Sabatini DM.lab_name: Sabatini Group, IOCB Prague (Prague, Czech Republic)
Sabatini DM.role: Identified mTOR (as RAFT1) in 1994. His lab then mapped much of the machinery around it: raptor and rictor at the core of mTORC1 and mTORC2, the Rag–Ragulator system that docks mTORC1 on the lysosome, and the sensors that detect leucine, arginine and SAM
Sabatini DM.sub: IOCB Prague · Howard Hughes Medical Institute (2008–2021) · Whitehead Institute & MIT (1997–2021) · Born 1968, New York, USA
Sabatini DM.credit: Portrait: Ceal Capistrano/Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research
story: David Sabatini grew up in a family of scientists — his father is a well-known cell biologist — and trained as an MD–PhD at Johns Hopkins in the laboratory of Solomon Snyder. As a graduate student he became fascinated by rapamycin, a drug found in the soil of Easter Island that could stop cells from growing. Nobody knew what it actually hit inside mammalian cells. In 1994 Sabatini answered that question: using rapamycin bound to its partner protein FKBP12 as 'bait', he fished a giant protein out of rat brain and named it RAFT1, the protein now called mTOR. That discovery opened the mammalian side of the field.

In 1997, still in his twenties, he started his own lab at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge. Over the next two decades the Sabatini lab identified many core parts of the mTOR machine: the two complexes mTORC1 and mTORC2, the Rag GTPases and Ragulator that dock mTORC1 onto the lysosome, and — most strikingly — the actual protein sensors (Sestrin2, CASTOR1, SLC38A9, SAMTOR) that let a cell literally taste individual amino acids such as leucine and arginine. Together this work explained how our cells decide, moment to moment, whether there is enough food to grow.

His discoveries earned major honours including the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize and the BBVA Frontiers of Knowledge Award. In 2021–2022 he left MIT and the Whitehead Institute. Since late 2023 he has led a laboratory at the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry (IOCB) in Prague. The timeline below traces his scientific path through the studies collected in this Atlas.

highlights.SAB1994: Three years after yeast TOR, Sabatini purifies the Target Of Rapamycin (RAFT1/mTOR) from rat brain, proposing it as the direct target of FKBP12-rapamycin and a mammalian homolog of the yeast TOR proteins.
highlights.KIM2002: Defines mTOR Complex 1 by discovering raptor (reported in parallel by the Yonezawa and Avruch labs), the partner protein that makes mTOR sensitive to nutrients.
highlights.SAR2004: Discovers mTOR Complex 2 (via rictor, in parallel with Michael Hall's lab), a second, rapamycin-insensitive mTOR machine that controls the cytoskeleton.
highlights.SAN2008: Shows, in parallel with Kun-Liang Guan's lab, that the Rag GTPases are the switch that relays the amino-acid signal to mTORC1.
highlights.SAN2010: Ragulator docks mTORC1 onto the surface of the lysosome — pinpointing where nutrient sensing physically happens.
highlights.WOL2015: Identifies Sestrin2 as a direct leucine sensor for the mTORC1 pathway.
highlights.SAB2017: Sabatini's own 25-year retrospective on mTOR: uncovering the link from nutrients to growth.
highlights.KAN2013: Senior author of the finding that mTORC1 phosphorylation sites encode their own sensitivity to rapamycin and starvation, so one activity level can produce different output profiles.
highlights.WYA2018: Senior author of the finding that NUFIP1 is a ribosome receptor for starvation-induced ribophagy, triggered by mTORC1 inhibition.
highlights.YIP2010: Co-authors the cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1, an obligate dimer that FKBP12-rapamycin gradually breaks apart in vitro.
highlights.YIL2012: Senior author: calorie restriction expands mouse intestinal stem cells by lowering mTORC1 in the Paneth cells of their niche, not in the stem cells themselves, and rapamycin reproduces the effect.

Hall MN.role: Discovered TOR in yeast in 1991 and established it as a central controller of cell growth that responds to nutrients. His lab later showed that TOR works in two distinct complexes, TORC1 and TORC2, only one of which is blocked by rapamycin
Hall MN.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Switzerland · Lasker, Gairdner & Breakthrough Prize laureate · Born 1953, Puerto Rico
story: Michael Hall was born in Puerto Rico, grew up in Peru and Venezuela, and came to the United States for school before training in molecular biology. As a young professor at the Biozentrum in Basel, Switzerland, he studied how yeast cells respond to the drug rapamycin. In 1991 his team found the genes rapamycin needs in order to work and named their product TOR — 'Target Of Rapamycin'. This was the original discovery on which the whole field is built.

Hall went on to show that TOR sits at the heart of a nutrient-sensing system controlling cell growth in organisms from yeast to humans, and that it forms two different machines, TORC1 and TORC2, with separate jobs. His lab connected TOR to metabolism, to the actin cytoskeleton, and to diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

For discovering TOR, Hall has received the Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award, the Canada Gairdner International Award, and the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences, among many others. The milestones below follow his contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.HEI1991: The founding discovery: Hall's team finds the TOR genes and coins the name Target Of Rapamycin.
highlights.LOE2002: Reveals that TOR forms two distinct complexes, only one of which is blocked by rapamycin.
highlights.JAC2004: Shows that mammalian TORC2 controls the actin cytoskeleton and is rapamycin-insensitive.
highlights.HAG2012: Senior author: liver mTORC2 drives glycolysis and fat synthesis after feeding through Akt, glucokinase and SREBP1c (mice).

Guan KL.lab_name: Guan Lab, Westlake University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Guan KL.role: Showed how growth-factor and energy signals reach mTORC1 through TSC2 and Rheb, and, in parallel with the Sabatini lab, that the Rag GTPases carry the amino-acid signal. His lab also found that AMPK and mTORC1 control autophagy by phosphorylating the kinase ULK1 at different sites
Guan KL.sub: Westlake University · UC San Diego · University of Michigan · MacArthur Fellow (1998) · Born 1963, Zhejiang, China
story: Kun-Liang Guan grew up in Zhejiang, China, studied biology at Hangzhou University, and earned his PhD at Purdue. He won a MacArthur 'genius' Fellowship in 1998 and built his career at the University of Michigan and UC San Diego before returning to China to lead a lab at Westlake University.

Guan's lab worked out how signals reach mTOR from above. They showed that the tumour-suppressor complex TSC1/TSC2 acts as an off-switch by shutting down the small GTPase Rheb, and that the cellular energy sensor AMPK feeds into this control — explaining how growth factors, energy levels and stress all converge on mTOR. His team also helped define how amino acids and the Rag GTPases switch mTORC1 on. Separately, Guan is a leader of the Hippo pathway field, which controls organ size.
The timeline below follows Guan's mTOR-related discoveries collected in this Atlas.

highlights.INO2002: Shows, in parallel with other groups, that TSC2 is switched off by Akt — wiring insulin and growth-factor signals into the control of mTOR.
highlights.INOK2003: One of several 2003 studies identifying Rheb as the direct target of TSC2's GAP activity and a key activator of mTOR.
highlights.INO2003: Links cellular energy status, via AMPK, to TSC2 and the control of cell growth and survival.
highlights.KIM2008: Shows the Rag GTPases regulate TORC1 in response to nutrients.
highlights.COR2004: Shows LKB1 acts upstream of TSC2 through AMPK to restrain mTOR signalling, linking tuberous sclerosis and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (senior author; cells).
highlights.ALE2010: Co-authors a study showing that ATM, in response to ROS, activates TSC2 in the cytoplasm through LKB1 and AMPK to repress mTORC1.
highlights.RUS2013: Shows ULK1 phosphorylates Beclin-1 to activate the ATG14L–VPS34 lipid kinase complex and start autophagy when mTORC1 is off (senior author; cells and worms).

Manning BD.lab_name: Manning Lab, Harvard Chan School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Manning BD.role: Was among the groups that in 2002 identified TSC2 as a direct target of Akt (MAN2002), linking insulin and PI3K signalling to mTORC1, and later found TBC1D7 as the third subunit of the TSC complex. His lab has shown how mTORC1 turns growth signals into the synthesis of lipids and nucleotides
Manning BD.sub: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health & Harvard Medical School · postdoc with Lewis Cantley · PhD, Yale
story: Brendan Manning studied at UMass Amherst and Yale, then joined Lewis Cantley's lab at Harvard for his postdoctoral work. There he made a defining discovery, reported in parallel by other groups: the tuberous sclerosis (TSC) tumour-suppressor proteins are the missing link between the PI3K–AKT pathway — which is switched on in most human cancers — and the mTOR growth machine (MAN2002, TEE2002). This tied a major cancer-signalling network directly to a nutrient sensor.

Running his own lab at Harvard, Manning has shown how mTORC1 acts as a 'metabolic rheostat', switching on production of the building blocks a growing cell needs — nucleotides, lipids and proteins — and how drugs such as metformin act on this network. His work explains how cell growth and metabolism are wired together in health and in cancer.
Manning has received an Outstanding Investigator Award from the National Cancer Institute. The milestones below trace his contributions in this Atlas.

highlights.DIB2012: Completes the TSC complex by identifying TBC1D7 as its third subunit — the master off-switch upstream of mTORC1.
highlights.MEN2014: Shows insulin moves the TSC complex off the lysosome, releasing the brake on mTORC1.
highlights.BEN2016: Reveals how mTORC1 drives purine synthesis through the mitochondrial folate cycle.
highlights.VAL2019: Frames mTORC1 signalling as a metabolic rheostat coupling growth signals to biosynthesis.
highlights.KAL2026: Senior author showing hepatic mTORC1's postprandial activation requires dietary protein, not just insulin — AKT-TSC2 phosphorylation drives insulin's effect but is dispensable for feeding-induced activation.
highlights.MAN2002: First author: identifies the TSC2 protein tuberin as a direct Akt substrate, linking PI3K–Akt growth-factor signalling to S6K1 and mTORC1 output (cells).
highlights.TEE2002: Co-author: TSC1 and TSC2 act together to inhibit mTOR signalling to S6K1 and 4E-BP1 (cells).
highlights.SHAW2004: Co-author: LKB1 is needed to turn mTOR signalling down when ATP falls, through AMPK and TSC2 (cells and mice).
highlights.DUV2010: Senior author: active mTORC1 switches on glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and lipid synthesis through HIF1α and SREBP1/2 (cells).

Blenis J.lab_name: Blenis Lab, Weill Cornell Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Blenis J.role: Showed early on that rapamycin blocks S6 kinase, then worked out how mTORC1 drives cell growth through its two main translation targets, S6K1 and 4E-BP1. His lab also found, in parallel with the Sabatini lab, that mTORC1 phosphorylates Grb10, a feedback brake on insulin signalling
Blenis J.sub: Weill Cornell Medicine, New York · Harvard Medical School (1989–2014) · PhD, Michigan State (1983)
story: John Blenis trained at UC Berkeley and Michigan State, did postdoctoral work at Harvard, and built his career at Harvard Medical School before moving to Weill Cornell Medicine in New York.

In the early days of the field, Blenis studied the ribosomal S6 kinases and showed, alongside other groups, that activation of p70 S6 kinase (S6K) depends on PI3-kinase and is blocked by rapamycin, making it one of the first known components of what we now call the PI3K–mTORC1 pathway. His lab helped define how this pathway is switched on through AKT, the Rheb GTPase and the TSC2 tumour suppressor (MAN2002, TEE2002), and how mTORC1 and S6K ultimately control protein synthesis and cell metabolism. He also mapped the parallel Ras–ERK–RSK pathway.
The timeline below follows Blenis's mTOR-related discoveries in this Atlas.

highlights.CHU1992: Early evidence that the rapamycin–FKBP complex specifically blocks growth signalling through the p70 S6 kinases.
highlights.FIN2002: Shows mammalian cell size is controlled by mTOR through its targets S6K1 and 4E-BP1/eIF4E.
highlights.HOL2005: Reveals how mTOR and S6K1 assemble the translation machinery through ordered phosphorylation.
highlights.MAN2002: Co-author: Akt phosphorylates the TSC2 protein tuberin, and a tuberin mutant lacking these sites blocks S6K1 activation (cells).
highlights.TEE2002: Senior author: TSC1 and TSC2 together inhibit mTOR signalling to S6K1 and 4E-BP1, and block amino-acid reactivation of S6K1.
highlights.POD2001: Co-author: an mTOR inhibitor reduces tumour growth and normalises S6 kinase activity in Pten+/- mice.

Zoncu R.lab_name: Zoncu Lab, UC Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Zoncu R.role: Showed as a postdoc that mTORC1 senses amino acids from inside the lysosome, through the v-ATPase and Ragulator. His Berkeley lab has since mapped how the Rag GTPases and the folliculin complex switch mTORC1 on, and how lysosomal cholesterol feeds into the same system
Zoncu R.sub: Professor, UC Berkeley (Molecular & Cell Biology) · postdoc with David Sabatini · PhD, Yale · neuroscience, University of Pisa · Born in Sardinia, Italy
Zoncu R.credit: Portrait: Cornell University, Weill Institute for Cell and Molecular Biology
story: Roberto Zoncu grew up in Sardinia in a family of physicians and studied neuroscience at the University of Pisa before crossing the Atlantic for a PhD in cell biology at Yale. He then joined David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute as a postdoc, turning his skill in live-cell imaging on a question nobody had answered: how does mTORC1 actually 'know' that amino acids are present inside the cell?

Zoncu helped show that mTORC1 is recruited to the surface of the lysosome — the cell's recycling organelle — by the Ragulator–Rag docking complex, and that amino acids inside the lysosome are read out from the inside by the v-ATPase proton pump, an 'inside-out' sensing mechanism. Since starting his own lab at UC Berkeley in 2014, he has extended this picture to cholesterol sensing and to how faulty lysosomal mTORC1 signalling contributes to neurodegenerative disease.
The timeline below traces Zoncu's studies gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SAN2010: Co-discovers that the Ragulator-Rag complex docks mTORC1 onto the lysosomal surface — the physical site where nutrient sensing happens.
highlights.ZON2011: Shows mTORC1 reads amino-acid levels from inside the lysosome via the v-ATPase, an 'inside-out' sensing mechanism.
highlights.LAW2019: Solves the structural mechanism of a Rag GTPase activation checkpoint involving the lysosomal folliculin complex.
highlights.ESP2026: Co-author identifying a nutrient-independent lysosomal TBK1/ULK1 pathway that inhibits FLCN to release TFEB, hijacked by ATP6V1B2 mutations in follicular lymphoma.
highlights.JAN2025: Senior author: cryo-EM structure of GATOR2 bound to CASTOR1, showing how arginine releases it.

Saxton RA.lab_name: Saxton Lab, UC Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Saxton RA.role: Solved, as a Sabatini-lab graduate student, the structures of the leucine sensor Sestrin2 and the arginine sensor CASTOR1, showing how each one grips its amino acid. He also co-wrote a widely cited 2017 review of mTOR signalling with David Sabatini
Saxton RA.sub: Assistant Professor of Immunology and Molecular Medicine and of Chemistry, UC Berkeley (Molecular & Cell Biology) · postdoc, Stanford University (K. Christopher Garcia lab) · PhD, Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute/MIT
story: As a graduate student in David Sabatini's lab, Robert Saxton took on the structural side of a question the lab had just opened: if Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 are the cell's leucine and arginine sensors, what do they actually look like, and how do they grab their amino acid?

Saxton solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine, showing a single pocket that specifically fits leucine's hydrophobic side chain, and did the equivalent structural work for CASTOR1 and arginine. Together with colleagues in the lab he also helped identify SAMTOR, the sensor for S-adenosylmethionine, rounding out the set of direct amino-acid and metabolite sensors upstream of mTORC1.
The timeline below follows his structural studies gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SAX2015: Solves the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine, explaining how a single pocket confers specificity for this one amino acid.
highlights.SAX2016: Solves the structural basis for arginine sensing by CASTOR1, the second direct amino-acid sensor upstream of mTORC1.
highlights.GU2017: Helps identify SAMTOR as the direct sensor for S-adenosylmethionine upstream of mTORC1.

Kim DH.lab_name: Kim Lab, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Kim DH.role: Co-discovered raptor, the defining partner of mTOR in mTORC1, and then mLST8 (GbetaL) as a Sabatini-lab postdoc. His Minnesota lab identified PRAS40 as an insulin-regulated link to mTORC1 and studies how mTORC1 controls autophagy
Kim DH.sub: Professor, Metabolic & Systems Biology, University of Minnesota · Postdoc, Whitehead Institute/MIT (Sabatini lab)
Kim DH.credit: Portrait: University of Minnesota College of Biological Sciences
story: Do-Hyung Kim did his postdoctoral work in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute, where in 2002 he identified raptor (reported in parallel by the Yonezawa and Avruch labs), the partner protein that binds mTOR and makes the resulting complex — now called mTORC1 — sensitive to nutrients. The discovery gave the field its first molecular handle on what would become mTOR's two distinct complexes.

Kim went on to identify GbetaL (mLST8), a second core component shared by both mTOR complexes, and later helped characterize PRAS40 and other regulators that tune mTORC1 activity in response to insulin and amino acids. He now runs his own lab at the University of Minnesota, studying the wider mTOR signalling network in growth control and disease.
The timeline below follows Kim's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.KIM2002: Identifies raptor, the defining partner protein that makes mTOR nutrient-sensitive and founds mTOR Complex 1.
highlights.KIM2003: Identifies GbetaL (mLST8), a positive regulator shared by both mTOR complexes.
highlights.KIM2012: Identifies SH3BP4 as a negative regulator that restrains Rag-GTPase signalling to mTORC1.

Sarbassov DD.role: Discovered rictor as a Sabatini-lab postdoc, in parallel with Michael Hall's lab, defining mTOR Complex 2, and showed that this complex is the long-sought kinase that phosphorylates Akt on serine 473. He also found that prolonged rapamycin treatment can block mTORC2 assembly
Sarbassov DD.sub: Professor of Biology, Nazarbayev University, Kazakhstan · formerly Dept. of Molecular & Cellular Oncology, MD Anderson Cancer Center · Postdoc, Whitehead Institute/MIT (Sabatini lab)
story: Dos Sarbassov trained as a postdoc in David Sabatini's lab, where he identified rictor (rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR), the protein that defines mTOR Complex 2 — a second mTOR machine, distinct from mTORC1, that is largely insensitive to short-term rapamycin treatment and instead controls the actin cytoskeleton.

Sarbassov then showed that mTORC2 directly phosphorylates Akt/PKB on serine 473, identifying mTORC2 as a missing kinase in the insulin-signalling pathway with direct relevance to cancer and metabolic disease. He continued this line of work as a faculty member in the Department of Molecular and Cellular Oncology at MD Anderson Cancer Center.
The timeline below follows Sarbassov's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SAR2004: Discovers rictor and defines mTOR Complex 2, a rapamycin-insensitive mTOR machine distinct from mTORC1.
highlights.SAR2005: Shows mTORC2 directly phosphorylates and activates Akt/PKB, wiring mTOR into insulin signalling.
highlights.SAR2006: Shows prolonged rapamycin treatment can also disassemble mTORC2, revealing an unexpected additional mechanism of action for the drug.

Sancak Y.lab_name: Sancak Lab, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Sancak Y.role: Showed as a Sabatini-lab graduate student, in parallel with Kun-Liang Guan's lab, that the Rag GTPases relay amino-acid signals to mTORC1, and that Ragulator anchors them to the lysosome where mTORC1 is switched on. She also identified PRAS40 as an insulin-regulated inhibitor of mTORC1
Sancak Y.sub: Associate Professor of Pharmacology, University of Washington · Pew Biomedical Scholar · postdoc, Vamsi Mootha lab, Massachusetts General Hospital & Broad Institute · PhD, Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute/MIT
story: Yasemin Sancak trained in David Sabatini's lab, where she identified, in parallel with Kun-Liang Guan's lab, the Rag GTPases as the long-sought link between amino acids and mTORC1: when nutrients are present, the Rags bind raptor and pull mTORC1 to the surface of the lysosome, its site of activation. She went on to show that the Ragulator complex anchors the Rags there and is itself required for amino-acid signalling.

Sancak also helped characterize PRAS40 as an insulin-regulated inhibitor of mTORC1 and DEPTOR as an mTOR-binding inhibitor overexpressed in some cancers. She now runs her own lab in the Department of Pharmacology at the University of Washington, where her focus has shifted to how mitochondria are regulated by calcium signalling.
The timeline below follows Sancak's mTOR-related discoveries gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SAN2008: Discovers, in parallel with Kun-Liang Guan's lab, that the Rag GTPases bind raptor and mediate amino-acid signalling to mTORC1.
highlights.SAN2010: Shows the Ragulator-Rag complex anchors mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface, required for its activation by amino acids.
highlights.SAN2007: Identifies PRAS40 as an insulin-regulated inhibitor of the mTORC1 kinase.

Strong R.lab_name: Faculty profile, Barshop Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Strong R.role: Leads the San Antonio site of the NIA Interventions Testing Program, which tests each compound in parallel at three sites under one shared protocol. He first-authored the program's reports on resveratrol and other supplements (2012) and on rapamycin combined with acarbose (2022)
Strong R.sub: Professor of Pharmacology · Co-Director, Nathan Shock Center of Excellence · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio
Strong R.credit: Portrait: UT Health San Antonio Faculty Directory
story: Randy Strong directs the San Antonio site of the National Institute on Aging's Interventions Testing Program (ITP), a multi-site effort that tests candidate longevity drugs in genetically heterogeneous mice under a strict, pre-registered protocol so that results replicate across independent laboratories.

In 2009, Strong's site co-led the landmark finding, published in Nature, that rapamycin extends mouse lifespan even when treatment starts late in life, which the authors described as the first pharmacological extension of lifespan in both sexes of a mammal. His group has since tested numerous other compounds through the ITP and, in 2026, is contributing scientific input to a large clinical trial of rapamycin in healthy older adults at UT Health San Antonio.
The timeline below follows Strong's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.WIL2012: Confirms rapamycin slows measures of aging in mice, extending earlier ITP lifespan findings.
highlights.MIL2014: Shows rapamycin's lifespan benefit in mice is dose- and sex-dependent and metabolically distinct from dietary restriction.
highlights.STR2012: Reports that none of the tested candidate compounds, including resveratrol, green tea extract and curcumin, significantly extended mouse lifespan in the Interventions Testing Program.
highlights.MAJ2012: Co-author: rapamycin started at 2 months of age, but not at 15 months, prevented age-related memory loss in mice, with lower IL-1beta and higher NMDA receptor signalling in the brain.

Miller RA.lab_name: Miller Lab, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Miller RA.role: Leads the University of Michigan site of the NIA Interventions Testing Program. His papers showed that rapamycin extends mouse lifespan when started in middle age, and that the size of the benefit depends on dose and differs between males and females
Miller RA.sub: Professor of Pathology, University of Michigan · Co-Director, Paul F. Glenn Center for Biology of Aging Research, University of Michigan · MD, PhD, Yale
story: Richard Miller has spent his career developing rigorous methods to test whether interventions actually slow aging in mice, rather than merely treating a single disease. He directs one of the three collaborating sites of the NIA's Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which he helped design specifically to guard against the false positives that had plagued earlier longevity research.

Through the ITP, Miller's group was one of the three ITP sites behind the 2009 discovery that rapamycin extends mouse lifespan even when treatment begins late in life, at 20 months of age — a result that reshaped the aging field's view of mTOR as a druggable target for healthy aging. His lab continues to study the genetics and cell biology of long-lived mouse strains.
The timeline below follows Miller's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.MIL2011: Shows rapamycin, but not resveratrol or simvastatin, extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice.
highlights.HAR2014: Shows acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extend mouse lifespan in a sex-preferential manner, broadening the ITP's drug set beyond rapamycin.
highlights.MIL2014: Shows rapamycin's lifespan effect in mice depends on dose and sex and is metabolically distinct from dietary restriction.

Harrison DE.lab_name: Faculty profile, The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA)
Harrison DE.role: Led the Jackson Laboratory site of the NIA Interventions Testing Program. His 2009 Nature paper showed that rapamycin extends the lifespan of genetically diverse mice even when feeding starts at 20 months of age, which the authors described as the first pharmacological extension of lifespan in both sexes of a mammal
Harrison DE.sub: Professor Emeritus, The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine · PhD, Stanford
story: David Harrison has worked for decades on aging in mouse models at the Jackson Laboratory, with a particular focus on hematopoietic stem cells and on genetic and pharmacological interventions that extend healthy lifespan. He directed the Jackson Laboratory site of the NIA's Interventions Testing Program (ITP).

Harrison was first author of the 2009 ITP report showing that rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice, an effect seen at all three ITP sites and now considered one of the best-established findings in the biology of aging. His group has continued to test additional compounds, including acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol, through the same rigorous multi-site design.
The timeline below follows Harrison's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.HAR2009: Landmark ITP result: rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice.
highlights.HAR2014: Shows acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extend mouse lifespan preferentially by sex.
highlights.MIL2011: Confirms rapamycin, but not resveratrol or simvastatin, extends lifespan in the ITP's mouse cohorts.

Thoreen CC.lab_name: Thoreen Lab, Yale (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Thoreen CC.role: Used Torin1, one of the first ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, to reveal functions of mTORC1 that rapamycin cannot block. He then showed that mTORC1 controls translation of mRNAs for the protein-making machinery mainly through the 4E-BP proteins
Thoreen CC.sub: Associate Professor of Cellular & Molecular Physiology, Yale School of Medicine · PhD, MIT (2008) · trained in the Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute
story: Carson Thoreen trained in David Sabatini's lab, where he helped characterize Torin1, an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor that, unlike rapamycin, fully blocks mTORC1 activity — revealing a whole set of rapamycin-resistant functions, especially in translation, that classic rapamycin treatment had been missing.

Building on that tool, Thoreen mapped how mTORC1 controls protein synthesis at the molecular level, proposing a unifying model in which mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP proteins to release the translation initiation factor eIF4E, selectively boosting translation of mRNAs needed for cell growth. He now runs his own lab at Yale, studying how mTOR-dependent translation is wired at the level of individual mRNA sequences.
The timeline below follows Thoreen's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.THO2009: Develops an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor that reveals rapamycin-resistant functions of mTORC1.
highlights.THO2012: Proposes a unifying model for how mTORC1 controls mRNA translation through 4E-BP and eIF4E.

Chantranupong L.lab_name: Chantranupong Lab, Boston University (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Chantranupong L.role: Showed as a Sabatini-lab graduate student that the Sestrins act through GATOR2 to regulate amino-acid signalling to mTORC1. She then discovered the CASTOR proteins, the cell's arginine sensors for the pathway
Chantranupong L.sub: Assistant Professor of Biology, Boston University (since 2024) · postdoc and Hanna Gray Fellow, Harvard Medical School (Bernardo Sabatini lab, 2016–2023) · PhD in Biology, MIT (David Sabatini lab, 2016) · BSc, University of Texas at Austin (2010)
Chantranupong L.credit: Portrait: Boston University Dept. of Biology
story: As a graduate student in David Sabatini's lab, Lynne Chantranupong helped identify GATOR1 and GATOR2, two multi-protein complexes that act as an off-switch and on-switch, respectively, for amino-acid signalling to mTORC1. She then showed that the Sestrin proteins bind directly to GATOR2, providing the missing physical link between intracellular leucine levels and this signalling machine.

That work, alongside the CASTOR1 arginine-sensor discovery, completed a core piece of the amino-acid-sensing pathway upstream of mTORC1: sensor proteins that directly bind specific amino acids and relay that information through GATOR1/2 and the Rag GTPases. Chantranupong later did postdoctoral work in neuroscience and now leads her own lab at Boston University.
The timeline below follows her contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.BAR2013: Co-discovers GATOR1, a tumor-suppressor complex with GAP activity that switches off Rag-GTPase signalling to mTORC1 in the absence of amino acids.
highlights.CHA2014: Shows the Sestrins bind GATOR2 to negatively regulate the amino-acid-sensing pathway upstream of mTORC1.
highlights.CHA2016: Co-identifies the CASTOR proteins as direct arginine sensors for the mTORC1 pathway.

Inoki K.lab_name: Inoki Lab, U. Michigan LSI (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Inoki K.role: Showed as a postdoc in Kun-Liang Guan's lab that Akt switches off TSC2, that TSC2 is the off-switch (GAP) for the small GTPase Rheb, and that AMPK and GSK3 feed energy and Wnt signals into the same brake. His Michigan lab studies mTOR signalling in metabolism and kidney disease
Inoki K.sub: Roger C. Wiggins Collegiate Professor of the Life Sciences · Research Associate Professor, Life Sciences Institute · Professor of Internal Medicine (Nephrology) and of Molecular & Integrative Physiology, University of Michigan Medical School · MD, PhD
Inoki K.credit: Portrait: University of Michigan Life Sciences Institute
story: Ken Inoki has focused his career on how the tuberous sclerosis complex proteins TSC1 and TSC2 control mTOR. Working in Kun-Liang Guan's lab and later independently, he showed that Akt directly phosphorylates and inhibits TSC2, wiring growth-factor signalling into the control of mTOR, and, as one of several groups reporting this in 2003, that TSC2 acts as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for the small GTPase Rheb, identifying Rheb as a direct, essential activator of mTORC1.

Inoki also showed that TSC2 integrates energy stress, via AMPK, and Wnt signalling into the same growth-control node, making the TSC–Rheb axis a central hub where nutrient, energy, growth-factor and developmental signals converge before reaching mTOR. His research at the University of Michigan continues to explore this axis in diabetes, aging and tuberous sclerosis, the inherited tumour disease caused by loss of TSC1 or TSC2.
The timeline below follows Inoki's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.INO2002: Shows, in parallel with other groups, that Akt phosphorylates and inhibits TSC2, linking growth-factor signalling to the control of mTOR.
highlights.INOK2003: One of several 2003 studies identifying Rheb as the direct target of TSC2's GAP activity and the essential activator of mTOR.
highlights.INO2003: Shows TSC2 mediates the cellular energy response, via AMPK, to control cell growth and survival.
highlights.COR2004: Co-authors the study placing LKB1 upstream of TSC2 through AMPK in the control of mTOR signalling (cells).
highlights.ALE2010: Co-authors a study showing that cytoplasmic ATM signals through LKB1, AMPK and TSC2 to repress mTORC1 when ROS rise.

Ali SM.role: Worked in the Sabatini lab on the papers that discovered raptor, mLST8 and rictor, and on the finding that the rictor-mTOR complex phosphorylates Akt. He later moved into cancer genomics and clinical diagnostics
Ali SM.sub: Head of Translational Medicine, Lunit · previously Foundation Medicine and EQRx · graduate research, Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute/MIT (co-author on the raptor, mLST8 and rictor papers)
story: The 2002 and 2004 papers that identified raptor and rictor — the defining subunits of mTORC1 and mTORC2 — depended on mass-spectrometry protein identification carried out with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center's proteomics core, led by Hediye Erdjument-Bromage and Paul Tempst. Siraj Ali, working in David Sabatini's lab, was a co-author of these studies, which identified the previously unknown proteins that co-purified with mTOR.

This kind of unbiased biochemical purification — pulling down a protein of interest and mass-spectrometry-sequencing everything that comes with it — was the method that physically revealed mTORC1's and mTORC2's core subunits, well before genome-scale tools existed. It remains a template for how signalling complexes are discovered.
The studies below, gathered in this Atlas, mark that contribution.

highlights.KIM2002: Co-author of the study that identified raptor, the defining subunit of mTORC1.
highlights.SAR2004: Co-author of the study that identified rictor, the defining subunit of mTORC2.

Erdjument-Bromage H.lab_name: Mass Spectrometry Core, NYU Langone (New York, New York, USA)
Erdjument-Bromage H.role: Ran the mass-spectrometry analyses in Paul Tempst's lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering that identified the unknown proteins in the raptor, mLST8 and rictor purifications, and contributed the same approach to work on how ERK inactivates TSC2
Erdjument-Bromage H.sub: Proteomics & mass spectrometry, NYU Langone Health Mass Spectrometry Core for Neuroscience · previously Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
story: Hediye Erdjument-Bromage is a biochemist whose postdoctoral training introduced her to mass spectrometry and proteomics, a technical specialty she has practiced ever since. For many years she managed the microchemistry and proteomics core laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, before moving to NYU Langone Health, where she is now lab manager of the Mass Spectrometry Core for Neuroscience.

Her core facility's protein-identification work was essential to the biochemical purification papers that discovered raptor and rictor — identifying, from tiny amounts of co-purified material, the specific proteins bound to mTOR that turned out to define its two distinct complexes. That kind of unbiased mass-spectrometry identification underlies much of the molecular parts-list this Atlas documents.
The studies below, gathered in this Atlas, mark her contribution.

highlights.KIM2002: Mass-spectrometry identification of raptor, the defining subunit of mTORC1.
highlights.SAR2004: Mass-spectrometry identification of rictor, the defining subunit of mTORC2.
highlights.MA2005: Contributes proteomics analysis to the identification of TSC2 phosphorylation by Erk.

Tempst P.lab_name: Tempst Lab, Sloan Kettering Institute (New York, New York, USA)
Tempst P.role: Developed mass-spectrometry methods for identifying proteins from tiny samples, and led the Memorial Sloan Kettering proteomics laboratory that identified the unknown partners of mTOR in the raptor, mLST8 and rictor purifications
Tempst P.sub: Molecular Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · mass-spectrometry protein identification
story: Paul Tempst built his career developing the technology and methods used to identify proteins and their modifications by mass spectrometry, work that made his laboratory's proteomics core at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center one of the reference facilities for the field. His techniques for polypeptide isolation and mass-spectrometric sequencing let researchers elsewhere identify unknown proteins from vanishingly small biochemical samples.

That capability was decisive for David Sabatini's lab when it purified mTOR-associated proteins and needed to know exactly what it had pulled down: Tempst's core identified raptor and rictor, the subunits that founded mTORC1 and mTORC2 respectively. The discoveries below, gathered in this Atlas, rest on that proteomics work.

highlights.KIM2002: Mass-spectrometry identification of raptor, the defining subunit of mTORC1.
highlights.SAR2004: Mass-spectrometry identification of rictor, the defining subunit of mTORC2.

Shaw RJ.lab_name: Shaw Lab, Salk Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Shaw RJ.role: Showed, in parallel with two other groups, that the tumour suppressor LKB1 directly activates AMPK, and that AMPK brakes mTORC1 by phosphorylating raptor. His Salk lab also linked AMPK to autophagy through ULK1 and helped explain how metformin acts in the liver
Shaw RJ.sub: Professor, Salk Institute for Biological Studies · postdoc with Lewis Cantley, Harvard Medical School · PhD, MIT (advisor: Tyler Jacks)
Shaw RJ.credit: Portrait: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
story: Reuben Shaw did his postdoctoral work with Lewis Cantley at Harvard, where in 2004 he showed, in parallel with two other groups, that the LKB1 tumour suppressor — mutated in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and in many lung cancers — directly activates AMPK, the cell's central energy-sensing enzyme. That discovery placed a major cancer gene squarely inside the pathway that senses whether a cell has enough energy to grow.

Since starting his own lab, now at the Salk Institute, Shaw has shown that AMPK directly phosphorylates raptor to shut down mTORC1 when cellular energy is low, a second brake alongside the AMPK-TSC2 route described by Kun-Liang Guan's lab, and that the diabetes drug metformin works partly through this same LKB1–AMPK–mTOR axis. His work ties energy stress, tumour suppression and mTOR signalling into a single, coherent pathway.
The timeline below follows Shaw's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SHW2004: Shows, in parallel with two other groups, that the LKB1 tumour suppressor directly activates AMPK, linking a major cancer gene to energy-stress signalling.
highlights.GWI2008: Shows AMPK phosphorylates raptor directly, creating a metabolic checkpoint that shuts down mTORC1 under energy stress.
highlights.HOW2017: Co-authors a Manning-lab study showing that metformin inhibits hepatic mTORC1 signalling through dose-dependent mechanisms involving AMPK.
highlights.SHAW2004: First author: shows LKB1 is needed to switch off mTOR signalling under low energy through AMPK and TSC2, with raised mTOR signalling in Lkb1 mutant mouse polyps.

Wolfson RL.lab_name: Wolfson Lab, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Wolfson RL.role: Identified Sestrin2 as the direct leucine sensor of the mTORC1 pathway as a Sabatini-lab MD-PhD student. She also co-discovered KICSTOR, the complex that recruits GATOR1 to the lysosome
Wolfson RL.sub: Assistant Professor of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School · postdoc, Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School · clinical training, Massachusetts General Hospital · MD, Harvard Medical School; PhD, MIT (Sabatini lab)
Wolfson RL.credit: Portrait: Harvard Medical School, Dept. of Cell Biology
story: As an MD-PhD student in David Sabatini's lab, Rachel Wolfson identified Sestrin2 as a direct biochemical sensor for the amino acid leucine: when leucine binds Sestrin2, it is released from the GATOR2 complex, relieving a brake on mTORC1 and switching growth signalling on. It answered a question the field had chased for years — how a single amino acid's concentration gets converted into a growth signal.

Wolfson went on to identify KICSTOR, a complex that recruits GATOR1 to the lysosome and is required for amino-acid or glucose deprivation to inhibit mTORC1, completing another structural piece of the pathway. She later trained in neurobiology and joined the Harvard Medical School faculty in 2024, where her lab now studies how sensory neurons detect signals from internal organs.
The timeline below follows her contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.WOL2015: Identifies Sestrin2 as a direct leucine sensor for the mTORC1 pathway.
highlights.WOL2017: Identifies KICSTOR, the complex that recruits GATOR1 to the lysosome and is required for nutrient signalling to mTORC1.

Lamming DW.role: Showed as a postdoc that rapamycin's harm to glucose metabolism comes largely from its effect on mTORC2, while the lifespan benefit tracks mTORC1. His Wisconsin lab studies intermittent rapamycin dosing and how restricting dietary protein or single amino acids affects metabolism and ageing
Lamming DW.sub: Professor of Medicine, University of Wisconsin–Madison · Co-director, Wisconsin Nathan Shock Center · Postdoc, Whitehead Institute/MIT (Sabatini lab)
story: During postdoctoral training in David Sabatini's lab, Dudley Lamming discovered that many of rapamycin's unwanted metabolic side effects, such as insulin resistance and elevated blood glucose, come from inhibition of mTORC2 rather than from blocking mTORC1, the complex thought to mediate the drug's lifespan benefit. This distinction reframed how the field thinks about designing safer mTOR-targeted longevity interventions.

Since 2014, Lamming has run his own lab at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he studies how nutrient-responsive pathways, especially dietary protein and branched-chain amino acids acting through mTOR, can be tuned to promote healthy lifespan without rapamycin's side effects. He served as president of the American Aging Association in 2023–2024.
The timeline below follows Lamming's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.LAM2012: Shows rapamycin-induced insulin resistance is mediated by mTORC2 loss, uncoupled from the drug's longevity benefit.
highlights.ARR2015: Shows alternative rapamycin dosing regimens can reduce its metabolic and immune side effects compared with daily dosing.
highlights.BAB2025: Shows restricting individual branched-chain amino acids has distinct effects on metabolism, Alzheimer's disease pathology and cognition in 3xTg mice, extending mTOR-nutrient research into diet design.
highlights.ARR2016: Shows an intermittent rapamycin schedule started late in life extends lifespan in female mice, the benefit side of the lab's work on separating rapamycin's effects from its side effects.
highlights.YIL2012: Co-author: shows that calorie restriction boosts mouse intestinal stem cells by lowering mTORC1 in the neighbouring Paneth cells, an effect rapamycin copies.

Bar-Peled L.lab_name: Bar-Peled Lab, MGH & Harvard (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Bar-Peled L.role: Showed as a Sabatini-lab graduate student that Ragulator switches the Rag GTPases on, acting as their GEF. He also discovered GATOR1 and GATOR2; GATOR1 switches the Rags off and its genes are mutated in some cancers
Bar-Peled L.sub: Rullo Family Endowed Chair in Cancer Research, Massachusetts General Hospital & Harvard Medical School · PhD, Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute/MIT
story: As a graduate student in David Sabatini's lab, Liron Bar-Peled showed that the Ragulator complex acts as a GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor) that switches the Rag GTPases on, and then identified GATOR1 as the GAP (GTPase-activating protein) complex that switches them back off — together defining the molecular on/off switch that gates amino-acid signalling to mTORC1.
Bar-Peled now leads his own lab at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, where his research has broadened to how cancer cells manage metabolic and oxidative stress.
The timeline below follows Bar-Peled's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.BAR2012: Shows Ragulator is a GEF for the Rag GTPases, switching them on to signal amino-acid sufficiency to mTORC1.
highlights.BAR2013: Identifies GATOR1 as a tumor-suppressor GAP complex that switches the Rag GTPases off in the absence of amino acids.

Cantley LC.role: Co-discovered PI3K, the pathway that feeds into mTOR from growth factors
Cantley LC.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute & Harvard Medical School · director of the Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center, Weill Cornell Medicine (2012–2022) · co-discovered PI3K (1985) · PhD, Cornell
story: Lewis Cantley and colleagues discovered and characterized phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) in the 1980s, a lipid-signalling enzyme that turned out to sit at the top of one of the most frequently mutated pathways in human cancer. PI3K activation, through Akt, is a principal route by which growth factors and insulin switch on mTORC1, directly linking Cantley's discovery to the biology this Atlas documents.

Over a career spanning Harvard, Tufts, Beth Israel Deaconess, Weill Cornell Medicine (where he directed the Meyer Cancer Center, 2012–2022) and now Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Cantley's lab has continued to map how PI3K signalling controls cell growth and metabolism, including work connecting LKB1, AMPK and TSC2 to the PI3K–mTOR network (SHAW2004). He has received the Breakthrough Prize and the Wolf Prize in Medicine, among many other honours.
The timeline below follows Cantley's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.CAN2002: Reviews the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway that Cantley discovered, and its role in growth-factor signalling to mTOR.
highlights.SHW2004: Co-authors one of the 2003–2004 studies showing that the LKB1 tumour suppressor directly activates AMPK, connecting energy stress to mTOR.
highlights.SAC2011: Co-author: Rac1 binds and regulates both mTORC1 and mTORC2 and controls cell size (cells).
highlights.MAN2002: Senior author of the study identifying tuberin (TSC2) as an Akt substrate, wiring PI3K signalling to the TSC complex and S6K1.
highlights.TEE2002: Co-authors the study showing that TSC1 and TSC2 work together to inhibit mTOR signalling to S6K1 and 4E-BP1.
highlights.SHAW2004: Senior author: LKB1 restrains mTOR signalling under low energy through AMPK and TSC2, with raised mTOR signalling in Lkb1 mutant mouse polyps.

Guertin DA.lab_name: Guertin Lab, UMass Chan (Worcester, Massachusetts, USA)
Guertin DA.role: Built the mouse genetics that defined mTORC2's biological roles
Guertin DA.sub: Professor of Molecular Medicine, UMass Chan Medical School · postdoc, Whitehead Institute/MIT (Sabatini lab) · PhD, UMass Chan Medical School
Guertin DA.credit: Portrait: UMass Chan Medical School, Guertin Lab
story: David Guertin did his postdoctoral training in David Sabatini's lab, where he built mouse models lacking raptor, rictor or mLST8 (first in the whole animal, then in specific tissues such as the prostate) to work out which biological functions depend on mTORC1 versus mTORC2. This genetic dissection was essential to separating the two mTOR complexes' distinct roles in a living animal, not just in cultured cells.

Since joining the faculty at UMass Chan Medical School in 2009, Guertin has focused mTORC2 genetics on fat tissue and cancer, showing for instance that mTORC2 is required for prostate cancer driven by loss of the tumour suppressor Pten, and more recently studying how mTORC2 signalling shapes brown and white adipose tissue function.
The timeline below follows Guertin's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.GUE2006: Uses knockout mice lacking raptor, rictor or mLST8 to show that mTORC1 is essential in early development and that mTORC2 is required for signalling to Akt-FOXO and PKCalpha, but not S6K1.
highlights.GUE2009: Shows mTOR Complex 2 is required for prostate cancer driven by loss of the Pten tumour suppressor.

Kaeberlein M.role: Extended TOR/aging research from yeast to mice to pet dogs
Kaeberlein M.sub: CEO, Optispan · co-founder & co-director, Dog Aging Project · co-founder, Dog Aging Institute · Affiliate Professor, University of Washington (previously Professor of Pathology) · PhD, MIT (2002)
Kaeberlein M.credit: Portrait: UW Healthy Aging and Longevity Research Institute
story: Matt Kaeberlein began his career studying replicative aging in budding yeast, showing that the TOR pathway and its downstream kinase Sch9 regulate yeast lifespan in response to nutrients — among the earliest direct evidence that TOR signalling controls aging itself, not just growth. He then built a career at the University of Washington extending that logic across species.

Kaeberlein has since studied rapamycin's effects on lifespan and healthspan in mice, including transient treatment protocols in middle-aged animals and one of the first randomized controlled trials of short-term rapamycin in companion dogs. He co-founded the Dog Aging Project, which uses pet dogs — a species that shares our environment and ages on a much faster clock — to test whether interventions like rapamycin can extend healthy lifespan in a genetically diverse, real-world population.
The timeline below follows Kaeberlein's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.KAE2005: Shows the TOR pathway and Sch9 regulate yeast replicative lifespan in response to nutrients, among the earliest evidence TOR controls aging.
highlights.BIT2016: Shows transient rapamycin treatment can increase both lifespan and healthspan in middle-aged mice.
highlights.URF2017: Reports one of the first randomized controlled trials of short-term rapamycin treatment in companion dogs.

Ballabio A.role: Discovered that the transcription factor TFEB is a master switch for building lysosomes (SAR2009) and for autophagy. His lab was one of the groups that showed in 2012 that mTORC1 keeps TFEB out of the nucleus from the lysosome surface, and later (2020) that constitutive TFEB activation drives the kidney disease of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome
Ballabio A.sub: Professor of Medical Genetics, University of Naples Federico II · founding director of the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Naples (1994–2024), now principal investigator there · MD, University of Naples
story: Andrea Ballabio trained as a pediatrician in Naples before moving into genetics, first identifying disease genes at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston and then, from 1994, building TIGEM (founded in Milan, based in the Naples area since 2000) into one of Europe's leading rare-disease research institutes.

His lab, in parallel with the groups of Rosa Puertollano and Shawn Ferguson, showed that TFEB, a transcription factor best known for driving lysosomal and autophagy genes, is itself a direct substrate of mTORC1: when nutrients are abundant, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB and keeps it out of the nucleus, and during starvation TFEB moves in and switches on a program of lysosomal biogenesis and clearance. The finding reframed the lysosome as a signalling hub that talks back to mTORC1, not just a passive recycling bin.
The timeline below follows Ballabio's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SET2011: Shows TFEB links autophagy induction to lysosomal biogenesis, with TFEB's nuclear localization controlled by ERK2-mediated phosphorylation.
highlights.SET2012: Shows mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at the lysosomal membrane and controls its nuclear entry, revealing a lysosome-to-nucleus signalling loop.
highlights.NAP2020: Shows a substrate-specific mTORC1 pathway underlies Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, tying TFEB/TFE3 regulation to a hereditary kidney-tumour disorder.
highlights.ZAU2026: Co-author on a study showing mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling state shapes bile-acid diversification during hepatic metabolic adaptation, linking his TFEB/TFE3 axis to liver bile-acid metabolism and MASLD.
highlights.ESP2026: Co-author on the TBK1/ULK1 pathway that regulates FLCN-dependent TFEB activation, linking lysosomal v-ATPase signalling to recurrent ATP6V1B2 mutations in follicular lymphoma.
highlights.ZHANG2026: Co-author: TSC1 loss drives non-canonical mTORC1-TFEB activation and aggressive liver cancer (mice, human HCC).
highlights.SAR2009: Senior author: identifies TFEB as the transcription factor that binds the CLEAR motif and coordinates lysosomal gene expression and lysosome production.
highlights.SET2013: Senior author: TFEB drives its own expression during starvation and controls liver lipid breakdown through PGC-1α and PPARα (mice, worms).

Jacinto E.lab_name: Jacinto Lab, Rutgers RWJMS (Piscataway, New Jersey, USA)
Jacinto E.role: Co-discovered mammalian mTORC2 as a postdoc in Michael Hall's lab, showing that it controls the actin cytoskeleton and is insensitive to rapamycin. Her Rutgers lab, with Bing Su's group, was among those that found SIN1 holds mTORC2 together and studies how both mTOR complexes control metabolism
Jacinto E.sub: Professor of Biochemistry & Molecular Biology, Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School · postdoc, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Michael Hall lab) · PhD, UC San Diego
story: Estela Jacinto did her postdoctoral training with Michael Hall at the Biozentrum in Basel, one of the labs that pioneered TOR biology, where she helped identify and characterize the second, rapamycin-insensitive mTOR complex, mTORC2.

Her 2004 and 2006 papers, alongside parallel work from the Sabatini lab and others, helped establish that mTORC2 contains rictor and the scaffold protein SIN1/MIP1, and that this complex — distinct from the raptor-containing mTORC1 — controls the actin cytoskeleton and phosphorylates Akt at a site required for its full activation. That work set up mTORC2 as a parallel signalling arm alongside mTORC1, now studied for its own roles in metabolism, cancer and immunity. She now runs her own lab at Rutgers, studying how mTORC1 and mTORC2 together shape metabolism in cancer, aging and immune cells.
The timeline below follows Jacinto's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.JAC2004: Shows mammalian TOR complex 2 (mTORC2) controls the actin cytoskeleton and, unlike mTORC1, is not directly inhibited by rapamycin.
highlights.JAC2006: Shows SIN1/MIP1 is required to maintain rictor-mTOR (mTORC2) complex integrity and its control of Akt phosphorylation and substrate specificity.
highlights.SZW2021: Reviews the distinct regulation and metabolic functions of mTORC1 and mTORC2.
highlights.FAC2008: Senior author: shows mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of Akt and PKC, which they need to fold correctly and stay stable.

Latek RR.role: Bioinformatics scientist at the Whitehead Institute who worked on the Sabatini-lab papers that described raptor, mLST8 (GbetaL) and rictor (raptor and rictor were reported in parallel by other labs), the core partners of mTOR in its two complexes
Latek RR.sub: Executive Director, Global Brand Lead, Boehringer Ingelheim · Bioinformatics Scientist, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (2001–2005) · contributed to the Sabatini lab's founding mTOR-complex papers (2002–2004)
story: Robert Latek was part of the Whitehead Institute team in David Sabatini's lab that, across three papers between 2002 and 2004, worked out the core protein composition of the mTOR complexes: first raptor, mTOR's partner in the nutrient-sensitive complex now called mTORC1; then GbetaL (mLST8), a third subunit that stabilizes the raptor-mTOR interaction; and then rictor, defining the separate, rapamycin-insensitive complex mTORC2.

Together with colleagues including Do-Hyung Kim, Dos Sarbassov and Siraj Ali, this run of papers gave the field its first parts list for the two mTOR complexes — the biochemical scaffolding that essentially all subsequent mTOR signalling research has built on.

Latek's role in those papers reflects his position at the Institute: he was on Whitehead's bioinformatics staff (Bioinformatics Scientist, then Senior Bioinformatics Scientist, 2001–2005), building expression, promoter and protein-structure analyses for Institute faculty rather than running a bench of his own. After Whitehead he moved into pharmaceutical development — more than a decade at Bristol-Myers Squibb in discovery medicine and immuno-oncology clinical research, then Kyowa Kirin, and since 2021 Boehringer Ingelheim, where he is now Executive Director and Global Brand Lead in oncology (career details from his public LinkedIn profile; no institutional portrait is available).
The timeline below follows Latek's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.KIM2002: Co-authors the discovery that raptor forms a nutrient-sensitive complex with mTOR that signals to the cell-growth machinery, one of the two 2002 papers (with Hara et al.) that first described mTORC1; Loewith et al. described the yeast TOR complexes the same year.
highlights.KIM2003: Co-authors the identification of GbetaL (mLST8) as a positive regulator that stabilizes the raptor-mTOR interaction.
highlights.SAR2004: Co-authors the discovery of rictor, defining a rapamycin-insensitive, raptor-independent mTOR complex (mTORC2) that controls the cytoskeleton.

Latek RR.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Latek RR.credit: Portrait: The Illio 1993, University of Illinois (via Internet Archive)

Mannick JB.lab_name: Profile, Altos Labs (Redwood City, California, USA)
Mannick JB.role: Ran early clinical trials of low-dose mTOR inhibitors in older adults, which improved their response to flu vaccination and, in a phase 2a trial, their rate of self-reported infections; a larger phase 3 trial of RTB101 (2021) did not confirm a reduction in respiratory illness. She led this work first at Novartis and then at resTORbio
Mannick JB.sub: SVP & Chief Medical Officer, Altos Labs · co-founder, resTORbio · led Novartis's clinical mTOR-inhibitor aging program · MD, Harvard Medical School
story: Joan Mannick trained in internal medicine at Harvard before moving into drug development, first at Genzyme and then, from 2010, in the New Indications Discovery Unit at Novartis. There she led the first randomized clinical trials testing whether low-dose mTOR inhibition could improve immune function in elderly volunteers, rather than just extending lifespan in animal models.

Her trials showed that low-dose mTOR inhibitors improved influenza-vaccine responses and, in a phase 2a trial, reduced the rate of self-reported infections in people over 65 (a phase 3 trial of RTB101 in 2021 did not confirm the clinical benefit) — among the first direct evidence in humans that partially inhibiting mTOR could counter an aspect of immune aging. She co-founded resTORbio, a Novartis spinout, to develop RTB101 along these lines, and has since led drug development at Life Biosciences and Tornado Therapeutics before becoming Chief Medical Officer at Altos Labs in 2025.
The timeline below follows Mannick's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.MAN2014: Reports that mTOR inhibition improves immune function in elderly volunteers, one of the first clinical demonstrations of an mTOR-targeted aging intervention in humans.
highlights.MAN2018: Phase 2a RCT (n=264): six weeks of low-dose BEZ235 (RTB101) plus everolimus was associated with fewer self-reported infections over the following year and a better flu-vaccine response; the later phase 3 trial of RTB101 alone did not confirm a clinical benefit (MAN2021).
highlights.MAN2021: Reports phase 2b/3 randomised trial results on targeting the biology of aging with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults.

Richardson A.lab_name: Faculty profile, OU Health (Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, USA)
Richardson A.role: Studies how rapamycin slows ageing in mice, including the broad changes it causes in the liver, and co-authored early studies showing that rapamycin protects memory in Alzheimer's-model mice
Richardson A.sub: Reynolds Chair in Aging Research, University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center · Director, Oklahoma Nathan Shock Center of Excellence in the Basic Biology of Aging (2015–2022) · PhD, Oklahoma State University
Richardson A.credit: Portrait: University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center
story: Arlan Richardson has spent five decades studying the biology of aging, from the free-radical theory of aging to dietary restriction, moving through Illinois State University, the Barshop Institute at UT Health San Antonio (which he directed), and now the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center.

Richardson's group helped characterize how rapamycin changes the liver transcriptome and other downstream biology in treated mice, and, as a co-author of studies led by Veronica Galvan's and Salvatore Oddo's groups, helped extend the question of mTOR's role in aging into models of Alzheimer's disease, showing that rapamycin can reduce amyloid-beta levels and prevent cognitive deficits in mouse models.
The timeline below follows Richardson's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SPI2010: Shows rapamycin abolishes cognitive deficits and reduces amyloid-beta levels in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
highlights.FOK2014: Shows mice fed rapamycin have an extended lifespan associated with major changes in the liver transcriptome.
highlights.CAC2010: Co-author of the 3xTg-AD mouse study showing that amyloid-beta raises mTOR signalling and that rapamycin restores memory and lowers amyloid-beta and tau, with autophagy required for the amyloid reduction.
highlights.FIS2015: Co-author of the lifelong rapamycin health study in C57BL/6J mice, which found mixed and strongly sex-specific effects on healthspan measures rather than improvement across the board.
highlights.MAJ2012: Co-author of the study showing that rapamycin fed from 2 months of age, but not from 15 months, protected spatial memory in normally ageing mice, alongside lower brain IL-1beta.

Ruggero D.lab_name: Ruggero Lab, UCSF (San Francisco, California, USA)
Ruggero D.role: Showed that oncogenic mTOR signalling reprograms which mRNAs are translated, and that tumours become addicted to this through the 4E-BP–eIF4E axis. His UCSF lab found that mTOR-driven translation of a specific set of mRNAs promotes prostate cancer invasion and metastasis
Ruggero D.sub: Professor of Urology & Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center · PhD, University of Rome La Sapienza
story: Davide Ruggero's lab was among the first to apply genome-wide ribosome profiling (a method developed by Nicholas Ingolia and Jonathan Weissman) to ask a question upstream of most cancer genomics: not which genes are transcribed, but which mRNAs actually get translated into protein when oncogenic signalling — including mTOR — is switched on.

His 2012 Nature paper with Andrew Hsieh mapped this 'translational landscape' in prostate cancer, identifying a specific set of pro-invasion mRNAs whose translation is selectively boosted by mTOR signalling, and showed that an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor could reprogram that signature and limit metastasis in mouse models. Earlier, he had contributed to a study led by Kevan Shokat's lab showing that active-site mTOR inhibitors reveal rapamycin-resistant outputs of both mTORC1 and mTORC2, and his lab had shown that the 4E-BP/eIF4E translation axis is a targetable node downstream of oncogenic mTOR.
The timeline below follows Ruggero's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.HSI2010: Shows genetic dissection of the oncogenic mTOR pathway reveals a druggable addiction to translational control via 4E-BP/eIF4E.
highlights.FEL2009: Shows active-site inhibitors of mTOR target rapamycin-resistant outputs of both mTORC1 and mTORC2.
highlights.HSI2012: Maps the translational landscape of mTOR signalling in prostate cancer and shows an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor reprograms it to limit metastasis.
highlights.GKO2013: Co-author: shows that mice lacking 4E-BP2, the brake on eIF4E, have autism-like behaviours linked to increased translation of neuroligin mRNAs, reversed by a drug that blocks eIF4E.

Thomas G.lab_name: Metabolism and Cancer group, IDIBELL (L'Hospitalet de Llobregat, Spain)
Thomas G.role: Purified and cloned S6K1, the kinase that became the classic readout of mTORC1 activity. His lab later showed that mice lacking S6K1 resist diet-induced obesity, and that amino acids signal to mTORC1 through the lipid kinase hVps34 (GUL2008)
Thomas G.sub: Principal investigator, Metabolism and Cancer group, Bellvitge Biomedical Research Institute (IDIBELL), Barcelona · previously Scientific Director, Metabolic Disease Institute, University of Cincinnati · Senior Group Leader, Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel (1979–2004) · PhD, University of California
story: George Thomas spent 25 years at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel, where his lab purified and cloned the cell-growth kinases S6K1 and S6K2 — among the first mTORC1 substrates to be identified — and then worked out much of the upstream signalling that controls them, including the TSC1/TSC2 tumour-suppressor complex.

His lab went on to trace S6K1/mTOR signalling into physiology and disease, at the FMI and then, from 2005, at the University of Cincinnati (and since 2012 at IDIBELL in Barcelona): showing that mice lacking S6K1 resist age- and diet-induced obesity while staying insulin-sensitive, that Rheb activation of mTOR/S6K is inhibited by TSC1/2 (one of several groups to report this in 2003), and that the diabetes drug metformin can inhibit mTORC1 independently of AMPK, in a Rag-GTPase-dependent manner.
The timeline below follows Thomas's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.GAR2003: Shows insulin activation of Rheb, a mediator of mTOR/S6K/4E-BP signalling, is inhibited by the TSC1/TSC2 complex.
highlights.UMX2004: Shows absence of S6K1 protects mice against age- and diet-induced obesity while enhancing insulin sensitivity.
highlights.KAL2010: Shows metformin inhibits mTORC1 independently of AMPK, in a Rag-GTPase-dependent manner.
highlights.DEN2001: Senior author: lowering cellular ATP reduces mTOR signalling independently of amino acids, leading to the proposal that mTOR senses ATP (cells).
highlights.MON1999: Senior author: flies lacking S6 kinase are smaller because their cells are smaller, not fewer.
highlights.OLD2000: Co-author: the fly TOR homologue dTOR controls growth through dS6K and points to a parallel amino-acid-sensing branch beside insulin signalling.
highlights.GUL2008: Senior author: amino acids raise intracellular calcium, and calcium-calmodulin binding to hVps34 is needed for amino-acid activation of mTORC1 (cells).
highlights.PEN2000: Senior author: S6K1-deficient mice have small pancreatic beta cells, low insulin and glucose intolerance.
highlights.SHI1998: Co-author: S6K1 knockout mice are small, and a second kinase, S6K2, partly takes over S6 phosphorylation.
highlights.JEF1997: Senior author: rapamycin suppresses translation of 5'TOP mRNAs through p70 S6 kinase (cells; the S6K step was later revised).
highlights.COT2006: Co-author: hypothalamic mTOR signalling acts as a fuel sensor in rats, with brain leucine lowering food intake and rapamycin blunting the effect of leptin on eating.

Valvezan AJ.lab_name: Valvezan Lab, Rutgers CABM (Piscataway, New Jersey, USA)
Valvezan AJ.role: Showed as a Manning-lab postdoc that mTORC1 matches nucleotide production to demand, creating a weak point that can be targeted in tumours with TSC loss. His Rutgers lab found that mTORC1 activity rises and falls through the cell cycle and helps drive entry into mitosis
Valvezan AJ.sub: Assistant Professor of Pharmacology, Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School · postdoc, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Brendan Manning lab) · PhD, University of Pennsylvania
Valvezan AJ.credit: Portrait: Center for Advanced Biotechnology and Medicine, Rutgers
story: Alexander Valvezan trained as a postdoc in Brendan Manning's lab at Harvard, where he worked out how mTORC1 links cell-growth signals to the metabolic pathways that build the nucleotides a growing or dividing cell needs.

His 2017 Cancer Cell paper showed that mTORC1 couples nucleotide synthesis to nucleotide demand, and that disrupting this coupling creates a targetable metabolic vulnerability in tumours with hyperactive mTORC1 signalling, such as those driven by loss of the TSC1/TSC2 tumour suppressors. He now runs his own lab at Rutgers, studying how mTORC1 coordinates metabolic networks and how oncogenic mutations can be exploited therapeutically.
The timeline below follows Valvezan's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.VAL2017: Shows mTORC1 couples nucleotide synthesis to nucleotide demand, revealing a targetable metabolic vulnerability in tumours with hyperactive mTORC1.
highlights.VAL2019: Reviews the molecular logic of mTORC1 signalling as a metabolic rheostat.
highlights.JOS2024: Shows mTORC1 activity oscillates through the cell cycle, promoting mitotic entry and differentially influencing autophagy induction.

Avruch J.lab_name: Profile, MGH Research Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Avruch J.role: Showed in 1998 that amino acids, not only insulin, are needed for mTOR to activate S6K1 and 4E-BP1. His Massachusetts General Hospital group, with Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's lab in Kobe, then co-discovered raptor in 2002 and found that Rheb binds mTOR directly
Avruch J.sub: Professor of Medicine, Harvard Medical School · Chief, Diabetes Unit, Massachusetts General Hospital (since 1979) · MD, Washington University in St. Louis
story: Joseph Avruch has led the Diabetes Unit at Massachusetts General Hospital since 1979, building a career tracing how insulin and growth-factor signalling control protein synthesis and cell growth — work that converged on mTOR as insulin's downstream growth-control checkpoint.

Together with Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's lab in Kobe, his lab identified raptor as mTOR's nutrient-sensitive binding partner in 2002 (in parallel with the Sabatini lab), and in 2005 showed that the small GTPase Rheb binds directly to mTOR's kinase domain and activates it. Together with the 2003 reports from several groups that Rheb is the target of the TSC1/TSC2 complex, this identified Rheb as a direct activator of mTORC1.
The timeline below follows Avruch's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.HAR1998: Shows amino acid sufficiency and mTOR regulate p70 S6 kinase and eIF-4E BP1 through a common effector mechanism, among the earliest evidence linking nutrients directly to mTOR substrates.
highlights.HARA2002: Independently identifies raptor as a binding partner of mTOR that mediates its action, alongside the Sabatini lab's 2002 raptor paper.
highlights.LON2005: Shows Rheb binds directly to mTOR and regulates its kinase activity, establishing Rheb as mTOR's direct GTPase activator.
highlights.PRI1992: Co-author: rapamycin inactivates the 70-kDa S6 kinase, an early readout of TOR signalling (cells).

Dibble CC.lab_name: Dibble Lab, BIDMC & Harvard (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Dibble CC.role: Identified TBC1D7 as the third subunit of the TSC complex that controls mTORC1, as a Manning-lab graduate student. His lab at Beth Israel Deaconess studies how PI3K signalling and nutrient supply are integrated to control mTORC1 and cell metabolism
Dibble CC.sub: Assistant Professor of Pathology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center & Harvard Medical School · PhD, Brendan Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · postdoc, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Lewis Cantley lab)
Dibble CC.credit: Portrait: Dibble Lab, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center
story: Christian Dibble did his PhD in Brendan Manning's lab at Harvard, where he worked out how the TSC1/TSC2 complex integrates growth-factor and nutrient signals to control mTORC1.

In 2012 he identified TBC1D7 as a third, stably associated subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, completing its core composition, and went on to review how PI3K signalling and nutrient cues are integrated by mTORC1 to coordinate a cell's biosynthetic output with its nutrient supply. He now runs his own lab at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.
The timeline below follows Dibble's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.DIB2012: Identifies TBC1D7 as a third, stably associated subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex upstream of mTORC1.
highlights.DIB2013: Reviews how mTORC1 performs signal integration, coordinating nutrient input with a cell's biosynthetic output.
highlights.DIB2015: Reviews how PI3K signalling regulates mTORC1.

Gray NS.role: Medicinal chemist whose lab designed Torin1, an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor that blocks functions of mTORC1 that rapamycin misses. His lab is also known for covalent kinase inhibitors and targeted protein degraders
Gray NS.sub: Krishnan-Shah Family Professor of Chemical and Systems Biology, Stanford University · previously Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School · PhD, UC Berkeley
story: Nathanael Gray is a chemical biologist whose lab designs small-molecule kinase inhibitors and, through long-running collaborations with mTOR biologists including David Sabatini's group, supplied some of the field's key chemical tools.

His lab developed Torin1, one of the first ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors (reported in 2009 alongside compounds such as Kevan Shokat's PP242 and Ku-0063794), which block both mTORC1 and mTORC2 far more completely than rapamycin does. These inhibitors revealed a whole set of rapamycin-resistant mTOR functions — particularly in translation control — that catalytic-site inhibitors, but not rapamycin, could shut down, reshaping how the field defines 'full' mTOR inhibition.
The timeline below follows Gray's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.THO2009: Co-develops an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor and shows it reveals rapamycin-resistant functions of mTORC1.
highlights.PET2009: Co-authors the discovery of DEPTOR, an mTOR inhibitor overexpressed in multiple myeloma and required for myeloma-cell survival.
highlights.THO2012: Co-authors a unifying model for how mTORC1 regulates mRNA translation.

Kang SA.role: Contributed to the Sabatini-lab studies that identified PRAS40 and DEPTOR, two of the cell's own mTOR inhibitors, and to the first characterisation of the mTOR inhibitor Torin1
Kang SA.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, MIT · contributed to the Sabatini lab's PRAS40 and DEPTOR papers (2007–2009)
story: Seong Kang was part of the Whitehead Institute team in David Sabatini's lab that identified (for PRAS40, in parallel with several other groups) two of mTORC1's own endogenous brakes: PRAS40, an insulin-regulated inhibitor that binds raptor, and DEPTOR, an mTOR-binding protein that restrains both mTORC1 and mTORC2 and is selectively overexpressed in multiple myeloma.

That work helped establish that mTORC1 is held in check by a layer of dedicated inhibitory subunits — not just activated by upstream signals — a theme that has since become central to understanding how cancers reactivate mTOR signalling.
The timeline below follows Kang's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SAN2007: Co-authors the discovery of PRAS40 as an insulin-regulated inhibitor of the mTORC1 protein kinase.
highlights.PET2009: Co-authors the discovery of DEPTOR, an mTOR inhibitor frequently overexpressed in multiple myeloma cells and required for their survival.
highlights.THO2009: Co-authors the development of an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor that reveals rapamycin-resistant functions of mTORC1.
highlights.KAN2013: First author of the study showing that each mTORC1 phosphorylation site has its own intrinsic substrate quality, which sets how sensitive it is to rapamycin and starvation.
highlights.YIP2010: Senior author of the cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1, a dimer that FKBP12-rapamycin dismantles in vitro while Torin1 leaves it intact.

Kang SA.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)

Peterson TR.lab_name: Profile, WashU Musculoskeletal Center (St. Louis, Missouri, USA)
Peterson TR.role: Discovered DEPTOR, an inhibitor that binds mTOR in both complexes and is overexpressed in some multiple myelomas. He also showed that mTORC1 controls fat synthesis by regulating where the enzyme lipin 1 sits in the cell, and through it the SREBP pathway
Peterson TR.sub: CEO, BIOIO · previously ran a lab at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis · PhD, David Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute/MIT
Peterson TR.credit: Portrait: Washington University Musculoskeletal Research Center
story: Tim Peterson did his graduate work in David Sabatini's lab, where in 2009 he led the discovery of DEPTOR, a protein that binds mTOR directly and inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2 — and that is selectively overexpressed in a subset of multiple myeloma cells, which depend on it for survival despite it being an mTOR inhibitor, a paradox his paper worked out mechanistically.

He went on to show that mTORC1 also controls lipin 1 localization to regulate the SREBP lipid-synthesis pathway, identifying a mechanism by which mTORC1 promotes SREBP function. He went on to run his own lab at Washington University in St. Louis, studying genomics, metabolism and aging, and now leads the company BIOIO.
The timeline below follows Peterson's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.SAN2007: Co-authors the discovery of PRAS40 as an insulin-regulated inhibitor of the mTORC1 protein kinase.
highlights.PET2009: Leads the discovery of DEPTOR, an mTOR inhibitor frequently overexpressed in multiple myeloma cells and required for their survival.
highlights.PET2011: Shows mTOR complex 1 regulates lipin 1 localization to control the SREBP lipid-synthesis pathway.

Powell JD.lab_name: Profile, Calico Life Sciences (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Powell JD.role: Showed that T cells lacking mTOR become regulatory T cells instead of effector cells, and that mTORC1 and mTORC2 each steer a different type of helper T cell
Powell JD.sub: Fellow, Calico Life Sciences · 20 years at Johns Hopkins University (Bloomberg-Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy) · MD, PhD, Emory University School of Medicine
story: Jonathan Powell spent two decades as a physician-scientist at Johns Hopkins, where his lab established mTOR as a central integrator of the metabolic and environmental signals that tell an immune cell what to become.
