story: Led the 2008 sirolimus trial (BIS2008): angiomyolipoma volume dropped to 53% of baseline by 12 months, crept back after stopping — suggesting mTOR blockade needs to be continuous. Key investigator on EXIST-2 (BIS2013) confirming the effect with everolimus in placebo-controlled design.
A 2023 Army-funded grant now tests whether blood-pressure drugs can prevent angiomyolipomas forming at all.

highlights.BIS2008: 24-month open-label sirolimus trial: AML volume drops to 53% of baseline, drifts back after stopping.
highlights.BIS2013: Key investigator on EXIST-2, confirming everolimus shrinks kidney AMLs in 42% vs 0% placebo.

Bissler JJ.credit: Portrait: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

Franz DN.lab_name: Tuberous Sclerosis Clinic, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Franz DN.role: Led the EXIST-1 trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus shrinks the brain tumours (SEGAs) of tuberous sclerosis, and helped run the first sirolimus trial for its kidney tumours
Franz DN.sub: Professor of Pediatrics, Univ. of Cincinnati · Founding Director, TSC Clinic, Cincinnati Children's · MD, pediatric neurologist
story: Led EXIST-1 (FRA2013, n=117): everolimus shrank SEGA brain tumors ≥50% in 35% vs 0% placebo — an alternative to high-risk neurosurgery. Collaborator on Bissler's 2008 sirolimus trial (BIS2008), groundwork for EXIST-1/2.
Founded and directs one of the longest-running, highest-volume TSC clinics in the US.

highlights.FRA2013: Led EXIST-1, proving everolimus shrinks SEGA brain tumors — cleanest randomized evidence blocking mTOR treats a genetic mTORopathy.
highlights.BIS2008: Collaborated on the earlier sirolimus trial establishing groundwork for EXIST trials.
highlights.FRA2006: First author: in five people with TSC, oral rapamycin shrank growing brain astrocytomas, and in one patient the tumour regrew when treatment was paused.
highlights.FRE2016: Senior author of EXIST-3, the phase 3 trial in which add-on everolimus reduced treatment-resistant seizures in TSC in a dose-dependent way (response 28% and 40% vs 15% on placebo).

Franz DN.credit: Portrait: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center

Kapahi P.lab_name: Kapahi Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Kapahi P.role: Showed that reducing TOR signalling extends fruit-fly lifespan, and that the translation repressor 4E-BP is needed for dietary restriction to extend it
Kapahi P.sub: Professor, Buck Institute for Research on Aging · postdoc, Caltech (S. Benzer) · postdoc, UC San Diego (M. Karin) · PhD, Univ. of Manchester (T. Kirkwood)
story: In Benzer's lab (KAP2004), showed genetically reducing TOR pathway activity (via TSC1/TSC2, TOR, S6K) extends fly lifespan, overlapping mechanistically with dietary restriction. In 2009 (ZID2009), closed the loop: dietary restriction upregulates the TOR target 4E-BP, which selectively boosts mitochondrial gene translation — required, not just correlated, for the lifespan extension.
Nathan Shock New Investigator Award (2010), NIA EUREKA Award (2010), Julie Martin Mid-Career Award (2011), Glenn Award (2015).

highlights.KAP2004: Genetically dialing down TOR in Drosophila extends lifespan, overlapping with dietary restriction.
highlights.ZID2009: Dietary restriction upregulates the TOR target 4E-BP, which boosts mitochondrial translation and is required for the lifespan extension.

Kapahi P.credit: Portrait: Buck Institute for Research on Aging

Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.lab_name: Clinical Biomarker Development, Loxo Oncology at Eli Lilly and Company (formerly Rosen Lab, Memorial Sloan Kettering) (Stamford, Connecticut, USA)
Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.role: Showed that tumours reactivate AKT after mTOR kinase inhibition, and that the third-generation inhibitor RapaLink-1 overcomes mTOR resistance mutations
Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.sub: Associate VP, Clinical Biomarker Development, Loxo Oncology at Lilly · Precision Medicine (Associate Director, then Director), Novartis Oncology (2017–2021) · Research Fellow to Senior Scientist, Rosen Lab, MSKCC (2006–2017) · PhD in Molecular Biology, CUNY Graduate Center (2006)
story: Led ROD2011 (Cancer Discovery): mTOR-kinase inhibitors trigger a biphasic AKT rebound via feedback release of upstream RTK signaling. Led follow-up ROD2016 (Nature, with Shokat's chemistry group): RapaLink-1, a bivalent third-gen inhibitor bridging mTOR's two drug pockets, overcomes resistance mutations.

After eleven years in Neal Rosen's lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering she moved from academic pharmacology into translational science: first precision medicine at Novartis Oncology, then clinical biomarker development at Lilly (Loxo Oncology), where she shapes biomarker strategy for precision-oncology trials.

highlights.ROD2011: mTOR-kinase inhibitors trigger feedback-dependent biphasic AKT rebound.
highlights.ROD2016: RapaLink-1 overcomes resistance mutations that defeat first/second-gen mTOR inhibitors.

Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.credit: Portrait: Clinical Genomic Biomarkers Summit 2025, speaker page

Rosen N.lab_name: Rosen Lab (Member Emeritus), Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Rosen N.role: Showed that blocking mTORC1 releases a feedback brake on receptor tyrosine kinases and AKT, explaining how tumours escape mTOR and PI3K inhibitors and shaping how these drugs are combined in the clinic
Rosen N.sub: Member Emeritus, MSKCC · fellowship, NCI · residency, Brigham and Women's Hospital · MD, PhD, Albert Einstein College of Medicine
story: In 2006 (ORE2006), showed mTOR inhibition paradoxically activates upstream RTK/Akt signaling via feedback release — foundational explanation for why single-agent mTOR inhibitors often fail. As senior author on ROD2011, extended this to mTOR-kinase inhibitors.
This 'feedback reactivation' framework became a central organizing principle of modern targeted-therapy combinations. NIH/NCI Outstanding Investigator Award (2016); AACR Academy Fellow (2022).

highlights.ORE2006: mTOR inhibition relieves feedback suppression of RTK signaling, paradoxically activating Akt.
highlights.ROD2011: Senior author: mTOR-kinase inhibitors cause feedback-dependent biphasic AKT rebound.

Rosen N.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Grabiner BC.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute / MIT (HHMI) (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Grabiner BC.role: Catalogued cancer-associated MTOR mutations and showed that many of them hyperactivate the kinase and can predict sensitivity to rapamycin; he also contributed to the discovery of GATOR1
Grabiner BC.sub: Senior Principal Scientist, Valo Health · Scientist to Senior Scientist, Biogen (2015–2021) · Postdoctoral Associate, Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute / MIT (jointly with David Root, Broad Institute) · PhD, UTHealth / MD Anderson Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences (Xin Lin lab)
story: Helped identify GATOR1 (BAR2013) — a GAP for the Rag GTPases; mutated in cancers, making tumors hypersensitive to rapamycin. Led follow-up (GRA2014) cataloguing cancer-associated MTOR mutations that hyperactivate the kinase and predict rapamycin sensitivity.

He came to the Sabatini lab as a postdoc after a PhD in Houston (UTHealth / MD Anderson, Xin Lin lab), then moved into industry: Biogen (translational genomics and target validation, 2015–2021), and since 2021 Valo Health (AI-driven drug discovery, neurology).

highlights.BAR2013: GATOR1 is a GAP shutting Rag GTPases (and mTORC1) off when amino acids run low.
highlights.GRA2014: Cancer-associated MTOR mutations are hyperactivating and predict rapamycin sensitivity.

Grabiner BC.credit: Portrait: Sabatini lab website, Whitehead Institute (2014, archived)

Guri Y.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Guri Y.role: Showed mTORC2 drives liver cancer by rewiring lipid and sphingolipid synthesis
Guri Y.sub: Botnar Research Centre for Child Health (BRCCH; affiliation on 2023 publications, renamed Basel Research Centre for Child Health in 2024) · University Hospital Basel (Internal Medicine) · MD-PhD, Biozentrum, Univ. of Basel (Hall lab)
story: In a fatty-liver-to-HCC mouse model, showed mTORC2 drives tumor formation by ramping up de novo lipid/sphingolipid synthesis (GUR2017); blocking synthesis prevented tumors. Co-authored a review (GUR2016) on mTOR as a resistance mechanism against targeted cancer drugs.
MD-PhD; returned to clinical medicine at University Hospital Basel (treated COVID-19 patients), now also affiliated with BRCCH.

highlights.GUR2017: mTORC2 promotes tumorigenesis via de novo lipid synthesis.
highlights.GUR2016: Review of mTOR signaling conferring resistance to targeted cancer drugs.

Guri Y.credit: Portrait: Botnar Research Centre for Child Health (BRCCH)

Loewith R.lab_name: Loewith Lab, University of Geneva (Geneva, Switzerland)
Loewith R.role: Showed, as first author in Michael Hall's lab, that yeast TOR exists as two distinct complexes, the basis of the TORC1/TORC2 framework
Loewith R.sub: Full Professor, Univ. of Geneva (faculty since 2005, full professor since 2015) · postdoc, Univ. of Basel (Michael N. Hall) · PhD, Univ. of Calgary (Dallan Young) · BSc, Univ. of Guelph
story: As Hall-lab postdoc, showed (LOE2002) TOR assembles into two biochemically distinct complexes — TORC1 (rapamycin-sensitive) and TORC2 (insensitive, controls actin polarity) — founding the field's organizing vocabulary. In 2009 (FEL2009), helped test some of the first ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors (TORKinibs) against this two-complex model.
Own lab at Univ. of Geneva since 2005; ERC Starting (2008) and Consolidator (2014) grants; Director (2019–2022), NCCR Chemical Biology; elected EMBO Member.

highlights.LOE2002: Defines TORC1/TORC2 as biochemically distinct complexes, founding the two-complex paradigm.
highlights.FEL2009: Helped test some of the first ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors (TORKinibs) against both complexes.

Yang H.lab_name: Pavletich Lab, Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Yang H.role: Solved, as first author in the Pavletich lab, the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase and the structure of mTORC1 activated by RHEB
Yang H.sub: Senior Research Scientist, Structural Biology Program, MSKCC (Pavletich Lab)
story: First author on the 2013 crystal structure of the mTOR kinase (YAN2013), revealing the FRB 'gatekeeper' domain. First author again in 2017 (YAN2017) on cryo-EM structures of mTORC1 alone and bound to RHEB, plus a crystal structure of a truncated mTOR–PRAS40 complex, revealing the allosteric activation/inhibition mechanism.
Both studies from Nikola Pavletich's lab (who has his own medailonek in the Atlas).

highlights.YAN2013: Solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, revealing the FRB gatekeeper domain.
highlights.YAN2017: Solved structures of mTORC1 bound to RHEB/PRAS40, revealing the allosteric activation mechanism.

Yang H.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Chen C.lab_name: The Chen-Liu Lab, State Key Laboratory of Biotherapy, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Chen C.role: Showed that blood stem cells need TSC to keep mTOR in check in order to stay dormant and self-renew, and that rapamycin restores the function of aged blood stem cells in mice
Chen C.sub: Professor, West China Hospital, Sichuan University · postdoc, Scott Lowe lab, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory & MSKCC · PhD, University of Michigan
story: First author (CHE2008): deleting Tsc1 (unleashing mTOR) drove resting blood stem cells into rapid division, flooded them with ROS, destroyed regenerative capacity — antioxidant partly rescued them. Follow-up (CHE2009): mTOR rises naturally in aged HSCs, and rapamycin restores regenerative capacity and vaccine response.
Postdoc'd with Scott Lowe (lineage plasticity/therapy resistance), now co-runs a lab with Yu (Kiki) Liu (co-author on both original papers) studying epigenetic reprogramming in cancer.

highlights.CHE2008: Deleting Tsc1 drives blood stem cells into rapid division, ROS flood, and exhausts self-renewal.
highlights.CHE2009: mTOR rises in aged HSCs; rapamycin restores their regenerative function and vaccine response.

Chen C.credit: Portrait: West China Hospital, Sichuan University

Zheng P.role: Showed as senior author that blood stem cells need TSC to keep mTOR in check in order to stay dormant, and that rapamycin restores the function of aged blood stem cells in mice
Zheng P.sub: Co-founder & CMO, OncoC4, Inc. · Professor, Univ. of Michigan, Ohio State, Children's National, Univ. of Maryland IHV · PhD, Yale · MD, Peking Union Medical College
story: Senior author on both CHE2008 and CHE2009 (HSC aging/mTOR). Long partnership with immunologist Yang Liu spanning Yale, Ohio State, Michigan, Children's National, Univ. of Maryland IHV; co-discovered the CD24–Siglec-10 checkpoint, translated into CD24Fc (tested for GVHD and severe COVID).
Co-founded OncoC4 (formerly OncoImmune), where she is now CMO directing global checkpoint-immunotherapy trials.

highlights.CHE2008: Senior author: TSC-mTOR keeps blood stem cells quiescent by repressing mitochondrial ROS.
highlights.CHE2009: Senior author: mTOR hyperactivation drives HSC aging; rapamycin restores function and immune competence.

Viollet B.role: Showed that metformin still lowers liver glucose production without AMPK or LKB1, pointing instead to a drop in cellular energy charge
Viollet B.sub: Directeur de Recherche (INSERM), Institut Cochin · shifted to AMPK biology late 1990s · trained in Axel Kahn's lab, Institut Cochin de Génétique Moléculaire
story: In 2010 (FOR2010), using AMPK/LKB1-knockout mice and hepatocytes, showed metformin still suppresses hepatic glucose production — contradicting the standard AMPK-dependent model, pointing instead to a drop in energy charge. His AMPK-knockout genetic tools were used in the 2011 ULK1 study (KIM2011), which separated AMPK's activating vs. mTORC1's inhibitory phosphorylation of ULK1.

Began career in liver gene transcription (Axel Kahn lab), then built AMPK-subunit knockout mouse lines used field-wide for two decades. Nutrition Research Award (2000), Institut Benjamin Delessert Prize (2004), Descartes-Huygens Prize (2015).

highlights.KIM2011: Contributed AMPK-knockout genetic tools to the study showing AMPK/mTORC1's opposing regulation of ULK1.
highlights.FOR2010: Metformin still suppresses hepatic glucose production without AMPK or LKB1.

Kim J.role: Showed as a Guan-lab postdoc that AMPK and mTORC1 control autophagy by phosphorylating ULK1 at different sites, with mTORC1's mark on Ser757 blocking activation by AMPK
Kim J.sub: Professor, Dept. of Oral Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Kyung Hee University, Seoul · training/postdoc in Kun-Liang Guan's lab, Univ. of Michigan Life Sciences Institute → UC San Diego
story: First author (KIM2011): AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1 at activating sites, mTORC1 phosphorylates Ser757 to keep it off and block AMPK access — the tug-of-war deciding autophagy on/off. Co-authored with Guan an influential 2019 review (KIM2019) reframing mTOR as the central hub of nutrient signaling.

Long apprenticeship in Guan's lab (Michigan → UCSD). Now Professor at Kyung Hee dental school, Seoul — extending AMPK/mTOR/autophagy biology into oral/dental contexts, retains UCSD Pharmacology affiliation.

highlights.KIM2011: First author: mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 at Ser757 to keep autophagy off and block AMPK's activating site.
highlights.KIM2019: Co-authors influential review reframing mTOR as the central hub integrating nutrient signals with cell growth.
highlights.RUS2013: Co-author: ULK1 phosphorylates Beclin-1 to activate the ATG14L–VPS34 complex and induce autophagy.

Demetriades C.lab_name: Demetriades Lab, European Research Institute for the Biology of Ageing (ERIBA), UMCG (Groningen, Netherlands)
Demetriades C.role: Showed as a postdoc in Aurelio Teleman's lab that starvation and other stresses pull TSC2 to the lysosome to switch mTORC1 off. His group, at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing in Cologne from 2017 and at ERIBA in Groningen since 2025, studies how cells sense nutrients and stress through mTORC1 and how this changes with age
Demetriades C.sub: Associate Professor, ERIBA, University Medical Center Groningen (since 2025) · Max Planck Research Group Leader, MPI for Biology of Ageing, Cologne (2017–2025) · postdoc, DKFZ Heidelberg (Aurelio Teleman lab, 2010–2016) · PhD, BSRC 'Alexander Fleming' & Aristotle Univ. (George Mosialos lab, 2003–2009) · BSc, Aristotle Univ. of Thessaloniki (2003)
story: As Teleman-lab postdoc, showed (DEM2014) starvation pulls TSC2 onto the lysosome to directly switch off Rheb/mTORC1 — the missing piece beyond Rag-GTPase relocation. Follow-up (DEM2016): many stress types (energy, hypoxia, osmotic, oxidative, growth-factor withdrawal) independently drive TSC2 to the lysosome — a general damage-control mechanism.

Own MPI-AGE group 2017–2025 (ERC Starting Grant), since 2025 at ERIBA Groningen, continuing to dissect the spatial logic of mTORC1 signaling (2024: mTORC1 does different jobs at different locations). FEBS Young Scientists' Fellowship (2014), Walther Flemming Award (2019).

highlights.DEM2014: Amino-acid starvation recruits TSC2 to the lysosome to inactivate Rheb and mTORC1.
highlights.DEM2016: Lysosomal TSC2 recruitment is a universal response to many cellular stresses.
highlights.FER2025: Senior author (preprint): CYLD deubiquitinates mTOR, limiting mTORC1/2 activity; its loss blocks lifespan extension in low-TORC1 worms.

Demetriades C.credit: Portrait: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing

Teleman AA.lab_name: Division of Signal Transduction in Cancer and Metabolism, DKFZ (Heidelberg, Germany)
Teleman AA.role: Uses fruit-fly genetics and human cells to study how growth signalling through TOR controls cell and body size. His lab showed that starvation and other stresses move TSC2 to the lysosome to switch mTORC1 off
Teleman AA.sub: Division Head, DKFZ (since 2012) · Junior Group Leader, DKFZ (2007) · McKinsey & Co. (2001–2002) · PhD, EMBL & Imperial College London (Stephen M. Cohen, 2004) · AB Biochemistry, Harvard (Richard Losick, 1998) · EMBO Member (2020)
story: As corresponding author, guided Demetriades to the TSC2/lysosome discoveries (DEM2014, DEM2016) — showing mTORC1's starvation shutdown depends on TSC2 acting at the lysosome, then generalizing to many stress types.
Trained as biochemist at Harvard, PhD with Stephen Cohen (fly growth signaling), briefly a McKinsey consultant. ERC Starting/Consolidator/Advanced grants.

highlights.DEM2014: Senior author: amino-acid starvation recruits TSC2 to the lysosome to inhibit Rheb and mTORC1.
highlights.DEM2016: Senior author: lysosomal TSC2 recruitment triggered by many cellular stresses, a general damage-control mechanism.
highlights.FER2025: Co-author on the preprint identifying CYLD as a deubiquitinase that restrains mTOR.

Markhard AL.lab_name: Long Lab, Stanford (formerly Mootha Lab, Broad/MGH) (Stanford, California, USA)
Markhard AL.role: Contributed, as a Sabatini-lab researcher, to the discovery that Ragulator docks mTORC1 on the lysosome, and now studies metabolite signals that tell the body it has eaten
Markhard AL.sub: Ph.D. student, NYU Grossman School of Medicine · Research Scientist, Long Lab, Stanford · Lab Manager, Mootha Lab, Broad/MGH (2012–2022) · Research staff, Sabatini Lab, Whitehead/MIT
story: Part of team showing (SAR2006) prolonged rapamycin also blocks mTORC2 assembly and Akt signalling in many cell types (later linked in mice to rapamycin's insulin resistance, LAM2012). Part of team (SAN2010) showing Ragulator recruits Rag GTPases to the lysosomal surface, docking mTORC1 next to Rheb.

Decade as Mootha-lab manager mapping mitochondrial proteins, then Stanford metabolomics (2024 Nature: enzyme PTER/taurine; 2026 Nature Metabolism: python-derived gut-brain feeding signal). Now pursuing a PhD at NYU.

highlights.SAR2006: Co-author: prolonged rapamycin treatment blocks mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB signalling in many cell types (later linked in mice to rapamycin's insulin resistance, LAM2012).
highlights.SAN2010: Helped show Ragulator recruits Rag GTPases to the lysosomal surface, docking mTORC1 next to Rheb.

Hsu PP.lab_name: Hsu Lab, University of Michigan Rogel Cancer Center (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Hsu PP.role: Identified, in parallel with Yonghao Yu's group, Grb10 as an mTORC1 substrate that feeds back to dampen insulin and growth-factor signalling, and now studies the earliest steps of lung cancer as a physician-scientist
Hsu PP.sub: University of Michigan · postdoc, Vander Heiden Lab, MIT · oncology fellowship, Dana-Farber & MGH · residency, Brigham and Women's · MD, Harvard · PhD, MIT (Sabatini Lab) · BA, Princeton
story: Used quantitative phosphoproteomics (HSU2011) to map mTOR's substrates directly, identifying Grb10 — mTORC1 phosphorylates/stabilizes it, and Grb10 suppresses PI3K/growth-factor signaling, explaining mTORC1-hyperactivation-causes-insulin-resistance. (Reported in parallel, in the same issue of Science, by Yonghao Yu and John Blenis.)

Physician-scientist path through MIT/Harvard/Dana-Farber/MGH; now thoracic oncologist and stem cell biologist studying how airway basal cells give rise to never-smoking, ALK-fusion lung cancer. NCI K08, Burroughs Wellcome Fund Career Award (2025), 2026 ASCI Young Physician-Scientist.

highlights.SAR2006: Co-author: prolonged rapamycin treatment blocks mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB signalling in many cell types (later linked in mice to rapamycin's insulin resistance, LAM2012).
highlights.HSU2011: Mapped the mTOR phosphoproteome, identifying Grb10 as a direct mTORC1 substrate feeding back on PI3K.

Hsu PP.credit: Portrait: American Society for Clinical Investigation (ASCI)

Sengupta S.role: Showed that mTORC1 controls whether the liver makes ketone bodies during fasting, and now leads biology for drug discovery at a metabolic-disease biotech
Sengupta S.sub: SVP, Head of Biology, Atavistik Bio · Associate Director, Agios · Lead Biologist, Navitor Pharmaceuticals · Broad Institute CDoT · Catabasis Pharmaceuticals · postdoc, Brugge Lab, Harvard Medical School · PhD, Whitehead/MIT (Sabatini Lab)
story: Showed (SEN2010) that during fasting the liver must switch mTORC1 off to make ketones — losing TSC1 locked the pathway on and blocked ketogenesis via PPARα/NCoR1; aged livers show chronically elevated mTORC1 and a similar ketogenesis defect.
Moved through Catabasis, Broad CDoT, Navitor (built on Sabatini-lab amino-acid-sensing biology), Agios, now heading biology at Atavistik Bio's metabolism pipeline.

highlights.SAR2006: Co-author: prolonged rapamycin treatment blocks mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB signalling in many cell types (later linked in mice to rapamycin's insulin resistance, LAM2012).
highlights.SEN2010: mTORC1 suppresses fasting-induced hepatic ketogenesis via PPARα; suppression worsens with age.
highlights.YIL2012: Co-author: calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 in Paneth cells, which then support more intestinal stem cells through the enzyme Bst1 (mice).

Ehninger D.lab_name: Translational Biogerontology Group, DZNE Bonn (Bonn, Germany)
Ehninger D.role: Showed that rapamycin reverses learning deficits in adult mice carrying a tuberous sclerosis mutation, and later tested carefully whether rapamycin's lifespan effect reflects a true slowing of ageing
Ehninger D.sub: Group Leader, DZNE Bonn (since 2010) · postdoc, UCLA (Alcino Silva lab, 2004–2009) · MD, Charité Berlin/UCL/Mount Sinai/Harvard (clinical training)
story: As UCLA postdoc, showed (EHN2008) Tsc2+/- mice have hyperactive mTOR/hippocampal learning deficits, reversible with a short rapamycin course — an early demonstration mTOR drugs could treat cognitive symptoms of a genetic disorder. At DZNE, led a rigorous large-scale phenotyping study (NEF2013): rapamycin extends mouse lifespan but leaves most classic aging phenotypes unchanged — a standard citation distinguishing 'longer life' from 'slower aging.'
Physician trained in neurology before full-time research; DZNE group continues skeptical, rigorous mouse-aging science.

highlights.EHN2008: Rapamycin reverses hippocampal learning/memory deficits in Tsc2+/- mice.
highlights.NEF2013: Rapamycin extends lifespan but leaves most classic aging markers unchanged.

Egan DF.lab_name: Shaw Lab, Salk Institute (where this work was done) (La Jolla, California, USA)
Egan DF.role: Showed as first author that AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1, linking low cellular energy to autophagy and mitophagy, and contributed to the finding that AMPK brakes mTORC1 by phosphorylating raptor
Egan DF.sub: Director, Eli Lilly · industry: Orna Therapeutics, ReNAgade Therapeutics, Casma Therapeutics · postdoc, Harvard Medical School (2014–2018) · PhD, UCSD/Salk (Reuben Shaw lab, 2008–2014) · BA, Colby College
story: Co-author (GWI2008): AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor, a second route (beyond TSC2) to shut mTORC1 down during energy stress. First author (EGA2010): AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1, connecting energy sensing to mitophagy.
Moved from Salk PhD through Harvard postdoc into a string of Boston biotechs, now a director at Eli Lilly — an academic-to-industry path that began with AMPK/autophagy biology.

highlights.GWI2008: AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor, a second route to shut down mTORC1 during energy stress.
highlights.EGA2010: AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1, linking energy sensing to mitophagy.

Egan DF.credit: Portrait: Spiegelman Lab, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

Wyant GA.lab_name: Wyant Lab, MGH Cardiovascular Research Center (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Wyant GA.role: Showed that the lysosomal protein SLC38A9 exports leucine and other essential amino acids out of the lysosome, letting cells grow on proteins they have taken up and broken down there
Wyant GA.sub: Assistant Professor, MGH/Harvard Medical School · postdoc, Dana-Farber (William Kaelin lab) · PhD, MIT/Whitehead (Sabatini lab) · BS, Northeastern Univ.
story: First author (WYA2017): SLC38A9, already known for arginine sensing, has a second job — effluxing essential amino acids like leucine out of lysosomes to activate mTORC1; pancreatic cancer cells scavenging protein by macropinocytosis depend on this efflux. Contributed to CHA2016 (CASTOR1 arginine sensor discovery).

Pivoted to oxygen sensing with Nobel laureate William Kaelin, now runs own MGH/Harvard lab studying oxygen, nutrients, mechanical stretch and electrical activity in heart/muscle growth — aimed at heart failure and cachexia.

highlights.WYA2017: SLC38A9 effluxes essential amino acids out of lysosomes to activate mTORC1.
highlights.CHA2016: Contributed to identifying CASTOR1 as the direct arginine sensor upstream of mTORC1.
highlights.WYA2018: First author: NUFIP1 acts as a receptor that delivers ribosomes to autophagy when mTORC1 is inhibited.

Rogala KB.lab_name: Rogala Lab, Stanford University (Stanford, California, USA)
Rogala KB.role: Solved the near-atomic cryo-EM structure that shows how mTORC1 physically docks at the lysosome by reading the Rag GTPases
Rogala KB.sub: Assistant Professor, Stanford (Structural Biology & Chemical & Systems Biology) · postdoc, MIT/Whitehead (Sabatini lab) · DPhil, Univ. of Oxford · MRes, UCL · BSc, Univ. of Edinburgh
story: First author (ROG2019, Science): cryo-EM at 3.2 Å of Raptor bound to Rag-Ragulator, revealing how mTORC1 reads the Rag GTPases' nucleotide state to dock at the lysosome. Co-first author (VAL2022, Nature): GATOR2's cryo-EM structure — a 1.1 MDa, two-fold symmetric cage with octagonal scaffold and 8 paired WD40 propellers, mapping Sestrin2/CASTOR1 docking sites.
Now leads his own Stanford lab, studying 'cellular intelligence' — how cells sense nutrients and growth signals — with an eye toward cancer and tuberous sclerosis therapeutics.

highlights.ROG2019: Cryo-EM shows how Raptor reads Rag GTPase nucleotide states to dock mTORC1 at the lysosome.
highlights.VAL2022: Co-first author: cryo-EM structure of GATOR2, mapping Sestrin2/CASTOR1 docking.
highlights.VAL2025: Senior author: structures of GATOR2 bound to Sestrin2 or CASTOR1, showing how the amino acid sensors detach.

Yu Yonghao.lab_name: Yu Lab, Columbia University Irving Medical Center (New York, New York, USA)
Yu Yonghao.role: Used phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises Grb10, which then acts as a feedback brake on insulin and IGF-1 signalling
Yu Yonghao.sub: Professor, Columbia University Irving Medical Center · Associate Professor, UT Southwestern · postdoc, Harvard Medical School (Steven Gygi & John Blenis) · PhD Chemistry, UC Berkeley (Julie Leary) · BS Chemistry, Fudan Univ.
story: As Blenis-lab postdoc, large-scale phosphoproteomics (YUX2011) identified Grb10 as a direct mTORC1 substrate whose stabilization suppresses PI3K/ERK-MAPK signaling downstream of insulin/IGF-1 receptor — discovered independently and near-simultaneously by Sabatini lab's Peggy Hsu (also in this Atlas).

Trained as a chemist before biology; built labs at UT Southwestern then Columbia, studying covalent protein modifications (phosphorylation, poly-ADP-ribosylation, tyrosine sulfation) and covalent drugs against 'undruggable' targets.

highlights.YUX2011: Phosphoproteomics identify Grb10 as a direct mTORC1 substrate creating negative feedback on insulin/PI3K signaling.

Ferguson SM.lab_name: Ferguson Lab, Yale School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Ferguson SM.role: Showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to keep the lysosome-building program switched off, and that folliculin is required at the lysosome for amino acids to recruit and activate mTORC1
Ferguson SM.sub: Professor of Cell Biology and Neuroscience, Yale School of Medicine · postdoc, Yale (Pietro De Camilli) · PhD Neuroscience, Vanderbilt · BS/MS, Univ. of Ottawa
story: Showed (ROC2012) mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (Ser211), recruiting 14-3-3 to trap it in the cytoplasm — independent, complementary work to the Settembre/Ballabio TFEB papers. Follow-up (PET2013): folliculin (FLCN, a Birt-Hogg-Dubé tumor suppressor) binds RagA at the lysosome and is required for amino acids to recruit mTORC1 there. Watch the direction, which the paper's title invites you to get backwards: FLCN's own lysosomal localisation rises when amino acids are WITHDRAWN. What depends on amino acids is the recruitment of mTORC1, and that step needs FLCN.
Trained in neuroscience before shifting to lysosome cell biology with De Camilli at Yale; now studies lysosomal adaptation and neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson's, ALS, FTD, Alzheimer's).

highlights.ROC2012: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to keep it cytoplasmically sequestered via 14-3-3.
highlights.PET2013: FLCN binds RagA at the lysosome and is required for amino-acid-driven recruitment of mTORC1; FLCN's own lysosomal localisation rises when amino acids are withdrawn.

Podlutskaya N.lab_name: BLaST Program, University of Alaska Fairbanks (Fairbanks, Alaska, USA)
Podlutskaya N.role: Contributed, at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, to mouse studies showing that rapamycin prevents Alzheimer's-like memory loss and improves cognition in normal ageing
Podlutskaya N.sub: Research advisor/mentor, BLaST Program, Univ. of Alaska Fairbanks (since 2015) · researcher, Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (Richardson/Galvan labs, c. 2008–2013) · MS Biology, Kharkov University, Ukraine
story: Contributed to SPI2010: long-term rapamycin prevented memory deficits and lowered amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's mouse model, tracking with increased autophagy. Contributed to HAL2012: a lifespan-extending rapamycin dose improved learning/memory, reduced anxiety/depression-like behavior in mice.
Part of the broader Barshop Institute comparative-aging tradition (oxidative stress, mitochondrial function across long-lived mammals).
Moved into science education/mentoring at UAF's BLaST program, training undergraduates in molecular biology.

highlights.SPI2010: Contributed to showing long-term rapamycin prevents memory deficits and lowers amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's model.
highlights.HAL2012: Contributed to showing a lifespan-extending rapamycin dose improves cognition and reduces anxiety/depression-like behavior.

Galvan V.lab_name: Galvan Lab, University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center (Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, USA)
Galvan V.role: Led mouse studies showing that rapamycin prevents Alzheimer's-like memory loss and amyloid build-up, and improves learning in normally ageing mice
Galvan V.sub: Professor & Donald W. Reynolds Endowed Chair, Univ. of Oklahoma HSC (since 2021); Editor-in-Chief, GeroScience · UT Health San Antonio, Barshop Institute (until 2021) · postdoc, Buck Institute (Dale Bredesen) · PhD virology, Univ. of Chicago (Bernard Roizman, 1999) · MS, Univ. of Buenos Aires (1994)
story: Senior author on SPI2010 (rapamycin prevents Alzheimer's-model cognitive decline, lowers amyloid-beta) and HAL2012 (chronic rapamycin enhances cognition across normal aging, no cost to the aging brain).

Work done with Barshop Institute collaborators Richardson and Strong (both already in the Atlas). Seeded her career-long focus on mTOR as a druggable node between brain aging and Alzheimer's; co-author on a 2025 pilot Phase 1 rapamycin/Alzheimer's clinical trial.
Moved to OU Health Sciences Center in 2021; directs the Oklahoma Nathan Shock Center on Aging; past President, American Aging Association (2021–2022); Editor-in-Chief, GeroScience (since 2021).

highlights.SPI2010: Senior author: long-term rapamycin prevents memory deficits and lowers amyloid-beta, tracking with increased autophagy.
highlights.HAL2012: Senior author: a lifespan-extending rapamycin dose enhances cognition and reduces anxiety/depression-like behavior.

Galvan V.credit: Portrait: University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center

Budanov AV.lab_name: Budanov Lab, Trinity College Dublin (Dublin, Ireland)
Budanov AV.role: Helped identify the Sestrins as stress-induced proteins and was among the groups that showed they inhibit mTORC1 through the GATOR complex, a brake that protects against age-related disease
Budanov AV.sub: Ussher Assistant Professor, Biochemistry, Trinity College Dublin · Assistant Professor, VCU Massey Cancer Center · postdoc, Michael Karin lab, UC San Diego
story: In flies (LEE2010, led by Jun Hee Lee in Michael Karin's lab), helped show loss of Sestrin lets TOR run unchecked, producing fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle wasting, heart failure — reversible by inhibiting TOR or activating AMPK; established a TOR–Sestrin negative feedback loop. Follow-up (PAR2014): Sestrins interact with GATOR2 (also reported by the Sabatini lab), blocking mTORC1 recruitment to the lysosome — an AMPK-independent brake.
Traces back to his postdoc with Michael Karin (Sestrin1/2 as p53 targets activating AMPK to inhibit mTOR after DNA damage, 2008 Cell, BUD2008). Now at Trinity College Dublin.

highlights.PAR2014: Sestrins block mTORC1 by binding GATOR2, preventing mTOR from reaching the lysosome.
highlights.LEE2010: Loss of Sestrin in flies lets TOR run unchecked, causing fat/mitochondrial/muscle/heart pathology reversible by blocking TOR or activating AMPK.
highlights.BUD2008: First author: p53 targets Sestrin1 and Sestrin2 activate AMPK and TSC2 to inhibit mTOR after DNA damage (cells and mice).

Betz C.lab_name: Michael N. Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (where these studies were done) (Basel, Switzerland)
Betz C.role: Traced mTORC2 to a specific address inside the cell — the mitochondria-ER contact site
Betz C.sub: Head of International Relations, Directorate of Health, Luxembourg (since 2022) · Luxinnovation (2017–2022) · research staff, vascular-biology groups, Biozentrum · PhD & postdoc, Michael Hall lab, Biozentrum
story: Showed (BET2013) mTORC2 concentrates at mitochondria-associated ER membranes (MAM), phosphorylating tether proteins via Akt; disrupting mTORC2 broke the ER-mitochondria tether, damaging membrane potential/ATP/calcium handling. Co-authored the widely cited review (BETZ2013) arguing mTOR's subcellular address is a regulatory layer in its own right.
PhD and postdoc in Hall's lab (later a co-author of a 2018 Nature paper on LHPP as a tumor suppressor). Moved into vascular biology, then public-health administration.

highlights.BETZ2013: Review arguing mTOR's subcellular location, not just activity, is a core regulatory layer.
highlights.BET2013: mTORC2-Akt signaling concentrates at mitochondria-ER contact sites, maintaining the tether required for normal mitochondrial function.
highlights.HAG2012: Co-author: liver-specific loss of mTORC2 blocks feeding-induced glycolysis and lipogenesis, acting mainly through Akt (mice).

Delgoffe GM.lab_name: Delgoffe Lab, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center / University of Pittsburgh (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA)
Delgoffe GM.role: Showed as a graduate student in Jonathan Powell's lab that T cells lacking mTOR become regulatory rather than effector T cells, and that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer different helper-T-cell fates
Delgoffe GM.sub: Professor of Immunology, Director of Tumor Microenvironment Center, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center; Editor-in-Chief, Immunology (Wiley) · postdoc, St. Jude (Dario Vignali lab) · PhD, Johns Hopkins (Jonathan D. Powell lab, 2010)
story: As PhD student with Powell (who has his own medailonek), showed (DEL2009) T cells lacking mTOR fail to differentiate into effector cells, defaulting toward Treg fate. Refined (DEL2011): mTORC1 required specifically for Th1/Th17, mTORC2 specifically for Th2 — which complex is active, not just mTOR on/off, dictates fate.

Built own program at Pitt around the idea that tumors selectively feed Tregs, not just starve killer T cells — tumor Tregs depend on taking up lactic acid through the transporter MCT1 (Nature 2021); dichloroacetate improves CAR-T persistence (Cell Metabolism 2025). Co-founded Novasenta and RemplirBio. CRI Lloyd J. Old STAR awardee.

highlights.DEL2009: T cells lacking mTOR fail to differentiate into effector cells, defaulting toward Treg fate.
highlights.DEL2011: mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively program distinct CD4 helper T-cell lineages.
highlights.POL2015: Co-author: mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer CD8 T cells differently, with constant mTORC1 driving short-lived glycolytic effectors and loss of mTORC2 favouring long-lived memory cells (mice).

Lawrence RE.lab_name: Lawrence Lab, UCLA David Geffen School of Medicine (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Lawrence RE.role: Working in Roberto Zoncu's lab, uncovered the nutrient-driven affinity switch and the FLCN checkpoint that gate mTORC1 activation at the lysosome
Lawrence RE.sub: Assistant Professor, UCLA (since January 2025) · postdoc, UCSF/HHMI (Peter Walter lab) · PhD, UC Berkeley (Roberto Zoncu lab) · BA, Swarthmore College
story: As Zoncu-lab PhD student (Zoncu has his own medailonek), showed (LAW2018) nutrients destabilize the Rag-Ragulator scaffold, requiring two simultaneous Rag-binding interfaces for mTORC1 capture — an affinity switch cancer mutations short-circuit. Solved (LAW2019), in parallel with a Sabatini-lab study, a 3.6 Å cryo-EM structure of the lysosomal folliculin (FLCN) complex, showing FLCN's RagC-GAP activity is auto-inhibited until the complex disassembles.

Moved to UCSF/HHMI studying the Integrated Stress Response (eIF2B allostery, ISRIB mechanism). Now own lab at UCLA since Jan 2025, studying stress-signaling feedback on metabolism and glial neurodegeneration.

highlights.LAW2018: Nutrients destabilize the Rag-Ragulator scaffold, requiring two engaged Rag interfaces for mTORC1 capture.
highlights.LAW2019: Cryo-EM shows FLCN's GAP activity is auto-inhibited within the intact lysosomal complex, gating mTORC1 activation.

Wang T.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute / MIT Biology (at time of both featured studies) (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Wang T.role: Co-developed genome-wide CRISPR screening in human cells (reported in parallel by Feng Zhang's lab) as a graduate student with David Sabatini and Eric Lander, and contributed to studies showing that the 4E-BPs mediate mTORC1's control of translation and that CASTOR1 senses arginine
Wang T.sub: Senior Scientist, Allen Institute for Neural Dynamics · postdoc (Helen Hay Whitney Fellow), Janelia Research Campus (Karel Svoboda lab) · PhD, MIT (Sabatini & Lander labs) · BS Bioengineering, UC Berkeley
story: Co-author (THO2012): ribosome profiling with Torin1 showed mTORC1 controls translation of TOP-motif mRNAs largely through 4E-BPs. Co-author (CHA2016): CASTOR1 identified as the direct arginine sensor upstream of mTORC1.

highlights.THO2012: Co-authored the ribosome-profiling study showing 4E-BPs are mTORC1's master translational effectors.

Garcia-Martinez JM.lab_name: MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, University of Dundee (at time of both featured studies) (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Garcia-Martinez JM.role: Discovered mTORC2 activates SGK1 and co-developed Ku-0063794, one of the first selective ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors
Garcia-Martinez JM.sub: Cancer Research, Boehringer Ingelheim RCV, Vienna · postdoc, Alessi Lab, MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, Dundee · PhD, Universitat de Barcelona/IDIBAPS (Alberch lab, Huntington's disease)
story: First author (GAR2008, with Dario Alessi, who has his own medailonek): mTORC2 — not mTORC1 — phosphorylates and activates SGK1, cleanly separating what each mTOR complex does. First author (GAR2009): co-developed Ku-0063794, one of the first genuinely selective ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors blocking both complexes.

Continued at Dundee testing PI3K/mTOR inhibitors in mouse lymphoma models, then moved into industry — Boehringer Ingelheim's Vienna oncology unit, developing bispecific antibody drugs (TRAILR2 agonists) for colorectal/pancreatic cancer (2020, 2024 papers).

highlights.GAR2008: mTORC2 (not mTORC1) phosphorylates and activates SGK1.
highlights.GAR2009: Co-developed Ku-0063794, a specific ATP-competitive inhibitor blocking both mTOR complexes.

Williams RL.lab_name: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), Cambridge (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Williams RL.role: Solved structures showing how the Rag GTPases bind mTORC1 and how TOR forms a dimer, working at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
Williams RL.sub: Group Leader, MRC LMB, Cambridge · Rutgers, Cornell, Boris Kidrič Institute Belgrade · PhD, UC Riverside (1986) · MS, Eastern Washington Univ. · BS, Purdue
story: Cryo-EM shows TOR dimerizes through an N-terminal helical solenoid (BAR2016), shaping how mTORC1 is built. Three years later, solved mTORC1 bound to Rag GTPases (ANA2019), showing how amino-acid status recruits the complex to the lysosome.
Leads a structural biology group at the storied MRC LMB, working across the PI3K superfamily. FRS (2017), FMedSci, EMBO Member, Biochemical Society Morton Lectureship.

Chi H.lab_name: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Department of Immunology (Memphis, Tennessee, USA)
Chi H.role: Showed that regulatory T cells need mTORC1 signalling to fuel their suppressive function, and studies how mTOR-driven metabolism steers T-cell fate
Chi H.sub: Chair, Department of Immunology, St. Jude; Robert G. Webster Endowed Chair in Immunology · PhD, University of Rochester
story: His 2012 review (CHI2012) became a foundational reference for immunometabolism. In 2013 (ZEN2013), with Hu Zeng, showed mTORC1 (via Raptor) is required for Tregs to integrate metabolic cues and mature into suppressive cells — overturning the assumption Tregs are simply low-mTOR cells.

Chairs St. Jude Immunology, co-directs the Center of Excellence for Pediatric Immuno-Oncology. NCI Outstanding Investigator Award (2021), AAAS Fellow (2023), ICIS-BioLegend William E. Paul Award (2025), elected to National Academy of Sciences (2026).

highlights.CHI2012: Foundational review synthesizing how mTOR governs T-cell fate decisions.
highlights.ZEN2013: mTORC1 (via Raptor) required for Tregs to integrate metabolic signals and establish suppressive function.

Abraham RT.role: Co-discovered the mammalian target of rapamycin in 1995, giving it the name mTOR, and showed that it directly phosphorylates the translation repressor 4E-BP1 (PHAS-I)
Abraham RT.sub: Chief Scientific Officer, Engine Biosciences (since 2025) · Odyssey Therapeutics · Vividion Therapeutics · Pfizer Oncology Research · Burnham Institute · Duke University Medical Center · Mayo Clinic
story: At Mayo Clinic, isolated mTOR using a rapamycin-FKBP12 bait (SAB1995), one of several independent 1994–95 papers (alongside Schreiber's FRAP and Sabatini/Snyder's RAFT1) founding the field. In 1997 (BRU1997), showed mTOR directly phosphorylates PHAS-I (4E-BP1) — the paper behind nearly every mTOR→translation diagram.

Moved through Duke, Burnham Institute (TOR/ATM-ATR/T-cell signaling), Pfizer Oncology (San Diego), Vividion Therapeutics, now Engine Biosciences — over 30 years still working at the chemical-biology/cancer-drug-discovery interface.

highlights.SAB1995: Isolated mTOR via a rapamycin-FKBP12 affinity matrix, one of several independent founding papers.
highlights.BRU1997: Showed mTOR directly phosphorylates PHAS-I (4E-BP1), the mechanistic link to protein synthesis control.

Maier T.lab_name: Maier Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Maier T.role: Solved some of the first cryo-EM structures of human mTORC1 (with Nenad Ban's group) and mTORC2, including a high-resolution map of mTORC2
Maier T.sub: Full professor of Structural Biology, Biozentrum (2023) · associate professor, Biozentrum (2016) · assistant professor, Biozentrum (2011) · postdoc, ETH Zurich (Nenad Ban) · PhD, Freie Universität Berlin (Wolfram Saenger)
story: With Nenad Ban's group, produced one of the first cryo-EM structures of complete human mTORC1 (AYL2015, 5.9 Å), revealing its rigid dimeric assembly. Five years later, solved mTORC2 at 3.2 Å (SCA2020), pinpointing Rictor's C-terminal tail as the reason mTORC2 isn't directly blocked by rapamycin.
Trained under crystallographer Saenger, then structural biologist Nenad Ban. Continues combining cryo-EM, X-ray, and computation to map large regulatory complexes at atomic resolution.

highlights.AYL2015: One of the first cryo-EM structures of complete human mTORC1, revealing dimeric architecture and active-site access.
highlights.SCA2020: Cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 pinpoints Rictor's C-terminus as source of rapamycin insensitivity.

Ben-Sahra I.lab_name: Ben-Sahra Lab, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (Chicago, Illinois, USA)
Ben-Sahra I.role: Showed as a postdoc in Brendan Manning's lab that mTORC1 drives both pyrimidine and purine synthesis, through two different mechanisms. His Northwestern lab has extended this to bicarbonate import, SAM synthesis and ERK control of purine production
Ben-Sahra I.sub: Associate Professor, Northwestern Feinberg (since 2023) · postdoc, Harvard T.H. Chan School (Brendan D. Manning lab) · PhD, Université de Nice Sophia Antipolis (now Université Côte d'Azur), France (Frédéric Bost lab, 2010)
story: As Manning-lab postdoc, showed (BEN2013), in parallel with Michael Hall's lab, that mTORC1–S6K1 switches on de novo pyrimidine synthesis by phosphorylating CAD. Three years later (BEN2016), showed mTORC1 also drives purine synthesis via ATF4-dependent activation of the mitochondrial tetrahydrofolate cycle — completing the picture that mTORC1 controls both nucleotide families.
Trained in Nice, France before Harvard postdoc; now runs his own lab at Northwestern's Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center studying how growth signaling rewires metabolism in cancer and aging.

highlights.BEN2013: mTORC1–S6K1 switches on de novo pyrimidine synthesis by phosphorylating CAD.
highlights.BEN2016: mTORC1 drives purine synthesis via ATF4-dependent activation of the mitochondrial tetrahydrofolate cycle.

Jiaqiang Jiang.lab_name: Department of General Surgery & Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China)
Jiaqiang Jiang.role: Member of the Nanfang Hospital gastric-cancer surgery team that traced how a tumor-enriched gut bacterium rewires CD8+ T cells through an mTOR-linked checkpoint to blunt anti-PD-1 therapy.
Jiaqiang Jiang.sub: Department of General Surgery · Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor · Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University · Guangzhou, China
story: Jiaqiang Jiang works in the gastrointestinal-tumor surgery group at Nanfang Hospital (Southern Medical University, Guangzhou) led by Yanfeng Hu. In the study behind this entry, the team found that the bacterium Streptococcus anginosus is enriched in gastric tumors that fail to respond to PD-1 checkpoint blockade, and that it produces a metabolite, kynurenic acid, which pushes up integrin α2 (ITGA2) on CD8+ T cells. ITGA2 in turn dampens an mTOR-dependent signaling step, keeping cathepsin V high and interferon-γ/granzyme B output low — effectively disarming the cytotoxic T cells the immunotherapy needs to work. Blocking ITGA2 restored T-cell killing activity and resensitized tumors to PD-1 blockade.

This is Jiang's only study currently in the Atlas under this name. PubMed shows the same Jiang, with the identical Nanfang Hospital affiliation, as a co-author on at least two other 2026 papers from the same lab on gut-microbiota–immune crosstalk in gastrointestinal cancers, suggesting a working researcher embedded in this specific research line rather than a one-off contributor.

highlights.REN2026: Co-author on the Nanfang Hospital team that identified the Streptococcus anginosus–kynurenic acid–ITGA2–mTOR–cathepsin V axis driving PD-1 blockade resistance in gastric cancer.

Shuai Yu.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou Municipal Hospital), Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Shuai Yu.role: Neurology researcher who contributed to a study showing that the lipid kinase PIP4K2A protects the brain after ischaemic stroke by relieving a block on autophagy and boosting AKT/mTOR signalling
Shuai Yu.sub: Department of Neurology · The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University · Suzhou Municipal Hospital · Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University · Suzhou, Jiangsu, China
story: Shuai Yu is part of the clinical neurology research group at Suzhou Municipal Hospital that studies mechanisms of ischemic stroke. The study behind this entry found that PIP4K2A is elevated in stroke patients' blood and, in mouse models, acts as a protective factor: raising PIP4K2A reduced a stress complex (TRIB3-p62) that otherwise clogs up autophagy, restored autophagic flux, and was accompanied by stronger AKT/mTOR signaling — together limiting brain damage and improving recovery.

PubMed shows Yu as a recurring member of this Suzhou stroke-research team, also contributing to other 2025–2026 studies on intracerebral hemorrhage biomarkers and basilar-artery stroke thrombectomy outcomes from the same hospital.

highlights.MA2026: Contributed to the Suzhou Municipal Hospital team's work showing PIP4K2A reduces the TRIB3-p62 autophagy block and boosts AKT/mTOR signaling after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.

Shiting Yu.lab_name: Northeast Asia Research Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine (Changchun, China)
Shiting Yu.role: Natural-products researcher who contributed to a study showing that a Chinese yam (Dioscorea polystachya) extract counters male reproductive ageing through the mTOR–Beclin-1 autophagy axis
Shiting Yu.sub: Northeast Asia Research Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine · Changchun University of Chinese Medicine · Changchun, Jilin, China
story: Shiting Yu works in the Northeast Asia Research Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine at Changchun University of Chinese Medicine. In this study, a protein extract from Chinese yam improved testicular histology, sperm parameters, and testosterone in aged rats, and rescued viability and reduced senescence markers in D-galactose-induced senescent Leydig and Sertoli cells in vitro. The effect was linked to restored autophagy through the mTOR-Beclin-1 axis and was largely lost when mTOR was activated.
PubMed shows Yu as a repeat contributor to this institute's broader natural-products work, indicating an active role in the lab's ongoing TCM pharmacology program.

highlights.ZHANG2026B: Co-author on the study showing Chinese yam protein extract activates mTOR-Beclin-1-mediated autophagy to counter reproductive aging in Leydig and Sertoli cells.

Yukun Zhang.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Yukun Zhang.role: Senior author of a study showing that failing chaperone-mediated autophagy lets midnolin accumulate and degrade TSC2, overactivating mTORC1 and accelerating intervertebral disc degeneration
Yukun Zhang.sub: Department of Orthopedics · Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College · Huazhong University of Science and Technology · Wuhan, China
Yukun Zhang.credit: Portrait: Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
story: Yukun Zhang is a corresponding/senior author in the spine research group at Union Hospital, Wuhan. The team showed that in degenerating intervertebral discs, a quality-control pathway (chaperone-mediated autophagy) fails, letting the protein Midnolin (MIDN) pile up; accumulated MIDN then binds and destroys TSC2, the brake on mTORC1. With that brake gone, mTORC1 hyperactivates, pushing disc cells into senescence and breaking down the disc's extracellular matrix. Restoring autophagy, removing MIDN, or directly inhibiting mTORC1 with rapamycin each attenuated the damage.

PubMed lists Zhang as corresponding author on multiple other 2026 Union Hospital papers on disc-degeneration biomaterials and cell therapy, indicating an active role in this hospital's intervertebral-disc-degeneration research.

highlights.CHEN2026C: Senior/corresponding author on the Union Hospital study defining the impaired-CMA → MIDN accumulation → TSC2 degradation → mTORC1 hyperactivation axis in intervertebral disc degeneration.

Yiwen Zhang.lab_name: Northeast Asia Research Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine (Changchun, China)
Yiwen Zhang.role: Researcher at Changchun University of Chinese Medicine who contributed to a study showing that a Chinese yam extract counters male reproductive ageing through mTOR–Beclin-1 autophagy
Yiwen Zhang.sub: Northeast Asia Research Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine · Changchun University of Chinese Medicine · Changchun, Jilin, China
story: Yiwen Zhang is confirmed on PubMed as the first author of the study evaluating a Chinese yam protein extract in aged rats and senescent Leydig/Sertoli cell models. The extract improved testicular function and reduced senescence markers, tied to restoring autophagy through the mTOR-Beclin-1 pathway.
Public record of this specific name at this institute is limited beyond this paper, so this bio stays close to the study itself.

highlights.ZHANG2026B: First author of the Changchun University of Chinese Medicine study of Chinese yam protein extract's mTOR-Beclin-1-dependent protection against male reproductive aging.

Meijie Li.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Systems Biology, Geisel School of Medicine, Dartmouth College (Luikart / Hong labs) (Hanover, New Hampshire, USA)
Meijie Li.role: Dartmouth researcher, working with the Luikart and Hong labs, studying how PTEN controls the neuronal microtubule cytoskeleton through mTORC2 rather than mTORC1
Meijie Li.sub: Department of Molecular and Systems Biology · Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth College · Hanover, NH, USA
story: Meijie Li works at Dartmouth's Geisel School of Medicine with Bryan Luikart (now at the University of Alabama at Birmingham) and Jennifer Hong studying how the tumor-suppressor PTEN shapes neuronal growth. The study behind this entry showed that PTEN loss accelerates microtubule polymerization in peripheral sensory neurons specifically via mTORC2 — not mTORC1 — and only at the axon's growth cone, pointing to the growth-cone microtubule cytoskeleton as a potential target for nerve-regeneration therapies.
PubMed shows Li as a co-author on an earlier (2022) paper from the same group on PTEN and dendritic arborization via microtubule polymerization, indicating a multi-year role in this research line.

highlights.EVA2026: Co-author on the Dartmouth study showing that PTEN loss accelerates microtubule polymerization in peripheral sensory neuron growth cones through mTORC2, not mTORC1.

Mei Li.lab_name: Pediatrics Research Institute, Children's Hospital of Soochow University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Mei Li.role: Scientist at the Pediatrics Research Institute of Children's Hospital of Soochow University studying brain injury, who contributed to a study of how PIP4K2A protects the brain after stroke
Mei Li.sub: Pediatrics Research Institute · Soochow Key Laboratory of Prevention and Treatment of Child Brain Injury · Children's Hospital of Soochow University · Suzhou, Jiangsu, China
story: Mei Li is based at the Pediatrics Research Institute, Children's Hospital of Soochow University, in a group focused on mechanisms of hypoxic-ischemic and developmental brain injury. She is a co-author on the Suzhou team's work identifying PIP4K2A as a protective factor in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.

PubMed also credits Li as the corresponding author of a 2026 study of Trim47 protecting the neonatal blood-brain barrier, a 2025 study of FAM20C in hypoxic-ischemic brain damage from the same institute, and a 2026 paper with a dual Soochow/Massachusetts General Hospital affiliation — pointing to an active, pediatrics-focused neuroscience researcher with an international collaboration.

highlights.MA2026: Co-author from the Children's Hospital of Soochow University Pediatrics Research Institute on the PIP4K2A/TRIB3-p62/AKT-mTOR stroke-protection study.

Lei Zhang.lab_name: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (Yantai, China)
Lei Zhang.role: Contributed to a 2026 mouse study showing that the plant compound pungenin relieves androgenic alopecia through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway
Lei Zhang.sub: College of Life Sciences · Yantai University, China
story: Lei Zhang is part of a Yantai University team that tested pungenin — a phenolic glucoside from Picea wilsonii — on DHT-induced hair follicle injury in a mouse model of androgenetic alopecia. The group found pungenin protected follicle cells, accelerated hair regrowth, and was associated with transcriptional regulation of the PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR axis.
No independent lab page or prior publication trail was found beyond this study, so this bio stays close to the paper itself.

highlights.ZHAI2026: Contributed to the Yantai University team's mouse study identifying pungenin as a PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR-pathway modulator that restores hair growth in DHT-induced androgenic alopecia.

Ling Zhang.lab_name: School of Public Health, Hubei Province Key Laboratory of Occupational Hazard Identification and Control, Wuhan University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Ling Zhang.role: Contributed to a 2026 toxicology study linking early-life exposure to microplastics and the plasticiser DEHP to autism-relevant brain changes through impaired mTOR-regulated autophagy
Ling Zhang.sub: School of Public Health, Hubei Province Key Laboratory of Occupational Hazard Identification and Control · Wuhan University of Science and Technology, China
story: Ling Zhang is part of a collaboration (with a Central China Normal University toxicology group) on a 2026 paper exposing young mice to food-grade polypropylene microplastics and the plasticizer DEHP. The combined exposure produced autism-spectrum-disorder-relevant behavioral and synaptic changes, traced to activation of mTOR signaling and impaired autophagy — partially reversed by the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin.

highlights.YANG2026: Co-author on the finding that early-life polypropylene-microplastic and DEHP co-exposure drives ASD-relevant neurodevelopmental damage in mice through mTOR-pathway activation and autophagy impairment.

Qingsong Liu.lab_name: Qingsong Liu Lab, Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences (Hefei, China)
Qingsong Liu.role: Medicinal chemist in Nathanael Gray's lab who helped discover Torin1, an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, and later built an independent kinase-inhibitor drug-discovery program in China
Qingsong Liu.sub: PI, Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences – formerly Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School (Gray lab)
story: In 2009, Qingsong Liu was a medicinal chemist in Nathanael Gray's lab (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School) and co-authored the Thoreen et al. paper reporting Torin1 — one of the first highly potent, selective ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors. The result reshaped the field: rapamycin only partially suppresses mTORC1, whereas directly blocking the kinase's ATP site with Torin1 hits those 'rapamycin-resistant' functions too — motivating a whole generation of second-generation mTOR kinase inhibitors.

Liu went on to lead his own kinase-inhibitor medicinal chemistry program at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, developing the 'CHMFL' series of inhibitors against FLT3, BCR-ABL, EGFR, c-KIT, RIPK1 and other kinases for leukemia, GIST and inflammatory disease. The institutional trail (Harvard/Dana-Farber → Hefei CAS) and unbroken focus on ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor chemistry make this identification highly likely, though not formally confirmed in a single source.

highlights.THO2009: As a chemist in Nathanael Gray's lab, contributed to the discovery and characterization of Torin1, one of the first potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, establishing that direct mTOR kinase inhibition blocks rapamycin-resistant functions of mTORC1.

Qianqian Liu.lab_name: Department of Population Health Sciences, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Qianqian Liu.role: Biostatistician on one of the first randomised pilot trials of rapamycin's safety in older adults
Qianqian Liu.sub: Department of Population Health Sciences · UT Health San Antonio, USA
story: Qianqian Liu contributed biostatistical work to the 2018 Kraig et al. paper — one of the earliest placebo-controlled human pilot trials testing whether low-dose rapamycin (1 mg/day) is safe and tolerable in healthy older adults (70-95 years old), run out of UT Health San Antonio's Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies.

The trial found short-term rapamycin was generally well tolerated, with only mild hematologic changes and no worsening of glucose metabolism, cognition, or physical performance — a result that helped pave the way for the larger human longevity trials of mTOR inhibition that followed.

highlights.KRA2018: Contributed biostatistical work to the UT Health San Antonio pilot trial showing short-term low-dose rapamycin is safe and tolerable in healthy older adults, an early human proof-of-concept for mTOR-inhibition longevity research.

Jing Wang.lab_name: Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Jing Wang.role: Showed as first author that the CORVET/HOPS trafficking machinery is needed for T cells to sense amino acids and activate mTORC1
Jing Wang.sub: Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology, Shanghai Key Laboratory of Metabolic Remodeling and Health · Fudan University, China
story: Jing Wang is first author of a 2026 PNAS paper from Fudan University's Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology (corresponding authors Tong-Jin Zhao and Xingrong Du). The study identifies the CORVET/HOPS membrane-tethering complexes as upstream gatekeepers of T-cell amino acid supply: they drive macropinocytosis to pull in extracellular nutrients, which dampens the cell's stress response and switches on mTORC1 signaling needed for T cells to proliferate and fight infection.
Deleting core CORVET/HOPS subunits starved T cells of amino acids, triggered a pathological stress response, blunted mTORC1 activity, and crippled immune responses in mice.

highlights.WANG2026: First author showing that CORVET/HOPS tethering complexes are required for T cells to import amino acids and activate mTORC1, linking nutrient trafficking to immune-cell metabolic resilience.

Jie Wang.lab_name: Wang Jie Lab, Department of Chemistry, Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) (Shenzhen, China)
Jie Wang.role: Corresponding author of a 2026 JACS paper identifying PKM2 as a direct methionine-sensing protein that signals into mTORC1 via GATOR2.
Jie Wang.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis · SUSTech, China – PhD, Peking University (2020)
story: Jie Wang is an associate professor of chemistry at SUSTech, where he runs a lab on bioorthogonal chemistry, genetic code expansion, and enzyme engineering, after training with Aiwen Lei at Wuhan University and Peng Chen/Chu Wang at Peking University.

As corresponding author on a 2026 JACS paper, his team designed a 'Trojan' photoaffinity methionine probe to fish out proteins that directly sense methionine in living cells. They found PKM2 — better known as a glycolytic enzyme — moonlights as a methionine sensor, binding methionine through a newly discovered pocket and relaying that signal through GATOR2 to control mTORC1. This adds a direct methionine sensor to mTOR's nutrient-sensing machinery, alongside the previously discovered SAMTOR, which senses the methionine metabolite SAM rather than methionine itself.

highlights.SANG2026: Corresponding author showing PKM2 acts as a novel direct methionine sensor that signals through GATOR2 into mTORC1, complementing the known SAMTOR sensing pathway.

Jie Wang.credit: Portrait: Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Wang Jie Lab People page

Xiaoge Sun.lab_name: Department of Radiation Oncology, Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (Hohhot, China)
Xiaoge Sun.role: Senior author of a 2026 study showing that the recurrent PIK3CA-E545K mutation drives cervical cancer growth and invasion through AKT/mTOR signalling
Xiaoge Sun.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology · Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University, Hohhot, China
story: Xiaoge Sun is the corresponding author of a 2026 study that sequenced paired tumor/non-tumor tissue from 61 cervical cancer patients and found PIK3CA among the most frequently mutated genes. In cell and mouse xenograft models, the mutant boosted tumor cell proliferation and invasiveness while suppressing apoptosis, acting through sustained AKT/mTOR pathway activation — supporting PI3K/AKT/mTOR-axis inhibitors as a rational therapeutic strategy for this cervical cancer subgroup.

highlights.HUANG2026: Corresponding author on genomic and functional work showing the PIK3CA-E545K mutation drives cervical cancer growth and invasion through sustained AKT/mTOR pathway activation.

Xiaojie Sun.lab_name: School of Public Health, Hubei Province Key Laboratory of Occupational Hazard Identification and Control, Wuhan University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Xiaojie Sun.role: Contributed to a 2026 toxicology study linking early-life exposure to microplastics and the plasticiser DEHP to autism-relevant brain changes through impaired mTOR-regulated autophagy
Xiaojie Sun.sub: School of Public Health, Hubei Province Key Laboratory of Occupational Hazard Identification and Control · Wuhan University of Science and Technology, China
story: Xiaojie Sun shares Ling Zhang's affiliation at Wuhan University of Science and Technology's School of Public Health, and is a co-author on the same 2026 paper on early-life microplastic and phthalate exposure, which found the combination produces autism-spectrum-disorder-relevant changes in mice driven by mTOR pathway activation and impaired autophagy.

Siming Wang.lab_name: Northeast Asia Research Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine (Changchun, China)

highlights.ZHO2009: First author of the paper showing pharmacological mTORC1 inhibition (rapamycin) reverses anatomical, cellular, and behavioral abnormalities in neural Pten-knockout mice.

highlights.TAO2026: Co-author on the largemouth bass study showing impaired mTOR/SREBP1 lipogenesis redirects excess carbohydrate into hepatic glycogen.

highlights.YAO2026: Co-author on the spinal-cord-injury study linking Salvianolic Acid B's pro-angiogenic, motor-recovery benefit to AKT/mTOR/HIF-1α activation.

Sunghoon Kim.lab_name: Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center, College of Pharmacy, Yonsei University (Incheon, South Korea)
Sunghoon Kim.role: Senior author of the 2012 study proposing leucyl-tRNA synthetase as an intracellular leucine sensor for mTORC1, part of his broader work on the signalling roles of tRNA synthetases
Sunghoon Kim.sub: Biochemist · Yonsei University (since 2020; Seoul National University 2001–2020) – known for work on the "moonlighting" signaling roles of tRNA synthetases · Ho-Am Prize laureate
story: Sunghoon Kim is one of the most decorated biochemists in South Korea. He is the senior/corresponding author of Han JM et al., Cell 2012, which proposed an answer to a long-standing puzzle: how cells directly sense intracellular leucine levels to switch on mTORC1. His group showed that leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LRS) — an enzyme whose textbook job is attaching leucine to its tRNA for protein synthesis — moonlights as a leucine sensor, binding the Rag GTPase in a leucine-dependent manner and acting as a GAP toward RagD. The model remains debated: Sestrin2 (2015) is now the best-supported leucine sensor upstream of mTORC1.

That discovery sits inside a decades-long research program: PhD at Brown University (1991), postdoctoral work at MIT, and a career at Seoul National University (2001–2020) and, since 2020, Yonsei University, directing a sequence of national research centers on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases — most recently the Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center. His lab found that several components of the multi-tRNA synthetase complex, notably the associated proteins AIMP2 and AIMP3, act as tumor suppressors, part of a wider body of work by several groups showing that tRNA synthetases also act as signaling molecules in human disease. He has received Korea's Top Scientist and Technologist Award (2006), the Korean National Academy of Science Award (2012), and the Ho-Am Prize in Medicine (2015) — often described as Korea's answer to the Nobel Prize.

highlights.HAN2012: Senior/corresponding author proposing leucyl-tRNA synthetase as an intracellular leucine sensor that activates mTORC1, a model that competes with the Sestrin2 model and remains debated.

Seongbin Kim.lab_name: Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST & Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions, Institute for Basic Science (IBS) (Daejeon, South Korea)
Seongbin Kim.role: Contributed to a 2026 study showing that abnormal ERBB4 in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's pathology through mTOR signalling
Seongbin Kim.sub: Neuroscience researcher · KAIST & IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions, South Korea
story: Seongbin Kim is affiliated with KAIST's Department of Biological Sciences and the IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions. The 2026 Nature study, led by Won-Suk Chung's group, found that a specific population of excitatory neurons abnormally switches on the receptor ERBB4 early in Alzheimer's disease, and that this, acting through mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4, is necessary for reactive gliosis, synapse loss, amyloid deposition and cognitive decline in mouse models, and sufficient to reproduce these changes apart from amyloid plaques.

highlights.LEE2026: Co-author on the Nature study identifying excitatory-neuronal ERBB4, acting through mTOR signalling, as an early driver of Alzheimer's disease pathology.

highlights.LIANG2026: Co-author on the study showing LINP1 suppresses radiation-induced keratinocyte senescence by blocking the mTOR–p53 interaction.

story: Chen Zhang is a PhD candidate in Wen-Xing Ding's laboratory at the University of Kansas Medical Center, studying alcohol-related liver disease, fatty liver disease and liver cancer. As first author on the 2026 J Clin Invest paper, Zhang showed that knocking out TSC1 in mouse hepatocytes paradoxically drives TFEB (the lysosomal/autophagy master regulator) into the nucleus despite hyperactive mTORC1 — a 'non-canonical' activation that pushes hepatocytes toward a more plastic, biliary-like state and ultimately high-grade hepatocellular carcinoma.

highlights.ZHANG2026: First author; led the Tsc1-knockout mouse studies showing non-canonical mTORC1-TFEB activation drives hepatocyte plasticity and high-grade malignancy in HCC.

Long He.lab_name: Blenis Lab, Dept. of Pharmacology & Meyer Cancer Center, Weill Cornell Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Long He.role: Research faculty member in John Blenis's lab at Weill Cornell who studies how mTORC1 controls cell metabolism, and first author of the lab's 2025 review of mTORC1 as a conductor of metabolism and growth
Long He.sub: Assistant Professor of Research in Pharmacology · Weill Cornell Medicine (Blenis Lab) – PhD, Chungnam National Univ., 2011
story: Long He has been a long-standing member of John Blenis's laboratory — one of the labs that, alongside David Sabatini's, defined much of modern mTOR signaling — first at Harvard and since its move to Weill Cornell Medicine, where he now holds the title Assistant Professor of Research in Pharmacology.

His publication record traces the Blenis lab's core scientific arc on how mTORC1 rewires metabolism: lipogenic splicing via S6K1-SRPK2 (2017), Foxk1-mediated metabolic reprogramming (2018), m6A-dependent mRNA degradation (2021), FAM120A coupling SREBP transcription to lipogenic splicing (2023), and direct sensing of dietary linoleic acid via FABP5-mTORC1 signaling (2025).

That work culminated in the paper flagged here: 'mTORC1, the maestro of cell metabolism and growth' (Genes & Development, 2025), where he is listed first and shares the corresponding-author line with Blenis.

highlights.HE2025: First and co-corresponding author (with John Blenis) of this comprehensive review of mTORC1's role in metabolic rewiring, disease, and drug targeting.

Linling He.role: Researcher in the Fudan team studying amino-acid sensing and stress resilience in T cells
Linling He.sub: Researcher · Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology, Fudan University, Shanghai
story: Linling He is affiliated with Fudan University's Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology, part of the team led by Xingrong Du and Tong-Jin Zhao.
