highlights.TAO2026: Co-author on the Shanghai Ocean University study showing impaired insulin/mTOR/SREBP1 signaling underlies hepatic glycogen overload in largemouth bass fed high-carbohydrate diets.

Ruoning Wang.lab_name: Center for Childhood Cancer, Abigail Wexner Research Institute, Nationwide Children's Hospital & Dept. of Pediatrics, Ohio State University College of Medicine (Columbus, Ohio, USA)
Ruoning Wang.role: Showed as first author, in Douglas Green's lab, that the transcription factor Myc drives the metabolic switch of activated T cells, and now leads an immunometabolism lab
Ruoning Wang.sub: Principal Investigator · Nationwide Children's Hospital – Professor of Pediatrics, Ohio State University
story: As a researcher in Douglas Green's laboratory at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Ruoning Wang first-authored the 2011 Immunity paper confirmed here, showing that of the two top candidate transcription factors induced by T-cell activation, only Myc was required for the glycolytic and glutaminolytic burst that fuels T-cell proliferation. This became one of the founding papers of the immunometabolism field, establishing Myc (alongside mTOR) as a master regulator of the metabolic switch accompanying lymphocyte activation.

He has since become an independent principal investigator, leading his own lab in the Center for Childhood Cancer at Nationwide Children's Hospital while holding a professorship in Pediatrics at Ohio State University, extending this trajectory into metabolic checkpoints, immune-cell metabolism, and pediatric cancer.

highlights.WAN2011: First author; identified Myc as the transcription factor required for the glycolytic/glutaminolytic metabolic reprogramming of activated T cells, a foundational immunometabolism finding.

Yanhui Xu.lab_name: Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center & Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Shanghai Medical College of Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Yanhui Xu.role: Structural biologist whose Fudan lab solved a cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 in 2018, showing how rictor and mSin1 block rapamycin's access to mTOR
Yanhui Xu.sub: Professor & Principal Investigator · Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center – structural biology of mTOR signaling and transcription
story: Yanhui Xu is a professor at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and one of China's most prominent structural biologists, using cryo-EM and biochemistry to determine how large multi-protein machines assemble and function.

On mTOR specifically, his lab, with Hong-Wei Wang's group at Tsinghua, reported a 4.4 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1 in 2016 (the first cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1 came from the Basel/Zurich groups of Michael Hall, Nenad Ban and Timm Maier) and then, in the 2018 Cell Research paper verified here, one of the first two cryo-EM structures of human mTORC2, published in parallel with the Basel/Zurich groups — revealing a hollow, two-fold-symmetric dimer in which Rictor and mSin1 sterically block FKBP12-rapamycin from binding mTOR, explaining mTORC2's relative rapamycin insensitivity compared with mTORC1.

His earlier work solved structures underlying DNA methylation, and since 2020 his group has published four papers in Science resolving the complete transcription pre-initiation complex — work named one of 'China's Top 10 Advances in Life Sciences' for 2021, and for which he received the 2021 Xplorer Prize from the Tencent Foundation.

highlights.CHE2018: Co-corresponding author; his team determined one of the first two cryo-EM structures of human mTORC2 (in parallel with Stuttfeld et al., eLife 2018), revealing the Rictor/mSin1 architecture that explains its rapamycin insensitivity relative to mTORC1.

Yulang Xu.lab_name: Division of Oncology, Department of Pediatric Surgery & Rare Diseases Center, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Yulang Xu.role: Paediatric surgeon-researcher who led a multicentre study showing that head-and-neck kaposiform hemangioendothelioma responds especially well to the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus
Yulang Xu.sub: Pediatric surgeon-researcher · West China Hospital, Sichuan University – multicenter sirolimus/KHE cohort study
story: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare, locally aggressive vascular tumor of infancy. Sirolimus, which blocks mTOR, is the standard drug for KHE, but doctors did not know whether tumor location changes how well it responds.

Xu led a five-center Chinese cohort of 71 children and found that head-and-neck KHE responded dramatically better to sirolimus alone than KHE elsewhere — anatomical location turned out to be the single strongest independent predictor of treatment response, which could let doctors tailor treatment by tumor site.

highlights.XU2026: First author; led a multicenter cohort study showing head-and-neck KHE tumors respond far better to sirolimus monotherapy than KHE elsewhere, identifying anatomical location as an independent predictor of mTOR-inhibitor treatment response.

Eunjung Kim.lab_name: Guan Laboratory, Department of Pharmacology & Moores Cancer Center, University of California San Diego (circa 2007–2010) (La Jolla, California, USA)
Eunjung Kim.role: Showed as first author, in Kun-Liang Guan's lab, that the Rag GTPases relay amino-acid availability to TORC1, in parallel with the Sabatini lab's discovery
Eunjung Kim.sub: Postdoctoral researcher, Kun-Liang Guan lab, UCSD (circa 2007–2010) · first author, landmark 2008 Rag GTPase discovery · later career not reliably traceable
story: Before 2008, scientists knew amino acids switch on mTORC1 but not how that signal physically reached the enzyme. In 2008, two labs independently reported the answer: Yasemin Sancak in David Sabatini's lab (Science) and Eunjung Kim in Kun-Liang Guan's lab (Nature Cell Biology) both showed that the Rag GTPases are needed for amino acids to switch on mTORC1. The Sabatini paper also showed that the Rags bind raptor and move mTORC1 to the compartment that holds its activator Rheb; that this is the lysosome surface was established by the same lab in 2010. Kim was first author on the Guan lab's paper, built largely on Drosophila genetics and mammalian cell experiments — now textbook mTOR biology.

Kim appears as a co-author on two other Guan-lab papers from the same period, indicating she continued in the lab for at least a couple more years. Her subsequent career could not be reliably traced — 'Eunjung Kim' is a very common Korean name and no confidently-matched later publication record was found.

highlights.KIM2008: First author on the 2008 discovery that Rag GTPases activate TORC1 in response to amino acids — one of two simultaneous, independent 2008 papers that established the amino-acid-sensing arm of the mTOR pathway.

Eunjoon Kim.lab_name: Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions, Institute for Basic Science & Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST (Daejeon, South Korea)
Eunjoon Kim.role: Neuroscientist who directs the IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions and studies synaptic scaffold proteins linked to autism; he contributed to work linking neuronal ERBB4 and mTOR signalling to Alzheimer's pathology
Eunjoon Kim.sub: Professor, KAIST Department of Biological Sciences · Director, IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions · over 200 papers · Asan Award in Medicine (2018), POSCO TJ Park Prize (2013)
story: Eunjoon Kim built his career mapping the molecular architecture of the synapse — in particular the SHANK family of postsynaptic scaffold proteins, whose mutations are among the best-established genetic causes of autism spectrum disorder. He now directs the IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions at KAIST, with over 200 papers published.

In this 2026 Nature paper from Won-Suk Chung's group (also at KAIST/IBS), Kim is a co-author on work showing that aberrant ERBB4 expression in excitatory neurons drives synapse loss, amyloid deposition, and cognitive decline via mTOR signaling — connecting his long-standing expertise in synaptic biology to the molecular front lines of neurodegeneration.

highlights.LEE2026: Co-author (director, IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions; KAIST) on a 2026 Nature study showing aberrant ERBB4 expression in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like synapse loss and pathology via mTOR signaling.

Shiwen Chen.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology & Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Shiwen Chen.role: Aquaculture physiologist studying why the largemouth bass, a carnivorous fish, tolerates dietary carbohydrate so poorly
Shiwen Chen.sub: Aquaculture nutrition researcher · Shanghai Ocean University
story: Chen and colleagues compared largemouth bass with tilapia on graded-carbohydrate diets and traced bass's poor carbohydrate tolerance to a blunted insulin → AKT1 → mTOR → SREBP1 signaling axis. Using gene knockdown in bass liver cells, the team showed the chain of command directly: silencing akt1 or s6k1 blocked SREBP1 activation, silencing tsc2 restored mTOR signaling, and blocking mTOR with rapamycin reproduced the glycogen-overload phenotype.

highlights.TAO2026: Second author on a comparative fish physiology study showing largemouth bass have a blunted insulin/AKT1/mTOR/SREBP1 axis that diverts excess dietary carbohydrate into liver glycogen rather than fat.

Sheng Chen.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Sheng Chen.role: Orthopaedic researcher who contributed to a study showing that the plant compound corilagin protects joint cartilage by calming inflammation and restoring autophagy
Sheng Chen.sub: Orthopedic surgeon-researcher · Tongji Hospital, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan
story: In inflamed mouse chondrocytes and a surgical osteoarthritis model, the plant compound corilagin reduced cartilage-degrading enzymes, restored markers of healthy cartilage, and dialed down both NF-κB signaling and overactive PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling — which let autophagy resume. Blocking autophagy chemically partly undid corilagin's benefit, confirming autophagy restoration as part of the mechanism.

highlights.ZHOU2026B: Co-author on a preclinical study showing the plant compound corilagin protects cartilage in an osteoarthritis model by blocking NF-κB inflammatory signaling and PI3K/AKT/mTOR overactivation, restoring chondrocytes' protective autophagy.

Yunwei Wang.lab_name: Department of Burn Plastic and Wound Repair Surgery, The Second Hospital of Lanzhou University (Lanzhou, China)
Yunwei Wang.role: Burn and wound-repair researcher who contributed to a study testing the plant flavonoid dihydromyricetin as an anti-scarring treatment
Yunwei Wang.sub: Burn & wound-repair surgery researcher · The Second Hospital of Lanzhou University
story: Wang and colleagues tested dihydromyricetin (a flavonoid found in vine tea) on hypertrophic scars. In scar-derived fibroblasts, it lowered fibrosis markers alongside reduced PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activity, and in a rabbit-ear hypertrophic scar model, it visibly improved scar appearance and reduced collagen buildup.

highlights.CAO2026B: Co-author on a study combining network pharmacology with lab experiments to show dihydromyricetin reduces fibrosis markers in hypertrophic scar tissue alongside decreased PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activity, replicated in a rabbit-ear scar model.

Yifei Wang.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Pesticide & Chemical Biology (Ministry of Education) & Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, Central China Normal University (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Yifei Wang.role: Environmental toxicologist who contributed to a study of how early-life exposure to food-contact microplastics and a common plasticiser disrupts brain development through mTOR signalling
Yifei Wang.sub: Environmental toxicology researcher · Central China Normal University, Wuhan
story: Exposed young mice showed autism-relevant behavioral changes alongside neuronal damage in the prefrontal cortex and reduced expression of two autism-risk genes. Proteomic screening pointed to the mTOR pathway as the central mechanism: exposure over-activated mTOR signaling, impairing autophagy and disrupting synapse-plasticity genes. Treating mice with rapamycin restored autophagy and ameliorated the behavioral changes.

highlights.YANG2026: Co-author on a toxicology study in young mice showing combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP produces autism-relevant behavioral changes via mTOR pathway overactivation and impaired autophagy — ameliorated by the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin.

Joy Zhao.lab_name: Cregan Laboratory, Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario (London, Ontario, Canada)
Joy Zhao.role: Researcher in Sean Cregan's lab studying how chronic cell-stress signalling through ATF4 suppresses mTOR and kills dopamine neurons in Parkinson's disease models
Joy Zhao.sub: Research staff/trainee, Cregan lab · Robarts Research Institute, Western University, London, Canada
story: Working in Parkinson's disease models, the Cregan lab found that sustained activity of the stress-response transcription factor ATF4 turns on a set of genes whose combined effect is to chronically suppress both mTORC1 and mTORC2. That suppression helps activate a pro-death protein, pushing dopamine-producing neurons toward death — identifying a maladaptive 'ATF4-mTOR' axis as a potential new drug target for slowing neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: Co-author on a mechanistic study identifying a maladaptive ATF4-mTOR signaling axis — chronic integrated-stress-response activation suppresses both mTORC1 and mTORC2, triggering dopaminergic neuron death in Parkinson's disease models.

Jiaqi Zhao.lab_name: Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis & State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) (Shenzhen, China)
Jiaqi Zhao.role: Co-author; chemical biologist who helped build a chemical probe revealing a glycolytic enzyme's secret second job as a methionine sensor for mTORC1.
Jiaqi Zhao.sub: Chemical biology researcher · Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Shenzhen
story: To find the cell's methionine sensor directly, Zhao and colleagues built a 'Trojan horse' chemical probe: a photoaffinity version of methionine that tags whatever protein grabs onto it when hit with light. That fishing expedition landed on PKM2 — an enzyme best known for its day job in glucose metabolism — which the team showed binds methionine through a newly identified pocket and relays that signal through GATOR2 to control mTORC1.

highlights.SANG2026: Co-author on a chemical-biology study using a photoaffinity methionine probe to identify PKM2 as a direct methionine-sensing protein that signals through the GATOR2 complex to regulate mTORC1.

Zhang Zhihong (Shanxi Medical University.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
Zhang Zhihong (Shanxi Medical University.role: Co-corresponding author of a study showing that the lncRNA LINP1 protects irradiated skin cells from radiation-induced senescence through the mTOR–p53 axis
Zhang Zhihong (Shanxi Medical University.sub: Corresponding author · Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health · Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, China
story: Zhang Zhihong is a co-corresponding author (with Liang Zhou of Southern Medical University) of the 2026 Mol Cell Biochem paper identifying the lncRNA LINP1 as a radioprotective factor in skin — it binds the FAT domain of mTOR and blocks its interaction with p53, holding off radiation-induced senescence in keratinocytes, validated in human skin explants.

Affiliated with the MOE Key Laboratory of Coal Environmental Pathogenicity and Prevention and the Center for Ecological Public Health Security of Yellow River Basin — consistent with a senior environmental-health/toxicology PI. Note: shares an identical name with a different co-author at Beihua University (see separate entry) — the two are distinct people confirmed by different institutions, fields, and non-overlapping co-author lists.

highlights.LIANG2026: Co-corresponding author on the study showing LINP1 suppresses radiation-induced keratinocyte senescence by blocking the mTOR–p53 interaction.

Zhang Zhihong (Beihua University).lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University (Jilin, China)
Zhang Zhihong (Beihua University).role: Pharmacology researcher who contributed to a study showing that forsythoside A eases hypertensive kidney damage by promoting mitophagy and blocking ferroptosis via the ASCL1–CCNB1/mTOR pathway
Zhang Zhihong (Beihua University).sub: Pharmacology researcher · College of Pharmacy · Beihua University, Jilin, China
story: Zhang Zhihong is part of a recurring pharmacology research group at Beihua University's College of Pharmacy. In this 2026 J Ethnopharmacol study, the group showed that Forsythoside A — a compound from Forsythia suspensa — protects the kidney in hypertension models by promoting mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria) and blocking ferroptosis (iron-dependent cell death) through the ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR pathway.

The same group, with overlapping co-authors, published a related 2025 paper on Schisanhenol inhibiting hepatocellular carcinoma cell proliferation with the identical affiliation for this Zhang Zhihong, confirming a recurring, locatable member of this specific lab — distinct from the Shanxi Medical University researcher of the same name, with no institutional or co-author overlap between the two.

highlights.CUI2026: Co-author on the study showing Forsythoside A promotes mitophagy and inhibits ferroptosis via the ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR pathway in hypertensive nephropathy.

Korolchuk VI.lab_name: Korolchuk Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Korolchuk VI.role: Showed that where lysosomes sit inside the cell tunes mTORC1 activity to nutrient supply. His Newcastle lab found that senescent cells can no longer switch mTORC1 off when nutrients or growth factors are withdrawn, and studies how autophagy and mitophagy decline with age
Korolchuk VI.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (since 2024) · Reader, Newcastle University (2017–2024) · Lecturer, Institute of Ageing and Health, Newcastle University (2011–2017) · postdoc, University of Cambridge (2003–2011, David Rubinsztein lab) · postdoc, University of Bristol (2000–2003) · PhD in Biochemistry, Institute of Biochemistry, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Kyiv (2000)
story: In 2011, working in David Rubinsztein's lab in Cambridge, Korolchuk showed that mTORC1 activity depends on a variable that had received little attention: where the lysosome physically sits in the cell. With nutrients available, lysosomes move out towards the cell periphery, close to the plasma-membrane signalling modules, and mTORC1 is active there. Starvation changes intracellular pH and pulls them into a cluster around the nucleus, mTORC1 output falls, and autophagy is released. The same positioning also sets how fast autophagosomes fuse with lysosomes — so one variable governs both the start and the finish of autophagic flux.

Since starting his own group at Newcastle in 2011, he has worked the other end of the same problem: what mTORC1 does in cells that have stopped dividing. His lab showed that in senescent human cells mTORC1 is constitutively active and deaf to the removal of serum or amino acids, and that the fault lies upstream — a depolarised plasma membrane, defective primary cilia, and an internal amino acid pool kept topped up by autophagy. Correct those inputs and the cells die, which makes persistent mTORC1 signalling a survival dependency of senescent cells rather than a side effect of senescence.

More recently the lab has tied rapamycin's effect on cellular ageing to mitochondrial housekeeping: healthy primary human cells run a high level of basal mitophagy that shuts down in senescence, and reactivating it turned out to be necessary for the anti-senescence effect of both rapamycin and NAD precursors. Alongside the research, Korolchuk is the human selector behind Autophagy and mTOR (bims-auttor), the weekly curated literature report on biomed.news that has been running since February 2019 — the same slice of the literature this Atlas curates.

highlights.KOR2011: First author: showed lysosomal positioning coordinates mTORC1 signalling with autophagic flux, adding a spatial axis to nutrient sensing.
highlights.CAR2017: Senior author: explained why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells, and that they depend on it to survive.
highlights.KEL2024: Senior author: reactivation of basal mitophagy is required for the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin and NAD precursors.
highlights.COR2018: Co-author: in nfkb1 mice rapamycin improved healthspan and lowered senescence markers without extending lifespan or reducing inflammaging.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author on the Cell study showing G3BP1/2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and thereby suppress mTORC1.

Kamada Y.lab_name: National Institute for Basic Biology, Okazaki (Okazaki, Japan)
Kamada Y.role: Showed as first author that TOR keeps autophagy switched off in yeast by controlling the Atg1 (Apg1) kinase complex, and has studied TOR's control of autophagy ever since
Kamada Y.sub: Assistant Professor, National Institute for Basic Biology, National Institutes of Natural Sciences, Okazaki, Japan · ORCID 0000-0001-7395-660X
story: In 2000, in Yoshinori Ohsumi's group, Kamada asked a question that sounds simple and was not: how does TOR actually stop a cell from digesting itself? The answer turned out to be a phosphorylation switch one step upstream of the autophagy machinery. Starving the cells, or treating them with rapamycin, raised the kinase activity of Apg1 (now Atg1, the yeast counterpart of mammalian ULK1). TOR was keeping Apg13 hyperphosphorylated, and phosphorylated Apg13 binds Apg1 poorly. Remove TOR signalling and Apg13 loses its phosphates, binds Apg1, and autophagy starts.

The same paper drew a line that is easy to miss: the Apg1–Apg13 association is needed for autophagy but not for the Cvt pathway, a related vesicle route that uses many of the same proteins during normal growth. That made the Apg1 complex a switch between two transport systems rather than a simple on/off for one, which is why the finding survived the move from yeast to mammals.

His group at NIBB still works on TORC1 in budding yeast, and the NIBB page lists the same three threads: how amino acids regulate TORC1, how TORC1 controls autophagy through Atg13 phosphorylation, and how TORC1 acts on eIF4E-binding proteins. The mammalian version of his 2000 result (ULK1–ATG13–FIP200) was published nine years later.

highlights.KAM2000: First author: TOR represses autophagy by keeping Apg13 hyperphosphorylated, so it cannot bind and activate the Apg1 kinase.

Kamada Y.credit: Portrait: National Institute for Basic Biology

Ohsumi Y.lab_name: Cell Biology Center, Institute of Integrated Research, Institute of Science Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Ohsumi Y.role: Found the genes that make autophagy work, and with them the link from TOR to the autophagy machinery
Ohsumi Y.sub: Honorary Professor, Cell Biology Center, Institute of Integrated Research, Institute of Science Tokyo · Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2016, “for his discoveries of mechanisms for autophagy” · PhD, University of Tokyo (1974) · postdoctoral research, Rockefeller University · born 1945
story: Autophagy had been described in the 1960s and then largely left alone, because nobody could see the genes behind it. Ohsumi's laboratory found them in budding yeast in the 1990s by a deliberately low-technology route: block the vacuolar proteases so that the delivered material piles up instead of being degraded, starve the cells, and look down a microscope for mutants in which nothing piles up. That screen produced the Atg genes and turned autophagy from a phenomenon into a pathway that could be taken apart.

KAM2000 is the point where that work meets this Atlas. Ohsumi is the senior author of the paper showing that TOR holds autophagy shut through Apg13 phosphorylation, and it supplied the mechanism for the TOR control of autophagy that his laboratory had first reported in 1998 (Noda and Ohsumi): the connection the Atlas draws between nutrient sensing and self-digestion starts with this yeast work, and was carried into mammalian cells afterwards.

He received the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discoveries of mechanisms for autophagy. He has been consistent in public about what the prize does and does not mean for medicine, and the Atlas treats the distinction the same way: the machinery is understood far better than its effect on any human outcome.

highlights.KAM2000: Senior author: TOR controls autophagy through the Apg1/Apg13 kinase complex in yeast, a mechanism for the TOR control of autophagy his laboratory had reported in 1998.

Byfield MP.lab_name: Department of Molecular Pharmacology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (affiliation on BYF2005) (Bronx, New York, USA)
Byfield MP.role: Showed as first author that the lipid kinase hVps34 is regulated by nutrients and is needed for amino acids to activate S6 kinase through mTOR, in parallel with a study from George Thomas's group
Byfield MP.sub: Professor of Biology, Seminole State College of Florida · postdoc, Burnett School of Biomedical Sciences, University of Central Florida · PhD in Molecular Pharmacology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine
story: BYF2005 does something unusual for its year: it separates two inputs that were being treated as one. Insulin reaches S6K1 through class I PI3K and Akt. Byfield showed that the class III PI 3-kinase hVps34 also sits upstream of S6K1, is required for the phosphorylation of both S6K1 and 4E-BP1, and yet is not part of the insulin arm at all — knocking it down leaves Akt and TSC2 phosphorylation untouched.

What makes hVps34 a candidate for the nutrient arm is how it behaves: it is switched off by amino acid or glucose starvation, and by activating AMPK. That is the profile of something reporting on supply rather than on hormones. The paper is careful about the limit of this — the sensor itself is not identified, and the evidence is knockdown, overexpression and antibody microinjection in cell lines.

After her PhD at Einstein she did a neuroscience postdoc at the University of Central Florida and then moved into teaching, as a professor of biology at Seminole State College of Florida, where she also founded the Phenomenal STEM(ist) outreach initiative.

highlights.BYF2005: First author: hVps34 is inhibited by amino acid and glucose starvation and is required for S6K1 activation, outside the insulin/class I PI3K route.

Byfield MP.credit: Portrait: Seminole State College of Florida

Backer JM.lab_name: Backer Lab, Department of Molecular Pharmacology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Bronx, New York, USA)
Backer JM.role: Showed that the class III PI 3-kinase hVps34, best known for its role in autophagy, is regulated by nutrients and is needed for amino acids to activate S6 kinase through mTOR, in parallel with George Thomas's group
Backer JM.sub: Professor of Molecular Pharmacology and of Biochemistry · Chair, Department of Molecular Pharmacology · William S. Lasdon Chair in Pharmacology · Associate Director of Shared Resources, Montefiore Einstein Comprehensive Cancer Center · Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY
story: Backer's laboratory works on phosphoinositide kinases — the enzymes that mark membranes with lipid tags and thereby decide which proteins get recruited where. Most of the pathway's attention goes to class I PI3K, the one insulin switches on. His senior-authored contribution to this Atlas is about the other one: hVps34, the class III enzyme that supplies most of the cell's PI(3)P and is best known for building the autophagosome. Class II PI3Ks make PI(3)P as well, at other membranes, so hVps34 is the main source rather than the only one.

BYF2005 put hVps34 upstream of mTORC1 and showed it responds to amino acid and glucose supply rather than to insulin. Published within weeks of a paper from George Thomas's group reaching the same conclusion by a different route (NOB2005), it opened a second account of how amino acids reach mTORC1 — one that has never been fully reconciled with the Rag/Ragulator story that later dominated the field. The Atlas keeps both, because the corpus contains both.

The rest of the laboratory's work is on how altered PI3K regulation drives cancer, with emphasis on breast cancer invasion and metastasis, on macropinocytosis, and on S100A4 signalling in macrophages.

highlights.BYF2005: Senior author: hVps34 is a nutrient-regulated lipid kinase required for S6K1 activation, distinct from the insulin input.

Backer JM.credit: Portrait: Albert Einstein College of Medicine

Nobukuni T.lab_name: Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization, Tohoku University (Sendai, Japan)
Nobukuni T.role: Showed as first author that amino acids activate mTOR through the lipid kinase hVps34, by a route separate from insulin signalling through TSC, in parallel with a study from Jonathan Backer's laboratory
Nobukuni T.sub: Associate Professor, Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization, Tohoku University · Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel (affiliation on NOB2005, 2005)
story: NOB2005 is written as an argument about evolution as much as about signalling. Its claim is that the amino-acid-driven TOR pathway came first, and that in animals the insulin/class I PI3K pathway was grafted onto it — so the two inputs should not be expected to run through the same machinery. Working in George Thomas's group at the FMI in Basel, Nobukuni showed that the amino acid signal to mTOR/raptor goes through class 3 PI3K (hVps34) rather than through the components of the insulin route.

The result matters for how the Atlas reads its own amino-acid branch. The Rag/Ragulator account that came later describes a different mechanism for the same input, and neither account has displaced the other; the corpus now carries both, with the disagreement stated rather than smoothed over.
His publication record after roughly 2019 is in population-scale health research at the Tohoku Medical Megabank rather than in mTOR signalling.

highlights.NOB2005: First author: amino acids signal to mTOR/raptor through class 3 PI3K, separately from the insulin/class 1 PI3K route.
highlights.GUL2008: Co-author: amino acids raise intracellular calcium, which acts through calmodulin and hVps34 to activate mTORC1 (cells).

Nobukuni T.credit: Portrait: Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization, Tohoku University

Hansen M.lab_name: Hansen Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Hansen M.role: Showed in worms, alongside a 2007 report from Beth Levine's laboratory, that autophagy is required for dietary restriction to extend lifespan
Hansen M.sub: Chief Scientific Officer and Professor, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (since 2021) · own laboratory, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, La Jolla (from 2007) · postdoctoral research with Cynthia Kenyon, University of California San Francisco (from 2001)
story: By 2008 two things were established separately: dietary restriction extends lifespan partly by lowering TOR, and lowering TOR releases autophagy. Whether the second explained the first had only begun to be tested: in 2007 Jia and Levine reported that autophagy genes are needed for the long life of eat-2 dietary-restriction mutants. Hansen tested it directly in C. elegans by knocking down the genes autophagy needs, and found that both dietary restriction and TOR inhibition stopped extending lifespan when autophagy was blocked.

The same paper is unusually careful about the opposite claim. Long-lived daf-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutants need both autophagy and the transcription factor DAF-16/FOXO, yet autophagy still runs in animals lacking DAF-16 — and those animals are not long-lived. So autophagy is necessary and not sufficient: it supplies the raw material, and something else has to decide what the cell builds from it.

Her laboratory at the Buck works on the same question at a finer grain: how autophagy is regulated in specific tissues, how it changes with age, and what the standard readouts do and do not measure. She has been Chief Scientific Officer there since 2021.

highlights.HAN2008: First author: blocking autophagy genes abolishes the lifespan extension produced by dietary restriction and by TOR inhibition, but autophagy alone is not sufficient.
highlights.HAN2007: First author: lowering protein synthesis in C. elegans, by knocking down ribosomal proteins, the S6 kinase rsks-1 or translation-initiation factors, extended lifespan and raised heat-stress resistance, much as TOR inhibition does.

Hansen M.credit: Portrait: Buck Institute for Research on Aging

Kenyon C.lab_name: Calico Life Sciences (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Kenyon C.role: Showed in 1993 that a single-gene change doubles the lifespan of the worm C. elegans, which opened the study of nutrient-sensing pathways as ageing pathways
Kenyon C.sub: Vice President, Aging Research, Calico (since 2014) · Herb Boyer Distinguished Professor and American Cancer Society Professor, University of California San Francisco (faculty from 1986) · PhD, Massachusetts Institute of Technology · postdoctoral research with Sydney Brenner, Cambridge · member of the US National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine
story: Before 1993 ageing was widely treated as accumulated wear; the age-1 mutant described by Friedman and Johnson in 1988 was an early sign that a single gene could change it. Kenyon's discovery that a mutation in daf-2 doubles the lifespan of healthy, fertile C. elegans — and that the effect requires DAF-16 — reframed it as a regulated process. Every nutrient-sensing arm in this Atlas inherits that reframing, including the TOR arm.

She is senior author of HAN2008 here, the paper from her UCSF laboratory that tied autophagy to the lifespan effect of dietary restriction and TOR inhibition. It is a good example of her laboratory's habit of asking which steps are actually required rather than which correlate.
Since 2014 she has led ageing research at Calico. The Atlas cites her for the worm genetics, not for any human claim.

highlights.HAN2008: Senior author: autophagy genes are required for dietary restriction and TOR inhibition to extend lifespan in C. elegans.
highlights.HAN2007: Senior author: reducing translation extended lifespan in C. elegans, and the results linked TOR, but not sir-2.1, to the lifespan effect of dietary restriction.

Eisenberg T.lab_name: Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (Graz, Austria)
Eisenberg T.role: Showed as first author that the dietary polyamine spermidine extends lifespan by inducing autophagy, and later that it protects the heart in an autophagy-dependent way
Eisenberg T.sub: Associate Professor and group leader, Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (group leader since 2016) · venia docendi in Molecular Biology (2020) · APART project leader, Austrian Academy of Sciences (2013–2016) · postdoctoral researcher, University of Graz (2008–2013) · PhD, University of Graz (2004–2008) · biochemistry studies, University of Tübingen (1997–2004)
story: EIS2009 is the opening of a branch the Atlas had been missing: a way to induce autophagy through a route other than mTOR kinase signalling (EIS2009 itself did not measure mTOR). Spermidine is a natural polyamine whose concentration falls with human age. Feeding it extended lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells, and the effect depended on autophagy. The mechanism runs through inhibition of histone acetyltransferases and the transcriptional upregulation of autophagy genes — chromatin, not kinase signalling.

EIS2016 is the mammalian follow-up and the reason the branch matters for human health claims. Oral spermidine extended mouse lifespan, reduced cardiac hypertrophy and preserved diastolic function in old mice. The load-bearing control is the negative one: in mice whose cardiomyocytes lack Atg5, the protection disappears. That makes autophagy necessary for the effect rather than a correlate of it.

The same paper reports that high dietary spermidine in a human cohort correlates with lower blood pressure and fewer cardiovascular events. That part is a food questionnaire, so it is observational and does not carry the causal weight the mouse data carry — a distinction worth keeping when this work is quoted.

highlights.EIS2009: First author: spermidine induces autophagy by inhibiting histone acetyltransferases and extends lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells.
highlights.EIS2016: First author: oral spermidine extends mouse lifespan and protects the ageing heart, and the protection is lost in mice lacking Atg5 in cardiomyocytes.

Madeo F.lab_name: Ageing and Cell Death Laboratory, Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (Graz, Austria)
Madeo F.role: Established spermidine as a dietary compound that extends lifespan in yeast, worms, flies and mice, and showed that the effect depends on autophagy
Madeo F.sub: Full Professor and Director of Research, Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (since 2004) · group leader, University of Tübingen (1997–2004) · PhD on tyrosine phosphorylation and apoptosis in yeast, University of Tübingen (1994–1997) · biochemistry studies, University of Tübingen (1987–1993)
story: Madeo came to ageing through cell death in yeast, and the habit shows in how his laboratory frames interventions: not “does this extend life” but “what has to be intact for it to work”. Spermidine is the case in point. EIS2009 established that the polyamine induces autophagy and extends lifespan across four systems; EIS2016 moved it into mammals and made the heart protection contingent on Atg5 in cardiomyocytes.

The branch matters to this Atlas because it reaches autophagy by a route that does not start at mTOR (EIS2009 did not measure mTOR directly). Where rapamycin releases autophagy by inhibiting mTORC1, spermidine does it by changing histone acetylation and the transcription of autophagy genes. That makes it a useful test of a claim the Atlas is careful about: if the benefits of mTOR inhibition really run through autophagy, an mTOR-independent autophagy inducer should reproduce part of them.
His laboratory also works on other caloric-restriction mimetics and on fasting regimens, and he is an editor of the yeast and cell-stress literature in this area.

highlights.EIS2009: Senior author: autophagy is required for spermidine to suppress necrosis and extend lifespan.
highlights.EIS2016: Senior author: spermidine extends mouse lifespan and prevents cardiac ageing, with the effect abolished in cardiomyocyte Atg5 knockouts.

Narita Masako.lab_name: Narita Group, Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Narita Masako.role: Discovered, as first author, the TASCC, a compartment in senescent cells where mTOR and autophagy work side by side to fuel the secretion of inflammatory proteins
Narita Masako.sub: Principal Scientific Associate, Narita Group, Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute, University of Cambridge
story: The textbook version says mTOR switches between building proteins and digesting them. NAR2011 found a place in the cell where both happen at once. In Ras-induced senescent cells, autolysosomes and mTOR gather on the trans side of the Golgi in a structure the paper named the TOR-autophagy spatial coupling compartment, or TASCC.

Two details make it more than an observation. mTOR's recruitment there is amino-acid- and Rag-dependent, which links the arrangement to the same machinery the Atlas draws for nutrient sensing. And disrupting mTOR's localisation to the TASCC suppresses interleukin-6 and interleukin-8 synthesis — so the compartment is how the senescent secretory programme is fuelled, with degradation supplying the amino acids that the synthesis consumes.

The same structure was seen during macrophage differentiation and in glomerular podocytes, both heavily secretory, which argues that it is a general solution to fast protein turnover rather than a quirk of senescence.

highlights.NAR2011: First author: identified the TASCC, where autolysosomes and mTOR co-localise so that a senescent cell can degrade and secrete at the same time.

Narita Masako.credit: Portrait: Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute

Narita Masashi.lab_name: Narita Group, Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Narita Masashi.role: Studies what senescent cells do to the tissue around them, and showed that mTOR position, not just mTOR activity, sets their secretory output
Narita Masashi.sub: Professor of Senobiology, Department of Oncology, University of Cambridge (since 2019) · Senior Group Leader, Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute
story: Narita's earlier work described senescence-associated heterochromatin foci, the chromatin rearrangement that locks a senescent cell out of the cell cycle. His group then moved to the harder question: a senescent cell is not simply switched off, it is doing something to its neighbours, and the secretory programme is the doing.

NAR2011 is where that meets mTOR. The group found the TASCC, a compartment at the trans-Golgi where autolysosomes and mTOR sit together, and showed that keeping mTOR out of it cuts IL-6/IL-8 synthesis. This is a specifically spatial claim: the same total amount of mTOR activity in the wrong place produces a different phenotype. It is the closest thing in this corpus to the question of how mTOR signalling is organised in space, alongside KOR2011 on lysosomal positioning.

For the Atlas the edge from mTORC1 to the senescent secretory phenotype had, until this paper was added, a single supporting study. NAR2011 supports the same claim by a different route, and bounds it: it explains how the secretome is fuelled, not whether suppressing it helps an animal.

highlights.NAR2011: Senior author: spatial coupling of mTOR and autophagy at the TASCC drives the senescent secretory phenotype; disrupting mTOR localisation suppresses IL-6/8.

Narita Masashi.credit: Portrait: Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute

Arias E.lab_name: Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Bronx, New York, USA)
Arias E.role: Showed that mTORC2, working with PHLPP1 and Akt at the lysosome, regulates chaperone-mediated autophagy
Arias E.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Medicine (Hepatology) and Department of Pathology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY
story: Chaperone-mediated autophagy is the tidy form of self-digestion: a cytosolic chaperone carries one protein at a time to the lysosomal surface, where it unfolds and is threaded through a translocation complex. No vesicle is built. How it was regulated was largely unknown, which is a gap worth noticing given how much is known about the regulation of macroautophagy.

ARI2015 filled part of it and reversed two of the usual terms while doing so. The complex sitting on the lysosomal membrane here is mTORC2, not mTORC1, and it inhibits CMA through lysosomal Akt; the phosphatase PHLPP1 pushes the other way. What that kinase-phosphatase pair actually controls is the assembly and disassembly of the translocation complex — the gate, not the cargo.

Her own laboratory works on metabolic liver injury: fatty liver disease, hepatic tumorigenesis, and how failing autophagy contributes to age-related liver disease and to the progression from steatohepatitis to hepatocellular carcinoma.

highlights.ARI2015: First author: a lysosomal mTORC2/PHLPP1/Akt axis controls chaperone-mediated autophagy by setting the assembly state of the translocation complex.

Cuervo AM.lab_name: Cuervo Lab, Institute for Geroscience, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Bronx, New York, USA)
Cuervo AM.role: Worked out much of the machinery of chaperone-mediated autophagy, a pathway first described in Fred Dice's laboratory, and showed it declines with age
Cuervo AM.sub: Distinguished Professor, Department of Developmental and Molecular Biology and Department of Medicine (Hepatology) · Robert and Renée Belfer Chair for the Study of Neurodegenerative Diseases · Co-Director, Institute for Geroscience, Albert Einstein College of Medicine · own laboratory at Einstein since October 2001
story: Most of what is said about autophagy in the ageing literature is about macroautophagy: the membrane wraps a piece of cytoplasm and delivers it to the lysosome. Cuervo's laboratory built the case that a second, selective route matters too. In chaperone-mediated autophagy the substrate is recognised by a targeting motif, carried by a chaperone, unfolded at the lysosomal membrane and pulled through a LAMP2A translocation complex one molecule at a time.

Two of her findings shape how the Atlas should read this branch. CMA activity falls with age, and restoring it in old animals improves proteostasis — which makes it a candidate mechanism for age-related decline rather than a curiosity. And in ARI2015 her group showed the pathway is under mTOR control, but through mTORC2 and lysosomal Akt, not through the mTORC1–ULK1 step that governs macroautophagy.

That difference is the useful part. The Atlas states that mTOR inhibits autophagy; ARI2015 shows the statement is complex-specific, and that a different mTOR complex regulates a different kind of autophagy by a different mechanism.

highlights.ARI2015: Senior author: mTORC2 inhibits chaperone-mediated autophagy at the lysosomal membrane via Akt, with PHLPP1 counteracting it.

Cuervo AM.credit: Portrait: Albert Einstein College of Medicine

Abu-Remaileh M.lab_name: Abu-Remaileh Lab, Stanford University (Stanford, California, USA)
Abu-Remaileh M.role: Worked out how to isolate lysosomes fast enough to measure what is inside them, and found that mTOR controls what gets out
Abu-Remaileh M.sub: Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering and of Genetics, Stanford University · postdoctoral research, Whitehead Institute and MIT, in David Sabatini's laboratory (to 2019) · PhD in Molecular Genetics, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem (2014)
story: The lysosome is where mTORC1 is switched on, so what is inside it matters — but lysosomal metabolites turn over in seconds, and conventional fractionation is far too slow to catch them. ABU2017 solves the measurement problem first: a rapid immunoprecipitation method that pulls lysosomes out of a cell in minutes, followed by metabolite profiling of the isolated organelles.

The biology that follows reverses an arrow the Atlas draws. Blocking the v-ATPase raised the luminal concentration of most metabolites but left most essential amino acids alone. Nutrient starvation did change them, and the effect traced back to mTOR: inhibiting mTOR strongly reduced the efflux of essential amino acids from the lysosome, converting the organelle into a store. So the lysosome is not only the platform that activates mTORC1; mTORC1 also decides what the lysosome releases.

His laboratory at Stanford works on how cells and organisms adapt to metabolic stress, with the lysosome at the centre and with applications in cancer and in neurodegeneration, including lysosomal storage disorders.

highlights.ABU2017: First author: rapid lysosome isolation plus metabolomics shows mTOR controls the efflux of essential amino acids from the lysosome.
highlights.WYA2018: Co-author: lysosome proteomics after mTORC1 inhibition identifies NUFIP1 as a receptor for starvation-induced ribophagy.

Sadoshima J.lab_name: Sadoshima Lab, Department of Cell Biology and Molecular Medicine, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School (Newark, New Jersey, USA)
Sadoshima J.role: Studies how mTOR, autophagy and mitophagy protect the heart under stress and in ageing, and contributed to the finding that spermidine protects the heart
Sadoshima J.sub: Professor and Chair, Department of Cell Biology and Molecular Medicine, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School (Chair since 2012, Professor since 2003) · Associate Professor, UMDNJ–New Jersey Medical School (2000–2003) · Allegheny University of the Health Sciences (1998–2000) · Assistant Professor, University of Michigan (1994–1998) · postdoctoral fellow, Beth Israel Hospital, Harvard Medical School (1990–1994) · PhD (1989) and MD (1983), Kyushu University
story: The heart is the organ where the autophagy story stops being abstract. Cardiomyocytes are not replaced, so whatever quality control they have has to last a lifetime, and both too little autophagy and too much of it damage the tissue. Sadoshima's laboratory works on exactly that balance, together with Hippo signalling and redox-sensitive pathways in cardiovascular disease.

His contribution to this corpus sits in two places. He is a co-author of EIS2016, the Graz-led spermidine study whose cardiac work includes the finding that the protection disappears in mice whose cardiomyocytes lack Atg5 — the control that turns a correlation into a requirement. He is also senior author of SCI2014, the Atlas's review of mTOR signalling in cardiac physiology and disease.

The point the Atlas takes from this line of work is a boundary rather than a promise: autophagy in the heart is protective within a range, and interventions that push it are not automatically good for the organ.

highlights.EIS2016: Co-author of the study showing spermidine's cardioprotection is lost when cardiomyocytes lack Atg5.
highlights.SCI2014: Senior author of the review of mTOR signalling in cardiac physiology and disease.

Sadoshima J.credit: Portrait: Sadoshima Lab, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School

Buettner S.lab_name: Büttner Lab, Institute of Integrative Cell Biology and Physiology, University of Münster (Münster, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Buettner S.role: Studies how organelles communicate inside cells and how that communication breaks down with age, and contributed to the Graz studies showing that spermidine extends lifespan by inducing autophagy
Buettner S.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Institute of Integrative Cell Biology and Physiology, University of Münster (since October 2024) · Professor of Molecular Cell Biology, Stockholm University (2015–2024) · Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (affiliation on EIS2009 and EIS2016)
story: Büttner came up through the Graz school of yeast cell death, and her own laboratory now asks a question one level up from a single pathway: how do organelles inside one cell stay coordinated, and what happens to protein homeostasis and cellular fitness when that coordination degrades with age.

In this corpus she appears on both spermidine papers. EIS2009 established that the polyamine induces autophagy and extends lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells; EIS2016 carried it into mice and made the cardiac protection depend on Atg5. Her presence on both is one reason the Atlas can treat them as one line of evidence rather than two unrelated results.

She is also a co-author of the yeast cell death nomenclature guidelines, which is the kind of work that keeps a field's terms usable — the same reason this Atlas is careful about what counts as autophagy and what counts only as autophagosome number.

highlights.EIS2009: Co-author: spermidine induces autophagy and extends lifespan across yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells.
highlights.EIS2016: Co-author: oral spermidine extends mouse lifespan and protects the ageing heart, with the effect abolished without Atg5.

Neff F.lab_name: Institute of Pathology and German Mouse Clinic, Helmholtz Zentrum München (Neuherberg (Munich), Germany)
Neff F.role: First author of the study that separated what rapamycin does to lifespan from what it does to ageing itself
Neff F.sub: Neuropathologist, Institute of Pathology, München Klinik Neuperlach · head of pathology, German Mouse Clinic, Helmholtz Zentrum München (from 2009) · habilitation in neuropathology, Technical University of Munich (2016) · MD, University of Marburg
story: NEF2013 is one of the more uncomfortable papers in this corpus, and one of the more useful. Rapamycin does extend murine lifespan — that part replicated. But when the same mice were put through a broad phenotyping battery covering many age-sensitive traits, most of them were not rejuvenated. Some of what looked like an anti-ageing effect was better explained as a direct pharmacological effect that happens to be beneficial.

The result is a boundary condition the Atlas keeps in view whenever the lifespan literature is quoted: living longer and ageing more slowly are separate claims that need separate evidence, and a single survival curve does not settle the second one.
She also appears in EIS2016 through the German Mouse Clinic's phenotyping of the spermidine-fed animals — the same discipline applied to a different intervention.

highlights.NEF2013: First author: rapamycin extended lifespan in mice while leaving most age-sensitive phenotypes unchanged, separating lifespan from ageing.
highlights.EIS2016: Co-author: contributed to the German Mouse Clinic phenotyping of spermidine-treated mice.

Neff F.credit: Portrait: Technical University of Munich, Institute of Pathology

Carmona-Gutierrez D.lab_name: Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (Graz, Austria)
Carmona-Gutierrez D.role: Studies how cell death and autophagy shape ageing at the University of Graz, and contributed to the studies showing that spermidine extends lifespan through autophagy
Carmona-Gutierrez D.sub: Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (affiliation on EIS2009 and EIS2016)
story: Carmona-Gutierrez works in the Graz group on yeast as a model for programmed cell death and ageing, and on the compounds that shift the balance — the caloric-restriction mimetics of which spermidine is the best-characterised.

He is a co-author of both corpus papers on that branch: EIS2009, which showed the effect depends on autophagy and works through histone acetylation, and EIS2016, which moved it into mammals and tied the cardiac benefit to Atg5.

A second strand of his work is definitional: he is among the authors of the yeast cell death nomenclature guidelines and an editor in that literature. This matters more than it sounds, because most disputes in the autophagy field turn out to be disputes about what a measurement means.

highlights.EIS2009: Co-author: spermidine extends lifespan in an autophagy-dependent way, via inhibition of histone acetyltransferases.
highlights.EIS2016: Co-author: spermidine feeding extends mouse lifespan and preserves diastolic function in old animals.

Rubinsztein DC.lab_name: Rubinsztein Lab, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research · UK Dementia Research Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Rubinsztein DC.role: Showed that rapamycin induces autophagy to clear the toxic protein of Huntington's disease, and that where lysosomes sit inside a cell helps set mTORC1 activity
Rubinsztein DC.sub: Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics, Department of Medical Genetics, University of Cambridge · Deputy Director, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research · Group Leader, UK Dementia Research Institute at Cambridge
story: David Rubinsztein leads a lab at Cambridge that has spent over two decades studying autophagy — the process cells use to break down and recycle their own worn-out parts — and how failures in that process contribute to neurodegenerative diseases like Huntington's and Parkinson's.

In this study, his team asked a question that sounds almost architectural: does it matter where inside the cell a lysosome is sitting? They found that it does. Lysosomes parked near the cell's outer edge sit close to the signals that activate mTORC1, so mTORC1 turns on there. When nutrients run low, lysosomes cluster near the nucleus instead, and mTORC1 activity drops while autophagy ramps up. Moving lysosomes around, it turns out, is itself a way the cell fine-tunes growth versus recycling.

highlights.KOR2011: Senior author on the discovery that lysosome positioning — spread toward the cell edge versus clustered near the nucleus — helps set how strongly mTORC1 activates and how efficiently autophagy proceeds.
highlights.BER2006: Senior author on the finding that rapamycin, by inducing autophagy, lowers the toxicity of several aggregate-prone proteins in cells and of tau in flies.

Bouquier N.lab_name: Perroy Team, Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle (IGF), CNRS/INSERM/Université de Montpellier (Montpellier, France)
Bouquier N.role: Built AIMTOR, a glowing biosensor that lets researchers watch mTOR activity move around inside a living cell in real time
Bouquier N.sub: Research Engineer, Perroy Team, Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle, CNRS · Université de Montpellier
story: Nathalie Bouquier is a research engineer in Julie Perroy's team in Montpellier, where she works on tools that make it possible to see cell signaling as it happens rather than reconstructing it afterward from snapshots.

For this study she helped build and validate AIMTOR, a genetically encoded biosensor that gives off a light signal whenever mTOR is active nearby. Because the sensor can be targeted to specific spots in the cell — the cytosol, the lysosome surface, the nucleus, near mitochondria — it let the team watch mTORC1 activity rise and fall in different compartments during muscle-cell differentiation and after amino-acid stimulation, and even catch mTOR-signaling abnormalities in neurons from mouse models of autism.

highlights.BOU2020: Helped build and validate AIMTOR, a light-emitting biosensor that tracks mTOR activity live in specific parts of a cell, and used it to watch mTORC1 respond to amino acids during muscle-cell differentiation.

Bouquier N.credit: Portrait: Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle (IGF), CNRS

Ollendorff V.lab_name: DMEM (Dynamique Musculaire et Métabolisme), INRAE · Université de Montpellier (Montpellier, France)
Ollendorff V.role: Co-led the Montpellier team that built AIMTOR, a light-emitting biosensor for watching mTOR activity inside living cells, as part of his work on muscle metabolism
Ollendorff V.sub: Director (since 2022), DMEM (Dynamique Musculaire et Métabolisme), INRAE · Université de Montpellier
story: Vincent Ollendorff studies how muscle cells manage their metabolism, at the DMEM unit run jointly by INRAE and the University of Montpellier. Muscle differentiation — the process by which young muscle precursor cells fuse and mature into working muscle fibers — is tightly controlled by nutrient-sensing pathways including mTOR.

As a corresponding author on the AIMTOR biosensor study, he co-led the effort to turn that biosensor into a working tool and to use it to track mTORC1 activity as muscle cells differentiate and respond to amino acids like leucine — giving a live readout of a signaling pathway that used to be measurable only after the fact.

highlights.BOU2020: Co-led development of the AIMTOR biosensor and its use to track mTORC1 activity live as muscle cells differentiate and respond to amino-acid stimulation.

Arriola Apelo SI.lab_name: Arriola Apelo Lab, Department of Animal and Dairy Sciences, University of Wisconsin–Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Arriola Apelo SI.role: Showed that giving rapamycin intermittently rather than daily lessens its effects on glucose metabolism and the immune system in mice
Arriola Apelo SI.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Animal and Dairy Sciences, University of Wisconsin–Madison
story: Sebastian Arriola Apelo now runs his own lab at UW-Madison studying nutrient metabolism and mTOR signaling, but this study was done while he was working in Dudley Lamming's lab, on one of the more practical problems in the rapamycin field: the drug extends lifespan in mice by blocking mTORC1, but it also causes glucose intolerance and weakens the immune system by blocking a second mTOR complex, mTORC2, that's much less sensitive to the drug.

The team tested whether the dosing pattern itself — daily versus intermittent dosing, or swapping in related drugs like everolimus and temsirolimus — could separate the two effects. They found an intermittent dosing schedule that still inhibited mTORC1 effectively while largely sparing glucose tolerance and immune function, suggesting the drug's downsides aren't an unavoidable package deal with its benefits.

highlights.ARR2015: Led the study showing that intermittent rapamycin dosing, or swapping in related drugs like everolimus, can preserve mTORC1 inhibition while reducing the drug's impact on blood sugar (and, for the intermittent schedule, on immune function).
highlights.ARR2016: Led the follow-up showing that the same intermittent schedule, rapamycin every five days started at 20 months of age, extended the lifespan of female mice.

Arriola Apelo SI.credit: Portrait: Arriola Apelo Lab, University of Wisconsin–Madison

Hurley JH.lab_name: Hurley Lab, UC Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Hurley JH.role: Structural biologist who uses cryo-EM to show how protein machines assembled on membranes control autophagy and nutrient signalling. His lab solved structures of the Rag–Ragulator complex and of the whole mTORC1–TFEB–Rag–Ragulator assembly on the lysosome
Hurley JH.sub: Professor of Molecular & Cell Biology and Kirsch Springer Chair in Biological Sciences, UC Berkeley (since 2013) · Faculty Scientist, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (since 2014) · Chief, Section on Structural Biology & Cell Signaling, NIDDK/NIH (1998–2013) · Senior Investigator, NIDDK/NIH (1997–2013) · Tenure-track Investigator, NIH (1992–1997) · Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Oregon (1990–1992) · PhD in Biophysics, UCSF (1990) · BA in Physics, San Francisco State University (1984) · Member, US National Academy of Sciences (2020) · Hans Neurath Award, Protein Society (2014)
story: mTORC1 only switches on when it is physically dragged to the surface of the lysosome, and the machine that does the dragging is a five-protein clamp called Ragulator together with the Rag GTPases. In the 2017 study, Hurley's laboratory solved the crystal structure of the whole human Ragulator at 1.4 angstrom resolution, which is sharp enough to see individual side chains. Lamtor1 turned out to wrap around the other four subunits like a belt, while the Lamtor2-Lamtor3 pair stacks on Lamtor4-Lamtor5 to build the platform the Rags sit on.

A crystal structure alone could not show where the Rags actually dock, so the team added two other methods. Hydrogen-deuterium exchange, which reports how exposed each stretch of protein is to water, mapped the Rag contact to the outer face of Lamtor2-Lamtor3 and to the floppy N-terminal tail of Lamtor1; electron microscopy then gave a lower-resolution picture of full-length RagA-RagC bound to Ragulator. Stitching these together produced a hybrid model in which the business ends of the Rags project away from the Ragulator core, held out like a handle for mTORC1 to grab.

Hurley spent two decades at the NIH before moving to Berkeley in 2013, and built his reputation on structures of the protein complexes that bend and cut membranes, especially the ESCRT machinery. His group now uses cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-electron tomography on the autophagy initiation machinery, on lysosome biology in cancer and Alzheimer's disease, and on how HIV hijacks membrane trafficking. The Ragulator work sits at the junction of those interests: it is a nutrient sensor, a membrane anchor and a drug-relevant target at the same time.

highlights.SUX2017: Senior author (with Roberto Zoncu); his laboratory determined the 1.4 angstrom Ragulator crystal structure and combined it with hydrogen-deuterium exchange and EM into the hybrid RagA/C-Ragulator model.
highlights.ESP2026: Co-author on the TBK1/ULK1-FNIP1-FLCN pathway that controls TFEB's release from the lysosome, independent of nutrient status.
highlights.JAN2025: Senior author: cryo-EM structure of GATOR2 bound to CASTOR1, showing how arginine releases it.

Ganley IG.lab_name: Ganley Lab, MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Ganley IG.role: Showed, in one of three 2009 studies (alongside the Mizushima and Kim laboratories), that the ULK1–ATG13–FIP200 complex relays mTOR signalling to start autophagy, and studies how cells select damaged mitochondria for destruction
Ganley IG.sub: Professor of Cellular Homeostasis, MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit, University of Dundee (since 2022) · Programme Leader, MRC PPU, University of Dundee (2016–2022) · Group Leader, MRC PPU, University of Dundee (2010–2016) · Postdoctoral Fellow, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (Xuejun Jiang lab) and Stanford University (Suzanne Pfeffer lab) (2002–2010) · PhD, University of Cambridge (Nick Ktistakis lab, 1998–2002) · Oxford GlycoSciences (1997–1998) · MBiochem, University of Oxford (1997) · Fellow, Royal Society of Edinburgh (2025) · Hooke Medal, British Society for Cell Biology (2025)
story: When a cell runs out of nutrients it starts eating parts of itself, and the 2009 paper, one of three published that spring alongside papers from Noboru Mizushima's and Do-Hyung Kim's laboratories, identified the switchboard where that decision is made. Working as a postdoc in Xuejun Jiang's laboratory, Ganley showed that the kinase ULK1 does not act alone but sits in a complex with two partners, ATG13 and FIP200, and that all three are needed for starvation-induced autophagy. Removing either partner left ULK1 unstable and in the wrong place, unable to reach the site where a new autophagosome is born.

The crucial link to mTOR came from two directions. In cells, ULK1 and ATG13 were phosphorylated in a way that tracked nutrient supply, and in a reaction rebuilt from purified components ATG13 and FIP200 each boosted ULK1 kinase activity, with both needed for the full effect. That made the complex a node: mTOR writes phosphate marks onto it when food is plentiful, and releasing those marks when food is scarce lets ULK1 fire and autophagy begin.

Since setting up his own group in Dundee at the end of 2010, Ganley has focused on mitophagy, the selective removal of damaged mitochondria. His laboratory built the mito-QC reporter, a colour-changing tag that turns from yellow to red when a mitochondrion reaches the acidic interior of a lysosome, which made it possible to count mitophagy events in living tissue rather than only in cultured cells. Using it, his group has shown that a great deal of mitophagy happens routinely in healthy tissue and has traced how the common Parkinson's mutation LRRK2 G2019S interferes with it.

highlights.GAN2009: First author; he identified and reconstituted the ULK1-ATG13-FIP200 complex and showed that ULK1 and ATG13 are phosphorylated through the mTOR pathway in a nutrient-dependent manner.

Ganley IG.credit: Portrait: MRC PPU, University of Dundee

Parent JM.lab_name: Parent Lab, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Parent JM.role: Neurologist and stem-cell researcher who rebuilds human epilepsies in patient-derived neurons to find what goes wrong
Parent JM.sub: William J. Herdman Professor of Neurology, University of Michigan Medical School (faculty since 2000) · Co-Director, Comprehensive Epilepsy Center, Michigan Medicine · Director, Human Stem Cell and Gene Editing Core, University of Michigan · Member, Michigan Neuroscience Institute · Staff Physician, VA Ann Arbor Healthcare System · Fellowship in Clinical Neurophysiology, UCSF (1996) · Residency in Neurology, UCSF (1994) · MD, Yale University School of Medicine (1990) · AB in Human Biology, Stanford University
story: Focal cortical dysplasia is a patch of mis-built cortex that causes epilepsy which drugs usually cannot control, and in most cases it traces back to a mutation that arose in a few brain cells during development and left the mTOR pathway stuck in the on position. Parent is the senior author of the 2026 screen that went looking for the genes that normally hold that pathway down. The key design choice was the cell type: instead of cancer lines, the screen used human neurons made from induced pluripotent stem cells, because a gene that restrains mTOR in a tumour cell need not do the same job in a neuron.

That platform is Parent's long-standing contribution. He directs Michigan's Human Stem Cell and Gene Editing Core and has spent nearly two decades turning patient skin and blood cells into neurons and, more recently, into brain organoids, in order to model Dravet syndrome and other genetic epilepsies in a dish. Earlier in his career he showed that seizures themselves change the adult brain, driving new neuron birth and rewiring in the hippocampus.

He remains a practising epilepsy neurologist and co-directs Michigan's epilepsy centre, which is what gives the screen its clinical point. Two of the six hits, PIK3R3 and HIP1, already had a candidate disease-causing variant reported in tissue removed from a patient during epilepsy surgery, so the screen is effectively handing surgeons and geneticists a longer list of genes worth checking in that tissue.

highlights.TID2026: Senior and co-corresponding author; his laboratory and stem-cell core supplied the human iPSC-derived neuron platform and the focal cortical dysplasia framing that the screen was built around.

Parent JM.credit: Portrait: University of Michigan Medical School

Tidball AM.lab_name: Tidball Lab, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Tidball AM.role: Stem-cell neuroscientist who builds human neuron and organoid models to find the genes behind brain malformations
Tidball AM.sub: Research Assistant Professor of Neurology, University of Michigan Medical School (since 2019) · Member, Michigan Neuroscience Institute · Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Michigan (Jack Parent lab, 2014–2019) · PhD, Vanderbilt University (Aaron Bowman lab, 2014) · BS, Calvin College (2008)
story: Tidball designed and ran the 2026 screen that is an unbiased, genome-wide hunt for brakes on mTOR carried out in human neurons. He converted induced pluripotent stem cells into neurons, then used CRISPR interference with a library of about 110,000 guide RNAs to turn down one gene at a time, and sorted the cells by how much phosphorylated S6 they carried, since that phospho-mark is the same biomarker pathologists use on focal cortical dysplasia tissue. Neurons that lit up brightly were the ones whose missing gene had been holding mTOR back.

Six genes came out of it: LRRC4, EIF3A, TSN, HIP1, PIK3R3 and URI1. Follow-up along the whole AKT-mTOR-S6 chain narrowed the list to PIK3R3 and HIP1 as the two that raise signalling at every step rather than only at the end, and each of those two had independently been reported with a candidate pathogenic variant in brain tissue resected from a patient. Knocking down any of the six also made the neurons indifferent to losing the growth factor GDNF, which normally keeps mTOR signalling switched on.

He came to this through two earlier stages. His Vanderbilt doctoral work with Aaron Bowman examined how neural progenitor cells handle manganese and how that feeds into ATM-p53 signalling, using Huntington's disease models; his postdoctoral years with Jack Parent were spent building stem-cell models of genetic epilepsies. His own laboratory now uses single-rosette brain organoids and CRISPR to study neural tube defects, focal cortical dysplasia and substances that disturb brain development before birth.

highlights.TID2026: First author and co-corresponding author; he built the human iNeuron CRISPRi platform, ran the genome-wide phospho-S6 FACS screen and validated the six hits.

Tidball AM.credit: Portrait: University of Michigan Medical School

Brown-Borg HM.lab_name: Brown-Borg Lab, University of North Dakota School of Medicine & Health Sciences (Grand Forks, North Dakota, USA)
Brown-Borg HM.role: Physiologist who measures how reduced growth-hormone signalling changes lifespan and what keeps long-lived mutant mice healthy
Brown-Borg HM.sub: Chester Fritz Distinguished Professor, Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of North Dakota School of Medicine & Health Sciences (since 2010) · Associate Professor, University of North Dakota (2002–2010) · Assistant Professor, University of North Dakota (1995–2002) · Research Associate, Physiology, Southern Illinois University School of Medicine · PhD, Physiology, North Carolina State University · MS, Animal Science, University of Nebraska–Lincoln · BS, University of Nebraska–Lincoln · President, American Aging Association (2010–2011) · Fellow, Gerontological Society of America (2006) · Denham Harman Lifetime Achievement Research Award (2013)
story: Brown-Borg is the first author of the 1996 Nature letter that reported Ames dwarf mice living far longer than their normal littermates. These mice carry a mutation in the Prop1 gene, so their pituitary never develops properly and never makes growth hormone, prolactin or thyroid-stimulating hormone. The size difference had been known for decades; what her lifespan curves showed was that the mutants outlived their siblings by roughly half again as long. She did the work with Andrzej Bartke, in whose group she trained before opening her own lab in North Dakota.

The result mattered because it turned a vague idea into a measurable one. If switching off a single growth-signalling hormone adds years to a mammal, then growth and lifespan are traded against each other by a specific, findable pathway. Less growth hormone means less circulating IGF-1, which means less signalling through PI3K, AKT and mTOR - the same nutrient-sensing chain that flies, worms and yeast use to decide between building and maintaining.

Her lab now works on why those mice are durable rather than merely small. It studies their antioxidant defences, especially glutathione handling, their methionine metabolism, mitochondrial function and DNA-methylation patterns, and asks which of these track with healthspan in muscle, liver and brain rather than with body size.

highlights.BRO1996: First author of the Nature letter reporting that growth-hormone-deficient Ames dwarf mice outlive their normal littermates, the founding lifespan measurement for this line of work.

Brown-Borg HM.credit: Portrait: University of North Dakota School of Medicine and Health Sciences

Bartke A.lab_name: Bartke Laboratory, Southern Illinois University School of Medicine (Springfield, Illinois, USA)
Bartke A.role: Endocrinologist who showed that Ames dwarf mice, which lack growth hormone because of a single-gene mutation, live much longer than normal mice
Bartke A.sub: Professor Emeritus & Director of Geriatrics Research, Departments of Internal Medicine and Physiology, Southern Illinois University School of Medicine (since 1984) · Faculty, Southern Illinois University Carbondale · Faculty, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · Fellow in Reproductive Physiology, Worcester Foundation for Experimental Biology · Faculty, Jagiellonian University, Kraków · PhD, Zoology, University of Kansas (1965) · MSc, Biology, Jagiellonian University, Kraków (1962) · Methuselah Mouse Prize (2003) · Endocrine Society Lifetime Achievement Award (2015)
story: Bartke is the senior author of the 1996 Nature letter on Ames dwarf mice. He had been studying that mutant strain for years as a reproductive endocrinologist, because a pituitary that cannot make growth hormone also cannot make prolactin, and his colony and his hormone measurements are what made a clean lifespan comparison possible. The letter is short, but it was the first demonstration that one gene mutation can extend life in a mammal.

He then pushed the same logic from the top of the pathway to its receiver. His group helped characterise growth-hormone-receptor knockout mice, which make growth hormone but cannot hear it; one of those animals, GHR-KO 11C, lived 1,819 days and won the first Methuselah Mouse Prize in 2003. Taken together, the two models say the signal itself is the variable: less growth-hormone signalling means less IGF-1, lower insulin, and reduced traffic down the PI3K-AKT-mTOR route that tells cells to grow.

Bartke has spent more than four decades on the genetic and hormonal control of ageing, with over 750 papers, and has kept asking the harder follow-up questions - how diet interacts with growth-hormone signalling, why these mice are unusually insulin-sensitive, and whether the same levers can be pulled pharmacologically in animals that are already old.

highlights.BRO1996: Senior author who supplied the Ames dwarf mouse colony and the endocrine framework behind the lifespan comparison.

Liu Yi.role: Drug-discovery scientist who builds selective kinase inhibitors, including the active-site mTOR inhibitor INK128
Liu Yi.sub: Chief Executive Officer, Kumquat Biosciences, San Diego · Co-founder and drug-discovery scientist, Intellikine, La Jolla · PhD; graduate training in the laboratory of Kevan M. Shokat
story: Liu is the co-first author of the 2012 Nature paper on the translational landscape of mTOR signalling, sharing that position with Andrew Hsieh. On the paper itself the affiliation is Intellikine Inc. in La Jolla, the company side of the collaboration rather than the Ruggero laboratory at UCSF. The contribution was the compound: INK128, an ATP-competitive inhibitor that binds the catalytic site of mTOR directly.

That distinction is the point of the study. Rapamycin does not switch mTORC1 off; it blocks some substrates and largely spares others, in particular the phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, the protein that clamps down on the translation initiation factor eIF4E. An active-site inhibitor shuts down both mTORC1 and mTORC2, restores 4E-BP1's grip on eIF4E, and so silences the small set of pro-invasion messages - among them YB1, vimentin, MTA1 and CD44 - that ribosome profiling had shown oncogenic mTOR was selectively translating in prostate cancer cells.

Intellikine was founded out of Kevan Shokat's chemical-biology work, together with Zachary Knight and Pingda Ren, and built a series of PI3K and mTOR inhibitors; INK128 later entered clinical development as sapanisertib. Liu is now chief executive of Kumquat Biosciences in San Diego, where Pingda Ren is president and chief operating officer, working on small molecules against targets long considered undruggable.

highlights.HSI2012: Co-first author on the industry side of the collaboration, responsible with the Intellikine team for developing and characterising INK128, the active-site mTOR inhibitor used to reverse the pro-invasion translation signature.

Liu Yu.lab_name: Chen-Liu Lab, National Key Laboratory of Biotherapy, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Liu Yu.role: Cancer biologist working on how tumour-suppressor loss and epigenetic state decide whether a cell stays differentiated
Liu Yu.sub: Professor, National Key Laboratory of Biotherapy, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (since 2015) · Postdoctoral Fellow, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory & Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (2010–2015) · Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Michigan (2008–2010) · PhD, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (2008) · MS, Beijing Normal University (2000) · BS, Beijing Normal University (1997)
