story: Liu is the second author of the 2008 Journal of Experimental Medicine paper on TSC-mTOR in blood stem cells, written in the Division of Immunotherapy at the University of Michigan with Chong Chen as first author and Yang Liu and Pan Zheng as senior authors. The experiment was a conditional deletion of Tsc1 in haematopoietic stem cells, which removes the brake on mTORC1 and leaves the pathway permanently on.

What happened next was not more stem cells but fewer working ones. Stem cells normally sit quiet and rely on glycolysis; with mTORC1 unrestrained they built more mitochondria, filled with reactive oxygen species, started cycling, and then failed in serial and competitive bone-marrow transplants - the strictest test of whether a stem cell can still renew itself. Giving the mice an antioxidant restored both their numbers and their function, which pinned the damage on ROS rather than on division itself.

The same group extended the finding in papers Liu co-authored: that mTOR activity rises in the blood stem cells of old mice and that rapamycin partly rejuvenates them, and that inflammatory cytokines switch mTOR on in stem cells during autoimmune disease. Liu now co-leads a laboratory at West China Hospital in Chengdu with Chong Chen, working on TP53 and chromosome-deletion tumour suppression and on differentiation-based therapies in acute myeloid leukaemia and bladder cancer.

highlights.CHE2008: Second author on the study, part of the Michigan team that deleted Tsc1 in haematopoietic stem cells and traced the resulting loss of quiescence and self-renewal to mitochondrial ROS.

Schroeder S.lab_name: Madeo group (Cell Ageing and Cell Death), Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (Graz, Austria)
Schroeder S.role: Researcher in Frank Madeo's group at Graz who has contributed to the spermidine studies from the first yeast longevity experiments to work in mice
Schroeder S.sub: Postdoctoral researcher, Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz · BioTechMed-Graz & Field of Excellence BioHealth, University of Graz · Madeo group, University of Graz (since 2009)
story: Schroeder appears in both spermidine papers in this atlas, and she is one of the people who actually ran the experiments rather than only supplying a technique. The 2009 Nature Cell Biology paper names her among the researchers who carried out the yeast work, which is where the central claim was built: feeding yeast spermidine made them live longer, and deleting the autophagy gene ATG7 took the benefit away. In the 2016 mouse follow-up she is listed third among more than fifty authors, at the Graz institute where the spermidine feeding and autophagy readouts were done.

Her own first-author paper, in Cell Reports in 2021, extended the story to the brain. She showed that spermidine given in drinking water reaches mouse brain tissue, raises hypusination of the translation factor eIF5A in the hippocampus and improves how the mitochondria there respire; old mice then learned spatial tasks better. In flies the boost in mitochondrial respiration required the autophagy gene Atg7 and the mitophagy genes Parkin and Pink1, and knocking down Pink1 in neurons abolished the improvement in olfactory learning, which is the argument that the memory effect runs through cellular recycling and not through some unrelated route.

That trio of papers is why the spermidine branch is interesting for an mTOR atlas even though spermidine is not an mTOR drug. Rapamycin switches autophagy on by blocking mTORC1; spermidine switches it on by inhibiting histone acetyltransferases, changing which genes the cell transcribes. Schroeder's work sits on the second route and keeps testing it with the same tool every time: remove an autophagy gene and see whether the benefit survives.

highlights.EIS2009: The paper's author-contribution statement lists her among the researchers who performed the yeast experiments on which the spermidine-autophagy link rests.
highlights.EIS2016: Third author of the mammalian follow-up, based at the Graz institute that ran the mouse spermidine feeding and the autophagy measurements.

Magnes C.lab_name: Bioanalytics and Metabolomics, HEALTH – Institute for Biomedicine and Health Sciences, Joanneum Research (Graz, Austria)
Magnes C.role: Analytical chemist at Joanneum Research whose group contributed the mass-spectrometry measurements of polyamines in the Graz spermidine studies
Magnes C.sub: Head of the Bioanalytics and Metabolomics research group, HEALTH – Institute for Biomedicine and Health Sciences, Joanneum Research, Graz · At Joanneum Research since 2003 · Doctorate in natural sciences (Mag. Dr. rer. nat.)
story: Magnes is not a cell biologist and does not run aging experiments. He heads a bioanalytics and metabolomics group at Joanneum Research, an applied research company in Graz that works to Good Laboratory Practice standards, and his job in both spermidine papers is measurement. The 2009 paper states plainly in its author-contribution note that he and Frank Sinner performed the polyamine measurements by mass spectrometry; the 2016 paper's methods describe a quantitative HPLC-MS/MS determination of ornithine, putrescine, spermidine and spermine in plasma, whole blood and heart tissue, run by his Joanneum team.

That role is easy to underrate and hard to replace. Spermidine is a small, chemically unremarkable molecule that is already present in every cell, so the whole claim of these papers depends on being able to say how much of it is in a sample, to a level that separates it cleanly from its close relatives putrescine and spermine. Liquid chromatography separates the molecules, the mass spectrometer weighs the fragments, and a spiked internal standard turns the signal into an actual concentration.

Without those numbers the 2016 mouse result would be a story about mice that drank something and lived longer. With them the paper can show that circulating spermidine actually rose after feeding, that ornithine fell, and that the arginine-to-ornithine balance shifted in a direction linked to blood pressure. His group also supplied the polyamine measurements for the 2021 Graz work on spermidine and cognition.

highlights.EIS2009: Credited in the author-contribution statement, together with Frank Sinner, with performing the polyamine measurements by mass spectrometry.
highlights.EIS2016: His Joanneum Research bioanalytics group ran the quantitative HPLC-MS/MS determination of ornithine, putrescine, spermidine and spermine in plasma, whole blood and cardiac tissue.

Ruckenstuhl C.lab_name: Ruckenstuhl group, Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz (Graz, Austria)
Ruckenstuhl C.role: Yeast geneticist who works out how amino-acid restriction and vacuole acidity set lifespan
Ruckenstuhl C.sub: Associate Professor and group leader, Institute of Molecular Biosciences, University of Graz · Researcher, Madeo group, University of Graz · Yeast sterol biochemistry, Turnowsky group, University of Graz (from 2003) · Mag. rer. nat. and Dr. rer. nat., University of Graz
story: Ruckenstuhl is one of the yeast people behind the 2009 spermidine paper: its author-contribution statement names him among the researchers who performed the yeast experiments, which were the backbone of the study. Yeast is where the mechanism could be tested cleanly, by deleting single autophagy genes and watching the lifespan benefit disappear. He is also a co-author on the 2016 mammalian follow-up from the same Graz institute.

His own line of work sits much closer to mTOR. In a 2014 PLoS Genetics paper he showed that restricting the amino acid methionine extends the chronological lifespan of yeast, and that the extension is abolished by deleting ATG5, ATG7 or ATG8 – autophagy is required, not incidental. He then found the step that comes next: methionine restriction makes the vacuole, the yeast equivalent of the lysosome, more acidic, and simply overexpressing components of the vacuolar ATPase proton pump was enough to lengthen lifespan on its own.

The same paper draws a direct line to the TOR pathway. Inhibiting or deleting TOR1 extended lifespan in normal yeast, but added nothing in methionine-restricted cells, which is the genetic signature of two interventions feeding into one shared mechanism. His group at Graz now works on methionine and sulphur metabolism as an entry point into that mechanism.

highlights.EIS2009: Named in the author-contribution statement among the researchers who ran the yeast experiments that tied spermidine's lifespan effect to autophagy.
highlights.EIS2016: Co-author from Madeo's Graz institute on the mammalian follow-up, the group that supplied the autophagy side of the mouse work.

Bitto A.lab_name: Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Bitto A.role: Showed that a short, three-month course of rapamycin in middle-aged mice can extend lifespan and improve healthspan
Bitto A.sub: Acting Assistant Professor, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington · Postdoctoral fellow, Kaeberlein lab, University of Washington (from 2013) · PhD in Molecular Pathobiology, Drexel University College of Medicine (2013)
story: Bitto is the first author of the 2016 eLife study that asked a question everyone else had skipped: does rapamycin have to be given for life? He treated 20-month-old mice – already middle-aged – for just three months and then stopped. Remaining life expectancy rose by as much as 60 percent, and measures of healthspan improved too, which means the benefit does not require permanent exposure to the drug.

Two secondary findings make the paper more than a dosing note. The treatment reshaped the gut microbiome, sharply increasing segmented filamentous bacteria in the small intestine, which hints that some of rapamycin's effect may be mediated outside the animal's own cells. And a particular dose in female mice failed to extend lifespan while shifting the cancer spectrum toward aggressive blood cancers and away from solid tumours – a reminder that dose and sex change the outcome, not just its size.

The practical point for an mTOR atlas is that transient dosing is testable in humans in a way lifelong dosing is not. Bitto now runs his own work at the University of Washington on the overlap between aging and mitochondrial disease, including Ndufs4-knockout mice, a model of the childhood disorder Leigh syndrome in which longevity interventions such as rapamycin are unusually effective.

highlights.BIT2016: First author: designed and ran the transient-rapamycin mouse experiment and the lifespan, healthspan, cancer-incidence and microbiome analyses, with Matt Kaeberlein as senior author.

Hussong SA.lab_name: Galvan Lab, University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center (Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, USA)
Hussong SA.role: Studies how mTOR damages the brain's blood vessels, and how blocking it restores blood flow, the blood-brain barrier and memory in aging and Alzheimer's models
Hussong SA.sub: Research Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Physiology & Center for Geroscience and Healthy Brain Aging, University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center · Oklahoma City VA Medical Center · Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (c. 2011–2021) · South Texas Veterans Health Care System (c. 2011–2021) · Retinal proteasome research, Department of Ophthalmology, University of Minnesota (c. 2006–2010)
story: Hussong joined Veronica Galvan's group at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, the lab that was asking a blunt question about the drug rapamycin: it makes mice live longer, but what does a lifetime of it do to the brain? In the 2012 study she is second author on the team that fed mice rapamycin-laced chow from youth to old age and then measured learning, memory, anxiety and depression-like behaviour at every stage. The answer was the reassuring one - young mice learned better, old mice were spared the usual age-related memory decline, and the animals were calmer, with higher levels of the brain's monoamine messengers.

Her earlier training was in a different organ entirely. At the University of Minnesota she worked on the immunoproteasome - a specialised version of the cell's protein-shredding machine - in the retina, showing that it is switched on not only by immune attack but by ordinary oxidative stress and aging, and that cells missing it die more readily. That is essentially the same question she still asks, one system over: how does a cell's quality-control machinery hold up over a lifetime?

In the Galvan lab she moved the focus to the brain's plumbing. Across a series of studies she helped show that mTOR drives the failure of cerebral blood flow, the breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, and the uncoupling of blood supply from neuronal activity - in Alzheimer's models, in vascular cognitive impairment, and in normal aging - and that rapamycin reverses much of it. The lab has since moved with Galvan to Oklahoma City, where Hussong continues this work with the VA.

highlights.HAL2012: Second author on the study, part of the Galvan team at the Barshop Institute that carried out the lifespan-long behavioural testing of rapamycin-fed mice.

Debnath J.lab_name: Debnath Lab, UC San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Debnath J.role: Physician-scientist who studies how autophagy - the cell's self-digestion system - keeps epithelial tissue healthy and how tumours hijack it
Debnath J.sub: Distinguished Professor & Chair, Department of Pathology, UC San Francisco (chair since 2018) · Professor, UCSF (2016) · Associate Professor, UCSF (2011) · Assistant Professor, UCSF (2005) · Internship, residency and fellowship in pathology, Brigham and Women's Hospital (1998–2003) · MD, Harvard Medical School (1998) · BS in Chemistry, Georgia Institute of Technology (1992) · Member, American Society for Clinical Investigation (2013) and American Association of Physicians (2023)
story: In the 2010 Alzheimer's study Debnath is the outside expert brought in for one specific job: reading the autophagy data. The San Antonio team had fed rapamycin to PDAPP mice, a model of Alzheimer's disease, and found that the mice kept their memories and accumulated less of the toxic amyloid-beta 42 peptide. The crucial question was whether autophagy was the reason, and the paper's author contributions credit Debnath with the interpretation of those autophagy measurements and, with Matthew Hart, the critical review of the manuscript.

His own laboratory at UCSF works on the same process in a different setting. Autophagy is the system by which a cell wraps up worn-out proteins and organelles in a double membrane and delivers them to the lysosome to be broken down and recycled. Debnath's group asks what that recycling does for epithelial cells - the sheets of cells that line our organs - and how cancer cells exploit it to survive detachment, starvation and chemotherapy, with a long-running focus on breast cancer and metastasis.

He trained as a physician first, taking an MD at Harvard and pathology training at Brigham and Women's Hospital, and did his cell biology in Joan Brugge's laboratory, where he helped develop three-dimensional cultures of mammary cells that behave like real tissue. He has led the UCSF Department of Pathology since 2018 while keeping the lab running.

highlights.SPI2010: Interpreted the autophagy data that linked rapamycin's memory and amyloid benefits to increased self-digestion in neurons, and co-reviewed the manuscript.

Mizushima N.lab_name: Mizushima Laboratory, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Mizushima N.role: Built much of the molecular map of autophagy in mammals - the ATG proteins that make an autophagosome, and the signals, including mTORC1, that decide when one is made
Mizushima N.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Graduate School of Medicine, University of Tokyo (since 2012) · Vice Dean, Graduate School and Faculty of Medicine, University of Tokyo (since 2021) · Professor, Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (2006–2012) · Laboratory Head, Department of Bioregulation and Metabolism, Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science (2004–2006) · Postdoctoral fellow and Assistant Professor, Department of Cell Biology, National Institute for Basic Biology (1997–2004) · PhD, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (1991) · MD, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (1985) · JSPS Prize (2008), Uehara Prize (2016), Medal with Purple Ribbon (2021), Beth Levine Prize in Autophagy Research (2023)
story: The 2009 study from Mizushima's laboratory, with Nao Hosokawa as first author and Mizushima as senior author, answered a question that had been open for a decade: everyone knew mTOR suppressed autophagy, but nobody knew how. His group, one of several that independently reported this complex in 2009 (others included the laboratories of Do-Hyung Kim and Xuejun Jiang), identified mammalian Atg13 and showed it sits in a roughly 3-megadalton complex with the kinase ULK1 and FIP200. When nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 docks onto that complex through ULK1 and phosphorylates both ULK1 and Atg13, holding the autophagy starter switch down. Starve the cells, or add rapamycin, and mTORC1 lets go.

That paper is one step in a much longer project. In 1998, working in Yoshinori Ohsumi's laboratory, Mizushima was first author on the discovery that Atg12 is covalently attached to Atg5 by a ubiquitin-like conjugation system - the first ubiquitin-like conjugation system found in the autophagy pathway, and the finding that made autophagy a tractable molecular problem rather than a phenomenon seen under an electron microscope. He then carried the yeast genetics into mammals, identifying mammalian counterparts of several ATG proteins.

His laboratory also built the tools and the animals the whole field now uses: GFP-LC3 reporter mice that let you watch autophagosomes form in living tissue, and Atg5-deficient mice. Those mice produced one of the field's defining results, published in 2004 with Mizushima as senior author - newborn mice survive the hours between losing the placenta and their first milk by digesting their own proteins for amino acids, and without autophagy they die within a day.

highlights.HOS2009: Senior author whose laboratory, in parallel with other groups in 2009, identified mammalian Atg13 and showed that mTORC1 physically joins the ULK1-Atg13-FIP200 complex and phosphorylates ULK1 to keep autophagy switched off.

Mizushima N.credit: Portrait: Mizushima Lab, University of Tokyo

Weichhart T.lab_name: Weichhart Lab, Center for Pathobiochemistry and Genetics, Medical University of Vienna (Vienna, Austria)
Weichhart T.role: Immunologist who showed that mTOR sets the tone of the innate immune response, and now studies how macrophage metabolism drives granulomatous disease
Weichhart T.sub: Associate Professor of Immunometabolism, Medical University of Vienna (since 2014) · Group Leader, Center for Pathobiochemistry and Genetics, Medical University of Vienna (since 2012) · Researcher, Clinical Division of Nephrology and Dialysis, Department of Internal Medicine III, Medical University of Vienna (c. 2005–2012) · PhD, University of Vienna (2005) · BSc in Biology and Genetics, University of Vienna (2000)
story: Weichhart is first author of the 2008 Immunity paper that forced immunologists to rethink what rapamycin does. Rapamycin was used clinically as an immunosuppressant, so the expectation was that blocking mTOR would damp inflammation down. His experiments in monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells showed the opposite for the innate arm: inhibiting mTOR raised pro-inflammatory cytokines through the transcription factor NF-kappaB while shutting off the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10, which depends on STAT3.

The reverse experiment made the case airtight. Deleting TSC2 - the brake that normally keeps mTOR quiet - flipped the cells the other way, lowering NF-kappaB activity and raising STAT3, so the cytokine balance moved back toward anti-inflammatory. The effect held in a live animal too: blocking mTOR changed the inflammatory response enough to protect genetically susceptible mice from lethal Listeria infection. The practical reading is that mTOR is a dial on the quality of an immune response, not simply an on-off switch for its strength - which matters for transplant patients, vaccines and cancer immunotherapy alike.

He did this work as a researcher in the nephrology division in Vienna with Marcus Saemann, and has since built his own group at the Medical University of Vienna. The lab now studies immunometabolism - how the metabolic state of a macrophage determines what it does to the tissue around it - with a particular focus on sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases, where mTOR-driven macrophages appear to build the granulomas themselves.

highlights.WEI2008: First author: designed and ran the monocyte, macrophage and dendritic cell experiments and the TSC2-deletion and Listeria infection work showing that the TSC-mTOR pathway controls the innate inflammatory response.

Weichhart T.credit: Portrait: Weichhart Lab, Medical University of Vienna

Kalaany NY.lab_name: Kalaany Lab, Boston Children's Hospital / Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Kalaany NY.role: Studies how a tumour's metabolism depends on the metabolic state of the whole body, and hunts for nutrient dependencies that can be turned into treatments
Kalaany NY.sub: Associate Professor of Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School · Principal Investigator, Division of Endocrinology, Boston Children's Hospital · Associate Member, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard · Postdoctoral Fellow, Whitehead Institute / MIT (Sabatini lab) · PhD, UT Southwestern Medical Center
story: Kalaany was a postdoctoral fellow in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute when the team took the two mTOR complexes apart in living animals instead of in a dish. GUE2006 deleted raptor, rictor or mLST8 in mice and then asked which downstream signals broke: raptor-null embryos died as early as mTOR-null ones, while rictor-null and mLST8-null embryos survived longer and lost only the mTORC2 outputs. The clean split - Akt and PKCalpha on one side, S6K1 untouched on the other - came from comparing the three knockouts side by side.

Her own training was in metabolism rather than kinases. Her PhD at UT Southwestern, with David Mangelsdorf, was on the liver X receptors, the sensors that read a cell's cholesterol load and shift the balance between storing fat and burning it; her earliest paper, from the American University of Beirut, was about how mammary cells coordinate differentiation through gap junctions.

She now runs her own lab at Boston Children's Hospital, asking what a tumour eats and how that changes when the body around it is obese or diabetic. Her group showed that pancreatic tumours build their own ornithine from glutamine using the enzyme OAT - a direction of flow that adult tissues normally abandon after infancy - which makes OAT a target that should hit the tumour far harder than healthy tissue.

highlights.GUE2006: Co-author on the Sabatini-lab team that generated and analysed the raptor-, rictor- and mLST8-knockout mice behind the complex-by-complex split of mTOR function.

Kundu M.lab_name: Kundu Lab, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital (Memphis, Tennessee, USA)
Kundu M.role: Physician-scientist who works out what the autophagy-initiating kinases ULK1 and ULK2 actually do when a cell runs short of fuel
Kundu M.sub: Member, Department of Cell and Molecular Biology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital · Faculty, Department of Pathology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital · Research training, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · Clinical Pathology Residency and Hematopathology Fellowship, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania · Postdoctoral Fellow, NHGRI / NIH · MD and PhD, Jefferson Medical College · BS, Pennsylvania State University · Elected member, American Society for Clinical Investigation (2017)
story: KIM2011 showed that ULK1, the kinase that starts autophagy, is a switch with two hands on it. When glucose runs out, AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 at Ser317 and Ser777 and switches it on; when nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 phosphorylates Ser757, which both keeps ULK1 quiet and physically peels AMPK off it. Kundu is the second author, and the Ulk1-knockout mouse cells in which the paper's rescue experiments are done come out of her own work on the kinase.

Three years earlier she had shown what ULK1 is for in an animal. A maturing red blood cell has to dispose of its mitochondria and ribosomes before it becomes an erythrocyte, and Kundu found that Ulk1-null mice fail at precisely that step - yet ordinary starvation-induced autophagy still worked in them. ULK1 therefore belongs to the selective clearance machinery rather than being a core requirement for autophagy itself.

She trained as a physician first: MD and PhD at Jefferson Medical College, then clinical pathology and hematopathology at the University of Pennsylvania, with postdoctoral research at the NIH and at Penn. Her lab at St. Jude now studies ULK1 and ULK2 as coordinators of the metabolic stress response and somatic mitochondrial DNA mutations, including recent work on how glucose starvation reroutes traffic from the ER to the Golgi and remodels what a cell displays on its surface.

highlights.KIM2011: Second author, supplying the ULK1 loss-of-function background - the kinase's in vivo biology and the Ulk1-null mouse cells - on which the paper's genetic rescue experiments rest.

Kundu M.credit: Portrait: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

Zalzala S.role: Family physician who co-founded AgelessRx and, as senior author, co-led PEARL, a year-long randomised trial of low-dose intermittent rapamycin in healthy older adults
Zalzala S.sub: Founder and Medical Director, Root Causes Medical · Co-Founder and Chief Medical Officer, AgelessRx · Family physician, Dearborn, Michigan · Residency in Family Medicine, Wayne State University (2009–2012) · MD, Wayne State University School of Medicine (2009) · Board certified in Family Medicine, American Board of Family Medicine
story: Zalzala is the senior author of MOE2025 and one of the four people the paper credits with designing and implementing the study. PEARL (NCT04488601) was a 48-week, decentralized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial sponsored by AgelessRx with the University of California, Los Angeles as collaborator, comparing 5 mg or 10 mg of compounded rapamycin per week against placebo in healthy adults aged 50 to 85. Its authors describe it as the first completed long-term randomized trial of rapamycin taken for ageing itself rather than for a disease.

The pre-registered primary endpoint - visceral fat measured by DXA - did not move at all (p = 0.942). Because the endpoint had been fixed in advance, the trial has to report a null result, and the more interesting secondary findings, such as better lean tissue mass and less self-reported pain in women on the 10 mg dose, stay where they belong: as hypotheses for the next trial rather than as conclusions. Adverse events were comparable across all three arms, which is the safety answer the study was mainly built to give.

He is a board-certified family physician who trained at Wayne State University in Detroit and practised in Dearborn, Michigan, before co-founding AgelessRx, a telemedicine company that prescribes off-label longevity drugs, and serving as its chief medical officer; he also founded the clinic Root Causes Medical. The paper states the obvious conflict openly: all seven authors are employees and shareholders of AgelessRx, which is why the pre-registered, placebo-controlled design and the honest reporting of the null primary endpoint matter so much here.

highlights.MOE2025: Senior author; the paper's author contributions list him among the four people who designed and implemented the PEARL trial.

Moel M.role: Analyses trial and real-world data on repurposed longevity drugs at AgelessRx and led the reporting of the PEARL rapamycin trial
Moel M.sub: Co-Founder, AgelessRx · Researcher, Division of Research and Applied Sciences, AgelessRx · Research in computational microbial ecology, Department of Biology, Boston University · BA in Neurobiology, Boston University
story: Moel is the first author of MOE2025, the PEARL trial report, and one of the three people the paper credits with the data analysis. That analysis is what makes the paper worth reading: the pre-registered primary endpoint, visceral fat on a DXA scan, moved essentially not at all (p = 0.942), and the report says so plainly instead of promoting a secondary finding into the headline.

The secondary results he analysed are narrower than the press coverage suggested. Among women taking 10 mg of rapamycin weekly, lean tissue mass and self-reported pain improved; participants on 5 mg reported better emotional well-being and general health; blood biomarkers stayed inside normal ranges and adverse events were similar in all three groups. With 114 people finishing 48 weeks, these are signals worth chasing in a properly powered follow-up, not evidence that the drug works.

Before he moved into longevity medicine he was at Boston University, where he took a BA in neurobiology and co-authored a computational study with Daniel Segre's group on 'costless' metabolites - compounds a bacterium can release without paying any growth penalty, which helps explain how stable cross-feeding between species can arise at all. At AgelessRx he has stayed on the data side, also co-authoring the company's work on how much rapamycin actually reaches the blood from compounded versus commercial formulations.

highlights.MOE2025: First author; the paper's author contributions list him as one of the three people who performed the data analysis for the PEARL trial.

Harinath G.lab_name: Division of Research and Applied Sciences, AgelessRx (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Harinath G.role: Designs, analyses and writes up human studies of repurposed drugs such as rapamycin at a longevity telehealth company, turning trial and real-world prescription data into peer-reviewed evidence
Harinath G.sub: Research Scientist, Division of Research and Applied Sciences, AgelessRx, Ann Arbor, MI · Researcher, Driscoll Lab, Department of Molecular Biology & Biochemistry, Rutgers University · Contributor, NIA Caenorhabditis Intervention Testing Program (CITP)
story: Harinath is the second author of the PEARL trial report, the first completed year-long randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rapamycin taken for healthy human aging rather than for disease (NCT04488601, AgelessRx as sponsor with UCLA as collaborator). Participants aged 50–85 took either placebo or 5 mg or 10 mg of compounded rapamycin once a week for 48 weeks, and the endpoint the team had committed to in advance was visceral fat measured by DXA scan. That endpoint did not move at all, while secondary measures — lean tissue mass and self-reported pain in women on 10 mg, and self-reported well-being on 5 mg — did improve.

His own first-author work explains part of why a null result there is hard to interpret. In a 2025 GeroScience paper he showed that compounded rapamycin, the formulation PEARL used, reaches only about 31% of the blood level per milligram that commercial sirolimus does, that blood levels peak roughly two days after a dose, and that different people on the same dose end up in very different places. In practical terms: a weekly 10 mg compounded tablet may inhibit mTOR far less than the number on the label suggests, which is an argument for measuring rapamycin in blood rather than trusting the dose.

Before joining AgelessRx he worked in Monica Driscoll's lab at Rutgers on the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, co-authoring studies on how swim exercise protects aging muscle and neurons, how spaceflight changes neuronal shape, and how metformin and antioxidants extend or shorten life depending on the animal's genetic background. That last theme carries into his human work: in a 2024 review he argued that quality-of-life questionnaires such as the SF-36 should count as real endpoints in geroscience trials, because waiting decades for disease and death outcomes is not a practical way to test drugs meant to keep people healthy.

highlights.MOE2025: Second author on the PEARL results paper, the AgelessRx report of the 48-week safety profile, DXA body-composition outcomes and quality-of-life measures for weekly low-dose rapamycin.

Ali ES.lab_name: Ali Lab (Metabolism & Signaling), Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, University of Kentucky College of Medicine (Lexington, Kentucky, USA)
Ali ES.role: Showed as a Ben-Sahra-lab postdoc that ERK2 directly activates the purine-synthesis enzyme PFAS, and that mTORC1 increases bicarbonate import through SLC4A7 to fuel nucleotide synthesis. His Kentucky lab studies how growth signals control nucleotide metabolism in cancer
Ali ES.sub: Assistant Professor of Cancer Metabolism, Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, University of Kentucky College of Medicine (since 2024); Markey Cancer Center and Center for Cancer and Metabolism · postdoc, Issam Ben-Sahra lab, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (2017–2024) · PhD, Flinders University, Adelaide (Greg Barritt lab) · MS, Stockholm University (Göran Widmalm lab)
story: A dividing cell needs nucleotides, and nucleotides need carbon. Ali showed in ALI2022 that mTORC1 does not only switch on the enzymes that build them – it also organises the delivery of the raw material. Through S6K and the translation factor eIF4B, mTORC1 selectively raises translation of the mRNA for SLC4A7, a sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter, so the cell pulls in more bicarbonate from its surroundings. Take SLC4A7 away from cells with hyperactive mTORC1 and flux through both purine and pyrimidine synthesis drops, along with cell and tumour growth – and the internal pH does not budge, so the transporter is acting as a supply line, not as a pH valve.

Two years earlier he had drawn a boundary around the same claim. In ALI2020 he found that the other big growth pathway reaches purine synthesis by its own route: ERK2, but not its close relative ERK1, phosphorylates the enzyme PFAS at threonine 619. Because this is a direct modification of the enzyme rather than a change in how much of it is made, the effect lands within minutes. A cell with a PFAS that cannot be phosphorylated makes fewer purines, forms fewer colonies and grows smaller tumours – so in a RAS-driven tumour, purine supply cannot be read from mTORC1 activity alone.

He trained as a carbohydrate chemist in Stockholm and then as a liver physiologist at Flinders, where he worked on how fat accumulation deranges calcium handling in hepatocytes, before joining Issam Ben-Sahra at Northwestern. There he also contributed to VIL2021, which turned the SAM story around: the Atlas already had SAMTOR as a sensor of S-adenosylmethionine, and that paper showed mTORC1 also controls how much SAM the cell makes. Since 2024 he has run his own laboratory at the University of Kentucky, asking how tumours keep their nucleotide supply running and where that supply can be cut.

Sahu U.lab_name: Department of Biochemical Engineering and Biotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi (New Delhi, India)
Sahu U.role: Showed that the building blocks of RNA also tell mitochondria how fast to burn fuel
Sahu U.sub: Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemical Engineering and Biotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi (since 2026) · Research Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (2024–2026) · postdoc, Issam Ben-Sahra lab, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center (2017–2024) · PhD, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru (Pundi N. Rangarajan lab)
story: Nucleotides are usually described as the letters of DNA and RNA, and little else. Sahu's own headline finding is that one of them moonlights as a fuel-gauge signal. Working at Northwestern, he showed that UTP – a pyrimidine nucleotide – is the preferred partner of the enzyme TPK1, which manufactures thiamine pyrophosphate, the active form of vitamin B1. Mitochondria need that cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. So when a cell runs short of pyrimidines, TPK1 slows, the cofactor thins out, pyruvate oxidation drops, and the cell stops making new fat. A shortage of RNA letters becomes, several steps later, a shortage of lipid.

That result grew out of several years spent mapping how growth signalling arranges nucleotide supply in Issam Ben-Sahra's lab. In ALI2020 he worked on the discovery that ERK2 acts directly on the purine-synthesis enzyme PFAS – a fast chemical modification of the enzyme rather than a slow change in how much of it the cell makes. In VIL2021 he helped trace a different thread: mTORC1 pushes up production of SAM, the cell's universal methyl donor, and through it the m6A marks placed on mRNA, which in turn set the pace of protein synthesis.

He came to this from an unlikely direction. His PhD at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru was on the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris, where he characterised the zinc-finger transcription factor Mxr1p as a master switch for how the yeast handles methanol, acetate and amino acids as carbon sources. Since June 2026 he has run his own group at IIT Delhi, using metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics and CRISPR screens to ask how these regulatory circuits go wrong in metabolic disease.

highlights.ALI2020: Second author; contributed to the finding that ERK2 phosphorylates the purine-synthesis enzyme PFAS, a fast posttranslational route to nucleotide supply running parallel to mTORC1.
highlights.VIL2021: Second author; helped show that mTORC1 raises SAM synthesis and m6A mRNA modification to control the rate of protein synthesis.

O'Hara BP.role: As lab manager of Issam Ben-Sahra's lab at Northwestern, contributed to its studies of how mTORC1 and ERK control nucleotide synthesis, SAM production and bicarbonate import
O'Hara BP.sub: Associate Director, Lab Manager, Dispatch Bio (since 2022) · Research Lab Manager, Issam Ben-Sahra lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (2019–2022) · research and postdoctoral-affairs roles, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis (2006–2019), including the Department of Genetics · MSc, Biochemistry, University of Bath
story: Behind almost every fast-moving metabolism lab there is someone who keeps the cell lines alive, the reagents stocked and the experiments reproducible – and who is often at the bench doing the work as well. For three years that person in Issam Ben-Sahra's lab at Northwestern was Brendan O'Hara, and his name sits on the run of papers that mapped how growth signalling arranges the supply of nucleotides: the ERK2–PFAS link (ALI2020), the SAM and m6A route from mTORC1 to protein synthesis (VIL2021), and the mTORC1–SLC4A7 bicarbonate import axis (ALI2022).

He arrived there from St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis, where he spent more than a decade in research and postdoctoral-affairs roles. In the Department of Genetics he was a co-author on the 2018 report proposing mTORC3 – a third, rapamycin-insensitive mTOR assembly built around the transcription factor ETV7, offered as one explanation for why rapamycin so often disappoints as a cancer drug. That claim remains debated, but it is a reminder that the standard two-complex picture of mTOR has been challenged from inside the field.

Since 2022 he has worked in industry, as lab manager at the cancer-immunotherapy start-up Dispatch Bio, while continuing to appear as a co-author on work begun at Northwestern – including the 2024 study showing that matrix stiffness pushes cells to accumulate sorbitol, which then helps proteins condense into droplets.

highlights.ALI2022: Co-author; contributed to the work showing mTORC1 raises SLC4A7 translation to import bicarbonate for de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis.
highlights.ALI2020: Co-author on the discovery that ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS at T619, speeding up purine synthesis without changing how much enzyme is present.
highlights.VIL2021: Co-author on the study linking mTORC1 to SAM synthesis, m6A mRNA modification and the control of protein synthesis.

Hong S.sub: Hobbs Lab & Li (Xiaochun) Lab, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center
story: Sen Hong is a structural biologist working across the Hobbs and Li labs at UT Southwestern, applying cryo-electron microscopy to membrane proteins involved in lipid and cholesterol biology.

story: Xiaochun Li earned his PhD in structural biology at Tsinghua University in 2012, then trained as a postdoctoral fellow with Nobel laureate Günter Blobel at Rockefeller University. In 2017 he joined the Department of Molecular Genetics at UT Southwestern, working alongside Nobel laureates Joseph Goldstein and Michael Brown.

His lab uses cryo-electron microscopy and protein engineering to study membrane proteins with Sterol-Sensing Domains — including Niemann-Pick C1, HMG-CoA reductase, and the Hedgehog receptors Patched and Dispatched — that govern how cells sense and traffic cholesterol.
He holds the Eugene McDermott Distinguished Chair in Molecular Genetics and has received the Damon Runyon–Rachleff Innovation Award and the American Heart Association Established Investigator Award.

highlights.HON2026: Senior-authored the cryo-EM structure of TM6SF1, identifying it as a lysosomal cholesterol-binding regulator of mTORC1 signaling via LAMTOR1.

Halle JL.lab_name: Miller Lab, Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation (Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, USA)
Halle JL.role: Muscle-biology researcher studying how cancer, chemotherapy and cachexia disrupt skeletal-muscle protein turnover and autophagy
Halle JL.sub: Aging and Metabolism Research Program (Miller Lab), Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation · PhD, Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory, University of Tennessee Health Science Center
Halle JL.credit: Portrait: Miller Lab, Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation
story: Halle earned her PhD in James Carson's Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center and now works in Benjamin Miller's laboratory at the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation. Her doctoral research centered on how cancer and its treatment disrupt skeletal muscle, including the feeding regulation of muscle protein synthesis in tumour-bearing mice and the mechanisms by which chemotherapy damages muscle independent of the tumour itself.

In the 2026 myotube study, she led the experiments dissecting how FOLFOX chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin and oxaliplatin) disrupts autophagy flux and protein synthesis in cultured muscle cells through altered mTORC1 and AMPK signalling, and tested whether the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin or the AMPK activator metformin could reverse the damage.

highlights.HAL2026: First author; led the myotube experiments testing how FOLFOX chemotherapy disrupts mTORC1/AMPK-regulated autophagy flux and protein synthesis, and whether rapamycin could restore it.

Carson JA.lab_name: Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory, Texas A&M University (College Station, Texas, USA)
Carson JA.role: Muscle physiologist studying cancer-associated cachexia and how chemotherapy and exercise remodel skeletal-muscle metabolism
Carson JA.sub: Professor, Department of Kinesiology & Sport Management, and Executive Director, Huffines Institute for Sports Medicine & Human Performance, Texas A&M University (since 2024) · formerly Senior Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Studies, College of Health Professions, University of Tennessee Health Science Center (2018–2024) · 19 years on faculty at the University of South Carolina, where he built its muscle-biology research program and directed its Exercise Science PhD program
story: Carson leads the Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory and is among the field's established voices on cancer-associated cachexia — the muscle wasting that accompanies tumours and their treatment. He moved the laboratory to Texas A&M University in 2024, after six years at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center (2018–2024) and, before that, 19 years at the University of South Carolina building a muscle-biology research program and its Exercise Science doctoral program.

His laboratory combines in vivo and in vitro models to examine how mechanical, inflammatory and hormonal signals converge on skeletal-muscle anabolic and metabolic plasticity. The 2026 study he senior-authored asked a narrower version of that question: whether the muscle damage caused by FOLFOX chemotherapy runs through mTORC1 and AMPK's control of autophagy, and whether rapamycin — by restoring autophagy flux — could partly undo it.

highlights.HAL2026: Senior and corresponding author; his laboratory's long-standing work on cancer-associated cachexia framed the study's focus on chemotherapy-induced disruption of muscle mTORC1/AMPK signalling.

Yang Y.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing (Beijing, China)
Yang Y.role: Showed as first author that the liver-secreted protein hepassocin protects against age-related liver senescence and helps the liver regenerate
Yang Y.sub: State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing · Department of Engineering Physics, Tsinghua University, Beijing
story: Yang is based at the State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics in Beijing, where the 2026 study on which Yang is first author asked why aged livers regenerate so poorly after injury. The team traced the answer to Hepassocin (HPS), a liver-secreted hormone whose levels fall with age in both mice and elderly humans, and that normally activates AMPK — restraining mTOR — through a relay running from Annexin A2 (ANXA2) through ERK and p90RSK to the LKB1 kinase.

In mice engineered to lack HPS, that restraint failed: aged animals showed elevated mTOR activity, impaired autophagy, worsened cellular senescence, and a severely blunted capacity to regrow liver tissue after partial hepatectomy. The AMPK activator AICAR rescued the liver aging phenotype and regenerative capacity of aged HPS-knockout mice, and giving HPS itself improved regeneration in aged normal mice, pointing to the HPS-AMPK-mTOR axis as a lever for age-related liver decline.

highlights.YAN2026B: First author; led the identification of Hepassocin (HPS) as an AMPK-activating hepatokine that restrains mTOR and protects against age-related liver senescence and regeneration failure.

Yang X.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing (Beijing, China)
Yang X.role: Showed as senior author that the liver-secreted protein hepassocin protects against age-related liver senescence and helps the liver regenerate
Yang X.sub: Corresponding author, State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, National Center for Protein Sciences (Beijing), Academy of Military Medical Sciences · School of Pharmacy, Guangdong Pharmaceutical University · School of Basic Medical Sciences, University of South China
story: Yang is the corresponding author on the 2026 study identifying Hepassocin (HPS) as a hepatokine that keeps aging livers regenerating. His laboratory traced how HPS activates AMPK through an ANXA2-ERK-p90RSK-LKB1 relay, restraining mTOR activity, and showed that this axis weakens with age — leaving HPS-deficient aged mice with elevated mTOR signalling, impaired autophagy, and a much-reduced ability to recover liver mass after injury.
The work points to restoring HPS or AMPK signalling, rather than blocking mTOR directly, as a route to counteracting age-related liver dysfunction and regeneration failure.

highlights.YAN2026B: Senior and corresponding author; his laboratory showed that the hepatokine Hepassocin activates AMPK and protects against liver senescence and regeneration failure.

Sun L.lab_name: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) (Chongqing, China)
Sun L.role: Researcher studying phosphorylation-based control of autophagy initiation and its role in metabolic liver disease
Sun L.sub: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University), Chongqing, China
story: Sun is based in the Department of Clinical Biochemistry at Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) in Chongqing, China. In the 2026 Nature Communications study, Sun (first author) led the work uncovering how the deubiquitinase OTUB1 is switched on by starvation: ERK phosphorylates OTUB1, stabilizing it against degradation and letting it drive up DEPTOR, a natural brake on mTOR.

The team showed in mice that restoring this fasting-triggered ERK-OTUB1-DEPTOR-mTOR relay could counteract the mTOR-activating effect of a Western diet and ease progression of MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease), offering a mechanistic account of why fasting benefits the liver.

highlights.SUN2026B: First author; led the identification of the ERK-OTUB1-DEPTOR axis that inhibits mTOR and drives starvation-induced autophagy, with relevance to fasting's protective effect against MASLD.

Lian J.lab_name: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) (Chongqing, China)
Lian J.role: Biochemist studying deubiquitinase signalling in autophagy and metabolic disease
Lian J.sub: Corresponding author, Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University), Chongqing, China
story: Lian is a corresponding author in the Department of Clinical Biochemistry at Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) in Chongqing, China. The 2026 study from Lian's group traced how cells sense starvation at the molecular level: ERK-driven phosphorylation stabilizes the deubiquitinase OTUB1, which in turn boosts DEPTOR to hold mTOR in check and switch on autophagy.

The work extended this mechanism to disease relevance, showing in a mouse model that reactivating the fasting-triggered OTUB1-mTOR axis could blunt Western-diet-driven mTOR activation and slow the progression of MASLD.

highlights.SUN2026B: Corresponding author; the laboratory identified the phosphorylation-dependent OTUB1-DEPTOR-mTOR mechanism linking starvation to autophagy initiation and its relevance to fasting-based protection against MASLD.

Kondratov RV.lab_name: Kondratov Lab, Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease, Cleveland State University (Cleveland, Ohio, USA)
Kondratov RV.role: Showed the circadian clock protein BMAL1 gates TOR/mTOR signaling to control aging, and that calorie restriction's lifespan benefits require a working circadian clock
Kondratov RV.sub: Professor & Associate VP for Research, Cleveland State University · Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease
story: Roman Kondratov leads a laboratory at Cleveland State University studying how the circadian clock — the internal 24-hour timekeeping system — shapes metabolism, cardiovascular physiology, and aging. His lab reported that mice lacking BMAL1, the core circadian clock protein, develop an early-aging syndrome: a lifespan of about 9 months versus 28 months in normal mice, along with sarcopenia, osteoporosis, cataracts, and other age-related pathologies.

Because BMAL1 is a transcription factor that can influence many pathways, the lab has worked out which downstream systems carry the aging signal, including TOR signaling, the Sirtuin pathway, and IGF/IGFR signaling — pathways that govern cell growth and the organism's response to nutrients and stress. A parallel line of work in the lab established that calorie restriction, one of the most robust lifespan-extending interventions known, works partly by resetting circadian rhythms in gene expression, and that an intact circadian clock is necessary for calorie restriction to extend lifespan.

That combination of circadian timing and mTOR signaling is the throughline of the lab's more recent work, including showing that calorie restriction's effect on liver mTOR signaling is time-of-day dependent — the same theme carried into VEL2026, comparing calorie restriction to fasting-refeeding cycles.

highlights.VEL2026: Senior/corresponding author; showed caloric restriction engages anticipatory, circadian-clock-aligned control of hepatic mTOR signaling, distinct from the reactive, cue-driven signaling seen under fasting-refeeding cycles.

Velingkaar N.lab_name: Kondratov Lab, Cleveland State University (where this work was done) (Cleveland, Ohio, USA)

Velingkaar N.sub: Postdoctoral Fellow, Kondratov Lab, Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease, Cleveland State University
Velingkaar N.credit: Portrait: Cleveland State University (Graduate Student Research Council)
story: Nikkhil Velingkaar trained as a PhD student in the Kondratov lab at Cleveland State University, where his dissertation research (supported by a CSU Dissertation Research Award) examined how internal circadian clocks interact to regulate daily rhythms in metabolic activity. He has continued in the lab as a postdoctoral fellow.

His work has focused on calorie restriction as a circadian phenomenon: earlier studies from the lab, the first with Velingkaar as second author (Tulsian et al., 2018) and the second as first author (2021), showed that calorie restriction's effect on liver mTOR signaling depends on time of day, and that a two-meal calorie-restriction schedule induces 12-hour metabolic rhythms and improves glucose homeostasis. VEL2026 extends that line of work by directly comparing calorie restriction to fasting-refeeding cycles matched for food intake and fasting duration.

highlights.VEL2026: First author; distinguished caloric restriction's anticipatory, clock-aligned metabolic control (including hepatic mTOR signaling) from the reactive signaling seen under fasting-refeeding cycles.

story: Mandeep Singh is a professor of medicine and interventional cardiologist in the Department of Cardiovascular Diseases at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, where he trained as an interventional cardiology fellow in the late 1990s.

In 2026 he was the corresponding author on a trial testing rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), working alongside aging researchers James Kirkland (Mayo's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging) and Dudley Lamming (University of Wisconsin-Madison).

Marchetti L.sub: University of Trento (CIBIO) · Fondazione COSBI, Rovereto
story: Luca Marchetti holds a PhD in computer science from the University of Verona and is an associate professor in the CIBIO department at the University of Trento, where he heads the Laboratory of Computational Modeling. He is also a consultant at the Microsoft Research - University of Trento Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI).

His work applies quantitative systems pharmacology and physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modeling, often with machine learning, to complex disease data. In 2026 he was senior author on a multivariate survival analysis of the RAP-ALS clinical trial of rapamycin in ALS patients, which found a signal of longer survival in treated C9orf72 mutation carriers.

Rainero E.role: Studies how cancer cells use the extracellular matrix as a nutrient and signaling source; senior author on a 2026 study linking collagen I to mTORC1 activation in cancer cells

story: Elena Rainero leads a lab in the School of Biosciences at the University of Sheffield studying the crosstalk between the extracellular matrix (ECM), integrin trafficking and cancer cell metabolism, including how cancer cells internalise and repurpose ECM components as a nutrient source under metabolic stress.

In 2026 her lab reported that collagen I drives alpha2beta1 integrin-dependent mTORC1/S6 activation and boosts amino acid import via the LAT1-4F2hc transporter, letting breast and pancreatic cancer cells survive and grow in nutrient-poor, collagen-rich tumor stroma.

highlights.NAZ2026: Senior author showing collagen I drives mTORC1/S6 activation and LAT1-4F2hc-mediated amino acid import in cancer cells.

Raffel S.lab_name: AG Raffel, Heidelberg University Hospital (Heidelberg, Germany)
Raffel S.role: Studies metabolic vulnerabilities of leukemia stem cells; senior author on a 2026 Blood paper on IDH3, citrate and mTORC1 in AML stem cell drug resistance
Raffel S.sub: Heidelberg University Hospital · Emmy Noether Group (DFG)
story: Simon Raffel runs an independent Emmy Noether research group at Heidelberg University Hospital studying the metabolic biology of leukemia stem cells (LSCs), building on earlier work (recognised with the 2017 Walter Schulz Prize) on amino acid breakdown in leukemia stem cells. He remains affiliated with HI-STEM and the Heidelberg-based LeukoSyStem consortium.

In 2026 his lab identified the TCA-cycle enzyme IDH3 as a selective regulator of AML leukemic stem cell maintenance: knocking down IDH3A raises intracellular citrate, activates AMPK and suppresses mTORC1, and sensitises resistant AML cells to the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax.

highlights.DEM2026: Senior author identifying the IDH3A-citrate-AMPK-mTORC1 axis as a route to overcome venetoclax resistance in AML stem cells.

Zhou X.role: Built TORCAR, an early genetically encoded FRET reporter that lets mTORC1 activity be watched in living cells
Zhou X.sub: Senior Scientist, Eikon Therapeutics · formerly postdoc (Johns Hopkins, 2010–2015) and Associate Project Scientist (UC San Diego, 2015–2022) in Jin Zhang's lab · PhD, Medicinal Chemistry, University of Minnesota
story: Xin Zhou earned a PhD in medicinal chemistry at the University of Minnesota, then joined Jin Zhang's lab at Johns Hopkins as a postdoc in 2010. The lab builds fluorescent sensors that show when an enzyme is working inside a living cell. When the lab moved to UC San Diego in 2015, Zhou moved with it as an associate project scientist and stayed until 2022, then went to industry as a scientist at Eikon Therapeutics in California.

TORCAR is a small protein that mTORC1 phosphorylates, built so that the phosphorylation changes how two fluorescent parts pass energy to each other (FRET). A microscope can read that change in a single living cell, second by second. Before such reporters, mTORC1 activity was usually measured in lysates of many cells at fixed time points. With TORCAR the team saw mTORC1 working not only at the lysosome but also in the cytosol, the nucleus and at the plasma membrane, and saw a short calcium spike after growth-factor stimulation feed into mTORC1 activity.

highlights.ZHO2015: First author on TORCAR, a FRET sensor that shows mTORC1 activity changing in living cells and in different parts of the cell, depending on which signal switched it on.

Kubota H.lab_name: Division of Integrated Omics, Kyushu University (Fukuoka, Japan)
Kubota H.role: Systems biologist who showed that the insulin pathway carries different messages in the timing of its signal, and that S6K, the mTORC1 target, reads only the fast part
Kubota H.sub: Professor, Division of Integrated Omics, Research Center for Transomics Medicine, Medical Institute of Bioregulation, Kyushu University · PhD in Science, University of Tokyo
story: Hiroyuki Kubota earned his doctorate at the University of Tokyo in 2001 and spent the following years there, from 2009 as an assistant professor in Shinya Kuroda's systems biology group. In 2014 he became a professor at Kyushu University's Medical Institute of Bioregulation, where his lab combines measurements of many molecular layers at once (proteins, their phosphorylation, metabolites) with mathematical models.

His two studies in the Atlas ask one question at two scales: can a cell tell a short burst of insulin from a steady level? In rat liver cells (KUB2012) and then in living rats (KUB2018), the answer was yes. The same pathway passes on both patterns, and each downstream molecule picks the part it responds to. S6K, which sits directly under mTORC1, followed the quick pulse. G6Pase, a glucose-making enzyme, followed the steady baseline. That makes the timing of a signal, not only its size, part of the message.

highlights.KUB2012: First author. In liver cells, a short insulin pulse and a steady insulin dose were passed through AKT as two different time patterns, and S6K responded only to the fast one.
highlights.KUB2018: First author. The in-vivo follow-up in rat liver: the insulin receptor carries every insulin pattern, and downstream molecules pick out different parts of it, with S6K reading the pulse-like extra secretion.

Kubota H.credit: Portrait: Medical Institute of Bioregulation, Kyushu University

Kuroda S.lab_name: Kuroda Lab (Systems Biology), University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Kuroda S.role: Leads a systems biology lab that studies how cells decode the timing of hormone signals, with insulin and mTORC1-S6K as the main test case
Kuroda S.sub: Professor, Department of Biological Sciences, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo
story: Shinya Kuroda runs the systems biology laboratory in the University of Tokyo's Department of Biological Sciences. His group starts from a simple observation: the same stimulus can lead to different outcomes depending on how it arrives over time. They pair experiments with computer models to work out how signalling networks turn a pattern into a decision, and more recently how whole metabolic networks shift in obesity.

He is senior author on both Atlas studies on this idea, KUB2012 in cultured liver cells and KUB2018 in the liver of living rats. Together they show that insulin information is split by timing. S6K, the kinase mTORC1 switches on, responds to fast insulin pulses, while other targets respond to the slow baseline. This is one of the clearest cases in the Atlas where the shape of a signal over time matters as much as how strong it is, which is the question behind my own focus on mTOR dynamics.

highlights.KUB2012: Senior author. Showed that the AKT pathway carries pulse and sustained insulin signals as separate time patterns, which downstream targets such as S6K decode selectively.
highlights.KUB2018: Senior author. Confirmed the same timing code in living rat liver and used modelling to explain it through network structure, sensitivity and time constants.

Zhang J.lab_name: Jin Zhang Lab, UC San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Zhang J.role: Builds fluorescent biosensors that show where and when signalling enzymes are active inside living cells; senior author of TORCAR, an early live-cell reporter of mTORC1
Zhang J.sub: Vice Chair and Professor of Pharmacology, UC San Diego School of Medicine (also Bioengineering and Chemistry & Biochemistry) · PhD, University of Chicago
story: Jin Zhang studied chemistry at Tsinghua University, earned her PhD at the University of Chicago and trained as a postdoc with Roger Tsien and Susan Taylor at UC San Diego. She led a lab at Johns Hopkins from 2003 and moved it back to UC San Diego in 2015. Her group makes genetically encoded sensors, proteins that glow differently when a particular kinase touches them, and uses them to map signalling inside single cells.

TORCAR, from her Johns Hopkins lab, applied that approach to mTORC1. It showed mTORC1 activity in several places at once (lysosome, cytosol, nucleus, plasma membrane) and showed that growth factors and amino acids light up different sets of those places. Watching mTORC1 in real time in one cell is the kind of measurement that later studies of mTORC1 oscillation depend on.

highlights.ZHO2015: Senior author on TORCAR, an early genetically encoded reporter of mTORC1 activity, which showed signal-specific mTORC1 activity in different parts of living cells.

Bobok N.role: Physician-scientist and founder of a Swiss longevity/skincare company; author of a 2026 review situating mTOR as an integrative signaling hub across the hallmarks of aging

story: Natalia Bobok is a physician (MD, PhD) and longevity scientist who founded INSTYTUTUM AG, a Zug, Switzerland-based skincare and longevity company, in 2014, where she serves as Chief Scientific Officer. Before INSTYTUTUM she held senior scientific and executive roles across biotech, pharmaceutical manufacturing and aesthetic medicine, including building the international skincare brand Hyalual.

In this Atlas she is the sole author of a 2026 review in Aging (Albany NY) that frames mTOR as a dynamic, context-dependent signaling hub linking nutrient sensing, proteostasis, autophagy and stress adaptation to the hallmarks of aging, and surveys how major geroprotective interventions partly converge on the pathway.

highlights.BOB2026: Sole author of a 2026 review arguing mTOR functions as an integrative signaling hub across the hallmarks of aging, with causal evidence for lifespan regulation strongest in model organisms and human data remaining associative.

story: Hongliang Li is Vice President of Gannan Medical University in Ganzhou, China, and Executive Director of its State Key Laboratory of New Targets Discovery and Drug Development for Major Diseases, where he also directs the Gannan Innovation and Translational Medicine Research Institute. His research focuses on the mechanisms, prevention and treatment of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, including cardiac remodeling, and on developing animal models of these diseases.

He is the senior author of a 2026 Circulation study identifying LAPTM4A as a novel booster of mTORC1 signaling in cardiomyocytes, showing that it drives pathological cardiac hypertrophy through a NEDD4L-AKT-mTORC1 axis, and that the FDA-approved compound magnolol suppresses LAPTM4A with cardioprotective effect in mice.

highlights.HU2026: Senior author identifying LAPTM4A as a novel mTORC1-activating driver of pathological cardiac hypertrophy via NEDD4L-mediated AKT ubiquitination.

Hu Y.role: First author of a 2026 Circulation study identifying LAPTM4A as a novel mTORC1 activator driving pathological cardiac hypertrophy
Hu Y.sub: Gannan Innovation and Translational Medicine Research Institute, School of Pharmacy, First Affiliated Hospital, Gannan Medical University, Ganzhou, China
story: Yufeng Hu is affiliated with the Gannan Innovation and Translational Medicine Research Institute at the First Affiliated Hospital of Gannan Medical University in Ganzhou, China. No further public biographical details were found.

Hu is first author of a 2026 Circulation study that screened lysosomal genes in cardiomyocytes and identified LAPTM4A as a novel booster of mTORC1 signaling, driving pathological cardiac hypertrophy through NEDD4L-mediated AKT ubiquitination.

highlights.HU2026: First author identifying LAPTM4A as a novel driver of mTORC1-dependent pathological cardiac hypertrophy in mice and rats.

Hu Y.lab_name: Gannan Innovation and Translational Medicine Research Institute, Gannan Medical University (Ganzhou, China)

Huang H.role: Senior/corresponding author of a 2026 Nature Communications study identifying the SPOP–ZMYND8–NEK7 mechanism of mTOR-inhibitor resistance in kidney cancer
Huang H.sub: Professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology & Professor of Urology, Mayo Clinic College of Medicine and Science, Rochester, MN
story: Haojie Huang is a professor at Mayo Clinic College of Medicine and Science, jointly appointed in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and in Urology. His lab has worked on prostate cancer biology and molecular oncology since the 1990s, with a long-standing focus on androgen-receptor signaling, phosphorylation pathways and the epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms of cancer cell growth.

In this Atlas he is senior/corresponding author of a 2026 Nature Communications study on why kidney cancer cells become resistant to mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus and temsirolimus. The work traces resistance to an SPOP-driven ubiquitination switch on the histone reader ZMYND8, which turns on the kinase NEK7 as an escape route around blocked mTOR signaling, and shows that a NEK7-targeting PROTAC restores drug sensitivity in mice.

highlights.TAN2026: Senior/corresponding author identifying a SPOP-ZMYND8-NEK7 mechanism of resistance to mTOR inhibitors (everolimus/temsirolimus) in kidney cancer, and validating a NEK7-targeting PROTAC that restores drug sensitivity in cells and mice.

Huang H.lab_name: Huang Lab, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)

Zhai Z.role: Senior author of a 2026 Nature study identifying Lsp2 as a rapamycin-resistant mTORC1 effector that extends lifespan in Drosophila when removed
Zhai Z.sub: Group Leader, Hunan Research Center of the Basic Discipline for Developmental Biology, College of Life Sciences, Hunan Normal University, Changsha, China · PhD, Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology & Heidelberg University
Zhai Z.credit: Portrait: Hunan Provincial Key Laboratory of Animal Intestinal Function and Regulation, Hunan Normal University
story: Zongzhao Zhai trained in Germany, first as a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology in Tübingen and then at Heidelberg University, before returning to China to lead his own group at Hunan Normal University. His lab studies innate immunity and physiology in Drosophila, including host defense, gut homeostasis, mTORC1 signaling and nutrient sensing.

In this Atlas he is senior author of a 2026 Nature study showing that Lsp2, previously known only as a fat-body storage protein, is also a nutrient-induced feedback activator of mTORC1 that drives translation of TOP-motif mRNAs (mostly ribosomal proteins) — a rapamycin-resistant arm of mTORC1 output. Genetically removing Lsp2 extends fly lifespan without a reproductive cost, revealing a route from mTORC1 activity to longevity that is distinct from rapamycin's own effects.

highlights.WAN2026: Senior author showing that Lsp2 is a nutrient-induced feedback activator of mTORC1 driving TOP mRNA translation, and that removing it extends Drosophila lifespan through a rapamycin-independent mechanism.

Zhai Z.lab_name: Zhai Lab, Hunan Normal University (Changsha, China)

Li TL.lab_name: Bateup Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Li TL.role: Co-first author of a 2026 Nature study showing mTORC1 hyperactivity drives reactive astrocytes as a primary, seizure-independent consequence of TSC2 loss, implicating glial dysfunction as a driver of tuberous sclerosis pathology
Li TL.sub: Postdoctoral Fellow, Bateup Lab · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology & Department of Neuroscience, University of California, Berkeley
story: Thomas (Tommy) L. Li is a postdoctoral fellow in Helen Bateup's lab at UC Berkeley (Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and Department of Neuroscience). He earned his PhD in Chemistry at Stanford University in the labs of Bianxiao Cui and Sergiu Pașca, where he worked on a genetically encoded magnetic protein crystal and on flexible mesh electrodes for long-term electrophysiological recording from brain organoids. In the Bateup lab he studies the function of a brain organoid model of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).

In this Atlas he is co-first author of a 2026 Nature study, from Helen Bateup's lab, using human brain organoids carrying TSC2 mutations plus patient-derived cortical tuber tissue to show that hyperactive mTORC1 signaling biases neural progenitors toward becoming enlarged, pro-inflammatory reactive astrocytes — independent of seizure activity — implicating glial dysfunction as a driver of tuberous sclerosis pathology rather than only a downstream consequence of seizures.

highlights.LI2026C: Co-first author using human brain organoids and patient tuber tissue to show that TSC2 loss drives neural progenitors into reactive, pro-inflammatory astrocytes independent of seizures.

Bateup HS.role: Senior/corresponding author of a 2026 Nature study showing mTORC1 hyperactivity drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis
Bateup HS.sub: Associate Professor of Molecular and Cell Biology & Neuroscience, University of California, Berkeley · Weill Neurohub Investigator · PhD, The Rockefeller University
story: Helen Bateup directs a lab in UC Berkeley's Department of Molecular and Cell Biology studying how genetic mutations linked to epilepsy and autism — especially in the TSC1/TSC2–mTORC1 pathway — disrupt neural development, synaptic function and circuit excitability. She trained as a PhD student at The Rockefeller University and is a Weill Neurohub Investigator.

In this Atlas she is senior/corresponding author of a 2026 Nature study using human brain organoids grown for 9+ months (to replicate human developmental timelines) alongside resected tuber tissue from tuberous sclerosis patients. The work shows that TSC2 loss biases neural progenitors toward reactive, pro-inflammatory astrocytes in a cell-autonomous manner — independent of seizures — implicating glial dysfunction, not just neuronal hyperexcitability, as a driver of TSC pathology and a potential therapeutic target.

highlights.LI2026C: Senior/corresponding author demonstrating that mTORC1-hyperactive neural progenitors become pro-inflammatory reactive astrocytes in a cell-autonomous manner, independent of seizure activity — implicating glial dysfunction as a driver, not only a consequence, of TSC pathology.
highlights.BAT2013: First author showing that Tsc1 loss in mouse hippocampal neurons weakens their inhibitory input and drives network hyperexcitability and seizure susceptibility, which rapamycin normalised.

Bateup HS.lab_name: Bateup Lab, UC Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)

Kell L.lab_name: Cox Lab of Ageing and Cell Senescence, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Kell L.role: First author identifying a direct genoprotective effect of rapamycin against DNA damage in ageing human immune cells
Kell L.sub: DPhil student, Department of Biochemistry, Oriel College, University of Oxford · Mellon Scholar in Ageing and Cell Senescence · BA, University College London
story: Loren Kell grew up in North Wales and read for a BA at University College London before moving to Oxford for postgraduate work. She is now a DPhil student in the Department of Biochemistry at Oriel College, working in Lynne Cox's laboratory on ageing and cell senescence as the college's Mellon Scholar in the field.

Her research asks how the immune system changes with time, and specifically whether mTOR inhibition can rejuvenate senescent immune cells — work that extends into clinical trials examining immune-system changes in older adults given mTOR inhibitors.

highlights.KEL2026: First author: shows rapamycin protects ageing human T cells from DNA damage directly, independent of protein synthesis, cell-cycle arrest or autophagy, and reduces a senescence marker (p21) in a placebo-controlled human trial of low-dose rapamycin.

Alsaleh G.lab_name: Alsaleh Group, Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Alsaleh G.role: Senior author studying autophagy and immune-cell ageing; identified a genoprotective mechanism for rapamycin
Alsaleh G.sub: Associate Professor & Versus Arthritis Career Development Fellow, Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, University of Oxford · Official Fellow, Reuben College · PharmD & PhD, University of Strasbourg
story: Ghada Alsaleh trained as a pharmacist before completing a PharmD and PhD at the University of Strasbourg. She joined Katja Simon's group at Oxford in 2017 as a postdoctoral researcher working on autophagy in ageing immune cells, and now leads her own group at the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology as a Versus Arthritis Career Development Fellow and Associate Professor.

Her lab studies how declining autophagy and lysosomal function — including falling TFEB activity — drive immune-cell dysfunction with age, with translational programmes spanning osteoarthritis and, through the UK's first Space Innovation Lab at the Botnar Institute, the effects of microgravity on ageing.

highlights.KEL2026: Senior author: identifies a previously unrecognised 'genoprotective' mechanism for rapamycin — direct protection of ageing human immune cells against DNA damage — including a placebo-controlled human trial showing reduced p21 (a senescence marker) with low-dose rapamycin.

Zaufel A.role: Researcher studying bile acid metabolism and mTORC1 signaling in liver disease
Zaufel A.sub: Researcher, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Medical University of Graz, Austria
story: Alex Zaufel works in the Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at the Medical University of Graz, where his research centers on bile acid metabolism and signaling — including how bile acid composition and stereochemistry intersect with nuclear receptor signaling (FXR) and, in his most recent work, with mTORC1 nutrient sensing.

First author of a 2026 Science Advances study identifying an mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling axis that reshapes hepatic bile acid metabolism during metabolic adaptation, with reversal by rapamycin and dietary protein restriction, and correlation to metabolic outcomes in human MASLD patients.

highlights.ZAU2026: First author: identifies an mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling axis controlling hepatic bile-acid diversification, reversible by rapamycin and protein restriction.

Zaufel A.lab_name: Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Medical University of Graz (Graz, Austria)
Zaufel A.credit: Portrait: Institute of Molecular Medicine III, University Hospital Düsseldorf

Moustafa T.role: Researcher in hepatic metabolism and bile acid signaling
Moustafa T.sub: University Assistant (Univ.-Ass., Mag. Dr. rer. nat.), Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Medical University of Graz, Austria
story: Tarek Moustafa is a University Assistant in the Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at the Medical University of Graz, working on metabolic regulation in the liver, including bile acid and nutrient-signaling pathways.

Senior/corresponding author of a 2026 Science Advances study showing that hepatic mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling state drives bile-acid diversification during metabolic adaptation, with effects reversed by rapamycin treatment or dietary protein restriction and correlating with metabolic outcomes in human MASLD patients.

highlights.ZAU2026: Senior/corresponding author: mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling shapes hepatic bile-acid metabolism, reversible by rapamycin and protein restriction, with correlation to human MASLD outcomes.
