Nolasco LNRA.role: Postdoctoral researcher in human molecular genetics
Nolasco LNRA.sub: Postdoctoral researcher and collaborating professor, Núcleo de Genética Humana e Molecular, Universidade Federal do Espírito Santo (UFES), Brazil · PhD in Biotechnology, UFES (2024)
story: Lyvia Neves Rebello Alves Nolasco is a postdoctoral researcher at the Núcleo de Genética Humana e Molecular at UFES in Brazil, where she has worked since her master's studies on molecular genetics and disease risk, more recently including cancer epigenetics and environmental exposures.

First author of a 2026 review in Biochimica et Biophysica Acta, General Subjects surveying rapamycin's biology and medicine, from its discovery as an antifungal macrolide through its role as the founding mTOR inhibitor and its clinical and healthspan applications.

highlights.NOL2026: First author of a comprehensive review of rapamycin/mTOR biology, pharmacology and clinical translation.

Nolasco LNRA.lab_name: Núcleo de Genética Humana e Molecular, Universidade Federal do Espírito Santo (Vitória, Brazil)

Louro ID.role: Professor of human and molecular genetics
Louro ID.sub: Full Professor, Núcleo de Genética Humana e Molecular, Universidade Federal do Espírito Santo (UFES), Brazil · PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, University of Alabama at Birmingham (1999)
story: Iúri Drumond Louro is a Full Professor at the Federal University of Espírito Santo (UFES) in Brazil, where he leads the Núcleo de Genética Humana e Molecular. He trained in medicine at UFES and completed a PhD and postdoctoral fellowship in molecular cancer genetics at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

His research spans cancer genetics, infectious-disease genetics and forensic genetics. Senior/corresponding author of a 2026 review in Biochimica et Biophysica Acta, General Subjects on rapamycin's mechanisms and clinical translation, co-authored with members of his UFES group.

highlights.NOL2026: Senior/corresponding author of a comprehensive review of rapamycin/mTOR biology, pharmacology and clinical translation.

Albeck JG.lab_name: Albeck Lab, UC Davis (Davis, California, USA)
Albeck JG.role: Measures mTORC1, AMPK and other metabolic signals in single living cells, following how they change over minutes and hours
Albeck JG.sub: Professor, Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of California, Davis · PhD, Computational and Systems Biology, MIT (2007)
story: John Albeck earned his PhD in computational and systems biology at MIT in 2007 and joined the University of California, Davis in 2013. His lab builds fluorescent reporters and imaging pipelines that follow cell signalling in individual living cells over time, instead of averaging a whole dish into one number.

For mTOR, that approach showed that mTORC1–TFEB signalling in single cells adjusts continuously to amino acids and insulin, fluctuating together with AMPK and AKT as nutrient levels shift. The lab has also built biosensors for AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, so that several metabolic signals can be imaged in the same cell at once.

highlights.SPA2023: Senior author: live single-cell imaging showing mTORC1–TFEB signalling adjusts continuously to amino acids and insulin.

Milias-Argeitis A.lab_name: Milias-Argeitis Lab, Molecular Systems Biology, University of Groningen (Groningen, Netherlands)
Milias-Argeitis A.role: Follows TORC1 activity through the cell cycle in single yeast cells and builds light-controlled tools to perturb it
Milias-Argeitis A.sub: Associate Professor, Molecular Systems Biology, Groningen Biomolecular Sciences and Biotechnology Institute, University of Groningen · PhD, Automatic Control Laboratory, ETH Zurich (2013)
story: Andreas Milias-Argeitis came to biology from engineering. He studied electrical engineering at the University of Patras, earned his PhD at the Automatic Control Laboratory of ETH Zurich in 2013, and was a postdoc in ETH's Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering before joining the University of Groningen in 2016.

His group films hundreds of single yeast cells to ask how growth signals are coordinated with division. They found that TORC1 and PKA activity towards ribosome biogenesis rises and falls in step with the cell cycle even when conditions outside the cell stay constant. In 2026 they added OPTO-Cln2, a light-controlled switch for G1 progression, to test how that oscillation is tied to the cycle.

highlights.GUE2022: Senior author: TORC1/PKA output to ribosome biogenesis oscillates with the yeast cell cycle under constant conditions.

Cappell SD.lab_name: Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, NCI (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Cappell SD.role: Studies how single cells commit to dividing; showed that mTOR briefly switches off the APC/C to give cells a pulse of glycolysis at cell cycle entry
Cappell SD.sub: Stadtman Investigator, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute · PhD, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
story: Steven Cappell did his PhD at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in the lab of Henrik Dohlman and was a Damon Runyon postdoctoral fellow with Tobias Meyer at Stanford University. He joined the National Cancer Institute in 2017, where his lab studies how individual cells decide to enter the cell cycle.

In 2025 his group showed that, right after growth-factor stimulation, mTOR phosphorylates CDH1 and briefly inactivates the APC/C, letting the glycolytic enzyme PFKFB3 build up until a slower phosphatase restores APC/C activity. The result is a short, timed pulse of glycolysis that cells need to enter the cycle — a case where the timing of an mTOR-driven signal, not only its size, does the work.

highlights.PAU2025: Senior author: transient mTOR-driven APC/C inactivation creates the pulse of glycolysis required for cell cycle entry.

Scadden DT.lab_name: Scadden Lab, Massachusetts General Hospital & Harvard Stem Cell Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Scadden DT.role: Stem cell and leukaemia biologist whose lab imaged mTORC1 activity in live mice and showed that well-timed mTORC1 inhibition kills more leukaemia cells
Scadden DT.sub: Gerald and Darlene Jordan Professor of Medicine, Harvard University · Director, Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital · Co-Director, Harvard Stem Cell Institute
story: David Scadden co-founded the Harvard Stem Cell Institute with Douglas Melton and founded the Center for Regenerative Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital, which he directs. He earlier led the Hematologic Malignancies Program at the MGH Cancer Center and was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2012.

His lab studies blood stem cells and the bone-marrow niche they live in. In a 2021 study of acute myeloid leukaemia, the group built fluorescent probes to follow mTORC1 activity in single leukaemia cells inside the bone marrow of live mice. mTORC1 activity fell as the disease progressed but rose at the point of maximal response to chemotherapy, and inhibiting mTORC1 at that moment killed more leukaemia cells.

highlights.OKI2021: Senior author: intravital imaging of mTORC1 dynamics in AML, supporting time-specific inhibitor therapy.

Ktistakis NT.lab_name: Ktistakis Group, Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Ktistakis NT.role: Uses live imaging to follow the first minutes of autophagy and of mTORC1 activation
Ktistakis NT.sub: Group Leader, Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute, Cambridge (since 1996)
story: Nicholas Ktistakis was a postdoctoral researcher and then an instructor at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas before starting his group at the Babraham Institute in Cambridge in 1996. His lab studies how autophagy begins — how the membrane that will engulf cellular material first forms — and the signals that switch it on and off.

In 2016 the group imaged the mTORC1 component RAPTOR in living cells and found that mTORC1 moves to lysosomes within two minutes of adding amino acids and peaks within five, while its classic targets are phosphorylated later. That gap suggests mTORC1 passes through the lysosome only briefly before acting on substrates elsewhere.

highlights.MAN2016: Senior author: live imaging of mTORC1 lysosomal translocation within minutes of amino acid addition.

Bally-Cuif L.lab_name: Zebrafish Neurogenetics Unit, Institut Pasteur (Paris, France)
Bally-Cuif L.role: Studies how adult neural stem cells in the zebrafish brain move between dormancy and activation
Bally-Cuif L.sub: Head, Zebrafish Neurogenetics Unit, Department of Developmental and Stem Cell Biology, Institut Pasteur (CNRS UMR3738)
story: Laure Bally-Cuif did her PhD in Paris, at the Hôpital de la Salpêtrière and the École Normale Supérieure, and was an EMBO postdoctoral fellow at Princeton. She joined the CNRS in 1996, led an independent group at the Helmholtz Center in Munich from 2000, became a CNRS research director at the Paris-Saclay Institute for Neuroscience in 2009, and has headed her unit at the Institut Pasteur since 2016.

Her lab uses the adult zebrafish brain, which keeps making new neurons throughout life, to study how neural stem cells stay dormant and when they wake up. A 2026 preprint from the group reports that mTORC1 activity is enriched during a long quiescent phase in which these stem cells become able to activate, and that mTORC1 sets the tempo of that progression while protecting stemness.

highlights.THE2026: Senior author (preprint): mTORC1 sets the tempo of quiescent neural stem cells' progression toward activation.

Perroy J.lab_name: Perroy Team, Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle (IGF) (Montpellier, France)
Perroy J.role: Neurobiologist who co-led AIMTOR, a biosensor for watching mTOR activity live in single cells and in separate parts of the cell
Perroy J.sub: CNRS Research Director (DR1) and team leader, Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle, Montpellier · PhD, University of Montpellier (2001)
story: Julie Perroy earned her PhD in cellular biology at the University of Montpellier in 2001 and leads a team at the Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle (CNRS, INSERM, University of Montpellier). She has been a CNRS research director since 2012 (DR1 since 2020) and held an ERC Consolidator Grant from 2015 to 2021.

With Vincent Ollendorff's group she co-led AIMTOR, a genetically encoded BRET biosensor that reports mTOR activity in living cells, in single cells and in specific compartments such as the lysosome surface, the nucleus and the area near mitochondria. In neurons it showed that higher neuronal activity increases mTOR signalling, and it picked up mTOR signalling defects in mouse models of autism spectrum disorder.

highlights.BOU2020: Co-senior author on AIMTOR, the BRET biosensor for live, subcellular readout of mTOR activity.

Kinoshita T.role: First author identifying how TCR-driven mTORC1 signaling epigenetically locks in Foxp3 expression in regulatory T cells
Kinoshita T.sub: Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, The University of Tokyo
story: Tomohide Kinoshita works in Shohei Hori's Laboratory of Immunology and Microbiology at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences.

First author of a 2026 PNAS study showing that strong, sustained T-cell receptor signaling activates mTORC1 to boost translation of the TET2 (and likely TET3) DNA-demethylation enzymes, epigenetically locking in stable Foxp3 expression during regulatory T cell differentiation — revealing an unrecognized role for mTORC1 in immune tolerance.

highlights.KIN2026: First author: shows TCR-mTORC1 signaling stabilizes Foxp3 expression in regulatory T cells by boosting TET2/TET3 translation and TSDR demethylation.

Kinoshita T.lab_name: Hori Lab (Laboratory of Immunology and Microbiology), The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)

Hori S.role: Senior author; laboratory head studying regulatory T cell differentiation and immune tolerance
Hori S.sub: Professor, Laboratory of Immunology and Microbiology, Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, The University of Tokyo
story: Shohei Hori leads the Laboratory of Immunology and Microbiology at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, having previously headed the Laboratory for Immune Homeostasis at RIKEN's Center for Integrative Medical Sciences.

Senior author of a 2026 PNAS study defining how mTORC1 activity downstream of the T-cell receptor epigenetically stabilizes the master Treg transcription factor Foxp3 through enhanced translation of TET DNA-demethylation enzymes.

highlights.KIN2026: Senior author: mTORC1 downstream of TCR signaling epigenetically stabilizes Foxp3 in regulatory T cells via TET protein translation.

Hori S.lab_name: Hori Lab (Laboratory of Immunology and Microbiology), The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)

Rivalta B.role: First author of a multicenter registry analysis comparing rapamycin and leniolisib in a rare immune disorder
Rivalta B.sub: Clinical Immunology and Vaccinology Unit, Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital, IRCCS, Rome, Italy
story: Beatrice Rivalta works in the Clinical Immunology and Vaccinology Unit at Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital in Rome.

First author of a 2026 retrospective ESID registry analysis of 95 patients with Activated PI3-Kinase-δ Syndrome (APDS), comparing real-world outcomes of rapamycin and the targeted PI3Kδ inhibitor leniolisib — finding comparable response rates for lymphoproliferation, with treatment-limiting adverse events reported only in the rapamycin group.

highlights.RIV2026: First author: multicenter registry of 95 APDS patients finds rapamycin and leniolisib produce comparable responses, but only rapamycin caused treatment-limiting adverse events.

Rivalta B.lab_name: Clinical Immunology and Vaccinology Unit, Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital (Rome, Italy)

Maccari ME.role: Senior author studying primary immunodeficiencies and their treatment
Maccari ME.sub: Institute for Immunodeficiency, Center for Chronic Immunodeficiency, Medical Center – University of Freiburg, Germany
Maccari ME.credit: Portrait: Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg (IMMediate programme)
story: Maria Elena Maccari works at the Institute for Immunodeficiency, Center for Chronic Immunodeficiency, at the University of Freiburg Medical Center, and in the pediatric hematology-oncology and stem cell transplantation division of Freiburg's Children's Hospital.

Senior author of a 2026 ESID registry-based analysis of 95 patients with Activated PI3-Kinase-δ Syndrome, comparing rapamycin against the newer targeted inhibitor leniolisib in real-world clinical practice.

highlights.RIV2026: Senior author: real-world ESID registry analysis of rapamycin vs. leniolisib in Activated PI3Kδ Syndrome.

Maccari ME.lab_name: Institute for Immunodeficiency, Center for Chronic Immunodeficiency, University of Freiburg Medical Center (Freiburg, Germany)

Esposito A.sub: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Naples · Scuola Superiore Meridionale (SSM), Genomics and Experimental Medicine programme
story: Alessandra Esposito is based at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) in Naples, with the Scuola Superiore Meridionale's Genomics and Experimental Medicine programme.

She is first author on a 2026 Nature paper identifying a nutrient-independent lysosomal signalling pathway in which the v-ATPase recruits TBK1 or ULK1 to phosphorylate FNIP1, inhibiting the FLCN:FNIP complex and releasing TFEB for nuclear translocation — a pathway hijacked by recurrent ATP6V1B2 mutations in follicular lymphoma.

highlights.ESP2026: First author on the Nature paper identifying the TBK1/ULK1-FNIP1-FLCN axis that releases TFEB from mTORC1 control, and showing ATP6V1B2 mutations hijack it in follicular lymphoma.

Napolitano G.sub: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Naples · Medical Genetics Unit, Federico II University, Naples
story: Gennaro Napolitano is based at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) in Naples, with the Medical Genetics Unit at Federico II University.

He is corresponding/senior author on a 2026 Nature paper describing a nutrient-independent lysosomal pathway in which TBK1/ULK1 inhibits the FLCN:FNIP complex to release TFEB from mTORC1 control — a pathway constitutively activated by ATP6V1B2 mutations in follicular lymphoma, driving TFEB-dependent tumour proliferation.

highlights.ESP2026: Corresponding author on the Nature paper describing the TBK1/ULK1-FLCN-TFEB lysosomal signalling axis and its hijacking by ATP6V1B2 mutations in follicular lymphoma.

Kalafut KC.lab_name: Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Kalafut KC.sub: Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School
story: Krystle C. Kalafut works in Brendan Manning's laboratory, jointly in the Department of Molecular Metabolism at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Department of Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School.

She is first author on a 2026 Nature Communications study using liver-specific mouse genetic models to show that AKT-mediated TSC2 phosphorylation drives insulin's induction of hepatic mTORC1 but is dispensable for feeding-induced activation — which instead requires dietary protein — and that hepatic mTORC1 signalling is not elevated in diet-induced obesity despite impaired insulin and glucose homeostasis.

highlights.KAL2026: First author showing hepatic mTORC1's postprandial activation depends on dietary protein, dissecting it from insulin/AKT/TSC2 signalling in liver-specific mouse models.

Kalafut KC.credit: Portrait: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Creevy KE.lab_name: Dog Aging Project, Texas A&M University College of Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences (College Station, Texas, USA)
Creevy KE.role: Runs the veterinary side of the Dog Aging Project and leads TRIAD, the trial testing whether rapamycin extends lifespan in pet dogs
Creevy KE.sub: Professor of Small Animal Internal Medicine, Texas A&M University College of Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences · Chief Veterinary Officer and scientific founder, Dog Aging Project · DVM, University of Tennessee · MS, University of Georgia · Diplomate, ACVIM (Small Animal Internal Medicine)
story: Kate Creevy is a veterinary internist who studies why some dogs live longer and healthier lives than others. As chief veterinary officer and a scientific founder of the Dog Aging Project, she helped set up the veterinary protocols and national infrastructure for a long-running study that has enrolled more than 50,000 companion dogs and shares its data openly with researchers.

Pet dogs live in our homes, share our environment and age much faster than we do, which makes them a practical test bed for ideas from mTOR biology. Creevy is senior author of a 2023 placebo-controlled trial of six months of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy dogs, which found no clinically significant adverse events but also no significant change in heart function, and she leads TRIAD, a multicentre trial that will test whether rapamycin extends lifespan in middle-aged dogs. In 2026 the American Veterinary Medical Association gave her its Career Achievement in Canine Research Award.
The timeline below follows Creevy's contributions gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.BAR2023: Senior author of a placebo-controlled six-month trial of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy dogs: well tolerated, but no significant change in heart function.
highlights.COL2025: Co-author of the design paper for TRIAD, the first placebo-controlled lifespan trial of rapamycin outside the laboratory, which she leads; no results yet.

Coleman AE.lab_name: Cardiology Service, University of Georgia College of Veterinary Medicine (Athens, Georgia, USA)
Coleman AE.role: Veterinary cardiologist and first author of the design paper for TRIAD, the lifespan trial of rapamycin in pet dogs
Coleman AE.sub: Professor, Small Animal Medicine & Surgery (Cardiology Service), University of Georgia College of Veterinary Medicine · Adjunct Professor of Pathology · DVM, University of Florida (2007) · Diplomate, ACVIM (Cardiology)
story: Amanda Coleman is a veterinary cardiologist at the University of Georgia College of Veterinary Medicine, where she works in the Small Animal Medicine and Surgery department's Cardiology Service.

She is first author of the 2025 GeroScience design paper for TRIAD, a double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled trial that will test whether rapamycin prolongs lifespan and improves healthspan measures in healthy middle-aged dogs from the Dog Aging Project. The paper sets out why and how the trial was built; it reports no results yet.
The timeline below follows Coleman's contribution gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.COL2025: First author of the design paper for TRIAD, a placebo-controlled trial testing rapamycin for lifespan in middle-aged dogs; no results yet.

Barnett BG.lab_name: Department of Small Animal Medicine and Surgery, University of Georgia College of Veterinary Medicine (Athens, Georgia, USA)
Barnett BG.role: First author of the six-month, placebo-controlled trial of low-dose rapamycin in healthy pet dogs
Barnett BG.sub: Department of Small Animal Medicine and Surgery, University of Georgia College of Veterinary Medicine (present address given in the 2023 paper) · Texas A&M University College of Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences (affiliation at the time of the trial)
story: Brian G. Barnett is a veterinary researcher who has published with the cardiology group at Texas A&M University's College of Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences, including Sonya Gordon, Sonya Wesselowski and Ashley Saunders, on heart disease and heart function in dogs. His 2023 paper gives his present address as the Department of Small Animal Medicine and Surgery at the University of Georgia.

He is first author of a 2023 placebo-controlled trial in Frontiers in Veterinary Science in which 17 healthy client-owned dogs received low-dose rapamycin or placebo for six months. The drug caused no clinically significant adverse events, but heart function measured by echocardiography did not differ significantly from placebo, so the heart benefit hinted at by an earlier 10-week trial was not reproduced. The work was supported by the Dog Aging Project.
The timeline below follows Barnett's contribution gathered in this Atlas.

highlights.BAR2023: First author of a placebo-controlled six-month trial of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy dogs: well tolerated, but no significant change in heart function.

Ferniani M.lab_name: Ballabio Lab, Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) / Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, Texas, USA)
Ferniani M.role: First author of the study showing mTORC1 hyperactivation, not TFEB/TFE3 activity itself, is the primary driver of kidney cystogenesis and tumorigenesis in mouse models of Birt-Hogg-Dubé and Tuberous Sclerosis
Ferniani M.sub: Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine · Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute, Texas Children's Hospital (Ballabio lab)
story: Marco Ferniani is first author of FER2026, from Andrea Ballabio's lab, which genetically uncoupled mTORC1 activity from TFEB/TFE3 activity in kidney-specific mouse models (Depdc5-KO, RagC-KO, Flcn/RagC double-KO) to ask which one actually drives the cystogenesis and tumorigenesis seen in Birt-Hogg-Dubé and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex. The answer: mTORC1 hyperactivation is the main driver, with constitutive TFEB/TFE3 activity accelerating disease on top of it.
Added to the Atlas 2026-10-03; profile is a stub pending a second corpus study (no portrait yet).

highlights.FER2026: First author of the study showing mTORC1 hyperactivation, not TFEB/TFE3 activity, is the primary driver of kidney cystogenesis and tumorigenesis in Birt-Hogg-Dubé and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex mouse models.

Chouchani ET.lab_name: Chouchani Lab, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Chouchani ET.role: Senior/corresponding author on a bioRxiv preprint showing dietary restriction licenses autophagy through oxidation of a single cysteine (Cys19) on the core autophagy protein ATG5
Chouchani ET.sub: Department of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute · Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA
story: Edward Chouchani is corresponding author of SHI2026 (bioRxiv), which built a tissue-resolved atlas of cysteine oxidation under dietary restriction and found that oxidation of Cys19 on ATG5 is required for it to bind ATG10 and form the ATG5-ATG12 conjugate that builds the autophagosome. Mice lacking this redox switch fail to induce autophagy on nutrient restriction and die rapidly, showing a single oxidized cysteine gates the autophagic response to fasting.
Added to the Atlas 2026-10-03; profile is a stub pending a second corpus study (no portrait yet).

highlights.SHI2026: Senior/corresponding author of a preprint showing a single oxidized cysteine (Cys19) on ATG5 licenses autophagosome formation and gates the autophagic response to nutrient restriction.

Asara JM.lab_name: Mass Spectrometry Core, Division of Signal Transduction, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Asara JM.role: Mass-spectrometry specialist whose core facility supplied metabolomics and proteomics for several mTOR studies, including measurements of purine, pyrimidine and SAM metabolism downstream of mTORC1.
Asara JM.sub: Director, Mass Spectrometry Core, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (founded 2004), and Associate Professor of Medicine, Harvard Medical School · postdoc in proteomics, Harvard University, then biotechnology industry · PhD in Analytical Chemistry, Michigan State University (1999)
story: Asara's core ran the mass spectrometry behind several Atlas studies. With Peng Gao he performed the LC-MS analysis showing that mTORC1 raises bicarbonate import through SLC4A7 to feed nucleotide synthesis (ALI2022), and he co-authored the related Ben-Sahra-lab studies on ERK2 control of purine synthesis (ALI2020) and mTORC1 control of SAM and m6A methylation (VIL2021). He was also a co-author on the study in which mass spectrometry mapped the S6K1 site on the clock protein BMAL1 (LIP2015).

Asara earned a PhD in analytical chemistry at Michigan State University in 1999, trained in proteomics at Harvard and worked briefly in biotechnology. In 2004 he founded the BIDMC Mass Spectrometry Core, which now covers proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics and stable-isotope flux analysis.

highlights.VIL2021: Co-author: mass-spectrometry support for the study showing mTORC1 controls SAM synthesis and m6A mRNA methylation.
highlights.ALI2020: Co-author: mass-spectrometry support for the finding that ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS to speed purine synthesis.
highlights.LIP2015: Co-author on the study in which LC-MS/MS identified S6K1 phosphorylation of BMAL1 at serine 42.
highlights.ALI2022: Performed the LC-MS analysis (with P. Gao) showing mTORC1–SLC4A7 bicarbonate import feeds nucleotide synthesis.

Baumeister R.lab_name: Baumeister Lab, Bioinformatics and Molecular Genetics, Institute of Biology III, University of Freiburg (Freiburg, Germany)
Baumeister R.role: Head of the Freiburg department that hosted the Thedieck group during the mTOR network modelling work; co-author on the dynamic mTOR model and the G3BP–TSC study.
Baumeister R.sub: Professor of Bioinformatics and Molecular Genetics, University of Freiburg (since 2003) · Professor of Metabolic Biochemistry, LMU Munich (2000–2003) · postdoc with Gary Ruvkun, Harvard Medical School (1992–1995) · PhD, University of Erlangen (1992)
story: Baumeister co-authored the 2012 dynamic network model of insulin–mTOR signalling, built while Kathrin Thedieck led a group in his Freiburg department (DAL2012). He is also a co-author on the 2021 study showing that G3BP proteins tether the TSC complex to lysosomes, which used zebrafish and other models across a European consortium (PRE2021).

He trained at the University of Erlangen (PhD 1992) and did a postdoc with Gary Ruvkun at Harvard Medical School. After group-leader and professor posts in Munich he moved to Freiburg in 2003, where his lab uses the nematode C. elegans to study disease genes, mTORC2 and autophagy; he was founding director of Freiburg's Center for Biological Systems Analysis (ZBSA).

highlights.DAL2012: Co-author and host department head: dynamic insulin–mTOR model showing mTORC2 is not regulated by TSC1-TSC2.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author on the finding that G3BPs anchor the TSC complex at lysosomes and suppress mTORC1.

Boyle LM.lab_name: Psychiatry Residency (Research Track), Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Boyle LM.role: Research assistant at Boston Children's Hospital who co-authored both studies linking mTOR to the clock protein BMAL1, including the tuberous sclerosis study where she was second author.
Boyle LM.sub: Psychiatry resident (research track, class of 2027), University of Pennsylvania · MD/PhD, Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons · research assistant, Lipton/Sahin labs, Boston Children's Hospital · undergraduate, Yale University
story: After college Boyle worked at Boston Children's Hospital on circadian biology in tuberous sclerosis models. She was a co-author on the paper showing that S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1 (LIP2015) and second author on the study showing that mTOR overactivity raises BMAL1 and disturbs circadian rhythms in these mice (LIP2017).

She studied at Yale, where she worked on chronic stress and fear learning, then completed an MD/PhD at Columbia University with a thesis on social recognition memory in mice. She is now a research-track psychiatry resident at the University of Pennsylvania, where she plans to study how stress and anxiety change neural activity and rhythms during sleep.

highlights.LIP2015: Co-author on the discovery that S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1 to link mTOR and circadian translation.
highlights.LIP2017: Second author: circadian abnormalities and BMAL1 deregulation in tuberous sclerosis mouse models.

Calcagnì A.lab_name: Ballabio Lab, Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) (Pozzuoli, Campania, Italy)
Calcagnì A.role: TIGEM researcher on the TFEB/TFE3 side of mTORC1 signalling; co-author on the lysosomal stress route to TFEB activation and on mouse models separating mTORC1 from TFEB/TFE3 in kidney cysts and tumours.
Calcagnì A.sub: Junior Investigator, Ballabio lab, Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli; also affiliated with the Medical Genetics Unit, Federico II University, Naples
story: She co-authored the study showing that lysosomal stress releases TFEB through a TBK1/ULK1–FNIP1 route independent of nutrients (ESP2026). In kidney-specific mouse models that uncouple mTORC1 from TFEB/TFE3, she is the second-to-last author of the work showing that mTORC1 hyperactivation drives cysts and tumours while TFEB/TFE3 activation speeds them up (FER2026).
She works in Andrea Ballabio's lab at TIGEM, where the lab page lists her as a Junior Investigator. Details of her training could not be verified from open sources.

highlights.ESP2026: Co-author: a v-ATPase–TBK1/ULK1–FNIP1 axis couples lysosomal stress to TFEB activation.
highlights.FER2026: Second-to-last author: mTORC1 hyperactivation, boosted by TFEB/TFE3, drives kidney cystogenesis and tumorigenesis in mice.

Carroll B.lab_name: Carroll Lab, School of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences, University of Bristol (Bristol, England, United Kingdom)
Carroll B.role: First author of the study showing why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells, and co-author on G3BP–TSC and senescence-mitophagy work; her own lab studies how nutrient sensing breaks down in ageing cells.
Carroll B.sub: Senior Lecturer in Molecular Cell Biology, University of Bristol · Vice-Chancellor's Fellow, then Wellcome Trust/Royal Society Sir Henry Dale Fellow, Bristol · postdoc with Viktor Korolchuk, Newcastle University · PhD, Imperial College London
story: As a postdoc in Viktor Korolchuk's lab in Newcastle, Carroll was first author of the 2017 paper showing that mTORC1 in senescent human fibroblasts no longer responds to amino acid or serum withdrawal because of defects upstream of the kinase (CAR2017). She is a co-author on the G3BP–TSC lysosome study (PRE2021) and on the 2024 paper linking loss of basal mitophagy to cellular ageing and to the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin (KEL2024).

Carroll did her PhD at Imperial College London and her postdoc at Newcastle University. She set up her lab at the University of Bristol as a Vice-Chancellor's Fellow and then a Sir Henry Dale Fellow; the lab asks why mTORC1 becomes unresponsive to nutrients in senescence.

highlights.CAR2017: First author: senescent cells keep mTORC1 active because amino acid and growth-factor sensing fail upstream.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author on G3BP1/2 anchoring the TSC complex at lysosomes.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author: suppressed basal mitophagy drives senescence; mitophagy is needed for rapamycin's anti-senescence effect.

Cissé MY.lab_name: Manning Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Cissé MY.role: Research associate in the Manning lab and co-author on the two 2026 mouse studies showing which feeding signals switch on mTORC1 in liver and in skeletal muscle.
Cissé MY.sub: Research Associate, Manning Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · previously at the Institut de Recherche en Cancérologie de Montpellier (Le Cam and Linares team, per PubMed affiliations)
story: Madi Cissé is a co-author on both Manning lab studies that used AKT-resistant TSC2 mice to separate feeding signals. In liver, insulin acts through AKT–TSC2, but the after-meal rise in mTORC1 depends on dietary protein (KAL2026). In muscle, feeding-induced mTORC1 drives postprandial protein synthesis but is not needed to keep muscle size (LAP2026).

Before Harvard he worked at the Institut de Recherche en Cancérologie de Montpellier on p53-independent roles of MDM2 in serine metabolism and mitochondrial respiration (Molecular Cell 2016 and 2018). The Manning lab describes his research as how cancer cells regulate their metabolism through these signalling mechanisms.

highlights.KAL2026: Co-author: dietary protein, not insulin–AKT–TSC2 signalling, drives postprandial hepatic mTORC1.
highlights.LAP2026: Co-author: muscle mTORC1 activated by feeding controls postprandial protein synthesis and endurance, not muscle size.

Cissé MY.credit: Portrait: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Manning Lab)

Cormerais Y.lab_name: Manning Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Cormerais Y.role: Research scientist in the Manning lab who works on how PI3K–AKT–TSC2 signalling controls mTORC1 in living tissues, using mouse models in which TSC2 cannot be phosphorylated by AKT.
Cormerais Y.sub: Research Scientist, Manning Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · PhD, Université de Nice (Nathalie Mazure and Jacques Pouysségur, 2016)
story: Yann Cormerais is second author on the liver study showing that insulin activates hepatic mTORC1 mainly through AKT phosphorylation of TSC2, but that the rise in mTORC1 after a meal depends on dietary protein (KAL2026). He is also a co-author on the companion muscle study, where the same TSC2 phospho-mutant blocked feeding-induced mTORC1 and protein synthesis without shrinking muscle (LAP2026). He was first author of the 2024 preprint that introduced the TSC2-5A mouse used in both studies.

His PhD thesis at the Université de Nice (2016), supervised by Nathalie Mazure and Jacques Pouysségur, studied the amino acid transporter LAT1 as a requirement for mTORC1 activity and tumor growth. In the Manning lab his stated interest is the in vivo role of PI3K–mTORC1 signalling in mammalian growth and metabolism.

highlights.KAL2026: Second author: AKT–TSC2 phosphorylation drives insulin-induced hepatic mTORC1, but feeding-induced activation needs dietary protein.
highlights.LAP2026: Co-author: feeding-induced muscle mTORC1 drives postprandial protein synthesis but is not needed for muscle size.

Cormerais Y.credit: Portrait: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Manning Lab)

Cui Z.lab_name: Cui Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Cui Z.role: Structural biologist who solved cryo-EM structures of the mTORC1–TFEB–Rag–Ragulator megacomplex and of mTORC1 switched on by RHEB and the Rags on a lipid membrane.
Cui Z.sub: Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, University of Colorado Anschutz (lab from June 2026) · postdoc, Hurley lab, University of California, Berkeley (affiliation on the 2023 and 2025 papers) · PhD, Texas A&M University · BSc, Jilin University
story: As first author he solved the structure of TFEB presented to mTORC1 by two Rag–Ragulator complexes, which explains why TFEB phosphorylation depends so strictly on RagC and FLCN (CUI2023). He then rebuilt mTORC1 activation on liposomes and showed by cryo-EM that Raptor and mTOR touch the membrane directly and that full kinase activity needs four steps of membrane engagement (CUI2025).

Both papers come from James Hurley's lab at UC Berkeley, with cell work from Andrea Ballabio's group at TIGEM. In June 2026 he started his own lab at the University of Colorado Anschutz, studying signalling on membrane surfaces: lysosomal mTORC1 control, small GTPases such as RAS, and membrane remodelling.

highlights.CUI2023: First author: cryo-EM structure of the lysosomal mTORC1–TFEB–Rag–Ragulator megacomplex.
highlights.CUI2025: First author: membrane-reconstituted cryo-EM shows Raptor and mTOR contact the lysosomal membrane in a four-step activation process.

Dalle Pezze P.role: First author of two Atlas modelling studies: the dynamic insulin–mTOR network model (TSC-independent mTORC2) and the systems study of concurrent AMPK and mTOR activation by amino acids.
Dalle Pezze P.sub: Lead Bioinformatics Engineer, Genomics England (since 2024, per theorg.com) · bioinformatics software engineer, Congenica · postdoc, Le Novère lab, Babraham Institute (2015–2018) · researcher, Institute for Ageing and Health, Newcastle University
story: Dalle Pezze built the mathematical models in two Atlas studies done with Kathrin Thedieck's experimental group. In 2012, working at Newcastle University's Institute for Ageing and Health, he was first author of the data-fitted dynamic model of the insulin–mTOR network that showed mTORC2 is not regulated by TSC1-TSC2 (DAL2012). In 2016 he was first author of the systems study showing that amino acids switch on AMPK and mTOR together (DAL2016); that model is deposited in BioModels.

From 2015 to 2018 he was a postdoc in Nicolas Le Novère's lab at the Babraham Institute, modelling early autophagosome formation and writing parameter-estimation software. Per theorg.com he later moved into genomics software and works at Genomics England.

highlights.DAL2012: First author: built the dynamic insulin–mTOR model; mTORC2 activation is TSC-independent.
highlights.DAL2016: First author: modelling showing amino acids activate AMPK and mTOR concurrently.

Davis F.lab_name: Davis Lab, Department of Biology, Northeastern University (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Davis F.role: Circadian biologist from Northeastern University who brought expertise on the brain's master clock to two studies linking mTOR and the clock protein BMAL1.
Davis F.sub: Professor of Biology, Northeastern University · PhD in Zoology, University of Texas at Austin · BSc and MSc in Biological Sciences, Stanford University
story: Davis was the outside circadian expert on both Boston Children's Hospital studies: the discovery that S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1 to drive rhythmic protein synthesis (LIP2015), and the finding that mTOR overactivity in tuberous sclerosis mouse models disturbs circadian behaviour through BMAL1 (LIP2017).

He is a Professor of Biology at Northeastern University. His research asks how the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master clock, coordinates daily rhythms across tissues, especially during development.

highlights.LIP2015: Co-author (Northeastern University) contributing circadian expertise to the BMAL1–S6K1 study.
highlights.LIP2017: Co-author (Northeastern University) on circadian defects in tuberous sclerosis mouse models.

De Virgilio C.lab_name: De Virgilio Lab, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland)
De Virgilio C.role: Yeast geneticist whose lab found the EGO/Rag GTPase complex that activates TORC1 and showed that the SEACIT complex (Iml1–Npr2–Npr3) switches TORC1 off by acting as a GAP for the Rag GTPase Gtr1.
De Virgilio C.sub: Full professor, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (since 2007) · SNSF professor, Faculty of Medicine, University of Geneva (from 2001) · group leader, University of Basel (1998) · postdoc with John Pringle, UNC Chapel Hill · PhD, University of Basel (Andres Wiemken and Thomas Boller, 1993)
story: His lab showed in yeast that when amino acids run out, the Iml1–Npr2–Npr3 complex (SEACIT, the yeast counterpart of human GATOR1) binds Gtr1 at the vacuole and stimulates its GTPase activity, turning TORC1 down (PAN2013). He is also one of the senior authors of the study showing that malonyl-CoA directly inhibits mTORC1; the first author, R. Nicastro, is from his Fribourg department, and the yeast data supported the claim that the mechanism is conserved (NIC2023).

He studied biology in Basel, did his PhD on trehalose and heat stress in yeast, and a postdoc on cell polarity with John Pringle in North Carolina. He has led his own group since 1998 and has been a full professor at Fribourg since 2007, working on how nutrient signals and TORC1 control entry into and exit from quiescence.

highlights.PAN2013: Senior author: Iml1–Npr2–Npr3 (SEACIT) is a GAP for Gtr1 that inhibits TORC1 when amino acids are removed.
highlights.NIC2023: Senior co-author: malonyl-CoA is a conserved endogenous ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor, with yeast work from his Fribourg department.
highlights.BON2012: Senior author: in yeast, leucyl-tRNA synthetase binds the Rag GTPase Gtr1 in a leucine-dependent way to pass the leucine signal to TORC1.

Dengjel J.lab_name: Dengjel Lab, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland)
Dengjel J.role: Mass-spectrometry proteomics specialist in autophagy and protein homeostasis; co-author on the TBK1/ULK1–TFEB lysosomal stress pathway and on the spermidine lifespan and cardioprotection study.
Dengjel J.sub: Professor of Biochemistry and Cell Biology, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (since 2016) · Professor of Medical Proteome Research, Department of Dermatology, University of Freiburg (2013) · junior fellow, Freiburg Institute for Advanced Studies (2009) · EMBO fellow, University of Southern Denmark (2006) · PhD, Department of Immunology, University of Tübingen (2005)
story: He is among the senior co-authors of the study showing that lysosomal stress activates TFEB through a v-ATPase–TBK1/ULK1–FNIP1 route that works independently of nutrients (ESP2026); his group runs mass-spectrometry proteomics. Earlier, from Freiburg, he co-authored the work showing that oral spermidine extends mouse lifespan and protects the heart through autophagy (EIS2016).

He studied biochemistry in Potsdam and Tübingen and did his PhD in Tübingen on MHC class II peptide presentation using mass spectrometry. After an EMBO fellowship in Odense working on proteomics and autophagy, he set up his group in Freiburg in 2009 and moved to Fribourg in 2016.

highlights.ESP2026: Senior co-author (proteomics lab): lysosomal stress activates TFEB via v-ATPase–TBK1/ULK1 phosphorylation of FNIP1.
highlights.EIS2016: Co-author: oral spermidine extends mouse lifespan and protects the heart in an autophagy-dependent way.

Fernandes SA.lab_name: Fernandes Group (Muscle Metabolism and Ageing), Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing (Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Fernandes SA.role: First author of the study showing that lysosomal and cytoplasmic pools of mTORC1 respond to different amino acid sources and phosphorylate different substrates.
Fernandes SA.sub: Minerva Fast Track Group Leader, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing (since 2025) · postdoc, Demetriades lab, MPI for Biology of Ageing (2023–2025) · PhD, University of Cologne / MPI for Biology of Ageing (Demetriades lab, 2017–2023)
story: She led the work showing that mTORC1 signalling is split in space: a lysosomal pool fed by protein breakdown inside lysosomes and a cytoplasmic pool fed by amino acids from outside the cell, each phosphorylating its own set of substrates (FER2024). She was also a co-author on the discovery that malonyl-CoA, a fatty-acid building block, directly inhibits mTORC1 (NIC2023).

She trained in Brazil (BSc and MSc, University of São Paulo) and did her PhD and postdoc in the Demetriades lab in Cologne. Since 2025 she runs her own Minerva Fast Track group at the same institute, studying how mTOR balances build-up and breakdown in skeletal muscle and how this changes with age; per her institute biography she became a full member of CECAD in 2026.

highlights.FER2024: First author: lysosomal and cytoplasmic mTORC1 pools sense different amino acid sources and target different substrates.
highlights.NIC2023: Co-author on the finding that malonyl-CoA is an endogenous ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor.
highlights.FER2025: First author (preprint): the tumor suppressor CYLD removes K63-linked ubiquitin from mTOR to restrain mTORC1 and mTORC2.

Gao P.lab_name: Metabolomics Core Facility, Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (Chicago, Illinois, USA)
Gao P.role: Directs the Northwestern metabolomics core that supplied mass-spectrometry metabolite measurements for three Ben-Sahra lab studies on how mTORC1 and ERK signalling drive nucleotide and SAM synthesis.
Gao P.sub: Research Associate Professor of Medicine and Director, Metabolomics Core Facility, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine · postdoc, Proteomics and Mass Spectrometry Facility, Medical University of South Carolina · PhD in Drug Discovery and Biomedical Sciences, Medical University of South Carolina
story: Peng Gao is listed with the Lurie Cancer Center Metabolomics Core Facility on three Ben-Sahra lab papers in the Atlas. Based on that affiliation, his contribution was metabolite measurement: SAM and methionine-cycle metabolites when mTORC1 drives MAT2A (VIL2021), purine synthesis flux after ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS (ALI2020), and purine and pyrimidine synthesis flux when SLC4A7 brings bicarbonate into mTORC1-driven cells (ALI2022).

Northwestern lists him as Research Associate Professor of Medicine and Director of the Metabolomics Core. His work there covers identifying and quantifying metabolites in cells, tissues and body fluids for preclinical and clinical cancer studies.

highlights.VIL2021: Co-author from the Metabolomics Core: mTORC1 drives SAM synthesis through MAT2A and m6A-dependent protein synthesis.
highlights.ALI2020: Co-author from the Metabolomics Core: ERK2 phosphorylation of PFAS stimulates de novo purine synthesis.
highlights.ALI2022: Co-author from the Metabolomics Core: mTORC1 raises SLC4A7 translation to import bicarbonate for nucleotide synthesis.

Gollwitzer P.lab_name: Frezza Lab, CECAD Cluster of Excellence, University of Cologne (Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Gollwitzer P.role: First author of the 'Rag dimer code' study showing that the four Rag GTPase paralogues are not interchangeable: RagC/D sets substrate choice and RagA/B sets the response to amino acid withdrawal.
Gollwitzer P.sub: Postdoc, Frezza Lab, CECAD, University of Cologne (since late 2022) · PhD, University of Cologne / MPI for Biology of Ageing (supervisor Constantinos Demetriades; thesis ‘Role of the Rag GTPases in Amino Acid sensing and mTORC1 signaling’, defended 2022)
story: His PhD project produced the finding that Rag GTPase dimers differ in function: only dimers containing RagD fully restore phosphorylation of TFEB and TFE3, and RagB-containing dimers keep mTORC1 at the lysosome during amino acid withdrawal (GOL2022). He also co-authored the malonyl-CoA study (NIC2023) and the work separating lysosomal and cytoplasmic mTORC1 (FER2024).

He did his doctorate in the Demetriades lab at the MPI for Biology of Ageing in Cologne, with the oral exam in September 2022. Since late 2022 he has been a postdoc in Christian Frezza's lab at CECAD, University of Cologne, where he studies how mitochondrial dysfunction feeds into cell signalling, currently through the integrated stress response. Before Cologne he trained at RWTH Aachen and spent time in David Ron's lab at the Cambridge Institute for Medical Research.

highlights.GOL2022: First author: RagC/D determines substrate specificity and RagA/B the response to amino acid removal.
highlights.NIC2023: Co-author on malonyl-CoA as an endogenous ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor.
highlights.FER2024: Co-author on the spatial separation of lysosomal and cytoplasmic mTORC1 signalling.

Inouye KE.lab_name: Hotamışlıgil Lab and Sabri Ülker Center, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Inouye KE.role: Metabolic physiologist who runs the Hotamışlıgil lab’s physiology facility, which specialises in glucose clamps, and co-authored two 2026 mouse studies on how feeding controls mTORC1 in liver and muscle.
Inouye KE.sub: Senior Research Scientist, Department of Molecular Metabolism, and Director, Sabri Ülker Center Physiology Lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · PhD in Physiology, University of Toronto (Mladen Vranic lab) · undergraduate, Queen’s University
story: Karen Inouye is a co-author on the Manning lab liver study, which found that hepatic mTORC1 is not elevated in diet-induced obesity even though insulin and glucose control are impaired (KAL2026). She also co-authored the muscle study that separated feeding-induced from contraction-induced mTORC1 (LAP2026). Her listed expertise is whole-animal metabolic physiology, which suggests she supported the in vivo metabolic measurements. The papers’ contribution statements were not checked.

She earned a PhD in Physiology at the University of Toronto under Mladen Vranic, where she learned the glucose clamp technique, after undergraduate study at Queen’s University. At Harvard she directs the physiology lab of the Sabri Ülker Center and studies non-adipose sources of FABP4 in the Hotamışlıgil lab.

highlights.KAL2026: Co-author: hepatic mTORC1 after a meal depends on dietary protein, and it is not elevated in diet-induced obesity.
highlights.LAP2026: Co-author: feeding-induced muscle mTORC1 controls postprandial protein synthesis and endurance, not muscle size.

Lapp SC.lab_name: Manning Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Lapp SC.role: First author of the muscle study showing that feeding-induced mTORC1 activation through AKT–TSC2 drives postprandial protein synthesis but is not needed to build or keep muscle mass.
Lapp SC.sub: Postdoctoral Research Fellow, Manning Lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · Doctoral student, Manning Lab (from 2020) · MS, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (2020) · BS, Tulane University (2018)
story: Samuel Lapp led the study of mice whose skeletal muscle expresses a TSC2 that AKT cannot phosphorylate. Feeding no longer switched on muscle mTORC1 or protein synthesis, but contraction still did, and muscle and fibre size stayed normal. The mice ran longer at maximal effort and had slightly more mitochondria (LAP2026). He is also a co-author on the matching liver study (KAL2026).

He earned a BS at Tulane University (2018) and an MS at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (2020), then joined the Manning lab as a doctoral student in 2020. Harvard now lists him as a postdoctoral research fellow. His work asks how TSC2 balances inputs such as insulin and how skeletal muscle balances protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

highlights.LAP2026: First author: AKT–TSC2 phosphorylation is required for feeding-induced muscle mTORC1 and protein synthesis, but not for muscle size.
highlights.KAL2026: Co-author: dietary protein governs postprandial hepatic mTORC1, with insulin acting through AKT–TSC2.

Lipton JO.lab_name: Lipton Lab, F.M. Kirby Neurobiology Center, Department of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Lipton JO.role: First author of the two studies that tie mTOR signalling to the circadian clock protein BMAL1: S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1 to drive translation, and constant mTOR activity in tuberous sclerosis disturbs the clock.
Lipton JO.sub: Assistant Professor of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School · postdoc with Mustafa Sahin, Boston Children's Hospital; clinical training in child neurology and sleep medicine (Boston Children's / Beth Israel Deaconess) · MD, PhD, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Scott Emmons lab)
story: As first author in Mustafa Sahin's lab, Lipton showed that S6K1, a main output of mTORC1, phosphorylates the clock protein BMAL1 at serine 42, which lets BMAL1 bind the translation machinery and drive daily rhythms of protein synthesis (LIP2015). Two years later his team found that mouse models of tuberous sclerosis, where mTOR is always on, keep abnormally high BMAL1 levels and have disturbed circadian behaviour, and that lowering BMAL1 restored the rhythms (LIP2017).

Lipton studied Classics at Brown University and did his MD/PhD at Albert Einstein College of Medicine, with a thesis on the genetics of motivated behaviour in Scott Emmons' lab. He trained in child neurology and sleep medicine in Boston, and his lab at Boston Children's Hospital now studies how circadian clocks relate to diseases of the developing brain.

highlights.LIP2015: First author: S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1, which then promotes translation and links mTOR to circadian protein synthesis.
highlights.LIP2017: First and corresponding author: mTOR overactivity in tuberous sclerosis models raises BMAL1 and disrupts circadian rhythms.

Miwa S.lab_name: Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Miwa S.role: Mitochondrial biologist who contributed to Newcastle studies on rapamycin in NF-κB-driven ageing mice and on basal mitophagy as a brake on cellular senescence.
Miwa S.sub: Lecturer in Translational Biology of Ageing, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University · PhD in Biochemistry, University of Cambridge (Martin Brand lab)
story: Miwa is a co-author on the 2018 study in which rapamycin improved healthspan but not inflammaging or lifespan in nfkb1 knockout mice (COR2018). She is also a co-author on the 2024 paper showing that basal mitophagy falls in senescent and aged human cells and is needed for the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin (KEL2024).

She trained first as a sport scientist, then did a PhD in biochemistry with Martin Brand at Cambridge on mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and ageing. At Newcastle she studies mitochondrial function in ageing and senescent-cell therapies.

highlights.COR2018: Co-author: rapamycin improved frailty and memory in nfkb1 mice without reducing inflammaging.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author: loss of basal mitophagy drives senescence; mitophagy needed for rapamycin's effect.

Monfregola J.lab_name: Ballabio Lab, Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) (Pozzuoli, Campania, Italy)
Monfregola J.role: TIGEM postdoc and co-author on the cryo-EM structure of the mTORC1–TFEB–Rag–Ragulator megacomplex and on the TBK1/ULK1 lysosomal stress route to TFEB.
Monfregola J.sub: Postdoc, Ballabio lab, Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli
story: She co-authored the megacomplex structure showing how two Rag–Ragulator units present TFEB to mTORC1 (CUI2023); she was part of the TIGEM team on the paper, which also tested the structure in cells (TFEB localization and phosphorylation in HeLa cells). She is also a co-author on the study showing that lysosomal stress activates TFEB through TBK1/ULK1 and FNIP1 (ESP2026).
She works in Andrea Ballabio's lab at TIGEM, listed there as a postdoc. Details of her training could not be verified from open sources.

highlights.CUI2023: Co-author: structure of the lysosomal mTORC1–TFEB–Rag–Ragulator megacomplex.
highlights.ESP2026: Co-author: a TBK1/ULK1 axis couples lysosomal stress to TFEB activation.

Nathan A.lab_name: Sahin Lab, F.M. Kirby Neurobiology Center, Department of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Nathan A.role: Co-author on both Boston Children's Hospital studies linking mTOR signalling to the circadian clock protein BMAL1.
Nathan A.sub: Listed at the F.M. Kirby Neurobiology Center, Boston Children's Hospital, on the 2015 and 2017 papers; current position not verified
story: Nathan was a co-author on the study showing that S6K1, downstream of mTORC1, phosphorylates BMAL1 so that it can promote protein synthesis (LIP2015), and on the follow-up showing that mTOR overactivity in tuberous sclerosis mouse models deregulates BMAL1 and the clock (LIP2017).
Both papers list him at the Department of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital. His later career could not be confirmed from an open source.

highlights.LIP2015: Co-author on the discovery that S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1 to link mTOR and circadian translation.
highlights.LIP2017: Co-author on the study of BMAL1 deregulation and circadian defects in tuberous sclerosis models.

Nüchel J.lab_name: Nüchel Lab, Center for Biochemistry, Medical Faculty, University of Cologne (Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Nüchel J.role: Co-author on two Demetriades-lab mTORC1 papers from Cologne: the spatial split of mTORC1 signalling by amino acid source and malonyl-CoA as a direct mTORC1 inhibitor.
Nüchel J.sub: Junior Group Leader, Center for Biochemistry, University of Cologne, and CMMC Career Advancement Program group leader (since 2024) · postdoc, Demetriades lab, MPI for Biology of Ageing (2021–2023) · PhD, Center for Biochemistry, Medical Faculty, University of Cologne (2017–2021)
story: As a postdoc in the Demetriades lab he co-authored the study showing that lysosomal and cytoplasmic mTORC1 respond to different amino acid sources (FER2024) and the discovery that malonyl-CoA binds the mTOR catalytic pocket and inhibits mTORC1 (NIC2023). His own interest is how mTORC1 and nutrient signals control protein secretion and the extracellular matrix, a topic he co-leads with Demetriades in the DFG research unit FOR2722 (project D3).

He studied biology at the University of Cologne and did his PhD at the Center for Biochemistry of its Medical Faculty. Since January 2024 he leads his own group there, studying how post-translational modifications control secretion and upkeep of the extracellular matrix in disease and ageing.

highlights.FER2024: Co-author: spatially separate lysosomal and cytoplasmic mTORC1 pools respond to different amino acid sources.
highlights.NIC2023: Co-author: malonyl-CoA acts as a conserved ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor.
highlights.FER2025: Co-author on the preprint identifying CYLD as a deubiquitinase that restrains mTOR.

Prentzell MT.lab_name: Opitz Lab (Division of Metabolic Crosstalk in Cancer), German Cancer Research Center DKFZ (Heidelberg, Germany)
Prentzell MT.role: First author of the study showing that G3BP proteins anchor the TSC complex to lysosomes, a physical brake on mTORC1; earlier co-author on the dynamic insulin–mTOR network model.
Prentzell MT.sub: Deputy Division Head, Metabolic Crosstalk in Cancer, DKFZ Heidelberg · earlier work with the Thedieck group (Freiburg) on mTOR signalling
story: Prentzell is first author of the 2021 Cell paper showing that G3BP1 and G3BP2, known as stress-granule proteins, also hold the TSC complex at the lysosome and so restrain mTORC1 (PRE2021). In the DKFZ press release she described the G3BP proteins as an anchor that lets the TSC complex bind to lysosomes. Nine years earlier she was a co-author on the data-fitted dynamic model of the insulin–mTOR network from the Freiburg and Newcastle groups (DAL2012).

She is listed as Deputy Division Head in Christiane Opitz's division Metabolic Crosstalk in Cancer at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, and took part in the EU MESI-STRAT consortium on metabolic signalling in breast cancer.

highlights.PRE2021: First author: G3BP1/2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes; their loss makes mTORC1 over-responsive to amino acids and insulin.
highlights.DAL2012: Co-author on the dynamic network model showing mTORC2 activation is independent of TSC1-TSC2.

Sahin M.lab_name: Sahin Lab, Rosamund Stone Zander and Hansjoerg Wyss Translational Neuroscience Center, Department of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Sahin M.role: Senior author of the studies showing that mTOR signalling reaches the circadian clock through BMAL1, and a physician-scientist focused on tuberous sclerosis, the classic disease of overactive mTOR.
Sahin M.sub: Neurologist-in-Chief (chair since 2024), Department of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital, and Professor of Neurology, Harvard Medical School · residencies in pediatrics (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia) and child neurology (Boston Children's, 2000) · MD, PhD in Neurobiology, Yale University School of Medicine (1995)
story: Sahin's lab showed that S6K1, downstream of mTORC1, phosphorylates the clock protein BMAL1, which lets it act as a translation factor and gives protein synthesis a daily rhythm (LIP2015). In mouse models of tuberous sclerosis, where mTOR is stuck on, his team found raised BMAL1 levels and disturbed circadian behaviour that improved when BMAL1 was genetically lowered (LIP2017).

He earned his MD and PhD at Yale and trained in pediatrics and child neurology in Philadelphia and Boston. He directs the Translational Neuroscience Center at Boston Children's Hospital, became chair of its Department of Neurology in 2024, cares for children with tuberous sclerosis and was elected to the National Academy of Medicine in 2023.

highlights.LIP2015: Senior author: S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1, making it a translation factor that links mTOR to the circadian clock.
highlights.LIP2017: Senior author: mTOR overactivity in tuberous sclerosis models deregulates BMAL1 and disrupts circadian rhythms.
highlights.TSA2012: Senior author: deleting Tsc1 in cerebellar Purkinje cells caused autism-like behaviour in mice, and rapamycin started in early life prevented it.

Sampson JR.lab_name: Institute of Medical Genetics, Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom)
Sampson JR.role: Clinical geneticist who led the consortium that identified the TSC2 gene and led trials of mTOR inhibitors in tuberous sclerosis, including the TRON trial of everolimus for cognition.
Sampson JR.sub: Emeritus Professor, Cardiff University School of Medicine · former Head of the Institute of Medical Genetics and Director of the Division of Cancer and Genetics, Cardiff · at Cardiff since 1989 (moved from Glasgow)
story: Sampson is a senior author on the TRON randomised trial, which found that 24 weeks of everolimus did not clearly improve neuropsychological function in tuberous sclerosis over placebo (SAX2026). He is also a co-author on the study showing that G3BP proteins tether the TSC complex to lysosomes (PRE2021).

He moved to the Institute of Medical Genetics in Cardiff in 1989 and led the international consortium that identified TSC2; he also took part in identifying TSC1 and led the TESSTAL trial of mTOR inhibitors for TSC kidney tumours. He received the 2017 Manuel R. Gomez Award and is now Emeritus Professor at Cardiff University.

highlights.SAX2026: Senior investigator, TRON trial: everolimus did not beat placebo on neuropsychological outcomes in TSC.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author on G3BP1/2 anchoring the TSC complex at lysosomes.

Shanley DP.lab_name: Shanley Lab, Biosciences Institute / Centre for Integrated Systems Biology of Ageing and Nutrition (CISBAN), Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Shanley DP.role: Systems biologist of ageing whose Newcastle modelling group built, with the Thedieck lab, the dynamic models of mTOR signalling in the Atlas.
Shanley DP.sub: Reader in Systems Biology of Ageing, Newcastle University, and Director of CISBAN (per Newcastle staff profile) · Research Associate, Newcastle and Manchester · PhD in Computational Biology, University of Manchester (Wellcome Trust Mathematical Biology studentship)
story: Shanley is joint senior author, with Kathrin Thedieck, on the 2012 dynamic model of the insulin–mTOR network (DAL2012) and the 2016 systems study showing that amino acids switch on AMPK and mTOR together (DAL2016). His group supplied the modelling side; Piero Dalle Pezze, first author on both papers, worked in his Newcastle unit.

He did a PhD in computational biology at the University of Manchester. Before academia he worked as a scientist at British Gas and the Institut Français du Pétrole. At Newcastle he models ageing processes, from senescent cells to theories of why ageing evolves.

highlights.DAL2012: Joint senior author (modelling): dynamic insulin–mTOR model; mTORC2 activation is TSC-independent.
highlights.DAL2016: Joint senior author (modelling): amino acids activate AMPK and mTOR concurrently.

Sonntag AG.lab_name: Baumeister Lab, Bioinformatics and Molecular Genetics, Institute of Biology III, University of Freiburg, at the time of the studies (Freiburg, Germany)
Sonntag AG.role: Experimental researcher in the Thedieck group who contributed cell data to the dynamic mTOR network model and the AMPK–mTOR amino acid study.
Sonntag AG.sub: Scientist, Discovery, Immatics Biotechnologies (Tübingen, since 2014) · doctoral research, Institute of Biology III, University of Freiburg (Thedieck group)
story: Sonntag is second author on the 2012 dynamic model of insulin–mTOR signalling, which combined her group's cell experiments with modelling from Newcastle (DAL2012), and a co-author on the 2016 study of concurrent AMPK and mTOR activation by amino acids (DAL2016). In 2012 she was also first author of a related FEBS Journal paper on IRS-dependent regulation of AMPK by insulin.

The 2012 University of Freiburg press release names her as a researcher at the Institute of Biology III. In 2014 she moved to the Tübingen immuno-oncology company Immatics Biotechnologies, where she built the RNA-sequencing pipeline and leads NGS-based HLA typing for its tumour-specific immunotherapies.

highlights.DAL2012: Second author: experimental data for the dynamic insulin–mTOR network model.
highlights.DAL2016: Co-author on the systems study of amino acid activation of AMPK and mTOR.

Thedieck K.lab_name: Lab for Metabolic Signaling (Thedieck Lab), Department Metabolism, Senescence and Autophagy, Faculty of Medicine, University of Duisburg-Essen (Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Thedieck K.role: Senior author of three Atlas studies that treat mTOR signalling as a dynamic network: TSC-independent mTORC2 activation, concurrent AMPK and mTOR activation by amino acids, and G3BP tethering of TSC to lysosomes.
Thedieck K.sub: Professor of Metabolism, Senescence and Autophagy, University of Duisburg-Essen (since 2025) · Professor and Director of Biochemistry, University of Innsbruck (2019–2024) · Associate Professor, Groningen and Oldenburg (2013–2019) · group leader, Freiburg (2008–2013) · postdoc with Michael N. Hall, Basel · PhD, Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research, Braunschweig (2005)
story: Thedieck is senior author on the 2012 data-fitted model of the insulin–mTOR network, which showed that TSC1-TSC2 does not regulate mTORC2 (DAL2012), and on the 2016 systems study finding that amino acids switch on AMPK and mTOR at the same time (DAL2016). Both came from a collaboration with Daryl Shanley's modelling group in Newcastle. She is also senior author of the 2021 Cell paper showing that G3BP proteins anchor the TSC complex to lysosomes (PRE2021).

She did her PhD at the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research and a postdoc with mTOR pioneer Michael N. Hall in Basel. She then led groups in Freiburg, Groningen/Oldenburg and Innsbruck before moving to the University of Duisburg-Essen in 2025; she holds an ERC Advanced Grant.

highlights.DAL2012: Senior author: dynamic insulin–mTOR model; mTORC2 activation runs independently of TSC1-TSC2 and the feedback loop.
highlights.DAL2016: Senior author: amino acids activate AMPK, PI3K and mTORC2 alongside mTORC1; AMPK keeps autophagy going via ULK1.
highlights.PRE2021: Senior author: G3BP1/2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and suppress mTORC1.

Turk BE.lab_name: Turk Lab, Department of Pharmacology, Yale School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Turk BE.role: Kinase biochemist who studies how protein kinases choose their substrates; co-author on the discovery that AMPK phosphorylates raptor and on the study showing that mTORC1 sites differ in intrinsic substrate quality.
Turk BE.sub: Professor of Pharmacology, Yale School of Medicine · PhD, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (1999) · BA, Oberlin College (1990)
story: Turk co-authored the Shaw-lab study that used a proteomic and bioinformatic search for AMPK substrates and found that AMPK directly phosphorylates raptor to shut down mTORC1 under energy stress (GWI2008). He was also a co-author on the Sabatini-lab study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates peptides from its substrates at very different rates, and that this 'substrate quality' predicts which sites resist rapamycin and starvation (KAN2013).

Turk received his PhD from MIT in 1999 and is Professor of Pharmacology at Yale School of Medicine. His lab uses peptide arrays, phage display and phosphoproteomics to learn how kinases recognise sequence motifs and how these signalling networks are rewired in cancer.

highlights.GWI2008: Co-author: AMPK directly phosphorylates raptor, a second route by which energy stress halts mTORC1.
highlights.KAN2013: Co-author: mTORC1 phosphorylation sites differ in intrinsic substrate quality, which sets their rapamycin sensitivity.

Uda S.lab_name: Information and Data Science Education Center, Yamaguchi University (Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi Prefecture, Japan)
Uda S.role: Systems biologist who uses information theory and modelling. He co-authored the studies showing that the insulin–AKT pathway encodes insulin’s timing pattern, and that S6K, downstream of mTORC1, reads only the fast, pulse-like part.
Uda S.sub: Associate Professor, Information and Data Science Education Center, Yamaguchi University (since 2024) · Associate Professor, Integrated Omics, Medical Institute of Bioregulation, Kyushu University (2014–2022) · Assistant Professor, Graduate School of Science, University of Tokyo (2013) · PhD (Science), Tokyo Institute of Technology
story: Shinsuke Uda is a co-author on the cell study showing that pulse and sustained insulin produce transient and sustained AKT phosphorylation, and that S6K, G6Pase and GSK3-beta each read a different part of that signal (KUB2012). He then co-authored the in vivo follow-up in rat liver, where insulin clamps and mathematical modelling showed the same selective decoding and linked it to network structure and time constants (KUB2018).

His background is in communication engineering, information statistical mechanics and machine learning, which he applies to systems biology and trans-omics. He was an associate professor in Kyushu University’s Integrated Omics division from 2014 and moved to Yamaguchi University’s Information and Data Science Education Center in January 2024.

highlights.KUB2012: Co-author: AKT multiplexes insulin patterns in time; S6K decodes only the transient, pulse-like component.
highlights.KUB2018: Co-author (second author): in rat liver, downstream molecules decode blood insulin patterns through AKT, explained with mathematical modelling.

Villa E.lab_name: Ben-Sahra Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (Chicago, Illinois, USA)
Villa E.role: First author of the study showing that mTORC1 raises production of the methyl donor SAM through MAT2A and boosts m6A mRNA methylation to support protein synthesis and cell growth.
Villa E.sub: Scientist, Frontier Medicines (per Ben-Sahra lab alumni page) · Postdoctoral fellow, Ben-Sahra Lab, Northwestern University (2018–2022) · PhD, Université Côte d’Azur, Nice (2017)
story: As a postdoctoral fellow in Issam Ben-Sahra’s lab, Elodie Villa led the work showing that mTORC1 controls how much S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) the cell makes: c-MYC raises MAT2A expression, mTORC1 raises WTAP protein, and the resulting rise in m6A mRNA methylation supports protein synthesis and tumor growth (VIL2021). She was also a co-author on the study showing that ERK2 phosphorylates the purine enzyme PFAS to speed up de novo purine synthesis, a growth input that runs in parallel to mTORC1 (ALI2020).

She earned her PhD at Université Côte d’Azur in Nice in December 2017 and was a postdoc in the Ben-Sahra lab from September 2018 to October 2022. The lab’s alumni page lists her next position as Scientist at Frontier Medicines.

highlights.VIL2021: First author: mTORC1 drives SAM synthesis via c-MYC/MAT2A and raises WTAP, increasing m6A mRNA methylation and protein synthesis.
highlights.ALI2020: Co-author: ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS at Thr619 to acutely stimulate de novo purine synthesis.

Wilhelm S.lab_name: Demetriades Lab, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing (Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Wilhelm S.role: Co-author on two Demetriades-lab studies of amino acid sensing by mTORC1: the Rag GTPase dimer code and the spatial split of mTORC1 signalling.
Wilhelm S.sub: Staff member, Demetriades lab, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Cologne (affiliation on the 2022 and 2024 papers)

Both papers list her at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing in Cologne. Her exact position and training could not be verified from open sources.

highlights.GOL2022: Co-author on the Rag GTPase dimer code study.
highlights.FER2024: Co-author on the spatial separation of mTORC1 signalling by amino acid source.
highlights.FER2025: Co-author on the preprint identifying CYLD as a deubiquitinase that restrains mTOR.

Yuan ED.lab_name: Sahin Lab, F.M. Kirby Neurobiology Center, Department of Neurology, Boston Children's Hospital (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Yuan ED.role: Second author on the study showing that S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1 to link mTOR signalling with circadian protein synthesis, and co-author on the follow-up in tuberous sclerosis models.
Yuan ED.sub: Research staff, Sahin Lab, Boston Children's Hospital (per 2015–2017 paper affiliations) · earlier co-author from the Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute (2015) · later listed at University of Massachusetts Medical School (2017, per PubMed)

She was also a co-author on the follow-up showing that mTOR overactivity in tuberous sclerosis mouse models raises BMAL1 and disturbs the clock (LIP2017).

PubMed also lists an Elizabeth D. Yuan at the Whitehead Institute as a co-author on the 2015 Sabatini-lab paper on the arginine transporter SLC38A9, and at the University of Massachusetts Medical School on a 2017 medical-education paper. Her current position could not be verified.

highlights.LIP2017: Co-author on the study of BMAL1 deregulation and circadian defects in tuberous sclerosis models.

von Zglinicki T.lab_name: von Zglinicki Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
von Zglinicki T.role: Cell-senescence researcher who co-authored the Newcastle studies on stuck-on mTORC1 in senescent cells and on loss of basal mitophagy as a driver of cellular ageing.
von Zglinicki T.sub: Professor of Cellular Gerontology, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University · founding member of ageing biology research at Newcastle and former Scientific Director of the Newcastle University Institute for Ageing (per BSRA, 2017)
story: Von Zglinicki is a co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 stays active in senescent fibroblasts because nutrient and growth-factor sensing fail upstream (CAR2017). He is also a co-author on the 2024 paper showing that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged cells, and that restoring it is needed for rapamycin's anti-senescence effect (KEL2024).

He is Professor of Cellular Gerontology at Newcastle University. His earlier work showed that oxidative stress speeds up telomere shortening, and he received the Lord Cohen of Birkenhead Medal of the British Society for Research on Ageing in 2017.

highlights.CAR2017: Co-author: senescent cells keep mTORC1 active through defects in amino acid and growth-factor sensing.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author: suppressed basal mitophagy drives senescence; reversible with a p62-targeting molecule.

Moreno TM.lab_name: Kumsta Lab, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Moreno TM.role: First author of a healthy-aging cohort study showing that human autophagy flux is remodeled with age in a sex- and cell type-specific way, uncoupled from autophagy-gene transcription, and responsive to a mild exercise intervention
Moreno TM.sub: Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute
story: Tatiana M. Moreno is the first author of MOR2026, a study from Caroline Kumsta's group at Sanford Burnham Prebys that measured autophagy flux directly across subject-matched human cell types (skin fibroblasts, induced neurons and blood immune cells) from a healthy aging cohort. The study found that autophagy-gene transcription rises with age but autophagic flux itself does not move in lockstep with it: flux fell in male fibroblasts, held steady in female fibroblasts, rose in female induced neurons, and grew more variable in blood cells, becoming associated with reduced physical function only after age 70. A small pilot exercise intervention lowered blood-cell autophagy flux in older adults in parallel with improved physical function, suggesting the measurement is responsive to a real intervention, not just a fixed trait.

highlights.MOR2026: First author of a healthy-aging cohort study showing human autophagy flux is sex- and cell type-specific, linked to physical function after age 70, and responsive to 12 weeks of mild exercise.

Kumsta C.lab_name: Kumsta Lab, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Kumsta C.role: Senior author of a healthy-aging cohort study measuring autophagy flux directly across human cell types, showing it is sex- and cell type-specific and linked to physical function in older adults
