Kumsta C.sub: Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute
Kumsta C.credit: Portrait: Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute
story: Caroline Kumsta studies how autophagy and proteostasis change with age, and is the senior author of MOR2026, which directly measured autophagic flux (not just gene expression) across matched human cell types from a healthy aging cohort. The study's central finding complicates the simple view that autophagy declines uniformly with age: flux changes differed by cell type and by sex, and in blood immune cells it trended higher, not lower, in older individuals, with higher flux associated with reduced physical function after age 70. A pilot exercise intervention lowered that flux in parallel with improved function, a result the Atlas also reads against the open question of whether a human autophagic-flux assay can serve as a practical readout for mTOR-pathway geroprotector trials.

highlights.MOR2026: Senior author of a direct, multi-cell-type measurement of human autophagy flux during aging, linking it to physical function and to responsiveness to exercise.

Hu K.lab_name: Feske Lab, NYU Grossman School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Hu K.role: First author identifying SLC4A7/NBCn1 as a pH regulator required for mTORC1 activity and antibody-secreting cell differentiation
Hu K.sub: Department of Pathology, New York University Grossman School of Medicine
story: Ke Hu is the first author of HU2026B, from Stefan Feske's lab at NYU Langone, identifying the sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter SLC4A7/NBCn1 as a selective regulator of antibody-producing plasmablast differentiation. The study showed that SLC4A7 keeps the inside of a differentiating B cell from becoming too acidic; without it, cells acidify internally, their lysosomes become abnormally alkaline, and mTORC1 activity falls, blunting antibody responses in mice after immunization and influenza infection. Restoring mTORC1 activity, or acidifying the cells by blocking a different transporter (the Na+/H+ exchanger), rescued differentiation, tying this pH-sensing step directly to mTORC1 function in humoral immunity.

highlights.HU2026B: First author identifying SLC4A7/NBCn1 as a pH-regulating input required for mTORC1 activity during antibody-secreting cell differentiation.

Feske S.lab_name: Feske Lab, NYU Grossman School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Feske S.role: Senior author identifying intracellular pH regulation via SLC4A7/NBCn1 as required for mTORC1 activity and antibody-secreting cell differentiation
Feske S.sub: Department of Pathology, New York University Grossman School of Medicine
story: Stefan Feske's lab studies ion transport and signalling in immune cells, including calcium and pH-sensing pathways in T and B lymphocytes. He is the senior author of HU2026B, which found that the Na/HCO3- cotransporter SLC4A7/NBCn1 is required to keep intracellular pH compatible with mTORC1 activity during B-cell differentiation into antibody-secreting cells, and that antibody responses are similarly impaired by extracellular acidosis in a mouse model of metabolic acidosis -- linking a basic physiological variable, pH, to the mTORC1-dependent step of humoral immunity.

highlights.HU2026B: Senior author showing that intracellular pH regulation through SLC4A7/NBCn1 is required for mTORC1-dependent antibody-secreting cell differentiation.

Trivedi H.role: First author of a 2026 PRISMA-guided systematic review of senolytic, senomorphic and anti-ageing drug trials in humans.
Trivedi H.sub: Department of Pharmacology, Zydus Medical College and Hospital · Dahod, India
story: Hitesha Trivedi is in the Department of Pharmacology at Zydus Medical College and Hospital in Dahod, India. In 2026 she led a PRISMA 2020 systematic review that pulled together every completed human clinical trial testing drugs meant to clear or calm senescent cells — senolytics such as dasatinib plus quercetin, alongside senomorphic and mTOR-targeting approaches — and judged the evidence against ageing to be real but still thin.

highlights.TRI2026: Led the systematic review of senolytic, senomorphic and mTOR-targeting human trials.

Trivedi H.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, Zydus Medical College and Hospital (Dahod, Gujarat, India)

Shaikh S.role: Senior author of the same 2026 systematic review of senolytic and anti-ageing drug trials in humans.
Shaikh S.sub: Department of Pharmacology, Zydus Medical College and Hospital · Dahod, India
story: Sohel Shaikh is in the Department of Pharmacology at Zydus Medical College and Hospital in Dahod, India, and is the senior author of the group’s 2026 PRISMA systematic review of human senolytic, senomorphic and mTOR-targeting clinical trials.

highlights.TRI2026: Senior author on the senolytic/anti-ageing human-trials systematic review.

Shaikh S.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, Zydus Medical College and Hospital (Dahod, Gujarat, India)

Lai M.role: First author of a 2026 study of immune aging across the canine lifespan and short-term responses to rapamycin.
Lai M.sub: Institute of Advanced Biotechnology & Institute of Homeostatic Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology · Shenzhen, China
story: Meiling Lai is at the Institute of Advanced Biotechnology and Institute of Homeostatic Medicine at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen, China. In 2026 she led a study profiling immune aging across the canine lifespan and testing short-term geroprotective interventions — rapamycin, the SGLT2 inhibitor canagliflozin, and dietary restriction — in young Beagles, finding rapamycin produced the broadest shift in blood cytokines of the three.

highlights.LAI2026: Led the canine immune-aging study testing rapamycin, canagliflozin and dietary restriction.

Lai M.lab_name: Institute of Advanced Biotechnology & Institute of Homeostatic Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
Lai M.credit: Portrait: Institute of Advanced Biotechnology, SUSTech (Zhu Jian-Kang Group member page)

Lyu YX.role: Corresponding/senior author of the same 2026 canine immune-aging and geroprotective-intervention study.
Lyu YX.sub: Institute of Advanced Biotechnology & Institute of Homeostatic Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen · Faculty of Medicine, Macau University of Science and Technology
story: Yu-Xuan Lyu is a corresponding author at the Institute of Advanced Biotechnology and Institute of Homeostatic Medicine at SUSTech in Shenzhen, with a joint appointment at the Faculty of Medicine, Macau University of Science and Technology. His group’s 2026 study found that canine immune aging is non-linear and sex-stratified, and that a 90-day course of rapamycin produced the broadest cytokine shift among three geroprotective interventions tested in young Beagles.

highlights.LAI2026: Corresponding author on the canine rapamycin/canagliflozin/dietary-restriction immune-aging study.

Lyu YX.lab_name: Institute of Advanced Biotechnology & Institute of Homeostatic Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
Lyu YX.credit: Portrait: Institute of Advanced Biotechnology, SUSTech (Zhu Jian-Kang Group member page)

Longo VD.lab_name: Longo Lab, USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology & USC Longevity Institute, University of Southern California (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Longo VD.role: Studies how nutrient-sensing pathways (including TOR and GH/IGF-1) and diet shape ageing and resistance to stress and disease, from yeast to mice and people.
Longo VD.sub: University of Southern California · Professor of Gerontology and Biological Sciences; Director, USC Longevity Institute · PhD UCLA (1997)
story: Valter Longo is a professor at the University of Southern California and directs the USC Longevity Institute. According to his USC profile, he studied at the University of North Texas (BS, 1992), earned his PhD at UCLA (1997) and did postdoctoral training at USC (2000). His lab works on how ageing is regulated in yeast and in mammals, and how cells resist stress.

The Atlas includes the 2010 Science review he wrote with Luigi Fontana and Linda Partridge, 'Extending healthy life span: from yeast to humans'. It brings together evidence that eating less, or turning down nutrient-sensing signals such as mTOR and growth hormone/IGF-1, lets yeast, worms, flies and rodents live longer and stay healthier for longer.

The review is careful about people. Dietary restriction and lower nutrient-sensing activity are linked to protection from diabetes, cancer and heart disease in monkeys and humans, but direct proof that they slow ageing in humans is limited. This is why the review also discusses possible side effects.

highlights.FON2010: Review proposing that dietary restriction and reduced nutrient-sensing signalling (mTOR, GH/IGF-1) may slow ageing through shared, evolutionarily conserved mechanisms, with Longo as senior author.

Rueegg MA.lab_name: Rüegg Group, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Rueegg MA.role: Neurobiologist who studies how nerves and skeletal muscle are built and maintained, including the role of mTOR signalling in muscle.
Rueegg MA.sub: University of Basel · Professor of Neurobiology (since 2004) · Co-founder and CEO, SEAL Therapeutics (since 2021)
story: Markus Rüegg is a professor of neurobiology at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel. His CV lists a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford University School of Medicine (1989 to 1992), then assistant professor (1992 to 1997), associate professor (1998 to 2004) and full professor (since 2004) in Basel.

The Atlas study from 2008, led by first author C. Florian Bentzinger in the lab of Rüegg and Michael Hall, asked what the two mTOR complexes do in skeletal muscle. The team removed raptor (a part of mTORC1) or rictor (a part of mTORC2) only in muscle of mice.

Muscles without raptor slowly became dystrophic, burned fuel less efficiently and the mice did not live as long. Muscles without rictor looked normal. The result showed that mTORC1 is essential for healthy muscle, while mTORC2 is not.

highlights.BEN2008: Showed that deleting raptor (mTORC1) in mouse skeletal muscle causes dystrophy and metabolic changes, whereas deleting rictor (mTORC2) does not; Rüegg was senior author.

Nathan CO.lab_name: Head and Neck Cancer Research, Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, LSU Health Shreveport (Shreveport, Louisiana, USA)
Nathan CO.role: Head and neck surgeon and cancer researcher who tests whether drugs such as the mTOR inhibitor everolimus can help patients whose tumours resist immunotherapy.
Nathan CO.sub: LSU Health Shreveport · Chair and Professor of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery · Feist-Weiller Cancer Center · Clinician-scientist
story: Cherie-Ann Nathan is a head and neck cancer surgeon and the chair of the Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery at LSU Health Shreveport. She also directs head and neck surgery and research there and works with the Feist-Weiller Cancer Center.

Her 2026 study in the Atlas looked at head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with a mutated TP53 gene. These tumours often stay 'immune-cold', meaning immune cells do not enter them, and they respond poorly to immunotherapy. In mouse models, the mTOR inhibitor everolimus slowed tumour growth.

The treatment brought more CD8+ T cells and dendritic cells into the tumour, reduced regulatory T cells and lowered PD-1 and PD-L1 levels. The authors suggest mTOR inhibition could be a way to prepare such tumours for immunotherapy. The work was done in mice, so it is not yet shown in patients.

highlights.NAT2026: In mouse models of TP53-mutant head and neck cancer, everolimus reprogrammed the immune-cold tumour environment and boosted anti-tumour T cell activity; Nathan was senior and corresponding author.

Sell C.lab_name: Sell Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Drexel University College of Medicine (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Sell C.role: Studies the basic biology of ageing, especially how mTOR, rapamycin, cellular metabolism and senescence are connected.
Sell C.sub: Drexel University College of Medicine · Associate Professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology; Director, Aging Initiative
story: Christian Sell is an associate professor at Drexel University College of Medicine in Philadelphia, where he directs the Aging Initiative. According to his Drexel profile, his work centres on mTOR and rapamycin and on how hormone signalling, metabolism and cellular senescence fit together.

The 2019 trial in the Atlas, led by dermatologist Christina Chung with Sell as senior author, asked whether rapamycin can slow ageing in a tissue that is easy to see and sample: the skin. Adults over 40 with signs of sun-related skin ageing applied rapamycin cream.

The skin showed lower levels of p16, a marker of senescent cells, and more collagen VII, which helps hold skin layers together. Some people also looked better. The trial was small: 36 people joined and 19 dropped out or were lost to follow-up, so it is an early signal and not proof.

highlights.CHU2019: Small randomised trial in which topical rapamycin lowered the senescence marker p16 and raised collagen VII in human skin; Sell was senior author.

Sell C.credit: Portrait: Drexel University College of Medicine

Lenardo MJ.lab_name: Molecular Development of the Immune System Section, Laboratory of Immunology, NIAID, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Lenardo MJ.role: Immunologist known for work on how immune cells die and are controlled; his lab also showed that mTOR reactivation ends autophagy and rebuilds lysosomes.
Lenardo MJ.sub: NIAID, NIH · Former Chief, Molecular Development of the Immune System Section (Senior Investigator from 1994) · National Academy of Sciences (2019)
story: Michael Lenardo is an immunologist at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) in the US National Institutes of Health. His NIAID profile says he set up an independent research unit there in 1989 and became a Senior Investigator and Section Chief in 1994. He trained at Johns Hopkins (BA), Washington University in St. Louis (MD) and, as a postdoctoral fellow, at the Whitehead Institute at MIT.

The 2010 Nature paper in the Atlas, with Li Yu as first author, looked at what happens to autophagy (the cell's recycling process) during long starvation. mTOR is switched off at first, which starts autophagy. After prolonged starvation, mTOR switches back on.

The reactivated mTOR stops autophagy and helps rebuild lysosomes, the cell's digestive compartments, from tubes that bud off the autolysosomes. This showed autophagy as a cycle that ends by restoring the lysosomes it used.

highlights.YUX2010: Showed that mTOR is reactivated during prolonged starvation, terminating autophagy and driving autophagic lysosome reformation; Lenardo was senior author.

Li XC.lab_name: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center, Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist (Houston, Texas, USA)
Li XC.role: Transplant immunologist who studies how the immune system rejects or tolerates transplants, and how drugs such as mTOR inhibitors act on immune cells.
Li XC.sub: Houston Methodist · Director, Immunobiology & Transplant Science Center; Professor of Transplant Immunology in Surgery
story: Xian Chang Li is a physician-scientist at Houston Methodist. His profile lists him as director of the Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center and vice chair of research in the Department of Surgery, and describes his research as the mechanisms of transplant rejection and tolerance.

The 2026 study in the Atlas deals with a known side effect. Transplant patients who take mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus sometimes develop a lung problem resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, in which the lungs fill with surfactant. Li's team asked whether mTOR is needed by alveolar macrophages, the lung cells that clear surfactant.

In mice, deleting mTOR in myeloid cells, or treating with temsirolimus, caused alveolar macrophages to die off, take up less material and fill with fat, producing PAP-like lung changes. This gives one cell-level explanation for the side effect. It is an animal study.

highlights.HEN2026: In mice, genetic deletion of mTOR or temsirolimus treatment depleted alveolar macrophages and caused PAP-like lung pathology; Li was senior author.

Superti-Furga G.lab_name: Superti-Furga Lab, CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences (Vienna, Austria)
Superti-Furga G.role: Systems biologist who maps how proteins and drugs interact in cells, with a focus on solute carrier (SLC) membrane transporters; his group helped identify SLC38A9 as a lysosomal amino-acid sensor for mTORC1.
Superti-Furga G.sub: CeMM, Vienna · Scientific Director (since 2005) · Professor of Medical Systems Biology, Medical University of Vienna (since 2015)
story: Giulio Superti-Furga is the scientific director of CeMM, the Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna, and a professor of medical systems biology at the Medical University of Vienna. Earlier he led a team at EMBL in Heidelberg and co-founded the company Cellzome.

His group uses large-scale proteomics to see which proteins sit together in cells and how drugs act on them. A big interest is the solute carrier (SLC) family, proteins that carry nutrients and other small molecules across membranes.

In the 2015 Nature paper in the Atlas (first author Manuele Rebsamen, with Lukas Huber's group in Innsbruck and others), the team described SLC38A9 as a protein in the lysosome membrane that can transport amino acids. It binds the Ragulator and Rag GTPase machinery, and cells without it responded poorly to amino acids. SLC38A9 thus became one of the lysosomal sensors that tell mTORC1 when amino acids are available.

highlights.REB2015: Identified SLC38A9 as a lysosomal amino-acid transporter and part of the Ragulator-Rag machinery required for amino-acid activation of mTORC1; Superti-Furga was senior author.

Parada LF.lab_name: Parada Lab, Cancer Biology & Genetics Program, Sloan Kettering Institute, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Parada LF.role: Uses genetically engineered mouse models to study nervous system tumours such as glioblastoma and neurofibromatosis-related tumours, and the brain effects of PTEN loss.
Parada LF.sub: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · Director, Brain Tumor Center; Albert C. Foster Chair · Member, National Academy of Sciences (2011)
story: Luis Parada is a neuroscientist and cancer biologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where he directs the Brain Tumor Center. His lab builds mouse models of nervous system tumours, including glioblastoma, neurofibromas and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours. When the Atlas study was done in 2009 his lab was at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

The 2009 paper in the Atlas, with Jing Zhou as first author, used mice that lack the PTEN gene in some neurons of the cortex and hippocampus. PTEN normally holds back the PI3K and AKT pathway upstream of mTOR, so these mice have overactive mTORC1, enlarged neurons, large brains and behaviours that resemble some features of autism.

Rapamycin, an mTORC1 inhibitor, both prevented and reversed the neuron enlargement and improved some of the abnormal behaviours. The work pointed to mTORC1 as a drug target for PTEN-related brain disorders. It was done in mice.

highlights.ZHO2009: Rapamycin prevented and reversed neuronal hypertrophy and improved some abnormal behaviours in neural-specific Pten knock-out mice; Parada was senior author.

Parada LF.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Kwiatkowski DJ.lab_name: Kwiatkowski Lab, Division of Translational Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Kwiatkowski DJ.role: Geneticist and physician who studies tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) and the TSC1/TSC2 genes that restrain mTORC1.
Kwiatkowski DJ.sub: Brigham and Women's Hospital · Senior Physician; Professor of Medicine, Harvard Medical School
story: David Kwiatkowski is a physician-scientist at Brigham and Women's Hospital and a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. His profile says his research covers the genetics of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), including mouse models (KWI2002), the roles of the TSC1 and TSC2 proteins, kidney and lung tumours linked to TSC, and genomic methods to find mutations.

TSC is caused by mutations in TSC1 or TSC2. The proteins they make normally keep mTORC1 in check, so without them mTORC1 becomes overactive. In the brain this causes epilepsy and learning and social difficulties.

The 2008 study in the Atlas, with Lynsey Meikle as first author, used a mouse in which Tsc1 is removed from most neurons. Treatment with rapamycin or its relative RAD001 raised median survival from 33 days to over 100 days and improved behaviour and brain cell structure. Even a short course, from day 7 to day 30 of life, gave lasting benefit. The work supported testing mTOR inhibitors for TSC brain disease.

highlights.MEI2008: Rapamycin and RAD001 greatly extended survival and improved neuronal and behavioural features in a mouse model of TSC brain disease; Kwiatkowski was senior author.
highlights.TEE2002: TSC1 and TSC2 act together to inhibit mTOR signalling to S6K1 and 4E-BP1, in a study from John Blenis's lab; Kwiatkowski was a co-author.
highlights.KWI2002: A Tsc1 knockout mouse develops kidney cystadenomas and liver hemangiomas, and Tsc1-null cells show rapamycin-sensitive S6K activation; Kwiatkowski was first author.

Laiho M.lab_name: Laiho Lab, Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Laiho M.role: Studies DNA damage, the nucleolar stress response and how RNA polymerase I (which makes ribosomal RNA) can be targeted in cancer.
Laiho M.sub: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine · Willard and Lillian Hackerman Professor of Radiation Oncology; Director, Division of Molecular Radiation Sciences · part-time Professor, University of Helsinki
story: Marikki Laiho is a professor of radiation oncology and molecular radiation sciences at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and co-director of a cancer chemical and structural biology programme at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center. Her lab studies how cells react to DNA damage and how the making of ribosomes can be targeted in cancer.

Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and fast-growing cancer cells need many of them. In the 2026 Genes & Development paper in the Atlas (first author Wenjun Fan), the team blocked RNA polymerase I and screened the genome for genes that let cancer cells survive this. Switching off mTOR was one of them.

This was surprising because mTOR is usually seen as a driver of growth. The authors found that mTORC1 inhibition did not restore ribosome production. Instead it moved the few remaining ribosomes away from 5'TOP mRNAs and toward transcripts needed for survival, which they call 'translational fitness'. This was shown in cancer cells in the lab.

highlights.FAN2026: Genome-wide screens showed mTORC1 inhibition lets cancer cells survive ribosome biogenesis deficiency by redirecting scarce ribosomes to survival transcripts; Laiho was senior and corresponding author.

Harris AL.lab_name: Department of Oncology, University of Oxford; formerly CRUK Molecular Oncology Laboratories, Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Harris AL.role: Medical oncologist who studies hypoxia, tumour blood-vessel growth and the metabolic response of breast cancer cells.
Harris AL.sub: University of Oxford · Emeritus Professor of Medical Oncology · First Professor of Medical Oncology at Oxford (1989–2017) · Emeritus
story: Adrian Harris is an emeritus professor of medical oncology at the University of Oxford. His Oxford page says he became Professor of Clinical Oncology at Newcastle-upon-Tyne in 1982 and in 1989 the first Professor of Medical Oncology at Oxford, a post he held until 2017. He directed the Cancer Research UK Molecular Oncology Laboratories at the Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine. His research focus is hypoxia, tumour angiogenesis and metabolism.

The 2016 Cell Metabolism review in the Atlas was written with Deborah Goberdhan and Clive Wilson, both at Oxford. It discusses how mTORC1 senses amino acids, and argues that transporters in different cell compartments, including lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus, mark the places where mTORC1 is switched on.

The authors propose that different amino acids in different compartments may activate different mTORC1 complexes, which could have different drug sensitivities and jobs. This is a proposal, not a final answer.

highlights.GOB2016: Review proposing that amino-acid transporters on lysosomes, endosomes and the Golgi mark sites of mTORC1 activation and may define distinct mTORC1 complexes; Harris was senior author.

Harris AL.credit: Portrait: University of Oxford, Department of Oncology

Sellers WR.lab_name: Sellers Lab, Cancer Program, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Sellers WR.role: Cancer biologist and physician-scientist whose work spans cancer genomics and cancer therapeutics, including how the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway drives tumours and how to target it.
Sellers WR.sub: Core Institute Member and Director of the Cancer Program, Broad Institute · Faculty, Harvard Medical School and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute · Formerly Vice President and Global Head of Oncology, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research
story: William Sellers is a physician-scientist who studies how cancers arise and how to treat them. His group at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston was an early contributor to the idea that the PI3K/AKT pathway, which feeds into mTOR, is a major driver of tumours when it is switched on too strongly. Later he led oncology research at Novartis, and he now directs the Cancer Program at the Broad Institute.

The study in the Atlas, published in 2004 with Pradip Majumder as first author, used mice that carry an active form of the human AKT1 gene in the prostate. These mice develop early prostate changes that resemble a pre-cancer. Treating them with an mTOR inhibitor reversed the changes, which showed that growth driven by AKT depends on mTOR. The work also showed that the cells die by a mitochondrial route and that HIF-1 alpha targets, including glycolysis genes, respond to AKT and mTOR inhibition.

The paper also raised a caution for patients. If tumours switch on the survival gene BCL2 or increase HIF-1 alpha activity, they might escape mTOR inhibitors. That kind of resistance question is still relevant for cancer drugs aimed at this pathway.

highlights.MAJ2004: Senior author: in mice with active AKT in the prostate, an mTOR inhibitor reversed the pre-cancerous change by triggering cell death and altering HIF-1 alpha-dependent metabolism.

Sellers WR.credit: Portrait: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard

Mockett RJ.lab_name: Mockett Lab, Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (Mobile, Alabama, USA)
Mockett RJ.role: Studies ageing in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, including how rapamycin and diet change lifespan.
Mockett RJ.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (since 2013) · Assistant Professor, University of South Alabama (2007–2013) · Research Assistant Professor, University of Southern California (2001–2007)
story: Robin Mockett studies why animals age, mostly using fruit flies. Flies live only weeks, so a lifespan experiment can be finished quickly. His work has covered oxidative stress, genes that affect longevity and, more recently, how the drug rapamycin changes the lifespan of flies.

The 2026 study in the Atlas followed an earlier finding from the same laboratory that rapamycin shortened the life of one male fly strain. The team tested five fly strains on two different foods. On a cornmeal and torula yeast food, rapamycin mostly did not help and was harmful in 19 experiments. On a richer brewer's yeast food it was beneficial in eight experiments and not significantly harmful in any.
The result is a reminder that a drug's effect on lifespan can depend on diet, sex and genetic strain, which matters when results from different laboratories seem to disagree.

highlights.JAC2026: Corresponding author: rapamycin extended or shortened fly lifespan depending on diet, strain and sex, so the drug can switch between helpful and harmful effects.

Behrends C.lab_name: Behrends Lab, Munich Cluster for Systems Neurology (SyNergy), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (Munich, Germany)
Behrends C.role: Studies autophagy and ubiquitin pathways, and in 2015 reported SLC38A9 as a member of the Rag-Ragulator complex that relays amino acid availability to mTORC1.
Behrends C.sub: Professor for Systems Biology of Neurodegenerative Diseases, SyNergy, LMU Munich (since 2016) · Emmy Noether Group Leader, Goethe University Frankfurt (2011–2016) · Postdoctoral fellow, Harvard Medical School (2007–2010)
story: Christian Behrends trained at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry near Munich and did postdoctoral work at Harvard Medical School with J. Wade Harper. He then started his own group at Goethe University in Frankfurt and since 2016 has been a professor at LMU Munich. His lab studies autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and ubiquitin signalling.

The study in the Atlas, from his Frankfurt group with Jennifer Jung as first author, looked at SLC38A9, a protein sitting on the lysosome, the compartment where mTORC1 is switched on by amino acids. They found that SLC38A9 binds the Rag GTPases and Ragulator in a way that depends on amino acids. Removing it lowered mTORC1 activity, and having too much of it made mTORC1 overactive even when amino acids were scarce.

This placed SLC38A9 inside the machinery that tells mTORC1 whether food is available. Related work from other laboratories at about the same time found that SLC38A9 can also act as a sensor of the amino acid arginine.

highlights.JUN2015: Senior author: identifies the lysosomal protein SLC38A9 as part of the Rag-Ragulator complex that passes amino acid availability on to mTORC1.

Green DR.lab_name: Green Lab, Department of Immunology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital (Memphis, Tennessee, USA)
Green DR.role: Cell death researcher known for work on apoptosis and the immune system, whose group also showed that the transcription factor Myc drives the metabolic switch of activated T cells.
Green DR.sub: Peter C. Doherty Endowed Chair of Immunology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital · PhD, Yale University (1981) · Member, National Academy of Sciences (2020)
story: Douglas Green is an immunologist at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis. He is best known for studying apoptosis, the controlled way in which cells die, in cancer and in the immune system. His honours include election to the US National Academy of Sciences in 2020.

The study in the Atlas, led by Ruoning Wang in his laboratory, asked how T cells prepare for a fight. When a T cell is activated it must grow and divide fast, so it changes how it uses sugar and the amino acid glutamine. The team found that the transcription factor Myc, not HIF1 alpha, controls this switch, and that glutamine feeds the making of polyamines, small molecules cells need to grow.

The paper connects immune cell activation to nutrient use, the same theme in which mTOR acts as a master controller of growth. It is included in the Atlas because the metabolic reprogramming it describes is part of the picture of how mTOR-linked growth signals shape T cell responses.

highlights.WAN2011: Senior author: Myc controls the glucose and glutamine metabolic reprogramming of activated T cells, linking glutaminolysis to polyamine synthesis.

Green DR.credit: Portrait: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

Kaelin WG.lab_name: Kaelin Lab, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Kaelin WG.role: Cancer researcher who worked out how cells sense oxygen through the VHL and HIF proteins, work recognised by the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Kaelin WG.sub: Sidney Farber Professor of Medicine, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School · Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator (since 1998) · Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 2019
story: William Kaelin is a physician-scientist who studies how mutations in tumour-suppressor genes cause cancer. His work on the VHL protein helped reveal how cells sense oxygen, and it led to drugs for kidney cancer. He shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Peter Ratcliffe and Gregg Semenza.

The study in the Atlas, published in 2004 with James Brugarolas as first author, asked how low oxygen (hypoxia) turns mTOR down. The team found that this needs the TSC1/TSC2 complex and a hypoxia-inducible gene called REDD1. Cells lacking REDD1 or TSC2 failed to shut mTOR off under low oxygen, unlike the energy-stress route, which uses AMPK.
This linked the oxygen-sensing field to the mTOR field. It also suggested a reason tumours lacking TSC2 can keep growing in oxygen-poor regions.

highlights.BRU2004: Senior author: low oxygen inhibits mTOR through REDD1 and the TSC1/TSC2 complex, independently of AMPK and LKB1.

Martin DDO.lab_name: NeurdyPhagy Lab, Department of Biology, University of Waterloo (Waterloo, Ontario, Canada)
Martin DDO.role: Studies protein mislocalization and disturbed protein recycling (proteostasis) in Huntington disease and ALS.
Martin DDO.sub: Associate Professor and Program Director, Medical and Biomedical Sciences, Department of Biology, University of Waterloo · PhD, University of Alberta (2011)
story: Dale Martin leads a group at the University of Waterloo that studies how proteins end up in the wrong place in brain cells and how that damages them, with a focus on Huntington disease and ALS. The lab also works on getting drugs across the blood-brain barrier.

The 2026 review in the Atlas, written with Fatima Abrar, covers SQSTM1, also called p62. This protein marks damaged or unwanted material for autophagy, the cell's recycling process, which mTORC1 helps to restrain. The review describes how chemical tags on SQSTM1, such as phosphate, ubiquitin and fatty acid groups, change where it sits and what it does.
Understanding these switches may help explain why autophagy fails in neurodegenerative diseases and where treatments could act.

highlights.ABR2026: Senior author of a review on how post-translational modifications of SQSTM1/p62 control autophagy and relate to neurodegeneration.

Foks AC.lab_name: Aging and Immunity group, Division of BioTherapeutics, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University (Leiden, Netherlands)
Foks AC.role: Studies how the immune system drives atherosclerosis and how it changes with age, including how rapamycin reshapes immune cells in aged atherosclerotic mice.
Foks AC.sub: Associate Professor (Universitair hoofddocent), LACDR, Leiden University
story: Amanda Foks is an associate professor in the Division of BioTherapeutics at the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research (Leiden University). Her group is called Aging and Immunity, and her university page lists her work on the immune system in cardiovascular disease such as atherosclerosis.

Atherosclerosis is the build-up of fatty, inflamed plaques in artery walls. It becomes more common with age, and immune cells are part of the problem. In the 2026 Aging Cell study in the Atlas, Foks was the last author. Her team gave rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, to aged mice that prone to atherosclerosis and looked at the immune cells in the plaques and in lymphoid tissue.

They found fewer plaque macrophages and T cells, more regulatory T cells, and fewer of the B cell types linked to autoantibodies. The authors read this as rapamycin acting as an immune rejuvenation treatment in old arteries. The work was done with colleagues in Leiden and at the Medical University of Vienna.

highlights.JIN2026C: Senior author of the Aging Cell study showing that rapamycin reduced plaque inflammation and shifted T and B cell populations toward a younger-looking profile in aged atherosclerotic mice.

Ohdo S.lab_name: Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Kyushu University (Fukuoka, Japan)
Ohdo S.role: Works on the body clock and drug timing (chronopharmacology), including how circadian rhythms control mTOR in cancer cells.
Ohdo S.sub: Specially Appointed Professor, Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Kyushu University
story: Shigehiro Ohdo is a pharmaceutical scientist at Kyushu University in Fukuoka, Japan. His university profile describes his aim as new chronotherapy based on the molecular clock: timing drug doses to the body's daily rhythms so they work better and cause fewer side effects.

In the 2013 Cancer Research paper in the Atlas, he was the last author. The team studied renal cell carcinoma, a kidney cancer, and asked how the circadian clock controls mTOR. They reported that the clock regulates mTOR through the ubiquitin system, the cell's protein tagging and disposal machinery.
For a student, the link is simple: the activity of mTOR is not constant over a day, and this work asks whether that rhythm matters for how cancers grow and how mTOR drugs might be timed.

highlights.OKA2013: Last author of the Cancer Research study describing circadian regulation of mTOR by the ubiquitin pathway in renal cell carcinoma.

Solit DB.lab_name: Solit Lab, Human Oncology and Pathogenesis Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Solit DB.role: Physician-scientist who used whole-genome sequencing of an exceptional responder to show that TSC1 mutations can predict sensitivity of bladder cancer to the mTOR inhibitor everolimus.
Solit DB.sub: Geoffrey Beene Chair · Director, Marie-Josée and Henry R. Kravis Center for Molecular Oncology, MSK · Genitourinary medical oncologist
story: David Solit is a medical oncologist who treats genitourinary cancers and runs a research lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York. He holds the Geoffrey Beene Chair and directs the Marie-Josée and Henry R. Kravis Center for Molecular Oncology. His work includes clinical trials of kinase inhibitors and the study of "extraordinary responders": patients with hard-to-treat cancers who respond very strongly to a drug that helps few others.

The 2012 Science paper in the Atlas began with one such patient. A man with metastatic bladder cancer had a long remission on everolimus, a drug that inhibits mTOR. The team sequenced the whole genome of his tumour and found a loss-of-function mutation in TSC1, a gene that normally restrains mTOR signalling.

They then checked 109 more bladder cancers and found TSC1 mutations in about 8 percent, and these mutations matched everolimus sensitivity. The study is an early example of finding a drug response marker by sequencing one unusual patient. Solit was the last author.

highlights.IYE2012: Last author of the Science study that sequenced an everolimus extraordinary responder and linked TSC1 mutation to sensitivity to mTOR inhibition in bladder cancer.

Solit DB.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Campisi J.lab_name: Campisi Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Campisi J.role: Pioneer of research on cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP); her 2015 paper showed that mTOR drives the inflammatory SASP.
Campisi J.sub: Deceased 19 January 2024 (1950–2024) · Buck Institute for Research on Aging (from 2002) · Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory · Boston University Medical School
story: Judith Campisi (1950–2024) was a cell biologist at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging in California, which she joined in 2002. Earlier she worked at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and at Boston University Medical School. She died on 19 January 2024. She is known for showing that cellular senescence, a state in which damaged cells stop dividing, is a key driver of ageing, and that it also protects against cancer.

Senescent cells do not simply sit quietly. They release inflammatory signals known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. In the 2015 Nature Cell Biology study in the Atlas, Campisi was the last author. The team found that rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, reduced the inflammatory output of senescent cells without bringing the cells back to dividing.

The mechanism they identified was selective: rapamycin cut translation of IL1A, a cytokine at the top of the inflammatory cascade, which lowered NF-kB activity. In mice, rapamycin also reduced the ability of senescent fibroblasts to stimulate prostate tumour growth. The paper gave one explanation for why rapamycin may help against age-related inflammation.

highlights.LAB2015: Senior author of the study showing that mTOR promotes IL1A translation and so drives the pro-tumorigenic SASP, and that rapamycin suppresses it.

Campisi J.credit: Portrait: Buck Institute for Research on Aging

Vissing K.lab_name: Department of Public Health, Sport Science, Aarhus University (Aarhus, Denmark)
Vissing K.role: Studies the control of protein balance in skeletal muscle and how this knowledge might counter muscle loss.
Vissing K.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Public Health, Sport Science, Aarhus University
story: Kristian Vissing is an associate professor of sport science at Aarhus University in Denmark. His university page lists two main interests: the regulatory mechanisms that keep protein balance in skeletal muscle, and how muscle activity might send signals that protect distant organs.

The 2026 paper in Experimental Gerontology in the Atlas asks how ageing changes the way muscle responds to being stretched passively. The abstract-level finding in the Atlas is that mTORC1 signalling was preserved with age, while the JNK-SMAD2L signalling was less sensitive.
Vissing is the last author of this four-author study, which fits his research line on how muscle controls its own growth and breakdown.

highlights.KRISTIANSEN2026: Last author of the Experimental Gerontology study showing that ageing preserved mTORC1 signalling but blunted JNK-SMAD2L sensitivity to passive stretch of muscle.

Trapnell BC.lab_name: Translational Pulmonary Science Center, Division of Pulmonary Medicine, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Trapnell BC.role: Pulmonologist-scientist who directs the Rare Lung Diseases Clinical Research Consortium whose MILES trial led to approval of sirolimus for lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM); also known for work on pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.
Trapnell BC.sub: Director, Translational Pulmonary Science Center · Professor, UC Department of Pediatrics · Pulmonologist, Cincinnati Children's
story: Bruce Trapnell is a lung doctor and researcher at Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center and a professor in the University of Cincinnati Department of Pediatrics. He directs the Translational Pulmonary Science Center. His group showed that GM-CSF autoantibodies cause autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and that a hereditary form comes from mutations in the genes CSF2RA and CSF2RB.

He also established and directs the Rare Lung Diseases Clinical Research Consortium. Its study of sirolimus (rapamycin) in lymphangioleiomyomatosis, or LAM, is the 2011 New England Journal of Medicine trial known as MILES. LAM is a rare disease, mostly in women, in which cells with overactive mTOR damage the lungs.

In MILES, sirolimus stabilised lung function over the treatment year, while lung function fell in people on placebo. Trapnell is listed as the last author. The trial led to FDA approval of sirolimus for LAM, one of the clearest examples of an mTOR drug helping patients.

highlights.MCC2011: Last author of the MILES trial, in which sirolimus stabilised lung function in lymphangioleiomyomatosis compared with placebo.

Trapnell BC.credit: Portrait: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center

Ueberheide B.lab_name: Proteomics Resource Center, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Ueberheide B.role: Mass spectrometry and proteomics specialist who directs NYU's proteomics core and contributed the protein profiling to the Down syndrome hippocampus mTOR study.
Ueberheide B.sub: Associate Professor, Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology and Neurology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine · Director, Proteomics Resource Center
story: Beatrix Ueberheide is an associate professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, in the departments of Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology and of Neurology, and director of the Proteomics Resource Center. Her profile lists work on biological mass spectrometry, de novo protein sequencing and the structure of peptide toxins.

Proteomics means measuring many proteins at once. In the 2026 Alzheimer's & Dementia paper in the Atlas, her laboratory is the proteomics group of a team led by neuroscientists at the University of Colorado and NYU. She is a middle author, not the senior author.

The study looked at hippocampal tissue from people with Down syndrome who also had Alzheimer's disease changes, and found disruption in upstream regulators of the mTOR and insulin pathways. The paper describes its observations as preliminary.

highlights.NOR2026: Proteomics co-author of the study reporting disrupted hippocampal upstream regulators of mTOR and insulin signalling in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's neuropathology (preliminary observations).

Ueberheide B.credit: Portrait: NYU Grossman School of Medicine

Cecconi F.lab_name: Cell Stress and Survival group, Danish Cancer Institute (Copenhagen, Denmark), and Department of Biology, University of Rome Tor Vergata (Rome, Italy)
Cecconi F.role: Discovered AMBRA1, a regulator of autophagy, and showed how mTOR restrains autophagy by acting on AMBRA1 and ULK1.
Cecconi F.sub: Full Professor, University of Rome Tor Vergata (since 2006) · Leads Cell Stress and Survival group, Danish Cancer Institute (since 2013) · Deputy Director, CARD, Copenhagen
story: Francesco Cecconi is a full professor at the University of Rome Tor Vergata and, since 2013, leads the Cell Stress and Survival group at the Danish Cancer Institute in Copenhagen. His group studies autophagy, the cell's recycling process, in development and in disease, especially tumours. He is known for discovering AMBRA1, an autophagy regulator, and earlier for identifying the developmental role of Apaf1 in apoptosis.

The 2013 Nature Cell Biology paper in the Atlas, with Cecconi as last author, asked how mTOR switches autophagy off. The team showed that when nutrients are plentiful, mTOR phosphorylates AMBRA1. When mTOR is inhibited, AMBRA1 loses that phosphate and works with the ubiquitin ligase TRAF6 to attach K63-linked ubiquitin chains to ULK1.
That modification stabilises ULK1 and helps it assemble, so autophagy can start. The paper is often cited for showing a direct link between mTOR and the machinery that begins autophagosome formation.

highlights.NAZ2013: Last author of the study showing that mTOR inhibits AMBRA1 by phosphorylation, and that without mTOR activity AMBRA1 and TRAF6 ubiquitylate and activate ULK1 to start autophagy.

Kummu O.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Kummu O.role: Studies how chemicals activate the nuclear receptor PXR and disturb metabolism; co-author of the study linking PXR-driven liver growth to the AKT-mTOR pathway.
Kummu O.sub: Senior Research Fellow, Faculty of Medicine, University of Oulu
story: Outi Kummu is a senior research fellow at the University of Oulu in Finland, in pharmacology and toxicology. Her page describes work on chemical exposure and the activation of nuclear receptors, especially the pregnane X receptor (PXR), and how this can disturb metabolism.

PXR is a sensor for foreign chemicals and drugs in the liver. In the 2026 Archives of Toxicology study in the Atlas, the Oulu team tested the drug rifampicin, a human PXR activator, in 16 healthy volunteers. After one week, the liver volume relative to body weight rose by about 2.7 percent.
In male mice, PXR activation made the liver grow and raised AKT-mTOR activity, without the YAP activation seen in earlier work. Kummu is the third author; the senior author is Jukka Hakkola.

highlights.LASSILA2026: Co-author of the controlled trial and mouse study showing that PXR activation enlarged the liver and activated the AKT-mTOR pathway in male mice.

Passos JF.lab_name: Cell and Molecular Aging Laboratory, Department of Physiology and Biomedical Engineering, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Passos JF.role: Studies how senescent cells, mitochondria and telomeres contribute to ageing and age-related disease.
Passos JF.sub: Professor of Physiology, Mayo Clinic · Newcastle University Institute for Ageing (affiliation on the 2018 paper)
story: João Passos is a professor of physiology at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, where he leads the Cell and Molecular Aging Laboratory. His page says he studies the role of senescent cells in ageing and age-related disease, with a focus on mitochondria and telomeres. He earned his PhD at Newcastle University.

In the 2018 Aging Cell paper in the Atlas, he was the last author, with the work done at the Newcastle University Institute for Ageing. The team gave rapamycin to mice lacking the gene nfkb1, which age fast and show chronic inflammation, and asked whether it would help.

Rapamycin improved healthspan in these mice, but it did not lower the chronic low-level inflammation of ageing, often called inflammaging. The result separates the two effects, which matters for deciding how rapamycin might act as an ageing treatment.

highlights.COR2018: Last author of the study showing that rapamycin improved healthspan in nfkb1 mutant mice without reducing inflammaging.

Wei W.lab_name: Wei Lab, Department of Pathology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Wei W.role: Studies how protein stability and cell signalling, including the PI3K-mTOR-AKT network, are controlled in cancer cells.
Wei W.sub: Professor of Pathology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center & Harvard Medical School (since 2017) · Director, Biochemistry Program, BIDMC Cancer Center (2015) · Postdoc with William Kaelin, Dana-Farber (2002–2005)
story: Wenyi Wei leads a laboratory in the Department of Pathology at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, part of Harvard Medical School. He trained as a PhD student at Brown University with John Sedivy and then as a postdoctoral fellow with William Kaelin at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. His research focuses on tumour formation, the cell cycle and cell signalling.

The Atlas includes his 2015 study in Cancer Discovery on how mTORC2 is switched on. mTORC2 is one of the two big mTOR protein complexes, and it activates a growth kinase called AKT. The team found that a part of the SIN1 protein normally holds mTOR back, and that a membrane lipid called PIP3 releases this brake, so mTORC2 turns on when growth signals arrive.

They also showed that mutations found in cancer patients weaken the brake, which raises mTORC2 activity and helps tumours grow. The work links the PI3K signal that sits upstream of AKT directly to mTORC2.

highlights.LIU2015: Showed that the SIN1 PH domain inhibits mTOR and that PIP3 relieves this inhibition to activate mTORC2; Wei was senior and corresponding author.

Puertollano R.lab_name: Protein Trafficking and Organelle Biology, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Puertollano R.role: Studies how lysosomes are regulated, including how mTORC1 controls the transcription factors TFEB and TFE3 that switch on autophagy and lysosome genes.
Puertollano R.sub: Senior Investigator, NHLBI, National Institutes of Health
story: Rosa Puertollano is a Senior Investigator at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute at the NIH. Her group treats the lysosome not just as the cell's recycling bin but as a control centre that senses conditions and sends signals.

In the 2012 study in the Atlas, her lab showed how mTORC1 controls autophagy at the level of genes. When nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 adds a phosphate to the transcription factor TFEB at position Ser211. That tag lets 14-3-3 proteins hold TFEB in the cytosol, away from its target genes.

When mTORC1 is blocked, TFEB is released, moves into the nucleus and turns on genes for autophagy and lysosomes. Her lab also works on TFEB and TFE3 and on animal models of lysosomal storage diseases.

highlights.MAR2012: Showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB on Ser211, trapping it in the cytosol with 14-3-3 proteins, and that mTORC1 inhibition frees TFEB to enter the nucleus and drive autophagy genes; Puertollano was senior author.
highlights.MAR2013: Showed that active Rag GTPases bind TFEB and recruit it, and some MITF isoforms, to the lysosome, where mTORC1 can phosphorylate it; Puertollano was senior author.

Bandyopadhyay S.lab_name: Bandyopadhyay Lab, Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Bandyopadhyay S.role: Uses functional genomics, drug screens and proteomics to understand why breast and lung cancers become resistant to drugs, including drugs that target the mTOR pathway.
Bandyopadhyay S.sub: Professor, Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, UCSF · PhD with Trey Ideker, UC San Diego · independent lab at UCSF since 2010
story: Sourav Bandyopadhyay is a professor at the University of California San Francisco. He earned his PhD in bioinformatics and systems biology with Trey Ideker at UC San Diego and started his own research group at UCSF in 2010. His lab studies drug resistance and synthetic lethal interactions in breast and lung cancers.

The 2023 study in the Atlas tested RMC-6272, a bi-steric molecule: it joins a rapamycin-like part to a part that blocks the mTOR active site. It hits mTORC1 more than 25 times more strongly than mTORC2, and it blocks 4E-BP1, a target that rapamycin-type drugs miss.

In breast cancer cell lines the drug triggered cell death, worked in tumours that were resistant to hormone therapy or to CDK4/6 inhibitors, and did better than everolimus. The authors suggest selective mTORC1 inhibition could help overcome several forms of resistance.

highlights.MEN2023: Showed that the bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-6272 kills ER+ breast cancer cells and overcomes hormone and CDK4/6 inhibitor resistance; Bandyopadhyay was senior and corresponding author.

Gonen T.lab_name: Gonen Lab, Departments of Biological Chemistry and Physiology, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Gonen T.role: Determines the 3D structures of membrane proteins and pioneered microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED); in the mTOR field he solved the structure of the lysosomal arginine transporter SLC38A9.
Gonen T.sub: Professor, Biological Chemistry and Physiology, UCLA · HHMI Investigator (2017) · PhD, University of Auckland (2002)
story: Tamir Gonen is a structural biologist and professor at UCLA, and an Investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. He studied at the University of Auckland, did structural biology training at Harvard Medical School and later led a group at HHMI's Janelia Research Campus before moving to UCLA.

The Atlas includes his 2018 study of SLC38A9, a protein in the lysosome membrane that moves amino acids and helps mTORC1 sense them. His team used X-ray crystallography on the zebrafish version of the protein with arginine bound.

The structure caught the transporter in a cytosol-open state and showed how a conserved stretch in its first helix holds arginine in place. Changing that stretch stopped arginine transport. This gave a molecular picture of how a lysosomal transporter could report amino acid levels to mTORC1.

highlights.LEI2018: Solved the crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9 from zebrafish, showing how the transporter grips arginine; Gonen was senior and corresponding author.

Yancopoulos GD.role: Industry scientist who co-founded Regeneron and led drug discovery there; in this Atlas he is senior author of an early paper showing that Akt/mTOR signalling controls muscle size.
Yancopoulos GD.sub: Founding Scientist, President & Chief Scientific Officer, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (joined 1989) · Member, US National Academy of Sciences (2004) · industry scientist
story: George Yancopoulos is a physician-scientist who joined Regeneron in 1989 as its founding scientist, working with co-founder Leonard Schleifer. He is now the company's president and chief scientific officer. He is listed as a principal inventor or developer on several approved drugs from Regeneron and was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences in 2004.
The study in the Atlas, published in Nature Cell Biology in 2001, came from Regeneron's muscle biology group led by Sue Bodine. It asked what makes skeletal muscle grow or shrink in living animals.

The team found that the Akt/mTOR pathway turns up during muscle growth and down during wasting. Rapamycin blocked growth, and switching on the pathway genetically was enough to cause growth and to oppose muscle loss from disuse.

highlights.BOD2001: Showed in rats that Akt/mTOR signalling is needed and sufficient for skeletal muscle hypertrophy and can oppose atrophy; Yancopoulos was last author, with Bodine as first author.

Finkel T.lab_name: Aging Institute, UPMC and University of Pittsburgh (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA)
Finkel T.role: Studies the biology of aging, including how mTOR levels and mitochondria influence lifespan and healthspan in mammals.
Finkel T.sub: Director, Aging Institute, UPMC & University of Pittsburgh (since 2017) · Chief, Center for Molecular Medicine, NHLBI, NIH (nearly 25 years at NIH) · MD, PhD, Harvard
story: Toren Finkel directs the Aging Institute at UPMC and the University of Pittsburgh, which he joined in 2017. Before that he spent nearly 25 years at the National Institutes of Health, most recently as chief of the Center for Molecular Medicine at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. He earned his MD and PhD at Harvard.
The Atlas study from 2013 asked a direct question: what happens if a mammal simply has less mTOR? The team built mice that make about 25 percent of normal mTOR, with lower mTORC1 and mTORC2 activity.

These mice were smaller but ate, handled glucose and burned energy normally. They lived about 20 percent longer at the median, and many tissue markers of aging were reduced. The slowing of aging was uneven, so some organs were protected more than others.

highlights.WUX2013: Showed that mice with about 25 percent of normal mTOR live roughly 20 percent longer with segmental, tissue-specific slowing of aging; Finkel was senior author.
highlights.SCH2006: Showed in human cells that the mTOR–raptor complex sets mitochondrial oxygen consumption and oxidative capacity, and that rapamycin lowers them; Finkel was senior author.

Schaffitzel C.lab_name: Berger-Schaffitzel Lab, School of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences, University of Bristol (Bristol, England, United Kingdom)
Schaffitzel C.role: Structural biologist who uses cryo-electron microscopy to study ribosomes and translation machinery; co-senior author of the first cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2.
Schaffitzel C.sub: Professor of Biochemistry, University of Bristol (since 2014) · Team leader, EMBL Grenoble (from 2007) · Postdoc and lecturer, ETH Zurich (from 2001)
story: Christiane Berger-Schaffitzel is a professor of biochemistry at the University of Bristol. She did her doctoral work at the University of Zurich, then worked at ETH Zurich and led a team at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory in Grenoble from 2007 before moving to Bristol in 2014. She also leads the GW4 Cryo-EM Facility.

The 2017 study in the Atlas was a joint effort with Robbie Loewith's group in Geneva. They used electron cryo-microscopy to solve the structure of TORC2 from baker's yeast, a complex of six proteins shaped like a rhombohedron.

The structure showed that the Avo3 protein (the yeast version of Rictor) covers the spot where the rapamycin-FKBP12 complex would bind. This explains why TORC2 is not blocked by rapamycin. It also showed how another subunit sits near the active site and may help recruit substrates.

highlights.KAR2017: Solved the cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2, explaining its rapamycin insensitivity through Avo3 covering the FKBP12-rapamycin binding site; Schaffitzel was last author, co-corresponding with Robbie Loewith.

Phillips PC.lab_name: Phillips Lab, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Eugene, Oregon, USA)
Phillips PC.role: Evolutionary geneticist who uses the nematode C. elegans to study aging, including how insulin/IGF-1 signalling, a pathway tightly connected to mTOR, shapes lifespan.
Phillips PC.sub: Professor, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon · Caenorhabditis Intervention Testing Program participant
story: Patrick Phillips is a professor at the University of Oregon. His group uses the roundworm C. elegans to ask how DNA turns into traits such as body size, reproduction and lifespan, and how evolution shapes these genetic systems. He takes part in the Caenorhabditis Intervention Testing Program, which tests compounds for effects on aging.

The 2026 study in the Atlas, led by Rose Al-Saadi, looked at the insulin/IGF-1 pathway in male worms. The researchers used a tool that removes the DAF-2 receptor on demand, called auxin-inducible degradation, so the pathway could be switched off in the whole animal.

Males lived much longer, with median lifespan up by more than 440 percent, and kept better reproductive health late in life. Insulin/IGF-1 signalling and mTOR are linked growth-and-nutrient pathways, which is why the result is relevant here.

highlights.ALS2026: Showed that removing the DAF-2/IGF-1 receptor throughout the body in C. elegans males raises median lifespan by more than 440 percent and improves late-life reproduction; Phillips was senior author.

Ahmed R.lab_name: Ahmed Laboratory, Emory Vaccine Center, Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Emory University (Atlanta, Georgia, USA)
Ahmed R.role: Immunologist who studies T-cell and B-cell memory and showed that mTOR is a major regulator of memory CD8 T-cell formation.
Ahmed R.sub: Director, Emory Vaccine Center · Professor of Microbiology and Immunology, Emory University · Georgia Research Alliance Eminent Scholar · Member, US National Academy of Sciences
story: Rafi Ahmed directs the Emory Vaccine Center and is a professor of microbiology and immunology at Emory University in Atlanta. His lab studies immune memory in T cells and B cells, with the aim of building better vaccines and treatments. He is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences.

His group is also known for showing that the receptor PD-1 helps T cells become exhausted during long-lasting viral infections, which led to PD-1 blocking antibodies being tried in infections and cancer.

The 2009 study in the Atlas, published in Nature, found that mTOR helps decide which CD8 T cells become long-lived memory cells. Surprisingly, rapamycin, usually seen as an immune suppressor, improved the number and quality of memory T cells in virus-infected mice, and in vaccinated monkeys.

highlights.ARA2009: Showed that mTORC1 acts inside CD8 T cells to control memory differentiation and that rapamycin treatment improves memory responses to infection and vaccines; Ahmed was senior author.

Hafen E.lab_name: Hafen Group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Hafen E.role: Developmental geneticist who used Drosophila to work out how insulin and TOR signalling control cell and body size, including the role of Rheb.
Hafen E.sub: Professor of Developmental Genetics, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (since 2006) · Professor, University of Zurich (1997–2005) · Postdoc with Gerald Rubin, UC Berkeley (1984–1986)
story: Ernst Hafen studied biology at the University of Basel, where he earned his PhD with Walter Gehring. After postdoctoral work with Gerald Rubin at UC Berkeley, he became a professor at the University of Zurich and has been a professor at ETH Zurich since 2006. He works on growth control and signal transduction in the fruit fly Drosophila.
In the 2003 study in the Atlas, his group studied Rheb, a small GTPase. Flies with mutations in the Rheb gene had smaller cells, while extra Rheb made cells grow larger.

Their genetic tests placed Rheb downstream of the tumour suppressors Tsc1 and Tsc2 in the TOR pathway, and showed that a main target is S6 kinase. This helped establish the order of parts in the pathway that controls cell growth.

highlights.STO2003: Showed in Drosophila that Rheb acts downstream of Tsc1-Tsc2 in the TOR pathway and signals mainly through S6K to promote cell growth; Hafen was senior author.
highlights.MON1999: Showed with George Thomas's group that flies lacking S6 kinase are small because their cells are smaller, not fewer; Hafen was a co-author.
highlights.OLD2000: Characterised dTOR, the fly TOR, as a cell-autonomous growth regulator acting through dS6K, likely on an amino-acid-sensing branch parallel to insulin signalling; Hafen was senior author.

Giguère V.lab_name: Giguère Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
Giguère V.role: Studies how nuclear receptors, especially the estrogen-related receptors (ERRs), control energy metabolism, and showed that mTOR and ERRα share target genes involved in lipid and TCA-cycle metabolism
Giguère V.sub: Professor of Biochemistry, McGill University · Goodman Cancer Institute · Fellow, Royal Society of Canada (2013)
story: Vincent Giguère is a professor in the Department of Biochemistry at McGill University and is affiliated with the Goodman Cancer Institute. His laboratory studies nuclear hormone receptors, proteins that sit in the cell and switch genes on and off in response to signals. A main focus is the estrogen-related receptors (ERRs), which have no known natural ligand but control how cells handle fat, sugar and mitochondria.

His lab page describes a link to mTOR: mTOR can act as a regulator of gene activity at many promoters, including genes shared with ERRα that are involved in the TCA cycle and fat synthesis. A 2013 paper from the lab examined how this crosstalk contributes to the fatty liver that can follow rapamycin treatment.

The study collected in the Atlas continues this theme. Rapamycin, an mTORC1 inhibitor, can cause fat to build up in the liver of mice. In this work, the antimalarial drug chloroquine reduced that effect, and the rescue depended on ERRα. The Atlas entry is a mouse study, so it does not by itself show the same thing happens in people.

highlights.BCH2026: Mouse study in which chloroquine co-treatment lessened rapamycin-induced fatty liver, with the protection depending on ERRα; the Atlas lists Giguère as senior author, consistent with his lab's ERRα–mTOR work.

Giguère V.credit: Portrait: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre

Oddo S.lab_name: Oddo Lab, University of Messina (Messina, Italy)
Oddo S.role: Alzheimer's disease researcher who showed that amyloid-beta raises mTOR activity and that lowering mTOR with rapamycin cuts amyloid and Tau pathology in mice through autophagy
Oddo S.sub: Associate Professor of Molecular Biology, University of Messina (from 2020, per his 2022 CV) · Associate Professor, School of Life Sciences, Arizona State University (2015–2020) · Assistant Professor, UT Health Science Center at San Antonio (2008–2013) · PhD, UC Irvine
story: Salvatore Oddo studies Alzheimer's disease, in which two sticky proteins, amyloid-beta and Tau, build up in the brain. He trained at the University of California, Irvine, where he earned his PhD in neurobiology, and ran his own lab at UT Health Science Center at San Antonio when the Atlas study was published in 2010. His CV lists later posts at Banner Sun Health Research Institute, Arizona State University and, since 2020, the University of Messina in Italy.

The 2010 paper, with Antonella Caccamo as first author, asked how amyloid-beta damages memory. In 3xTg-AD mice, which develop both amyloid and Tau pathology, rising amyloid-beta increased mTOR signaling, and high mTOR in turn reduced autophagy, the cell's recycling system that clears protein clumps. This forms a loop in which the disease feeds itself.

Treating the mice with rapamycin broke the loop: memory improved and both amyloid and Tau pathology fell. The team also showed that autophagy was needed for the drop in amyloid. The work is in mice, so it is evidence for a mechanism, not proof of a treatment for people.

highlights.CAC2010: Showed in 3xTg-AD mice that amyloid-beta raises mTOR activity and that rapamycin rescues memory while lowering amyloid and Tau through autophagy; Oddo is senior author.
highlights.MAJ2012: Showed in normally ageing mice that rapamycin from 2 months of age preserved spatial memory at 18 months while a start at 15 months did not, with lower brain IL-1beta and higher NR2B and CREB phosphorylation; Oddo is senior author.

Hortobagyi GN.lab_name: Department of Breast Medical Oncology, Division of Cancer Medicine, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas, USA)
Hortobagyi GN.role: Breast cancer physician-scientist and senior author of BOLERO-2, the phase 3 trial that showed adding the mTOR inhibitor everolimus improves outcomes in advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer
Hortobagyi GN.sub: Professor of Medicine, Breast Medical Oncology, MD Anderson Cancer Center · Chairman, Department of Breast Medical Oncology (1995–2015) · Nellie B. Connally Chair in Breast Cancer (1998–2015) · Clinician and clinical trialist
story: Gabriel Hortobagyi is a medical oncologist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston. He earned his MD at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia in 1970, trained in internal medicine at Case Western Reserve University, and did his oncology fellowship at MD Anderson, where he has worked since the 1970s. He chaired the Department of Breast Medical Oncology from 1995 to 2015.

Many hormone-receptor-positive breast cancers stop responding to hormone therapy, and this resistance is linked to activation of mTOR signaling. BOLERO-2 tested whether blocking mTOR could help. In 724 postmenopausal women whose cancer had progressed on a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor, adding everolimus to the drug exemestane was compared with exemestane plus placebo.

Progression-free survival was 10.6 months with everolimus versus 4.1 months with placebo by central review. Side effects included mouth sores (stomatitis), anemia and pneumonitis. The trial supported approval of everolimus for this use and remains one of the clearest human proofs that targeting mTOR can help cancer patients. Hortobagyi is a clinician and trialist, not a bench scientist.

highlights.BAS2012: Phase 3 randomized trial (n=724) in which adding everolimus to exemestane raised median progression-free survival from 4.1 to 10.6 months (central review); Hortobagyi is the senior author.
highlights.PIC2014: Final overall-survival analysis of BOLERO-2: the progression-free survival gain held (7.8 vs 3.2 months) but overall survival was not significantly longer (31.0 vs 26.6 months, P = 0.14); Hortobagyi is a co-author (second author).

Fields S.lab_name: Fields Lab, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Fields S.role: Technology-driven geneticist whose yeast screens helped show that lowering TOR signaling extends chronological lifespan in yeast
Fields S.sub: Professor Emeritus of Genome Sciences, University of Washington School of Medicine
story: Stanley Fields is a professor emeritus in the Department of Genome Sciences at the University of Washington. His faculty page says his lab works on developing new technologies, based on the idea that a good new method can open many areas of biology. The lab often uses baker's yeast as a test system and has applied its methods to topics including aging, cancer-associated proteins and malaria.

The 2006 paper, led by first author R. Wilson Powers, used that approach on aging. Yeast cells that sit in a dish without dividing can stay alive for a while, and the length of that time is called chronological lifespan. The team built a high-throughput assay and measured it for about 4,800 yeast strains, each missing one gene.

Several of the longest-lived strains had mutations in the TOR pathway. Rapamycin and another TOR-inhibiting compound also extended lifespan, and removing certain amino acids from the medium did too. The authors proposed that lower TOR signaling triggers a stress-resistance response that helps cells survive longer, an idea that connected TOR to calorie restriction.

highlights.POW2006: Screened about 4,800 yeast deletion strains and found that decreased TOR pathway signaling, genetic or by rapamycin, extends chronological lifespan; Fields is the senior author.

Fields S.credit: Portrait: University of Washington Department of Genome Sciences

Kim HS.lab_name: Myokine Research Center, Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Seoul, South Korea)
Kim HS.role: Muscle biologist working on muscle-secreted factors and treatments for sarcopenia and muscle wasting, and senior author of a study on a leucine-like drug that activates mTORC1 through Sestrin2
Kim HS.sub: MD, PhD, Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine · Myokine Research Center, Korea University
story: Hyeon Soo Kim holds an MD and PhD and works in the Department of Anatomy at Korea University College of Medicine in Seoul. He is listed in the university's Myokine Research Center, whose focus is basic muscle research, substances released by muscle, and treatments for sarcopenia and other muscle-wasting conditions.

Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. The amino acid leucine switches on mTORC1 by binding the sensor protein Sestrin2, which helps muscle build protein, but leucine is broken down quickly in the body. In the 2026 study, the group made DLMEH, a modified form of D-leucine designed to last longer, and showed that it binds Sestrin2 about as tightly as leucine does.

In human muscle cells and in rats with steroid-induced muscle wasting, DLMEH restored protein synthesis and preserved muscle mass, grip strength and endurance better than oral L-leucine, and its effect depended on Sestrin2. These are cell and rat results, so human benefit is not yet shown.

highlights.SHIM2026: Showed that the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH binds Sestrin2 and activates mTORC1 in a Sestrin2-dependent way, restoring muscle protein synthesis and function in a rat atrophy model; Kim is the senior and corresponding author.

Kim HS.credit: Portrait: Korea University Myokine Research Center

Ocampo A.lab_name: Ocampo Lab, University of Lausanne (Lausanne, Switzerland)
Ocampo A.role: Aging researcher known for work on partial cellular reprogramming as a way to rejuvenate tissues, and senior author of a cross-species platform for screening lifespan-extending compounds
Ocampo A.sub: Professor, University of Lausanne · EPITERNA (Épalinges, Switzerland)
story: Alejandro Ocampo leads a laboratory at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland and is also listed with the company EPITERNA in Épalinges. A bio on a Nature collection page describes his lab's work as epigenetic rejuvenation, including mouse models in which reprogramming factors can be switched on in specific tissues or the whole body.

The 2026 Cell Reports study in the Atlas is a different kind of project: a screening platform. It tests whether drugs extend lifespan in five species, from yeast and worms to flies, killifish and mice, using automated imaging and deep-learning software that detects when animals die. More than 400 compounds were tested across thousands of conditions.

Comparing species lets the team pick out compounds that work in several of them and point to longevity pathways shared across species. mTOR is one of the best-known of these pathways, and rapamycin is the classic compound that extends lifespan in many species.

highlights.PEREZ2026: Built a high-throughput lifespan-screening platform across yeast, nematodes, flies, killifish and mice and evaluated more than 400 compounds; Ocampo is the last and corresponding author.

Ocampo A.credit: Portrait: Alpian (interview with Prof. Alejandro Ocampo)

Chung WS.lab_name: Glia Biology Lab, Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST and Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (Daejeon, South Korea)
Chung WS.role: Neuroscientist who studies how glial cells (astrocytes and microglia) shape synapses, and senior author of the 2026 study linking neuronal ERBB4 and mTOR signaling to early Alzheimer's disease changes in mice
Chung WS.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST · Associate Director, Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (IBS)
story: Won-Suk Chung is an associate professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at KAIST and associate director of the Center for Vascular Research at the Institute for Basic Science, both in Daejeon, South Korea. His group's website is named for glia, the support cells of the brain.

In the 2026 Nature paper, the team followed Alzheimer's disease in mice. They found that astrocytes and microglia clear away excitatory synapses while sparing inhibitory ones. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing then showed a group of excitatory neurons that switch on an unusual gene, Erbb4, very early in the disease.

Deleting Erbb4 in these neurons prevented synapse loss, gliosis, amyloid plaques and memory problems in AD mice, while adding Erbb4 to healthy mouse neurons reproduced most of those changes, except plaques. The authors report that these effects needed mTOR signaling downstream of ERBB4. All of this is in mice, with supporting analysis of human transcriptomic data.

highlights.LEE2026: Showed in AD mouse models that ectopic excitatory-neuron ERBB4, acting through mTOR signaling, is necessary and sufficient for early synapse loss, gliosis and cognitive deficits; Chung is the senior and corresponding author.

Chakraverty R.lab_name: Chakraverty Group, Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Chakraverty R.role: Haematologist and transplant immunologist who studies why T cell immunotherapies succeed or fail, including how tuning T cell metabolism through mTORC1 changes their function.
Chakraverty R.sub: Professor of Haematology, University of Oxford (since 2020) · University College London (2005–2020; Professor from 2013)
story: Ronjon Chakraverty is a doctor and scientist who treats patients who receive bone marrow transplants and studies the immune cells that are used as therapy.
