He trained in medicine at the University of Birmingham and completed a PhD at the Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine in Oxford, followed by postdoctoral work with Megan Sykes at Harvard Medical School.

He moved to University College London in 2005 and became a professor there in 2013. In 2020 he joined the University of Oxford as Professor of Haematology, where he also helps run first-in-human trials of advanced cell and gene therapies.

His group asks why T cell treatments for cancer work in some patients and fail in others. One idea is to boost the metabolism of therapeutic T cells. In the study in this Atlas, his team turned up mTORC1 in helper CD4+ T cells by overexpressing RHEB. The cells lasted longer after transfer, but many became exhausted, so the boost was a trade-off.

highlights.SIL2026: Showed that forcing mTORC1 activity on with RHEB in therapeutic CD4+ T cells increased persistence after transfer but led to exhaustion and weaker tumour clearance; Chakraverty is the senior author.

Chakraverty R.credit: Portrait: MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine, University of Oxford

Lin AL.lab_name: Lin Lab, Department of Radiology, University of Missouri (Columbia, Missouri, USA)
Lin AL.role: Neuroimaging scientist who studies brain blood flow and metabolism in ageing and Alzheimer's risk, including the effect of rapamycin in people who carry APOE4.
Lin AL.sub: Professor and Vice Chair for Research, Department of Radiology, University of Missouri · NextGen Precision Health Investigator
story: Ai-Ling Lin is a professor of radiology at the University of Missouri. Her page describes her as an expert in translational neuroimaging of brain vascular and metabolic function in ageing, which means using brain scans to study how blood flow and energy use change as we grow older.
Her group is interested in people who carry the APOE4 gene variant, which raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease and is linked to blood vessel changes in the brain years before symptoms appear.

In the pilot trial in this Atlas, 23 healthy adults aged 45 to 65 took 1 mg of rapamycin a day for four weeks. Brain blood flow rose by more than 15 percent in several regions in the nine APOE4 carriers, but not in non-carriers. It was a small study with no control group, so it points to an idea to test rather than a proven benefit.

highlights.AWARE2026: Single-arm pilot trial in which low-dose rapamycin raised cerebral blood flow in APOE4 carriers; Lin is the senior (last) author.

Lin AL.credit: Portrait: University of Missouri School of Medicine

Budde K.lab_name: Department of Internal Medicine, with a focus on Nephrology and Internal Intensive Care, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin (Berlin, Germany)
Budde K.role: Kidney and transplant physician who took part as an investigator in the EXIST-2 trial of everolimus for kidney tumours in tuberous sclerosis and LAM; clinician-investigator rather than a bench mTOR researcher.
Budde K.sub: Professor, Department of Nephrology and Internal Intensive Care, Charité Berlin · clinician and transplant specialist
story: Klemens Budde is a physician at the Charité hospital in Berlin. He works in nephrology, the medicine of the kidneys, with a focus on kidney transplantation.
Transplant doctors use mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus and sirolimus to help prevent organ rejection, so mTOR drugs are part of everyday practice in his field.

He is the last author of EXIST-2, a phase 3 trial in 118 adults with kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas, caused by tuberous sclerosis complex or by LAM. Everolimus shrank the tumours by at least half in 42 percent of treated patients and in none on placebo. He is a clinician-investigator, so his role here is on the clinical side.

highlights.BIS2013: Companion phase 3 trial (EXIST-2) showing that everolimus shrank angiomyolipomas in 42% of patients versus 0% on placebo; Budde is listed as last author.

Liu AC.lab_name: Liu Lab, Department of Physiology and Aging, College of Medicine, University of Florida (Gainesville, Florida, USA)
Liu AC.role: Circadian biologist who studies how the body clock works at the molecular level and how it connects with metabolism and signalling pathways such as mTOR.
Liu AC.sub: Professor, Department of Physiology and Aging, University of Florida (since 2018) · University of Memphis (Assistant and Associate Professor, 2008–2017)
story: Andrew Liu studies the circadian clock, the roughly 24 hour timer that runs inside nearly every cell. He earned a PhD in biochemistry at the University of Michigan, did postdoctoral training at The Scripps Research Institute, and has worked on mammalian clocks since 2003.
He ran a lab at the University of Memphis from 2008 to 2017 and joined the University of Florida in 2018.

The study in this Atlas asked whether mTOR affects the clock. Lowering mTOR activity made the clock run slower and with a weaker swing, and raising it made the clock run faster with a stronger swing. This was seen in cells, in brain and liver tissue and in mice with less mTOR, so nutrient signalling and daily timing are tied together.

highlights.RAM2018: Showed that mTOR activity sets the speed and strength of the circadian clock in cells, brain (SCN) and liver clocks, and in mTOR heterozygous mice; Liu is the senior author.

Bolger TA.lab_name: Bolger Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Georgia (Athens, Georgia, USA)
Bolger TA.role: Studies how RNA helicases such as yeast Ded1 and human DDX3X control protein production under stress, including after TORC1 inhibition.
Bolger TA.sub: Principal investigator, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Georgia
story: Timothy Bolger leads a lab at the University of Georgia that studies translation, the step where a cell reads messenger RNA to build proteins. His group focuses on DEAD-box RNA helicases, enzymes that reshape RNA-protein complexes, and works mostly in budding yeast.
A main interest is the yeast protein Ded1 and its human relative DDX3X. Mutations in DDX3X are common in medulloblastoma, the most frequent brain cancer in children.

In the study in this Atlas, yeast carrying medulloblastoma-type mutations in Ded1 kept growing when rapamycin switched off TORC1. They made more protein from messages with simple, unstructured starts. The authors suggest that mutant DDX3X may help tumour cells escape stress-linked growth controls, though this has been shown in yeast, not yet in tumours.

highlights.SWA2026: Modelled medulloblastoma DDX3X mutations in yeast Ded1 and found rapamycin-resistant growth and selective translation changes after TORC1 inhibition; Bolger is the senior and corresponding author.

Knævelsrud H.lab_name: Autophagy regulation in development and disease, Department of Molecular Cell Biology, Institute for Cancer Research, Oslo University Hospital, and Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, University of Oslo (Oslo, Norway)
Knævelsrud H.role: Autophagy researcher who studies how cells recycle their own material and how this process is regulated in development and disease, including cancer.
Knævelsrud H.sub: Group leader and Associate Professor, University of Oslo & Oslo University Hospital · ERC Starting Grant · member of The Young Academy of Norway
story: Helene Knævelsrud leads a research group in Oslo that studies autophagy, the process by which cells break down and recycle their own parts. Her group page lists an ERC Starting Grant and membership in The Young Academy of Norway.

The study in this Atlas looks at Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition caused by mutations in the FLCN gene that raises the risk of kidney tumours. Without FLCN, the transcription factor TFEB stays in the nucleus and mTORC1 signalling is overactive.

Her team found that overall autophagy still worked in patient-derived kidney cancer cells, but the protein p62 piled up in enlarged clusters. The same p62 build-up appeared in a cohort of Norwegian BHD kidney tumour samples.

highlights.ULL2026: Showed that FLCN loss in BHD kidney cancer cells keeps TFEB in the nucleus and mTORC1 overactive, yet autophagy flux is intact while p62 accumulates; Knævelsrud is the senior author.

Knævelsrud H.credit: Portrait: Oslo University Hospital (Institute for Cancer Research)

Clardy J.lab_name: Clardy Lab, Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Clardy J.role: Chemist who solved the crystal structure of the FKBP12-rapamycin-FRB (mTOR) complex, showing how rapamycin acts as a molecular glue between two proteins.
Clardy J.sub: Professor of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (since 2002) · Cornell University (1978–2002)
story: Jon Clardy is a chemist who studies small molecules made by bacteria and fungi and how they control biological processes. He earned his PhD in chemistry at Harvard in 1969, taught at Iowa State and then at Cornell from 1978 to 2002, and joined Harvard Medical School in 2002.
With Stuart Schreiber he determined the crystal structures of the immunosuppressant drugs FK506 and rapamycin bound to FKBP12. He is also a co-founder of Harvard's chemical biology PhD program.

The 1996 study in this Atlas, from his Cornell lab, showed the structure of FKBP12 and rapamycin bound to the FRB domain of mTOR (then called FRAP). Rapamycin sits in two pockets at once and glues the two proteins together. It became a textbook example of a small molecule that brings two proteins into contact.

highlights.CHO1996: Crystal structure at 2.7 angstroms of FKBP12-rapamycin bound to the FRB domain of human FRAP/mTOR, showing rapamycin as a molecular glue; Clardy is the senior (last) author.

Sargeant TJ.lab_name: Lysosomal Health in Ageing, Hopwood Centre for Neurobiology, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Sargeant TJ.role: Studies lysosomal recycling and autophagy in ageing and Alzheimer's disease, and develops ways to measure autophagy flux in people.
Sargeant TJ.sub: Associate Professor and Head, Lysosomal Health in Ageing, SAHMRI (since 2015) · School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Science, Adelaide University
story: Tim Sargeant heads the Lysosomal Health in Ageing group at SAHMRI in Adelaide. He completed a PhD in neuroscience at Victoria University of Wellington and did two postdoctoral positions at the University of Cambridge before starting his group in 2015.
His group studies how the cell's recycling system, the lysosome, is damaged in diseases such as Alzheimer's and how to measure and improve that recycling in humans.

The trial in this Atlas tested a common idea from animal work: eating less protein lowers mTORC1 and should switch on autophagy. In 63 healthy adults who ate average-protein and reduced-protein diets for four weeks each, autophagic flux in blood cells did not change. The result suggests that cutting protein alone may not be enough to boost autophagy in human blood.

highlights.SIN2026: Randomised crossover trial in 63 healthy adults showing that four weeks of reduced protein intake did not change autophagic flux in blood cells; Sargeant is the senior and corresponding author.

Sargeant TJ.credit: Portrait: South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI)

Su B.lab_name: Shanghai Institute of Immunology, Department of Immunology and Microbiology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (Shanghai, China)
Su B.role: Immunologist who studies how mTOR and MAPK signaling shape immune regulation and vascular function, and senior author of the study showing that SIN1 is a core part of mTORC2.
Su B.sub: Director, Shanghai Institute of Immunology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine · Adjunct Professor, Yale School of Medicine · Joined SJTU 2012 · PhD, Yale (1991)
story: Bing Su is a professor at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, where he directs the Shanghai Institute of Immunology and chairs the Department of Immunology and Microbiology. He also co-directs an institute for immune metabolism run jointly with Yale University, where he holds an adjunct appointment. He earned his PhD at Yale in 1991 and did postdoctoral training at the University of California, San Diego.

His lab studies how signaling inside cells, especially through mTOR and MAPK proteins, controls the immune system and blood vessels. In the Atlas he appears as senior author of a 2006 Cell paper led by Estela Jacinto. It asked how the mTORC2 complex switches on the kinase Akt. The team found that a protein called SIN1 is needed to hold mTORC2 together. Without SIN1, Akt was not phosphorylated at serine 473, but only some Akt targets were affected.
This showed that mTORC2 does not simply turn Akt on or off. It tunes which of Akt's targets are switched on, and it left the other mTOR complex, mTORC1, working normally.

highlights.JAC2006: Showed that SIN1 holds the rictor-mTOR complex together and is needed for Akt Ser473 phosphorylation, which affects only a subset of Akt targets such as FoxO1/3a; Su is senior (last) author.
highlights.FAC2008: Showed that mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of Akt and conventional PKC, helping the new kinases fold and stay stable; Su was a co-author, with Estela Jacinto as senior author.

Su B.credit: Portrait: Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine

Costa-Mattioli M.lab_name: MCM Lab, Department of Neuroscience, Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, Texas, USA)
Costa-Mattioli M.role: Neuroscientist who studies how mTOR signaling and protein synthesis control learning, memory and brain function, including the role of mTORC2 in long-term memory.
Costa-Mattioli M.sub: Adjunct Professor of Neuroscience, Baylor College of Medicine · PhD, University of Nantes (2002) · Postdoctoral fellow, McGill University
story: Mauro Costa-Mattioli studied in Uruguay and France before earning his PhD at the University of Nantes in 2002 and training as a postdoctoral fellow at McGill University in Montreal. He is listed at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston in the Department of Neuroscience, and runs the MCM Lab.

His lab asks how the brain turns a short-lived experience into a lasting memory, and how cells control protein production to make this possible. The 2013 Nature Neuroscience study in the Atlas, led by Wei Huang, looked at mTORC2, the rapamycin-insensitive form of mTOR. Mice that lacked its key partner Rictor in the forebrain could learn, but could not keep long-term memories.

The team traced the problem to actin, the protein scaffold that reshapes the connections between neurons. Restoring actin polymerization rescued memory, and a compound that boosted mTORC2 activity improved it.

highlights.HUA2013: Deleting Rictor in the mouse forebrain impaired long-term memory and late-phase LTP through reduced actin polymerization; restoring actin rescued both, and an mTORC2-boosting compound enhanced memory. Costa-Mattioli is senior (last) author.
highlights.COS2009: Narrative review arguing that the start of mRNA translation, controlled by the mTORC1 and eIF2alpha pathways, is a main control point for long-lasting synaptic plasticity and long-term memory; Costa-Mattioli is first author.

Fruman DA.lab_name: Fruman Lab, Department of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry, University of California, Irvine (Irvine, California, USA)
Fruman DA.role: Immunologist and cancer biologist who studies PI3K and mTOR signaling in lymphocytes and leukemia cells and the drugs that target them.
Fruman DA.sub: Professor and Chair, Molecular Biology and Biochemistry, UC Irvine · Director, UCI Cancer Research Institute
story: David Fruman is a professor and chair of the Department of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry at the University of California, Irvine, and directs the UCI Cancer Research Institute. His lab studies the signals that control growth and survival in immune cells and blood cancers.

A main theme is the PI3K/mTOR pathway and how it controls protein production in lymphocytes. The 2010 Nature Medicine paper in the Atlas, led by Matthew Janes, tested PP242, a drug that blocks the active site of mTOR and so inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2, in leukemia carrying the Philadelphia chromosome.
Unlike rapamycin, PP242 killed leukemia cells. It had much weaker effects on normal lymphocytes, suggesting that such inhibitors could treat leukemia without fully shutting down the immune system.

highlights.JAN2010: The mTOR kinase inhibitor PP242 killed Ph+ leukemia cells where rapamycin did not, with much weaker effects on normal lymphocytes; Fruman is senior (last) author.

Blau HM.lab_name: Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology, Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Stanford University School of Medicine (Stanford, California, USA)
Blau HM.role: Stem cell biologist known for work on muscle stem cells, regeneration, cell reprogramming and rejuvenation, including how aging muscle loses strength.
Blau HM.sub: Donald E. and Delia B. Baxter Foundation Professor and Director, Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology, Stanford · Stanford faculty since 1978 · National Medal of Science (2025)
story: Helen Blau studied at the University of York in England and earned her PhD at Harvard. After postdoctoral work at the University of California, San Francisco, she joined Stanford in 1978 and has directed the Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology since 2000.

Her lab studies muscle stem cells, how they repair muscle, and how cells can be reprogrammed or made younger. The Atlas includes a 2026 review in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, led by Sara Ancel, on new treatments for sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength with age, for which no drug is approved.

The review compares several strategies. It highlights mTORC1 inhibitors for their ability to restore autophagy, the cell's recycling system, in aging muscle, and places this next to other approaches such as urolithin A and myostatin inhibitors.

highlights.ANC2026: Review of drug strategies against sarcopenia that highlights mTORC1 inhibitors for restoring impaired autophagy in aging muscle; Blau is senior (last) author.

Karin M.lab_name: Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, Departments of Pharmacology and Pathology, UC San Diego School of Medicine (La Jolla, California, USA)
Karin M.role: Cell biologist best known for discovering AP-1 and JNK signaling and the IKK-NF-kB inflammation pathway, whose lab also co-led the study of Sestrin as a feedback inhibitor of TOR.
Karin M.sub: Distinguished Professor of Pharmacology and Pathology, UC San Diego · Ben and Wanda Hildyard Chair for Mitochondrial and Metabolic Diseases · Born 1951, Tel Aviv, Israel
story: Michael Karin is a Distinguished Professor of Pharmacology and Pathology at the University of California, San Diego. His lab identified the AP-1 transcription factors and the JNK family of kinases, and cloned the IKK complex that switches on NF-kB, a central driver of inflammation.

More recently his group has studied how inflammation, fatty liver disease and metabolism feed into liver cancer. His lab also contributed to a 2010 Science paper led by Jun Hee Lee, together with fly geneticists at Sanford-Burnham.

That study found that Sestrin is switched on by TOR activity and in turn inhibits TOR, forming a feedback loop. In flies lacking Sestrin, signs of aging such as fat build-up, mitochondrial problems and muscle and heart decline appeared, and TOR inhibition or AMPK activation prevented them.

highlights.LEE2010: In flies, Sestrin acts as a feedback inhibitor of TOR, and its loss causes age-related fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction and muscle and heart decline that TOR inhibition or AMPK activation prevents; Karin is senior (last) author.
highlights.BUD2008: The p53 target genes Sestrin1 and Sestrin2 activate AMPK and TSC2 to switch off mTOR signalling after DNA damage; Karin is senior (last) author.

Karin M.credit: Portrait: UC San Diego Department of Pharmacology

Rasmussen BB.lab_name: Rasmussen Lab, Department of Cellular & Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Rasmussen BB.role: Muscle physiologist who studies how mTORC1 and nutrient signaling control muscle growth and loss in people, including during exercise and aging.
Rasmussen BB.sub: Professor and Chair, Cellular & Integrative Physiology, UT Health San Antonio (chair since 2024)
story: Blake Rasmussen is a professor and, since 2024, chair of the Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology at UT Health San Antonio. His lab studies muscle growth and wasting in aging and disease, using human studies and transgenic mice.

The 2009 Journal of Physiology study in the Atlas, led by Micah Drummond, asked whether mTORC1 is really needed for muscle to build protein after exercise in people. Volunteers took rapamycin before a bout of resistance exercise.

Rapamycin blocked the normal rise in muscle protein synthesis after exercise, and blunted several downstream mTORC1 signals. This was direct evidence in humans that mTORC1 helps drive the muscle response to exercise.

highlights.DRU2009: Rapamycin taken before resistance exercise blocked the contraction-induced rise in human muscle protein synthesis; Rasmussen is senior (last) author.
highlights.MARCHANT2026: Senior author: constant mTORC1 activity in mouse muscle raised inflammation but did not by itself impair glucose tolerance (mice).

Winter D.lab_name: AG Winter, Lysosomal Proteome Dynamics, Research Center One Health Ruhr, University of Duisburg-Essen (Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Winter D.role: Proteomics researcher who uses mass spectrometry to map lysosomal proteins and their modifications, including phosphorylation, in health and disease.
Winter D.sub: Professor, lysosomal proteome dynamics group, University of Duisburg-Essen (previously Institute of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Bonn)
story: Dominic Winter leads a research group on lysosomal proteome dynamics. The group page says it has moved from the University of Bonn to the Research Center One Health Ruhr at the University of Duisburg-Essen. Lysosomes are the cell's main digestive compartments, and their proteins are present in very low amounts, so special mass spectrometry methods are needed to study them.

His group develops ways to enrich lysosomes and to measure their proteins, phosphorylation, protein partners and half-lives. This fits the 2026 preprint in the Atlas, led by Prasanna Muthukottiappan, which links cholesterol exchange between the ER and the lysosome to lysosome movement.

The preprint reports that this control runs through mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of LAMTOR1, part of the Ragulator complex that anchors the Rag GTPases on the lysosome. It is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

highlights.MUT2026: Preprint reporting that ER-lysosome cholesterol exchange regulates lysosome motility via mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of LAMTOR1 in the Ragulator complex; Winter is senior (last) author.

Winter D.credit: Portrait: University of Duisburg-Essen (photo: UDE/Anke Wälischmiller)

Blackwell TK.lab_name: Blackwell Lab, Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Blackwell TK.role: Geneticist who uses the worm C. elegans to study how the SKN-1/Nrf stress-response factor, insulin signaling and TOR shape stress resistance and lifespan.
Blackwell TK.sub: Professor of Genetics, Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School
story: Keith Blackwell is a professor of genetics at the Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School in Boston. His lab uses the roundworm C. elegans to study how organisms defend themselves against environmental and metabolic stress, and how those defenses affect aging.

Much of the work centers on SKN-1, the worm relative of the human Nrf stress-response proteins. The 2012 Cell Metabolism paper in the Atlas, led by Stacey Robida-Stubbs, asked how TOR signaling affects lifespan. When TORC1 was inhibited genetically, SKN-1 and DAF-16/FoxO activated protective genes and the worms lived longer.
Rapamycin extended worm lifespan through SKN-1 but not DAF-16, which the authors think is because it also interferes with TORC2.

highlights.ROB2012: In C. elegans, TORC1 inhibition extends lifespan via SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO, while rapamycin's effect needs SKN-1 but not DAF-16, apparently because it also affects TORC2; Blackwell is senior (last) author.

Duman RS.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Duman RS.role: Psychiatric neuroscientist who showed that ketamine's rapid antidepressant effect depends on mTOR signaling and the growth of new synapses in the prefrontal cortex.
Duman RS.sub: Deceased. 1954–2020 · Professor of Psychiatry and of Neuroscience, Yale School of Medicine · Yale Psychiatry from 1988
story: Ronald Duman (1954 to 2020) was a neuroscientist at Yale School of Medicine, where he joined the Department of Psychiatry in 1988. With Eric Nestler he co-founded the Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry. He died suddenly in February 2020 while hiking near his home in Connecticut.

He proposed that stress weakens the growth-factor signals that keep brain cells and their connections healthy, and that antidepressants work in part by restoring them. He also showed that antidepressants promote the birth of new neurons in the adult hippocampus.

The 2010 Science paper in the Atlas, led by Nanxin Li, found that ketamine rapidly activates mTOR in rat prefrontal cortex and increases the number of synapses. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin stopped both the new synapses and the antidepressant-like behavior.

highlights.LIX2010: Ketamine's rapid antidepressant-like action in rats requires mTOR-dependent synapse formation in the prefrontal cortex; Duman is senior (last) author.

Duman RS.credit: Portrait: Brain Behavior Mind conference (Amygdala, Stress & PTSD)

Pass M.lab_name: Oncology drug discovery, AstraZeneca (Cheshire, England, United Kingdom)
Pass M.role: Pharmaceutical drug-discovery leader who worked on AstraZeneca's oncology small-molecule programs, including the ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor AZD8055.
Pass M.sub: Chief Development Officer, Amphista · Formerly Vice President and Head of Projects, Early Oncology, AstraZeneca · Industry scientist, not an academic
story: Martin Pass is a drug-discovery scientist from industry rather than a university lab. According to the page of his current company, he became a program leader in the oncology group at AstraZeneca, nominating drug candidates for the clinic and leading development, and later served as Vice President, Head of Projects in early oncology. He is now Chief Development Officer at Amphista.

The 2009 Cancer Research paper in the Atlas, led by Christine Chresta, describes AZD8055. Unlike rapamycin, which blocks only part of mTORC1, AZD8055 binds the active site of the mTOR kinase and so inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2, including rapamycin-resistant outputs such as 4E-BP1 phosphorylation.
The compound shrank or stopped the growth of many human tumor types in mouse models and moved into phase I clinical trials.

highlights.CHR2009: Introduced AZD8055, an ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor that blocks mTORC1 and mTORC2 and rapamycin-resistant outputs, with antitumor activity in mouse xenografts; Pass is senior (last) author.

Cate JHD.lab_name: Cate Lab, Departments of Molecular and Cell Biology and of Chemistry, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Cate JHD.role: Structural and molecular biologist who studies how ribosomes and the initiation factor eIF3 control which mRNAs are translated into protein.
Cate JHD.sub: Professor of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, UC Berkeley
story: Jamie Cate is a professor in the Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. His lab studies how genetic information is turned into protein, using cryo-EM, biophysics and genomics. One focus is how the initiation factor eIF3 switches translation of particular mRNAs on or off.
The 2026 RNA Biology paper in the Atlas, led by Erica Pledger, used ribosome profiling to look at how human CD8+ T cells translate their mRNAs after chronic activation, a model of T cell exhaustion.

The team found that 5' TOP mRNAs, a class normally under mTOR control, were strongly repressed in translation even though mTOR activity looked elevated. This points to a layer of translational control that can override or bypass mTOR in exhausted T cells.

highlights.PLEDGER2026: Ribosome profiling of chronically activated human CD8+ T cells showed strong translational repression of 5' TOP mRNAs despite elevated mTOR activity; Cate is senior (last) author.

Cate JHD.credit: Portrait: UC Berkeley College of Chemistry

Ban N.lab_name: Ban Group, Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Ban N.role: Structural biologist known for atomic structures of the ribosome and for work on how cells make, fold and sort proteins.
Ban N.sub: Professor of Structural Molecular Biology, ETH Zurich (since 2000) · Born 1966, Zagreb, Croatia
story: Nenad Ban was born in Zagreb and trained in molecular biology there, then earned his PhD at the University of California, Riverside, and did postdoctoral work at Yale with Thomas Steitz. He has been a professor of structural molecular biology at ETH Zurich since 2000.

His group works out the three-dimensional shape of the machines that make proteins. His work on the large ribosomal subunit helped show that the ribosome is a ribozyme, an RNA-based catalyst. The group also studies how proteins fold and reach the right membranes while still being made.

In the 2018 eLife paper in the Atlas, led by Edward Stuttfeld, Ban's group and Michael Hall's group in Basel reported the architecture of the human mTORC2 core, made of mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8. The structure showed a binding site for accessory proteins on mTOR and helped explain why mTORC2 is insensitive to rapamycin.

highlights.STU2018: Cryo-EM architecture of the human mTORC2 core (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1, mLST8) revealing a conserved accessory-protein site and the basis of rapamycin insensitivity; Ban is senior (last) author.

Du X.lab_name: Du Group, Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Du X.role: Studies how cellular metabolism and signaling shape the function of T cells, regulatory T cells and dendritic cells in tumor immunity, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency.
Du X.sub: Principal investigator, Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology (IMIB), Fudan University
story: Xingrong Du is a principal investigator at the Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology at Fudan University in Shanghai. According to the institute's page, her group studies how metabolism and the signals that control it shape immune cells, including T cells, regulatory T cells and dendritic cells, in tumor immunity, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency.

The study in the Atlas asks how activated T cells keep their supply of amino acids high enough to grow and divide. The team found that two protein complexes, CORVET and HOPS, help the cell take in nutrients from outside by macropinocytosis, a kind of cell drinking. Without them the T cells run short of amino acids, a stress program called the integrated stress response switches on, and mTORC1 shuts down.

Restoring mTORC1 activity rescued the failure to multiply, while deleting the cell-death gene BIM rescued survival. This separated two ways the cells fail and placed nutrient uptake upstream of the lysosomal amino-acid sensors that control mTORC1.

highlights.WANG2026: Showed that CORVET/HOPS complexes supply amino acids to activated T cells via macropinocytosis; loss of VPS18 or VPS11 triggers the integrated stress response and turns off mTORC1. Du is the last author on the paper.

Du X.credit: Portrait: Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology, Fudan University

Pagano M.lab_name: Pagano Laboratory, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Pagano M.role: Studies ubiquitin ligases, the enzymes that tag proteins for destruction, including how the S6K1 kinase triggers degradation of the translation brake PDCD4.
Pagano M.sub: Chair, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology · May Ellen and Gerald Jay Ritter Professor of Oncology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine
story: Michele Pagano is a physician-scientist at NYU Grossman School of Medicine in New York, where he chairs the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology. His laboratory works on ubiquitin ligases, enzymes that attach a molecular tag to other proteins so the cell breaks them down. Controlled protein destruction helps decide when cells divide, grow or stop.

The study in the Atlas, led by first author N. Valerio Dorrello, connected this field to mTOR signaling. Growth signals activate the kinase S6K1, which sits downstream of mTORC1. The team showed that S6K1 phosphorylates a protein called PDCD4, a tumor suppressor that blocks the translation helper eIF4A. The tag lets the ubiquitin ligase SCF-betaTRCP recognize PDCD4 and destroy it.

With PDCD4 gone, cells can build proteins more efficiently. A mutant PDCD4 that resisted destruction slowed translation, made cells smaller and slowed their cycle. The work gave a concrete link between mTOR signaling and the control of protein synthesis and cell size.

highlights.DOR2006: Showed that S6K1 phosphorylates PDCD4 so that SCF-betaTRCP degrades it, allowing efficient translation and cell growth. Pagano is the senior (last) author.

Pagano M.credit: Portrait: NYU Grossman School of Medicine

Cregan SP.lab_name: Cregan Laboratory, Robarts Research Institute and Neuroscience Program, Western University (London, Ontario, Canada)
Cregan SP.role: Studies the molecular pathways that trigger neuron death, aiming to find drug targets that protect neurons in stroke and in diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer and Huntington.
Cregan SP.sub: Scientist, Robarts Research Institute · Neuroscience Program, Western University
story: Sean Cregan is a scientist at the Robarts Research Institute at Western University in London, Ontario. According to the institute, his lab studies the molecules that trigger cell death in the brain and how they are switched on, with the goal of finding drug targets that help neurons survive in stroke and in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson disease.

The study in the Atlas, led by Matthew Demmings, looked at the integrated stress response, a cell program that is switched on by stress. When the stress does not go away, the transcription factor ATF4 raises three genes, SESN2, DDIT4 and Trib3, which together turn down both mTORC1 and mTORC2.

In mouse and cell models of Parkinson disease, this lasting drop in mTOR activity helped kill dopamine neurons through a cell-death protein called PUMA. The result is unusual in mTOR research, because here too little mTOR activity is harmful, not too much.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: Showed that chronic ATF4 signaling raises SESN2, DDIT4 and Trib3, suppressing mTORC1 and mTORC2 and driving dopamine neuron death via PUMA in Parkinson disease models. Cregan is the senior author.

Cregan SP.credit: Portrait: Robarts Research Institute, Western University

Cantrell DA.lab_name: Cantrell Group, Cell Signalling and Immunology, School of Life Sciences, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Cantrell DA.role: Studies how signaling and metabolism control T-cell fate, including how amino-acid uptake and mTORC1 steer T-cell differentiation.
Cantrell DA.sub: Professor, Cell Signalling and Immunology, University of Dundee · Wellcome Trust Principal Research Fellow · FRS (2011), CBE (2014)
story: Doreen Cantrell is a professor at the University of Dundee in Scotland, where she works in the division of Cell Signalling and Immunology. Her university profile lists her as a Wellcome Trust Principal Research Fellow, a Fellow of the Royal Society and a Commander of the Order of the British Empire. Her group studies the signals that decide what a T cell becomes.

The Atlas study, led by Linda Sinclair, asked how T cells get the building blocks they need when an infection starts. When the T-cell receptor detects antigen, the cell raises many amino-acid transporters, but one of them, Slc7a5, does most of the work of importing large neutral amino acids such as leucine.

T cells lacking Slc7a5 could not switch their metabolism, could not multiply and could not become effector cells. The reason was that they could not bring in enough leucine to switch on mTORC1 and to make the growth factor c-Myc. Amino-acid transport therefore acts as a metabolic checkpoint for T cells.

highlights.SIN2013: Showed that antigen receptor signaling upregulates the amino-acid transporter Slc7a5, whose leucine uptake is needed for mTORC1 activity, c-Myc and T-cell differentiation. Cantrell is the senior author.

Silva AJ.lab_name: Silva Lab, Department of Neurobiology and Integrative Center for Learning and Memory, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Silva AJ.role: Studies the molecular and cellular basis of learning and memory, including how overactive mTOR signaling in tuberous sclerosis impairs memory and how rapamycin can reverse it in mice.
Silva AJ.sub: Distinguished Professor of Neurobiology · Director, Integrative Center for Learning and Memory, UCLA
story: Alcino Silva is a Distinguished Professor of Neurobiology at the University of California, Los Angeles, and directs UCLA's Integrative Center for Learning and Memory. His research asks how memories form in the brain and what goes wrong in genetic disorders that affect learning.

In the study in the Atlas, led by Dan Ehninger, the team worked with mice that carry one broken copy of the Tsc2 gene, a model of tuberous sclerosis. People with this condition often have learning and memory problems, even when they have normal intelligence. The mice also had learning deficits, without seizures or visible brain damage.

The cause was too much mTOR signaling in the hippocampus, a memory region, which disturbed a form of synaptic strengthening called long-term potentiation. A short treatment of adult mice with rapamycin restored both the synaptic plasticity and the behavior, which suggested that some cognitive problems in the disorder can be reversed.

highlights.EHN2008: Showed that Tsc2+/- mice have hippocampal mTOR hyperactivity and learning deficits, and that brief rapamycin treatment in adults rescued synaptic plasticity and behavior. Silva is the senior author.

Sehgal SN.lab_name: Ayerst Research Laboratories (later Wyeth) (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
Sehgal SN.role: Led the team at Ayerst that isolated rapamycin from an Easter Island soil bacterium and kept the program alive until the drug reached the clinic.
Sehgal SN.sub: Ayerst Research Laboratories, Montreal (from 1959), later Wyeth · 1932–2003 (deceased)
story: Surendra Nath Sehgal, known as Suren, was a scientist at Ayerst Research Laboratories in Montreal, a company that later became part of Wyeth. He died in 2003. His name is tied to the first description of rapamycin, a compound that later led researchers to the mTOR protein.

The 1975 paper in the Atlas reports a Streptomyces bacterium from a soil sample collected on Easter Island. The bacterium made a substance that stopped the growth of fungi such as Candida albicans. The team extracted it, obtained it in crystal form and named it rapamycin. It was first seen as an antifungal drug, and it had low toxicity in mice.

According to his biography, when the company's rapamycin program was cancelled, Sehgal kept bacterial samples in a freezer at home, and after the Ayerst and Wyeth merger he argued for restarting the work. Rapamycin was approved by the FDA in 1999 to prevent rejection of transplanted organs.

highlights.VEZ1975: Reported the isolation of rapamycin from an Easter Island Streptomyces strain and its antifungal activity, the first step in the discovery that led to mTOR. Sehgal is the last author.

Maier AB.lab_name: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Programme, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (Singapore)
Maier AB.role: Geriatrician-researcher who studies biological ageing and healthy longevity, including a systematic review of what rapamycin and its derivatives do in humans.
Maier AB.sub: Professor of Medicine, Healthy Longevity Translational Research Programme, National University of Singapore · also affiliated with Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
story: Andrea Maier is a professor of medicine at the National University of Singapore, where she works in the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Programme. The paper's byline also lists a link to the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Her work focuses on how people age and on ways to measure and improve healthy longevity.

The systematic review in the Atlas, led by Deborah Lee, asked what is actually known about rapamycin and its relatives (rapalogs) as anti-ageing treatments in people. The team searched five databases, screened 18,400 articles and included 19 studies.

Rapamycin and rapalogs improved some measures in the immune, cardiovascular and skin systems. No significant effects were found for the endocrine, muscle or nervous systems. No serious side effects were reported in healthy people, but people with age-related disease had more infections and higher cholesterol and triglycerides. The authors called for studies of the systems not yet tested and for long-term exposure.

highlights.LEE2024: First systematic review of rapamycin and rapalogs for ageing in humans (19 studies): benefits in immune, cardiovascular and skin measures, no significant effects elsewhere, and more infections and raised lipids in people with age-related disease. Maier is the senior author.

Maier AB.credit: Portrait: National University of Singapore (NUS SCALE)

Withers DJ.lab_name: Metabolic Signalling Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences, Imperial College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Withers DJ.role: Studies how hormone and nutrient signaling pathways control metabolism and ageing, including the finding that loss of S6K1 extends lifespan in mice.
Withers DJ.sub: Professor of Diabetes and Endocrinology, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences, Imperial College London · Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences · formerly University College London (at the time of the 2009 paper)
story: Dominic Withers is a professor of diabetes and endocrinology at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences, which is part of Imperial College London, and a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences. When the study in the Atlas was published in 2009, the first author was at the Institute of Healthy Ageing at University College London.

The study, led by Colin Selman, asked whether a part of the mTOR pathway controls how long mammals live. S6K1 is a kinase that mTORC1 switches on. Mice lacking S6K1 were protected from several age-related problems, including declines in bone, immune and motor function and in insulin sensitivity.

In the Atlas, the key finding is that the lifespan gain was seen in female mice, about 19 percent in median lifespan, and was not significant in males. The mice also showed gene activity resembling that of calorie restriction and of activated AMPK. The result suggests that one branch of mTOR signaling can carry much of the effect on ageing.

highlights.SEL2009: Showed that deleting S6K1 extends lifespan in female mice (not significantly in males) and protects against age-related bone, immune and motor decline. Withers is the senior author.

Withers DJ.credit: Portrait: MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences

Jung YK.lab_name: Laboratory of Apoptosis & Molecular Disease, School of Biological Sciences, Seoul National University (Seoul, South Korea)
Jung YK.role: Studies programmed cell death and autophagy and their roles in ageing and disease, including mice with extra copies of the autophagy gene Atg5 that live longer.
Jung YK.sub: Professor, School of Biological Sciences, Seoul National University (since 2005) · earlier Professor, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (1996–2005)
story: Yong-Keun Jung is a professor of biological sciences at Seoul National University in South Korea. According to his lab page, he trained for his PhD at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, did postdoctoral work at Harvard Medical School, and was a professor at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology before moving to Seoul. His lab studies genes that control cell death, and autophagy and its role in ageing.

Autophagy is the cell's recycling system, and mTOR is one of its main brakes. The study in the Atlas, led by Jong-Ok Pyo, asked whether turning autophagy up is enough to extend lifespan in a mammal. The team made mice with extra copies of Atg5, a protein needed to build the autophagosome, the recycling bubble.

These mice had more autophagy, lived about 17 percent longer in median lifespan, were leaner and were more sensitive to insulin. Their cells also resisted oxidative damage better, and blocking autophagy removed that protection.

highlights.PYO2013: Showed that moderate overexpression of Atg5 raises autophagy and extends median lifespan of mice by about 17 percent, with leanness and better insulin sensitivity. Jung is the senior author.

Jung YK.credit: Portrait: School of Biological Sciences, Seoul National University

Fujio K.lab_name: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Fujio K.role: Rheumatologist and immunologist who studies how self-tolerance breaks down in autoimmune disease, including lupus, and how nutrient sensing by CASTOR1 shapes B-cell responses.
Fujio K.sub: Professor, Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo
story: Keishi Fujio is a professor and physician at the University of Tokyo, working in allergy and rheumatology. The university lists his research theme as the mechanisms by which the body's tolerance to its own tissues breaks down, which is the basis of autoimmune diseases such as lupus.

The study in the Atlas, led by Takeshi Kusuda, looked at CASTOR1, a protein that senses the amino acid arginine and holds mTORC1 in check. The team examined mice lacking Castor1 and a mouse line lacking it only in B cells. These mice made more plasma cells and more IgG antibodies, produced antibodies against DNA and developed kidney inflammation like that of lupus.

In people with lupus, the activity of the CASTOR1 gene in plasmablasts was lower when the disease was more active (r = -0.32). The work links an upstream amino-acid sensor of mTORC1 to a human autoimmune disease.

highlights.KUS2026: Showed that loss of CASTOR1 in mice causes plasma cell expansion, anti-DNA antibodies and lupus-like kidney disease, and that CASTOR1 in human lupus plasmablasts is lower when disease activity is higher. Fujio is the senior author.

Fujio K.credit: Portrait: The University of Tokyo Hospital

Kellogg DL.lab_name: Kellogg Lab, Division of Geriatrics, Gerontology & Palliative Medicine, Department of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Kellogg DL.role: A geriatrician who co-leads clinical trials of rapamycin in older adults at the Barshop Institute, with a focus on safety and cardiovascular effects.
Kellogg DL.sub: Professor of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · GRECC, South Texas Veterans Health Care System
story: Dean Kellogg is a physician-scientist with both an MD and a PhD. He is a professor in the Division of Geriatrics, Gerontology and Palliative Medicine at UT Health San Antonio, and he works at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies. His lab studies how drugs that may slow aging affect people, paying particular attention to drug safety and to the blood vessels and heart.

In the 2018 pilot trial in this Atlas, he was the senior author. Twenty-five healthy people aged 70 to 95 took either 1 mg of rapamycin or a placebo each day, and 11 on rapamycin and 14 on placebo completed at least 8 weeks. The question was simple: is it safe? There were small drops in some red blood cell measures, but blood sugar, insulin sensitivity, thinking tests and walking tests did not change over that short time.

Kellogg now co-leads a larger National Institute on Aging-funded program at UT Health San Antonio. It looks for the lowest rapamycin dose that reaches useful biological targets in older adults and includes a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of about 84 people.

highlights.KRA2018: Senior author of a small randomized pilot (25 adults aged 70-95) showing that 8+ weeks of daily low-dose rapamycin was well tolerated, with no change in blood glucose or insulin sensitivity.

Klickstein LB.lab_name: New Indications Discovery Unit, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Klickstein LB.role: A physician-scientist who led the clinical studies at Novartis showing that low-dose mTOR inhibitors can boost immune function and cut infections in older adults.
Klickstein LB.sub: Head of Translational Medicine, New Indications Discovery Unit, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research · MD, PhD
story: Lloyd Klickstein is a physician-scientist with MD and PhD degrees. According to a profile page, he is Head of Translational Medicine in the New Indications Discovery Unit at the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research. In 2018 he was the senior author of a clinical trial that asked whether blocking mTOR in a gentle way could help the aging immune system.

In that phase 2a trial, 264 older adults took a low dose of two mTOR inhibitors, BEZ235 and everolimus (RAD001), for 6 weeks. During the following year they reported fewer infections, their cells switched on more antiviral genes, and they responded better to a flu vaccine. The result made low-dose mTOR inhibition a serious idea for treating aging-related decline in immunity.
A later phase 3 trial of RTB101 (BEZ235) alone did not confirm a clinical benefit, so the 2018 result is best read as an encouraging first step that was not borne out in larger testing.

highlights.MAN2018: Senior author of a phase 2a randomized trial (264 older adults) in which 6 weeks of low-dose BEZ235 plus everolimus was linked to fewer infections over the next year and a better flu-vaccine response.

Klickstein LB.credit: Portrait: Springer Lab, Harvard Medical School

Edgar BA.lab_name: Edgar Lab, Department of Oncological Sciences, Huntsman Cancer Institute, University of Utah (Salt Lake City, Utah, USA)
Edgar BA.role: A Drosophila geneticist who studies how cells and tissues control their growth, including the role of Rheb in the insulin/TOR network.
Edgar BA.sub: Professor, Oncological Sciences, University of Utah · Huntsman Cancer Institute (since 2016) · ZMBH & DKFZ Heidelberg (2009–2016) · Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (from 1993)
story: Bruce Edgar studies how cells and whole tissues decide how big to grow, mostly using the fruit fly Drosophila. He did postdoctoral work at UCSF with Pat O'Farrell and at Oxford with Paul Nurse, started his own lab at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle in 1993, and worked in Heidelberg, Germany, from 2009 to 2016. Since 2016 his lab has been at the Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah.

In the 2003 study in this Atlas, his group screened for new regulators of growth and found Rheb, a small GTP-binding protein. Flies with extra Rheb grew larger cells and sped up the cell cycle, while flies lacking Rheb stopped growing as young larvae. Genetic and biochemical tests placed Rheb in the insulin pathway, below the Tsc1-Tsc2 complex and above TOR.
Rheb is now a textbook part of the mTORC1 pathway, the switch that links growth signals to the TOR kinase. The same lab went on to study growth and stem cells in the fly gut.

highlights.SAU2003: Senior author of the Drosophila study that identified Rheb as a growth regulator acting downstream of Tsc1-Tsc2 and upstream of TOR, and showed it can drive cell growth in starved animals.

Crabtree GR.lab_name: Crabtree Lab, Departments of Pathology and Developmental Biology, Stanford University School of Medicine (Stanford, California, USA)
Crabtree GR.role: Helped define the calcineurin-NFAT pathway behind cyclosporine and FK506, and showed in 1992 that rapamycin blocks IL-2 activation of p70 S6 kinase.
Crabtree GR.sub: David Korn Professor, Pathology and Developmental Biology, Stanford University · Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator (since 1988) · Born 1946, West Virginia, USA
story: Gerald Crabtree is a physician-scientist at Stanford who has spent his career on how signals reach the genes in the cell nucleus. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, with Stuart Schreiber, his work helped explain the calcineurin-NFAT pathway, which is how the drugs cyclosporine and FK506 switch off immune responses.

The 1992 paper in this Atlas, led by Calvin Kuo with Crabtree as senior author, asked how rapamycin stops T cells from dividing. The team found that the immune signal interleukin-2 switches on an enzyme called p70 S6 kinase, and that very low rapamycin doses blocked it at the same concentrations that stop T cells entering S phase. FK506 competed with rapamycin, showing that both drugs act through the FKBP protein. This tied rapamycin to a growth-signalling pathway that later became known as the mTOR pathway.

Crabtree's later work focuses on chromatin regulation in development and cancer, including a remodeling complex whose subunits are mutated in many human cancers. He is also a founder of several biotechnology companies.

highlights.KUO1992: Senior author of the study showing that rapamycin selectively and rapidly blocks IL-2-driven phosphorylation and activation of p70 S6 kinase at doses that stop T-cell entry into S phase.
highlights.CHU1992: Co-author: rapamycin-FKBP12 blocks growth-factor activation of p70 S6 kinase (T cells, in vitro).

Crabtree GR.credit: Portrait: Stanford University School of Medicine

Rosenberg JE.lab_name: Genitourinary Oncology Service, Division of Solid Tumor Oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Rosenberg JE.role: A bladder and urothelial cancer oncologist whose clinical trial work includes the case of an exceptional responder to everolimus with activating MTOR mutations.
Rosenberg JE.sub: Chief, Genitourinary Oncology Service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (since 2018) · Dana-Farber/Brigham and Women's Cancer Center (until 2012) · MD, Harvard Medical School
story: Jonathan Rosenberg is a medical oncologist who treats bladder and other urinary tract cancers. Since 2018 he has been Chief of the Genitourinary Oncology Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York. Before joining MSK in 2012 he directed the Bladder Cancer Center at Dana-Farber/Brigham and Women's Cancer Center in Boston.

The 2014 study in this Atlas began with one unusual patient. In a phase I trial of everolimus (an mTOR inhibitor) plus pazopanib, a person with advanced bladder cancer had a complete response lasting 14 months. Sequencing the tumor found two mutations in the MTOR gene itself, and lab experiments showed both made mTOR more active, which may explain why the drug worked so well in this person.
This is a single-patient observation. It suggests that mTOR pathway mutations could help pick patients for mTOR-targeted therapy, but it does not prove that they predict response in general.

highlights.WAG2014: Senior author on the report of an exceptional responder to everolimus plus pazopanib whose tumor carried two activating MTOR mutations; a hypothesis-generating single case.

Rosenberg JE.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Oberg K.lab_name: Endocrine Oncology, Department of Medical Sciences, Uppsala University (Uppsala, Sweden)
Oberg K.role: A leading figure in neuroendocrine tumor research and care, and a co-author of the RADIANT-3 trial that supported everolimus for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.
Oberg K.sub: Professor of Endocrine Oncology, Uppsala University · Dean of the Medical Faculty, Uppsala (2002–2008) · Co-founder of the European Neuroendocrine Tumor Network (ENET, from 1995)
story: Kjell Öberg is a Swedish physician and professor of endocrine oncology at Uppsala University and Uppsala University Hospital. He founded the Department of Endocrine Oncology there, served as dean of the medical faculty from 2002 to 2008, and helped found the European Neuroendocrine Tumor Network in the 1990s.

RADIANT-3 was a phase 3 trial that randomly assigned 410 people with advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors to everolimus or placebo. Median time without progression was 11.0 months on everolimus and 4.6 months on placebo, a 65% reduction in the risk of progression or death. Side effects such as mouth sores and rash were mostly mild.
The trial helped make everolimus a standard treatment for these tumors, one of the approved uses of an mTOR inhibitor in cancer.

highlights.YAO2011: Co-author (listed last) of RADIANT-3, the phase 3 trial (n=410) in which everolimus raised median progression-free survival from 4.6 to 11.0 months in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

Li MO.lab_name: Ming Li Lab, Immunology Program, Sloan Kettering Institute, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Li MO.role: An immunologist who studies how tumors trigger immune responses and who found that SZT2 organizes the GATOR complexes controlling mTORC1.
Li MO.sub: David H. Koch Chair in Immunologic Studies and Professor, Immunology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · PhD, Columbia University
story: Ming Li leads a lab in the Immunology Program at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, where he holds the David H. Koch Chair in Immunologic Studies. His group studies the cellular and molecular basis of immune responses to tumors, aiming for treatments based on those mechanisms.

In the 2017 Nature paper in this Atlas, his lab looked at how cells sense nutrients to control mTORC1. They showed that a protein called SZT2, which is mutated in a form of epilepsy, pulls the GATOR1 and GATOR2 complexes together at the lysosome. Cells lacking SZT2 kept mTORC1 switched on even when starved, and mice lacking it died soon after birth.
The work showed that GATOR1 and GATOR2 need SZT2 to read amino acid levels properly, and it linked an epilepsy gene to the mTORC1 pathway.

highlights.PEN2017: Senior author of the study showing that SZT2 assembles GATOR1 and GATOR2 into a lysosomal complex needed to switch mTORC1 off during nutrient deprivation; SZT2-deficient mice died as newborns.

Li MO.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Levine B.lab_name: Center for Autophagy Research, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Levine B.role: Discovered beclin 1, the first mammalian autophagy gene, and showed that autophagy matters for lifespan, tumor suppression and defense against viruses.
Levine B.sub: Deceased 2020 (1960–2020) · Professor of Internal Medicine and Microbiology, UT Southwestern (2004–2020) · HHMI Investigator (from 2008) · Columbia University (1994–2004)
story: Beth Levine (1960-2020) was a physician-scientist who identified beclin 1, the first mammalian gene known to drive autophagy, the process cells use to recycle their own damaged parts. She worked at Columbia University and from 2004 at UT Southwestern in Dallas, where she directed the Center for Autophagy Research. She became a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator in 2008 and was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences in 2013. She died in June 2020.

The 2003 Science paper in this Atlas, from her Columbia lab with Alicia Meléndez as first author, tested autophagy in the roundworm C. elegans. Worms with weak insulin-like signaling normally live much longer and can enter a resting 'dauer' stage. When the autophagy gene bec-1 was missing, both effects were lost.
This was early evidence that autophagy is required, not just present, when reduced insulin or TOR-type signaling extends lifespan.

highlights.MEL2003: Senior author of the C. elegans study showing that the autophagy gene bec-1 is needed for dauer development and for the lifespan extension caused by reduced insulin-like signaling.

Schulze A.lab_name: Division of Tumor Metabolism and Microenvironment, German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) (Heidelberg, Germany)
Schulze A.role: Studies how growth signaling, including PI3K/Akt and mTORC1, drives the metabolism that cancer cells need, notably fat synthesis through SREBP.
Schulze A.sub: Head of Division, Tumor Metabolism and Microenvironment, DKFZ Heidelberg
story: Almut Schulze heads the Division of Tumor Metabolism and Microenvironment at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg. Her group studies how cancer-driving signals reshape cell metabolism, using RNA sequencing, metabolic flux analysis and mouse models. Topics include lipid metabolism, ferroptosis and how tumors adapt to low oxygen and low nutrients.

In the 2008 paper in this Atlas, done when her group was in London, the team asked how Akt, a growth signal, gets cells to build fats as well as protein. They found that mTORC1 is needed to activate SREBP, a transcription factor that turns on genes for making lipids. Blocking mTORC1 with rapamycin kept SREBP out of the nucleus, and silencing SREBP reduced cell size, in cultured cells and in flies.
The study showed that mTORC1 coordinates fat and protein production so a growing cell can make both at once.

highlights.POR2008: Senior author of the study showing that mTORC1 activates SREBP to drive lipid synthesis, which is required for Akt-dependent cell growth in cells and flies.

Jozwiak S.lab_name: Department of Child Neurology, Medical University of Warsaw (Warsaw, Poland)
Jozwiak S.role: A child neurologist known for work on tuberous sclerosis complex and a senior author of the EXIST-1 trial of everolimus.
Jozwiak S.sub: Department of Child Neurology, Medical University of Warsaw
story: Sergiusz Jóźwiak is a child neurologist at the Medical University of Warsaw in Poland. He works on tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), a genetic disease in which the mTOR pathway is permanently switched on. He has co-edited a collection of articles on TSC diagnosis and management.

EXIST-1 was a phase 3 trial in 117 people with TSC and brain tumors called subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. Patients got everolimus or placebo in a 2 to 1 ratio. In 35% of those on everolimus the tumors shrank by at least 50%, compared with none on placebo, and side effects were mostly mild to moderate.

Because TSC is caused by overactive mTOR, this is among the clearest randomized results that blocking mTOR helps in a genetically defined disease. It does not show the same benefit in people without such a mutation.

highlights.FRA2013: Senior author on EXIST-1, the phase 3 trial (n=117) in which everolimus shrank TSC-related brain tumors by 50% or more in 35% of patients versus none on placebo.

Scheffer IE.lab_name: Epilepsy research, The Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health / Austin Health, University of Melbourne (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia)
Scheffer IE.role: Paediatric neurologist and epilepsy researcher who defined new epilepsy syndromes and helped identify epilepsy genes, including DEPDC5, a GATOR1 gene that connects inherited focal epilepsy to the mTOR pathway.
Scheffer IE.sub: Professor, University of Melbourne · Honorary Senior Principal Research Fellow, The Florey Institute · Director of Paediatrics, Austin Health · Fellow of the Royal Society (2018) · Officer of the Order of Australia (2014)
story: Ingrid Scheffer is a doctor and researcher who works on epilepsy in children. Her work includes describing new epilepsy syndromes and finding the genes behind them. According to the Royal Society, her research led to the identification of the first epilepsy gene in 1995, and many more genes have been found since.

In the study in this Atlas she is the last author of a paper on families with an inherited form of focal epilepsy, in which seizures start in different brain regions in different relatives. The team found that loss-of-function changes in a gene called DEPDC5 ran in these families. DEPDC5 makes part of GATOR1, a protein complex that holds the mTORC1 pathway in check.

The paper did not measure mTORC1 itself, so the link to mTOR comes from other molecular work. What it adds is a human case: damage to one part of the brake on mTORC1 is enough to cause a brain disorder in people.

highlights.DIB2013B: Last author. Families with focal epilepsy of variable foci carry loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5 (a GATOR1 subunit), found in about 12% of smaller families tested; a genetic association, with no mTORC1 readout in the paper itself.

Ravussin E.lab_name: Pennington Biomedical Research Center, Louisiana State University System (Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA)
Ravussin E.role: Human energy-metabolism researcher who studies why people differ in how they burn energy and what long-term calorie restriction does to the body, including in the CALERIE trial.
Ravussin E.sub: Associate Executive Director for Clinical Science and Boyd Professor, Pennington Biomedical Research Center, LSU · PhD, University of Lausanne (1980)
story: Eric Ravussin studies human metabolism: why some people burn more energy than others, how genetics shapes this, and how obesity relates to type 2 diabetes. He is originally from Lausanne, Switzerland, and works at the Pennington Biomedical Research Center in Louisiana.

The study in this Atlas comes from CALERIE, a randomized trial in which healthy adults who were not obese ate about 25% fewer calories than usual for two years, compared with people who ate as they pleased. This paper looked at safety. Overall the diet was safe and well tolerated, but bone density at the spine, hip and femoral neck fell more in the calorie-restriction group, so the authors advised watching for bone loss and anemia.

Calorie restriction is of interest to mTOR researchers because it is one of the best-studied ways to slow ageing in animals and is thought to involve nutrient-sensing pathways such as mTOR. This paper is a human safety study and did not measure mTOR.

highlights.ROM2016: Co-author (fourth in the byline, from Pennington Biomedical): two years of 25% calorie restriction in healthy non-obese adults was safe overall, with lower bone density than the control group.

Puigserver P.lab_name: Puigserver Lab, Department of Cell Biology and Cancer Biology, Harvard Medical School and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Puigserver P.role: Metabolism researcher who studies how mitochondrial energy production and nutrient metabolism are controlled, including the finding that mTOR drives mitochondrial gene activity through YY1 and PGC-1alpha.
Puigserver P.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School · Professor of Cell Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
story: Pere Puigserver leads a laboratory at Harvard Medical School and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. His group studies how cells regulate core metabolism: how mitochondria are built and controlled, how liver and fat cells handle nutrients, and how cancer cells use metabolism to grow and survive.

In the 2007 paper in this Atlas, he was the senior author. The team showed that mTOR is needed to keep mitochondria working well. In muscle tissue and cells, rapamycin lowered the activity of genes that control mitochondria, and oxygen use fell. They found that mTOR works with a protein called YY1, which in turn partners with PGC-1alpha, a master switch for mitochondrial genes.
The result showed that mTOR does more than control protein building. It also helps set how much energy a cell can make, which is part of the reason mTOR inhibition changes whole-body metabolism.

highlights.CUN2007: Senior author. mTOR is needed to keep mitochondrial gene expression and oxygen use up, through a YY1-PGC-1alpha complex; rapamycin lowered both.

Kozma SC.lab_name: Kozma Laboratory, Department of Cancer and Cell Biology, Genome Research Institute, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Kozma SC.role: Studies the S6K/mTOR pathway and how it controls cell growth, ribosome production, diabetes and cancer, including mTOR signalling in liver cancer.
Kozma SC.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Cancer and Cell Biology, University of Cincinnati (since 2004) · Associate Investigator, Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel (1987–2003)
story: Sara Kozma works on the S6K/mTOR signalling pathway, which links nutrients and growth signals to cell growth. Her laboratory asks how this pathway controls the making of ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, and how that connects to cell division. Her listed career runs from graduate work at the University of Liege through postdoctoral posts in Germany and Switzerland, the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel, and then the University of Cincinnati.

The 2010 study in this Atlas, with George Thomas's group, looked at how metformin, the common diabetes drug, switches mTORC1 off. It is often said to work through AMPK, an energy sensor. The team found that metformin still blocked mTORC1 in cells lacking AMPK or the TSC1/TSC2 brake, and that the effect needed the Rag GTPases, the proteins that signal amino-acid supply.
The work suggests that a large part of metformin's action on mTORC1 does not go through AMPK. It was done in cells, not in people.

highlights.KAL2010: Co-author with George Thomas (last author) and Adem Kalender: metformin inhibits mTORC1 without AMPK or TSC1/TSC2, in a Rag GTPase-dependent manner.
highlights.DEN2001: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): lowering ATP reduces mTOR signalling independently of amino acids (cells).
highlights.MON1999: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): Drosophila lacking S6 kinase are small because their cells are smaller.
highlights.GUL2008: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): amino acids activate mTORC1 through calcium-calmodulin signalling to hVps34 (cells).
highlights.PEN2000: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): S6K1-deficient mice have smaller beta cells, low insulin and glucose intolerance.
highlights.SHI1998: Senior author: S6K1 knockout mice are small, and the newly found S6K2 partly compensates for S6 phosphorylation.
highlights.COT2006: Co-author with Daniela Cota (first author) and Randy Seeley (last author): hypothalamic mTOR signalling tracks energy status, and raising it with leucine in the brain lowers food intake and body weight (rats).

Melov S.lab_name: Melov Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Melov S.role: Geroscientist who studies how cells and tissues change with age or drug treatment, including the finding that late-life rapamycin improves heart function in old mice.
Melov S.sub: Professor, Buck Institute for Research on Aging · Founding editor, Aging Cell
story: Simon Melov leads a laboratory at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging. The group uses worms, mice, human cells and tissues together with large-scale genomic analysis to find the core mechanisms of ageing, and aims to develop treatments that reduce damage from ageing itself. He was also a founding editor of the journal Aging Cell.

In the 2013 study in this Atlas, he was the senior author. The team gave rapamycin to female mice that were already 24 months old, which is old for a mouse, for three months. Ultrasound tests of heart function showed that age-related changes in the heart were reversed or reduced. Gene-activity data pointed to lower inflammation and less heart-muscle enlargement as likely reasons.
The result matters because it suggests mTOR inhibition can help even when started late in life, not only slow ageing when started early. It was done in mice, not in people.

highlights.FLY2013: Senior author. Three months of rapamycin in 24-month-old female mice reversed or reduced age-related heart changes, with gene-expression changes pointing to less hypertrophy and inflammation.

Melov S.credit: Portrait: Buck Institute for Research on Aging

Hunter T.lab_name: Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (La Jolla, California, USA)
Hunter T.role: Cell biologist who showed that tyrosine phosphorylation is a master on/off switch for proteins, work that informed cancer drugs such as Gleevec; his lab also studied the TSC/Rheb/mTOR/S6K feedback to insulin signalling.
Hunter T.sub: American Cancer Society Professor and Renato Dulbecco Chair, Salk Institute · BA and PhD, University of Cambridge · Fellow of the Royal Society (1987) · Wolf Prize in Medicine (2005)
story: Tony Hunter studies how cells use phosphate groups added to and removed from proteins to switch them on and off. He showed that tyrosine phosphorylation is a master switch for many proteins, and this work informed the design of the leukemia drug Gleevec. He works at the Salk Institute and trained at the University of Cambridge.

In the 2004 paper in this Atlas, Hunter was the last author with O. Jameel Shah and Zhiyong Wang. In cultured cells, the team showed that when the TSC/Rheb/mTOR/S6K chain is switched on too much, the cells lose two insulin-signalling proteins, IRS1 and IRS2. The result is cellular insulin resistance and weaker survival signals.

Together with a companion paper, this helped establish a negative feedback loop in which S6K1 dampens insulin signalling. It links overactive mTOR to insulin resistance, though this paper used cultured cells.

highlights.SHA2004: Last author. Constant activity in the Rheb/mTOR/S6K chain depletes IRS1 and IRS2 in cultured cells, causing insulin resistance and impaired survival signalling.

Hunter T.credit: Portrait: Salk Institute for Biological Studies

Jiang X.lab_name: Xuejun Jiang Lab, Cell Biology Program, Sloan Kettering Institute, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Jiang X.role: Cell biologist who studies autophagy and programmed cell death, including the ULK1-ATG13-FIP200 complex that links mTOR signalling to autophagy.
Jiang X.sub: Virginia and Daniel K. Ludwig Chair and Lab Head, Cell Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · PhD, UT Southwestern Medical Center
story: Xuejun Jiang leads a laboratory in the Cell Biology Program of the Sloan Kettering Institute. His group studies programmed cell death, such as apoptosis and ferroptosis, and autophagy, the process by which cells recycle their own parts, and how both matter in cancer.

In the 2009 paper in this Atlas, he was the senior author with first author Ian Ganley. The team found a protein complex made of ULK1, ATG13 and FIP200, and showed that all three are needed for autophagy triggered by starvation. ATG13 and ULK1 are phosphorylated through the mTOR pathway depending on nutrient supply.
This made the complex a switchboard: when nutrients are plentiful, mTOR keeps autophagy in check, and when they run low, the complex is released to start building autophagosomes.

highlights.GAN2009: Senior author. The ULK1-ATG13-FIP200 complex is essential for starvation-induced autophagy, and ULK1 and ATG13 are phosphorylated by the mTOR pathway in a nutrient-dependent way.

Jiang X.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Wu D.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, Yale School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Wu D.role: Signalling biologist who studies Wnt signalling and receptor-driven cell migration, and who showed that PIP3 can directly stimulate mTORC2 kinase activity.
Wu D.sub: Gladys Phillips Crofoot Professor of Pharmacology, Yale School of Medicine · PhD, Clarkson University (1991)
story: Dianqing Wu is a pharmacologist at Yale. His research looks at how cells pass on signals from receptors at the cell surface, especially the Wnt pathway, which matters in development, bone and cancer, and the signals that guide white blood cells to move toward sites of inflammation.

In the 2011 study in this Atlas, with first author Xiaoqing Gan, the team asked whether the lipid PIP3 only acts upstream of mTORC2 or can switch it on directly. In cells, insulin and active PI3K raised phosphorylation of the Akt hydrophobic-motif site, and a PI3K inhibitor blocked it. In test-tube assays, PIP3 stimulated mTORC2 complexes to phosphorylate Akt.
The result links PI3K signalling to mTORC2, one of the two main mTOR complexes. It was done in cultured cells and in vitro.

highlights.GAN2011: Senior author. PIP3 directly stimulates the kinase activity of immunoprecipitated mTORC2 in vitro, one of several ways PI3K signalling can drive Akt phosphorylation.

Deretic V.lab_name: Deretic Laboratory, Autophagy, Inflammation and Metabolism (AIM) Center, Department of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology, University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center (Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA)
Deretic V.role: Studies how autophagy shapes infection, immunity and inflammation, including early work showing that autophagy restricts Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and how galectins and TRIM proteins control mTOR and AMPK.
Deretic V.sub: Distinguished Professor, Chair of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology & Director of the AIM Center, University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center
story: Vojo Deretic is a cell biologist and microbiologist at the University of New Mexico, where he chairs the Department of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology and directs the Autophagy, Inflammation and Metabolism (AIM) Center. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system, in which parts of the cell are wrapped up and broken down in the lysosome. His group is known for showing that this system can also destroy invading bacteria such as the tuberculosis germ, and for studying how it is switched on and off.

KOR2011 is a Nature Cell Biology study from David Rubinsztein's group in Cambridge, with Deretic as one of the later authors. It found that where lysosomes sit inside the cell helps decide whether mTORC1 is on. When nutrients are plentiful, lysosomes move toward the cell edge and mTORC1 is active; when they are clustered near the centre, mTORC1 is weaker and autophagy rises.

Later work from his own group linked galectins, sugar-binding proteins that sense damaged lysosomes, to the control of mTOR and AMPK. His awards listed on the University page include an NIH MERIT Award (2018) and UNM's Annual Research Lecturer title (2022).

highlights.KOR2011: Co-author (later position) of a study showing that lysosome positioning inside the cell helps set mTORC1 activity and autophagy.

Deretic V.credit: Portrait: University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center

Motzer RJ.lab_name: Genitourinary Oncology Service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Motzer RJ.role: Kidney-cancer oncologist who led the RECORD-1 phase III trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus extends progression-free survival in metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
Motzer RJ.sub: Section Head, Kidney Cancer, Genitourinary Oncology Service & Jack and Dorothy Byrne Chair in Clinical Oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
story: Robert Motzer is a medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York who heads its kidney cancer section.
