According to the MSK profile he has led more than 80 clinical trials, mostly in kidney and testicular cancer, and he chairs the NCCN guidelines panel for kidney cancer.

MOT2008 is the RECORD-1 trial, with Motzer as first author in The Lancet. Patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma whose disease had progressed on sunitinib, sorafenib or both received either everolimus (272 patients) or placebo (138). Median progression-free survival was 4.0 months with everolimus and 1.9 months with placebo, and the trial was stopped early. Common side effects were mouth sores, rash and fatigue, and 8% of treated patients developed pneumonitis.
This was one of the first large randomised trials to show that blocking mTOR helps cancer patients, and it supported the use of everolimus after other targeted drugs fail.

highlights.MOT2008: First author of RECORD-1, the double-blind phase III trial in which everolimus roughly doubled progression-free survival (4.0 vs 1.9 months) in metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
highlights.HUD2007: Senior author (Global ARCC trial): temsirolimus extended survival to 10.9 vs 7.3 months with interferon in poor-prognosis kidney cancer (phase 3, humans).

Motzer RJ.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Piccart M.lab_name: Institut Jules Bordet, Université libre de Bruxelles (Brussels, Belgium)
Piccart M.role: Breast cancer oncologist who co-founded the Breast International Group and has led or co-led major academic trials such as HERA, MINDACT and ALTTO.
Piccart M.sub: Professor of Oncology, Université libre de Bruxelles · Institut Jules Bordet, Brussels · Former President of ESMO (2012–2013) and ECCO (2014–2015)
story: Martine Piccart is a Belgian breast cancer specialist. She is Professor of Oncology at the Université libre de Bruxelles and works at the Jules Bordet Institute in Brussels. She co-founded the Breast International Group, a network of academic research groups that runs breast cancer trials worldwide, and has been president of ESMO and ECCO.

BAS2012 is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer whose disease had returned on aromatase inhibitors. Adding the mTOR inhibitor everolimus to exemestane raised median progression-free survival from 2.8 to 6.9 months by local assessment (10.6 vs 4.1 months by central review). Piccart is one of the authors of the paper, which was led by José Baselga and Gabriel Hortobagyi.
The trial showed that resistance to hormone therapy in breast cancer can be tackled by blocking mTOR, and it led to everolimus being used in this setting.

highlights.BAS2012: Author of the BOLERO-2 phase 3 trial, in which adding everolimus to exemestane more than doubled progression-free survival in hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer.
highlights.PIC2014: First author of the final BOLERO-2 overall-survival report: everolimus plus exemestane kept its progression-free survival gain but did not significantly lengthen overall survival (31.0 vs 26.6 months).

Mootha VK.lab_name: Mootha Laboratory, Department of Molecular Biology, Massachusetts General Hospital; Department of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School; Broad Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Mootha VK.role: Studies how mitochondria are built and work and how their genes cause disease, including the MitoCarta inventory of the mitochondrial proteome and the mitochondrial calcium uniporter.
Mootha VK.sub: Investigator, Howard Hughes Medical Institute · Professor of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School · Massachusetts General Hospital & Broad Institute · Member, National Academy of Sciences
story: Vamsi Mootha is a physician-scientist who studies mitochondria, the structures that make most of a cell's usable energy. His lab at Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School and the Broad Institute combines biochemistry and physiology with genomics and proteomics. It produced MitoCarta, a catalogue of the proteins in mitochondria, and helped define parts of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter. He is an HHMI investigator and a member of the National Academy of Sciences.

CUN2007 is a Nature paper led by John Cunningham and Pere Puigserver, with Mootha as a co-author. It showed that mTOR is needed to keep mitochondria working well. Rapamycin lowered the activity of genes that drive mitochondria and reduced oxygen use in muscle, and the effect ran through the transcription factor YY1 and its partner PGC-1alpha.
The Atlas includes it because it tied mTOR to energy production, not only to protein building and cell growth.

highlights.CUN2007: Co-author of the Nature study showing that mTOR controls mitochondrial gene expression and respiration through a YY1-PGC-1alpha complex.

Brugarolas J.lab_name: Kidney Cancer Program, Harold C. Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Brugarolas J.role: First author of the 2004 study showing that hypoxia switches off mTOR through REDD1 and the TSC1/TSC2 complex; now directs a kidney cancer research program studying signalling and resistance to targeted drugs.
Brugarolas J.sub: Professor of Internal Medicine & Director, Kidney Cancer Program, UT Southwestern Medical Center · Sherry Wigley Crow Cancer Research Endowed Chair
story: James Brugarolas is a physician-scientist at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. He directs the Kidney Cancer Program and is a professor in the Division of Hematology and Oncology. His interests include signalling mechanisms, resistance to targeted drugs, and the genetics of kidney cancer. He was elected to the American Society for Clinical Investigation in 2013 and is a principal investigator of the kidney cancer SPORE grant renewed in 2022.

BRU2004 was done at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in William Kaelin's laboratory, with Brugarolas as first author. Low oxygen is known to turn mTOR down, but the route was unknown. The study showed that it needs the TSC1/TSC2 complex and the gene REDD1, which is switched on by hypoxia. Cells lacking TSC2 kept growing under low oxygen, which fits TSC2 acting as a tumour suppressor.
The paper became a standard reference for how oxygen shortage reaches mTORC1, and it links the Atlas to later work on hypoxia and kidney cancer.

highlights.BRU2004: First author of the study showing that hypoxia inhibits mTOR through REDD1 and the TSC1/TSC2 complex, independent of AMPK and LKB1.
highlights.PEN2011: Senior author of the study showing that mTORC1 raises V-ATPase gene expression through TFEB in Tsc2-null cells and mouse tissues.

Fontana L.lab_name: Charles Perkins Centre, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of Sydney (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia)
Fontana L.role: Studies how diet and calorie restriction affect human ageing and metabolic health, and co-wrote a widely cited Science review linking dietary restriction to nutrient-sensing pathways such as mTOR
Fontana L.sub: Professor and Leonard Pullmann Chair in Translational Metabolic Health, University of Sydney · Royal Prince Alfred Hospital · Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis (affiliation on FON2010, 2010)
story: FON2010 is a review written by Luigi Fontana, Linda Partridge and Valter Longo. It collects evidence from yeast, worms, flies, mice, monkeys and people that eating less, or turning down nutrient-sensing pathways such as mTOR and growth hormone/IGF-1 signalling, can slow ageing and lower the risk of age-related disease. The authors argue that dietary restriction and reduced pathway activity may work through similar mechanisms that evolution has conserved.

When the paper appeared, Fontana was at the Division of Geriatrics and Nutritional Science of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He is now a professor at the University of Sydney, based at the Charles Perkins Centre and linked to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, where he holds a chair in translational metabolic health.

His honours include the AFAR Breakthroughs in Gerontology Award (2009), the Glenn Award for Research in Biological Mechanisms of Aging (2011) and the AFAR Vincent Cristofalo Award (2016). In the Atlas the review is useful as a bridge: it connects the molecular mTOR work to what is known about diet and ageing in humans.

highlights.FON2010: First author of a Science review arguing that dietary restriction and reduced nutrient-sensing signalling, including mTOR, may slow ageing by similar conserved mechanisms.

Hotamışlıgil GS.lab_name: Hotamışlıgil Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Hotamışlıgil GS.role: Leads a Harvard laboratory on metabolic disease and was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences in 2026 for achievements in metabolic research
Hotamışlıgil GS.sub: James Stevens Simmons Professor of Genetics and Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health · Director, Center on Causes and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease · Elected to the National Academy of Sciences (2026)
story: KAL2026 asks how the liver switches on mTORC1 after a meal. Working in mouse models in which parts of the insulin pathway were removed from the liver, the authors found that insulin acts through AKT and the protein TSC2 to activate mTORC1, but that this route is not required for feeding to activate it. Dietary protein turns out to decide how much insulin signalling matters. Hotamışlıgil is the sixth of seven authors; Brendan Manning is the last author.

Hotamışlıgil is the James Stevens Simmons Professor of Genetics and Metabolism in the Department of Molecular Metabolism at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, and he directs the Center on Causes and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease. On 28 April 2026 the School announced his election to the National Academy of Sciences, citing distinguished and continuing achievements in metabolic research.
For the Atlas this paper is a reminder that mTORC1 in the liver listens to both hormones and food, and that the same pathway can be reached by more than one route.

highlights.KAL2026: Sixth author of a mouse study showing that dietary protein governs whether insulin signalling is needed for postprandial activation of hepatic mTORC1.

Rabinovitch PS.lab_name: Rabinovitch Lab, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Rabinovitch PS.role: Uses mouse models to study how improving mitochondrial function changes lifespan and healthspan, including catalase-overexpressing mice and the drug elamipretide (SS-31)
Rabinovitch PS.sub: Professor Emeritus, Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington · Joint member, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center · Fellow of the AAAS
story: JOH2013 is a Nature review by Simon Johnson, Peter Rabinovitch and Matt Kaeberlein, all at the University of Washington. It argues that mTOR is a leading target for slowing ageing: inhibiting the pathway extends lifespan in model organisms and protects against a growing list of age-related diseases. The authors also note that approved mTOR inhibitors exist, but that side effects currently rule out use in otherwise healthy people.

Rabinovitch joined the University of Washington Department of Pathology in 1992 and became a joint member of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in 1998. His own laboratory works on mitochondria and ageing in mice, including animals that make extra catalase in their mitochondria and treatment with the peptide elamipretide, and on how mitochondrial energy production interacts with cell signalling.
His honours include election as a Fellow of the AAAS and the Denham Harman Lifetime Achievement in Research Award of the American Aging Association. He is now Professor Emeritus.

highlights.JOH2013: Middle author of the Nature review that presents mTOR inhibition as a route to slowing ageing and age-related disease.

Rabinovitch PS.credit: Portrait: University of Washington Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology

Meyerson M.lab_name: Meyerson Lab, Center for Cancer Genomics, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Meyerson M.role: Cancer geneticist whose group has helped identify key genes mutated in lung cancer, and who contributed the cancer-genome analysis to the discovery that GATOR1 is a tumour suppressor acting on mTORC1
Meyerson M.sub: Charles A. Dana Chair in Human Cancer Genetics · Professor of Genetics and Medicine, Harvard Medical School · Director, Center for Cancer Genomics, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute · Member, Broad Institute
story: BAR2013 is a Science paper from David Sabatini's group that found GATOR, a protein assembly that talks to the Rag GTPases which tell mTORC1 whether amino acids are available. One part, GATOR1, switches the Rags off when amino acids run low. Its genes are mutated in human cancers, and cells with such mutations keep mTORC1 active even without amino acids and are unusually sensitive to rapamycin. Meyerson is the second to last author.

Meyerson is a professor of genetics and medicine at Harvard Medical School, holds the Charles A. Dana Chair in Human Cancer Genetics, and directs the Center for Cancer Genomics at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, with membership at the Broad Institute. His group, which he started at Dana-Farber in 1998, uses genomic and genetic methods to find the causes of cancer, with a focus on lung cancer.
His honours include election to the National Academy of Medicine (2018), the Alfred G. Knudson Award in Cancer Genetics (2019) and the Paul Marks Prize in Cancer Research (2009).

highlights.BAR2013: Senior co-author of the Science paper identifying GATOR1 as a tumour suppressor complex that switches off Rag GTPase signalling to mTORC1.

Ingolia NT.lab_name: Ingolia Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Ingolia NT.role: Known for ribosome profiling, a method that reads out which messenger RNAs ribosomes are translating across a whole genome; the study in the Atlas used this approach to map mTOR-controlled translation in prostate cancer.
Ingolia NT.sub: Professor of Biochemistry, Biophysics and Structural Biology, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, UC Berkeley
story: Nicholas Ingolia is a professor in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, where he leads the Ingolia Lab. His name is tied to ribosome profiling, a technique that lets researchers see, across all genes at once, which messenger RNAs are being turned into protein by ribosomes at a given moment.

HSI2012 is a 2012 Nature paper led by Andrew Hsieh and Davide Ruggero. Ingolia is one of the co-authors. The team used ribosome profiling to ask what oncogenic mTOR signalling changes in prostate cancer cells. They found that it does not simply speed up all protein production. It selectively boosts the translation of a specific group of messenger RNAs involved in cell proliferation, metabolism and invasion.

A class of those pro-invasion messages was shown to drive prostate cancer invasion and metastasis downstream of mTOR, and an ATP-site mTOR inhibitor, INK128, reversed this pattern with benefit in a metastasis model. For the Atlas, the paper is a key example of mTOR acting through selective translation, and ribosome profiling is the tool that made that visible.

highlights.HSI2012: Co-author of the 2012 Nature study that used ribosome profiling to show how oncogenic mTOR selectively reprograms translation to drive prostate cancer invasion and metastasis.

Ingolia NT.credit: Portrait: UC Berkeley, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology

Knight ZA.lab_name: Knight Lab (The Neurobiology of Homeostasis), Department of Physiology, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Knight ZA.role: Neuroscientist whose lab studies the brain mechanisms behind appetite, thirst and body-temperature preference; he is a co-author of the 2009 study that introduced the TORKinibs PP242 and PP30.
Knight ZA.sub: Professor, Department of Physiology, UCSF · Investigator, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (named 2018) · Weill Institute for Neurosciences
story: Zachary Knight is a professor of physiology at the University of California, San Francisco, a member of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences, and an investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, a title he received in 2018. His lab, called the Neurobiology of Homeostasis, studies how the brain controls appetite, thirst and the choice of a comfortable temperature.

FEL2009 was published in PLoS Biology with Morris Feldman as first author and Knight among the co-authors. The paper describes two new drugs, PP242 and PP30, that block the active site of the mTOR kinase. Unlike rapamycin, which only partly blocks mTORC1 and does not directly hit mTORC2, these drugs inhibit both complexes.

The authors used them to show that mTOR is needed for phosphorylation of Akt at S473, and that PP242 shuts down cap-dependent translation in conditions where rapamycin has no effect. A study from another group in the same year reached a similar conclusion, and together they showed that part of mTORC1 output is resistant to rapamycin.

highlights.FEL2009: Co-author of the PLoS Biology study introducing the active-site mTOR inhibitors PP242 and PP30, which hit rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 and mTORC2.

Scorrano L.lab_name: Scorrano Lab, Department of Biology, University of Padova (Padova, Italy)
Scorrano L.role: Mitochondrial biologist known for showing how the shape of mitochondria and their inner folds (cristae) control energy production and cell death.
Scorrano L.sub: Chiara Fama Professor of Biochemistry, Department of Biology, University of Padova · Scientific Director of the Veneto Institute of Molecular Medicine (2014–2020) · EMBO member
story: Luca Scorrano is a professor of biochemistry at the University of Padova. He trained as a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Stanley Korsmeyer at Dana-Farber and Harvard Medical School, then ran a group at the Dulbecco-Telethon Institute and became a full professor at the University of Geneva in 2006, before moving to Padova. From 2014 to 2020 he was Scientific Director of the Veneto Institute of Molecular Medicine. He is a member of EMBO and of Academia Europaea.

His work centres on the architecture of mitochondria. His lab described how remodelling of the cristae, the folds of the inner membrane, controls the release of cytochrome c during cell death, and how variants of the protein mitofusin-2 tether the endoplasmic reticulum to mitochondria.

EIS2016, a Nature Medicine paper from the group of Frank Madeo and colleagues, reports that the natural polyamine spermidine extends lifespan in mice and protects the heart. Scorrano is among its many co-authors. For the Atlas it is the mammalian follow-up to the earlier spermidine and autophagy work, linking this branch of nutrient and ageing biology to mitochondrial health.

highlights.EIS2016: Co-author of the Nature Medicine study showing that spermidine extends mouse lifespan and protects the heart.

Carracedo A.lab_name: Cancer Cell Signaling and Metabolism Laboratory, CIC bioGUNE (Bilbao, Spain)
Carracedo A.role: Cancer biologist who, as first author in 2008, showed that blocking mTORC1 can switch on the MAPK pathway through a PI3K-dependent feedback loop.
Carracedo A.sub: Ikerbasque Research Professor, CIC bioGUNE (Bilbao, Spain) · Beth Israel Deaconess Cancer Center, Harvard Medical School (affiliation on CAR2008)
story: Arkaitz Carracedo is an Ikerbasque research professor at CIC bioGUNE in Bilbao, where his group studies the signalling and metabolic changes that make cancer cells different from normal cells, with a focus on prostate and breast cancer. His work has been supported by an ERC Consolidator Grant, and in 2023 he received a Leonardo Grant from the BBVA Foundation.

CAR2008 comes from his time at the Beth Israel Deaconess Cancer Center at Harvard Medical School, in the group of Pier Paolo Pandolfi. The question was practical. Rapamycin and its relative RAD001 (everolimus) were being tested as cancer drugs, but results in patients were often modest. The authors found that when mTORC1 is blocked, cells lose a brake on a feedback loop that runs through S6K, PI3K and Ras, and the MAPK pathway switches on.

They saw this in biopsies from patients treated with RAD001, in a mouse model of prostate cancer, and in cell lines. Adding a MAPK inhibitor made rapamycin work better in cells and in a xenograft model. In the Atlas this is a standard example of why mTOR inhibitors often work best in combination.

highlights.CAR2008: First author: mTORC1 inhibition activates MAPK through a PI3K-dependent feedback loop, supporting combined mTORC1 and MAPK blockade in cancer.

Krnjevic K.lab_name: Department of Physiology, McGill University (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
Krnjevic K.role: Neurophysiologist who helped identify glutamate and GABA as the brain's main excitatory and inhibitory transmitters and described slow modulatory actions of acetylcholine in the cortex.
Krnjevic K.sub: Professor Emeritus of Physiology, McGill University · 1927–2021 · Gairdner International Award (1984)
story: Krešimir Krnjević was born in Zagreb in 1927, studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh and joined McGill University in 1964, where he stayed for about fifty years, serving as Director of Research in Anesthesia and later chair of Physiology. He died in 2021. His honours include the Gairdner International Award (1984), election to the Royal Society of Canada (1975) and the Order of Canada (1987).

Using microiontophoresis on single neurons, he helped show which chemicals the brain uses to excite and to inhibit nerve cells. He also showed that acetylcholine can slowly excite cortical neurons by reducing potassium conductance, and that rising calcium inside a neuron opens potassium channels and links metabolism to excitability.

HUA2013 is a Nature Neuroscience paper from the Costa-Mattioli group with Krnjević as a late co-author. Deleting Rictor, a core part of mTORC2, in the mouse forebrain lowered mTORC2 activity and impaired long-term memory and the late phase of hippocampal long-term potentiation. The effect traced to actin polymerization, so mTORC2 appears to be needed for memory to be stored for the long term.

highlights.HUA2013: Co-author of the Nature Neuroscience study showing that mTORC2 controls actin polymerization needed for long-term memory consolidation.

Huber LA.lab_name: Huber Laboratory, Institute of Cell Biology, Medical University of Innsbruck (Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria)
Huber LA.role: Cell biologist who studied the p14-MP1 scaffold on late endosomes, a complex later recognised as part of Ragulator (LAMTOR), the lysosomal platform that holds mTORC1 in place
Huber LA.sub: Director, Institute of Cell Biology, Medical University of Innsbruck · Professor of Cell Biology, Innsbruck (since 2002) · Director, Austrian Drug Screening Institute (since 2012) · Founding Director, Biocenter Innsbruck (2005–2013) · Group Leader, IMP Vienna (1996–2002) · MD, University of Innsbruck (1989)
story: Lukas Huber trained as a medical doctor in Innsbruck and did postdoctoral work at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory in Heidelberg before running his own group at the Institute of Molecular Pathology in Vienna. In the early 2000s his team described a small protein pair, p14 and MP1, that sits on late endosomes and helps a signalling kinase cascade (MAPK) work at the right place in the cell. At the time it looked like a niche trafficking story.

It turned out to be the seed of a much larger discovery. p14 and MP1 are two of the five subunits of Ragulator, the complex that Sabatini's group later showed anchors the Rag GTPases and therefore mTORC1 on the lysosome. Huber's laboratory in Innsbruck has continued on this LAMTOR/Ragulator complex, and links it to nutrient sensing, immune disease and Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.

The study in the Atlas, from 2023, is a cryo-electron microscopy structure led by James Hurley's group at Berkeley with Andrea Ballabio's group in Naples and Huber's in Innsbruck. It shows two Rag-Ragulator complexes together presenting the transcription factor TFEB to mTORC1 for phosphorylation, and gives a physical explanation for why TFEB depends so strongly on the FLCN protein.

highlights.CUI2023: Co-author of the Nature cryo-EM structure of the mTORC1-TFEB-Rag-Ragulator megacomplex; his Innsbruck laboratory works on the LAMTOR/Ragulator complex at the core of the structure.

Tavernarakis N.lab_name: Neurogenetics and Ageing Laboratory, Medical School, University of Crete and Institute of Molecular Biology and Biotechnology, FORTH (Heraklion, Crete, Greece)
Tavernarakis N.role: Geneticist who uses the roundworm C. elegans to study how ageing, neurodegeneration, necrotic cell death, autophagy and protein turnover are controlled
Tavernarakis N.sub: Professor of Molecular Systems Biology, Medical School, University of Crete · Research Director, IMBB-FORTH; heads the Neurogenetics and Ageing laboratory · Member, German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina (2019)
story: Nektarios Tavernarakis works in Heraklion on Crete, where his laboratory uses the tiny transparent roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans to ask why cells and animals age and why neurons die. Worms live only a few weeks and their genes are easy to switch off, so a lifespan experiment that would take years in mice takes days. His interests include autophagy (the cell's recycling system), necrotic cell death, mitochondria and lysosomes.

The Atlas study is the 2009 spermidine paper led by Tobias Eisenberg and Frank Madeo in Graz. Spermidine is a natural molecule found in foods such as wheat germ and soy that tends to fall with age. The paper reported that adding it lengthened lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells, and that the effect required autophagy. Tavernarakis is one of the authors of this multi-laboratory work, which opened the 'caloric restriction mimetic' idea to a wide audience.
He is a Professor at the University of Crete Medical School and a Research Director at the research institute FORTH, and was elected to the German academy Leopoldina in 2019.

highlights.EIS2009: One of the co-authors of the Nature Cell Biology spermidine paper, which showed lifespan extension in yeast, flies, worms and human cells through autophagy; the work with worms is the kind of ageing genetics his laboratory does.

Tavernarakis N.credit: Portrait: Tavernarakis Lab, FORTH / University of Crete

Bos JL.lab_name: Group Bos, Department of Molecular Cancer Research, Center for Molecular Medicine, University Medical Center Utrecht (Utrecht, Netherlands)
Bos JL.role: Cancer biologist known for work on Ras mutations and for the small GTPase Rap1 and its activator Epac, a cAMP-regulated switch for cell adhesion
Bos JL.sub: Professor of Physiological Chemistry, Utrecht University (since 1991) · Head, Department of Molecular Cancer Research, UMC Utrecht · Member, Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (2006) · Member, EMBO (1996) · Josephine Nefkens Prize for Cancer Research (2014) · Born 1950
story: Hans Bos studied biochemistry in Amsterdam, earned his doctorate in 1980 and began studying mutated Ras genes in 1984, when the link between Ras and cancer was still new. Since 1991 he has been a professor in Utrecht, where his group studies Ras-like small GTPases, molecular switches that flip between an off and an on state, and in particular Rap1 and the cAMP sensor Epac.

In 2005 Bos took part in a study from George Thomas's laboratory in Basel that asked how amino acids switch on mTOR. Until then most pictures put insulin and class 1 PI3-kinase in charge. The paper found a separate route in which amino acids act through a different enzyme, class 3 PI3-kinase hVps34, which helped establish that nutrients and hormones feed into mTORC1 by different inputs.

Besides his own research, Bos has led large Dutch cancer research programmes, including a 2013 international 'Dream Team' project co-led with Hans Clevers. He is a member of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences and of EMBO.

highlights.NOB2005: Co-author of the PNAS paper showing that amino acids reach mTOR/raptor through class 3 PI3-kinase hVps34, separate from the insulin route; he contributed as a small-GTPase specialist from Utrecht.

Green R.lab_name: Green Lab, Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Green R.role: Biochemist who studies how the ribosome works and how cells detect and rescue stalled or colliding ribosomes, including links to the integrated stress response
Green R.sub: Bloomberg Distinguished Professor and Director, Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine · Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator (since 2000) · Johns Hopkins faculty since 1998
story: Rachel Green studies the ribosome, the molecular machine that reads messenger RNA and builds proteins. Her laboratory in Baltimore combines biochemistry, genetics and ribosome profiling in bacteria, yeast and human cells, and asks what happens when translation goes wrong: how cells spot stalled ribosomes, clear them, and trigger stress responses such as the integrated stress response.

The 2026 Atlas study asks how cancer cells survive when ribosome production is blocked. A genetic screen found that switching off mTOR let cells live despite severe translation problems. Rather than rebuilding ribosomes, mTORC1 inhibition redirected the few available ribosomes away from the highly translated 5'TOP messages, mostly ribosomal proteins, toward transcripts needed for survival. The authors call this 'translational fitness'.

Green's group at Johns Hopkins supplied the translation expertise for this collaboration, which was led by Marikki Laiho's cancer research group at the same university. She has been an HHMI Investigator since 2000.

highlights.FAN2026: Co-author in the Genes & Development study showing that mTOR inactivation lets cells survive ribosome biogenesis deficiency by redistributing ribosomes away from 5'TOP mRNAs; she is a ribosome and translation specialist at Johns Hopkins.

Green R.credit: Portrait: Johns Hopkins University, Department of Biology

Kahan BD (Rapamune US Study Group).lab_name: Division of Immunology and Organ Transplantation, Department of Surgery, McGovern Medical School, University of Texas Health Science Center (Houston, Texas, USA)
Kahan BD (Rapamune US Study Group).role: Transplant surgeon-scientist who was the named author of the large US trial that made sirolimus (rapamycin) an approved immunosuppressant for kidney transplant patients
Kahan BD (Rapamune US Study Group).sub: Emeritus Professor and Director Emeritus, Division of Immunology and Organ Transplantation, University of Texas Medical School at Houston · Chief of Organ Transplant Services, Hermann Hospital (30+ years) · Past President, American Society of Transplant Surgeons (1989–1990) · MD, PhD
story: Barry Kahan spent most of his career at the University of Texas Medical School in Houston, where he ran the organ transplant service at Hermann Hospital for more than thirty years. He took part in the early clinical work on cyclosporine, basiliximab and sirolimus, and later became editor-in-chief of the journal Transplantation Proceedings. He served as president of the American Society of Transplant Surgeons in 1989 and 1990.

Sirolimus is the drug name for rapamycin, the molecule that led scientists to discover mTOR. The 2000 Lancet trial in the Atlas, run by the Rapamune US Study Group with Kahan as author, randomised 719 kidney transplant recipients to sirolimus 2 mg, 5 mg or azathioprine on top of cyclosporin and prednisone. At six months, biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was 16.9% and 12.0% on sirolimus compared with 29.8% on azathioprine, and graft and patient survival at one year were similar.
This trial was one of the studies behind the approval of sirolimus (Rapamune) for preventing kidney transplant rejection, the first clinical use of an mTOR inhibitor.

highlights.KAH2000: Author for the Rapamune US Study Group of the randomised Lancet trial showing sirolimus reduced acute kidney transplant rejection compared with azathioprine.

Yaffe MB.lab_name: Yaffe Lab, Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Yaffe MB.role: Cancer biologist and physician-scientist known for working out how phosphorylation creates binding sites on proteins, including the 14-3-3 family of phosphoserine/threonine-binding proteins, and how kinases choose their targets.
Yaffe MB.sub: David H. Koch Professor in Science and Biological Engineering, MIT · Director, MIT Center for Precision Cancer Medicine · Intramural Faculty, Koch Institute · Margaret MacVicar Faculty Fellow · Fellow, Association of American Physicians (2021)
story: Michael Yaffe is both a physician and a biochemist, and he has spent his career on one question: how does a cell read a phosphate tag? Adding a phosphate group to a protein is the main way kinases such as mTOR pass messages, but the tag only matters if something reads it. Yaffe's work on the 14-3-3 proteins and on the short sequence patterns that kinases prefer helped show how those messages are read and routed.

That background made him a natural partner for the Sabatini laboratory in the 2013 Science study in the Atlas. The team asked why some mTORC1 phosphorylation sites stay switched on when the kinase is partly blocked by rapamycin or starvation, while others switch off first. The answer was that each site has its own built-in quality as a substrate, so a single level of mTORC1 activity can give different outputs depending on the target.

Today Yaffe is a professor at MIT and a member of the Koch Institute, where he also directs the MIT Center for Precision Cancer Medicine. His group studies how cancer cells and the immune system respond to DNA damage and drug treatment through signalling networks.

highlights.KAN2013: Co-author with the Sabatini group on the finding that mTORC1 phosphorylation sites encode their own sensitivity to starvation and rapamycin.

Hockemeyer D.lab_name: Hockemeyer Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Hockemeyer D.role: Stem-cell biologist whose laboratory builds engineered human stem-cell and mouse models of disease, using genome editing and functional genomics screens.
Hockemeyer D.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Development and Physiology, Molecular and Cell Biology, UC Berkeley (promoted 2025)
story: Dirk Hockemeyer runs a laboratory at UC Berkeley that makes human disease models from stem cells. The group edits the genome of human pluripotent stem cells, which can become almost any cell type, and then uses those cells, along with mouse models and genome-wide screens, to study what a given mutation actually does.

That approach is the backbone of the 2026 Nature study in the Atlas, done with Helen Bateup's laboratory. Brain organoids (small, lab-grown clusters of human brain cells) carrying loss-of-function mutations in TSC2, the gene mutated in tuberous sclerosis, together with tissue from patients, showed that overactive mTORC1 pushes neural progenitor cells to become reactive astrocytes. The effect arises inside the cells themselves rather than from outside signals.
For a reader of the Atlas the paper is a useful reminder that mTORC1 hyperactivity in tuberous sclerosis is not only a neuron story. It also changes which glial cells the developing brain produces.

highlights.LI2026C: Senior author with Helen Bateup; stem-cell engineered TSC2-mutant brain organoids showed that hyperactive mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity.

Hogenesch JB.lab_name: Hogenesch Lab, Division of Human Genetics, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Hogenesch JB.role: Circadian-rhythm geneticist who uses genome-wide methods to map which genes the body clock controls in each tissue.
Hogenesch JB.sub: Thomas F. Boat Chair, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center · Appointments in Human Genetics, Pulmonary Medicine and Immunobiology
story: John Hogenesch studies the body clock, the roughly 24-hour timer that tells cells when to be active and when to rest. His laboratory is known for large genomic surveys that ask which genes switch on and off with the clock in different organs, and for building tools that other chronobiologists use to detect rhythms in data.

In the 2018 PLoS Genetics paper in the Atlas, led by Andrew Liu's group, he is a co-author on work showing that mTOR sets how the clock runs. Blocking mTOR made the clock tick more slowly and with a weaker swing, while activating mTOR made it faster and stronger, in both brain and peripheral tissues.
Hogenesch now holds the Thomas F. Boat Chair at Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, where his lab moved to work on circadian medicine.

highlights.RAM2018: Co-author of the study showing that mTOR signalling controls the period and amplitude of the central and peripheral circadian clocks.

Hogenesch JB.credit: Portrait: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center

McCormack FX.lab_name: Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
McCormack FX.role: Pulmonologist who led the MILES trial, which showed that sirolimus (rapamycin) halts the decline in lung function in lymphangioleiomyomatosis, a rare mTOR-driven lung disease.
McCormack FX.sub: Professor and Division Chief, Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, University of Cincinnati · Gordon and Helen Hughes Taylor Chair (since 2006) · Co-leader, Rare Lung Diseases Consortium
story: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis, or LAM, is a rare lung disease mostly in women. Cells with overactive mTOR form cysts that slowly destroy lung tissue. Because the problem sits in the mTOR pathway, rapamycin (sirolimus) was an obvious candidate drug, but it had to be tested properly.

Francis McCormack is first author of the MILES trial, a 12-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 89 patients. Lung function fell by about 12 ml per month on placebo and held steady on sirolimus. When the drug was stopped, the decline resumed, so the benefit lasted only while patients kept taking it. Side effects were more common on sirolimus.

McCormack leads the pulmonary division at the University of Cincinnati and co-leads the Rare Lung Diseases Consortium with Bruce Trapnell. In the Atlas, MILES stands as one of the clearest human demonstrations that blocking mTOR can change the course of a disease.

highlights.MCC2011: First author of the MILES randomized trial: 12 months of sirolimus stabilized lung function in 89 patients with LAM, with decline resuming after the drug was stopped.

de Angelis MH.lab_name: Institute of Experimental Genetics, Helmholtz Munich, and Chair of Experimental Genetics, Technical University of Munich (Munich, Germany)
de Angelis MH.role: Mouse geneticist who directs large-scale phenotyping of mouse mutants and the German Mouse Clinic, a platform that tests how genes affect health and disease.
de Angelis MH.sub: Director, Institute of Experimental Genetics, Helmholtz Munich (since 2000) · Chair of Experimental Genetics, Technical University of Munich (since 2003) · Research Director, Helmholtz Munich · Member, Leopoldina (2018) · Paul Langerhans Medal (2021)
story: Martin Hrabě de Angelis leads the Institute of Experimental Genetics at Helmholtz Munich and holds the chair of experimental genetics at the Technical University of Munich. His institute runs systematic, standardized health checks on mice, covering heart, metabolism, behaviour and more, so that the effects of a gene or a treatment can be measured across the whole animal.

That expertise is why he appears on the 2016 Nature Medicine paper from Frank Madeo's group in the Atlas. The study found that spermidine, a natural polyamine, extended lifespan in mice and protected the heart from age-related stiffening and thickening. Mouse phenotyping platforms like his are what make claims about whole-body effects checkable.

He is also a founding member and board chair of the German Center for Diabetes Research, a member of the executive committee of the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium, and a member of the Leopoldina, Germany's national academy of sciences.

highlights.EIS2016: Co-author on the spermidine study, in which oral spermidine extended mouse lifespan and improved cardiac function; the mouse phenotyping work is his field.

Kuehl WM.lab_name: Genetics Branch, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Kuehl WM.role: Physician-scientist who spent decades working out the genetic and molecular biology of multiple myeloma and its precursor condition MGUS.
Kuehl WM.sub: Deceased (1939–2023) · Senior Investigator, Genetics Branch, NCI Center for Cancer Research · Deputy Chief of the branch (2001–2006) · Retired 2015 · Waldenström Award, International Myeloma Workshop (2011)
story: Michael Kuehl was a physician-scientist who spent more than thirty years at the National Cancer Institute studying multiple myeloma, a cancer of antibody-producing plasma cells. He identified several mechanisms behind the disease and helped establish the link between the pre-cancer condition MGUS and myeloma, which matters for early diagnosis.

His expertise was central to the 2009 Cell paper in the Atlas, led by Timothy Peterson in David Sabatini's laboratory. The paper identified DEPTOR as a built-in brake on both mTOR complexes. In most cancers DEPTOR is low, but in a subset of myelomas with specific chromosomal translocations it is strongly overexpressed, and those cells need it to survive, because it keeps pro-survival Akt signalling active.
Kuehl died in April 2023. The NCI described him as someone who continued to advise colleagues in the Genetics Branch for several years after his retirement in 2015.

highlights.PET2009: Co-author of the DEPTOR paper; his myeloma expertise supported the finding that some myeloma cells depend on high DEPTOR levels to survive.

Kuehl WM.credit: Portrait: National Cancer Institute (public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Kroemer G.lab_name: Metabolism, Cancer and Immunity team, Cordeliers Research Centre (Inserm) & Gustave Roussy (Paris, France)
Kroemer G.role: Cell biologist known for work on programmed cell death, mitochondria and autophagy, and for linking autophagy to ageing and cancer immunity.
Kroemer G.sub: Director of the Metabolomics and Cellular Biology Platforms, Gustave Roussy · Head, Inserm team Metabolism, Cancer and Immunity · Deputy Director, Cordeliers Research Centre · Professor, Paris-Descartes University · Member, Academia Europaea (2007) · Carus Medal, Leopoldina (2007) · Descartes Prize, European Commission (2006)
story: Guido Kroemer is a cell biologist in Paris whose work centres on how cells die and how they clean up after themselves. He leads an Inserm team called Metabolism, Cancer and Immunity and directs the metabolomics and cellular biology platforms at Gustave Roussy, a cancer centre near Paris. He is also deputy director of the Cordeliers Research Centre.

In the Atlas he appears on the 2009 Nature Cell Biology study led by Frank Madeo and Tobias Eisenberg. The team showed that spermidine, a small natural molecule called a polyamine whose level falls as people age, extended the lifespan of yeast, flies and worms, and of human immune cells in culture. The effect depended on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, which is the same process that mTORC1 holds back when nutrients are plentiful.

The paper became the starting point for the idea that some natural compounds can mimic parts of caloric restriction. Kroemer is a senior author on it, and it sits in the Atlas as the opening study of the spermidine branch.

highlights.EIS2009: Senior author with Frank Madeo: spermidine induces autophagy and extends lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells.

Berkovic SF.lab_name: Epilepsy Research Centre, Austin Health & Department of Medicine, University of Melbourne (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia)
Berkovic SF.role: Neurologist who helped establish the genetic causes of many epilepsies, including the discovery that DEPDC5 mutations, which affect the mTORC1 brake GATOR1, cause familial focal epilepsy.
Berkovic SF.sub: Laureate Professor, Department of Medicine, University of Melbourne · Director, Epilepsy Research Centre, Austin Health · Fellow of the Royal Society (2007) · Fellow, Australian Academy of Science (2005) · Companion of the Order of Australia (2014)
story: Sam Berkovic is a neurologist in Melbourne who studies epilepsy, a condition where brain cells fire in abnormal bursts. He directs the Epilepsy Research Centre at Austin Health and is a Laureate Professor at the University of Melbourne. His honours include Fellow of the Royal Society and Companion of the Order of Australia.

The 2013 Nature Genetics study in the Atlas, led by Leanne Dibbens with Berkovic and Ingrid Scheffer as the final authors, looked at families in which different relatives had seizures starting in different parts of the brain. Exome sequencing, which reads all the protein-coding genes, found mutations in DEPDC5 in two families, and in five of six further published large families. About 12 percent of smaller families with focal epilepsy (10 of 82) also carried DEPDC5 mutations.

DEPDC5 is a subunit of GATOR1, the complex that switches mTORC1 off when amino acids are scarce. When it is damaged, mTORC1 can stay too active in brain cells. This is why the paper is a link between a human genetic disease and the mTOR pathway, although the paper itself pointed only to a role in neuronal signalling.

highlights.DIB2013B: Senior author (with Ingrid Scheffer): DEPDC5 loss-of-function mutations cause familial focal epilepsy with variable foci.

Berkovic SF.credit: Portrait: Epilepsy Research Centre, Austin Health / University of Melbourne

Brown EJ.lab_name: Brown Lab, Department of Cancer Biology, Abramson Family Cancer Research Institute, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Brown EJ.role: Co-discoverer of mTOR: as first author he isolated the mammalian protein bound by the rapamycin-FKBP12 complex (FRAP) and cloned its gene in 1994.
Brown EJ.sub: Associate Professor of Cancer Biology, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · PhD in Immunology, Harvard University (1996) · BA in Genetics, UC Berkeley (1989)
story: In the early 1990s rapamycin was known to stop cells from dividing, and it was known to work by first binding a small protein called FKBP12. Nobody knew what the drug-bound complex actually hit in mammalian cells. In the 1994 Nature paper in the Atlas, Eric Brown and colleagues in Stuart Schreiber's laboratory at Harvard used the rapamycin-FKBP12 complex to pull a large protein out of cell extracts, which they called FRAP.

They sequenced pieces of the purified protein and used them to find the human gene. It turned out to be closely related to the yeast TOR1 and TOR2 genes, which had already been linked to rapamycin. That match is why the protein is now called mTOR, mammalian target of rapamycin. A paper from David Sabatini's laboratory, also in the Atlas, reached the same protein from rat brain in the same year.

Brown later moved his research away from mTOR. His lab at the University of Pennsylvania now studies how cells protect their DNA while it is being copied, with a focus on the ATR kinase and on ATR inhibitors as cancer treatments.

highlights.BRO1994: First author: purified FRAP, the mammalian protein bound by the rapamycin-FKBP12 complex, and cloned the human gene, which resembles yeast TOR.

Brown EJ.credit: Portrait: Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania

Driscoll M.lab_name: Driscoll Lab, Department of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry, Rutgers University (Piscataway, New Jersey, USA)
Driscoll M.role: Studies the biology of ageing in the roundworm C. elegans, including interventions that extend healthspan and the mechanisms that protect neurons from damage.
Driscoll M.sub: Distinguished Professor, Department of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry, Rutgers University · Member, US National Academy of Sciences (2023)
story: Monica Driscoll is a Distinguished Professor at Rutgers University. Her laboratory uses the tiny roundworm C. elegans to ask how ageing works and how neurons stay healthy, testing genetic, chemical and exercise interventions that extend healthspan. She was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences in 2023.

She is one of the authors of the 2008 PLoS Genetics study in the Atlas, led by Malene Hansen and Cynthia Kenyon at UCSF. The team asked whether autophagy, the cell's recycling system, is needed for dietary restriction to lengthen life in worms. Dietary restriction and TOR inhibition both produced signs of autophagy, and switching off autophagy genes prevented them from extending lifespan.

The study also found that the autophagy response to dietary restriction depends on the transcription factor PHA-4, and that autophagy alone was not sufficient to extend lifespan. It is one of the early experiments tying TOR signalling, autophagy and longevity together.

highlights.HAN2008: Co-author: autophagy is required for dietary restriction and TOR inhibition to extend lifespan in C. elegans.

Heitman J.lab_name: Heitman Lab, Department of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology, Duke University School of Medicine (Durham, North Carolina, USA)
Heitman J.role: Co-discovered the TOR genes in yeast in 1991 as a first author with Rao Movva and Michael Hall, the genetic identification of what became known as mTOR in mammals
Heitman J.sub: Duke Health Distinguished Professor of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology, Duke University · Member, US National Academy of Sciences (2021) · University of Basel (affiliation on HEI1991, 1991)
story: Rapamycin was known to stop yeast cells from dividing, but nobody knew what it acted on. In HEI1991, Joseph Heitman, working in Michael Hall's group at the University of Basel, treated yeast with rapamycin and found that the cells froze in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. He showed that the drug works by first binding a small protein called FKBP, and that this drug-protein pair is the actual toxic agent: yeast lacking FKBP survived the drug.

The same paper reported two other genes that mattered for rapamycin toxicity. Heitman named them TOR1 and TOR2, short for Target Of Rapamycin. This was the first genetic identification of the TOR pathway. Mammalian mTOR was purified a few years later, and the name carries through from these yeast genes.

Heitman went on to run his own laboratory at Duke University, where he is a professor and a member of the US National Academy of Sciences. His group studies disease-causing fungi such as Cryptococcus, including how rapamycin and related drugs act against them through FKBP12 and TOR.

highlights.HEI1991: First author. Showed that rapamycin arrests yeast through an FKBP-rapamycin complex and named the TOR1 and TOR2 genes that take part in its toxicity.

Heitman J.credit: Portrait: Duke University School of Medicine

Baselga J.lab_name: Division of Hematology/Oncology, Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center, Harvard Medical School (affiliation on BAS2012) (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Baselga J.role: Breast cancer oncologist who led the BOLERO-2 trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus added to hormone therapy lengthens progression-free survival
Baselga J.sub: Deceased (1959–2021) · Executive Vice President, Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca (2019–2021) · Physician-in-Chief, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · President, AACR (2015–2016) · Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center (affiliation on BAS2012, 2011)
story: Breast cancers that depend on oestrogen are treated with hormone therapy, but many eventually stop responding. Laboratory work had linked this resistance to activation of the mTOR pathway. José Baselga led BOLERO-2, a phase 3 trial of 724 women, to test the idea: everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, added to the hormone drug exemestane versus exemestane with a placebo.

At the interim analysis, median progression-free survival was 6.9 months with everolimus and 2.8 months with placebo as judged by local investigators, and 10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review. Side effects included mouth sores, anaemia and lung inflammation. The trial is one of the clearest tests in people that mTOR matters in a common cancer.

Baselga was born in Barcelona in 1959 and trained at Memorial Sloan Kettering, later led oncology at Vall d'Hebron in Barcelona and became Physician-in-Chief at Memorial Sloan Kettering. He took part in developing several breast cancer drugs, including trastuzumab, pertuzumab, alpelisib and everolimus, and was president of the American Association for Cancer Research in 2015–2016. He joined AstraZeneca in 2019 and died in March 2021.

highlights.BAS2012: First author of BOLERO-2, the phase 3 trial in which adding everolimus to exemestane improved progression-free survival in hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer.
highlights.PIC2014: Senior author of the final BOLERO-2 overall-survival report, in which adding everolimus to exemestane did not significantly lengthen overall survival (31.0 vs 26.6 months), although the progression-free survival gain held.

Kirkland JL.lab_name: Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Kirkland JL.role: Founder of the field of senolytics, drugs that clear senescent cells, and a leader of clinical trials of ageing-targeted therapies
Kirkland JL.sub: Director, Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics, Cedars-Sinai · Principal Investigator, Translational Geroscience Network · formerly Mayo Clinic
story: James Kirkland is a physician-scientist whose main focus is how senescent cells, which stop dividing but stay alive and release inflammatory signals, contribute to age-related disease. He is described as a founder of senolytics, the idea of using drugs to remove such cells.

LAN2026 is a Mayo Clinic Proceedings study of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), a common heart condition of older age. Kirkland is one of the listed authors, alongside other researchers working on ageing biology and mTOR, including Dudley Lamming. In the Atlas this study sits at the point where mTOR inhibition is tested directly in older patients.

Kirkland spent many years at Mayo Clinic and, according to a 2025 Cedars-Sinai article, now directs the new Cedars-Sinai Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics and leads the Translational Geroscience Network, which runs many clinical trials.

highlights.LAN2026: Listed author of a Mayo Clinic Proceedings study of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; Kirkland's role as an ageing-biology and senescence researcher on the team.

Benzer S.lab_name: Benzer Laboratory, Division of Biology, California Institute of Technology (Pasadena, California, USA)
Benzer S.role: Pioneer of fine-structure gene mapping in phage and founder of neurogenetics, whose Drosophila work found the first circadian-rhythm mutants
Benzer S.sub: Boswell Professor of Neuroscience, Emeritus, Caltech · 1921–2007 (deceased) · Wolf Prize, Lasker Award, Crafoord Prize, National Medal of Science
story: Seymour Benzer began as a physicist. He took a PhD at Purdue in 1947, then moved into biology after reading Schrödinger's What Is Life?, working with Max Delbrück at Caltech and later at the Pasteur Institute. In the 1950s he used mutant bacteriophages to map the inside of a single gene, showing that a gene is divisible and that mutations are spread along it.

From the 1960s at Caltech he turned to behaviour and used the fruit fly to ask which genes shape it. His laboratory found the first circadian-rhythm mutants and identified genes such as per (the biological clock) and dunce (learning). His honours include the Lasker Award, Wolf Prize, Crafoord Prize and National Medal of Science, and he was a member of the National Academy of Sciences and the Royal Society. He died in 2007.

In the Atlas he appears as a co-author of ZID2009, a Drosophila study from Pankaj Kapahi's group. It found that the mTOR target 4E-BP is switched on by dietary restriction and is needed for the lifespan gain, partly by boosting mitochondrial gene translation. The fly was Benzer's own model organism, and this is a late paper in a long career.

highlights.ZID2009: Co-author of the Drosophila study showing that 4E-BP, a target of mTOR, mediates lifespan extension under dietary restriction by enhancing mitochondrial activity.

Gingras AC.lab_name: Gingras Lab, Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute, Sinai Health; Department of Molecular Genetics, University of Toronto (Toronto, Ontario, Canada)
Gingras AC.role: Showed in 1999 that mTOR phosphorylates 4E-BP1 in a priming two-step mechanism, and now leads work on interaction proteomics (including BioID) that maps how cells read signals such as mTORC1
Gingras AC.sub: Senior Investigator & Director, Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute · Vice President, Research, Sinai Health · Professor, University of Toronto
story: Anne-Claude Gingras did the work in GIN1999 at McGill University in Nahum Sonenberg's field, which studies how cells start making proteins. The protein 4E-BP1 holds back the factor eIF4E; when 4E-BP1 is phosphorylated it lets go, and protein synthesis speeds up. The paper asked which sites mTOR itself phosphorylates and in what order.

The answer was a two-step mechanism. mTOR first adds phosphate to two sites, Thr-37 and Thr-46, and this acts as a priming event that is needed before the later, serum-sensitive sites can be phosphorylated. It was an early, concrete picture of how mTOR turns a growth signal into more translation.

Today she is Senior Investigator and Director of the Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute in Toronto and Vice President, Research, at Sinai Health. Her laboratory develops mass spectrometry and proximity-labelling methods to map protein interactions and locations, and studies signalling pathways including mTORC1, relevant to cancer, neurodegeneration and rare diseases. She holds a Canada Research Chair in Functional Proteomics.

highlights.GIN1999: First author: mTOR phosphorylates 4E-BP1 at Thr-37 and Thr-46 as a priming step required for later phosphorylation sites that release eIF4E.
highlights.TAN2002: Co-author: mTOR, 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2 and eIF4E sit in hippocampal dendrites near synapses, and rapamycin reduced late-phase LTP in rodent hippocampal slices.

Gingras AC.credit: Portrait: Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute, Sinai Health

Mair WB.lab_name: Mair Lab, Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Mair WB.role: Studies how nutrient and energy sensors, and dietary restriction, control the rate of ageing, using models from yeast to mammals
Mair WB.sub: Professor of Molecular Metabolism · Director, Harvard Chan School Aging Initiative · Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
story: William Mair leads the Mair Lab at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, where he is Professor of Molecular Metabolism and directs the school's Aging Initiative. His group asks why ageing raises the risk of chronic disease, and how food and metabolism change the pace of ageing. Their aim is to find genetic pathways that could copy the benefits of dietary restriction without its drawbacks.

He has received the American Federation for Aging Research Breakthrough in Gerontology Award, along with scholar awards from the Glenn and Ellison foundations (as listed on his Harvard profile). Much of his work looks at how cells' nutrient and energy sensors, including the pathways that meet at mTOR, stop working well with age.

In the Atlas he appears as a co-author of SHI2026, a 2026 preprint led from Edward Chouchani's laboratory. It reports that dietary restriction oxidises a selected set of protein cysteines, and that oxidation of Cys19 on the autophagy protein ATG5 is needed for autophagy during nutrient restriction. It has not been peer reviewed.

highlights.SHI2026: Co-author of the preprint showing that dietary restriction oxidises selected cysteines and that oxidation of ATG5 Cys19 licenses autophagy upon nutrient restriction.

Mair WB.credit: Portrait: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Jewell JL.lab_name: Jewell Lab, Department of Molecular Biology, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Jewell JL.role: Studies how cells sense nutrients such as amino acids to control growth and metabolism through mTORC1
Jewell JL.sub: Associate Professor of Molecular Biology · UT Southwestern Medical Center
story: Jenna Jewell is an Associate Professor in the Department of Molecular Biology at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. Her lab studies how cells sense nutrients to control cell growth and metabolism, and how this sensing goes wrong in human disease.

She earned her PhD at Indiana University with Debbie Thurmond and then trained as a postdoctoral fellow with Kun-Liang Guan at the University of California, San Diego. Her awards include an American Cancer Society Research Scholar Award and a FASEB Junior Investigator Award.

In the Atlas she is first author of JEW2015, a Science paper from the Guan lab. It showed that two amino acids reach mTORC1 by different routes: leucine works through the Rag GTPases, while glutamine can switch mTORC1 on even in cells that lack RagA and RagB, using the small GTPase Arf1 instead.

highlights.JEW2015: First author: leucine and glutamine activate mTORC1 by different routes, with glutamine using a Rag-independent, Arf1-dependent path (cells).

Gwinn DM.lab_name: Shaw Lab, Salk Institute for Biological Studies, at the time of the study (La Jolla, California, USA)
Gwinn DM.role: First author of the 2008 study showing that the energy sensor AMPK switches off mTORC1 by phosphorylating raptor
story: Dana Gwinn did this work in Reuben Shaw's laboratory at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California, which is the affiliation PubMed gives for the study. The Atlas has no other sourced details of her career, so this profile covers only that paper.

In the Atlas she is first author of GWI2008. The paper found a second way that AMPK, the cell's low-energy alarm, shuts down mTORC1. Besides acting through TSC2, AMPK directly phosphorylates raptor, a core part of mTORC1, and this step is needed for cells to stop growing and pause their cell cycle when energy runs low.

highlights.GWI2008: First author: AMPK phosphorylates raptor on two serines, a step required for mTORC1 shutdown and cell-cycle arrest under energy stress (cells).

Mihaylova MM.lab_name: Mihaylova Lab, Department of Biological Chemistry and Pharmacology, The Ohio State University (Columbus, Ohio, USA)
Mihaylova MM.role: Studies how intestinal stem cells change with age and how diet shapes their metabolism
Mihaylova MM.sub: Assistant Professor of Biological Chemistry and Pharmacology · The Ohio State University · Pew Biomedical Scholar (2022)
story: Maria Mihaylova is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biological Chemistry and Pharmacology at The Ohio State University. Her lab studies how intestinal stem and progenitor cells change with age, how those changes affect nutrient absorption and gut health, and what role diet plays.

She earned her PhD in biology from the University of California, San Diego and the Salk Institute in 2012, then did postdoctoral work at the Whitehead Institute until 2018. She was named a Pew Biomedical Scholar in 2022.
In the Atlas she is a co-author of GWI2008 from Reuben Shaw's lab at the Salk Institute, which showed that the energy sensor AMPK phosphorylates raptor to switch off mTORC1 when energy is low.

highlights.GWI2008: Co-author: AMPK phosphorylates raptor to enforce a metabolic checkpoint on mTORC1 (cells).

Vander Haar E.lab_name: Kim Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota, at the time of the study (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Vander Haar E.role: First author of the 2007 study identifying PRAS40 as the link that carries insulin signals from Akt to mTOR
story: Emilie Vander Haar did this work in Do-Hyung Kim's laboratory in the Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics at the University of Minnesota, the affiliation PubMed gives for the study. The Atlas has no other sourced details of her career, so this profile covers only that paper.

In the Atlas she is first author of VAN2007 in Nature Cell Biology. It identified PRAS40 as a protein that binds mTOR and holds it back. When insulin switches on Akt, Akt phosphorylates PRAS40, PRAS40 lets go, and mTOR signalling can proceed. This gave a second route from insulin to mTOR, alongside the better-known one through TSC2.

highlights.VAN2007: First author: PRAS40 binds and inhibits mTOR, and its phosphorylation by Akt passes insulin signals to mTOR (cells).

Fingar DC.lab_name: Fingar Lab, Department of Cell and Developmental Biology, University of Michigan Medical School (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Fingar DC.role: Studies how mTORC1 and mTORC2 are regulated, especially through site-specific phosphorylation
Fingar DC.sub: Professor of Cell and Developmental Biology · Associate Chair · University of Michigan Medical School
story: Diane Fingar is Professor of Cell and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan Medical School, where she is also Associate Chair of the department. Her lab studies how the two mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, are switched on and off, especially through phosphorylation at specific sites, and how they talk to other signalling systems.

She earned her PhD at Harvard Medical School (1995), did postdoctoral work at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and was an Instructor in Cell Biology at Harvard before moving to Michigan.

In the Atlas she is first author of FIN2002 from John Blenis's lab. It showed that mammalian cell size depends on mTOR, separately from cell division, and that mTOR controls size through two downstream targets, S6K1 and the 4E-BP1/eIF4E pair.

highlights.FIN2002: First author: mTOR sets mammalian cell size through S6K1 and 4E-BP1/eIF4E, separately from cell-cycle progression (cells).
highlights.TEE2002: Co-author: the TSC1–TSC2 complex inhibits mTOR signalling to S6K1 and 4E-BP1 (cells).

Fingar DC.credit: Portrait: University of Michigan Medical School

Krueger DA.lab_name: Tuberous Sclerosis Clinic, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Krueger DA.role: Child neurologist who led the first trial of an mTOR inhibitor for brain tumours in tuberous sclerosis complex
Krueger DA.sub: Director, Tuberous Sclerosis Clinic · Associate Professor of Clinical Pediatrics and Neurology · Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center
story: Darcy Krueger is a child neurologist who directs the Tuberous Sclerosis Clinic at Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, where he is Associate Professor of Clinical Pediatrics and Neurology. His work focuses on how tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) causes disease and on treatments that could prevent or reverse it.

He earned both a PhD (2000) and an MD (2002) at Saint Louis University and trained in pediatrics, neurology and child neurology in Cincinnati. He was a founding member and the first director (2011–2013) of the TSC Clinical Research Consortium.

In the Atlas he is first author of KRU2010 in the New England Journal of Medicine. In 28 patients with TSC, the mTOR inhibitor everolimus shrank subependymal giant-cell astrocytomas (a type of brain tumour) by at least 30% in three out of four. This open-label study led to the first FDA-approved treatment for TSC in 2010.

highlights.KRU2010: First author: everolimus shrank TSC-related brain tumours by 30% or more in 75% of 28 patients (open-label, humans).

Ravikumar B.lab_name: Rubinsztein Lab, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, University of Cambridge, at the time of the study (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Ravikumar B.role: First author of the 2004 study showing that switching off mTOR clears the toxic protein of Huntington disease by autophagy
story: Brinda Ravikumar did this work in David Rubinsztein's laboratory at the Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, the affiliation PubMed gives for the study. The Atlas has no other sourced details of her career, so this profile covers only that paper.

In the Atlas she is first author of RAV2004 in Nature Genetics. The study found that mTOR gets trapped inside the clumps formed by the mutant huntingtin protein, which turns autophagy on. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin in flies, or with the related drug CCI-779 in mice, helped cells clear the toxic protein and eased disease signs. It was early proof that inducing autophagy could be a treatment strategy for this kind of brain disease.

highlights.RAV2004: First author: blocking mTOR induced autophagy, cleared mutant huntingtin and reduced toxicity in fly and mouse models of Huntington disease.
highlights.BER2006: Co-author: rapamycin-induced autophagy cleared several polyglutamine and polyalanine proteins in cells and reduced tau toxicity in flies.

Selman C.lab_name: School of Molecular Biosciences, University of Glasgow (Glasgow, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Selman C.role: Biogerontologist who studies how diet and nutrient-sensing pathways such as insulin/IGF-1 and mTOR set the pace of ageing
Selman C.sub: Professor of Biogerontology · Head of School of Molecular Biosciences · University of Glasgow
story: Colin Selman is Professor of Biogerontology and Head of the School of Molecular Biosciences at the University of Glasgow. His research covers ageing, dietary restriction, insulin/IGF-1 and mTOR signalling, mitochondria and frailty.

He studied zoology at Glasgow and earned his PhD at Durham University on how a migrating shorebird changes its metabolism. Postdoctoral work in Aberdeen, at the University of Florida and at Imperial College and UCL moved him towards metabolism and ageing. He lectured at Aberdeen from 2007 and returned to Glasgow as professor in 2013.

In the Atlas he is first author of SEL2009 in Science. Mice lacking S6K1, a kinase directly downstream of mTORC1, lived longer and stayed healthier in old age. The lifespan gain (about 19% median) was clear in females but not significant in males.

highlights.SEL2009: First author: deleting S6K1 extended median lifespan in female mice (not significant in males) and protected against age-related decline (mice).

Bjedov I.lab_name: UCL Cancer Institute, University College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Bjedov I.role: Studies DNA repair and protein synthesis in ageing; showed that rapamycin extends lifespan in fruit flies
Bjedov I.sub: CRUK Senior Cancer Research Fellow · UCL Cancer Institute
story: Ivana Bjedov leads a laboratory at the UCL Cancer Institute in London that studies DNA repair and protein synthesis. She is a Cancer Research UK Senior Cancer Research Fellow.

She studied molecular biology at the University of Zagreb and earned her PhD in Paris with Miroslav Radman, working on DNA repair in bacteria. As an EMBO postdoctoral fellow with Linda Partridge at UCL she studied how rapamycin improves health and lifespan in flies. She set up her own group at UCL after winning an ERC Starting Grant.

In the Atlas she is first author of BJE2010 in Cell Metabolism. Adult fruit flies fed rapamycin lived longer, and the effect worked through mTORC1 by changing both autophagy and protein synthesis. Rapamycin still extended life in flies already on a lifespan-maximising diet, which points to more than one mechanism.

highlights.BJE2010: First author: rapamycin extended fly lifespan via TORC1, autophagy and translation, even on top of dietary restriction (Drosophila).

Findlay GM.lab_name: MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Findlay GM.role: Uses pluripotent stem cells to study how faulty signalling by protein kinases causes intellectual disability
Findlay GM.sub: Principal Investigator, MRC PPU · Senior Lecturer · University of Dundee · Sir Henry Dale Fellow
story: Greg Findlay is a Principal Investigator at the MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit at the University of Dundee. His group, set up in 2014, uses pluripotent stem cells to study understudied protein kinases and to learn how faulty signalling causes intellectual disability. He is a Wellcome Trust/Royal Society Sir Henry Dale Fellow.

He studied biochemistry at Dundee and did his PhD at the Institute of Cancer Research in London with Richard Lamb, looking for new parts of the mTOR pathway. He then worked as a postdoc with Tony Pawson in Toronto on protein complexes in stem cells.

In the Atlas he is a co-author of HAR2004 from his PhD lab. That study showed that when TSC1-2 is lost, S6K1 stays active and shuts down IRS-1, cutting the cell's response to insulin. This is one of the papers that placed mTORC1's main negative feedback loop.

highlights.HAR2004: Co-author: loss of TSC1-2 keeps S6K1 active, which suppresses IRS-1 and blunts insulin-PI3K signalling (cells).

Findlay GM.credit: Portrait: MRC PPU, University of Dundee

Harrington LS.lab_name: Cancer Research UK Centre for Cell and Molecular Biology, Institute of Cancer Research, at the time of the study (London, England, United Kingdom)
Harrington LS.role: First author of the 2004 study showing that TSC1-2 loss blunts insulin signalling through S6K1-driven feedback on IRS proteins
story: Laura Harrington did this work in Richard Lamb's laboratory at the Cancer Research UK Centre for Cell and Molecular Biology, Institute of Cancer Research, London, the affiliation PubMed gives for the study. The Atlas has no other sourced details of her career, so this profile covers only that paper.

In the Atlas she is first author of HAR2004 in the Journal of Cell Biology. Cells without TSC1-2 keep S6K1 switched on, and S6K1 then shuts down IRS-1, both by lowering its gene expression and by phosphorylating it directly. The result is a weak insulin-PI3K response. The authors suggested this may explain why tumours caused by TSC loss rarely become malignant.

highlights.HAR2004: First author: TSC1-2 loss keeps S6K1 active, which represses and phosphorylates IRS-1 and blunts insulin-PI3K signalling (cells).

Lamb RF.lab_name: School of Health Sciences, Liverpool Hope University (Liverpool, England, United Kingdom)
Lamb RF.role: Studied how amino acids and growth signals reach mTOR, including the IRS feedback loop and nutrient signalling through MAP4K3
Lamb RF.sub: Institute of Cancer Research, London (2004) · University of Alberta (2010) · University of Liverpool (2013) · Liverpool Hope University (2017)
story: Richard Lamb led the laboratory at the Institute of Cancer Research in London where HAR2004 was done, and Greg Findlay's PhD on new components of the mTOR pathway was carried out under his supervision. By 2010 he was at the University of Alberta, where his group reported that amino acids reach mTOR partly through the kinase MAP4K3, which is held in check by the phosphatase PP2A-T61ε.

In the Atlas he is senior author of HAR2004, which showed that loss of TSC1-2 keeps S6K1 active and that S6K1 then shuts down IRS-1, weakening the cell's insulin-PI3K response. This negative feedback loop is one reason that drugs blocking mTORC1 can end up switching Akt back on.

highlights.HAR2004: Senior author: TSC1-2 loss drives S6K1-mediated suppression of IRS-1, establishing mTORC1 negative feedback onto insulin-PI3K signalling (cells).

Hong J.lab_name: Departments of Surgery and Molecular and Systems Biology, Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth (Hanover, New Hampshire, USA)
Hong J.role: Neurosurgeon-scientist who studies peripheral nerve regeneration and epilepsy
Hong J.sub: Associate Professor of Surgery and of Molecular and Systems Biology · Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth
story: Jennifer Hong is Associate Professor of Surgery and of Molecular and Systems Biology at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth. She is a practising stereotactic and functional neurosurgeon and runs a translational research programme on peripheral nerve regeneration and epilepsy.

In the Atlas she is senior author of EVA2026. In mouse sensory neurons lacking PTEN, the team deleted either raptor (to block mTORC1) or rictor (to block mTORC2). Only blocking mTORC2 brought the faster microtubule growth back to normal, so the signal from PTEN loss to the cytoskeleton runs through mTORC2, not mTORC1.

highlights.EVA2026: Senior author: in PTEN-null sensory neurons, mTORC2 rather than mTORC1 drives faster microtubule polymerisation (mouse neurons).

Ji Y.lab_name: Division of Oncology, Department of Pediatric Surgery, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Ji Y.role: Paediatric surgeon whose team studies sirolimus treatment of kaposiform hemangioendothelioma in children
Ji Y.sub: Department of Pediatric Surgery · West China Hospital, Sichuan University
story: Yi Ji works in the Department of Pediatric Surgery at West China Hospital, Sichuan University, in Chengdu. A 2022 hospital news item lists him as Associate Professor and describes his team's work on sirolimus-based treatment of kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE), a rare vascular tumour of children, including a Blood paper on sirolimus plus steroids for KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.

In the Atlas he is senior author of XU2026. In 71 children with KHE but without the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, sirolimus alone gave a 100% radiological response at 12 months for head and neck lesions, against 76% for lesions elsewhere.

highlights.XU2026: Senior author: sirolimus monotherapy gave 100% 12-month response in head and neck KHE versus 76% elsewhere (n=71 children).

Säemann MD.lab_name: Chair of Nephrology, Sigmund Freud University Vienna (Vienna, Austria)
Säemann MD.role: Nephrologist who showed that the TSC-mTOR pathway controls the innate inflammatory response
Säemann MD.sub: Professor and Chair of Nephrology · Sigmund Freud University Vienna
story: Marcus Säemann has held the Chair of Nephrology at Sigmund Freud University in Vienna since 2017. His research interests include the renin-angiotensin system, HDL in kidney failure and diabetes after transplantation. At the time of the Atlas study he was in the Clinical Division of Nephrology and Dialysis at the Medical University of Vienna.

In the Atlas he is senior author of WEI2008 in Immunity. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin, or removing TSC2, changed how monocytes and macrophages respond to bacteria: blocking mTOR boosted inflammatory messengers through NF-κB and cut the calming messenger IL-10, while losing TSC2 did the opposite. This showed that the TSC-mTOR pathway is a regulator of innate immunity, not only of cell growth.

highlights.WEI2008: Senior author: the TSC-mTOR pathway regulates the inflammatory response of monocytes and macrophages (mouse and human cells).
