Johnson CM.sub: Head of the Biophysics Facility, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (2009–2022, semi-retired since) · MRC Centre for Protein Engineering, Cambridge (from 1992) · postdoc, University of Glasgow · PhD in protein folding, Department of Biochemistry at a Scottish university
story: Christopher Johnson is a co-author of two structural papers in the Atlas from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge. BAR2016 used cryo-electron microscopy to show that the Tor kinase, bound to its partner Lst8, pairs up into a dimer through a long coiled stretch of helices at its front end. ANA2019 solved structures of the human Rag GTPases, the switch proteins that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome when amino acids are present, and showed how they bind mTORC1. Pictures from microscopes and crystals are usually checked with solution measurements, for example of how tightly two proteins bind or whether a complex stays together in liquid, and that is the kind of work a biophysics facility provides.

Johnson studied biology, then did a PhD on protein folding in a biochemistry department in Scotland and a postdoc at the University of Glasgow on protein thermodynamics and calorimetry, the measurement of the heat released or absorbed when molecules bind. From 1992 he worked at the MRC Centre for Protein Engineering in Cambridge. When that centre closed he joined the LMB in 2009 as head of its new Biophysics Facility, which came to serve more than 50 research groups with calorimetry, spectroscopy and kinetic methods. He also built and adapted instruments with the LMB workshop.
In 2022 Stephen McLaughlin became head of the facility, and the LMB described Johnson as semi-retired and still supporting the team part-time with training.

highlights.BAR2016: Co-author of the cryo-EM study showing that Tor forms a dimer through a long helical region at its N-terminus.
highlights.ANA2019: Co-author of the structural study of the human Rag GTPases and their complex with mTORC1.

Ancel S.lab_name: Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Ancel S.role: Muscle stem-cell biologist at Sanford Burnham Prebys, trained at Nestle Research and EPFL in Lausanne, who studies why muscle repair fails with age
Ancel S.sub: Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (2025–2026) · Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology, Stanford University, with Helen Blau (2021) · Nestle Research and School of Life Sciences, EPFL, Lausanne, with Jerome Feige (2019–2024)
story: Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. It makes falls and frailty more likely, and no drug is approved for it. In a 2026 review in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, with Helen Blau as senior author, Sara Ancel and colleagues survey the drug strategies now being tested. Among them are mTORC1 inhibitors, which may help because aging muscle has too little autophagy, the cell's clean-up system, and lowering mTORC1 activity can restore it. The review sets this against other approaches such as NAD-boosting molecules, urolithin A, myostatin blockers, drugs that mimic male hormones in muscle and blockers of the enzyme 15-PGDH. A review collects earlier work; it does not test these drugs itself.

Ancel trained in Lausanne, Switzerland, at Nestle Research and the School of Life Sciences of EPFL in Jerome Feige's group. There, Ancel was first author of a 2019 study showing that fat-forming progenitor cells in muscle help keep muscle stem cells young, and co-author of a 2019 Cell Stem Cell paper showing that aging disrupts muscle stem cells by reducing the protein WISP1 made by these neighbouring cells. In 2024, Ancel was first author of a study describing a two-colour reporter mouse for tracking different kinds of muscle stem cells in repair and aging.

Ancel co-authored a 2021 study from Helen Blau's lab at Stanford on heart muscle cells in muscular dystrophy, and now works at the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases of Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla. Ancel's exact position title could not be confirmed.

highlights.ANC2026: First author of the review of emerging drug treatments for sarcopenia, including mTORC1 inhibitors that restore autophagy in aging muscle.

Araki K.lab_name: Department of Microbiology and Immunology and Emory Vaccine Center, Emory University (Atlanta, Georgia, USA)
Araki K.role: Immunologist in Rafi Ahmed's group at Emory who discovered that rapamycin improves memory killer T cells, a finding that linked mTOR to vaccine design
Araki K.sub: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Emory University (papers to 2026) · Emory Vaccine Center, Rafi Ahmed lab (2009)
story: After an infection, most killer CD8 T cells die off, but a few become long-lived memory cells that guard against the same germ in future. Koichi Araki is first author of a 2009 paper from Rafi Ahmed's lab at the Emory Vaccine Center that found mTOR helps decide this fate (ARA2009). In mice infected with a virus, low doses of rapamycin, an mTOR blocker best known as a drug that suppresses the immune system, actually increased the number and quality of memory CD8 T cells. Blocking mTOR inside the T cells themselves had the same effect, and rapamycin also improved T cell memory after vaccination in monkeys. The result changed how immunologists think about mTOR: besides acting as a growth switch, it is a decision point between short-lived effector cells and long-lived memory cells.

Araki has continued at Emory's Department of Microbiology and Immunology. A 2026 study, with Araki as a co-author, tested the idea in an HIV-like vaccine model: rhesus macaques given rapamycin during booster shots of an SIV vaccine had more and better memory CD8 T cells, lower virus levels in the gut and blood after infection, and longer survival. The current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.ARA2009: First author: showed that mTOR regulates memory CD8 T-cell differentiation and that rapamycin enhances memory responses after infection and vaccination.

Baar EL.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Baar EL.role: Researcher in Dudley Lamming's group at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who mapped how mTOR signalling changes with age in different mouse tissues and helped test gentler rapamycin dosing schedules
Baar EL.credit: Portrait: Lamming Lab, University of Wisconsin-Madison
Baar EL.sub: Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison, and William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital (Lamming lab, papers 2014–2020, at the time of the study)
story: Emma Baar is a co-author of two linked mouse studies from Dudley Lamming's lab in this Atlas (ARR2015, ARR2016). Rapamycin is the best-tested drug for extending lifespan in mice, but given every day it causes side effects such as poor blood sugar control and weaker immune responses. In ARR2015, mice given rapamycin daily (2 mg/kg) became glucose intolerant and their insulin-producing islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every five days left glucose and insulin tolerance normal, while dosing every three days was already too frequent. In ARR2016, female mice that started the every-five-days schedule at 20 months of age, which is old for a mouse, lived longer than untreated females. Taken together, the two mouse studies suggest that rapamycin's lifespan benefit can be partly separated from its side effects by giving it intermittently. This conclusion comes from combining two experiments in mice, not from a single study, and has not been tested this way in people.

Baar was first author of a 2015 Aging Cell paper that measured mTOR signalling in several tissues of male and female mice at different ages and found that the changes with age differ by sex and by tissue. As a member of the Lamming group, Baar also co-authored work showing that losing Rictor, a core part of the second mTOR complex mTORC2, shortens the life of male mice (2014), that eating fewer branched-chain amino acids improves metabolic health (2016), that a new rapamycin-like drug can block mTORC1 selectively in animals (2019), and that the better insulin sensitivity seen with calorie restriction depends on mTORC2 in fat tissue (2019).
The most recent paper in PubMed with Baar's name is from 2020. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.ARR2015: Co-author: helped show that rapamycin given once every five days avoids the glucose intolerance seen with daily dosing in mice.
highlights.ARR2016: Co-author: helped show that the same every-five-days schedule, started at 20 months of age, extended the lifespan of female mice.

Cummings NE.role: Graduate researcher in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and first author of a 2017 study reporting that eating fewer branched-chain amino acids restores metabolic health
Cummings NE.credit: Portrait: Lamming Lab, University of Wisconsin-Madison
Cummings NE.sub: Endocrinology and Reproductive Physiology Graduate Training Program and Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Lamming lab, papers 2015–2019, at the time of the study)

Aware C.lab_name: Lin Lab, Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health, University of Missouri (Columbia, Missouri, USA)
Aware C.role: Researcher in Ai-Ling Lin's group at the University of Missouri who studies how rapamycin and the gut microbiome affect brain blood flow and metabolism in people and mice at genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease
Aware C.sub: Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health, University of Missouri (Ai-Ling Lin lab, papers 2024–2026)
story: APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Carriers often show lower blood flow and weaker energy use in the brain years before any memory problems. In the Atlas study AWARE2026, Chetan Aware was first author of a small pilot trial at the University of Missouri. Twenty-three cognitively normal adults aged 45 to 65 took 1 mg of rapamycin a day for four weeks. In the nine APOE4 carriers, blood flow in several brain regions rose by more than 15%, while non-carriers showed no clear change. Blood markers of metabolism and inflammation improved, and the gut microbiome shifted. There was no placebo group and very few participants, so this is early evidence that needs a controlled trial.

Aware works in Ai-Ling Lin's group in the Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health at the University of Missouri. The group had earlier shown in mice carrying human APOE4 that 16 weeks of rapamycin improved mitochondrial function and nerve-cell signalling in the brain, with different effects in APOE3 mice; Aware was a co-author of that 2024 study. In 2026 Aware was first author of a mouse study in which gut bacteria taken from stroke patients sped up tau changes and brain inflammation in Alzheimer's model mice, pointing to the gut-brain connection as a possible link between stroke and later dementia. No official profile page was found.

highlights.AWARE2026: First author: ran the pilot trial in which four weeks of low-dose rapamycin raised brain blood flow in APOE4 carriers aged 45 to 65.

Aylett CH.lab_name: Aylett Group, Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology, Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Aylett CH.role: Structural biologist who solved the first cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1 at ETH Zurich and now leads a cryo-EM group at Imperial College London
Aylett CH.sub: Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology, Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London (papers 2020–2026) · Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2015–2018) · MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (2012 paper with Jan Löwe)
story: Christopher Aylett is first author of AYL2015, the first detailed 3D architecture of human mTORC1, made by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The structure showed that mTORC1 is a dimer, two copies of mTOR, Raptor and mLST8 joined into a lozenge-shaped complex with the two kinase active sites sitting in deep clefts. That arrangement explains how the complex limits which proteins can reach the active site, and how the drug pair rapamycin-FKBP12 narrows the entrance further. Aylett is also a co-author of STU2018, the matching architecture of the mTORC2 core.

Aylett's earlier work, at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge with Jan Löwe, was on bacterial proteins that push plasmids apart before cell division; a 2012 paper there described a DNA-protein filament at the heart of the TubZRC system. The mTOR structures came from a period at the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics of ETH Zurich, working with Nenad Ban and Timm Maier.

Since about 2020 Aylett has led a group in the Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology of the Department of Infectious Disease at Imperial College London. The lab uses cryo-EM on large molecular machines, including the unusual RNA polymerase of the giant bacteriophage PhiKZ, a virus being explored as a treatment for Pseudomonas infections (2026), and develops simpler ways to prepare cryo-EM samples, such as a 3D-printed tool for moving fragile carbon and graphene support films.

highlights.AYL2015: First author: determined the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1, a dimer with recessed active sites.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Boehringer D.lab_name: Cryo-EM Knowledge Hub, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Boehringer D.role: Electron microscopy specialist at ETH Zurich whose cryo-EM work underpins the Atlas structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2
Boehringer D.sub: Cryo-EM Knowledge Hub (CEMK), ETH Zurich (papers since 2020) · Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2015–2019)
story: Daniel Boehringer is a co-author on all three Atlas papers that showed the shapes of the two mTOR complexes: the first architecture of human mTORC1 (AYL2015), the architecture of the human mTORC2 core (STU2018), and the 3.2-angstrom structure of mTORC2 (SCA2020). These papers relied on cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM): protein complexes are frozen in a thin layer of ice and imaged many thousands of times, and a computer combines the images into a 3D map. Together they explain why mTORC1 is a two-part dimer with its active sites hidden in clefts, and why mTORC2 ignores rapamycin.

The publication record shows Boehringer as a regular cryo-EM contributor to structural projects at ETH Zurich, many with Nenad Ban's group on ribosomes and their assembly. Since about 2020 the papers list the Cryo-EM Knowledge Hub of ETH Zurich, a shared facility, and include method work such as a 2020 study with Christopher Aylett's Imperial College group on transferring fragile support films for cryo-EM samples. No personal web page was opened, so the exact current title is not confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: contributed electron microscopy to the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author: contributed to the 3.2-angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2.

Imseng S.lab_name: Maier Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Imseng S.role: Structural biologist from Timm Maier's group at the Biozentrum Basel who helped solve the first detailed structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2 and then worked on a drug to block mTORC1 specifically
Imseng S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation 2013–2021, at the time of the studies) · PhD, University of Basel (2016, thesis on the structure of mTORC1, advisors Timm Maier and Tilman Schirmer)
story: To see how a protein machine works, structural biologists try to see its shape. Stefan Imseng is a co-author of three Atlas studies that did this for the two mTOR complexes using cryo-electron microscopy, which photographs frozen protein molecules and combines thousands of images into a 3D model. The 2015 Science paper (AYL2015) showed the architecture of human mTORC1, the growth-control complex: two copies of mTOR and its partners form a diamond-shaped dimer, and the structure showed how rapamycin bound to its helper protein FKBP12 narrows the entrance to the active site. The 2018 eLife paper (STU2018) did the same for the core of mTORC2, and the 2020 Science Advances paper (SCA2020) sharpened that picture to 3.2 angstroms, showing that the end of the partner protein Rictor covers the spot where rapamycin would bind. That explains why mTORC2 resists rapamycin.

Imseng did doctoral work in Timm Maier's structural biology group at the Biozentrum. The 2016 thesis, supervised by Maier and Tilman Schirmer, was titled 'Structural studies on the target of rapamycin complex 1'. Imseng was first author of a 2018 review on the architecture and activation of the PI3K-related kinase family to which mTOR belongs, and a co-author of later Basel studies on how DEPTOR regulates both mTOR complexes (2021) and on how mTORC1 recognises its substrate 4E-BP1 (2021).

In 2018 the Biozentrum announced an Innosuisse-funded project in which Imseng and Asier Gonzalez, supported by Timm Maier and Michael Hall, set out to develop a lead compound that blocks mTORC1 specifically, as a possible drug for tuberous sclerosis. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: part of the team that solved the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1, including its complex with FKBP12-rapamycin.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the first architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author: contributed to the 3.2 angstrom structure of human mTORC2 that pinpoints Rictor as the cause of its rapamycin insensitivity.

Sauer E.role: Structural biologist at the Biozentrum Basel who worked on the structure of the mTOR kinase and contributed to the cryo-EM structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2
Sauer E.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation 2013–2018, at the time of the studies)
story: Evelyn Sauer is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Basel that used cryo-electron microscopy to show the shape of the mTOR complexes. The 2015 Science paper (AYL2015) gave the first detailed architecture of human mTORC1, the growth-control complex, including how rapamycin bound to its helper protein FKBP12 narrows access to the active site. The 2018 eLife paper (STU2018) did the same for the core of mTORC2, made of mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8, and helped explain why mTORC2 resists rapamycin.

Sauer was first author, with Stefan Imseng, Timm Maier and Michael Hall, of a 2013 review in Biochemical Society Transactions on the conserved sequence motifs and structure of the mTOR kinase domain, the part of the enzyme that transfers phosphate groups. Earlier Basel work by Sauer was in protein crystallography: a 2013 single-author paper on the structure and RNA binding of the bacterial protein Hfq, and a 2014 study of the cell-death regulator BCL-W solved with designed binding proteins.
PubMed lists Sauer at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel on all of these papers. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: contributed to the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Babygirija R.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Babygirija R.role: Researcher in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how restricting single amino acids in the diet affects metabolism, memory and Alzheimer's disease in mice
Babygirija R.sub: Graduate Program in Cellular and Molecular Biology and Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Lamming lab, papers from 2022) · earlier: Department of Surgery and Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Medical College of Wisconsin, and Aurora Research Institute, Milwaukee (papers 2012–2021)
story: Reji Babygirija was first author of a 2026 Advanced Science paper in this Atlas (BAB2025), first posted as a preprint. Branched-chain amino acids, leucine, isoleucine and valine, are building blocks of protein, and they act differently on mTORC1, the growth-control complex: leucine is a strong activator. The study restricted each of the three separately in 3xTg mice, a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The effects on memory and Alzheimer's-type brain changes were distinct for each amino acid and differed between males and females. Cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. The results come from mice and point to diet composition, not just total protein, as something that matters.

Before joining Lamming's group, Babygirija worked at the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. As first author of a 2012 Brain Research paper from Takahashi's group in the Department of Surgery, Babygirija showed in rats that social interaction softened stress responses after chronic stress in animals separated from their mothers early in life. Later papers from Milwaukee covered visceral pain after bladder inflammation in young rats (2017), irritable bowel symptoms in inflammatory bowel disease (2019) and electro-acupuncture against chronic stress (2021).

At the University of Wisconsin-Madison, in the graduate program in cellular and molecular biology, Babygirija has co-authored many of the Lamming lab's diet studies, including a 2022 Cell Metabolism paper showing that sex and genetic background shape how mice respond to protein restriction. PubMed lists more than 60 papers with the name.

highlights.BAB2025: First author: restricted each branched-chain amino acid separately in Alzheimer's model mice and found distinct, sex-specific effects, with isoleucine and valine restriction improving metabolic health.

Knopf BA.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Knopf BA.role: Graduate student in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and first author of a 2026 review that sets out the hallmarks of protein and amino acid restriction in aging
Knopf BA.credit: Portrait: University of Wisconsin-Madison (Cellular and Molecular Biology Graduate Program)
Knopf BA.sub: Graduate student, Cellular and Molecular Biology program, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Lamming lab, Department of Medicine and William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital, papers from 2025) · BS in Cell and Developmental Biology, University of Iowa
story: Bailey Knopf was first author of a 2026 review in Cell Press Blue (KNO2026) that asks what eating less protein does to an aging body. Across many organisms, cutting dietary protein, or only certain essential amino acids such as methionine, isoleucine and valine, improves metabolic health and can lengthen healthy life and lifespan. The review argues that the make-up of the protein, which amino acids it contains, matters as much as the amount, and that much of the effect runs through nutrient-sensing pathways, including mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Most of the evidence it summarises comes from animals.

Knopf is also a co-author of the Lamming lab's 2026 study on restricting single branched-chain amino acids in Alzheimer's model mice (BAB2025), in which cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. PubMed lists about a dozen papers with Knopf's name since 2025, all from Lamming's group, including a 2025 preprint showing that the body's production of ketone bodies is not needed for the metabolic changes caused by calorie restriction in mice. Knopf studied cell and developmental biology at the University of Iowa (BS) and is now a graduate student in the Cellular and Molecular Biology program at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, doing doctoral research in the Lamming lab.

highlights.KNO2026: First author of this review defining the hallmarks of protein and amino acid restriction in aging.
highlights.BAB2025: Co-author of the study restricting single branched-chain amino acids in Alzheimer's model mice.

Banerjee C.lab_name: Division of Neuroscience, Department of Pharmacology, ISF College of Pharmacy (Moga, Punjab, India)
Banerjee C.role: Pharmacology researcher at ISF College of Pharmacy in Punjab who writes reviews on signalling pathways and repurposed drugs for multiple sclerosis and other brain diseases
Banerjee C.sub: Division of Neuroscience, Department of Pharmacology, ISF College of Pharmacy, affiliated to IK Gujral Punjab Technical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the immune system attacks myelin, the fatty insulation around nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord. Chandrayee Banerjee is first author of a 2026 review on how two signalling systems talk to each other in MS (BANERJEE2026). One is the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which controls growth and metabolism in immune cells and in the oligodendrocytes that make myelin. The other is JAK/STAT, which carries signals from inflammatory messengers into the cell nucleus. The review argues that the two pathways reinforce each other in driving Th17 inflammatory T cells and microglia, the brain's immune cells, and that mTOR has two faces in MS: it helps oligodendrocytes mature and rebuild myelin, but too much of it feeds damage. It is a review of earlier studies, not new experiments, and drugs that hit both pathways at once have not been tested in people with MS.

PubMed lists three 2026 papers with Banerjee, all from Sidharth Mehan's neuroscience group in the Department of Pharmacology at ISF College of Pharmacy in Moga. The other two are reviews on repurposing older drugs for brain disease: the antihistamine clemastine as a promoter of myelin repair, and the osteoporosis drug raloxifene as a possible neuroprotective agent. No institutional profile page was found, so the position shown is the one on these papers.

highlights.BANERJEE2026: First author of the review mapping crosstalk between PI3K/Akt/mTOR and JAK/STAT signalling in multiple sclerosis.

Tongra M.role: Chief Scientific Officer of Celagenex Research in Mumbai, senior author of reviews and animal studies that link the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway to brain and immune disorders
Tongra M.sub: Chief Scientific Officer, Celagenex Research, Thane, Mumbai (2026)
story: Multiple sclerosis is a disease in which the immune system attacks the fatty myelin sheath around nerve fibres. In a 2026 review in Immunologic Research, with Manoj Tongra as senior author, the authors map how two signalling routes interact in this disease: the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which steers cell growth and the activity of immune cells, and the JAK/STAT pathway, which carries signals from inflammatory messengers called cytokines. They argue that drugs acting on both routes could reduce immune damage and loss of myelin. A review collects and interprets earlier work; it does not test this idea.

PubMed lists Tongra as Chief Scientific Officer of Celagenex Research in Thane, Mumbai. All of Tongra's papers found on PubMed date from 2026. They include reviews on how muscarinic and histamine receptor signals converge on PI3K/Akt/mTOR, on pentadecanoic acid as a possible mTOR modulator in age-related female infertility, and on growth-factor and immune signalling in autism, as well as rodent studies testing sulforaphane, a compound from broccoli, in models of multiple sclerosis-like and ALS-like nerve damage. Earlier training and career details could not be confirmed.

highlights.BANERJEE2026: Senior author of the review on crosstalk between PI3K/Akt/mTOR and JAK/STAT signalling in multiple sclerosis.

Baretic D.lab_name: Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Baretic D.role: Structural biologist who, while at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, solved early cryo-EM structures of Tor and its relatives, and now works on ADP-ribosylation enzymes at Oxford
Baretic D.sub: Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, University of Oxford (papers since 2024) · MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (Roger Williams group, then Joseph Yeeles group, papers 2014–2020)
story: mTOR is a huge protein, and for years nobody knew what its long front section looked like. Domagoj Baretić's 2016 paper in Nature Communications (BAR2016), from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, used cryo-electron microscopy, a method that images frozen protein particles and combines thousands of pictures into a 3D model. Working with Tor bound to its partner protein Lst8, the team found that Tor pairs up into a dimer, and that its N-terminal region forms a long solenoid of stacked helices with an unusually complex fold. This helped explain the overall shape of mTORC1, which is also built as a dimer.

Baretić had earlier co-written a 2014 review with Williams on the structural basis of mTOR function, and in 2019 was first author of a review on the related DNA-damage sensors DNA-PKcs, ATM and ATR, which share mTOR's kinase design. A 2020 Molecular Cell paper, from Joseph Yeeles' group at the LMB, then showed by cryo-EM how the fork protection complex sits on the DNA replication machinery.

Since 2024 Baretić has published from the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology at the University of Oxford, in structural work with Ivan Ahel's and Marcin Suskiewicz's groups on enzymes that attach ADP-ribose to proteins. This includes a 2025 Nature Structural and Molecular Biology paper, as first author, on filament formation by the unusual human sirtuins FAM118, and contributions on PARP enzymes in the interferon response and in cancer drug action.

highlights.BAR2016: First author: solved the cryo-EM structure showing that Tor dimerizes through a long N-terminal helical solenoid.

Burris HA.lab_name: Sarah Cannon Research Institute (Nashville, Tennessee, USA)
Burris HA.role: Medical oncologist who led the Sarah Cannon Research Institute in Nashville as President and Chief Medical Officer, has run hundreds of early-phase cancer drug trials, including the first trial of the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552, and was ASCO President in 2019–2020
Burris HA.sub: President and Chief Medical Officer, Sarah Cannon Research Institute, Nashville (retirement from this role announced for end of 2025, advisory role after) · at Sarah Cannon since 1997 · President, American Society of Clinical Oncology (2019–2020) · earlier Director of Clinical Research, Institute for Drug Development, San Antonio · U.S. Army physician, Brooke Army Medical Center (service ended 1997)
story: Howard Burris is a co-author of two Atlas trial papers about mTOR drugs in cancer. PIC2014 is the final report of BOLERO-2, which added everolimus, a rapamycin-like mTORC1 blocker, to the hormone drug exemestane in women with advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. The combination kept the cancer in check for longer (7.8 against 3.2 months) but did not significantly lengthen overall survival. SCH2025 was the first trial in patients of RMC-5552, a newer bi-steric drug designed to block mTORC1 fully while sparing mTORC2. In 57 patients with advanced solid tumours, high blood sugar, a typical side effect of older mTOR drugs, was uncommon (4 percent). Without a comparison group, the trial is an early signal, not proof.

Burris joined the Sarah Cannon Research Institute in Nashville in 1997. It became one of the largest centres in the United States for early-phase (phase 1) cancer trials, where new drugs are first given to patients to find a safe dose. PubMed lists him with a Sarah Cannon affiliation on more than 200 trial papers, which shows how many new cancer drugs pass through this kind of centre on the way to approval.

Burris studied at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point and at the University of South Alabama College of Medicine. He served as an Army doctor, finishing his service at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio in 1997, and before that directed clinical research at the Institute for Drug Development in San Antonio. At Sarah Cannon he became Chief Medical Officer and Executive Director of the Drug Development Program, and later President and Chief Medical Officer. He was President of the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) for 2019 to 2020. In October 2025 Sarah Cannon announced that he would retire from the President and Chief Medical Officer role at the end of 2025 and stay on as an adviser.

highlights.SCH2025: Trial investigator and co-author on the first-in-human phase 1 trial of RMC-5552, a bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor.
highlights.PIC2014: Co-author of the final BOLERO-2 report, which confirmed longer progression-free survival with everolimus plus exemestane but no significant overall survival gain.

Battaglioni S.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Battaglioni S.role: Cell biologist in Michael Hall's group at the Biozentrum Basel, first author of a 2022 Cell review that catalogued the direct substrates of mTOR
Battaglioni S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall group (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024) · Institute of Biochemistry, ETH Zurich (PubMed affiliation 2020)
story: mTOR is a kinase, an enzyme that switches other proteins on or off by attaching phosphate groups to them. Which proteins it acts on decides what mTOR does in the cell. Stefania Battaglioni is first author of the 2022 Cell review in this Atlas (BAT2022), written with Michael Hall, which gathered the known direct substrates of mTOR and explained how the two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, end up acting on different targets. It is a reference map for anyone trying to trace a signal from mTOR to an effect.

Battaglioni's own lab work in the Hall group looks for new mTOR substrates. A 2024 PNAS paper, with Battaglioni as first author, showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises a protein called LST2, which in turn holds back the EGF receptor, a growth-factor receptor. A 2023 EMBO Journal study, on which Battaglioni is a co-author, found that yeast TORC1 switches off Stm1, a factor that keeps ribosomes dormant, so that protein synthesis can restart when nutrients return.

Battaglioni also contributed to a 2020 Nature Metabolism study, led from ETH Zurich, showing that the pH inside cells helps drive cell division and tumour growth by raising cyclin D1. PubMed lists Battaglioni at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel through 2024. A current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.BAT2022: First author: wrote, with Michael Hall, the Cell review that catalogues direct mTOR substrates and how mTORC1 and mTORC2 choose their targets.

B'chir W.lab_name: Vincent Giguère laboratory, Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
B'chir W.role: Metabolism researcher in Vincent Giguère's laboratory at McGill who studies how the nuclear receptor ERR-alpha controls fat handling in the liver, including the fatty liver caused by rapamycin
B'chir W.sub: Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University, Montreal (papers 2018–2026) · INRA Human Nutrition Unit and Université Clermont 1, Clermont-Ferrand, France (papers to 2013)
story: Wafa B'chir was first author of a 2026 Journal of Endocrinology study (BCH2026) on a side effect of rapamycin. Rapamycin blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and is used to prevent organ rejection. In mice it can also cause fatty liver, where fat builds up inside liver cells. The team added chloroquine, an old antimalarial drug, and found that it made the rapamycin-induced fatty liver milder. Measuring all the genes switched on in the liver showed that chloroquine undid much of rapamycin's push on fat-handling genes, and the nuclear receptor ERR-alpha, a master switch for energy metabolism, came out as a top controller. In mice lacking ERR-alpha, chloroquine no longer helped. This is a mouse study, and it does not show that the combination is safe or useful in patients.

B'chir came to this from nutrition and stress biology. In 2013, at the INRA Human Nutrition Unit in Clermont-Ferrand, France, B'chir was first author of a Nucleic Acids Research paper showing that when amino acids run out, the GCN2 and PERK stress kinases act through ATF4 and CHOP to switch on a whole set of autophagy genes. At McGill's Goodman Cancer Research Centre B'chir moved to the liver: a 2018 first-author paper in Endocrinology found that mice without ERR-alpha are protected from fatty liver on a high-fat diet but cannot clear fat from the liver normally when fed again after fasting.
B'chir has continued with the Giguère group at the Goodman Cancer Institute on work about ERR-alpha in the heart (2022) and in the progression of fatty liver to liver inflammation in mice (2023).

highlights.BCH2026: First author: showed in mice that chloroquine softens rapamycin-induced fatty liver and that this rescue needs ERR-alpha.

Bentzinger CF.lab_name: Bentzinger Lab, Department of Pharmacology-Physiology, Université de Sherbrooke (Sherbrooke, Quebec, Canada)
Bentzinger CF.role: Muscle stem cell biologist at the Université de Sherbrooke who, as a PhD student in Basel, showed that mTORC1 but not mTORC2 is essential for healthy skeletal muscle
Bentzinger CF.sub: Professor, Department of Pharmacology-Physiology, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Université de Sherbrooke, and researcher at the CRCHUS (since 2016) · Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences, Lausanne (2014–2016) · postdoc, Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (2009–2013) · PhD, Biozentrum, University of Basel (2005–2009)
story: mTOR works in two complexes. mTORC1 needs the partner protein raptor, and mTORC2 needs rictor. Florian Bentzinger was first author of the 2008 Cell Metabolism study in this Atlas (BEN2008) from Markus Ruegg's group at the Biozentrum in Basel. The team deleted raptor or rictor only in the skeletal muscle of mice. Without raptor, the muscles changed their metabolism and developed muscular dystrophy, a progressive breakdown of muscle tissue. Without rictor, the muscles stayed normal. This showed that mTORC1, not mTORC2, is the complex that muscle depends on, a result from mice that has guided later thinking about mTOR drugs and muscle.

Bentzinger did an MSc and then a PhD at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel (2005 to 2009). From 2009 to 2013 Bentzinger was a postdoc at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute in Canada, and from 2014 to 2016 worked at the Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences in Lausanne.

Since 2016 Bentzinger has been a professor in the Department of Pharmacology-Physiology at the Université de Sherbrooke and a researcher at its hospital research centre, the CRCHUS. The lab studies muscle stem cells and their niche, the surrounding tissue and extracellular matrix that tell the stem cells when to rest and when to rebuild muscle, and how these signals fail in aging and muscular dystrophy. The group has also developed a protocol for making muscle stem cells from induced pluripotent stem cells.

highlights.BEN2008: First author: showed in mice that losing raptor, not rictor, in skeletal muscle causes metabolic changes and muscular dystrophy.

Howell JJ.role: Metabolism biologist who, as a postdoc in Brendan Manning's lab at Harvard, worked out how the diabetes drug metformin switches off mTORC1 in the liver, and who later moved into drug and gene-therapy research in industry
Howell JJ.sub: Lead (Principal) Scientist and Project Manager, Spark Therapeutics (per Manning lab alumni page) · scientist, Navitor Pharmaceuticals, Cambridge, Massachusetts (2019 paper) · postdoctoral fellow, Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2010–2016) · Markus Stoffel's group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (papers 2008–2009)
story: Metformin is the most widely prescribed diabetes drug and is also tested as a possible anti-aging medicine, yet how it acts inside cells has long been debated. In HOW2017, Jessica Howell, working in Brendan Manning's lab, asked how metformin reaches mTORC1, the growth-control complex that tells cells when to build proteins and fats. In mouse liver and in liver cells the study found that metformin lowers the cell's energy supply and that, at lower doses, this shuts down mTORC1 through two known brakes: the energy sensor AMPK and the TSC complex. At higher doses other routes come into play. The study is a direct mechanistic link between a common drug, cellular energy sensing and the mTOR pathway, though it was done in mice and cultured cells, not in people.

Howell's earlier research was on how insulin controls the liver. In Markus Stoffel's group at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich, Howell studied the transcription factor Foxa2 and showed in 2009 that insulin turns it off by phosphorylation rather than by moving it out of the nucleus. Howell joined the Manning lab in 2010, co-wrote reviews on how mTOR links nutrient sensing to whole-body metabolism and drives the building of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, and contributed to the finding that chronic mTORC1 activation in mouse liver is enough to cause liver cancer.

After the Manning lab Howell worked at Navitor Pharmaceuticals in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on a 2019 study that found small molecules which selectively block mTORC1 by inhibiting glucose transporters. The Manning lab alumni page lists the current position as Lead (Principal) Scientist and Project Manager at Spark Therapeutics, a gene-therapy company.

highlights.HOW2017: First author: showed in mouse liver and liver cells that metformin lowers cell energy and, at low doses, inhibits mTORC1 through AMPK and the TSC complex.

Berger Z.lab_name: Rubinsztein Lab, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, University of Cambridge (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Berger Z.role: Neuroscientist who, in David Rubinsztein's lab in Cambridge, showed that rapamycin-induced autophagy lowers the toxicity of several disease proteins that form clumps, including tau in fruit flies
Berger Z.sub: Department of Medical Genetics, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, Addenbrooke's Hospital, University of Cambridge (at the time of the study, 2006)
story: Several brain diseases, including Huntington's disease and some dementias, are caused by proteins that misfold and clump together. Autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, can remove such clumps, and rapamycin switches autophagy on by blocking mTOR. In BER2006, Zdenek Berger, working in David Rubinsztein's lab in Cambridge, extended the group's earlier huntingtin work. In cultured cells, rapamycin increased the clearance of several proteins with long stretches of the amino acid glutamine, and of a protein with an extended alanine stretch, and reduced their toxicity. In fruit flies carrying normal or mutant human tau, rapamycin lowered tau toxicity and the amount of insoluble tau. The authors proposed that inducing autophagy might help in a range of clumping-protein diseases. The evidence comes from cells and flies only, with no data in mammals or people.

PubMed lists about 14 papers under this name on huntingtin, tau, LRRK2 and alpha-synuclein, the proteins behind Huntington's, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.BER2006: First author: showed that rapamycin speeds the clearance and lowers the toxicity of several aggregate-prone proteins in cells, and of tau in flies.

de Vries PJ.role: Child and adolescent psychiatrist at the University of Cape Town known for work on TAND, the behavioural, learning and mental-health problems of tuberous sclerosis complex, and co-author of major everolimus trials in TSC
de Vries PJ.sub: Sue Struengmann Professor of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Cape Town · Founding Director, Centre for Autism Research in Africa · President, International Society for Autism Research · earlier clinical and research career in the United Kingdom (PhD, University of Cambridge)
story: Petrus de Vries appears in this Atlas on two trials of everolimus, an mTOR blocker, in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), the genetic disease in which mTORC1 runs unchecked. EXIST-3 (FRE2016) was a large phase 3 trial in 366 children and adults whose focal seizures had not responded to standard drugs. Adding everolimus at a higher blood level halved seizure frequency in 40% of patients, against 15% on placebo, and it became the basis for approving the drug for TSC epilepsy. TRON (SAX2026) asked a harder question in adults: does everolimus improve memory and thinking? Both everolimus and placebo groups improved, so the trial found no clear drug effect on cognition.

de Vries studied medicine at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, then trained in psychiatry and in child and adolescent psychiatry in the United Kingdom and earned a PhD in developmental neuroscience at the University of Cambridge. Work on TSC began in 1997, with a focus on its behavioural, intellectual, psychiatric and learning problems, now grouped under the name TSC-Associated Neuropsychiatric Disorders (TAND), on which de Vries has led international consensus recommendations.

In 2012 de Vries returned to South Africa as the Sue Struengmann Professor of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at the University of Cape Town and became founding director of the Centre for Autism Research in Africa. Current work covers autism and child mental health in low- and middle-income settings, alongside the TSC programme. In 2014 de Vries received the Manuel R Gomez Award from the TSC community.

highlights.FRE2016: Co-author of EXIST-3, the phase 3 trial showing that adjunctive everolimus reduces treatment-resistant seizures in TSC.
highlights.SAX2026: Co-author of the TRON trial report, which found no clear benefit of everolimus over placebo for neuropsychological deficits in TSC.

Glass DJ.role: Muscle biologist and Regeneron vice president for ageing research, member of the US National Academy of Sciences, who helped discover the muscle-wasting enzymes MuRF1 and MAFbx and co-authored the first trials of low-dose mTOR inhibition in older people
Glass DJ.sub: Vice President, Aging/Age-Related Disorders, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (since 2019) · Senior Lecturer in Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School · head of the musculoskeletal programme, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research · Regeneron (about 15 years, earlier) · postdoc with Charles Cantor and Stephen Goff, Columbia University · MD, New York Medical College
story: David Glass is a co-author of two Atlas trials from the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research that asked whether a short course of a low-dose mTOR inhibitor can help the ageing immune system. In MAN2014, older volunteers took everolimus (RAD001), a rapamycin-like drug, for six weeks before a flu shot, and their antibody response to the vaccine rose by about 20 percent; fewer of their T cells carried PD-1, a marker of exhausted immune cells. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of everolimus and BEZ235 (a drug that blocks PI3K and mTOR at the active site) was linked to fewer reported infections over the following year.

These trials are the main human basis for the idea of weekly low-dose rapalogs as an anti-ageing intervention. Their limits matter: a stronger vaccine response is a lab marker, not proof of fewer infections, and a later phase 3 trial of BEZ235 (RTB101) alone did not confirm a clinical benefit.

Glass trained as a physician, with an MD from New York Medical College, and chose research over further clinical training. Postdoctoral work followed with Charles Cantor and then Stephen Goff at Columbia University. During about 15 years at Regeneron, Glass began studying skeletal muscle and helped identify MuRF1 and MAFbx, two muscle-specific enzymes that tag proteins for destruction when muscle wastes away (MAFbx was found independently by Alfred Goldberg's group, who named it atrogin-1). The lab later showed that myosin heavy chain, the main motor protein of muscle, is a key target of MuRF1, and that the kinase Akt drives muscle growth and links growth and wasting through the FOXO proteins.

At Novartis, Glass led the musculoskeletal research programme, working on myostatin, GDF-11 and activin A and leading development of the antibody bimagrumab. As senior author there, Glass led a 2019 study in aged rats showing that partial inhibition of mTORC1 with a rapalog counteracted the age-related loss of muscle mass. In 2019 Glass returned to Regeneron as Vice President of Aging/Age-Related Disorders and also holds a post as Senior Lecturer in Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School. Recent papers cover how common low muscle mass is among people with obesity in the USA, a 2025 trial identifying GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A as the main brakes on muscle mass in postmenopausal women, and, in 2026, why keeping muscle matters during drug-induced weight loss. In April 2024 Glass was elected to the US National Academy of Sciences.

highlights.MAN2014: Co-author of the trial in which a short course of everolimus improved the flu-vaccine response of older volunteers by about 20 percent.
highlights.MAN2018: Co-author of the phase 2a trial in which low-dose BEZ235 plus everolimus was linked to fewer infections in older adults over the following year.

Caccamo A.role: Neuroscientist who, with Salvatore Oddo, showed in Alzheimer's model mice that amyloid-beta and mTOR feed each other in a loop that rapamycin can break
Caccamo A.sub: Department of Chemical, Biological, Pharmaceutical and Environmental Sciences, University of Messina (papers 2024–2026) · ASU-Banner Neurodegenerative Disease Research Center, Arizona State University (papers to about 2020) · Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (2010)
story: Alzheimer's disease has two hallmarks: clumps of amyloid-beta outside nerve cells and tangles of the protein tau inside them. In a 2010 mouse study (CAC2010), Antonella Caccamo, first author in Salvatore Oddo's group at the University of Texas Health Science Center in San Antonio, found that the two are tied to mTOR in a loop. Amyloid-beta raised mTOR activity. High mTOR in turn blocked autophagy, the cell's clean-up process, so more amyloid and tau built up. In 3xTg-AD mice, a model that develops both hallmarks, rapamycin broke the loop, improved memory and lowered both amyloid-beta and tau. When autophagy was blocked, the drop in amyloid disappeared, which showed that autophagy was needed for the benefit. All of this was in mice, not in people.

Caccamo and Oddo later moved to the ASU-Banner Neurodegenerative Disease Research Center at Arizona State University, where they continued to publish together, including work on autophagy in Alzheimer's model mice.

PubMed records since 2024 list Caccamo, again with Oddo, at the Department of Chemical, Biological, Pharmaceutical and Environmental Sciences of the University of Messina in Italy. Recent work includes a 2024 review on DNA methylation and histone changes in Alzheimer's disease and a 2026 mouse study on the lipid enzyme diacylglycerol kinase theta, whose levels rose with amyloid and with activation of support cells called astrocytes in older APP/PS1 mice.

highlights.CAC2010: First author: showed in 3xTg-AD mice that amyloid-beta raises mTOR, that high mTOR blocks autophagy, and that rapamycin breaks this loop and improves memory.

Cao ZL.role: Urologist in Zhejiang who works with colleagues on inherited endocrine tumour syndromes and wrote a review re-examining how FLCN loss changes mTORC1 signalling in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Cao ZL.sub: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University (2026) · Department of Urology / Oncologic and Urologic Surgery, 903rd PLA Hospital, Hangzhou Medical College (2023–2025)
story: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is an inherited condition caused by faults in the FLCN gene. People with it can get benign skin bumps, air-filled cysts in the lungs that may cause a collapsed lung, and kidney tumours. For years the explanation was simple: lose FLCN and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on everywhere. In a 2026 review in Frontiers in Oncology (CAO2026), Zhi-Lie Cao, first author, with Wei-Ying Chen as senior author, argues that this picture does not fit the evidence. FLCN acts on the RagC/D switch proteins, which control only some mTORC1 targets, above all the MiT/TFE transcription factors. Losing both copies of FLCN lets these factors pile up in the nucleus and drives kidney tumours, while losing one copy may be enough for lung and skin changes. As a review, it reports no new experiments.

PubMed shows Cao as a urologist. In 2023 and 2025 papers the address is the urology and oncologic surgery department of the 903rd PLA Hospital of Hangzhou Medical College; by 2026 it is the Department of Urology of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University. With Chen and Xiao-Ping Qi, Cao has co-authored case reports and literature reviews on rare tumours, including a primary seminoma of the prostate (2023) and families with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A caused by RET mutations (2025, 2026). No official profile page was found.

highlights.CAO2026: First author: argued in a review that FLCN controls mTORC1 selectively through RagC/D, and that FLCN gene dosage explains why kidney, lung and skin are affected differently.

story: In Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, faults in the FLCN gene cause skin bumps, lung cysts and kidney tumours. Wei-Ying Chen was the last author, usually the senior author, of the 2026 review CAO2026 in Frontiers in Oncology. Losing both FLCN copies lets these factors build up in the nucleus and drives kidney tumours, while one lost copy may be enough for lung and skin problems. It is a review of existing work, not a new experiment.

PubMed lists Chen in the Department of Urology of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University, on papers from 2023 to 2026. Together with Zhi-Lie Cao and Xiao-Ping Qi, Chen has co-authored case reports and reviews on rare hereditary tumours, such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A, a pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma syndrome now called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (2024), and a primary seminoma of the prostate (2023). Cao P.role: Wound-repair researcher at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center in Wuxi who tests natural compounds against scarring and diabetic wound inflammation
Cao P.sub: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University, and Wuxi School of Medicine, Jiangnan University (2026)
story: Hypertrophic scars are thick, raised scars that form after burns or surgery when skin cells called fibroblasts lay down too much collagen. In a 2026 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology, Peng Cao and colleagues tested dihydromyricetin, a plant compound, on fibroblasts taken from such scars and on scars in the rabbit ear, a standard animal model. The compound lowered collagen I and III and the scar marker alpha-smooth muscle actin, and the rabbit scars became flatter. At the same time the activating chemical tags on AKT and mTOR, two growth-signalling proteins, fell. The authors state that this does not prove the compound works through the mTOR pathway.

Cao works at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University and at Jiangnan University's Wuxi School of Medicine, in a group led by Guozhong Lyu that also belongs to a Ministry of Education engineering research centre for wound repair technology. In another 2026 first-author paper Cao studied alpha-mangostin, a compound from the mangosteen fruit, and found in cultured mouse immune cells that it reduced inflammation and oxidative stress caused by high glucose, a model of diabetic wounds. Earlier career details could not be confirmed.

highlights.CAO2026B: First author: dihydromyricetin reduced scar markers in fibroblasts and rabbit ear scars, with lower AKT and mTOR phosphorylation.

Lovat P.role: Professor of Cellular Dermatology and Oncology at Newcastle University who studies autophagy in melanoma, and whose work on the autophagy protein AMBRA1 and the skin protein loricrin underlies a test, developed with AMLo Biosciences, to identify early melanomas at low risk of spreading
Lovat P.credit: Portrait: European Society for Dermatological Research (ESDR 2026)
Lovat P.sub: Professor of Cellular Dermatology and Oncology, Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University · Chief Scientific Officer, AMLo Biosciences, Newcastle upon Tyne
story: Penny Lovat is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Viktor Korolchuk's lab at Newcastle University on why ageing cells behave as they do. CAR2017 showed that in senescent human cells (cells that have permanently stopped dividing) mTORC1, the growth-control complex, stays switched on even when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals, and the cells come to depend on this signal to survive. KEL2024 showed that healthy human cells constantly recycle damaged mitochondria (basal mitophagy), that this stops when cells become senescent, and that part of rapamycin's anti-ageing effect on cells needs mitophagy to be restored. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Lovat's own research centres on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, in skin cancer. PubMed lists her at Newcastle University on more than 50 papers on melanoma and autophagy. Her group found that the autophagy regulator AMBRA1 and the skin barrier protein loricrin are lost from the skin above melanomas that are more likely to spread. With collaborators in Rome she showed that the HPV virus breaks down AMBRA1 in throat cancers, which lowers autophagy and makes the tumour cells easier to kill with cisplatin (2020). A 2026 study tested AMBRA1 and loricrin staining to help pathologists tell high-grade moles from thin melanomas.

Lovat is Professor of Cellular Dermatology and Oncology at Newcastle University and Chief Scientific Officer of AMLo Biosciences, the Newcastle company that brings the AMBRA1 and loricrin test to clinical use. PubMed papers list her at the university's Translational and Clinical Research Institute.

highlights.CAR2017: Co-author on the Newcastle study showing that senescent human cells keep mTORC1 switched on because their sensing of amino acids and growth factors is broken.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author on the study showing that loss of basal mitophagy drives cellular ageing and that rapamycin's anti-senescence effect depends on restoring it.

Nelson G.role: Microscopy specialist who manages Newcastle University's Bioimaging Unit and has worked for many years on the signalling networks that keep senescent cells in their arrested state
Nelson G.sub: Specialist Experimental Scientific Officer and manager, Bioimaging Unit, Newcastle University · postdoc with Thomas von Zglinicki, Newcastle University · postdocs at the University of Liverpool and AstraZeneca · BSc and PhD, University of Edinburgh
story: Senescent cells have stopped dividing for good but stay alive and active, and they build up in aging tissues. Glyn Nelson is a co-author of two Newcastle studies in this Atlas that look at how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, behaves in these cells. The 2017 paper (CAR2017), on which Nelson is second author, found that mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent human fibroblasts and no longer responds when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream of mTORC1, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals. The 2024 paper (KEL2024) found that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria shuts down as cells become senescent or old. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Nelson studied at the University of Edinburgh for a BSc and a PhD, then worked as a postdoc at AstraZeneca and at the University of Liverpool, and later joined Thomas von Zglinicki's group at Newcastle, which studies cell senescence. That research thread, on the signalling networks that start and maintain senescence, continues alongside Nelson's imaging role.

Nelson now manages Newcastle University's Bioimaging Unit, which gives researchers across the university access to light microscopes, training and image analysis help. Nelson also develops standard quality-control methods for light microscopy with the international QUAREP-LiMi initiative.

highlights.CAR2017: Second author: contributed to the study showing that mTORC1 stays active in senescent human cells because nutrient and growth-factor sensing upstream of it is faulty.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged human cells.

Castilho RM.role: Dentist and cell biologist who showed, as a postdoc at the US National Institutes of Health, that Wnt signalling wears out skin stem cells through mTOR and that rapamycin can prevent it, and whose University of Michigan lab now studies how histone marks control epithelial healing and treatment resistance in head and neck cancer
Castilho RM.sub: Professor of Dentistry (promotion recommended 2024), Associate Professor with tenure (2018–2024) and Assistant Professor (2010–2018), Department of Periodontics and Oral Medicine, School of Dentistry, University of Michigan · postdoctoral fellow, National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, NIH (about seven years) · PhD (2003) and MS (2000), University of Sao Paulo · DDS, Pontifical Catholic University of Campinas (1995)
story: In the Atlas paper (CAS2009), Rogerio Castilho and colleagues in J. Silvio Gutkind's group at the US National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research looked at the stem cells that renew the skin and hair. They kept the Wnt signal, which tells these stem cells to divide, switched on in mice. At first the hair grew fast, but soon the stem cells stopped working, became senescent (a state where cells stop dividing for good) and the hair was lost. The cause was mTOR: Wnt kept mTOR active, and when the mice were given rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, the stem cells kept going. The study is in mice and in cultured cells, and it helped connect mTOR to the way stem cells run out with age.

Castilho trained as a dentist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Campinas in Brazil (DDS 1995) and earned an MS and a PhD in oral pathology at the University of Sao Paulo (2003), where he also taught surgical and experimental pathology. He then spent nearly seven years as a postdoctoral fellow at the NIDCR, part of the National Institutes of Health, studying how the lining of the mouth and skin stays healthy, heals wounds and turns into cancer.

He joined the University of Michigan School of Dentistry in 2010 and was recommended for promotion to full professor in 2024. His lab studies the histone code, the chemical marks on the proteins that package DNA, in tissue injury, chronic inflammation and cancer. It asks how histone acetylation controls healing and stem cell function, and how head and neck tumours, including salivary gland cancers, use these marks to resist chemotherapy and radiation. The group also tests drugs that change these marks, and works on better healing of burns.

highlights.CAS2009: First author: showed in mice that constant Wnt signalling exhausts epidermal stem cells through mTOR and that rapamycin prevents this stem cell loss.

Castellano BM.role: Cell biologist who, in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley, showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome switches on mTORC1 through the SLC38A9 and NPC1 proteins
Castellano BM.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Zoncu lab, papers 2015–2017, at the time of the study)
story: Castellano was first author of a 2017 Science paper in this Atlas (CAS2017). Every cell has to decide whether it has enough raw materials to grow. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, makes that decision on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, where it is switched on when nutrients are present. Amino acids were the best-known signal; CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is another one. SLC38A9, a transporter-like protein already known to sense the amino acid arginine, is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and it uses separate cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein to do it. NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The experiments used cell lines and fibroblasts from patients, not whole animals.

The finding opened a new line of work. If cholesterol feeds mTORC1, then diseases in which cholesterol gets stuck in lysosomes, like Niemann-Pick type C, may also disturb growth signalling, and later papers from the same lab followed this up.

During the Berkeley years Castellano also co-authored a 2015 Nature Genetics paper on recurrent mutations in RRAGC, a gene for one of the Rag GTPases that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, which keep mTORC1 switched on in follicular lymphoma, and a 2017 Cell Reports study on how proteins from the bacterium Legionella pneumophila turn mTORC1 up and down. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.CAS2017: First author: showed that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9, and that NPC1 restrains this signal.

Covey DF.role: Medicinal chemist and Andrew C and Barbara B Taylor Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry at Washington University in St. Louis who designs synthetic steroids and sterols to study neurosteroids, GABA-A receptors and cholesterol sensing, including in two Atlas studies on cholesterol and mTORC1
Covey DF.credit: Portrait: Department of Developmental Biology, Washington University School of Medicine
Covey DF.sub: Andrew C and Barbara B Taylor Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry · Professor of Developmental Biology, of Anesthesiology and of Psychiatry, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis · Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research
story: Douglas Covey is a co-author of two Atlas studies from the Zoncu lab on how lysosomes tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that cholesterol is available. In CAS2017 the team showed that cholesterol in the lysosome membrane switches on mTORC1. The transporter SLC38A9 is needed for this through cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein, separate from its role in sensing arginine, while NPC1, the protein that exports cholesterol out of the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. In SHI2022 they found a second sensor, LYCHOS (formerly called GPR155). When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS binds GATOR1, a brake on mTORC1, and takes it out of action, so mTORC1 can be recruited to the lysosome. Both studies were done mainly in cultured cells.

Covey's own field is the chemistry of steroids and sterols. Covey's group at Washington University makes modified versions of these molecules and tests how small changes in shape alter what they do. Much of this work, often with Mennerick, concerns neurosteroids, natural brain steroids that act on GABA-A receptors, the main inhibitory receptors of the brain, and their potential for treating psychiatric disorders. Recent papers use machine learning and screening to find new neurosteroid targets (2025), test steroid and sterol analogues on inflammation in brain immune cells (2026) and show that flipping the orientation of one hydroxy group in cholesterol changes how the molecule moves inside cells (2026).

Covey holds the Andrew C and Barbara B Taylor Distinguished Professorship of Psychiatry at Washington University School of Medicine, together with professorships in developmental biology, anesthesiology and psychiatry. PubMed also lists the Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research. In September 2026 the Department of Developmental Biology held a half-day symposium named after Covey.

highlights.SHI2022: Co-author: identified LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor that releases mTORC1 by binding GATOR1.

Davis OB.role: Cell biologist who did a PhD in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley on how lysosomal cholesterol controls mTORC1, and first author of a 2020 study proposing NPC1-mTORC1 signalling as a drug target in Niemann-Pick type C disease

story: Oliver Davis is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas on cholesterol and mTORC1. Every cell has to decide whether it has enough raw materials to grow. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, makes that decision on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, where it is switched on when nutrients are present. Amino acids were the best-known signal; CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is another one. SLC38A9, a transporter-like protein already known to sense the amino acid arginine, is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and it uses separate cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein to do it. NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The experiments used cell lines and fibroblasts from patients, not whole animals. SHI2022 then found the cholesterol sensor itself: LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein previously known only as GPR155. Cholesterol binds one end of LYCHOS, and when cholesterol is high LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that normally keeps mTORC1 off, which lets mTORC1 be recruited to the lysosome. This work was done in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Davis followed this up as first author of a 2020 Developmental Cell paper titled 'NPC1-mTORC1 signaling couples cholesterol sensing to organelle homeostasis and is a targetable pathway in Niemann-Pick type C'. Niemann-Pick type C is a rare inherited disease in which cholesterol gets trapped in lysosomes and the brain and liver are damaged. The paper linked this cholesterol signal to the health of the cell's organelles and suggested that blocking mTORC1 could be a way to treat the disease. Davis was also second author of a 2019 Nature Cell Biology paper showing that contacts between the endoplasmic reticulum and the lysosome let mTORC1 sense cholesterol and drive abnormal growth signalling in the same disease.

Davis completed a PhD dissertation at UC Berkeley in 2020 with Roberto Zoncu as advisor, titled 'The Role of Lysosomal Cholesterol Transport in Cellular Nutrient Sensing and Organelle Homeostasis'. It gathers the cholesterol and mTORC1 work described above. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.
