Nomura DK.role: Chemical biologist and professor at UC Berkeley who uses chemoproteomics to find druggable sites on proteins, including covalent handles that turn ordinary drug molecules into protein degraders
Nomura DK.credit: Portrait: UC Berkeley College of Chemistry
Nomura DK.sub: Professor of Chemical Biology and Molecular Therapeutics, Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, UC Berkeley (assistant professor 2011, associate 2015, professor since 2019) · Director, Novartis-Berkeley Translational Chemical Biology Institute (since 2017) · Investigator, Innovative Genomics Institute · Postdoc with Benjamin Cravatt, Scripps Research (to 2011) · PhD, UC Berkeley (2008)
story: Daniel Nomura is a co-author of two papers from Roberto Zoncu's lab in this Atlas about cholesterol as a signal for growth. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is one of these nutrient signals: the protein SLC38A9 is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, holds the signal back. The experiments used cell lines and patient fibroblasts. SHI2022 found the cholesterol sensor itself, LYCHOS (previously known as GPR155): when cholesterol is high, LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that keeps mTORC1 off, and so lets mTORC1 reach the lysosome. This was shown in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Nomura's own lab works at the border of chemistry and biology. It uses chemoproteomics, methods that use reactive chemical probes and mass spectrometry to map where small molecules can attach to proteins across the whole cell. A 2019 Nature Chemical Biology paper from the lab, with Zoncu lab member Hijai Shin as second author, showed that a compound attaching covalently to the vacuolar H+-ATPase, the proton pump that acidifies lysosomes, switches on autophagy by inhibiting mTORC1. More recently the lab has designed small chemical 'handles' that bind the E3 ligase RNF126 and, when attached to a drug, make the cell destroy the drug's target protein. In 2026 it used an improved handle to degrade BRD4 and the androgen receptor variant AR-V7, which drives drug-resistant prostate cancer.

Nomura studied molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley (BA 2003) and earned a PhD in molecular toxicology there in 2008 with John Casida. Postdoctoral work in chemical biology followed at the Scripps Research Institute with Benjamin Cravatt, who developed many of the chemoproteomic methods the lab now uses. Nomura joined the Berkeley faculty in 2011 and became a full professor in 2019. Today Nomura is Professor of Chemical Biology and Molecular Therapeutics in the Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, directs the Novartis-Berkeley Translational Chemical Biology Institute (since 2017) and is an investigator of the Innovative Genomics Institute. Nomura has also co-founded drug discovery companies, including Frontier Medicines.

highlights.CAS2017: Co-author of the study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9 and NPC1.
highlights.SHI2022: Co-author of the study identifying LYCHOS as the lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

Nomura DK.lab_name: Nomura Lab, Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)

Perera RM.role: Professor of Anatomy at UCSF whose lab studies how autophagy and the lysosome, the cell's recycling centre, help cancer cells cope with stress, and a co-author of two Science papers on how lysosomal cholesterol switches on mTORC1
Perera RM.credit: Portrait: Hirshberg Foundation for Pancreatic Cancer Research
Perera RM.sub: Professor of Anatomy and Deborah Cowan Endowed Professor, University of California San Francisco
story: The lysosome is the cell's recycling centre, and its outer surface is also where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. Perera is a co-author of two Atlas studies led by Zoncu that showed cholesterol is one of the nutrients mTORC1 reads there. In CAS2017, the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 was needed for cholesterol to activate mTORC1, and NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome, held mTORC1 back. In SHI2022, a lysosomal protein named LYCHOS was identified as a cholesterol sensor: when cholesterol is high it binds and ties up GATOR1, a brake on mTORC1, so mTORC1 can be recruited and switched on. Both are studies in cells.

Perera is a professor in the Department of Anatomy at the University of California San Francisco and holds the Deborah Cowan Endowed Professorship. According to the university profile, the lab studies how autophagy and the lysosome regulate the response to cellular stress in ways that promote cancer progression.

highlights.CAS2017: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9, with NPC1 acting as a brake.
highlights.SHI2022: Co-author: contributed to the identification of LYCHOS as the lysosomal cholesterol sensor that signals to mTORC1 by binding GATOR1.

Perera RM.lab_name: Perera Lab, Department of Anatomy, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)

Thelen AM.role: Cell biologist who did graduate work in Roberto Zoncu's lysosome lab at UC Berkeley, first author of a 2017 review on the lysosome's roles in lipid metabolism, and later a postdoctoral scholar in Philip Greenberg's lab at Fred Hutch
Thelen AM.credit: Portrait: UC Berkeley Department of Molecular and Cell Biology
Thelen AM.sub: Postdoctoral scholar, Philip Greenberg lab, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle (per Zoncu lab alumni page) · graduate student, Zoncu Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (about 2017–2019)
story: Ashley Thelen is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is one of these nutrient signals: the protein SLC38A9 is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, holds the signal back. The experiments used cell lines and patient fibroblasts. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited. Loss of FLCN causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition with kidney tumours.
Together the two papers show how mTORC1 reads the state of the lysosome: what nutrients it holds, and whether the Rag switch on its surface is in the 'on' position. Both are cell and protein studies.

Thelen did graduate work in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley, which studies how the lysosome senses nutrients. There Thelen was first author of a 2017 Trends in Cell Biology review, written with Zoncu, on the emerging roles of the lysosome in lipid metabolism, and co-authored a 2019 Molecular Biology of the Cell paper from Schekman's lab at Berkeley on how an autophagy-specific PI3-kinase complex controls LC3 lipidation, an early step in building autophagosomes. The Zoncu lab's alumni list gives Thelen's next position as postdoctoral scholar in Philip Greenberg's lab at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle.

highlights.CAS2017: Co-author of the study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9 and NPC1.
highlights.LAW2019: Co-author of the structural study showing the folliculin complex as a checkpoint for Rag GTPase activation.

Thelen AM.lab_name: Greenberg Lab, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (Seattle, Washington, USA)

Orozco JM.role: Researcher trained in David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute and MIT who showed that mTORC1 senses glucose through the glycolysis metabolite DHAP
Orozco JM.sub: Harvard/MIT MD-PhD Program; PhD student in the Sabatini laboratory, Whitehead Institute and MIT Department of Biology (papers 2014–2021; at the time of the studies) · undergraduate research in Erin Cram's lab, Northeastern University
story: Jose Orozco is a co-author of four Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute that mapped how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, learns what nutrients a cell has. Sestrin proteins bind the GATOR2 complex to dampen amino acid signalling (CHA2014). A complex named KICSTOR holds the GATOR1 brake at the lysosome so that nutrients can control mTORC1 (WOL2017). A protein named SAMTOR senses S-adenosylmethionine, a molecule made from the amino acid methionine (GU2017), which links mTORC1 to diet in a way that may matter for why methionine restriction affects aging. And genome-wide CRISPR screens showed that the kinases AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial problems to mTORC1 (CON2021). These are laboratory studies, mostly in cultured cells.

Orozco's own first-author paper, in Nature Metabolism in 2020, answered a question the field had left open: how mTORC1 knows that glucose is present, separately from the energy sensor AMPK. Working in human cells engineered to lack AMPK, the team traced the signal to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), a molecule made partway through glycolysis. DHAP is also a starting material for making fats, a process that mTORC1 controls, which gives a reason for the cell to watch it.

Orozco came to the work through the Harvard/MIT MD-PhD Program, which trains doctors who also do research. After two years at Harvard Medical School, Orozco started a PhD as an MIT Biology graduate student in Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute. Before medical school, Orozco studied at Northeastern University and did research there in Erin Cram's lab on the roundworm C. elegans. In a Whitehead Institute podcast recorded during the fifth year of the PhD, Orozco described the DHAP finding and said the plan was to finish the medical degree without further clinical training and to build a research career. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.CHA2014: Co-author of the study showing that Sestrins bind GATOR2 to restrain amino acid signalling to mTORC1.
highlights.WOL2017: Co-author of the study showing that KICSTOR recruits GATOR1 to the lysosome.
highlights.GU2017: Co-author of the study identifying SAMTOR as an S-adenosylmethionine sensor for mTORC1.
highlights.CON2021: Co-author of the CRISPR screen study showing that AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1.

Spooner E.role: Manager of the Whitehead Institute's Proteomics Core Facility, whose mass spectrometry work identified proteins in complexes for many Whitehead studies, including two on amino acid sensing upstream of mTORC1
Spooner E.sub: Facility manager, Proteomics Core Facility, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Whitehead profile, 2020; PubMed affiliation through 2024)
story: Many discoveries about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, began by pulling one protein out of cells and asking which other proteins came with it. The answer comes from mass spectrometry, which weighs protein fragments and identifies them. Eric Spooner runs that step at the Whitehead Institute, and he is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab that relied on it.

In TSU2013, the lab showed that folliculin, a tumour suppressor, works with its partner FNIP as a GAP for the Rag GTPases RagC and RagD; a GAP is a helper that makes a switch protein turn itself off. RagC or RagD in this GDP-bound state is needed for the Rags to bind mTORC1 and bring it to the lysosome when amino acids are present. In CHA2014, the lab found that the Sestrin proteins bind GATOR2 and so damp the amino acid signal to mTORC1. Both were done in cultured cells.

A 2020 Whitehead Institute profile describes Spooner as manager of the Proteomics Core Facility, with more than 20 years of protein analysis behind him, most of it running the core. The facility measures protein levels, maps how complexes are built and studies protein interactions, using labelling methods such as SILAC and iTRAQ, high-resolution mass spectrometry and cross-linking. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute on more than forty papers, the most recent in 2024.

highlights.TSU2013: Co-author on the cell study showing that folliculin-FNIP is a GAP for RagC and RagD, needed for amino acids to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.CHA2014: Co-author on the cell study showing that the Sestrins bind GATOR2 to damp amino acid signalling to mTORC1.

Spooner E.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)

Chen Xizi.role: Structural biologist in Yanhui Xu's group at Fudan University who was first author of the 2018 cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 and co-first author of an earlier structure of human mTORC1
Chen Xizi.sub: Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Fudan University, Shanghai (papers 2016–2018, at the time of the study)
story: Xizi Chen was first author of the 2018 Cell Research paper (CHE2018) that gave the first close look at human mTORC2, the second of the two mTOR complexes. The team used cryo-electron microscopy, which freezes purified proteins in thin ice and builds a 3D model from many thousands of images, and reached 4.9 angstrom resolution. The complex is a hollow, diamond-like shape in which two copies of mTOR form the scaffold. The partner proteins Rictor and mSin1 sit right next to the spot where the drug rapamycin would bind. They block it, which explains at the level of shape why rapamycin hits mTORC1 but not mTORC2.

The structure also showed that Rictor and Raptor, the defining partner of mTORC1, use overlapping contacts on mTOR, so a single mTOR cannot belong to both complexes at once. These are results from purified human proteins, not from cells or animals.

Two years earlier Chen was one of four co-first authors of a 4.4 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1 in Protein & Cell. The paper credits Chen with purifying the protein, running biochemical tests and helping with crosslinking mass spectrometry. Both papers came from Yanhui Xu's laboratory at Fudan University in Shanghai, in collaboration with Hong-Wei Wang's cryo-EM group at Tsinghua University. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.CHE2018: First author: solved the 4.9 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2, showing how Rictor and mSin1 block rapamycin binding.

Chen Xizi.lab_name: Yanhui Xu laboratory, Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)

Chen K.role: Researcher in plastic surgery at Wenzhou Medical University and first author of a mouse study on engineered stem-cell exosomes that speed wound healing by changing fibroblast metabolism
Chen K.sub: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Chronic wounds, such as foot ulcers in people with diabetes, can stay open for months. In the Atlas study CHEN2026 in Cellular Signalling, Kewei Chen was first author. The team engineered adipose-derived stem cells, stem cells taken from fat tissue, so that the tiny vesicles they release (exosomes) carried FGF21, a hormone that affects energy use. When these exosomes were given to skin fibroblasts, the cells that rebuild tissue, the fibroblasts switched up glycolysis, the quick sugar-burning pathway, with the energy sensor AMPK turned on and mTOR signalling turned down. The fibroblasts divided and moved faster, and wounds in a mouse model closed sooner. The evidence comes from cells and mice.

PubMed lists Chen in the Department of Plastic Surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, with Li L as senior author. Because the name is very common, no other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, and no official profile page was found.

highlights.CHEN2026: First author: showed in fibroblasts and a mouse wound model that FGF21-loaded stem-cell exosomes boost glycolysis, activate AMPK, lower mTOR signalling and speed wound closure.

Chen K.lab_name: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Wenzhou, China)

Chen Xianglong.role: Orthopedic researcher at Union Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 study that found a new route by which failing autophagy switches on mTORC1 and drives spinal disc degeneration
Chen Xianglong.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: The discs between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers, and their slow degeneration is a major cause of back pain. Xianglong Chen's 2026 study in Advanced Science, with Y. Zhang as senior author, focused on chaperone-mediated autophagy, a selective clean-up route in which single proteins are fed one by one into the lysosome through a receptor called LAMP2A.

In disc cells from patients and in rat models, this pathway was weakened. One of its usual cargoes, the protein midnolin, then built up. Midnolin bound TSC2, part of the main brake on mTORC1, and sent it to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, without the usual ubiquitin tag. With the brake gone, mTORC1 became overactive, and the disc cells became senescent, released inflammatory signals and lost their matrix. Reducing midnolin, adding back LAMP2A or giving rapamycin each blocked the damage in cells and rats. The study describes a new upstream route to mTORC1 overactivity; it has not been tested as a treatment in people.

PubMed lists Xianglong Chen at the Department of Orthopedics of Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.CHEN2026C: First author: showed that impaired chaperone-mediated autophagy lets midnolin accumulate and destroy TSC2, overactivating mTORC1 and driving disc degeneration in human cells and rats.

Chen Xianglong.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)

Chung CL.role: Dermatologist specialising in skin disease of organ transplant recipients, and first author of a small randomised trial showing that topical rapamycin lowers a senescence marker in aging human skin
Chung CL.sub: Montgomery Dermatology and Lankenau Institute for Medical Research, Pennsylvania (papers 2019–2026) · Department of Dermatology, Drexel University College of Medicine, Philadelphia (papers 2012–2019)
story: Christina Lee Chung is first author of the Atlas study CHU2019, with Christian Sell of Drexel University as senior author. Skin is a good place to test an anti-aging drug in people, because it can be seen, photographed and sampled with a small biopsy. In this exploratory randomised trial, older adults were randomised to rapamycin or placebo skin cream. Rapamycin lowered p16, a marker of senescent cells (old cells that have stopped dividing and send out inflammatory signals), and raised collagen VII, a protein that anchors the skin layers. Some participants' skin also looked better.

The trial was small: 36 people enrolled and 17 completed it. So it is early evidence that topical rapamycin can reduce a senescence marker in human skin, not proof that it slows skin aging. It is one of the few human studies in the Atlas in which rapamycin was applied to a tissue rather than given as a pill.

Chung's clinical research centres on skin disease in organ transplant recipients, who take drugs that suppress the immune system and develop skin cancers far more often than other people. At Drexel Chung led studies comparing skin disease after transplant across racial groups (2017) and on genital lesions in transplant recipients (2018). Later papers list Montgomery Dermatology and the Lankenau Institute for Medical Research in Pennsylvania, including expert consensus work on skin cancer screening and prevention after transplant (2019, 2021) and on topical treatment of precancerous skin lesions (2026).

highlights.CHU2019: First author: ran the randomised trial in which topical rapamycin lowered p16 and raised collagen VII in aging human skin.

Chung CL.lab_name: Montgomery Dermatology and Lankenau Institute for Medical Research (Wynnewood, Pennsylvania, USA)

Correia-Melo C.role: Ageing biologist who showed with João Passos in Newcastle that rapamycin can improve healthspan in mice without lowering inflammation, and later studied metabolite sharing between cells in Markus Ralser's lab
Correia-Melo C.sub: Leibniz Institute on Aging, Fritz Lipmann Institute, Jena (paper 2025) · Molecular Biology of Metabolism Laboratory, The Francis Crick Institute, London (Markus Ralser lab, papers 2019–2023) · PhD, Newcastle University Institute for Ageing and GABBA Program, University of Porto (papers 2016–2018)
story: Rapamycin extends life in mice, and a popular explanation is that it calms inflammaging, the low-grade inflammation that builds up with age. Clara Correia-Melo's 2018 paper in Aging Cell (COR2018), from João Passos' group at Newcastle University, tested this in mice lacking the gene nfkb1. These mice have overactive NF-kB, a master switch of inflammation, and they age early. Rapamycin did not lengthen their lives and did not lower their inflammation. It did make them less frail, improved long-term memory, coordination and the structure of several tissues, and lowered markers of senescent cells, which are cells that have stopped dividing and send out harmful signals.

The result separates two effects of rapamycin that are usually assumed to go together: in these mice the healthspan benefit happened without any drop in inflammation. The outcome was mixed, with positive healthspan results and null results for lifespan and inflammaging.

Correia-Melo did doctoral research at the Newcastle University Institute for Ageing through the GABBA graduate program of the University of Porto. As first author of a 2016 EMBO Journal paper with Passos, Correia-Melo showed that mitochondria are needed for many pro-ageing features of senescent cells. Postdoctoral work followed in Markus Ralser's Molecular Biology of Metabolism Laboratory at the Francis Crick Institute in London, where Correia-Melo was first author of a 2023 Cell paper showing that yeast cells that share metabolites with each other create a pro-survival environment that extends lifespan, and contributed to proteomic studies of COVID-19. In 2025 Correia-Melo was listed at the Leibniz Institute on Aging in Jena on a Science paper about protein translation in the ageing killifish brain.

highlights.COR2018: First author: showed that rapamycin improved healthspan in nfkb1 knockout mice without extending lifespan or reducing inflammaging.

Correia-Melo C.lab_name: Leibniz Institute on Aging, Fritz Lipmann Institute (Jena, Thuringia, Germany)

Chresta CM.role: Cancer biologist at AstraZeneca who led the preclinical description of AZD8055, one of the first ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors to reach clinical testing
Chresta CM.sub: Oncology iMed, AstraZeneca, Alderley Park (PubMed affiliation 2009–2016, at the time of the study) · School of Biological Sciences, University of Manchester (1996, with John Hickman)
story: Rapamycin does not block mTOR completely. It sticks to the side of the enzyme and blocks only some outputs of mTORC1, and it leaves mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, largely untouched. Christine Chresta was first author of the 2009 Cancer Research paper in this Atlas (CHR2009) that described AZD8055, a drug that plugs the ATP pocket of mTOR, the site where the enzyme takes up its energy source. AZD8055 therefore blocks both complexes, including the outputs that resist rapamycin. In cancer cells and in mouse tumour models it slowed growth. The result was in cells and animals, not patients.

Chresta was one of the AstraZeneca scientists on a 2009 Biochemical Journal paper with Dario Alessi's group in Dundee describing Ku-0063794, another selective mTOR kinase inhibitor, and on a 2012 study combining AZD8055 with the MEK inhibitor selumetinib in mouse models of lung and colorectal cancer.

Earlier, at the University of Manchester, Chresta worked with John Hickman on how p53 and apoptosis, the cell's programmed death, shape the response of tumours to chemotherapy (1996 and 1999). Later AstraZeneca papers place the author in Oncology iMed at Alderley Park, working on molecular subtypes of lung and colorectal cancer (2013 to 2016). A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.CHR2009: First author: described AZD8055, an ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor that blocks both mTORC1 and mTORC2 and slows tumour growth in mice.

Chresta CM.lab_name: Oncology iMed, AstraZeneca, Alderley Park (Macclesfield, England, United Kingdom)

Cosulich S.role: Cancer drug discovery scientist at AstraZeneca whose work spans PI3K and mTOR pathway inhibitors, PARP1 inhibitors and phosphoinositide lipid signalling
Cosulich S.credit: Portrait: American Association for Cancer Research (AACR Journals)
Cosulich S.sub: Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca, Cambridge (PubMed affiliation 2019–2026; Projects Group, 2022) · AstraZeneca, Alderley Park, Macclesfield (2009–2016)
story: Cancer cells can escape mTOR-blocking drugs by mutating mTOR itself. Sabina Cosulich is a co-author of the 2016 Nature paper in this Atlas (ROD2016), led from Memorial Sloan Kettering and UCSF, which found such mutations in breast cancer cells treated with mTOR inhibitors. Some mutations raised mTOR's own activity. The team then built RapaLink-1, a third-generation drug that joins rapamycin to an ATP-site inhibitor in one molecule, and showed in cells and mice that it still works against the resistant mutants. Cosulich was the AstraZeneca contributor on the author list.

Cosulich has worked on the mTOR pathway at AstraZeneca for many years. A 2009 Biochemical Journal paper with Dario Alessi's group in Dundee, describing the selective mTOR kinase inhibitor Ku-0063794, lists Sabina C. Cosulich together with AstraZeneca colleague Christine Chresta.

Later papers place Cosulich in AstraZeneca Oncology R&D in Cambridge, UK: on a 2019 review and a 2025 study with the Babraham Institute about the fatty-acid make-up of phosphoinositides, the membrane lipids that PI3K signalling uses, on the 2022 preclinical description of the PARP1 inhibitor AZD5305, and on a 2026 paper about a TEAD inhibitor for Hippo-pathway cancers.

highlights.ROD2016: Co-author: AstraZeneca contributor to the study that found mTOR resistance mutations and designed RapaLink-1 to overcome them.

Cosulich S.lab_name: Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)

de Araujo MEG.lab_name: Huber Lab, Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck (Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria)
de Araujo MEG.role: Cell biologist in Lukas Huber's group in Innsbruck who solved the crystal structure of the Ragulator (LAMTOR) complex, the lysosomal platform on which mTORC1 is switched on
de Araujo MEG.credit: Portrait: Medical University of Innsbruck, Institute of Cell Biology
de Araujo MEG.sub: Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck (papers with Lukas Huber, 2004–2026)
story: Mariana de Araujo appears in three Atlas studies about the lysosome surface, where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on and off. In NAP2020 (cells and mice), mTORC1 was shown to reach the transcription factor TFEB by a special route that depends on the RagC and RagD proteins, and this route drives kidney disease in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. In PRE2021 (cells), the stress-granule proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 were found to hold the TSC complex, a brake on mTORC1, on the lysosome. CUI2023 is a cryo-EM structure showing how two Rag-Ragulator units hand a TFEB molecule to the mTOR active site. De Araujo is a co-author in the middle of the author list on all three.

These collaborations build on de Araujo's own first-author work. In a 2017 Science paper from Innsbruck, de Araujo and colleagues solved the crystal structure of the human LAMTOR complex, also called Ragulator: five small proteins held together by LAMTOR1 that anchor the Rag GTPases to the lysosome and set their orientation for meeting mTORC1. The paper also showed which short stretches of LAMTOR1 are needed to recruit and hold the Rags. This structure is one of the reference points for how amino acid signals reach mTORC1.

De Araujo has published with Lukas Huber's group at the Medical University of Innsbruck since a 2004 study on the p14/MP1 scaffold, an earlier-known part of the same complex. The group studies how late endosomes and lysosomes organise signaling. In 2026 de Araujo was first author of a PNAS paper showing that the BORC complex, which moves lysosomes along the cell's tracks, can combine with subunits of a related complex, BLOC-1, to take on different transport jobs. No personal profile page was found, so the current job title is not confirmed.

highlights.NAP2020: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB through a RagC/D-dependent route that drives Birt-Hogg-Dube kidney disease.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author: contributed to the discovery that G3BP1 and G3BP2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes to restrain mTORC1.
highlights.CUI2023: Co-author: contributed to the cryo-EM structure of the mTORC1-TFEB-Rag-Ragulator megacomplex.

Cui X.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University (Jilin, China)
Cui X.role: Pharmacologist at Beihua University who studies how plant-derived compounds protect the kidney and heart from damage caused by high blood pressure in mice
Cui X.sub: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University, Jilin (papers 2026)
story: High blood pressure slowly damages the kidney. In the Atlas study CUI2026 in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology, Xiaoli Cui was first author. Mice received angiotensin II, a hormone that raises blood pressure and injures the kidney. Treatment with forsythoside A, a compound from the medicinal plant Forsythia, protected the kidney. The team reports that forsythoside A binds a protein called ASCL1 and so blocks a downstream CCNB1/mTOR axis. With mTOR held back, the cells cleared more damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) and suffered less ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Blood pressure itself did not fall, so the protection came from inside the kidney cells. The work was done in mice and cells.

Cui works in the Department of Pharmacology of the College of Pharmacy at Beihua University in Jilin, China, with Mengyang Wang, the senior author of CUI2026. In 2026 the same group reported that fangchinoline, an alkaloid from the plant Stephania tetrandra, protected mouse hearts from angiotensin II-induced heart failure through mitophagy and less ferroptosis, and that schisandrin B eased fatty liver disease in mice through the receptor PPAR-gamma. No official profile page was found, so the career path before 2026 is not known.

highlights.CUI2026: First author: led the mouse study in which forsythoside A blocked an ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR axis, increased mitophagy and reduced ferroptosis in kidneys damaged by angiotensin II.

Cunningham JT.lab_name: Department of Cancer Biology, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Cunningham JT.role: Cancer biologist who showed in Puigserver's lab at Dana-Farber that mTOR controls mitochondrial activity, later worked on protein synthesis and nucleotide metabolism in cancer in Davide Ruggero's lab at UCSF, and now works at the University of Cincinnati
Cunningham JT.sub: Department of Cancer Biology, University of Cincinnati (PubMed affiliation, 2026) · Department of Urology and Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, UCSF (Davide Ruggero lab, papers 2014–2016) · Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (Puigserver lab, 2007)
story: mTOR is best known for switching on protein production when nutrients are plentiful. In the Atlas study CUN2007, Cunningham and colleagues in Puigserver's lab showed that mTORC1 also runs the cell's power plants, the mitochondria. Working in cultured cells and mouse muscle, they found that mTORC1 helps two proteins, the transcription factor YY1 and its partner PGC-1alpha, switch on genes for mitochondrial function. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin lowered these genes and cut the cells' oxygen use. The paper explains part of why mTOR inhibitors change metabolism, and why long-term rapamycin can affect energy use in tissues.

Cunningham then moved to Davide Ruggero's lab at the University of California, San Francisco. A 2014 first-author paper in Cell showed that the cancer gene Myc couples protein synthesis and nucleotide production through a single enzyme, PRPS2, whose own production is controlled at the translation step. In 2016 Cunningham was a co-author on a method to measure mTORC1 activity in living animals by PET scanning with radioactively labelled transferrin.

A 2026 paper lists Cunningham at the Department of Cancer Biology, University of Cincinnati, on work showing that the enzyme caspase-1 acts as a scaffold that binds raptor, a part of mTORC1, to hold back excess inflammatory NF-kB signalling in leukemia cells. The same mTOR focus and the earlier Ruggero connection tie this record to the same person.

highlights.CUN2007: First author: showed that mTORC1 drives mitochondrial gene expression and oxygen use through a YY1-PGC-1alpha complex, and that rapamycin lowers both.

Heberle AM.lab_name: Institute of Biochemistry, University of Innsbruck (Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria)
Heberle AM.role: Cell biologist and Junior Group Leader at the University of Innsbruck who studies how mTOR balances growth signalling and metabolism when cells are under stress, trained in Kathrin Thedieck's systems-biology group
Heberle AM.sub: Junior Group Leader and postdoctoral researcher, Institute of Biochemistry, University of Innsbruck · earlier in the Thedieck group, Section Systems Medicine of Metabolism and Signaling, University Medical Center Groningen (papers 2016–2021)
story: Alexander Heberle is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Kathrin Thedieck's group. The 2016 study (DAL2016) combined lab experiments with a computer model of the signalling network. It found that when amino acids are given back to starved cells, AMPK, the cell's energy-shortage sensor, switches on at the same time as mTOR, even though the two are usually described as opposites. AMPK then helps keep autophagy, the cell's recycling system, running through the kinase ULK1. The 2021 Cell paper (PRE2021) found a new brake on mTORC1, the growth-control complex: two proteins called G3BP1 and G3BP2, best known from stress granules, sit on the surface of the lysosome and hold the TSC complex there, so that TSC can keep mTORC1 in check. Without G3BPs, mTORC1 overreacts to nutrients and insulin. Both studies were mainly done in cultured cells.

Heberle's publication list follows the same line of questions: how stress switches mTOR on and off (a 2014 review), how the mitotic kinase PLK1 inhibits mTORC1 and promotes autophagy (2017), how the PI3K and p38 pathways control stress granule assembly (2019), and reviews on mTORC1 and stress granules in aging and on systems approaches to mTOR signalling (2021). Collaborations extend to cardiac IGF-1 receptor signalling and mass spectrometry methods.

PubMed lists Heberle at the University Medical Center Groningen on both Atlas papers. The current University of Innsbruck page lists Heberle as a Junior Group Leader at the Institute of Biochemistry, with a lab that studies how cells survive stress by balancing signalling and metabolism, with mTOR at the centre, and that aims to develop treatments for mTOR- and stress-related diseases.

highlights.DAL2016: Co-author of the systems study showing that amino acids switch on AMPK and mTOR at the same time in starved-then-fed cells.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author of the Cell study showing that G3BP proteins hold the TSC complex on lysosomes and so restrain mTORC1.

Stork B.lab_name: Molecular Biology of Cellular Stress Responses group, Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Medical Faculty and University Hospital Düsseldorf, Heinrich Heine University (Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Stork B.role: Heisenberg Professor for the molecular biology of cellular stress responses at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, who studies the ULK1 complex, the switch that starts autophagy, and how it is wired to the energy sensor AMPK and to mTOR
Stork B.sub: Heisenberg Professor (W2), Molecular Biology of Cellular Stress Responses, Medical Faculty, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (since 2017) · Group leader, Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Düsseldorf (2011–2017) · Junior group leader, University of Tübingen (2006–2011) · PhD, Bielefeld, Göttingen and Kansai Medical University, Osaka (2002–2006)
story: Autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system, is started by a protein kinase called ULK1. When energy runs low, the energy sensor AMPK switches ULK1 on, and when nutrients are plentiful mTORC1 switches it off. In LOF2011, from Björn Stork's group, then at the University of Tübingen, Antje Löffler and colleagues found that the signal also runs backwards: ULK1 adds phosphate groups to AMPK and dampens its activity. This makes a negative feedback loop, a built-in way for the autophagy machinery to limit the signal that started it, rather than a one-way switch. The work was done in cell and biochemical experiments.

Stork studied biochemistry in Bielefeld, with a semester at McGill University in Montreal, and did a PhD in biochemistry and molecular immunology from 2002 to 2006 under J. Wienands and T. Kurosaki, with the work split between Bielefeld, Göttingen and Kansai Medical University in Osaka. From 2006 to 2011 Stork led a junior research group at the University of Tübingen, where LOF2011 was done, and then moved to the Institute of Molecular Medicine I at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf as a group leader, completing the habilitation (the German qualification to teach and supervise at university level) in molecular medicine there in 2013. In 2015 the team mapped the short stretch of the protein ATG13 that holds ULK1 in place and found that cells lacking this contact still keep some autophagy, which points to routes that bypass the usual ULK1-ATG13 link.

Since 2017 Stork has held a Heisenberg Professorship, a German research council post for established researchers, for the molecular biology of cellular stress responses at the Düsseldorf medical faculty. The group's central theme is how signals switch autophagy on and off, with the longer-term aim of using autophagy control in cancer, infection and nerve development. In 2026, as senior author, Stork reported that human induced pluripotent stem cells and nerve progenitor cells have working autophagy machinery but do not switch it on after low-dose DNA damage, unlike many cancer cell lines.

highlights.LOF2011: Senior author: led the study showing that ULK1 phosphorylates and inhibits AMPK, forming a negative feedback loop in autophagy signalling.

Dan L.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Dan L.role: Yeast geneticist at Chengdu University who studies reversible mutations that let cells switch drug resistance on and off, using rapamycin resistance in fission yeast as the model
Dan L.sub: School of Pharmacy and Antibiotics Innovation and Resistance Control Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu University (PubMed affiliation 2025–2026) · Life Sciences Institute, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou (Xiangwei He lab, PubMed affiliation 2021)
story: Fission yeast is a single-celled fungus used to study how cells control growth. Its TORC1 complex is the yeast version of mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and it can be blocked with rapamycin plus caffeine. Lufeng Dan is first author of the 2026 Microbiology Spectrum study in this Atlas (DAN2026). Some yeast cells became resistant to the drugs, then lost the resistance again a few generations later. The team showed that this was not an epigenetic switch. Mutations that broke the gaf1 gene appeared under drug pressure and then reverted to the normal DNA sequence when the drug was gone. Gaf1 is a GATA transcription factor that slows growth downstream of TORC1. The authors warn that such hidden switches can quietly change laboratory yeast stocks.

The paper continues a line of work Dan began at the Life Sciences Institute of Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, in the group of Xiangwei He. A 2021 PNAS paper with Dan as first author found drug-resistance mutations in fission yeast that are made by short tandem duplications of DNA and then flip back to the original sequence, and used deep genome sequencing to find thousands of such duplications in a single population.

By 2025 Dan was at the School of Pharmacy of Chengdu University, where a paper in the Chinese journal Hereditas described a screen that isolated 14 yeast strains with unstable rapamycin resistance, again with Xiangwei He as a co-author.

highlights.DAN2026: First author: showed that on-and-off resistance to TORC1 inhibitors in fission yeast comes from reversible mutations in gaf1.

Demir A.lab_name: Simon Raffel group, Heidelberg University and Heidelberg University Hospital (Heidelberg, Germany)
Demir A.role: Leukaemia researcher at Heidelberg University and first author of the 2026 study showing that the enzyme IDH3 keeps acute myeloid leukaemia stem cells metabolically fit and resistant to venetoclax
Demir A.sub: Heidelberg University, Heidelberg (Simon Raffel group, at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Aykut Demir was first author of a 2026 paper in Blood (DEM2026) about acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), a fast-growing blood cancer. AML returns after treatment because a small group of leukaemic stem cells survives. These cells depend on the TCA cycle, the chain of reactions in mitochondria that burns fuel for energy, more than healthy blood stem cells do. The team found that the enzyme IDH3, one step of that cycle, is more abundant in leukaemic stem cells.

When they lowered IDH3A, the working part of the enzyme, citrate piled up inside the cells and both main energy pathways slowed. The resulting energy shortage switched on AMPK, the cell's fuel gauge, which shut down mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and so cut protein production. The cells then became more sensitive to venetoclax, a drug that blocks the survival protein BCL2. Healthy blood formation was spared. The work used patient cells, bone marrow organoids (miniature lab-grown tissue) and mice, and in a patient group, stem cells from people whose leukaemia resisted venetoclax plus azacitidine showed gene programmes of an active TCA cycle.

The paper lists Demir at Heidelberg University, in a team led by Simon Raffel at Heidelberg University Hospital with Andreas Trumpp of the German Cancer Research Center and Carsten Müller-Tidow among the co-authors. Other PubMed records under the same initials belong to different people, and a fuller career history could not be confirmed.

highlights.DEM2026: First author: showed that loss of IDH3A in AML stem cells raises citrate, activates AMPK and shuts down mTORC1, making the cells more sensitive to venetoclax.

Zamboni N.lab_name: Zamboni Group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Zamboni N.role: Group leader at ETH Zurich's Institute of Molecular Systems Biology who develops mass spectrometry methods to measure hundreds of metabolites at once, used in many collaborations on cell metabolism
Zamboni N.credit: Portrait: ETH Zurich, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology
Zamboni N.sub: Group leader, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (since 2005) · postdoc, Stanford Genome Technology Center (2004) · PhD, Institute of Biotechnology, ETH Zurich, Jay Bailey group (2003)
story: Nicola Zamboni is a co-author of two Atlas studies that measured cell metabolism. GEI2016 tracked metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells and found that the amino acid L-arginine drops sharply after activation; raising L-arginine pushed the cells toward oxidative metabolism, made them live longer and improved their anti-tumor activity in a mouse model. DEM2026 found that losing the enzyme IDH3A in leukemic stem cells of acute myeloid leukemia slows the citric acid cycle and raises citrate, which switches on AMPK, turns down mTORC1 and makes the cells more sensitive to the drug venetoclax.

In both studies the key data came from metabolomics, the large-scale measurement of small molecules in cells. Zamboni earned a PhD at ETH Zurich in 2003 in the group of Jay Bailey at the Institute of Biotechnology, working on metabolic engineering and 13C flux analysis, a method that follows carbon atoms from a labelled nutrient to see which metabolic routes a cell uses. A postdoc at the Stanford Genome Technology Center from 2004 added mass spectrometry and metabolomics in eukaryotic cells.

Zamboni returned to ETH Zurich in 2005 and leads a group at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology. The lab builds mass spectrometry, metabolomics and stable-isotope tracer methods, together with software for analysing the data, to measure how whole metabolic networks respond inside living cells. More than 30 papers are shared with Uwe Sauer, a systems biologist at the same institute, and many others are collaborations in microbiology, immunology, aging and cancer biology.

highlights.GEI2016: Co-author: contributed metabolomics to the study showing that raised L-arginine shifts activated T cells to oxidative metabolism and improves their survival.
highlights.DEM2026: Co-author: contributed metabolite measurements to the study linking IDH3A loss, citrate build-up, AMPK activation and lower mTORC1 activity in AML stem cells.

Demmings MD.lab_name: Neuroscience Program, Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry, University of Western Ontario (London, Ontario, Canada)
Demmings MD.role: Neuroscience researcher in Sean Cregan's lab at Western University who showed that chronic ATF4 stress signalling shuts down mTOR and kills dopamine neurons in models of Parkinson's disease
Demmings MD.sub: Neuroscience Program, Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry, and Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario (Sean Cregan lab, papers 2020–2026)
story: In Parkinson's disease the dopamine-making neurons of the midbrain die. Matthew Demmings' 2026 paper in Cell Reports (DEMMINGS2026), from Sean Cregan's lab at Western University in Canada, traced one route to that death. In cell and animal models of the disease, a long-lasting stress response called the integrated stress response kept the transcription factor ATF4 active. ATF4 turned up three genes, SESN2, DDIT4 and TRIB3, whose proteins together lowered the activity of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. That sustained loss of mTOR signalling switched on PUMA, a protein that triggers cell suicide, and the neurons died.

Much of the ageing literature treats lower mTOR activity as good. This study is a reminder that neurons need some mTOR signalling to survive, and that chronic shutdown can be harmful. The results come from cell and animal models, not from patients.

The paper builds on Demmings' earlier first-author study from the same lab, published in Cell Death and Differentiation in 2020, which showed that ATF4 promotes the death of neurons exposed to Parkinson's toxins and to clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein. In 2025 Demmings was also first author of a review on how neurons and glial cells interact from brain development to disease, and a co-author of a review on metabolic networks in the healthy brain.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: First author: showed that chronic ATF4 signalling suppresses mTORC1 and mTORC2 through SESN2, DDIT4 and TRIB3 and drives PUMA-dependent death of dopamine neurons in Parkinson's models.

De Nardi A.lab_name: Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI), Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (Rovereto, Italy)
De Nardi A.role: Mathematical modeller in Trento who applies survival and epidemic models to medical data, and first author of the 2026 re-analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial in ALS
De Nardi A.sub: COSBI, Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (2026)
story: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease in which the nerve cells that control muscles die. RAP-ALS was a small clinical trial of rapamycin, the drug that blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, in people with ALS. In the Atlas study DEN2026B, De Nardi and colleagues went back to the trial data (63 patients) and asked which factors predicted survival. Among carriers of a mutation in the C9orf72 gene, the most common genetic cause of ALS, those treated with rapamycin survived longer, and the same pattern held against a separate group of 40 C9orf72 carriers.

This is a secondary, exploratory analysis. The number of treated C9orf72 carriers was small, and the patients were not randomised for this question, so the drug may not be the cause of the difference. The result is a reason for a proper trial in this genetic group, not evidence that rapamycin works in ALS.
PubMed lists De Nardi in 2026 at COSBI in Rovereto, a computational biology centre run jointly by Microsoft Research and the University of Trento.

highlights.DEN2026B: First author: re-analysed RAP-ALS trial survival and found a possible survival benefit of rapamycin in C9orf72 mutation carriers, flagged as exploratory.

de Oliveira Isídio BE.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Studies and Experimental Therapy, Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (Recife, Brazil)
de Oliveira Isídio BE.role: Researcher in Antonio Carlos de Freitas's laboratory at the Federal University of Pernambuco who studies whether human papillomavirus (HPV) is active in breast tumours
de Oliveira Isídio BE.sub: Laboratory of Molecular Studies and Experimental Therapy, Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (papers 2024–2026, at the time of the study)
story: HPV, the virus that causes most cervical cancers, carries three cancer-promoting genes called E5, E6 and E7. A question still under debate is whether the virus also plays a part in some breast cancers. In DEOLIVEIRA2026, Beatriz Eda de Oliveira Isídio and colleagues in Recife measured these viral genes and the RNA messages of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway in breast tumour samples. Of 92 patients, 48 had usable RNA. Tumours expressing HPV16 genes had higher PI3K and lower mTOR transcript levels. The design only shows an association between two sets of RNA measurements in tissue, so it does not prove that the virus switches the mTOR pathway on or off.

The work continues a line from the same laboratory, led by Antonio Carlos de Freitas in the Department of Genetics at the Federal University of Pernambuco. In a 2024 study of 56 patients from northeastern Brazil, on which de Oliveira Isídio was a co-author, the group detected HPV in about a third of breast tumours, mostly HPV16, often with high viral load and active E5. No institutional profile was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.DEOLIVEIRA2026: First author: measured HPV16 E5, E6 and E7 expression and PI3K/AKT/mTOR transcripts in breast tumour samples, finding an association but not a causal link.

Dibbens LM.lab_name: Epilepsy Research Group, Australian Centre for Precision Health, University of South Australia (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Dibbens LM.role: Epilepsy geneticist at the University of South Australia who found that mutations in DEPDC5, part of the GATOR1 brake on mTORC1, cause familial focal epilepsy
Dibbens LM.sub: Epilepsy Research Group, Clinical and Health Sciences, Australian Centre for Precision Health, University of South Australia (papers to 2025)
story: Some families pass down epilepsy in which seizures start in one part of the brain, a different part in different relatives. Leanne Dibbens is first author of a 2013 study that found a gene behind it (DIB2013B). By reading the protein-coding DNA of affected families and tracking which stretch of DNA travelled with the disease, the team found loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5 in most large families studied and in about 12% of smaller ones. DEPDC5 is part of GATOR1, a complex that switches off mTORC1 when amino acids are scarce, so the finding tied a common form of inherited epilepsy to the mTOR pathway. The study is genetic; it did not measure mTOR activity itself, and the link to mTORC1 rests on the known role of GATOR1.

Dibbens leads epilepsy genetics work in Adelaide, with about 80 papers on PubMed. A 2025 study with the group used the structure of the KCNT1 potassium channel to screen known drugs for ones that block the overactive channel found in severe childhood epilepsies, tested them in cells and in fruit flies carrying the human mutation, and identified antrafenine as a candidate that also reaches the brain in mice.

highlights.DIB2013B: First author: identified loss-of-function DEPDC5 mutations, a GATOR1 subunit, as a cause of familial focal epilepsy with variable foci.

Dorrello NV.lab_name: Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine and Hospital Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons (New York, New York, USA)
Dorrello NV.role: Pediatric critical care physician-scientist at Columbia University whose training in Michele Pagano's lab at NYU showed how S6K1 removes the translation brake PDCD4, and who now works on repairing injured children's lungs
Dorrello NV.sub: Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine and Hospital Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons · Department of Pathology, NYU Cancer Institute, New York University School of Medicine (Pagano lab, 2003–2008)
story: To grow, a cell must make proteins, and to make proteins it must unwind the folded start of each messenger RNA. The helicase eIF4A does this, and the tumour suppressor PDCD4 holds eIF4A back. In 2006, in a Science paper with Michele Pagano as senior author, N. Valerio Dorrello showed how growth signals lift this brake. S6K1, a kinase switched on by mTORC1, phosphorylates PDCD4, which marks it for the ubiquitin ligase betaTRCP; PDCD4 is then destroyed, eIF4A is freed and translation and cell growth go up.

The paper added a new branch to the map of what mTORC1 does: besides acting on ribosomal protein S6 and on 4E-BP1, the pathway also removes an inhibitor of the translation machinery. Because PDCD4 is a tumour suppressor, its loss through this route also links mTOR signalling to cancer growth.

Dorrello's PubMed record has papers with the Pagano group at NYU from 2003 to 2008, then a later line of work at Columbia University. The later papers come from the Department of Pediatrics and its Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine, often with bioengineers, for example a 2017 study with Gordana Vunjak-Novakovic on delivering and imaging stem cells in the lung. As senior author of a 2026 npj Regenerative Medicine paper, Dorrello showed that healthy alveolar type II cells, the cells that make surfactant, can be engrafted into mice lacking surfactant protein C and reduce lung injury, a step toward cell therapy for childhood interstitial lung disease.

highlights.DOR2006: First author: showed that S6K1 triggers betaTRCP-mediated degradation of PDCD4, releasing the translation helicase eIF4A and promoting protein synthesis and cell growth.

Drummond MJ.lab_name: Drummond Lab, Department of Physical Therapy and Athletic Training, University of Utah (Salt Lake City, Utah, USA)
Drummond MJ.role: Muscle physiologist at the University of Utah who studies why older muscle wastes during inactivity and recovers poorly, and who showed that mTORC1 drives part of the protein-building response to exercise in humans
Drummond MJ.sub: Professor, Department of Physical Therapy and Athletic Training, University of Utah · postdoc in muscle biology, University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston (to 2008) · PhD in Exercise Sciences, Brigham Young University (2006)
story: When you lift weights, your muscles start building new protein within an hour or two. In 2009, Micah Drummond, then at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston with Blake Rasmussen, tested whether mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is needed for that response in people (DRU2009). Healthy volunteers took a single dose of rapamycin before a session of resistance exercise. In the control group, muscle protein synthesis rose by about 40% in the first one to two hours. Rapamycin blocked that rise. Rapamycin also blunted ERK1/2 and MNK1 signalling, so the authors concluded that mTORC1 drives the response only in part. The study measured protein synthesis over a few hours, not muscle growth over weeks.

Drummond studied at California Lutheran University, earned a PhD in exercise sciences at Brigham Young University in 2006 and trained in muscle biology at the University of Texas Medical Branch until 2008.

At the University of Utah, Drummond is a Professor of Physical Therapy and Athletic Training, with adjunct appointments in nutrition and integrative physiology and other departments. The lab studies how aging, physical inactivity and immune changes combine to cause muscle loss and poor recovery after disuse, such as bed rest, hospital stays or surgery, with a focus on inflammation, cellular senescence and metabolic disease in aged rodents and in people.

highlights.DRU2009: First author: showed in healthy volunteers that rapamycin blocks the early rise in muscle protein synthesis after resistance exercise.

Duran RV.lab_name: Centro Andaluz de Biología Molecular y Medicina Regenerativa (CABIMER), CSIC (Seville, Spain)
Duran RV.role: Cell biologist who showed that glutamine breakdown feeds amino acid signalling to mTORC1, and who now leads research on mTOR, glutamine metabolism and cancer at CABIMER in Seville
Duran RV.sub: Senior Researcher, Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), CABIMER, Seville · group leader, Institut Européen de Chimie et Biologie, INSERM U1218 and University of Bordeaux (PubMed affiliation 2015–2017) · postdoc, Michael N. Hall lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (2012) · doctoral work, Instituto de Bioquímica Vegetal y Fotosíntesis, University of Seville and CSIC (2006)
story: Cells check whether they have enough amino acids before they grow, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is the checkpoint. Raúl Durán was first author of the 2012 Molecular Cell study in this Atlas (DUR2012), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel. In cultured cells, glutamine together with leucine switched on mTORC1 by speeding up glutaminolysis, the breakdown of glutamine into alpha-ketoglutarate. Alpha-ketoglutarate then acted through the Rag GTPases, the switches that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome. The work linked a metabolic pathway that many cancer cells overuse to the main growth signal.

Durán started in a different field. A 2006 first-author paper from the Instituto de Bioquímica Vegetal y Fotosíntesis in Seville studied how electron-carrier proteins feed photosystem I in cyanobacteria. After the postdoc in Basel, Durán led a team at the Institut Européen de Chimie et Biologie in Bordeaux (INSERM and University of Bordeaux). There the group described 'glutamoptosis', a form of cell death caused when glutaminolysis runs unchecked during nutrient shortage and autophagy is blocked (2017).

Durán is now a Senior Researcher of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) at CABIMER in Seville. A 2026 paper from the group, with Durán as senior author, found that the FGFR1 receptor drives a metabolic rewiring that lets glioblastoma cells resist the chemotherapy drug temozolomide, and that blocking FGFR1 restored sensitivity in cells and mouse models.

highlights.DUR2012: First author: showed in cells that glutaminolysis, through alpha-ketoglutarate, activates Rag-mTORC1 signalling.

Robitaille AM.lab_name: Thermo Fisher Scientific (San Jose, California, USA)
Robitaille AM.role: Mass spectrometry scientist who, as a PhD student in Michael Hall's lab, used phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 switches on the cell's production of pyrimidines, and who now works on proteomics applications at Thermo Fisher Scientific
Robitaille AM.credit: Portrait: LCGC International (Thermo Fisher Scientific headshot)
Robitaille AM.sub: Senior Product Applications Specialist, Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose · postdoc, Randall Moon lab, University of Washington, Seattle · PhD, Michael N. Hall lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel
story: To grow and divide, a cell must copy its DNA and make lots of RNA, and both need pyrimidines, a family of chemical building blocks. Aaron Robitaille was first author of the 2013 Science paper in this Atlas (ROB2013), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel. Using quantitative phosphoproteomics, a mass spectrometry method that measures thousands of phosphorylation sites at once, the team found 335 proteins whose phosphorylation depended on mTOR. One of them was CAD, the enzyme that runs the first three steps of making pyrimidines. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches CAD on through S6 kinase. The work, done in cultured cells, tied the main growth signal directly to the supply of DNA and RNA building blocks.

Robitaille did the PhD at the University of Basel in Michael Hall's laboratory and then moved to the University of Washington in Seattle as a postdoc in Randall Moon's lab, using quantitative proteomics to measure protein levels and protein partners and to find regulators of embryonic stem cell differentiation. The thread through this work is the use of mass spectrometry to follow how cells respond to their surroundings when they decide to grow or change identity.
Robitaille now works at Thermo Fisher Scientific in San Jose, California, as a Senior Product Applications Specialist for mass spectrometry and proteomics.

highlights.ROB2013: First author: used quantitative phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 activates pyrimidine synthesis through S6 kinase and CAD.

Duran-Ortiz S.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University (Athens, Ohio, USA)
Duran-Ortiz S.role: Researcher in John Kopchick's group at Ohio University who studies how switching off growth hormone action, even in middle age, lengthens life in mice
Duran-Ortiz S.sub: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University (papers 2025–2026) · Edison Biotechnology Institute, Ohio University (papers from 2019)
story: Silvana Duran-Ortiz is first author of an Atlas study (DUR2026) that asked whether blocking growth hormone still helps if you wait until middle age. Mice born without the growth hormone receptor are small, very insulin sensitive and the longest-lived laboratory mice known, but that may be because they never grew normally. Here the team deleted the receptor at 12 months, when the mice were adults. Both sexes still lived significantly longer, without big changes in body size. Males also kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone structure as they aged, and the liver showed sex-specific changes in gene activity.

Growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1 and mTOR are linked growth signals, so the result fits the wider idea that turning growth signals down in adult life can slow ageing. It is a mouse study; in people, growth hormone receptor defects cause Laron syndrome, which is not the same as switching the receptor off in midlife.

Duran-Ortiz has published with the Ohio University growth hormone group of John Kopchick, Edward List and Darlene Berryman since at least 2019, first listed at the Edison Biotechnology Institute and more recently at the Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging. The work uses mice in which the growth hormone receptor is removed from the whole body or from single tissues such as fat, liver or muscle, and asks how each affects metabolism, immunity and lifespan; a 2026 paper found that old female mice without the receptor kept younger-looking B and T cell populations. No personal profile page was found, so the job title is not confirmed.

highlights.DUR2026: First author: showed that deleting the growth hormone receptor at 12 months of age still extends lifespan in both sexes of mice, with extra metabolic and muscle benefits in males.

Ikeno Y.lab_name: Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ikeno Y.role: Pathologist at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies in San Antonio whose examinations of tissues from aged mice help ageing studies tell whether an intervention changes disease, especially cancer, late in life
Ikeno Y.credit: Portrait: Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio
Ikeno Y.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (affiliation on PubMed papers)
story: Yuji Ikeno is a co-author of two Atlas papers on ageing. LAB2015, from Judith Campisi's group, studied senescent cells, old cells that stop dividing but keep releasing inflammatory signals called the SASP. These signals can harm nearby tissue and even help tumours grow. The team showed that mTOR drives the SASP by boosting the production of IL1A, the signal at the top of the cascade, and that rapamycin turned this off and stopped senescent cells from feeding prostate tumour growth in mice. DUR2026, from John Kopchick's group, deleted the growth hormone receptor in mice at 12 months of age, which is middle age for a mouse. The mice still lived longer, in both sexes, and the males kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone. This matters because most growth-hormone longevity mice lack the hormone signal from birth, while this study shows that a midlife start is still enough.

PubMed lists Ikeno on more than 120 papers on ageing, many of them from the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, where the long-lived mouse models and anti-ageing drug studies need careful pathology to show what the animals died of and which diseases were delayed. In both Atlas papers the role is consistent with this: examining tissues from the mice.
No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given here.

highlights.LAB2015: Co-author on the study showing that mTOR drives the senescence-associated secretory phenotype through IL1A translation and that rapamycin blocks it.
highlights.DUR2026: Co-author on the study showing that deleting the growth hormone receptor in midlife still extends healthy lifespan in mice.

Evans S.lab_name: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (Hanover, New Hampshire, USA)
Evans S.role: Neuroscience researcher at Dartmouth who studies how growth signals shape the skeleton of sensory nerve fibres, and first author of work showing that PTEN acts on microtubules through mTORC2 rather than mTORC1
Evans S.sub: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: PTEN is a brake on the PI3K growth pathway. When nerve cells lose PTEN, they grow larger and their axons, the long fibres that carry signals, extend faster. Both mTOR complexes sit downstream of PTEN: mTORC1, best known for driving protein synthesis, and mTORC2, which acts more on the cell's internal skeleton. In EVA2026, Simone Evans and colleagues at Dartmouth asked which of the two carries the signal in peripheral sensory neurons. Using mouse genetics, they removed PTEN together with either Raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, or Rictor, an essential part of mTORC1's sister complex mTORC2. Removing mTORC2, but not mTORC1, brought the fast growth of microtubules, the protein tracks inside axons, and the enlarged size of PTEN-deficient neurons back to normal. The effect was seen at the growth cone, the moving tip of the axon, not along the axon shaft. The work adds evidence on the less studied mTORC2 side of the pathway.

Evans is a member of the Department of Integrative Neuroscience at Dartmouth's Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, the school that runs Dartmouth's PhD programmes. EVA2026 is the only PubMed paper found under this name and affiliation, so no wider research record is described here.

highlights.EVA2026: First author: used Raptor or Rictor co-deletion in PTEN-deficient sensory neurons to show that mTORC2, not mTORC1, drives faster microtubule growth at the axon tip.

Fan W.lab_name: Laiho Lab, Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Fan W.role: Cancer biologist in Marikki Laiho's lab at Johns Hopkins who studies ribosome production as a weak point of cancer cells, and who showed how mTOR inhibition helps cells survive when ribosomes run short
Fan W.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Marikki Laiho lab, papers 2022–2026)
story: Ribosomes are the machines that build every protein in the cell, and cancer cells need huge numbers of them. Drugs that block ribosome production are being tested against cancer. In the Atlas study FAN2026 in Genes & Development, Wenjun Fan, first author in Marikki Laiho's lab, asked what happens to mTOR signalling when ribosome production fails. Turning mTORC1 off did not restore ribosome production. Instead it shifted the few ribosomes left away from 5'TOP mRNAs, a family of messages that normally take up a large share of ribosomes, and toward messages the cell needs to survive. The authors call this translational fitness. The work was done in cancer cells.

All of Fan's papers with Laiho in PubMed come from the Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences at Johns Hopkins. As first author in 2022, Fan used whole-genome data from 2,504 people in the 1000 Genomes Project to show that human ribosomal RNA genes vary much more between people than expected. A 2025 first-author paper in Cell Chemical Biology found that cancer cells with faulty RPL22, a ribosomal protein, are especially sensitive to drugs that block RNA polymerase I, the enzyme that makes ribosomal RNA, and that RPL22 also controls how many other messages are spliced. The Atlas paper also lists the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

highlights.FAN2026: First author: showed in cancer cells that mTORC1 inhibition redirects scarce ribosomes from 5'TOP mRNAs to survival transcripts when ribosome production fails.

Feldman ME.lab_name: Shokat lab, Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, UCSF and Howard Hughes Medical Institute (San Francisco, California, USA)
Feldman ME.role: Chemical biologist who, in the Shokat lab at UCSF, introduced PP242 and the TORKinib class of drugs that block mTOR's active site and reach the outputs rapamycin misses
Feldman ME.sub: Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology and Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California San Francisco, Shokat lab (papers 2006–2012, at the time of the study)
story: Morris Feldman is first author of the Atlas study FEL2009 from the Shokat lab at UCSF. Rapamycin does not bind mTOR's active site. It sticks to the side of mTORC1 and blocks only some of its outputs, and it barely touches the second complex, mTORC2. Feldman and colleagues made small molecules called TORKinibs, including PP242 and PP30, that sit in the ATP pocket of the mTOR kinase itself. These hit both complexes.

The key result was that active-site inhibitors shut down cap-dependent translation, the main way cells start making proteins, much more strongly than rapamycin. A parallel study by Thoreen and colleagues reported the same conclusion in the same year. Together the two papers opened a new class of mTOR drugs beyond rapamycin and its analogues. The work was done in cultured cells.

PP242 then became a common research tool. Feldman is a co-author on several papers that used it, including the 2012 Nature study from the Ruggero group showing that mTOR-controlled translation steers cancer initiation and metastasis, a 2010 study showing that mTORC2 activates the kidney sodium channel ENaC through SGK1, a 2010 study of a herpesvirus protein that keeps mTORC1 switched on, and a 2012 study combining active-site mTOR inhibitors with chemotherapy for colorectal cancer. No current position could be confirmed.

highlights.FEL2009: First author: developed the active-site mTOR inhibitors PP242 and PP30 and showed they block rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 and mTORC2, including cap-dependent translation.

Flynn JM.lab_name: Melov Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Flynn JM.role: Aging researcher from Simon Melov's lab at the Buck Institute who showed that a short course of rapamycin late in life can partly reverse heart aging in mice
Flynn JM.sub: Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Simon Melov lab (2012–2017, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Department of Cell Biology, University of North Texas Health Science Center, Fort Worth (2005–2008) · current position not confirmed
story: Most rapamycin studies in mice start the drug early and ask whether aging is slowed. In 2013 James Flynn, working with Simon Melov at the Buck Institute, asked a different question: can rapamycin help an organ that has already aged? Already old female mice, aged 24 months, received rapamycin for three months. Several age-related changes in heart function were reversed or reduced. Reading the active genes in the heart (RNA sequencing) pointed to less inflammation, changes in metabolism and less growth of heart muscle. The study was done in mice and does not show the same effect in people.

Flynn came to aging research from mitochondrial biology. At the University of North Texas Health Science Center in Fort Worth, Flynn studied how the hormone estrogen protects mitochondria in cells of the eye lens, as first author of a 2008 paper in this line of work with Patrick Cammarata.

At the Buck Institute, Flynn was first author of a 2012 study that measured gene activity in single bone-forming cells, and co-authored work from Judith Campisi's lab on cell senescence, the state in which damaged cells stop dividing, including a 2012 study linking mitochondrial oxidative stress to skin aging and a 2017 study on how senescent cells differ from one another. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.FLY2013: First author: three months of rapamycin in 24-month-old female mice reversed or reduced age-related heart dysfunction.

Diaz V.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Diaz V.role: Aging researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who has worked for more than a decade on the mouse lifespan studies behind rapamycin's reputation as an anti-aging drug, including the Interventions Testing Program
Diaz V.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2013–2026)
story: Vivian Diaz is a co-author of two Atlas studies from San Antonio. In FOK2014, mice fed rapamycin lived longer, and their livers showed large changes in which genes were switched on, a first look at what long-term rapamycin does inside an organ. In STR2022, from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which tests drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites, male mice given rapamycin plus acarbose from 9 months of age lived longer than males on rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts, while in females the combination matched rapamycin alone. Both studies are in mice.

PubMed lists Diaz at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio on a long run of mouse aging studies. Several test rapamycin directly: it extended life and health in C57BL/6 mice (2013), it raised mortality in db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes (2015), and chronic rapamycin reduced age-related motor decline in a sex-dependent way (2026). Diaz is also a co-author on ITP reports on canagliflozin (2020) and on epicatechin, halofuginone and mitoglitazone (2025), and on a 2026 Nature study of genetic and body-wide trade-offs in aging and mortality.
These papers show steady work on the San Antonio mouse aging studies; Diaz's exact role in the team was not stated in the sources checked.

highlights.FOK2014: Co-author: mice fed rapamycin lived longer and showed large changes in the liver transcriptome.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author from the San Antonio ITP site: rapamycin plus acarbose from 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts.

Fok WC.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Structural Biology and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Fok WC.role: Biologist of aging who, in Viviana Pérez's group in San Antonio, compared rapamycin with dietary restriction in mouse liver and showed that rapamycin's lifespan gain comes with large changes in liver gene activity
Fok WC.sub: Department of Cellular and Structural Biology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2012–2015, at the time of the study)
story: Wilson Fok is first author of the Atlas study FOK2014, with A. Richardson as senior author. Mice fed rapamycin in their food lived longer, and their livers showed large changes in which genes were turned on or off, measured across the whole transcriptome. The study helped connect rapamycin's effect on lifespan with concrete changes in an organ that controls much of the body's metabolism. It is a mouse study.

Fok's other first-author papers from San Antonio, with Viviana Pérez, compared rapamycin with dietary restriction, the best-known way to extend lifespan in lab animals. Short-term treatment in young mice showed that the two had overlapping but distinct effects (2012), and combining them changed the liver transcriptome and metabolome more than either alone (2013). Fok was also a co-author on a 2014 study showing that rapamycin and dietary restriction cause metabolically distinct changes in mouse liver.

In 2015 Fok is listed at the Barshop Institute on a study of a mitochondrial protease in muscle cells. No later position could be confirmed from sources that tie directly to this work, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.FOK2014: First author: showed that rapamycin-fed mice lived longer and had large changes in the liver transcriptome.

Foretz M.lab_name: Institut Cochin, Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Inserm (Paris, France)
Foretz M.role: Researcher at the Institut Cochin in Paris who studies how the liver controls sugar and fat, and whose 2010 work showed that metformin can lower liver glucose output without AMPK
