Foretz M.sub: Institut Cochin, CNRS, Inserm, Université Paris Cité (papers 2010–2025) · Inserm U465, Centre de Recherches Biomédicales des Cordeliers, Paris (1999 paper)
story: Marc Foretz is first author of an Atlas study (FOR2010) that changed how scientists explain metformin, the most widely used diabetes drug. For years the simple story was that metformin works by switching on AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, which then shuts down sugar production in the liver. The team tested this in mice and liver cells that lacked AMPK or its activating kinase LKB1. Metformin still lowered glucose production. Instead, the drug lowered the liver's energy charge, the balance of ATP to its used-up forms, and that alone was enough to slow the making of new glucose.

For the Atlas this matters because metformin is often described as an indirect mTOR blocker acting through AMPK. The paper shows that its main sugar-lowering effect in the liver does not need that route, so any claim that metformin works mainly through AMPK and mTOR needs separate evidence. The experiments were in mice and isolated liver cells.

Foretz has worked on liver metabolism for more than 25 years. A 1999 paper from the Inserm unit at the Centre des Cordeliers in Paris, with Pascal Ferré and Fabienne Foufelle, showed that the transcription factor SREBP-1c carries insulin's message to genes for sugar and fat handling in liver cells. At the Institut Cochin, working closely with Benoit Viollet, Foretz went on to study AMPK and metformin in the liver, and in 2025 co-wrote a major review on how metformin lowers blood sugar. No official profile page could be opened, so the exact current title is not confirmed; the 2025 affiliation is the Institut Cochin.

highlights.FOR2010: First author: showed in mice and liver cells lacking AMPK or LKB1 that metformin still blocks glucose production by lowering the liver's energy charge.

Curatolo P.lab_name: Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Systems Medicine Department, Tor Vergata University (Rome, Italy)
Curatolo P.role: Child neurologist at Tor Vergata University in Rome who has spent much of a long career on tuberous sclerosis complex, the genetic disease of overactive mTOR, with a focus on epilepsy and brain development in children
Curatolo P.sub: Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Systems Medicine Department, Tor Vergata University, Rome · Tor Vergata University Hospital (EXIST-3, 2016)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease caused by faulty TSC1 or TSC2 genes. These genes normally act as a brake on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, so in TSC mTORC1 runs too high and benign growths form in the brain, kidneys, skin and other organs. Many children with TSC have epilepsy that standard drugs do not control. Paolo Curatolo is a co-author of EXIST-3 (FRE2016), a phase 3, double-blind trial published in the Lancet in 2016 that tested whether everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR, could reduce these seizures.

The trial enrolled 366 patients aged 2 to 65 with treatment-resistant focal seizures and randomly assigned them to placebo, a low everolimus dose or a high everolimus dose. About 15% of patients on placebo had their seizures cut by half or more, against 28% on the low dose and 40% on the high dose. Because the drug targets the cause of the disease and not just the seizures, EXIST-3 is one of the clearest examples in people of what blocking mTOR can do.

PubMed lists Curatolo on more than 140 papers about tuberous sclerosis. A 2025 review in eBioMedicine, written with colleagues in Rome and Amsterdam, sets out how biomarkers such as EEG findings, gene variants and brain imaging can pick out infants at high risk, and how early treatment with vigabatrin or mTOR inhibitors might prevent the severe epilepsy and developmental problems that often follow. On that paper Curatolo is listed at the Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Systems Medicine Department, Tor Vergata University.

highlights.FRE2016: Co-author of the phase 3 EXIST-3 trial showing that everolimus reduces treatment-resistant seizures in tuberous sclerosis complex.

Frias MA.lab_name: Department of Biology, St. Francis College (Brooklyn, New York, USA)
Frias MA.role: Cancer biologist who did her doctoral research on mTORC2 in David Sabatini's lab and now teaches biology at St. Francis College in Brooklyn, while continuing work with David Foster on how the lipid phosphatidic acid controls mTOR
Frias MA.sub: Assistant Professor and Chair of Biology, St. Francis College, Brooklyn (since 2021) · postdoctoral research, The Rockefeller University and Hunter College, City University of New York (David Foster lab) · PhD in Cancer Biology, Medical School of the University of Lisbon (2008), with the research done in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute
story: mTOR, the cell's central growth kinase, works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 is the one rapamycin blocks; mTORC2 was the less understood partner, and one of its main jobs is to switch on Akt, a kinase that keeps cells alive and responds to insulin. In 2006, as first author of a Current Biology paper from David Sabatini's lab (FRI2006), Maria Frias showed in human cells that a protein called mSin1 is needed to build mTORC2 and for mTORC2 to add a phosphate to Akt at serine 473. The mSin1 gene makes several versions of the protein, and the paper found that three of them each sit in a distinct form of mTORC2, so there is more than one mTORC2 in a cell.

Frias did this work as a doctoral student from Portugal. Her official faculty pages say her PhD in Cancer Biology was awarded by the Medical School of the University of Lisbon in 2008, with the research carried out in the Sabatini lab at the Whitehead Institute and funded by a Portuguese government fellowship. She then did postdoctoral research at The Rockefeller University and at Hunter College of the City University of New York, and received a grant for a Master of Science in Clinical and Translational Investigation at Weill Cornell Medicine.

At Hunter College she worked with David Foster on phosphatidic acid, a membrane lipid that binds mTOR and helps hold its complexes together. PubMed lists her on papers from that group on how cells keep phosphatidic acid levels steady for mTOR (2014), on the two-way link between the energy sensor AMPK and phospholipase D (2015), on why rapamycin works at different doses in different settings (2016), on glutamine switching on mTORC1 through phospholipase D (2018), on cancer cells that resist rapamycin when RB and CDKN2A are both mutated (2021), and a 2023 review on how phosphatidic acid regulates mTOR. She joined St. Francis College in Brooklyn in 2021 and is Assistant Professor and Chairperson of Biology there; her stated research aim is to work out what controls mTORC1, how cancer cells exploit it and which drugs could block it.

highlights.FRI2006: First author: showed in human cells that mSin1 is required to assemble mTORC2 and for Akt phosphorylation, and that mSin1 variants define three distinct mTORC2s.

Xu C.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The Seventh Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University (Shenzhen, China)
Xu C.role: Hematologist in Shenzhen who studies drug resistance and drug safety in multiple myeloma, and senior author of a study linking a small RNA fragment to autophagy-driven resistance to bortezomib
Xu C.sub: Department of Hematology, The Seventh Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen (papers 2025–2026)
story: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, the antibody factories of the bone marrow. A standard drug against it is bortezomib, which blocks the proteasome, the machine that destroys unwanted proteins, so that myeloma cells choke on their own protein waste. Many patients eventually stop responding. In FU2026, Cong Xu's group found that a small RNA piece cut from a transfer RNA, called tRF-17-8SPOL52, is raised in relapsed or treatment-resistant myeloma. It lowers RUBCN, a protein that normally holds back autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system. With the brake removed, autophagy speeds up and helps myeloma cells survive bortezomib. The link to mTOR is indirect: autophagy is one of the main processes mTORC1 keeps in check.

Xu works in the Department of Hematology of the Seventh Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University in Shenzhen. In 2025 Xu was senior author of a study that used the US FDA adverse event reporting database to map lung side effects, such as pneumonia and interstitial lung disease, linked to the antibody drugs approved for myeloma. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.FU2026: Senior and corresponding author: led the study showing that tRF-17-8SPOL52 drives bortezomib resistance in myeloma by suppressing RUBCN and increasing autophagy.

Gan X.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Gan X.role: Biochemist at Fudan University who showed as a Yale postdoc that the lipid messenger PIP3 directly switches on mTORC2, and who now studies Wnt and mTORC2 signalling in metabolism
Gan X.sub: Researcher, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Fudan University (since 2013) · postdoc, Yale University School of Medicine (2009–2013) · PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (2008)
story: mTORC2 is the second mTOR complex. One of its main jobs is to switch on Akt, a kinase that tells cells to take up sugar, grow and survive. By 2011 it was known that growth factors acting through PI3K turn on mTORC2, but not how. PI3K makes a lipid called PIP3 in the cell membrane. In the Atlas study GAN2011, Xiaoqing Gan, working in Dianqing Wu's lab at Yale, showed in cultured cells and in test-tube kinase assays that PIP3 directly raises the activity of mTORC2. This gave a simple chemical link between PI3K and mTORC2.

Gan earned a PhD in biochemistry and molecular biology at the Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2008 and was a postdoc at Yale University School of Medicine from 2009 to 2013.

Since 2013 Gan has been a researcher (principal investigator) in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology of the School of Basic Medical Sciences at Fudan University in Shanghai. The group works on metabolism and cell signalling, with themes that include Wnt signalling in stem cell differentiation, communication between bone and brown fat, and G protein-coupled receptor and mTORC2 signalling.

highlights.GAN2011: First author: showed in cells and in kinase assays that the lipid PIP3 directly stimulates mTORC2, linking PI3K to mTORC2.

Gao X.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Gao X.role: Geneticist who, in Duojia Pan's lab, used fruit flies and mammalian cells to show that the tumour suppressors Tsc1 and Tsc2 restrain TOR signalling and make it sensitive to amino acids
Gao X.sub: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center at Dallas (Duojia Pan lab, papers 2000–2005, at the time of the study)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex is an inherited disease in which benign tumours grow in the brain, skin, kidneys and other organs. It is caused by faults in either of two genes, TSC1 or TSC2. Around 2002 the big question was how these two tumour suppressors hold back growth. In the Atlas study GAO2002 in Nature Cell Biology, Xinsheng Gao, first author in Duojia Pan's lab at UT Southwestern in Dallas, showed in fruit flies and mammalian cells that Tsc1 and Tsc2 can physically associate with TOR, the nutrient-sensing kinase, and act upstream of it in fly genetic tests. Cells lacking Tsc1 or Tsc2 had more activity of S6K, a kinase that TOR switches on, and this rise depended on TOR. Normally S6K switches off when cells are starved of amino acids, but cells without Tsc1 or Tsc2 kept it on. The work placed the TSC proteins in the nutrient-sensing TOR pathway, which later helped make rapamycin-type drugs a treatment option for tuberous sclerosis.

PubMed lists seven papers from 2000 to 2005 in which Gao and Pan appear together on fly growth control and the Tsc genes. No later record could be tied to this person with confidence, because the name is common, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.GAO2002: First author: showed in flies and mammalian cells that Tsc1 and Tsc2 act upstream of TOR and that cells lacking them keep S6K active even without amino acids.

Gao K.lab_name: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), School of Medicine, Northwest University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Gao K.role: Urology researcher at Xi'an People's Hospital and first author of a 2026 multicentre study showing that the fat content of TSC kidney tumours predicts how well they shrink on everolimus
Gao K.sub: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University · also listed at the State Key Laboratory of Cancer Biology, Air Force Medical University, Xi'an (2026)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which the brake on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is missing. One result is angiomyolipoma, a benign kidney tumour made of blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat that can grow large and bleed. Everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, is the standard medical treatment. Ke Gao is first author of a prospective study from several Chinese hospitals that followed 183 patients with these tumours (GAO2026B).

Everolimus cut tumour volume by half or more in 44% of patients after 3 months and in 83% after 6 months. Tumours with little fat shrank better than fat-rich ones, which makes sense if the drug acts mainly on the growing muscle and vessel cells rather than on the fat. A lower dose seemed to work about as well and caused fewer mouth ulcers, but that comparison was exploratory and not randomised, so it needs a proper trial. Tumours grew back when treatment stopped.

On PubMed, Gao's other recent papers come from the same urology department at Xi'an People's Hospital, part of Northwest University's School of Medicine. They include a 2025 rat study on how a high-salt diet raises blood pressure and cholesterol through the immune signal IL-17, and a 2026 review on gut bacteria in cachexia, the wasting syndrome of cancer, written with the State Key Laboratory of Cancer Biology at the Air Force Medical University. No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the papers.

highlights.GAO2026B: First author of the multicentre prospective cohort of 183 patients, which linked lower tumour fat content to a better response to everolimus.

Ni J.lab_name: Department of Urology, Urology and Nephrology Hospital, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Ni J.role: Urologist at Xi'an People's Hospital and senior author of a 2026 multicentre study of everolimus for TSC kidney tumours, with further work on prostate cancer
Ni J.sub: Department of Urology, Urology and Nephrology Hospital, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University
story: Jianxin Ni is the last author, usually the person who leads the project, of a 2026 prospective study from several Chinese centres on everolimus for kidney angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex (GAO2026B). In TSC the brake on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is missing, and everolimus puts part of that brake back. In 183 patients the drug shrank tumours by half or more in 44% at 3 months and 83% at 6 months. Tumours with little fat responded better than fat-rich ones, so a scan of tumour fat could help predict who benefits. A lower dose looked similar and caused fewer mouth ulcers, but only in an exploratory, non-randomised comparison. Tumours regrew after the drug was stopped.

PubMed lists about ten papers with Ni at the urology department of Xi'an People's Hospital since 2023. They include a 2026 study in cells and mice showing that the protein PEAK1 helps prostate cancer resist the chemotherapy drug docetaxel by pushing nearby immune cells, macrophages, into a tumour-helping state, and a 2025 rat study on salt, IL-17 and cholesterol. No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on these papers.

highlights.GAO2026B: Last author who led the multicentre cohort linking tumour fat content to everolimus response in TSC angiomyolipoma.

Garami A.lab_name: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research (Basel, Switzerland)
Garami A.role: First author of the 2003 study, from George Thomas's group at the Friedrich Miescher Institute, showing that insulin switches on Rheb and that the TSC1-TSC2 complex switches it off
Garami A.sub: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel (at the time of the study, 2003)
story: Attila Garami was first author of a 2003 Molecular Cell paper (GAR2003) that helped fix the order of steps above mTOR. Rheb is a small GTPase, a molecular switch that is on when it holds GTP and off when it holds GDP. The study showed that insulin raises the amount of active, GTP-loaded Rheb. The tumour-suppressor proteins TSC1 and TSC2 work together as Rheb's GAP, an enzyme that makes Rheb burn its GTP and so turns it off. Active Rheb in turn drives the signals that mTOR sends to S6K and 4E-BP, the proteins that boost protein synthesis.

Put together, this placed Rheb directly upstream of mTOR and directly downstream of TSC1-TSC2. It explained why losing TSC1 or TSC2, as in the disease tuberous sclerosis complex, leaves mTOR stuck on. The work used cultured cells and fruit-fly genetics.

The paper came from the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel, where Garami worked in George Thomas's group. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.GAR2003: First author: showed that insulin activates Rheb and that TSC1-TSC2 acts as Rheb's off-switch, placing Rheb directly upstream of mTOR.

Stocker H.lab_name: Hafen group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Stocker H.role: Drosophila geneticist who worked for nearly two decades in Ernst Hafen's group in Zurich and helped show how insulin and TOR signalling set cell and body size in the fruit fly, including the discovery that Rheb is essential for TOR-S6K driven growth
Stocker H.sub: Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich, Hafen group (PubMed affiliation 2008–2016) · Zoological Institute, University of Zurich, Hafen group (1999–2007) · current position not confirmed
story: In 2003 the TOR pathway had a gap. Geneticists knew that the tumour suppressors Tsc1 and Tsc2 hold growth back and that TOR and its target S6K drive growth, but not what connected them. Hugo Stocker, first author of the Nature Cell Biology paper STO2003 from Ernst Hafen's group, found that the small GTPase Rheb sits in that gap. In fruit flies, cells lacking Rheb stopped growing, and cells with extra Rheb grew larger. Genetic tests placed Rheb downstream of Tsc1-Tsc2 and upstream of S6K. The study was done in Drosophila.

PubMed lists Stocker on about forty papers with Hafen between 1999 and 2016, first at the Zoological Institute of the University of Zurich and later at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology at ETH Zurich. The early papers belong to the work that made the fly a model for growth control: CHICO, the fly version of the insulin receptor substrate, controls cell and organ size (1999); fly S6 kinase regulates cell size (1999, with George Thomas's group in Basel); and the fly insulin receptor and seven insulin-like peptides control growth (2001).

Later papers list Stocker as senior or corresponding author. A 2010 Journal of Biology study showed that Madm works with Bunched A to promote growth, and a 2015 Journal of Cell Science paper with Catherine Rabouille's group found that TORC2 helps flies survive heat stress by promoting stress granules, protective clusters of RNA and protein. The most recent record found is from 2016 at ETH Zurich. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.STO2003: First author: showed in Drosophila that Rheb is required for cell growth and acts between Tsc1-Tsc2 and S6K in the TOR pathway.

Goberdhan DC.lab_name: Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Goberdhan DC.role: Oxford cell biologist who studies how amino acid transporters and the cell's secretory compartments control growth signalling, often using the fruit fly, and who argued that intracellular transporters mark where mTORC1 is switched on
Goberdhan DC.sub: Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health, University of Oxford (2025–2026) · Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics, University of Oxford (papers to 2025)
story: mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is switched on by amino acids, but where in the cell does that happen? In a 2016 review in Cell Metabolism (GOB2016), written with Adrian Harris, Deborah Goberdhan argued that amino acid transporters sitting in the membranes of compartments inside the cell, such as late endosomes, lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus, mark the spots where mTORC1 is activated. The review proposed that different amino acids in different compartments may switch on different pools of mTORC1. It is a synthesis of existing evidence, not a new experiment.

Goberdhan has worked for many years in the Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics at the University of Oxford, often with Clive Wilson, and has more than 50 papers in PubMed. The work moves between fly genetics and human cancer. With Harris, Goberdhan's group reported in 2020 that the glutamine transporter SNAT2 helps triple-negative breast cancer cells resist oxidative stress and is linked to worse survival. Goberdhan was also a co-author of MISEV2018, the international guidelines for research on extracellular vesicles, the small membrane packets that cells release.

More recent papers use the prostate-like secondary cells of male fruit flies to watch secretion live. A 2025 study in The EMBO Journal showed that the Alzheimer's protein APP and amyloid-beta disturb how dense-core secretory granules form in recycling endosomes, and a 2026 review proposed that faulty regulated secretion might start Alzheimer's pathology. These papers list Goberdhan at the Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health at Oxford.

highlights.GOB2016: First author: proposed in a review that amino acid transporters inside the cell mark the sites where mTORC1 is activated.

Goul C.lab_name: Leonetti Group, Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Goul C.role: Cell biologist who did graduate work in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley on lysosomes and mTORC1, first author of a major review of how mTORC1 senses nutrients and of a 2026 Nature study on how damaged lysosomes are repaired, now a scientist at CZ Biohub
Goul C.sub: Scientist, Leonetti group, Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco · graduate student, Zoncu lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (papers 2022–2026)
story: Claire Goul was first author of a 2023 review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology (GOU2023) that explains how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, senses nutrients. mTORC1 is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when amino acids, glucose, cholesterol and growth signals are all present, and it then drives the making of proteins, fats and new cell parts. The review walks through the sensors and switches involved, including the Rag GTPases that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, and how faults in this system contribute to metabolic disease, cancer and other conditions. It is a good entry point for a reader who wants the whole pathway in one place.

Goul's research in Roberto Zoncu's lab centres on the lysosome. In 2022 Goul co-wrote a short Developmental Cell commentary on lysosome repair, and in 2026 was first author of a Nature paper describing LASER, which links the sensing of lysosome damage to the assembly of the ESCRT machinery that patches the membrane. Goul also co-authored a 2025 EMBO Journal study showing that autophagosomes anchor a checkpoint that shapes PKA signalling in neurons.

Goul did this work as a graduate student in the Zoncu lab, which lists Goul among its alumni. After leaving Berkeley, Goul became a scientist in the Leonetti group at the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub in San Francisco.

highlights.GOU2023: First author of this review of how mTORC1 senses nutrients and signals in metabolism and disease.

Gu X.lab_name: Gu Lab, Department of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Gu X.role: Cell biologist who discovered SAMTOR, the sensor that lets mTORC1 read the methyl donor SAM, as a PhD student at MIT, and who now leads a lab at Dana-Farber and Harvard Medical School studying ubiquitin-independent protein destruction by the midnolin-proteasome pathway
Gu X.credit: Portrait: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Xin Gu Lab)
Gu X.sub: Assistant Professor of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (since 2024) · postdoc, Michael Greenberg lab, Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School (2021–2024) · PhD in Biology, MIT (David Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute) · BS in Biology, Peking University
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only switches on when a cell has enough nutrients. By 2017 the Sabatini lab had found sensors for the amino acids leucine and arginine. Xin Gu, first author of the 2017 Science paper on SAMTOR (GU2017), found that mTORC1 also reads a metabolite. SAMTOR binds S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the molecule cells use to hand out methyl groups, which is made from the amino acid methionine. When methionine runs low, SAM falls, SAMTOR is freed to bind GATOR1, a complex that turns mTORC1 off, and mTORC1 signalling drops. The work was done in human cells. This is relevant to why restricting methionine in the diet affects ageing.

Gu is also a co-author on three other Atlas papers from the same lab: KICSTOR, a complex that holds GATOR1 on the lysosome so nutrients can control mTORC1 (WOL2017); the cryo-EM structure that shows how raptor docks on the Rag-Ragulator complex at the lysosome (ROG2019); and the cryo-EM structure of GATOR2, a large cage-shaped complex that sits upstream of mTORC1 (VAL2022).

According to the lab's official page, Gu studied biology at Peking University and earned a PhD in Biology at MIT, then did postdoctoral work in the Department of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School; the Greenberg lab lists Gu as a postdoctoral fellow from 2021 to 2024. There Gu was first author of a 2023 Science paper showing that a protein called midnolin delivers many nuclear proteins, including transcription factors made from immediate-early genes, to the proteasome for destruction without the usual ubiquitin tag. Since 2024 Gu has been Assistant Professor of Cancer Biology at Dana-Farber and of Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School. The lab studies how cells keep their protein content stable, starting with the midnolin-proteasome pathway; a 2025 Molecular Cell paper from the lab solved structures of the midnolin-proteasome complex and linked low midnolin to the survival of myeloma cells.

highlights.GU2017: First author: identified SAMTOR as the SAM sensor that links methionine supply to mTORC1 through GATOR1.
highlights.WOL2017: Co-author on the discovery of KICSTOR, which tethers GATOR1 to the lysosome and is needed for nutrient control of mTORC1.
highlights.ROG2019: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure showing how raptor reads the nucleotide state of the Rag GTPases before mTORC1 docks on the lysosome.
highlights.VAL2022: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure of the nutrient-sensing hub GATOR2.

Guerrero-Morín JG.lab_name: Unidad Monterrey, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN (Apodaca, Nuevo León, Mexico)
Guerrero-Morín JG.role: Researcher at the Monterrey unit of Cinvestav in Mexico and first author of a 2020 mathematical model of how mTORC1 could tune the body's daily clock
Guerrero-Morín JG.sub: Unidad Monterrey, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN (Cinvestav), Apodaca, Nuevo León (at the time of the study, 2020)
story: Almost every cell in the body runs a circadian clock, a loop of genes and proteins that rises and falls over about 24 hours. One of the central clock proteins is BMAL1. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is one of the signals thought to affect the clock through BMAL1. José Guerrero-Morín was first author of a 2020 paper in the Journal of Theoretical Biology (GUE2020) that turned these observations into a mathematical model.

The model suggests that mTORC1 makes the clock's swings bigger by boosting the making (translation) of BMAL1, and changes the length of each cycle by controlling where BMAL1 sits inside the cell. Both effects together were needed for a strong, regular rhythm in the model. This is a computer model, not an experiment: it makes predictions that still have to be tested in cells or animals. It matters for the Atlas because it gives a testable picture of how growth signalling and daily timing might be linked.

The paper was written at the Monterrey unit of Cinvestav, a national research centre in Mexico, with Santillán as senior author. PubMed lists no other papers under this name, so later career steps could not be traced.

highlights.GUE2020: First author: built a mathematical model in which mTORC1 sets circadian clock amplitude through BMAL1 translation and period through BMAL1 location.

Guerra P.lab_name: Molecular Systems Biology, Groningen Biomolecular Sciences and Biotechnology Institute, University of Groningen (Groningen, Netherlands)
Guerra P.role: Systems biologist who tracked TORC1 and PKA signalling in single yeast cells and showed that their growth signals rise and fall with the cell cycle
Guerra P.sub: PhD, University of Groningen (2022, thesis on single-cell analysis of TORC1 and PKA signalling during the budding yeast cell cycle; Andreas Milias-Argeitis group; at the time of the study)
story: Textbook diagrams show TORC1 (the yeast version of mTORC1) as a switch that is either on, when food is plentiful, or off, when it is not. Paolo Guerra's 2022 paper in the Journal of Cell Science (GUE2022), from Andreas Milias-Argeitis' group at the University of Groningen, looked at single cells instead of averages. Using time-lapse microscopy on hundreds of budding yeast cells, the team followed where two target proteins of TORC1 and of PKA (another nutrient-sensing kinase) sat inside the cell, which shows how active the kinases are. Their activity towards ribosome building rose and fell in step with the cell cycle, even though the food supply stayed the same the whole time. Mutations in regulators upstream of TORC1 and PKA changed the rhythm, which suggests that signals from the cell's own metabolism drive part of it.
For mTOR research this means that growth signalling is not only a reaction to the outside world but also has its own internal timing tied to cell division. The work was done in yeast.

The paper was part of Guerra's 2022 doctoral thesis at the University of Groningen, on single-cell analysis of TORC1 and PKA signalling and how growth and division are coordinated. In the same period Guerra contributed to a neural-network tool that outlines yeast cells in microscope images without hand-labelled training data, and to a 2022 study on what sets the timing of the Start checkpoint that commits a yeast cell to divide. No later position could be confirmed.

highlights.GUE2022: First author: showed by single-cell time-lapse imaging that TORC1 and PKA activity towards ribosome biogenesis oscillates with the yeast cell cycle.

Heim MH.lab_name: Department of Biomedicine, University of Basel, and Clarunis (Basel, Switzerland)
Heim MH.role: Basel hepatologist who studies how the liver responds to viral infection and how liver cancer develops, and a co-author of the study linking mTORC2 to fat synthesis in liver tumours
Heim MH.credit: Portrait: Clarunis, University Digestive Health Care Center Basel
Heim MH.sub: Department of Biomedicine, University of Basel, and Clarunis, Basel (recent papers) · Department of Biomedicine, University Hospital Basel (at the time of the 2017 study)
story: Markus Heim is a co-author of GUR2017, a Cancer Cell paper led by Michael Hall's group at the Biozentrum in Basel. The team used a mouse model in which overactive mTOR signalling in the liver causes fatty liver that later turns into liver cancer. They found that mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, drives the cell's own production of fatty acids and of sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking the making of fatty acids or sphingolipids prevented tumours in these mice. In tissue from people with liver cancer, higher lipid synthesis went along with higher mTORC2 activity, which links the mouse result to human tumours, though only as an association.

Heim's contribution came from the clinical and liver biology side in Basel. PubMed lists close to sixty papers under this name with a Basel affiliation on interferon or hepatitis C, the line of work on how the liver's antiviral interferon system responds to hepatitis viruses, and a similar number on hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common liver cancer. Recent papers, up to 2026, also list Clarunis, a university centre for digestive and liver diseases in Basel.
No official profile page could be opened, so title and training are not given here. Other Atlas records under this name carry no affiliation in PubMed and were not counted.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author on the Basel study showing that mTORC2 drives fatty acid and sphingolipid synthesis to promote liver cancer in mice, with a matching pattern in human tumours.

Jenoe P.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Jenoe P.role: Protein chemist who ran mass spectrometry and protein sequencing at the Biozentrum Basel for decades and contributed protein analysis to many mTOR studies from Michael Hall's lab
Jenoe P.sub: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation to 2022) · Department of Biochemistry, Biozentrum, University of Basel (1995)
story: Many discoveries about mTOR depend on identifying proteins and the phosphate tags on them, and that is the job of mass spectrometry. Paul Jenö is a co-author of the 2017 Cancer Cell study in this Atlas (GUR2017) from Michael Hall's lab. In a mouse model where too much mTOR signalling causes fatty liver that turns into liver cancer, the team found that mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, drives the production of fatty acids and sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking either kind of fat synthesis prevented tumours in the mice, and in human liver cancer samples high lipid synthesis went together with mTORC2 activity.

Jenö has worked on protein analysis at the Biozentrum since at least the 1990s. A 1995 paper with Jenö as first author, from the Department of Biochemistry, described a simple method to digest proteins inside polyacrylamide gels to obtain internal sequences, a step that became routine in protein identification. Later papers list Jenö at the Biozentrum's Proteomics Core Facility, usually together with Suzette Moes, on studies ranging from mTOR signalling to maternal blood markers of Down syndrome (2009) and prostate cancer (2022).

PubMed shows more than 100 papers under this name, many of them from Michael Hall's lab, including the 2013 phosphoproteomics study that linked mTORC1 to pyrimidine synthesis. A current position after 2022 could not be confirmed.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author: provided protein mass spectrometry for the mouse study showing that mTORC2 drives liver cancer through lipid synthesis.

Moes S.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Moes S.role: Protein scientist at the Biozentrum Basel's proteomics facility who, with Paul Jenö, carried out mass spectrometry for many mTOR studies from Michael Hall's lab
Moes S.sub: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed records 1995–2022)
story: Suzette Moes is a co-author of the 2017 Cancer Cell study in this Atlas (GUR2017) from Michael Hall's lab. In mice in which too much mTOR signalling causes fatty liver that progresses to liver cancer, the team found that mTORC2 drives the production of fatty acids and sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking either kind of fat synthesis prevented tumours, and in human liver cancer samples high lipid synthesis went together with mTORC2 activity.

Moes's role in this and many other Basel papers was protein analysis by mass spectrometry. PubMed shows Moes working with Paul Jenö from at least 1995, when the two published a method for digesting proteins inside polyacrylamide gels to read their internal sequences, through work at the Biozentrum's proteomics facility on topics from mTOR signalling to maternal blood markers of Down syndrome (2009).
The PubMed record under this name and Basel runs to 2022. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author: contributed protein mass spectrometry to the mouse study showing that mTORC2 drives liver cancer through lipid synthesis.

Ahmed AAE.lab_name: Pharmacology and Toxicology Department, Faculty of Pharmacy, Helwan University (Ein Helwan, Egypt)
Ahmed AAE.role: Pharmacologist at Helwan University in Cairo who leads animal studies of how existing drugs and natural compounds protect tissues from inflammation, fibrosis and injury
Ahmed AAE.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology Department, Faculty of Pharmacy, Helwan University, Cairo, Egypt (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2020 to 2026)
story: Amany Ahmed is the senior (last) author of HAFEZ2026, a mouse study of psoriasis, the skin disease with thick, red, scaly patches. The team caused psoriasis-like skin disease in mice with imiquimod cream and then gave melittin, the main peptide in bee venom. Melittin reduced the severity of the skin disease by about 60 percent. In the treated skin the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway was turned down and autophagy, the cell's recycling system, was turned up. This is a mouse study at a high injected dose, so it shows a mechanism worth testing, not a treatment for people.

PubMed lists Ahmed at the Pharmacology and Toxicology Department of Helwan University's Faculty of Pharmacy on about 25 papers since 2020, usually as senior author. The studies follow a common plan: a disease is induced in rats or mice and a drug or plant compound is tested for protection. Examples include the diabetes drug lixisenatide in a rat model of stroke (2020), the weight-loss drug semaglutide in a rat model of osteoporosis after loss of the ovaries (2024), and the plant compound phloridzin against lung scarring caused by the cancer drug bleomycin (2026), where autophagy was again one of the processes measured.
No university profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given here.

highlights.HAFEZ2026: Senior author: showed in mice that melittin from bee venom eases psoriasis-like skin disease while lowering PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling and raising autophagy.

Hafez SA.lab_name: Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health (Abha, Saudi Arabia)
Hafez SA.role: Researcher with the Aseer Health Cluster in Abha, Saudi Arabia, and first author of a 2026 mouse study testing the bee-venom peptide melittin against psoriasis-like skin inflammation
Hafez SA.sub: Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health, Abha (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Saeed A Hafez was first author of a 2026 Saudi Pharmaceutical Journal study (HAFEZ2026) on psoriasis, a common skin disease in which skin cells grow too fast and the skin becomes red, thick and scaly. The team produced a psoriasis-like rash in mice by rubbing imiquimod cream on the skin, a standard laboratory model. They then injected melittin, the main active peptide of bee venom. At the higher dose the rash score fell by about 60 percent.

The study links the effect to the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, the chain of signals that tells cells to grow. Melittin lowered the activity of this pathway in the skin and raised markers of autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system that mTOR normally holds back. This is one mouse model, with melittin given by injection into the abdomen, so it does not show that bee venom or melittin would help people with psoriasis.

PubMed lists Hafez at the Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, part of the Saudi Ministry of Health, in Abha. No other publication could be tied to this author with confidence, and a fuller career history could not be confirmed.

highlights.HAFEZ2026: First author: tested melittin in a mouse model of psoriasis and linked the lower rash score to reduced PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling and more autophagy.

Hagiwara A.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Hagiwara A.role: First author of a 2012 mouse study from Michael Hall's lab showing that liver mTORC2 tells the liver that the animal has eaten, by switching on sugar breakdown and fat production
Hagiwara A.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall group (at the time of the study, 2012)
story: After a meal, insulin tells the liver to stop making glucose and to start burning it and storing the extra as fat. Asami Hagiwara was first author of the 2012 Cell Metabolism study in this Atlas (HAG2012), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel, which asked what role mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, plays in that switch. The team deleted rictor, a core part of mTORC2, only in the liver of mice.

In fed mice without liver mTORC2, the kinase Akt lost its activating phosphate at serine 473, and the enzyme glucokinase and the fat-making regulator SREBP1c became less active. The liver kept making glucose while glycolysis (sugar breakdown) and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice developed high blood sugar and high insulin with low blood lipids. In liver cells lacking mTORC2, an always-active form of Akt2 restored both sugar breakdown and fat production, while extra glucokinase restored only the sugar side, so Akt is the main route from mTORC2 to these outputs. The study, in mice and mouse liver cells, placed mTORC2 at the centre of the liver's response to insulin.
PubMed lists Hagiwara at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel on this paper. No other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, so the later career is not known.

highlights.HAG2012: First author: showed in mice that liver mTORC2 activates glycolysis and fat synthesis through Akt, glucokinase and SREBP1c.

Polak P.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Polak P.role: Cell biologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed, in mice, that switching off mTORC1 in fat tissue alone makes animals lean and protects them from diet-induced obesity
Polak P.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2006–2012, at the time of the study) · current position not confirmed
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex built around the mTOR kinase, needs a partner protein called raptor to work. In 2008 Pazit Polak and colleagues in Michael Hall's lab removed raptor only in the fat cells of mice. The animals stayed lean, resisted weight gain on a high-fat diet and handled insulin better. Their fat tissue burned more energy because its mitochondria were more uncoupled, meaning they released energy as heat instead of storing it. The study showed that mTORC1 in one tissue, fat, can shape the metabolism of the whole body. It is a mouse result and says nothing direct about people.

Polak worked at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel throughout these papers. With Hall, Polak wrote a 2006 commentary on how mTORC2 activates the kinase Akt with the help of its subunit SIN1, and a 2009 review on how mTOR controls metabolism across the whole body. Polak is also a co-author of a 2007 study that identified PRAS40 and PRR5-like protein as new mTOR partners, of a 2009 study on mice lacking rictor (the core mTORC2 subunit) in fat, and of the 2012 liver mTORC2 paper.
A current position for Pazit Polak could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.POL2008: First author: removed raptor from fat cells of mice and found lean, insulin-sensitive animals with more uncoupled mitochondria in their fat.

Han JM.lab_name: College of Pharmacy, Yonsei University (Incheon, South Korea)
Han JM.role: Pharmacologist at Yonsei University who found that leucyl-tRNA synthetase, the enzyme that loads leucine onto its tRNA, doubles as the cell's leucine sensor for mTORC1, and who now studies how this enzyme links nutrients to growth signalling
Han JM.sub: College of Pharmacy and Department of Integrated OMICS for Biomedical Science, Yonsei University (papers since 2017) · Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center, Seoul National University (Sunghoon Kim group, at the time of HAN2012)
story: Leucine is the amino acid that switches mTORC1 on most strongly, but in 2012 nobody knew which protein inside the cell actually detects it. Jung Min Han's 2012 Cell paper (HAN2012), from Sunghoon Kim's group at Seoul National University, proposed an answer. Leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LRS) is the enzyme that attaches leucine to its matching transfer RNA so the ribosome can use it to build proteins. The team showed in cultured cells that LRS also binds the Rag GTPases, the switch proteins that dock mTORC1 on the lysosome, and acts as a GAP for one of them in a leucine-dependent way. That turns the Rags to their active form and switches mTORC1 on. An enzyme everyone knew for its housekeeping job turned out to be a sensor as well.
The finding comes from cell experiments, and it gave the field a concrete candidate for the sensor that links leucine to mTORC1.

Han has kept working on LRS at Yonsei University, where Han is a faculty member in the College of Pharmacy and the Department of Integrated OMICS for Biomedical Science. As corresponding author, Han led a 2017 Nature Communications study showing that small molecules blocking the contact between LRS and the Rag protein RagD can dampen leucine-driven mTORC1 signalling, and later work on a pyrazolone-based inhibitor series built from that idea. Han also contributed to a 2019 Science paper showing that LRS1 controls leucine use depending on glucose supply, and was senior author on work showing that a sugar tag on LRS1 links leucine and glucose availability to mTORC1.

highlights.HAN2012: First author: showed in cells that leucyl-tRNA synthetase senses leucine and activates mTORC1 by acting on the Rag GTPases.

Hands JM.lab_name: Department of Pathology, University of Southern California (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Hands JM.role: Researcher in integrative medicine and nutrition science, trained at George Washington University, who wrote a cautious review of whether off-label rapamycin is justified for healthy adults
Hands JM.sub: Department of Pathology, University of Southern California (2026 paper) · earlier at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences (2025)
story: Jacob Hands was first author of a 2025 review in Aging (HAN2025) that asked a direct question: what does the human evidence say about taking low-dose rapamycin, or related mTOR-blocking drugs, to slow aging in healthy adults? Some people already take rapamycin off-label for this reason, based mostly on animal studies in which it lengthened life. The review collected the clinical studies and re-analysed one group of people using PhenoAge, a 'biological age' score calculated from routine blood tests.

Its verdict was careful. The animal data on lifespan are strong, but the human studies are small, short and use different doses and measures, and they have not shown that rapamycin slows aging in healthy people. The review is useful as a reminder of the gap between results in mice and evidence in people.

PubMed lists Hands at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences on the 2025 review. A 2026 narrative review in Nutrients, on common genetic variants that affect blood fats and heart disease risk and how diet might interact with them, lists Hands at the Department of Pathology of the University of Southern California, with co-authors from George Washington University's Office of Integrative Medicine and Health. No personal page was found to confirm job title or training.

highlights.HAN2025: First author: reviewed the human evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults and concluded that it does not yet show a slowing of aging.

Rosen B.role: Los Angeles physician, originally trained as a retina specialist, who runs a longevity-medicine practice built around rapamycin and metformin, and senior author of a cautious review of the human evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults
Rosen B.sub: Physician, MTOR MD longevity practice, Los Angeles · retina fellowships, Lions Eye Institute (Perth) and Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital (Melbourne) · ophthalmology residency, Jules Stein Eye Institute, UCLA · MD, University of Florida
story: Rapamycin extends lifespan in laboratory animals, and some doctors now prescribe it in low doses to healthy people hoping to slow ageing. HAN2025, a 2025 review in Aging with Bradley Rosen as last author, asks what the human evidence actually shows. The authors gathered the clinical studies of rapamycin and related mTOR inhibitors in healthy adults and re-analysed one cohort with PhenoAge, a biological-age score calculated from blood tests. Their conclusion is careful: the animal data are strong, but human studies have not yet shown that rapamycin slows ageing in healthy people. The review is useful because it holds human data to a strict standard.

Rosen came to this field from eye medicine. A podcast biography says he studied mathematics and statistics, earned an MD at the University of Florida, trained in ophthalmology at the Jules Stein Eye Institute at UCLA, and did retina fellowships at the Lions Eye Institute in Western Australia and the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital in Melbourne. PubMed has a 1999 case report from the Lions Eye Institute with him as first author, on eye inflammation in cat scratch disease. According to the same biography, he turned to the biology of ageing in 2013.

He now runs MTOR MD, a longevity-medicine practice in Los Angeles. Its website describes mTOR inhibition with rapamycin and AMPK targeting with metformin as its core treatments, alongside work on diet, exercise, sleep and metabolic health. On the review PubMed lists his affiliation as an mTOR medicine practitioner in Los Angeles.

highlights.HAN2025: Last author: a review concluding that human evidence does not yet show that low-dose rapamycin slows ageing in healthy adults, with a PhenoAge re-analysis of one cohort.

Javors MA.lab_name: Biological Psychiatry Analytical Laboratory, Department of Psychiatry, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Javors MA.role: Pharmacologist and professor at UT Health San Antonio who directs an analytical laboratory for biochemical and drug measurements, and a co-author of rapamycin studies in mice and in older people
Javors MA.sub: Professor, Departments of Psychiatry and Pharmacology, and Director, Biological Psychiatry Analytical Laboratory, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · Adjunct Professor, College of Pharmacy, University of Texas at Austin · PhD in pharmacology, University of Colorado at Boulder (1979)
story: A drug can only be judged if you know how much of it actually reaches the blood. Martin Javors appears as a co-author on rapamycin studies from San Antonio, where the measurement of drug levels is part of the work. In the Atlas pilot trial KRA2018, 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95 took daily rapamycin or placebo for at least eight weeks. The drug was well tolerated, with only small changes in red blood cells and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance over that short period. The trial was small and short and only checked safety, but it laid groundwork for larger human studies.

Javors is also a co-author of the Atlas study STR2022 from the NIA Interventions Testing Program, which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin plus acarbose, a drug that slows sugar uptake from the gut, started at nine months of age gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had given in earlier groups. In females the combination did about as well as rapamycin alone.

PubMed lists 16 papers with Javors that involve rapamycin, including earlier Interventions Testing Program reports such as the 2016 study in which metformin plus rapamycin extended mouse lifespan, and a 2015 study in which rapamycin shortened life in db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes. Most give the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio as the address.

Javors earned a degree in pharmacy at the University of Texas at Austin and a PhD in pharmacology at the University of Colorado at Boulder in 1979, followed by a pharmacology internship at the UT Health Science Center at San Antonio. Javors is a tenured professor in the Departments of Psychiatry and Pharmacology there and directs the Biological Psychiatry Analytical Laboratory, which makes biochemical measurements for psychiatric research, including tests for psychiatric drugs. Javors' own research has covered biochemical markers of alcohol and nicotine use, the brain messengers serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline and their transporters, and how serotonin function relates to impulsivity.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author: part of the team behind the pilot trial showing that eight weeks of daily rapamycin was well tolerated in healthy adults aged 70 to 95.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author: part of the Interventions Testing Program study in which rapamycin plus acarbose gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts.

Fernandez E.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Fernandez E.role: Aging researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who has worked on rapamycin studies in mice and common marmosets, including the NIA Interventions Testing Program
Fernandez E.credit: Portrait: Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio
Fernandez E.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, and Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System (PubMed affiliation 2014–2026) · Department of Pharmacology, UT Health San Antonio
story: Rapamycin lengthens life in mice, but mice are far from people. Elizabeth Fernandez is a co-author of two Atlas studies that tried the drug in the common marmoset, a small, short-lived monkey. The 2014 study (TAR2014) worked out how to give rapamycin by mouth in a coated form, reached blood levels similar to those in mouse and human work, and saw lower mTORC1 signalling, the growth-control pathway, in the animals' tissues. The 2015 study (ROS2015) found that long-term treatment had only minor effects on body weight, activity, blood fats and glucose handling. Neither study measured lifespan.

Fernandez is also a co-author of a 2022 report from the NIA Interventions Testing Program (STR2022), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin combined with acarbose, a diabetes drug, gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had in earlier cohorts. In females the combination was no better than rapamycin alone.

PubMed places Fernandez at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and at the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the South Texas Veterans Health Care System on papers from 2014 to 2026. A 2026 paper with Randy Strong found that long-term rapamycin protected aging mice against the decline in motor function, with a larger effect in females. A current job title could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.TAR2014: Co-author: part of the team that first described oral rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in common marmosets.
highlights.ROS2015: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that long-term rapamycin had only minor metabolic effects in marmosets.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author: contributed to the Interventions Testing Program report in which rapamycin plus acarbose extended male mouse lifespan beyond rapamycin alone.

Nelson JF.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Nelson JF.role: Physiologist of aging at UT Health San Antonio who studies how calorie restriction, sex hormones and drugs change mouse lifespan, and a co-investigator on the Interventions Testing Program
Nelson JF.sub: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2003–2026)
story: James Nelson is a co-author of the Atlas study STR2022 from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP). The ITP tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at the same time, so a result has to hold up in different labs. In this cohort, male mice given rapamycin together with acarbose, a drug that slows sugar uptake from the gut, starting at 9 months of age lived longer than males on rapamycin alone in earlier ITP cohorts. In females the combination was neither better nor worse than rapamycin alone. The drug captopril also gave a small lifespan gain. All of this is in mice.

Nelson's own research at the Barshop Institute asks why some interventions slow aging and why the sexes differ. Nelson's group found that how well a mouse keeps its body fat predicts whether dietary restriction will lengthen its life (2011), that the higher stress-hormone levels of calorie-restricted mice help explain their lower inflammation (2019), and that castration before puberty removed the lifespan difference between male and female mice (2023).

As part of the San Antonio ITP team, Nelson is a co-author on many of the program's reports, including the 2016 study in which acarbose, an antioxidant and other compounds lengthened male lifespan, the 2021 report that 17-alpha-estradiol given late in life helped male mice, and a 2026 report of eight compounds that did not extend lifespan.

highlights.STR2022: Co-author from the San Antonio ITP site: rapamycin plus acarbose from 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts.

Wilkinson JE.lab_name: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Wilkinson JE.role: Pathologist at the University of Michigan who examines animal tissues for aging and cancer studies, and first author of the 2012 paper showing that rapamycin slows many signs of aging in mice
Wilkinson JE.sub: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor (papers 2012–2026)
story: When rapamycin was shown to lengthen mouse lifespan in 2009, a key question remained: did it slow aging itself, or did it simply delay the cancers that kill most laboratory mice? John Wilkinson was first author of the 2012 Aging Cell paper (WIL2012), with Richard Miller as senior author, that tackled this question by looking closely at many tissues. A pathologist studies tissue under the microscope to find disease and damage.

In mice given rapamycin, age-related changes in the heart, liver, adrenal glands, endometrium and tendon developed more slowly, and the age-related fall in spontaneous activity was smaller. The paper also reported harms: treated mice had more testicular degeneration and more cataracts. Because the benefits showed up across many organs, beyond a drop in tumours, the authors argued that rapamycin slows aging more broadly. These results are from mice.

PubMed lists Wilkinson at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor on dozens of papers, often as the pathologist on mouse studies from other groups. The most recent, from 2026 in Nature Immunology, is a study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory on how the fat-sensing factor PPAR-delta changes the balance between cancer cells and immune cells.

highlights.WIL2012: First author: showed that rapamycin slows age-related change in heart, liver, adrenal gland, endometrium and tendon in mice, while increasing cataracts and testicular degeneration.

Allison DB.lab_name: Department of Biostatistics, University of Alabama at Birmingham (Birmingham, Alabama, USA)
Allison DB.role: Biostatistician and obesity researcher, long at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and later dean of public health at Indiana University, known for work on nutrition, obesity and research rigour
Allison DB.sub: Dean, Indiana University School of Public Health-Bloomington (appointed 2017) · Distinguished Professor, Quetelet Endowed Professor and Director of the NIH Nutrition Obesity Research Center, University of Alabama at Birmingham · fellowship, Columbia University and St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital Center (1994) · postdoc, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (1991) · PhD, Hofstra University (1990)
story: David Allison is a co-author of MAT2017, a Nature Communications paper that brought together the two long-running studies of caloric restriction in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging and one at the University of Wisconsin. The two studies had seemed to disagree: Wisconsin reported longer survival with fewer calories, the NIA study did not. Looking at both side by side, the authors found that calorie-restricted monkeys were healthier in both studies. Whether they also lived longer depended on how each study was designed, including the age at which restriction started and what the control monkeys ate. Monkeys are close relatives of humans, so these studies are among the best animal evidence on eating less and ageing. Caloric restriction is one of the conditions in which mTOR activity falls, which is why it appears in this Atlas.

Allison's part in such work is mainly statistical. After a PhD at Hofstra University in 1990, with a thesis on types of obese persons, he did postdoctoral work at Johns Hopkins and a fellowship at Columbia University and St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital Center. At the University of Alabama at Birmingham he was a Distinguished Professor, Quetelet Endowed Professor and Director of the NIH-funded Nutrition Obesity Research Center. His research covers obesity and nutrition, biostatistics, quantitative genetics and clinical trials, and the rigour and reproducibility of research; he helped organise a 2017 National Academy of Sciences colloquium on reproducibility.

In 2017 Allison was appointed dean of the Indiana University School of Public Health-Bloomington. The current position after that could not be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAT2017: Co-author of the joint analysis of the NIA and Wisconsin monkey studies, which found health benefits of caloric restriction in both and survival effects that depended on study design.

He Y.lab_name: Xuefeng Yu group, Division of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
He Y.role: Endocrinology researcher in Xuefeng Yu's group at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan who studies the liver- and fat-derived hormone ANGPTL8 in aging and diabetes
He Y.sub: Division of Endocrinology, Department of Internal Medicine, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (papers 2024–2026)
story: Yi He is first author of the Atlas study HE2026, with Xuefeng Yu as senior author. ANGPTL8 is a hormone-like protein released into the blood that helps control fat and sugar metabolism. In a large human cohort, higher ANGPTL8 levels went along with an older biological age and a higher risk of death. In mice, deleting the Angptl8 gene lengthened life and lowered markers of senescence, the state in which cells stop dividing and release inflammatory signals.

The team traced the mechanism in fat tissue. ANGPTL8 binds AKT2, a kinase in the insulin pathway, and drives the AKT-mTOR-S6K chain that pushes fat cells into senescence; blocking that chain removed the effect. The human data are associations, while cause and mechanism come from mice and cells, so ANGPTL8 is a candidate driver of fat-tissue aging rather than a proven one in people.

Yi He's other papers come from the same Tongji endocrinology group and follow ANGPTL8 into other organs: it steers bone marrow stem cells towards fat instead of bone during skeletal aging (2025), it drives inflammation and scarring in kidney tubule cells in diabetic kidney disease through AKT2 (2025), and blocking it protected against diabetes-related memory problems in mice (2024).

highlights.HE2026: First author: linked circulating ANGPTL8 to biological age in people and showed in mice that it drives fat-cell senescence through AKT2 and mTOR-S6K.

Hennessy-Strahs S.lab_name: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center, Houston Methodist Hospital (Houston, Texas, USA)
Hennessy-Strahs S.role: Researcher who moved from studying heart pumps and blood vessels at Penn to transplant immunology in Houston, and first author of a study showing that the lung's cleaning macrophages need mTOR to survive
Hennessy-Strahs S.sub: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center and Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, and Texas A&M University College of Medicine (papers 2025–2026) · Texas A&M University (2022 paper) · Division of Cardiovascular Surgery, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (papers 2017–2021)
story: Samson Hennessy-Strahs is first author of an Atlas study (HEN2026) on alveolar macrophages, the immune cells that sit in the tiny air sacs of the lung and swallow up surfactant, the soapy film that keeps the sacs open. In mice, the team removed mTOR only from myeloid cells, the family that includes macrophages. The alveolar macrophages slowly disappeared, the ones left could not eat particles well, fat built up inside them, and the lungs filled with material in a pattern resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a rare human lung disease. Treating normal mice with the mTOR-blocking drug temsirolimus gave a similar picture.

The finding matters because mTOR inhibitors are used in transplant patients and in cancer, and some patients develop lung problems on them. The study suggests one possible reason: the drugs may starve the lung's own cleaning crew. The work was done in mice, so whether the same happens in patients still has to be shown.

The publication record shows two research phases. From 2017 to 2021 Hennessy-Strahs worked in the Division of Cardiovascular Surgery at the University of Pennsylvania, mostly with Carlo Bartoli, on how left ventricular assist devices (mechanical heart pumps) damage blood proteins such as von Willebrand factor and cause abnormal blood vessels in the gut. A 2022 paper lists Texas A&M University. Since 2025 the papers come from Xian C. Li's transplant immunology group at Houston Methodist Hospital, including a 2025 study on reprogramming macrophages to protect heart transplants in mice. The 2026 Atlas paper also lists the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine. No official profile page was found, so the current role could not be confirmed.

highlights.HEN2026: First author: showed in mice that alveolar macrophages need mTOR to survive and that losing it, by gene deletion or the drug temsirolimus, causes a lung disease resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

Holz MK.lab_name: Department of Cell and Molecular Physiology, Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, New York Medical College (Valhalla, New York, USA)
Holz MK.role: Cell biologist who, as a postdoc with John Blenis, showed how mTOR and S6K1 trade places on eIF3 to start protein synthesis, and who now studies mTOR in breast cancer and the rare lung disease LAM at New York Medical College
Holz MK.sub: Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences and Department of Cell and Molecular Physiology, New York Medical College (2026) · Department of Cell Biology and Anatomy, New York Medical College (from 2018) · Department of Biology, Stern College for Women, Yeshiva University, and Albert Einstein Cancer Center (papers to 2017) · Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, John Blenis lab (2005)
story: Marina Holz is first author of the Atlas study HOL2005, done in John Blenis's lab at Harvard Medical School. It answered a basic question: how does mTOR, once switched on by growth signals, get the cell's protein-making machinery started? The answer centred on eIF3, a large protein platform that helps ribosomes find the start of a messenger RNA. In resting cells the kinase S6K1 sits on eIF3 in an inactive state. When the cell is stimulated, mTOR arrives with its partner raptor, phosphorylates S6K1, and S6K1 lets go of eIF3 to phosphorylate its own targets, which helps assemble the complex that begins translation. The paper turned a list of phosphorylation events into an ordered sequence on one scaffold. It was done in cultured human cells.

After Harvard, Holz set up a lab in the Department of Biology at Stern College for Women of Yeshiva University, with a link to the Albert Einstein Cancer Center. The group studied how estrogen and mTOR signalling feed each other in breast cancer: mTOR and S6K1 together with the MAPK pathway phosphorylate estrogen receptor alpha (2010), estrogen raises S6K1 levels in a loop that drives breast cancer cell growth (2012), and estrogen tunes the eIF3 subunit eIF3f through mTORC1 (2018).

A second line of work is lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease of women caused by overactive mTORC1. In mice carrying TSC2-deficient tumours, rapamycin combined with resveratrol switched on cell death (2015), and Holz was senior author of a small clinical study of resveratrol plus sirolimus in LAM patients (2023). At New York Medical College in Valhalla, Holz's recent papers report that CDK4/6 inhibitors suppress mTOR activity in LAM cells (2026) and that education level affects how quickly LAM patients are diagnosed and treated (2026).

highlights.HOL2005: First author: showed in cultured cells that mTOR/raptor and S6K1 swap places on the eIF3 complex in an ordered sequence that starts translation.

Horvath S.lab_name: Department of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Horvath S.role: Biostatistician and geneticist who built the first pan-tissue epigenetic clock, a DNA methylation test that estimates biological age, and co-developed the network method WGCNA
Horvath S.sub: Principal investigator, Altos Labs · Professor of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, and of Biostatistics, Fielding School of Public Health, University of California, Los Angeles (faculty since 2000) · ScD in Biostatistics, Harvard School of Public Health (2000) · PhD in Mathematics, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (1995) · Diplom in Mathematics and Physics, Technische Universität Berlin (1989)
story: Cells carry chemical tags on their DNA, called methyl groups, and the pattern of these tags shifts with age in a predictable way. An epigenetic clock reads the pattern at selected sites and turns it into an age estimate. In HOR2021, Steve Horvath and colleagues, with Adam Salmon's group in San Antonio, built two such clocks for the blood of common marmosets, small short-lived monkeys used in aging research. One clock, trained on both human and marmoset data, also tracked age reasonably well in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate group of marmosets they asked whether rapamycin, the mTOR-blocking drug that lengthens life in mice, would make blood look younger by this measure. The clocks did not detect a significant change. This is a null result for one biomarker in blood; it does not show that rapamycin has no effect on aging in marmosets.

Horvath trained first in mathematics and physics at the Technische Universität Berlin, took a PhD in mathematics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1995 and an ScD in biostatistics at the Harvard School of Public Health in 2000. He joined UCLA that year as a professor of human genetics and of biostatistics. With members of his lab he developed weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA), a widely used method for finding groups of genes that act together. In 2013 he published the Horvath clock, a DNA methylation age estimator that works across nearly all tissues and cell types, and he co-founded the non-profit Clock Foundation.
He is now a principal investigator at Altos Labs, a company that studies cell rejuvenation, and is still listed as a professor at UCLA.

highlights.HOR2021: First author: built marmoset epigenetic clocks for blood and found no significant effect of rapamycin on epigenetic age.

Mattison JA.role: Primate aging researcher at the US National Institute on Aging who led the NIA study of calorie restriction in rhesus monkeys and its comparison with the Wisconsin study
Mattison JA.sub: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, NIH (papers to 2026) · Laboratory of Experimental Gerontology, NIA, NIH Animal Center, Dickerson, Maryland (2012)
story: Julie Mattison was first author of the 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that compared the two long-term studies of calorie restriction in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin. Eating less without malnutrition extends life in many animals, and lower mTOR activity is one of the routes thought to explain it. The two monkey studies had reached different conclusions about survival. Looking at both data sets together, the authors found consistent health benefits, while the survival effect depended on study design and on the diet of the control animals. This is evidence from monkeys, not from people.

Mattison was also first author of the 2012 Nature paper reporting that calorie restriction had not improved survival in the NIA monkeys, at that time listed at the Laboratory of Experimental Gerontology at the NIH Animal Center in Dickerson, Maryland, with Rafael de Cabo as senior author. That result, at odds with the Wisconsin study, set up the 2017 comparison.

In the Atlas, Mattison is also a co-author of a 2021 study (HOR2021) that built epigenetic clocks for the common marmoset, a small monkey, and found that rapamycin did not significantly change epigenetic age in these animals. PubMed lists Mattison at the NIA Translational Gerontology Branch on more recent papers, including a 2026 preprint on muscle aging that used cells from old and young rhesus monkeys.

highlights.MAT2017: First author: led the direct comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin rhesus monkey calorie restriction studies.
highlights.HOR2021: Co-author of the marmoset study that built epigenetic clocks and found no significant effect of rapamycin on epigenetic age.

Mattison JA.lab_name: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, National Institutes of Health (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)

Hosokawa N.lab_name: Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (Tokyo, Japan)
Hosokawa N.role: Cell biologist who, in Noboru Mizushima's lab, showed how mTORC1 directly holds the autophagy starter complex in check and helped discover the autophagy protein Atg101
Hosokawa N.sub: Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (Noboru Mizushima lab, 2009, at the time of the study) · Department of Bioregulation and Metabolism, Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science (2007)
story: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane and breaks them down for raw materials. Cells should only do this when food is short, so something has to keep autophagy off when nutrients are plentiful. In 2009, Nao Hosokawa, first author of the Atlas study HOS2009 from Noboru Mizushima's lab, showed in cultured cells how mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, does it. The autophagy starter kinase ULK1 sits in a large complex with Atg13 and FIP200. When nutrients are present, mTORC1 physically joins this complex and adds phosphate groups to ULK1 and Atg13, which keeps them inactive. Starvation or the drug rapamycin releases this brake, and autophagy begins. This gave a direct molecular link between nutrient sensing and autophagy.

In the same year Hosokawa was also first author of a paper in Autophagy that identified Atg101, a new mammalian protein that binds Atg13 and is needed for autophagy to proceed. An earlier first-author paper from 2007, at the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science and again with Mizushima, built mouse cell lines in which autophagy can be switched on and off with an antibiotic, and used them to show that autophagy helps cells shrink during starvation.
PubMed records under this name with autophagy work stop after 2009, and no later institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.HOS2009: First author: showed in cultured cells that mTORC1 binds the ULK1-Atg13-FIP200 complex when nutrients are plentiful and phosphorylates ULK1 and Atg13 to keep autophagy off.

Talbott G.lab_name: Manning Lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Talbott G.role: Research assistant in Brendan Manning's mTOR lab at Harvard in 2013 and 2014, who contributed to studies on where the TSC complex sits in the cell and how metformin reaches mTORC1
Talbott G.sub: Research Associate, The Jackson Laboratory (per Manning lab alumni page) · research assistant, Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2013–2014, at the time of the studies)
story: George Talbott appears in this Atlas on two papers from Brendan Manning's lab at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. MEN2014 showed that the TSC complex, the main brake on mTORC1 (the growth-control complex), works by sitting on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment where mTORC1 is switched on. Insulin pushes the TSC complex off the lysosome, which releases the brake, so the cell can combine signals about hormones and nutrients at one place. HOW2017 showed in mouse liver and liver cells that the diabetes drug metformin lowers cell energy and, at low doses, inhibits mTORC1 through the energy sensor AMPK and the TSC complex.

The Manning lab alumni page lists Talbott as a research assistant in the lab from 2013 to 2014 and gives a later position as Research Associate at The Jackson Laboratory, a mouse genetics research institute. No other official page was found, so the present role could not be confirmed.
