highlights.HOW2017: Co-author, from the time as a research assistant in the Manning lab, on the paper showing metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.
highlights.MEN2014: Co-author on the paper showing that insulin moves the TSC complex off the lysosome, releasing the brake on mTORC1.

Turner M.lab_name: Manning Lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Turner M.role: Research assistant and lab manager in Brendan Manning's mTOR lab at Harvard from 2014 to 2016, who contributed to studies on nucleotide synthesis in tumour cells and on metformin's route to mTORC1
Turner M.sub: Postdoctoral Fellow, University of California, San Francisco (per Manning lab alumni page) · research assistant and lab manager, Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2014–2016, at the time of the studies)
story: Marc Turner is a co-author on two Atlas papers from Brendan Manning's lab. VAL2017 studied cells that lack the TSC genes, so their mTORC1 (the growth-control complex) is always on. Such cells make DNA building blocks, nucleotides, at a high rate to keep up with growth; when nucleotide supply falls behind demand, DNA copying stalls, a condition called replication stress. The study used this imbalance as a weak point that drugs can target, tested in cells and mouse tumour models. HOW2017 showed in mouse liver and liver cells that the diabetes drug metformin lowers cell energy and, at low doses, inhibits mTORC1 through AMPK and the TSC complex.

The Manning lab alumni page lists Turner as research assistant and lab manager from 2014 to 2016 and gives a later position as Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of California, San Francisco. The common surname made it impossible to match later PubMed papers with confidence, so present research is not described here.

highlights.VAL2017: Co-author on the paper linking hyperactive mTORC1 to nucleotide demand and a drug-sensitive weakness in TSC-deficient cells.
highlights.HOW2017: Co-author on the paper showing metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.

Huang W.lab_name: Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Huang W.role: Neuroscientist trained in Mauro Costa-Mattioli's memory lab at Baylor, first author of the study that showed mTORC2 is needed for long-term memory through control of the actin skeleton
Huang W.sub: Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (latest PubMed affiliation, 2017) · Department of Neuroscience and Memory and Brain Research Center, Baylor College of Medicine (Costa-Mattioli lab, 2011–2017)
story: Long-term memories need new proteins, and most memory work on mTOR had focused on mTORC1, the complex that drives protein synthesis. Wei Huang's 2013 Nature Neuroscience paper, with Mauro Costa-Mattioli as senior author, looked at the other complex, mTORC2. Deleting its essential partner Rictor in the mouse forebrain after birth lowered mTORC2 activity and selectively impaired long-term memory and the late, protein-dependent phase of long-term potentiation (LTP), the strengthening of synapses thought to store memories. Flies lacking TORC2 showed a similar long-term memory defect.

The team traced the problem to actin, the protein filaments that shape dendritic spines, the small knobs where synapses sit. Actin polymerisation was reduced in the mutant hippocampus, and restoring it rescued both late LTP and long-term memory. A compound that raised mTORC2 activity turned short-lasting LTP into the long-lasting form and improved memory in normal mice. The work showed that mTORC2, not only mTORC1, is needed to consolidate long-term memories.

Huang's PubMed record with Costa-Mattioli runs from 2011 to 2017 and includes a pharmacogenetic study showing mTORC1 is required for late LTP and memory storage (2011) and a 2016 eLife paper showing that translational control by eIF2alpha phosphorylation explains why adolescent mice are more sensitive to cocaine. A 2017 paper lists Huang at both Baylor and the Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience at Johns Hopkins. The current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HUA2013: First author: showed that forebrain mTORC2 loss impairs long-term memory and late LTP through reduced actin polymerisation, and that boosting mTORC2 enhances memory.

Huang C.lab_name: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (Hohhot, China)
Huang C.role: Radiation oncology researcher in Hohhot and first author of a study linking the PIK3CA E545K mutation to faster growth and invasion of cervical cancer through AKT/mTOR signalling
Huang C.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: PIK3CA is the gene for the catalytic part of PI3K, an enzyme at the top of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway. Certain spelling mistakes in this gene, called hotspot mutations, keep the enzyme switched on. In the Atlas study HUANG2026 in Molecular Genetics and Genomics, Congxiu Huang was first author. The team sequenced tumours from 61 patients with cervical cancer and found PIK3CA among the most often mutated genes. They then put the E545K mutation, one of the common hotspots, into cervical cancer cell lines. The cells grew and invaded faster, died less, and showed stronger AKT/mTOR signalling. Human cancer cells grown as tumours in mice (a xenograft model) behaved the same way. The work suggests that patients whose tumours carry this mutation might be candidates for drugs against the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, but it did not test such drugs in patients.

PubMed lists Huang at the Department of Radiation Oncology of the Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University in Hohhot, with Sun X as senior author. Because the name is common, no other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, and no official profile page was found.

highlights.HUANG2026: First author: found PIK3CA among the most often mutated genes in 61 cervical tumours and showed in cells and xenografts that E545K drives growth and invasion through AKT/mTOR.

Hudes G.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Hudes G.role: Medical oncologist at Fox Chase Cancer Center who led the phase 3 trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus lengthens survival in poor-prognosis advanced kidney cancer
Hudes G.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia (at the time of the study, 2007)
story: In HUD2007, Gary Hudes was first author of the large randomised trial of temsirolimus, one of the first mTOR inhibitors tested in cancer. Patients with advanced kidney cancer and a poor outlook were given temsirolimus, interferon alfa (the standard treatment of the time), or both. Temsirolimus alone extended median overall survival to 10.9 months, compared with 7.3 months on interferon alfa. Rash, high blood sugar and high blood fats were more common with temsirolimus, which fits with mTOR's role in controlling metabolism. The trial is one of the strongest human data sets in this Atlas because it is a randomised phase 3 study.

At the time of the trial Hudes worked in the Department of Medical Oncology at Fox Chase Cancer Center in Philadelphia. The PubMed record under 'Hudes G' and 'Hudes GR' runs to more than 170 papers, but the name matches other authors as well, so the later career is not described here.

highlights.HUD2007: First author: reported the phase 3 trial in which temsirolimus alone gave longer survival than interferon alfa in poor-prognosis advanced kidney cancer.

Yang Q.lab_name: Kun-Liang Guan lab, Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Yang Q.role: Researcher in Kun-Liang Guan's Michigan lab and first author of the 2006 study that identified Sin1 as an essential part of mTOR complex 2
Yang Q.sub: Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (Kun-Liang Guan lab, at the time of the study)
story: mTOR, the cell's growth-control enzyme, works inside two separate protein complexes. mTORC1 is the one blocked by rapamycin and controls protein production and growth. mTORC2 is not blocked by short rapamycin treatment and adds a phosphate group to Akt, a protein that keeps cells alive and helps them respond to insulin. In 2006 the parts of mTORC2 were still being worked out.

Qian Yang's paper in Genes and Development (YAN2006), from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at the University of Michigan, showed that a protein called Sin1 belongs to mTORC2 but not to mTORC1. The team used fly and human cells and mouse genetics. When Sin1 was lowered, Akt phosphorylation dropped and Rictor, the defining partner of mTORC2, no longer held on to mTOR. In a test tube, mTORC2 needed Sin1 to be active. Sin1 is now counted as one of the core subunits of mTORC2, and this paper was one of the first to show it.
The name Qian Yang is common, and no web page could be tied with confidence to this author, so the profile shows only the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.YAN2006: First author: showed that Sin1 is an essential mTORC2 component needed for the complex to hold together and to phosphorylate Akt.

Iyer G.lab_name: Genitourinary Oncology Service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Iyer G.role: Medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering who heads its bladder cancer section and studies the genetics behind how bladder tumors respond to drugs
Iyer G.sub: Section Head, Bladder Cancer, Genitourinary Oncology Service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · Medical Oncology fellowship, Memorial Sloan Kettering · Internal Medicine residency, University of Michigan · MD, Vanderbilt University School of Medicine
story: Gopa Iyer is first author of an Atlas study (IYE2012) that started with one unusual patient. In a clinical trial of everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR, in advanced bladder cancer, one patient had a complete and unusually long-lasting remission. The team sequenced the whole genome of that patient's tumor and found a mutation that knocks out TSC1. TSC1 is part of the brake that normally keeps mTOR in check, so a tumor without it depends heavily on mTOR and is easy to hit with an mTOR blocker.

The group then checked 109 more bladder tumors and found TSC1 mutations in about 8 percent. In the trial, patients whose tumors carried such mutations tended to do better on everolimus. Because the idea grew from a single patient, the Atlas treats it as a strong hypothesis rather than proof. The paper helped start the practice of studying exceptional responders: sequencing the rare patient for whom a drug works unusually well to learn who else might benefit.

Iyer trained in medicine at Vanderbilt University, did a residency in internal medicine at the University of Michigan, and completed a medical oncology fellowship at Memorial Sloan Kettering. Today Iyer is a genitourinary medical oncologist and early drug development specialist there and heads the bladder cancer section. The research centers on the genetic makeup of bladder cancer through MSK's Bladder Cancer Oncogenome Project, and on clinical trials of new drugs for cancers of the bladder, kidney and prostate.

highlights.IYE2012: First author: led the genome sequencing of an exceptional everolimus responder and the follow-up that linked TSC1 loss to drug sensitivity in bladder cancer.

Jackson LN.lab_name: Mockett Lab, Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (Mobile, Alabama, USA)
Jackson LN.role: Researcher in Robin Mockett's lab at the University of South Alabama who showed that rapamycin's effect on fruit fly lifespan swings from harmful to helpful depending on the food
Jackson LN.sub: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (at the time of the 2026 study)
story: Lauren Jackson is the first author of JAC2026, a GeroScience paper from Robin Mockett's lab at the University of South Alabama. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, is often described as a drug that lengthens life in many animals. This fruit fly (Drosophila) study tested that claim carefully across five fly strains, both sexes and two kinds of food.

The answer depended on the diet. On a cornmeal and torula yeast food, rapamycin shortened life in 19 of 26 experiments. On a richer brewer's yeast food it helped in 8 experiments, made no difference in 14, and never caused clear harm. Changes in median lifespan ranged from a 51 percent loss to a 5 percent gain and varied with sex and strain. Rapamycin was also toxic to developing flies at higher doses. The lesson for a reader is that a lifespan result in one lab, on one food, may not carry over to other conditions. It is a fly study, so it says nothing direct about people.
PubMed shows only this paper under this name with Mockett, and no official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.JAC2026: First author: showed across five fly strains that rapamycin's effect on lifespan depends on diet, from clearly harmful to modestly helpful.

Kim YC.lab_name: Vallon Lab, Division of Nephrology and Hypertension, University of California San Diego and VA San Diego Healthcare System (La Jolla, California, USA)
Kim YC.role: Cell biologist who studied mTOR and autophagy in Kun-Liang Guan's lab at UC San Diego and later moved to kidney research in Volker Vallon's group
Kim YC.sub: Division of Nephrology and Hypertension, UC San Diego, and VA San Diego Healthcare System (papers with Volker Vallon, 2024–2026) · Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego (Kun-Liang Guan lab, papers 2013–2015)
story: mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, only switches on when amino acids are around. Before 2015 the accepted route was the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bring mTORC1 to the surface of the lysosome. The Atlas study JEW2015 in Science, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab, showed that two amino acids use different routes. Leucine works through the Rags, but glutamine could still turn on mTORC1 in cells that lacked Rags, through a pathway that needed another small GTPase, Arf1. Young Chul Kim was second author. The work was done in cultured cells.

In the Guan lab Kim also wrote, with Guan, a 2015 review on mTOR as a drug target for controlling autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and co-authored studies on how the energy sensor AMPK steers different Vps34 complexes during starvation and on how Wnt signals switch on the growth regulators YAP and TAZ. The 2015 Cell paper already listed a second address at the Veterans Medical Research Foundation in San Diego.

Later PubMed records place Kim at the Division of Nephrology and Hypertension of UC San Diego and the VA San Diego Healthcare System, in Volker Vallon's group. That work studies the kidney: how diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor drugs and GLP1 receptor drugs change gene activity in the proximal tubule, and how glucagon-receptor agonists affect kidney injury in mice.

highlights.JEW2015: Second author: helped show in cultured cells that glutamine can activate mTORC1 without the Rag GTPases, through Arf1, unlike leucine.

Park HW.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University (Seoul, South Korea)
Park HW.role: Biochemist at Yonsei University who trained with Kun-Liang Guan on the Hippo-YAP/TAZ growth pathway and now studies how cancer cells change their signalling and metabolism to spread
Park HW.credit: Portrait: Translational Cancer Research Lab, Yonsei University
Park HW.sub: Department of Biochemistry, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University, Seoul (papers since 2020) · postdoc, Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego (Kun-Liang Guan lab, papers to 2015)
story: The Atlas study JEW2015 in Science, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at UC San Diego, asked how different amino acids switch on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex. Leucine acted through the Rag GTPases, the usual route to the lysosome, while glutamine could activate mTORC1 in cells without Rags, through a route that needed the small GTPase Arf1. Hyun Woo Park was a co-author. The experiments were done in cultured cells.

Park's main work in the Guan lab was on the Hippo pathway and its targets YAP and TAZ, proteins that control organ size and are often overactive in cancer. As first author of a 2015 Cell paper, Park showed that the alternative Wnt signals Wnt5a/b and Wnt3a switch on YAP/TAZ through a chain of receptors, G proteins and Rho GTPases, separate from the classic beta-catenin route.

Park now runs a group in the Department of Biochemistry at Yonsei University in Seoul. Recent papers from the group, some still with Guan as co-author, describe an adherent-to-suspension transition in which solid tumour cells borrow blood-cell gene programs, switch off YAP/TEAD-driven adhesion genes and detach to become circulating tumour cells. The group has also reviewed how signalling pathways such as PI3K/AKT and Hippo rewire cancer metabolism.

highlights.JEW2015: Co-author: part of the Guan-lab team that showed in cultured cells that glutamine activates mTORC1 through Arf1 without the Rag GTPases.

Jung J.lab_name: Behrends Lab, Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University School of Medicine (Frankfurt am Main, Germany)
Jung J.role: Biochemist from Christian Behrends' group in Frankfurt who showed that the lysosomal amino acid transporter SLC38A9 helps switch on mTORC1, and who studied regulators of autophagy
Jung J.sub: Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University School of Medicine, Frankfurt (papers 2015–2019, Christian Behrends group; at the time of the study)
story: Jennifer Jung is first author of an Atlas study (JUN2015) in human cells about SLC38A9, a protein in the membrane of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the lysosome surface when amino acids are plentiful, with the help of the Rag GTPases and a scaffold called Ragulator. The study found SLC38A9 bound to the Rags and Ragulator. Removing SLC38A9 weakened mTORC1 activation by amino acids, and adding extra SLC38A9 made mTORC1 overactive. The same year two other groups reported similar findings, and SLC38A9 became known as a lysosomal arginine sensor for mTORC1.

Jung did this work in Christian Behrends' group at the Institute of Biochemistry II of Goethe University Frankfurt, which uses proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins and their partners, to map how autophagy and lysosomes are controlled. As first author of a 2017 eLife paper, Jung used an image-based RNAi screen to find autophagy regulators and showed that SMCR8, a partner of the ALS-linked protein C9ORF72, acts as a brake on the autophagy kinase ULK1. The publication record with the Behrends group runs from 2015 to 2019. Later positions could not be confirmed.

highlights.JUN2015: First author: showed that the lysosomal protein SLC38A9 binds the Rag-Ragulator machinery and is needed for full amino acid activation of mTORC1.

Jin P.lab_name: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University (Chongqing, China)
Jin P.role: Pharmaceutical scientist in Lei Luo's group at Southwest University in Chongqing who studies the drug pump P-glycoprotein, and first author of the study showing that oxidative stress boosts P-glycoprotein production through mTOR
Jin P.sub: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, Chongqing (Lei Luo group, papers 2025–2026)
story: P-glycoprotein is a pump in the cell membrane that throws drugs back out of the cell. Cancer cells that make a lot of it can resist many drugs at once. In the Atlas study JIN2026, Jin and colleagues in Lei Luo's group showed in cells that oxidative stress (a build-up of reactive oxygen molecules) switches on a chain of signals, PI3K to AKT to mTORC1 to the RNA-unwinding protein eIF4A, that makes the cell translate more P-glycoprotein from its existing messenger RNA. Because this skips the slower step of making new RNA, it is a fast route to drug resistance.
For the Atlas, the study is an example of mTORC1 acting through eIF4A to pick which proteins get made. It was done in cultured cells; whether it happens in tumours in patients is not shown.

On PubMed, Jin works with Luo at the College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, on how drugs are absorbed and pumped out of cells. Earlier papers in the group include a 2025 study showing that glucosamine directly switches on intestinal P-glycoprotein and reduces drug absorption, and a 2026 study on making the colorectal cancer drug trifluridine better absorbed when taken by mouth. Career stage could not be confirmed.

highlights.JIN2026: First author: showed in cells that oxidative stress drives fast production of the drug pump P-glycoprotein through a PI3K-AKT-mTORC1-eIF4A route.

Jin L.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Jin L.role: Cardiology researcher in Qiangsun Zheng's group in Xi'an who studies how metabolism and aging make the heart's upper chambers prone to atrial fibrillation
Jin L.sub: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (papers 2023–2026)
story: Lingyan Jin is first author of the Atlas study JIN2026B on rapamycin and atrial fibrillation, the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder. Its risk climbs steeply with age. To mimic aging, the team injected mice with D-galactose, a sugar that speeds up age-like damage. Rapamycin in the food lowered how easily the aged mice could be pushed into atrial fibrillation, and it eased the structural and electrical changes in the atria, the heart's upper chambers. Mitochondria worked better and the animals responded better to insulin.

The unusual part is the mechanism. Rapamycin is known as an mTOR blocker, but here the protective effect ran mainly through lower activity of HIF-1 alpha, a protein that reshapes cell metabolism when oxygen is short, and the authors describe it as independent of mTOR. This is one mouse model of accelerated aging, so it is a lead for heart rhythm research rather than evidence for treating people.

Jin's other papers come from the same Xi'an group, led by cardiologist Qiangsun Zheng with Xinghua Qin of Northwestern Polytechnical University. They treat atrial fibrillation partly as a metabolic disease: an exercise-released molecule, BAIBA, protected obese mice (2024); the metabolite succinate made mice more prone to the arrhythmia (2025); branched-chain amino acids raised the risk while swimming exercise lowered it (2025); and very hard exercise raised the risk through excess autophagy (2025). Jin also co-authored a 2024 review on how energy metabolism and the electrical activity of the atria are coupled.

highlights.JIN2026B: First author: in D-galactose-aged mice, dietary rapamycin reduced atrial fibrillation susceptibility and atrial remodelling, mainly through lower HIF-1 alpha activity rather than mTOR.

Zheng Q.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Zheng Q.role: Cardiologist at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University whose group studies atrial fibrillation as a disorder of heart metabolism, in mice and in patients
Zheng Q.sub: Department of Cardiology (Cardiovascular Medicine), The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University
story: Qiangsun Zheng is the senior author of the Atlas study JIN2026B. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular rhythm of the heart's upper chambers, becomes much more common with age. The team aged mice quickly with D-galactose injections and fed some of them rapamycin. Rapamycin lowered the animals' susceptibility to atrial fibrillation and eased the structural and electrical remodelling of the atria. It also improved mitochondrial function and insulin sensitivity. The authors traced the effect mainly to lower activity of HIF-1 alpha, a protein that switches cell metabolism under low oxygen, and described it as independent of mTOR. The evidence comes from one mouse aging model.

Zheng leads a cardiology group that works closely with Xinghua Qin's laboratory at Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi'an. Their mouse studies treat atrial fibrillation as partly a metabolic disease: a molecule released during exercise (BAIBA) protected obese mice through the energy sensor AMPK (2024), excess succinate raised the risk by harming mitochondria (2025), branched-chain amino acids raised it and swimming lowered it (2025), and very intense exercise raised it through over-active autophagy (2025). The group also studies reperfusion injury after heart attack.

On the clinical side, Zheng's recent papers look for blood markers that predict outcomes, such as an inflammation and nutrition score that forecast whether atrial fibrillation returns after catheter ablation (2026) and inflammation-related proteins in acute coronary syndrome (2026).

highlights.JIN2026B: Senior author: led the study showing that rapamycin reduced atrial fibrillation susceptibility in D-galactose-aged mice, mainly through HIF-1 alpha rather than mTOR.

de Mol J.lab_name: Aging and Immunity group (Foks lab), Division of BioTherapeutics, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University (Leiden, Netherlands)
de Mol J.role: Immunologist at Leiden University who studies how the aging immune system, especially aged B cells, drives atherosclerosis, and first author of a 2026 study of rapamycin as an immune rejuvenator in old mice
de Mol J.sub: Postdoc, Aging and Immunity group, Division of BioTherapeutics, LACDR, Leiden University · PhD candidate in Amanda Foks's group, Leiden University
story: Atherosclerosis is the build-up of fatty, inflamed plaques in artery walls, and it gets worse with age partly because the immune system ages too. Jill de Mol is first author of a 2026 study from Amanda Foks's group in Leiden that gave rapamycin, which blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, to old mice prone to atherosclerosis (JIN2026C). The plaques held fewer macrophages and T cells. Killer CD8 T cells shifted from an aggressive effector state to a calmer memory state, regulatory T cells that dampen inflammation increased in the aorta, and the antibody-making arm of immunity quietened, with fewer germinal-centre B cells, plasma cells and autoantibodies. Age-associated B cells dropped and the immune cells in the aorta looked less senescent, or worn out. The authors read this as rapamycin acting like an immune rejuvenation therapy. It is a mouse result; whether the same happens in older people is untested.

de Mol did a PhD in Foks's Aging and Immunity group at the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research and continues there as a postdoc. The group's work centres on aged B cell immunity in the plaque environment: the team found age-associated B cells in the blood and plaques of people with coronary artery disease and wants to understand them well enough to design targeted immune therapies for heart disease. In 2024 de Mol won a best poster award at the GEMSEQ meeting.

highlights.JIN2026C: First author: showed in aged atherosclerotic mice that rapamycin reduced plaque inflammation and reset T and B cell responses toward a younger profile.

Johnson SC.lab_name: School of Geography and Natural Sciences, Northumbria University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Johnson SC.role: Biologist of aging and mitochondrial disease, first author with Peter Rabinovitch and Matt Kaeberlein of the 2013 Nature review that made the case for mTOR as a central controller of aging, now a professor at Northumbria University
Johnson SC.sub: Professor, School of Geography and Natural Sciences, Northumbria University · Assistant Professor of Neurology, University of Washington, and Principal Investigator, Center for Integrative Brain Research, Seattle Children's Research Institute (earlier) · postdoc in Genetics, Albert Einstein College of Medicine · PhD in Molecular Basis of Disease, University of Washington (2013)
story: In 2013, while a PhD student in the Department of Pathology at the University of Washington, Simon Johnson was first author of the Nature review "mTOR is a key modulator of ageing and age-related disease", with Matt Kaeberlein as senior author. The review gathered the evidence that turning down mTOR signalling, genetically or with rapamycin, extends lifespan in model organisms from yeast to mice, and that it protects against a growing list of age-related diseases in animal models. It was also frank about the problem: side effects of the existing drugs stood in the way of giving them to healthy people. The paper became a standard starting map for the field.

Johnson's own research joins aging biology to mitochondrial disease, the inherited disorders in which the cell's power plants fail. One line of work asks what mTOR inhibition does in mitochondrial disease, including how the dose of an mTOR inhibitor shapes its effects on body weight and on the disease itself. Johnson studied biochemistry and biophysics at Oregon State University, earned the PhD in Molecular Basis of Disease at the University of Washington and was a postdoctoral fellow in genetics at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York.

Johnson then led a laboratory as Assistant Professor of Neurology at the University of Washington and Principal Investigator in the Center for Integrative Brain Research at Seattle Children's Research Institute, studying the molecular and developmental mechanisms of pediatric genetic disease, mainly mitochondrial disease. Johnson is now a professor in the School of Geography and Natural Sciences at Northumbria University in Newcastle, where the research interests listed are mitochondrial disease and biology, the basic biology of anaesthesia, biogerontology and the cell and molecular basis of human genetic disease. Oregon State University gave Johnson its Young Alumni Award in 2023.

highlights.JOH2013: First author: wrote the Nature review that set out the case for mTOR as a key modulator of aging and age-related disease across species.

Powers RW.lab_name: Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox P.L.L.C. (Washington, DC, USA)
Powers RW.role: Molecular biologist who, as a PhD student in Seattle, built high-throughput lifespan screens in yeast and showed that lowering TOR signalling extends chronological lifespan, and who later became a patent attorney
Powers RW.sub: Associate, Litigation Group, Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox (patent law) · PhD in molecular biology, University of Washington and Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (Stanley Fields lab, Department of Genome Sciences) · BA in biology, University of Virginia
story: Yeast cells age in two ways that can be measured in the lab. Replicative lifespan counts how many times a mother cell can divide; chronological lifespan measures how long cells that have stopped dividing stay alive, a rough model for non-dividing tissues in animals. In POW2006, R. Wilson Powers, working in Stanley Fields's lab at the University of Washington with Matt Kaeberlein and Brian Kennedy, built a high-throughput assay and measured chronological lifespan for about 4,800 yeast strains, each missing one gene. Several long-lived strains carried mutations in the TOR pathway, the nutrient-sensing system that mTOR belongs to in animals. Removing the amino acids asparagine or glutamate from the growth medium, or blocking TOR with rapamycin or methionine sulfoximine, also lengthened survival. The study, done only in yeast, supported the idea that lower TOR signalling is one way calorie restriction extends life.

Powers did a BA in biology at the University of Virginia and a PhD in molecular biology at the University of Washington and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, where he developed high-throughput assays for measuring the lifespan of yeast cells. He was also a co-author of the 2005 Science paper by Kaeberlein and colleagues showing that TOR and Sch9 regulate yeast replicative lifespan in response to nutrients.

He then moved into intellectual property law. A professional profile lists him as an associate in the Litigation Group of Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox, working on patent litigation, patent drafting and freedom-to-operate opinions in the life sciences.

highlights.POW2006: First author: ran the genome-wide yeast screen showing that reduced TOR signalling extends chronological lifespan.

Kalender A.lab_name: George Thomas group, Metabolic Diseases Institute, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Kalender A.role: Cell biologist who, in George Thomas's group at the University of Cincinnati, showed that metformin can switch off mTORC1 without AMPK by acting through the Rag GTPases
Kalender A.sub: Department of Cancer and Cell Biology and Division of Hematology-Oncology, Metabolic Diseases Institute, University of Cincinnati (papers 2010–2011, at the time of the study)
story: Adem Kalender is first author of the Atlas study KAL2010, which asked how metformin, the most widely used diabetes drug, holds back cell growth. The usual explanation was that metformin lowers cellular energy, which switches on the energy sensor AMPK, which in turn shuts down mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Kalender and colleagues tested cells that lacked AMPK or the TSC1/TSC2 brake proteins. Metformin and its stronger relative phenformin still blocked mTORC1 in those cells. What the drugs needed instead were the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome when nutrients are present.

The team checked the idea in two mouse settings, one for cancer and one for diabetes, and saw the same AMPK-independent effect. Together with a liver study by Foretz and colleagues from the same year, the paper moved part of metformin's action away from the AMPK route that textbooks gave it. The work was done in cells and mice, so it says how the drug can act, not how much of its benefit in patients runs through this route.

Kalender worked in George Thomas's laboratory at the University of Cincinnati's Metabolic Diseases Institute. With Thomas, Kalender also co-wrote two short commentaries in 2010 and 2011, one on how the bending of primary cilia feeds into TOR signalling and one on how the stress kinase p38 beta connects energy stress to mTORC1. No later publications or a current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KAL2010: First author: showed in AMPK- and TSC-deficient cells and in mice that metformin and phenformin inhibit mTORC1 through the Rag GTPases rather than through AMPK.

Pacold ME.lab_name: Pacold Lab, Department of Radiation Oncology and Laura and Isaac Perlmutter Cancer Center, NYU Langone Health (New York, New York, USA)
Pacold ME.role: Radiation oncologist and chemical biologist at NYU Langone who studies the metabolism of brain tumours, and a co-author of the Sabatini lab's structure of the leucine sensor Sestrin2
Pacold ME.sub: Assistant Professor of Radiation Oncology, NYU Langone Health · postdoc, David Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute and MIT, with Department of Radiation Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (2010s) · earlier structural work, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (Roger Williams group, 2001)
story: Michael Pacold is a co-author of SAX2015, a Science paper from David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute and MIT. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only switches on when amino acids are present, and leucine is one of the most important. Sestrin2 is the protein that senses leucine for mTORC1. The team solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine. It shows a single pocket for leucine, closed by a lid-like loop. When the pocket was mutated so that it held leucine less tightly, cells needed more leucine before mTORC1 switched on. This tied a physical shape to a signalling job.

Pacold's training mixed structural biology and medicine. In 2001 Pacold was a co-author, with Roger Williams's group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, of the crystal structure of the PX domain of p40phox bound to a lipid. As a postdoc in the Sabatini lab, while also linked to the Department of Radiation Oncology at Dana-Farber, Pacold was first author of a 2016 Nature Chemical Biology paper describing a small-molecule inhibitor of PHGDH, the first enzyme in the pathway that makes serine from glucose, and showing how serine synthesis guides the use of one-carbon units for building DNA.

Pacold now leads a lab at NYU Langone Health as Assistant Professor of Radiation Oncology. The lab uses chemical biology, enzymology, structural biology and mass spectrometry to find the metabolic adaptations that let tumour cells survive in unusual settings, especially in the brain, and to design inhibitors against them.

highlights.SAX2015: Co-author on the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine, which revealed the pocket that makes it a leucine sensor for mTORC1.

Zid BM.lab_name: Zid Lab, Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Zid BM.role: Biochemist at UC San Diego who studies how cells decide which messenger RNAs to translate under stress, and who showed as a Caltech student that the mTOR target 4E-BP is needed for dietary restriction to lengthen fly lifespan
Zid BM.credit: Portrait: UC San Diego (Interfaces Graduate Training Program)
Zid BM.sub: Faculty, Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California San Diego (from about 2017) · postdoc, Harvard University, Erin O'Shea lab (2014) · graduate research, California Institute of Technology, Seymour Benzer lab, with Pankaj Kapahi (2004–2009)
story: Eating less without malnutrition lengthens life in many animals, and lower mTOR activity is one suspected reason. In 2009 Brian Zid, first author of a Cell paper with Pankaj Kapahi, showed in fruit flies that a restricted diet raises the level of 4E-BP, a protein that mTOR normally keeps switched off. 4E-BP shifted the cell's protein production toward messenger RNAs for mitochondrial parts, which raised mitochondrial activity, and flies without 4E-BP did not get the lifespan gain. It pinned one specific mTOR target to the benefit of eating less. The result is in flies.

Zid did this work at the California Institute of Technology in Seymour Benzer's lab. Zid was second author of the 2004 Current Biology paper that showed turning down the TOR pathway extends fly lifespan, and co-authored a 2009 study showing that the water content of fly food can confound dietary restriction experiments.

As a postdoc with Erin O'Shea at Harvard, Zid found that, in starving yeast, a gene's promoter sequence decides where its messenger RNA goes in the cytoplasm and how well it is translated (Nature, 2014). Zid now runs a lab in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at UC San Diego that studies how messenger RNAs are sorted and translated during stress, including how glucose starvation couples transcription to translation and how ribosomes sitting on the surface of mitochondria help import proteins into them.

highlights.ZID2009: First author: 4E-BP is needed for dietary restriction to extend fly lifespan and works by boosting translation of mitochondrial genes.

Karuppasamy M.lab_name: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble Outstation (Grenoble, France)
Karuppasamy M.role: Structural biologist who used cryo-electron microscopy at EMBL Grenoble to solve the first structure of yeast TORC2, explaining why it resists rapamycin
Karuppasamy M.sub: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble, Schaffitzel group (papers 2016–2020, at the time of the study)
story: TOR works in two complexes. TORC1 is blocked by rapamycin, but TORC2 is not, and for years nobody could see why. Manikandan Karuppasamy is first author of a 2017 study from Christiane Schaffitzel's group at EMBL Grenoble that solved the structure of yeast TORC2 by cryo-electron microscopy, a method that images frozen protein molecules in an electron microscope and combines many pictures into a 3D model (KAR2017). The structure showed the overall layout of the complex and that the protein Avo3 sits over the spot where rapamycin, with its partner FKBP12, would need to bind, which explains the drug's lack of effect. The work was done on purified yeast proteins.

At EMBL Grenoble Karuppasamy also helped solve the cryo-EM structure of a human 48S translation pre-initiation complex, the ribosome machinery that starts protein production (2018), and contributed to a 2020 method for imaging long non-coding RNAs by atomic force microscopy. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KAR2017: First author: solved the cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2, revealing its architecture and the structural basis for rapamycin insensitivity.

Kelly G.lab_name: Korolchuk Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Kelly G.role: Cell biologist from Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University who showed that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria fails as human cells become senescent
Kelly G.sub: Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024, Korolchuk lab, at the time of the study)
story: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell, and damaged ones are removed by a process called mitophagy. George Kelly is first author of the 2024 Developmental Cell study in this Atlas (KEL2024). In healthy primary human cells, mitophagy ran at a steady high level, started by superoxide made in the mitochondria and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the receptor that tags mitochondria for removal. This housekeeping shut down when cells became senescent, the non-dividing state that builds up with age, and in cells from older donors. Blocking mitophagy in young cells was enough to push them into senescence.

The study also matters for rapamycin. Turning mitophagy back on was needed for rapamycin and NAD precursors to hold back senescence, which suggests that part of rapamycin's effect on cell aging works through mitochondrial quality control. A small molecule that targets p62 could restore mitophagy and reverse aging features in the cells. All of this was shown in cultured human cells.

PubMed links Kelly to Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University from 2020, starting with a review on reactive oxygen species and autophagy in neurons. Kelly is also a co-author of a 2022 Developmental Cell paper from the same lab showing that autophagy keeps cells alive by maintaining NAD levels, of a 2022 eLife study on short senolytic treatments in irradiated mice, and of a 2023 Nature paper with Joao Passos on how stressed senescent cells release mitochondrial DNA. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.KEL2024: First author: showed that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged human cells and that its return is needed for rapamycin's anti-senescence effect.

Khapre RV.lab_name: Kondratov Lab, Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease, Cleveland State University (Cleveland, Ohio, USA)
Khapre RV.role: Circadian biologist who did her PhD in Roman Kondratov's lab at Cleveland State University, where she showed that the clock protein BMAL1 acts as a brake on mTORC1 and that feeding times set a daily rhythm in mTORC1 activity
Khapre RV.sub: Postdoctoral fellow, Cleveland Clinic (listed by the Kondratov lab; 2016 paper from the Lerner Research Institute) · PhD student, Kondratov lab, Cleveland State University (2009–2014)
story: The body runs on a roughly 24-hour internal clock, and the protein BMAL1 is one of its core gears. Mice that lack BMAL1 age early and die young. In the Atlas study KHA2014, Khapre and colleagues asked whether this early ageing runs through mTORC1, the growth-control complex that rapamycin blocks. In mouse tissues and in cultured cells without BMAL1, mTORC1 was more active than normal. When Bmal1 knockout mice were given rapamycin, their lifespan rose by about 50 percent. The result places the clock upstream of mTORC1 as a brake, and suggests that losing that brake is part of why these mice age fast. It is a mouse and cell result, not a human one.

A companion paper from the same year, with Khapre as first author, found that mTORC1 activity in mouse tissues rises and falls on a 24-hour rhythm that is set by feeding times, not by light, and keeps going during fasting. The authors proposed that this food-driven rhythm is a second clock that runs alongside the light-driven one. An earlier first-author paper (2011) showed more senescent cells in the tissues of Bmal1 knockout mice and linked BMAL1 to how cells handle oxidative stress.

Khapre trained as a PhD student in Roman Kondratov's lab at Cleveland State University from 2009 to 2014, according to the lab's alumni list. The same list names her current post as a postdoctoral fellow at Cleveland Clinic, and a 2016 paper lists her at the Neuroinflammation Research Center of the Lerner Research Institute there, on a study of memory loss after brain bleeding in mice. No more recent position could be confirmed.

highlights.KHA2014: First author: showed in mice and cells that loss of the clock protein BMAL1 raises mTORC1 activity, and that rapamycin lengthens the life of Bmal1 knockout mice by about 50 percent.

Kidani Y.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Kidani Y.role: Researcher who, in Steven Bensinger's lab at UCLA, showed that activated killer T cells need SREBP-driven fat and cholesterol synthesis to expand
Kidani Y.sub: Steven Bensinger group, David Geffen School of Medicine, UCLA (papers 2011–2016, at the time of the study)
story: Yoko Kidani is first author of an Atlas study (KID2013) on what CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill virus-infected cells, need when they wake up. Within hours of activation they switch on genes for making fatty acids and cholesterol, the raw material for new cell membranes. The paper showed that this switch depends on SREBP proteins, the master regulators of lipid synthesis, and that the signal runs from PI3K through mTOR to SREBP: rapamycin given 30 minutes before stimulation blocked it in cells. T cells without SREBP activity could not grow and divide properly, and in mice infected with a virus they failed to expand.

The study is one of the clearest links between mTOR and immune cell metabolism. It helps explain why rapamycin and related drugs suppress the immune system: by blocking mTOR they also cut off the lipid supply that a dividing T cell needs. The key experiments were in mouse cells and mice.

Kidani worked in Steven Bensinger's group at the David Geffen School of Medicine, UCLA, where Bensinger, the senior author, studies how lipid metabolism shapes immune cells. Other papers from that period include a 2011 study with the same group on how liver X receptors help keep neutrophil numbers in balance. Later positions could not be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.KID2013: First author: showed that activated CD8 T cells need SREBP-driven lipid synthesis, switched on through PI3K and mTOR, to expand during viral infection.

Kim YM.lab_name: Do-Hyung Kim Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Kim YM.role: mTOR researcher in Do-Hyung Kim's University of Minnesota lab who found SH3BP4 as a brake on the amino acid sensing Rag GTPases and showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG to slow autophagy
Kim YM.sub: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (papers with Do-Hyung Kim, 2007–2016)
story: Young-Mi Kim is the first author of KIM2012, a Molecular Cell paper from Do-Hyung Kim's lab at the University of Minnesota. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only works when it sits on the surface of the lysosome, and it is brought there by the Rag GTPases, switches that flip on when amino acids are plentiful. The study, done in human cells, found that the protein SH3BP4 binds the inactive form of the Rag complex when amino acids are scarce and keeps it from switching on. As a result mTORC1 stays away from the lysosome, its activity and cell growth drop, and autophagy, the cell's recycling system, goes up.

Kim followed this with a short 2012 review on SH3BP4 and other Rag binders in Molecules and Cells, and was first author of the lab's 2014 Molecular Cell paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG, a protein that helps autophagosomes and endosomes mature. Phosphorylation of UVRAG slows that maturation, so mTORC1 brakes autophagy at a late step as well as at the start. Earlier papers in the same lab, from 2007 and 2009, include the discovery of PRR5 as a part of mTORC2 and the finding that mTOR phosphorylates the ULK-ATG13-FIP200 complex that starts autophagy.

These papers all list the University of Minnesota. Because this is a common name, only papers shared with Do-Hyung Kim at Minnesota were counted. No official profile was found, so the current position is not known and the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KIM2012: First author: identified SH3BP4 as a protein that binds inactive Rag GTPases under amino acid shortage and keeps mTORC1 off.

Benavides AD.lab_name: Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Molecular Genetics, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Benavides AD.role: Immunologist who worked at UT Health San Antonio and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and a co-author of the first small safety trial of rapamycin in healthy older people
Benavides AD.sub: Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Molecular Genetics, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (at the time of the study, 2018) · Infectious Disease Research Division, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (papers 2015–2016)
story: Adriana Benavides is a co-author of KRA2018, a small trial in San Antonio that asked a basic question before any longevity trial: is daily rapamycin safe for healthy older people? In this randomised pilot trial, 25 people aged 70 to 95 were followed for eight weeks or more. The drug was well tolerated, with only minor changes in red blood cells, and in this short window it did not raise blood glucose or cause insulin resistance, a side effect seen with daily rapamycin in mice. The trial was too small and too short to measure any effect on aging itself, but it laid groundwork for larger studies such as PEARL.

PubMed links Benavides to rapamycin and immune research in San Antonio and Philadelphia. Benavides co-authored a 2012 Aging Cell study from San Antonio showing that lifelong rapamycin improved age-related memory problems in mice, a 2015 review on how invariant natural killer T cells, a type of immune cell, attack tumours (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia), and a 2016 paper on how mice adapt to long-term rapamycin, which lists both institutions. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author of this pilot trial, which tracked immune, metabolic and other safety measures in older adults taking rapamycin.

Kraig E.lab_name: Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Kraig E.role: Immunologist at UT Health San Antonio who studies how aging changes immune regulation and who led the first small safety trial of rapamycin in healthy older people at the Barshop Institute
Kraig E.credit: Portrait: The University of Texas System
Kraig E.sub: Professor and Deputy Chair of Faculty Development, Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · Distinguished Fellow, American Association of Immunologists · postdoc, Leroy Hood lab, Caltech · PhD, Brandeis University (Jim Haber lab)
story: Before anyone can test whether rapamycin slows human aging, someone has to show that healthy older people can take it safely. Ellen Kraig was first author of the 2018 trial in this Atlas (KRA2018) that asked this question. Twenty-five healthy adults aged 70 to 95 took low-dose rapamycin or a placebo every day for at least 8 weeks. The drug was generally well tolerated. There were small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was small and short, so it says nothing about long-term benefit, but it was early groundwork for larger aging trials.

Kraig trained in genetics and immunology. As a graduate student at Brandeis University in Jim Haber's lab Kraig studied mating type in yeast, and then joined Leroy Hood's lab at Caltech as a postdoc. At UT Health San Antonio Kraig is Professor and Deputy Chair of Faculty Development in the Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy. Kraig's research uses molecular and cellular assays to study how aging affects immune regulation, work developed with colleagues at the Barshop Institute. Kraig has also won several teaching awards, including a 2018 Regents' Outstanding Teaching Award, and was named a Distinguished Fellow of the American Association of Immunologists.

The question from the pilot trial continues. In 2026 UT Health San Antonio announced a larger randomized, placebo-controlled study of rapamycin and everolimus in about 84 healthy adults aged 65 to 90, co-led by Kraig with Dean Kellogg Jr. and Brett Ginsburg, to work out dosing and short-term effects in older people.

highlights.KRA2018: First author: ran the randomized pilot trial showing that daily low-dose rapamycin was well tolerated by healthy adults aged 70 to 95 over 8 weeks.

Musi N.lab_name: Diabetes and Aging Center, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Musi N.role: Endocrinologist and aging researcher who directs the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism and the Diabetes and Aging Center at Cedars-Sinai, and who studies how aging drives insulin resistance, frailty and senescence
Musi N.sub: Director, Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, and Director, Diabetes and Aging Center, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (since 2022) · Kathi and Gary Cypres Chair in Diabetes Research (2024) · earlier at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, and South Texas Veterans Health Care System (PubMed affiliation 2018)
story: Nicolas Musi is a co-author of the 2018 trial in this Atlas (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot study in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. That last point matters because rapamycin can disturb sugar handling in mice. The trial was small and short.

At the time Musi worked at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and the Department of Medicine of UT Health San Antonio, and at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System. Musi's research covers how aging affects metabolism and cells in diabetes, obesity and sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), the effects of exercise on glucose and fat metabolism, and cellular senescence, the state in which damaged cells stop dividing but stay active.

Musi moved to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles in 2022. There Musi directs the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism and the Diabetes and Aging Center, and in 2024 became the first holder of the Kathi and Gary Cypres Chair in Diabetes Research. The current work includes a clinical trial testing whether removing senescent cells improves glucose metabolism and physical function. Musi is an elected member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author: part of the San Antonio team that ran the pilot safety trial of daily rapamycin in healthy adults aged 70 to 95.

Kristiansen JB.lab_name: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University (Aarhus, Denmark)
Kristiansen JB.role: Exercise biologist at Aarhus University, working with Kristian Vissing, who studies how aging changes muscle's response to mechanical load and to food
Kristiansen JB.sub: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University, Vissing group (papers 2025–2026)
story: Muscles grow when they are stretched and loaded, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is one of the main switches that turns that signal into new protein. Older muscle often responds less, a problem called anabolic resistance. Jonas Boritz Kristiansen is first author of a 2026 study from Kristian Vissing's exercise biology group at Aarhus University that tested which part of the signal is lost (KRISTIANSEN2026). Muscles from adult and old female mice were stretched in a dish. mTORC1 signalling switched on just as strongly in old muscle as in young, but a second stress pathway, JNK-SMAD2L, responded less with age. So, at least in this mouse model, the mTORC1 sensor for stretch seems to stay intact with age.

Kristiansen's other papers fit the same theme. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, as first author, pooled 46 human studies and found that older adults make muscle protein slightly more slowly than young adults at rest and after a meal, but respond about as well to exercise. A 2025 rat study, with the same group, looked at how weeks of voluntary wheel running affect oxidative stress and DNA repair in the brain. No institutional profile was found, so career stage is not given.

highlights.KRISTIANSEN2026: First author: showed in ex vivo mouse muscle that stretch activates mTORC1 equally in adult and old females while JNK-SMAD2L signalling is blunted with age.

Kusuda T.lab_name: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Kusuda T.role: Rheumatologist and researcher at the University of Tokyo who studies how B cells go wrong in lupus, and first author of the 2026 study tying the arginine sensor CASTOR1 to mTORC1 in antibody-making cells
Kusuda T.sub: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (group of senior author Fujio, 2026) · Department of Medicine and Rheumatology, Tokyo Metropolitan Geriatric Hospital (2023) · Department of Rheumatology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (2016)
story: Cells check whether they have enough of each amino acid before they grow. CASTOR1 is a sensor for the amino acid arginine: when arginine is low, CASTOR1 holds mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in check. In the Atlas study KUS2026, Kusuda and colleagues in the University of Tokyo group of senior author Fujio gave CASTOR1 a clear job in the body. In mice without CASTOR1, mTORC1 was overactive in B cells, the immune cells that make antibodies. The mice made more plasma cells (antibody factories), more antibodies including ones against their own DNA, and developed kidney inflammation like that seen in lupus.

Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. In blood from people with lupus, plasmablasts with less CASTOR1 went with more active disease. That human result is a correlation; the cause-and-effect evidence comes from mice. The study is one of few that link a specific nutrient sensor upstream of mTORC1 to a human autoimmune disease.

PubMed shows Kusuda as a clinician as well as a researcher: a 2016 case report from the Department of Rheumatology at Tokyo Medical and Dental University, and a 2023 letter on COVID-19 vaccination and rheumatoid arthritis in older patients from the Tokyo Metropolitan Geriatric Hospital, with a joint affiliation at the University of Tokyo. Rank and training details could not be confirmed.

highlights.KUS2026: First author: showed in mice that losing the arginine sensor CASTOR1 overactivates mTORC1 in B cells and leads to lupus-like autoantibodies and kidney disease, with a matching correlation in patients.

Laberge RM.lab_name: UNITY Biotechnology (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Laberge RM.role: Biologist of cell senescence, trained in Judith Campisi's lab, who showed how mTOR drives the inflammatory signals of senescent cells and then moved to drug development against senescence at UNITY Biotechnology
Laberge RM.sub: UNITY Biotechnology, South San Francisco (2017–2023, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Judith Campisi lab (2012–2017) · Institute of Parasitology, McGill University, Montreal (Elias Georges lab)
story: When cells are badly damaged they can stop dividing for good and become senescent. Senescent cells release a mix of inflammatory signals, called the SASP (senescence-associated secretory phenotype), which can harm nearby tissue and even help tumours grow. In 2015, as first author of a Nature Cell Biology paper with Judith Campisi, Remi-Martin Laberge showed that mTOR drives the SASP by raising translation of IL1A, a signal near the top of this cascade. Rapamycin lowered IL1A production and the SASP, and in mice it stopped senescent cells from helping prostate tumours grow. The work used cultured human cells and mouse tumour models.

Laberge also worked at McGill University's Institute of Parasitology in Montreal with Elias Georges; a 2014 first-author paper from that group asks how cancer cells that resist many drugs through the pump P-glycoprotein become extra sensitive to steroid hormones. At the Buck Institute, Laberge moved into senescence biology. A 2012 first-author paper showed that glucocorticoid drugs suppress parts of the SASP.

Later Laberge joined UNITY Biotechnology, a company developing drugs that remove senescent cells. From there, Laberge co-authored a 2017 Nature Medicine study showing that clearing senescent cells locally in the knee slowed post-traumatic osteoarthritis in mice, and later studies on the secreted signals of stressed cells (Science, 2021) and on senescence markers in patient tissues (2023). A current position after 2023 could not be confirmed.

highlights.LAB2015: First author: mTOR drives the senescence-associated secretory phenotype by promoting IL1A translation, and rapamycin blocks it.

Lane CM.lab_name: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Lane CM.role: Cardiologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, working in interventional cardiology, and first author of a trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Lane CM.sub: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine (Division of Interventional Cardiology), Mayo Clinic, Rochester (2023–2026) · Department of Internal Medicine, Mayo Clinic (2020–2021)
story: Conor Lane is first author of the Atlas entry LAN2026, a 2026 Mayo Clinic Proceedings report on rapamycin in frail older people who have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). In HFpEF the heart pumps out a normal share of its blood with each beat but is stiff and fills poorly. It is common in older adults, and there are few treatments that help. Rapamycin, the classic mTOR blocker, slows aging processes in animals, so a trial in this group tests whether that idea carries over to a real age-related disease in people.

The team joined Mayo Clinic cardiologists, including senior author Mandeep Singh, with aging researchers James Kirkland at Mayo and Dudley Lamming and Judith Simcox at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The abstract was not yet public when the Atlas entry was made, so the results are not summarised here.

Lane's other papers trace a clinical career at Mayo Clinic in Rochester. In 2020 and 2021 PubMed lists the Department of Internal Medicine, on studies of heart ultrasound methods and of medicines linked to microscopic colitis. From 2023 the affiliation is cardiovascular medicine, with case reports and commentary on catheter-based treatments, such as removing infected material from a mitral valve, repairing a coronary aneurysm and opening a blocked bypass graft. By 2025 Lane is listed in the Division of Interventional Cardiology.

highlights.LAN2026: First author of the Mayo Clinic and University of Wisconsin report on low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with HFpEF.

Landoas A.lab_name: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital, Universite Grenoble Alpes (Grenoble, France)
Landoas A.role: Hospital pharmacist at Grenoble Alpes University Hospital who studies how everolimus is used after lung transplantation and whether it protects the new lungs from long-term rejection
Landoas A.sub: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital and Universite Grenoble Alpes, France (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2021 to 2026)
story: Agathe Landoas is the first author of LANDOAS2026, a study of people who had received a lung transplant. The biggest long-term threat to a transplanted lung is chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), a slow scarring and narrowing of the airways caused largely by the immune system. Everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR and calms immune cells, is often added to the standard anti-rejection drugs, mainly to spare the kidneys. Landoas and colleagues looked back at the records of patients treated in Grenoble and asked whether the timing and continuity of everolimus mattered. Starting it later and stopping and restarting it more often were both linked to a higher risk of CLAD. Because this was a retrospective, single-hospital study, it shows an association and not proof that early, steady everolimus prevents CLAD.

The paper follows an earlier study from the same Grenoble team, with Landoas as first author (2024), which compared 59 lung transplant patients who received everolimus on top of standard treatment with 37 who did not. CLAD was less frequent and came later in the everolimus group. PubMed lists Landoas at the Pharmacy Department of Grenoble Alpes University Hospital on five papers since 2021, including a French nursing-journal article on insulin with the hospital pharmacy team, and with Pierrick Bedouch, a professor of clinical pharmacy, as senior author on the transplant work.
No official profile was available, so training and current position beyond the PubMed affiliation are not given.

highlights.LANDOAS2026: First author: in a retrospective single-centre study of lung transplant patients, later start and more interruptions of everolimus were linked to a higher risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction.

Morita M.lab_name: Morita Lab, Department of Molecular Medicine and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Morita M.role: Biochemist at UT Health San Antonio who studies how mTORC1 controls protein synthesis, mRNA decay and mitochondria, and how these links go wrong in cancer and metabolic disease
Morita M.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Molecular Medicine and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio · postdoc in cancer metabolism, McGill University (Nahum Sonenberg lab) · postdoc in medical sciences, University of Tokyo · PhD in Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of Tokyo (2008)
story: Masahiro Morita is the first author of MOR2013, a Cell Metabolism paper from Nahum Sonenberg's lab at McGill University. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, was known to switch on protein synthesis. The study showed that it also builds up and powers mitochondria, the cell's power plants, by raising the translation of messenger RNAs for mitochondrial proteins. It does this through the 4E-BP proteins, brakes on translation that mTORC1 switches off. In simple terms, when mTORC1 is active the cell makes more of the parts it needs to produce energy for growth. The work was done in cultured cells and mice.

The paper won Morita a McGill MedStar Award in 2015 as a postdoctoral fellow. A 2017 Molecular Cell paper, also with Sonenberg, followed the same thread: mTORC1 raises translation of MTFP1, a protein that drives mitochondrial fission, and when mTOR is blocked the mitochondria fuse into long networks that help cells survive.

Morita earned a BS, MS and PhD at the University of Tokyo, finishing the PhD in 2008, and did postdoctoral work there before moving to McGill. In Tokyo Morita worked with Tadashi Yamamoto on the CCR4-NOT complex, which shortens the poly(A) tails of mRNAs and so speeds their decay. Morita is now an associate professor in the Department of Molecular Medicine and the Barshop Institute at UT Health San Antonio, where the lab studies how mTOR signalling, mRNA translation and decay, and mitochondrial dynamics contribute to cancer and metabolic disease, including the role of CCR4-NOT in metabolic disorders.

highlights.MOR2013: First author: showed that mTORC1 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and activity by raising the translation of mitochondria-related mRNAs through the 4E-BPs.

Hakkola J.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Hakkola J.role: Professor of Pharmacology at the University of Oulu who studies the pregnane X receptor (PXR), a liver sensor of drugs and foreign chemicals, and how it changes liver growth and metabolism
Hakkola J.sub: Professor of Pharmacology (since 2009) and Head of the Research Unit of Biomedicine (since 2014), Faculty of Medicine, University of Oulu · Biocenter Oulu and Medical Research Center Oulu
story: Jukka Hakkola is the senior author of LASSILA2026, a study that joins a small clinical trial with mouse work. The pregnane X receptor (PXR) is a protein in liver cells that detects many drugs and chemicals and switches on genes to deal with them. Rifampicin, an antibiotic, activates it strongly. In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin made the liver about 2.7 percent larger relative to body weight. In male mice, activating PXR also enlarged the liver, and this came with higher activity of the AKT-MTOR growth pathway but not of YAP, another known driver of liver growth. The human part shows the effect is real in people, while the mTOR link comes from the mice.

Hakkola has worked on PXR for many years. PubMed lists him on more than 25 PXR papers from the University of Oulu, usually as senior author. A 2025 study from the group, for example, found Lasp2, a small cell-adhesion protein, as a new PXR target gene in mouse liver, with partners at Charles University in Hradec Kralove, Czech Republic. The wider theme is how drug-sensing receptors in the liver also change glucose and fat metabolism and the size of the organ.

Hakkola, who holds an MD and a PhD, has been Professor of Pharmacology at the University of Oulu since 2009 and head of its Research Unit of Biomedicine since 2014. The team works on nuclear receptors, proteins that switch genes on when they bind a signal molecule, and on cytochrome P450 enzymes, which break down drugs in the liver. Its main current target is PXR and how it shapes glucose and fat metabolism and metabolic disease. Other topics include sirtuins, PGC-1alpha and vitamin D metabolism.

highlights.LASSILA2026: Senior author: led the trial showing that a week of rifampicin enlarges the human liver and the mouse work tying PXR-driven liver growth to AKT-MTOR signalling.

Lassila P.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Lassila P.role: Researcher in Jukka Hakkola's pharmacology group at the University of Oulu who led a clinical and mouse study showing that activating the drug sensor PXR makes the liver grow
Lassila P.sub: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Biocenter Oulu, University of Oulu and Oulu University Hospital (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2025 to 2026)
story: Piia Lassila is the first author of LASSILA2026. The study gave the antibiotic rifampicin, which strongly activates the liver's drug-sensing receptor PXR, to 16 healthy volunteers for a week, and measured liver size. The liver grew by about 2.7 percent relative to body weight. In male mice, activating PXR also enlarged the liver, and the growth came with more activity in the AKT-MTOR pathway, the cell's main growth-signalling route, without activation of the YAP pathway. This matters because many common medicines activate PXR, and it shows that such drugs can change the size of a human organ within days.

PubMed lists Lassila on two papers, both from Jukka Hakkola's group at the University of Oulu. In the other, from 2025, she was a co-author of the discovery that the cell-adhesion protein Lasp2 is a new PXR target gene in mouse liver.
No official profile was found, so training and current position beyond the University of Oulu affiliation are not given.

highlights.LASSILA2026: First author: a week of rifampicin enlarged the liver in healthy volunteers, and PXR activation in mice grew the liver with higher AKT-MTOR activity.

Kim DJ.lab_name: Denali Therapeutics (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Kim DJ.role: Structural biologist, now at Denali Therapeutics, who worked in James Hurley's lab at UC Berkeley on the protein machines of autophagy and on the Rag-Ragulator complex that brings mTORC1 to the lysosome
Kim DJ.sub: Denali Therapeutics, South San Francisco (Hurley lab alumni list) · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences, University of California, Berkeley (Hurley lab, papers 2014–2019)
story: Do Jin Kim is a co-author of three Berkeley papers in this Atlas that describe, in atomic detail, the docking station for mTORC1, the growth-control complex, on the lysosome. SUX2017 combined several structural methods into a 'hybrid' model of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex, the scaffold that holds the Rag GTPases on the lysosome surface. LAW2018 found that nutrients change how tightly the Rag GTPases bind their lysosomal scaffold, Ragulator, a switch that controls whether mTORC1 is pulled to the lysosome. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited. Loss of FLCN causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition with kidney tumours.
Structures like these explain how a nutrient signal is turned into a physical change in proteins, and they show where drugs might act. They come from purified proteins and cells, not from animals.

Kim's earlier papers with Hurley's group, from 2014 and 2015, mapped the protein complexes that start autophagy: the Atg1/ULK1 complex, the autophagy PI3-kinase complex and the Atg13-Atg101 pair. The Hurley lab's alumni list now places Kim at Denali Therapeutics, a biotechnology company in South San Francisco. It does not give a job title.

highlights.SUX2017: Co-author of the hybrid structural model of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex.
highlights.LAW2018: Co-author of the study showing that nutrients flip an affinity switch between the Rag GTPases and Ragulator.
highlights.LAW2019: Co-author of the structural study showing the folliculin complex as a checkpoint for Rag GTPase activation.

Lim CY.lab_name: School of Basic Medical Sciences, Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou Medical University (Guangzhou, China)
Lim CY.role: Cell biologist who trained in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley on how cholesterol controls mTORC1, and now publishes as corresponding author from Guangzhou National Laboratory on lysosome signalling in immunity and nutrient sensing
Lim CY.sub: School of Basic Medical Sciences, Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou Medical University (corresponding author, 2025–2026) · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Zoncu lab, papers 2017–2022)
story: Chun-Yan Lim is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited to the lysosome. SHI2022 identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein previously known only as GPR155, as a cholesterol sensor for mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Cholesterol binds one end of LYCHOS, and mutating that site weakens mTORC1 activation. When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that normally keeps mTORC1 off, and so lets mTORC1 be recruited to the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. The work was done in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Lim's own Berkeley work tied these pieces to disease. As first author of a 2019 Nature Cell Biology paper, Lim showed that contact points between the endoplasmic reticulum and the lysosome let mTORC1 sense cholesterol, and that in Niemann-Pick type C, a disease in which cholesterol is trapped in lysosomes, these contacts drive abnormal growth signalling. Lim also co-authored a 2017 Cancer Discovery study on drugs that target both the recycling and the growth-signalling roles of the lysosome.

PubMed now lists Lim at the School of Basic Medical Sciences of Guangzhou National Laboratory and Guangzhou Medical University. As senior author of a 2026 EMBO Journal paper, Lim reported that the lysosomal LAMTOR-Rag complex, the same docking station that recruits mTORC1, acts as a checkpoint for the production of the antiviral signal interferon-beta in macrophages. Lim also co-authored a 2025 structure of the KICSTOR and GATOR1-KICSTOR complexes, which hold an mTORC1 brake on the lysosome, with Ming-Yuan Su, another Berkeley alumnus in this Atlas.

highlights.LAW2019: Co-author of the structural study showing the folliculin complex as a checkpoint for Rag GTPase activation.
highlights.SHI2022: Co-author of the study identifying LYCHOS as the lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

Lee JH.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Integrative Physiology, University of Michigan Medical School (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Lee JH.role: Physiologist at the University of Michigan who first showed in flies that Sestrin is a feedback brake on TOR that protects against age-related decline, and has since studied Sestrins as stress-induced regulators of mTORC1
Lee JH.sub: Department of Molecular and Integrative Physiology, University of Michigan Medical School (papers 2016–2022) · Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, University of California San Diego (Michael Karin lab, 2010 paper)
story: Jun Hee Lee is first author of LEE2010, a Science paper from Michael Karin's laboratory at the University of California San Diego. In fruit flies, the team found that Sestrin levels rise when TOR stays active, and that Sestrin then pushes TOR back down by switching on AMPK, the cell's energy sensor. This makes Sestrin a feedback brake. Flies without Sestrin built up fat and developed mitochondrial damage, muscle weakness and heart problems that looked like early ageing. Treating them with rapamycin or with an AMPK activator prevented these problems.
