The paper put Sestrins on the map of ageing research. Later work by other groups showed that in mammals Sestrin2 binds the amino acid leucine and passes that signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex, so Sestrins are now seen as both stress sensors and nutrient sensors for mTORC1.

Lee moved to the University of Michigan, where PubMed lists the Department of Molecular and Integrative Physiology of the Medical School. Lee's group there continued the Sestrin work, including a 2016 review on the biochemical basis of Sestrin activity, which describes Sestrins as stress-induced proteins that hold down both reactive oxygen species and mTORC1, and a 2022 commentary with Robert Wessells on how Sestrin links exercise to body temperature control. No profile page was opened, so the current title is not confirmed.

highlights.LEE2010: First author: showed in fruit flies that Sestrin acts as a feedback inhibitor of TOR and that its loss causes age-like fat, mitochondrial, muscle and heart defects that TOR inhibition prevents.

Lee DJW.lab_name: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (Singapore)
Lee DJW.role: First author of the first systematic review of rapamycin and related drugs given to people for ageing, from the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program at the National University of Singapore
Lee DJW.sub: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (at the time of the study, 2024)
story: Deborah J W Lee was first author of a 2024 systematic review in The Lancet Healthy Longevity (LEE2024). A systematic review gathers every study that meets fixed rules and judges them together, which makes it stronger than any single trial. The team screened about 18,400 records and kept 19 studies in which people took rapamycin or a related drug (a rapalog) with ageing-related outcomes in mind. The authors describe it as the first systematic review of its kind.

The picture was mixed. Measures of the immune system, the heart and blood vessels, and the skin improved in some studies. Hormone, muscle and brain measures showed no clear change. Healthy people had no serious side effects, but people who already had age-related diseases had more infections and higher cholesterol and triglycerides. For the Atlas this is one of the strongest summaries of what rapamycin does in humans, and it also shows how few human studies there are.

The paper lists Lee at the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program of the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore. No other publication could be tied to this author with confidence, and a current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.LEE2024: First author: led the systematic review of 19 human studies of rapamycin and rapalogs for ageing, which found gains in immune, cardiovascular and skin measures but none for hormones, muscle or the nervous system.

Lee SY.lab_name: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science, and Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST (Daejeon, South Korea)
Lee SY.role: Neuroscientist in Won-Suk Chung's group at KAIST and the Institute for Basic Science who studies how neurons, astrocytes and immune cells interact in Alzheimer's disease, and first author of the 2026 Nature study on ERBB4 in excitatory neurons
Lee SY.sub: Senior researcher, Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (2026) · Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST (Won-Suk Chung group, papers 2024–2026)
story: In Alzheimer's disease, brain circuits become unbalanced long before memory fails. In the Atlas study LEE2026, Lee and colleagues in Won-Suk Chung's group found that the receptor protein ERBB4 turns up in a group of excitatory (signal-sending) neurons very early in Alzheimer's model mice. Removing ERBB4 from these neurons reduced synapse loss, inflammation from support cells called glia, amyloid plaques and memory problems. Putting ERBB4 into the excitatory neurons of healthy mice was enough to cause synapse loss, glial inflammation and memory problems, though not plaques. These effects needed mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

For the Atlas, the study adds a new route into mTOR in the brain: a receptor that appears in the wrong cell type and drives damage through mTOR. The causal experiments were done in mice. The team also reported higher ERBB4 in excitatory neurons in human brain tissue from people with Alzheimer's disease, which is an association, not proof of cause.

On PubMed, Lee has worked with Chung at the Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST, including a 2024 review on how astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells of the brain, talk to neurons, blood vessels and immune cells, and a 2025 study with collaborators in Bonn on the receptor Tyro3 and brain inflammation in Alzheimer's models. Korean press coverage of the Nature paper describes Lee as a senior researcher who led the study at the Institute for Basic Science Center for Vascular Research, where Chung is deputy director.

highlights.LEE2026: First author: showed in mice that ERBB4 switched on in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like synapse loss, inflammation and memory decline through mTOR signalling.

Lei HT.lab_name: Gonen Lab, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Lei HT.role: Structural biologist from Tamir Gonen's lab who solved crystal structures of the lysosomal arginine sensor SLC38A9, showing how it holds arginine and how its own tail plugs the binding pocket
Lei HT.sub: Tamir Gonen lab, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California, Los Angeles (papers 2020–2023) · Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Ashburn, Virginia (papers 2018–2019)
story: Hsiang-Ting Lei is first author of LEI2018, the crystal structure of SLC38A9 from zebrafish with an arginine molecule bound. SLC38A9 is a transporter in the lysosome membrane that also acts as a sensor: when arginine builds up inside the lysosome, SLC38A9 helps tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that amino acids are plentiful. The structure, caught in a state open toward the cytosol, shows exactly where arginine sits and which parts of the protein grip it, giving a physical basis for arginine sensing.

In a 2020 follow-up in the journal Structure, again as first author, Lei solved a second SLC38A9 structure in which the protein's own N-terminal tail is inserted deep into the pocket where arginine normally binds. The team proposed a ball-and-chain model: when arginine is scarce the tail plugs the transporter, and when arginine is abundant the tail is pushed out and becomes free to activate the Rag GTPases and mTORC1.

Lei worked with Tamir Gonen, first at the Janelia Research Campus of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Ashburn, Virginia, where the lab also solved structures of an alanine transporter (2019), and then at HHMI at the University of California, Los Angeles, where Lei contributed to cryo-EM structures of the omega-3 fatty acid transporter Mfsd2a (2023). Later positions could not be confirmed.

highlights.LEI2018: First author: solved the crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9, the lysosomal arginine sensor for mTORC1.

Lelegren M.lab_name: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Lelegren M.role: First author of a 2016 study of how rapamycin changes the protein-quality-control machinery in marmoset liver, muscle and fat, carried out in Adam Salmon's group in San Antonio
Lelegren M.sub: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (at the time of the study, 2016)
story: Cells keep their proteins in good shape with a set of systems called the proteostasis network. Proteasomes chop up damaged proteins, chaperones help proteins fold, and autophagy recycles larger pieces of the cell. Blocking mTOR is thought to boost some of these systems, which may be part of how rapamycin slows aging in mice.

Matthew Lelegren was first author of the 2016 Atlas study (LEL2016) that checked this idea in a primate, using tissue from common marmosets treated with rapamycin in an earlier pilot. In liver and muscle, rapamycin went with more of PSMB5, a core proteasome subunit, but proteasome activity did not change. Chaperones that work inside mitochondria rose in muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in muscle and fat but not liver. Only parts of the network responded, and differently in each tissue. The samples came from a small group of animals, and the changes are protein levels, not proven effects on health.

The work was done at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System and the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, with Adam Salmon as senior author. No later research paper tied to this person could be confirmed, so the current position is not known.

highlights.LEL2016: First author: measured proteasome, chaperone and autophagy markers in rapamycin-treated marmoset tissues and found tissue-specific changes.

Ross C.lab_name: Ross Lab, Southwest National Primate Research Center, Texas Biomedical Research Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ross C.role: Primate biologist at Texas Biomedical Research Institute who uses the common marmoset to test whether drugs such as rapamycin can protect health during aging
Ross C.sub: Professor and Principal Investigator, Texas Biomedical Research Institute · Associate Director for Research, Southwest National Primate Research Center · earlier at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and Texas A&M University San Antonio (PubMed affiliation 2014–2016) · postdoc in the Biology of Aging, UT Health San Antonio · PhD in Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln (2005)
story: Rapamycin extends life in mice, but no one knows yet whether it does the same in primates. The common marmoset, a small South American monkey that lives about 10 to 15 years, is a practical test case. Corinna Ross was first author of the 2015 Atlas study (ROS2015) on long-term oral rapamycin in marmosets. Body weight, daily activity, blood fats and glucose handling barely changed, so the metabolic side effects that worry people about the drug were small in these animals. In the liver, one enzyme that makes glucose (G6Pase) became less active.

Ross is also a co-author of the 2014 study that first worked out how to dose rapamycin in marmosets (TAR2014) and of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016). These three papers belong to a longer San Antonio project that set up the marmoset as a model for testing anti-aging drugs.

Ross studied biology at Cornell University and the University of Nebraska Omaha, earned a PhD in biological sciences at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln in 2005, and trained as a postdoctoral Biology of Aging fellow at UT Health San Antonio. At the time of these studies PubMed lists Ross at the Barshop Institute and at Texas A&M University San Antonio. Ross now runs a laboratory as Professor at Texas Biomedical Research Institute and is Associate Director for Research at the Southwest National Primate Research Center, still using marmosets to study interventions for healthy aging.

highlights.ROS2015: First author: showed that long-term oral rapamycin had only minor metabolic effects in common marmosets.
highlights.TAR2014: Co-author: part of the team that first described rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author: contributed marmoset tissue work to the study of proteasome, chaperone and autophagy changes under rapamycin.

Tardif S.lab_name: Southwest National Primate Research Center, Texas Biomedical Research Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Tardif S.role: Primate biologist who spent more than 30 years developing the common marmoset as a research model, and who led the first studies of rapamycin dosing and safety in this small monkey
Tardif S.sub: Scientist and Associate Director of Primate Research, Texas Biomedical Research Institute · Associate Director of Research, Southwest National Primate Research Center · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (PubMed affiliation 2014–2016)
story: Suzette Tardif was first author of the 2014 Atlas study (TAR2014) that first described how to give rapamycin to the common marmoset. The drug was put in a protective coating and fed by mouth at about 1 mg per kg each day. Blood levels were similar to those in mouse aging studies and within the range used in human medicine. In treated animals, the marker of mTORC1 activity, the growth-control complex, fell in blood cells, liver and fat. The monkeys showed no anemia, lung scarring or mouth ulcers, side effects known from patients on the drug.

Tardif was senior author of the 2015 follow-up (ROS2015), which found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment, and a co-author of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016). Together these papers made the marmoset a usable model for testing anti-aging drugs in a primate, though none of them measured lifespan.

Tardif's research covers metabolism, behaviour and reproduction in marmosets, and more recently their use as a model of obesity and aging. A 2025 study with Corinna Ross on predicting obesity and blood-sugar problems in adult marmosets lists Tardif at the Southwest National Primate Research Center of Texas Biomedical Research Institute, where Tardif has served as Associate Director of Research.

highlights.TAR2014: First author: first described oral rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in common marmosets.
highlights.ROS2015: Senior author: led the study showing only minor metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author: provided the marmoset cohort for the study of proteasome and autophagy markers under rapamycin.

Wang Zhenhai.lab_name: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (Yinchuan, Ningxia, China)
Wang Zhenhai.role: Neurologist in Yinchuan who leads cell studies of microglia, the brain's immune cells, and of how Brucella bacteria survive inside them
Wang Zhenhai.sub: Neurology Center and Diagnosis and Treatment Engineering Technology Research Center of Nervous System Diseases of Ningxia, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (papers 2011–2026)
story: Brucellosis is an infection passed from farm animals to people, and it can reach the brain. The bacteria survive inside immune cells instead of being destroyed. Zhenhai Wang was senior author of LI2026B, a 2026 paper in the Journal of Medical Microbiology that asked how a Brucella strain does this in microglia, the immune cells of the brain. The team used BV2 cells, a mouse microglia cell line, infected with Brucella suis vaccine strain 2. The bacteria pushed the cells into a mixed state between M1 (the inflammatory, bacteria-killing mode) and M2 (the calmer, repair mode) and switched on autophagy. The M2 state and autophagy together helped the bacteria multiply inside the cells, and the effect ran through the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway.

Normally, autophagy helps immune cells destroy invading microbes. This study suggests that some bacteria can turn it to their own advantage, with mTOR signalling as part of the switch. It was done in a cell line, so it shows a possible mechanism and not what happens in infected patients.

Wang works in neurology at the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University in Yinchuan and in the hospital's engineering research centre for nervous system diseases. The group's PubMed record goes back to a 2011 study of how hepatitis C virus stimulates mouse microglia, and includes a cerebrospinal fluid research laboratory, BV2 cell lines engineered to lack particular phosphatases, a 2024 study on how exosomes from microglia affect myelin repair, and a 2025 study on how doxycycline kills human microglial cells infected with the same Brucella strain.

highlights.LI2026B: Senior author: led the cell study showing that Brucella suis vaccine strain 2 drives M2 polarisation and autophagy in microglia through PI3K/Akt/mTOR to favour its own replication.

Liang X.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
Liang X.role: Toxicology and environmental health researcher who found that the long non-coding RNA LINP1 protects skin cells from radiation-induced senescence by binding mTOR
Liang X.sub: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (2026) · Department of Toxicology, School of Public Health, Southern Medical University, Guangzhou (2025)
story: Xiaoting Liang is first author of the Atlas study LIANG2026, with Liang Zhou of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou as senior author. Radiotherapy often damages the skin, and part of that damage comes from senescence, the state in which cells stop dividing for good. The team found that LINP1, a long non-coding RNA (an RNA that regulates other molecules without making a protein), rises sharply in keratinocytes, the main cells of the outer skin, after radiation.

LINP1 binds the FAT domain of mTOR through a central stretch of the RNA. This weakens the contact between mTOR and the tumour suppressor p53, so less p53 is phosphorylated at serine 15, and the cells are less likely to become senescent. Removing LINP1 made radiation damage worse in cultured keratinocytes and in pieces of human skin kept alive in the lab. Here mTOR acts as a partner of p53 in the stress response, not as a nutrient sensor.

Before moving to Shanxi Medical University in Taiyuan, Liang was listed at the Department of Toxicology of Southern Medical University's School of Public Health, as a co-author with Zhou on a 2025 study of how another long non-coding RNA drives drug resistance in melanoma.

highlights.LIANG2026: First author: showed in keratinocytes and human skin explants that LINP1 binds mTOR, reduces p53 Ser15 phosphorylation and limits radiation-induced senescence.

Li N.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Li N.role: Neuroscientist in Ronald Duman's Yale psychiatry lab who showed in rats that ketamine's fast antidepressant effect depends on mTOR switching on new synapse growth in the prefrontal cortex
Li N.sub: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (papers with Ronald Duman, 2010–2015; at the time of the study)
story: Most antidepressants take weeks to work. Ketamine, a drug that blocks the NMDA type of glutamate receptor, can lift mood within hours. Nanxin Li's 2010 Science paper (LIX2010) from Ronald Duman's lab at Yale looked for the reason in rats. A single dose of ketamine quickly switched on mTOR signalling in the prefrontal cortex, the brain region behind planning and mood control. Within a day the neurons there grew more synaptic spines, the small bumps where one nerve cell receives signals from another. When the team blocked mTOR with rapamycin injected into the brain, both the new spines and the antidepressant-like behaviour disappeared.

The study tied a fast-acting antidepressant to a specific growth pathway and became one of the most cited pieces of evidence that mTOR activity in the brain can be helpful rather than harmful. It was done in rats, so it explains a possible mechanism and does not prove that the same steps happen in depressed patients.

Li followed up the work in the same lab. A 2011 paper in Biological Psychiatry, also as first author, showed that NMDA blockers rapidly reversed the synapse loss and behavioural changes caused by chronic stress in rats. Li also contributed to later Duman-lab papers on scopolamine, on the growth factor neuritin and on stress-driven inflammation in the brain, the last published in 2015. No current institutional page could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.LIX2010: First author: showed in rats that ketamine rapidly activates mTOR in the prefrontal cortex and that blocking mTOR stops both new synapse formation and the antidepressant-like effect.

Wullschleger S.lab_name: MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Wullschleger S.role: Biochemist trained in Michael Hall's Basel lab on TOR complex 2 in yeast, and first author of the widely cited 2006 Cell review that laid out the two TOR complexes and what each controls
Wullschleger S.sub: MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, University of Dundee, Dario Alessi lab (2007–2011, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Biozentrum, University of Basel (PhD 2004, review 2006)
story: In 2006 Stephan Wullschleger, with Robbie Loewith and Michael Hall, wrote the review "TOR signaling in growth and metabolism" in Cell. A review collects many earlier studies into one picture rather than reporting new experiments. This one described the two TOR complexes: TORC1, which is blocked by the drug rapamycin, and TORC2, which is not. It explained how each complex links nutrients and growth signals to cell growth, from yeast to mammals, and became one of the standard starting points for people entering the field.

Wullschleger did a doctorate at the University of Basel. Wullschleger's 2004 thesis characterised TOR complex 2 in baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), the second TOR complex, which was then newly discovered. Wullschleger is also a co-author of the 2002 Molecular Cell paper that first described the two yeast TOR complexes.

Wullschleger then moved to the MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit at the University of Dundee in Dario Alessi's group. There, Wullschleger co-authored the 2007 discovery of Protor, a new subunit of mTORC2, and a 2008 mouse study showing that the LKB1-AMPK energy-sensing pathway holds back tumours in PTEN-deficient mice. As first author in 2011, Wullschleger used knock-in mice to test how the adaptor proteins TAPP1 and TAPP2, which bind a membrane lipid made by PI3K, affect insulin sensitivity. Wullschleger's most recent paper found on PubMed is a 2013 colorectal cancer classification study in Nature Medicine. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.WUL2006: First author of the Cell review that set out TORC1 and TORC2 and their roles in growth and metabolism.

Löffler AS.lab_name: Stork group, Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Löffler AS.role: Cell biologist who worked in Björn Stork's group on how the autophagy kinase ULK1 talks back to the energy sensor AMPK
Löffler AS.sub: Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (papers to 2015) · Department of Internal Medicine I, University of Tübingen (at the time of LOF2011)
story: In LOF2011, Antje Löffler was first author of the study from Björn Stork's group at the University of Tübingen showing that ULK1, the kinase that starts autophagy, phosphorylates and inhibits AMPK, the energy sensor that normally switches ULK1 on. The result is a negative feedback loop: once autophagy has been triggered, ULK1 turns down the signal that started it. This matters for the mTOR field because AMPK and mTORC1 both act on ULK1 from opposite sides, so a loop back to AMPK changes how the whole system responds to starvation. The work was done in cell and biochemical experiments.

Löffler appears on seven PubMed papers from 2011 to 2015, all on autophagy signalling with Stork and Sebastian Wesselborg, first in Tübingen and then at the Institute of Molecular Medicine I of Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf. They include a 2015 study mapping the ULK1-binding site on the autophagy protein ATG13. No later papers or institutional page were found, so the affiliation shown is the last one on these papers.

highlights.LOF2011: First author: showed that ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK and inhibits it, a negative feedback loop in autophagy signalling.

Lv S.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Lv S.role: Kidney researcher at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, and first author of a 2026 study tracing a chain of enzymes that switches on mTOR and drives scarring in damaged kidneys
Lv S.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Chronic kidney disease often ends in fibrosis, a slow scarring in which working kidney tissue is replaced by stiff connective tissue. In the 2026 study led by Shiqi Lv, with Xiaoyan Zhang as senior author, the team followed a chain of four molecules. USP7 is a deubiquitinase, an enzyme that removes ubiquitin tags, the labels that send proteins to be destroyed. By removing them from KDM5B, USP7 keeps KDM5B stable. KDM5B is a histone demethylase, an enzyme that strips activating marks from the proteins that package DNA, and here it silences the gene for TSC1. TSC1 is part of the brake on mTOR, so less TSC1 means more mTOR activity and more scarring.

The evidence comes from two mouse models of kidney injury, where blocking USP7 genetically or with a drug restored TSC1, damped mTOR and reduced fibrosis, and from human kidney samples, where USP7 levels were higher in chronic kidney disease and tracked with how much scarring was present. The human part is a correlation; the cause-and-effect steps were shown in mice and cells.

PubMed lists Shiqi Lv at the Department of Nephrology of Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, in Shanghai. No official profile page could be checked, so the current position is given as at the time of the study.

highlights.LV2026S: First author: showed that USP7 stabilizes KDM5B, which silences TSC1 and activates mTOR, driving kidney fibrosis in mice; USP7 was raised in human CKD kidneys.

Zhang Xiaoyan.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Zhang Xiaoyan.role: Nephrologist at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, and senior author of a 2026 study linking the enzyme USP7 to mTOR activation and kidney scarring
Zhang Xiaoyan.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Xiaoyan Zhang is the senior author of a 2026 study on kidney fibrosis, the scarring that slowly destroys function in chronic kidney disease. The team, with Shiqi Lv as first author, described a chain of control. The enzyme USP7 removes destruction tags from KDM5B, an enzyme that edits the chemical marks on DNA packaging proteins. Stable KDM5B shuts down the gene for TSC1, one half of the main brake on mTOR, and mTOR activity then rises and promotes scarring.

Blocking USP7, by deleting it or with a drug, brought TSC1 back, lowered mTOR activity and reduced fibrosis in two mouse models of kidney injury. In human kidney biopsies USP7 was higher in chronic kidney disease and rose with the amount of scarring, which is an association rather than proof of cause. The authors propose the USP7-KDM5B-TSC1-mTOR axis as a possible drug target.

PubMed gives the Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai, as the affiliation. Because Xiaoyan Zhang is a very common name, no wider publication record or career details are given here without a second independent link.

highlights.LV2026S: Senior author: led the study showing that the USP7-KDM5B axis silences TSC1, activates mTOR and promotes kidney fibrosis in mice, with supporting correlations in human CKD tissue.

Feng H.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Feng H.role: Neurologist at Suzhou Municipal Hospital and senior author of a 2026 stroke study proposing PIP4K2A as a protector of brain tissue through AKT/mTOR signalling and autophagy
Feng H.sub: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou Municipal Hospital), Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: When a stroke blocks a brain artery, doctors try to restore blood flow as quickly as possible. The returning blood, however, causes a second wave of damage called ischemia/reperfusion injury. The 2026 study led by Bodun Ma, with Hongxuan Feng as senior author, looked at PIP4K2A, a lipid kinase, in laboratory models of this injury.

Raising PIP4K2A levels reduced the injury. The team linked the effect to two things: less of a TRIB3-p62 protein complex, which can clog autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and changed AKT/mTOR signalling, so that autophagy could run properly again. The study proposes PIP4K2A-AKT/mTOR as a protective axis, a result from experimental models that has not been tested in patients.

PubMed lists Hongxuan Feng at the Department of Neurology of the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. No official profile could be checked, so the position is given as at the time of the study.

highlights.MA2026: Senior author: led the study showing that PIP4K2A lessens ischemia/reperfusion brain injury by reducing the TRIB3-p62 complex and adjusting AKT/mTOR signalling to restore autophagy.

Ma B.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Ma B.role: Neurology researcher in Suzhou and first author of a 2026 study on how the enzyme PIP4K2A protects the brain after stroke by restoring autophagy through AKT/mTOR
Ma B.sub: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou Municipal Hospital), Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Restoring blood flow after a stroke saves brain tissue, but the sudden return of oxygen also injures cells. Bodun Ma's 2026 study, with Hongxuan Feng as senior author, asked whether the lipid kinase PIP4K2A could limit this reperfusion damage.

In the team's experimental models, more PIP4K2A meant less injury. Two changes went with it: less of a TRIB3-p62 complex that can jam autophagy, the cell's recycling pathway, and altered AKT/mTOR signalling, which let autophagy flow again. mTOR normally holds autophagy back when growth signals are high, so tuning this pathway changes how well damaged neurons clear debris. These are laboratory findings, not results in stroke patients.
PubMed gives the Department of Neurology at the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University as Bodun Ma's affiliation. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.MA2026: First author: showed that PIP4K2A overexpression reduces ischemia/reperfusion brain injury by lowering the TRIB3-p62 burden and modulating AKT/mTOR to restore autophagic flux.

Elshal M.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
Elshal M.role: Pharmacologist at Mansoura University who tests whether existing drugs can protect the brain, liver and other organs in rodent models of disease
Elshal M.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (papers 2024–2026)
story: Epilepsy often develops over time after an injury or a series of seizures, a process called epileptogenesis. In the Atlas study MADKOUR2026, Mahmoud Elshal was last author, the position that usually marks the senior scientist who supervised the work. Rats received repeated small doses of PTZ, a chemical that lowers the seizure threshold, so that seizures grow stronger with each dose (kindling). Rats pre-treated with carvedilol, a common heart and blood-pressure drug, had lower seizure scores, less damage in the hippocampus, the memory region of the brain, and less inflammation driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome. Levels of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway proteins changed at the same time. The authors state that these are associations and do not prove that mTOR signalling causes the benefit.

Elshal works in the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Mansoura University in Egypt. PubMed lists dozens of papers with this affiliation, most of them rodent studies that repurpose approved drugs. In 2026 the same team reported that empagliflozin, a diabetes drug, reduced PTZ-induced seizures in rats and strengthened the effect of the antiseizure drug levetiracetam, and a 2024 study in mice found that the diabetes drug sitagliptin protected the liver against chemically induced cholestasis, a blockage of bile flow. No official profile page was found.

highlights.MADKOUR2026: Last author: supervised the rat study in which carvedilol lowered PTZ-kindled seizures, hippocampal damage and NLRP3 inflammation, alongside changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related proteins.

Madkour AH.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
Madkour AH.role: Pharmacologist at Mansoura University who tests approved drugs as protection against seizures and kidney injury in rats
Madkour AH.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (papers 2022–2026) · Faculty of Health Science Technology, Mansoura National University (2026)
story: Ahmed Madkour was first author of the Atlas study MADKOUR2026 in Scientific Reports, which asked whether carvedilol, a beta-blocker used for heart failure and high blood pressure, could slow the development of epilepsy. Rats received repeated doses of PTZ, a chemical that makes seizures easier to trigger, until seizures became stronger over time (kindling). Rats given carvedilol beforehand had lower seizure scores, less damage in the hippocampus and less inflammation linked to the NLRP3 inflammasome, an alarm system of immune cells. Proteins of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which controls cell growth and survival, changed at the same time. The authors say the study shows associations only, so it does not prove that mTOR signalling is the reason carvedilol helped.

PubMed lists Madkour at the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Mansoura University, Egypt, from 2022 onward. An earlier first-author paper (2022) found that lactoferrin, an iron-binding milk protein, protected rat kidneys in a dose-dependent way after muscle breakdown caused by glycerol. A 2026 first-author paper in Neurotoxicology, again with Mahmoud Elshal, reported that the diabetes drug empagliflozin reduced PTZ-induced seizures in rats and worked best together with a lower dose of levetiracetam. That paper also lists the Faculty of Health Science Technology at Mansoura National University. No official profile page was found.

highlights.MADKOUR2026: First author: ran the rat PTZ-kindling study in which carvedilol lowered seizure scores, hippocampal damage and NLRP3 inflammation, with matching changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related proteins.

Majumder PK.lab_name: Sellers Lab, Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Majumder PK.role: Cancer biologist who, in William Sellers's lab at Dana-Farber, showed that mTOR inhibitors reverse AKT-driven early prostate cancer in mice
Majumder PK.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (at the time of the study, 2004)
story: AKT is a growth kinase that is often overactive in prostate cancer, usually because the brake PTEN is lost. In MAJ2004, Pradip Majumder and colleagues in William Sellers's lab used mice that make active AKT in the prostate. These mice develop prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN), an early, pre-invasive stage of prostate cancer. Treating them with the mTOR inhibitor RAD001 (everolimus) reversed the PIN. The authors traced the effect to two routes: the drug caused the abnormal cells to die by apoptosis, and it switched off a set of genes controlled by HIF-1, a transcription factor that drives growth and blood vessel formation. The study, done in mice, helped make the case that tumours driven by AKT depend on mTOR and could respond to mTOR inhibitors.
No current institutional page was found. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAJ2004: First author: showed in AKT-transgenic mice that the mTOR inhibitor RAD001 reverses prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia through apoptosis and HIF-1-dependent pathways.

Manifava M.lab_name: Ktistakis Group, Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Manifava M.role: Cell biologist in Nicholas Ktistakis's group at the Babraham Institute whose live-cell imaging work spans more than two decades of research on lipid signalling, autophagosome formation and mTORC1
Manifava M.sub: Ktistakis Group, Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (papers 2001–2026)
story: Maria Manifava was first author of the 2016 eLife study (MAN2016) that filmed mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in living human cells as amino acids were added back after starvation. mTORC1 arrived on lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, within about 2 minutes and peaked by 5 minutes, in step with the amino acid leucine reaching the inside of the lysosomes. The chemical marks that mTORC1 places on its usual target proteins appeared later. The authors suggested that mTORC1 makes a short stop at the lysosome to be switched on and then acts on its targets elsewhere in the cell. Timing like this is hard to see with methods that only take snapshots, which is why live imaging mattered here. The work was done in cultured cells.

Manifava has published with Nicholas Ktistakis at the Babraham Institute in Cambridge since at least 2001, when PubMed lists a paper on the lipid-binding FYVE-domain proteins FENS-1 and DFCP1. DFCP1 became central to a 2008 study in the Journal of Cell Biology, on which Manifava is a co-author, that described the omegasome: a membrane platform rich in the lipid phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate, connected to the endoplasmic reticulum, from which autophagosomes grow. The group's most recent paper, in Nature Communications in 2026 with Roger Williams's group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, describes a positive feedback loop between GABARAP and the PI3-kinase complex that helps autophagosome membranes expand quickly.
PubMed still lists Manifava in the Signalling Programme at the Babraham Institute on the 2026 paper. No personal page was found, so the exact job title is not shown.

highlights.MAN2016: First author: imaged living human cells to show that mTORC1 reaches lysosomes within 2 minutes of amino acid addition and acts on its targets after it leaves.

Quinn D.role: Clinical trial investigator at P3 Research in Wellington, New Zealand, who was a co-author of the resTORbio trials that tested low-dose mTOR inhibitors to strengthen immunity in older adults
Quinn D.sub: P3 Research, Newtown, Wellington, New Zealand (affiliation on PubMed papers) · listed with resTORbio, Boston, on the 2021 trial report
story: Dean Quinn is a co-author of two Atlas papers on whether short, low-dose courses of mTOR-blocking drugs can make older people's immune systems work better. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of BEZ235 and everolimus was followed by fewer reported infections over the next year, more active antiviral genes and a better response to the flu vaccine. MAN2021 then tested BEZ235 alone (renamed RTB101) in two bigger trials. The phase 2b trial (652 people) showed fewer lab-confirmed respiratory infections only in an analysis that was not corrected for multiple testing, and the phase 3 trial (1,024 people) found no difference in its main endpoint. Taken together, these are human trials that gave an early signal and then a negative confirmatory result, a useful lesson in how drug evidence develops.

Trials like these recruit volunteers at specialised research clinics. PubMed lists Quinn at P3 Research in Newtown, Wellington, a clinical trials company in New Zealand, on about ten trial reports, and the 2021 paper also lists him with resTORbio, the Boston company that ran the RTB101 program.
No official profile was found to confirm Quinn's medical training or current position, so this profile is limited to what the publications show.

highlights.MAN2018: Trial investigator and co-author on the phase 2a study linking a short low-dose course of BEZ235 plus everolimus with fewer infections in older adults.
highlights.MAN2021: Co-author, listed with resTORbio and P3 Research, on the phase 2b and phase 3 trials of RTB101, where the phase 3 trial did not confirm a clinical benefit.

Shergill S.role: Senior author of the 2021 report of resTORbio's phase 2b and phase 3 trials of the mTOR inhibitor RTB101 to protect older adults from respiratory infections
Shergill S.sub: resTORbio, Boston (PubMed affiliation, 2021, at the time of the study) · current position not confirmed
story: The immune system weakens with age, and the idea tested here was that blocking mTOR could improve immune function in older adults. MAN2021, published in Lancet Healthy Longevity in 2021 with Sarb Shergill as last author and the authors listed at resTORbio, reports two large tests of that idea with RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, taken once a day for 16 weeks by adults aged 65 and over.

In the phase 2b trial (652 people), fewer people on 10 mg had a laboratory-confirmed respiratory infection than on placebo (19% against 28%), but this came from a pooled analysis not corrected for multiple testing, and the corrected analysis was not significant. The phase 3 trial (1,024 people) used a different main endpoint agreed with the FDA, illness with or without a lab test, and found no difference (26% against 25%). Blood tests in both trials still showed more antiviral genes switched on. For readers, the lesson is that a promising biological signal in older people did not turn into fewer illnesses in the larger trial.
PubMed lists only this paper for Sarb Shergill, with the affiliation resTORbio, Boston. No official biography was found, so the role at the company and the current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.MAN2021: Last author of the report of the RTB101 phase 2b and phase 3 trials in adults over 65; phase 3 showed no reduction in respiratory illness.

Marchant ED.lab_name: Rasmussen Lab, Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Marchant ED.role: Graduate student in Blake Rasmussen's lab in San Antonio who studies what overactive mTORC1 in skeletal muscle does to metabolism, inflammation and exercise adaptation in aging and overnutrition
Marchant ED.sub: Graduate student, Biology of Aging discipline, Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, UT Health San Antonio (Rasmussen lab) · MS in nutritional science, Brigham Young University (2022) · BS in nutritional science, Brigham Young University (2019)
story: Erik Marchant is first author of the Atlas study MARCHANT2026, with B. B. Rasmussen as senior author. Overactive mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in muscle is often linked with insulin resistance, the state in which the body handles sugar poorly. To test whether one causes the other, the team switched mTORC1 on permanently in mouse skeletal muscle by removing GATOR1, a protein complex that normally turns mTORC1 off when amino acids are scarce.

The muscles showed more signs of inflammation, but the mice still handled a glucose load normally. So muscle mTORC1 overactivity alone was not enough to cause glucose intolerance, and other metabolic inputs must be needed. A companion paper from the same group in 2026, with Marchant as second author, found that this kind of hyperactive muscle mTORC1 blunted the benefits of endurance training even though mitochondria and lipids changed. Both studies are in mice.

Marchant earned a bachelor's degree (2019) and a master's degree (2022) in nutritional science at Brigham Young University in Utah. Papers from that time include a 2020 study showing that, unlike a high-fat diet, bed rest did not appear to cause insulin resistance through mitochondrial oxidants, and a 2018 commentary on restricting branched-chain amino acids for metabolic health. Marchant is now a graduate student in the Biology of Aging discipline at UT Health San Antonio, in the lab of Blake Rasmussen, working on muscle metabolism in aging and overnutrition. Besides the mTORC1 work, the projects include testing ultrasound as a possible treatment for insulin resistance in old mice, and co-authored human studies of muscle disuse and rehabilitation in middle-aged adults (2025) and of PDE-5 inhibitors (2026).

highlights.MARCHANT2026: First author: showed that permanently active mTORC1 in mouse skeletal muscle, made by deleting GATOR1, raises inflammation but does not by itself impair glucose tolerance.

Anderson RM.lab_name: Division of Geriatrics and Gerontology, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Anderson RM.role: Professor of medicine at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies the basic biology of aging and how calorie restriction slows it, and senior author of the 2017 comparison of the two long-running rhesus monkey calorie restriction studies
Anderson RM.sub: Professor, Division of Geriatrics and Gerontology, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison · Health Officer, Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital, Madison · earlier: postdoctoral fellow, UW-Madison Institute on Aging · postdoctoral fellow, Harvard Medical School (David Sinclair's group, papers 2002–2003) · PhD in biochemistry, University College Dublin
story: Rozalyn Anderson was senior author of a 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that resolved an apparent conflict between two of the longest experiments in aging research. One group at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin had followed rhesus monkeys on calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, for decades. Wisconsin had reported longer survival and the NIA had not. Analysing both studies side by side, the paper found consistent health benefits in both, and showed that the survival effect depended on study design and on what the control monkeys were fed.

Calorie restriction is the oldest known way to slow aging in animals, and lower mTORC1 activity is one of the routes through which it is thought to work. Monkeys are much closer to humans than mice are, so this comparison is among the strongest primate evidence that eating less improves health. It leaves open how large any lifespan gain would be.

Anderson earned a PhD in biochemistry at University College Dublin. As a postdoctoral fellow in David Sinclair's group at Harvard Medical School she worked on calorie restriction in yeast, and in 2003 she was first author of papers in Nature and Science showing that the enzyme PNC1, which removes nicotinamide, is needed for calorie restriction to extend yeast lifespan, and that this effect does not depend on swings in the cell's NAD+ to NADH ratio. A second postdoctoral fellowship at the UW-Madison Institute on Aging moved her to the mechanisms by which calorie restriction delays aging in mammals. She is now a professor in the Division of Geriatrics and Gerontology of the Department of Medicine, a faculty member of the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, and Health Officer at the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the Madison VA hospital. Her lab asks why aging makes people more vulnerable to cancer, diabetes, heart disease and neurodegeneration. Recent papers cover how calorie restriction remodels the mouse brain, how an acetyl-CoA transporter in the endoplasmic reticulum changes neuron metabolism, and sex differences in aging.

highlights.MAT2017: Senior author: led the joint analysis of the NIA and Wisconsin monkey studies, which found consistent health benefits of calorie restriction and a survival effect that depended on study design.

de Cabo R.lab_name: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, National Institutes of Health (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
de Cabo R.role: Aging researcher at the US National Institute on Aging who has studied calorie restriction, fasting and drugs that mimic them in mice and rhesus monkeys, including the long-running NIA monkey study
de Cabo R.sub: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, NIH, Baltimore (papers to 2026)
story: Rafael de Cabo is a co-author of the 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that put side by side the two longest studies of calorie restriction in primates: one run by the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin. Calorie restriction, eating 10 to 40% less while still getting all nutrients, lengthens life in many animals, and part of its effect is thought to run through lower mTOR activity. The two monkey studies had seemed to disagree on survival. Comparing them directly, the authors found clear health benefits in both, while the effect on survival depended on study design and on what the control monkeys were fed. This is evidence from rhesus monkeys, the closest animal model to humans for this question.

De Cabo was also the senior author of the 2012 Nature paper, with Julie Mattison as first author, that first reported that calorie restriction in the NIA monkeys had not improved survival, in contrast to the Wisconsin study. That apparent clash is what the 2017 comparison resolved. PubMed lists more than 400 papers under the name, many on how diet, fasting and candidate drugs affect health and lifespan in mice.

De Cabo works in the Translational Gerontology Branch of the NIA Intramural Research Program in Baltimore, and recent 2026 papers with collaborators in Madrid and at the NIA cover aging of the blood system and of human skeletal muscle.

highlights.MAT2017: Co-author of the comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin rhesus monkey studies, which showed consistent health benefits of calorie restriction and survival effects that depended on study design.

Ma XM.lab_name: Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics, Genentech (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Ma XM.role: Cell biologist who trained with John Blenis on how mTOR and S6K1 control protein synthesis, wrote a widely used review of mTOR-driven translation, and later worked in cancer research at Genentech
Ma XM.sub: Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics, Genentech (2009–2015) · John Blenis lab (papers 2008–2011)
story: Making protein is one of the most energy-hungry things a cell does, so cells only do it at full speed when conditions are good. mTOR is the sensor that decides. In 2009 Xiaoju Max Ma wrote, with John Blenis, a review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology (MAX2009) that explains how mTOR takes in signals about nutrients, energy, stress and growth factors and passes them on to the protein-making machinery. It covers the two best-known mTORC1 targets, S6K1 and the 4E-BP proteins that hold back the start of translation. As a review, it summarises earlier experiments rather than reporting new ones.

PubMed lists four papers under this name tied to Blenis or Genentech: a 2008 research paper and the 2009 review with Blenis, the 2011 phosphoproteomics study that identified Grb10 as an mTORC1 target (also in the Atlas), and a 2015 Science Translational Medicine paper from Genentech and AbbVie on BCL-2 family inhibitors, cancer drugs that make tumour cells more likely to die. The 2009 review gives the Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics at Genentech as the address.
No current institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAX2009: First author: wrote, with John Blenis, the review explaining how mTOR links nutrient, energy and growth signals to the control of protein synthesis.

McNeill M.lab_name: Division of Hematology-Oncology, Department of Pediatrics, The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto, Ontario, Canada)
McNeill M.role: Paediatric haematology researcher at SickKids in Toronto and first author of a 2026 cohort study of sirolimus for Evans syndrome and other autoimmune blood-count disorders in children
McNeill M.sub: Division of Hematology-Oncology, Department of Pediatrics, The Hospital for Sick Children, and Department of Pediatrics, University of Toronto (at the time of the study)
story: In Evans syndrome the immune system attacks the body's own blood cells, usually red cells and platelets together, so children can become anaemic and bruise or bleed easily. Steroids often help only for a while. Sirolimus (rapamycin) blocks mTOR in overactive immune cells and has been tried as a gentler long-term option. Maggie McNeill is first author of a 2026 retrospective study from the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) in Toronto that looked back at children treated with sirolimus for Evans syndrome and for autoimmune cytopenias, low blood counts, linked to other conditions (MCNEILL2026). The authors report that sirolimus was effective. A look-back study from one centre cannot show how much of the improvement was due to the drug, and the abstract was not yet indexed when this profile was written, so the exact numbers are still to be added.

PubMed lists McNeill in the Division of Hematology-Oncology at SickKids and the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Toronto, working with senior author Manuel Carcao. No other papers clearly by the same person were found, and no personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the paper.

highlights.MCNEILL2026: First author of the single-centre retrospective cohort reporting that sirolimus is effective for paediatric Evans syndrome and secondary autoimmune cytopenias.

Meikle L.lab_name: Division of Translational Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Meikle L.role: Researcher in David Kwiatkowski's tuberous sclerosis lab at Brigham and Women's Hospital who built a mouse model of TSC in the brain and showed that mTOR blockers rescue it
Meikle L.sub: Division of Translational Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Kwiatkowski lab (papers 2005–2009, at the time of the study)
story: In tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), loss of the TSC1 or TSC2 gene removes the brake on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and the brain is often hit hardest, with seizures, learning problems and autism. Lynsey Meikle, working in David Kwiatkowski's lab in Boston, first built a mouse in which most nerve cells of the cerebral cortex lose Tsc1 during development. Published in 2007, these mice had enlarged, misplaced neurons, delayed myelination, seizures and a median survival of only 35 days, which made them a model of the human brain disease.

In the Atlas paper (MEI2008), Meikle and colleagues treated these mice with rapamycin and the related drug RAD001 (everolimus). The drugs switched off the overactive mTORC1 signal, restored Akt signalling, and greatly improved survival and brain function. This mouse work was part of the evidence that led to testing mTOR blockers in people with TSC, where everolimus is now used for brain and kidney tumours and for seizures.

Meikle also contributed to a 2009 study with Mustafa Sahin's group showing that neurons lacking the TSC complex suffer high stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, a protein-folding compartment, which rapamycin reversed. No later papers or current position could be found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MEI2008: First author: showed that rapamycin and RAD001 improve survival and function in a neuronal Tsc1 mouse model of tuberous sclerosis.

Melendez A.lab_name: Meléndez Lab, Department of Biology, Queens College, City University of New York (New York, New York, USA)
Melendez A.role: Developmental geneticist at Queens College, CUNY, who showed as a postdoc in Beth Levine's lab that autophagy genes are needed for the long life of insulin-signalling mutant worms. Her lab studies autophagy in C. elegans development, from germline stem cells to meiosis
Melendez A.sub: Professor, Department of Biology, Queens College, CUNY · Director, Office of Undergraduate Research, Queens College (since 2023) · postdoc with Beth Levine and before that with Iva Greenwald, Columbia University · PhD in Biology, Columbia University (Daniel Kalderon lab) · BA, Princeton University
story: In 2003, working in Beth Levine's lab at Columbia University, Alicia Meléndez was first author of a Science paper (MEL2003) that tied autophagy, the cell's self-recycling system, to lifespan in an animal. The roundworm C. elegans lives much longer when its insulin-like signalling is turned down by mutations in the receptor gene daf-2. When bec-1, the worm version of the autophagy gene beclin 1, was switched off in these long-lived worms, they lost their extra lifespan. They also could not properly form dauer larvae, a tough resting stage that young worms enter when food is short.

Why does this matter for mTOR? mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is one of the main brakes on autophagy, and several ways of extending lifespan in animals, from eating less to taking rapamycin, switch autophagy on. This paper was among the first to show that autophagy is required for a genetic lifespan extension, not just present alongside it. The work was done in worms, so it shows a mechanism in one animal rather than an effect in people.

Meléndez did her undergraduate thesis with Eric Wieschaus at Princeton University and earned a PhD in Biology at Columbia University with Daniel Kalderon. She was a postdoc with Iva Greenwald at Columbia before moving to Levine's lab to study autophagy in worms. Her own lab at Queens College, City University of New York, studies the role of autophagy in C. elegans development, with a focus on germline stem cell proliferation and the accuracy of meiosis, the cell division that makes eggs and sperm. She is a Professor of Biology and since 2023 also directs the college's Office of Undergraduate Research.

highlights.MEL2003: First author: showed in long-lived daf-2 worms that losing the autophagy gene bec-1 removes the extra lifespan and blocks normal dauer formation.

Goodarzi H.lab_name: Goodarzi Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of California, San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Goodarzi H.role: Systems biologist at UCSF and the Arc Institute who combines computation and experiments to find hidden gene-regulation programs that drive cancer, and a co-author of two Atlas studies on mTORC1 in drug-resistant cancers
Goodarzi H.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, UCSF · Core Investigator, Arc Institute (since 2023) · postdoc in cancer systems biology, Rockefeller University (to 2016) · PhD in computational biology and genomics, Princeton (2010)
story: Goodarzi appears in the Atlas on two cancer studies about mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In MEN2023, the bi-steric inhibitor RMC-6272, which is more than 25 times more selective for mTORC1 than for mTORC2, fully shut down mTORC1, including its control of 4E-BP1, a target that rapamycin only partly blocks. It overcame resistance to hormone therapy and to CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer cells and in tumours grown from patient samples in mice. In YAN2026, from Davide Ruggero's lab, B cell lymphomas that import small protein fragments (dipeptides) through the transporter SLC15A3 kept mTORC1 switched on and resisted the chemotherapy drug 6-mercaptopurine; the resistant tumours became sensitive to rapamycin.

Goodarzi earned a PhD in computational biology and genomics at Princeton in 2010 and did postdoctoral training in cancer systems biology at Rockefeller University, finishing in 2016. According to the UCSF profile, his lab studies how cancer cells reach disordered gene expression states that drive progression, using unbiased computational and experimental methods to find regulatory pathways that are not yet known.
He is a professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at UCSF and has been a Core Investigator at the Arc Institute in Palo Alto since 2023.

highlights.MEN2023: Co-author: contributed to the breast cancer study showing that the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-6272 overcomes hormone-therapy and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance.
highlights.YAN2026: Co-author: contributed to the lymphoma study showing that SLC15A3-driven dipeptide import keeps mTORC1 on and causes chemotherapy resistance that rapamycin can reverse.

Meng D.lab_name: Bandyopadhyay Lab, Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Meng D.role: Cancer researcher at UCSF who led the preclinical test of RMC-6272, a drug that blocks mTORC1 much more strongly than mTORC2, in drug-resistant breast cancer
Meng D.sub: Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California San Francisco (at the time of the 2023 study, with Sourav Bandyopadhyay)
story: Delong Meng is the first author of MEN2023, an Oncogene paper from Sourav Bandyopadhyay's group at UCSF, written with colleagues at Revolution Medicines, the company that makes the drug. mTOR works in two complexes. mTORC1 drives growth, and in many breast cancers it stays switched on because of mutations in PIK3CA or PTEN. Older drugs either block mTORC1 only partly, like rapamycin, which misses the target 4E-BP1, or block both complexes, which causes side effects such as high blood sugar. RMC-6272 is a bi-steric inhibitor: one molecule that grips mTOR at two sites at once. It is more than 25 times more selective for mTORC1 than for mTORC2 and shuts mTORC1 down completely, including its control of 4E-BP1.

In the study the drug killed ER-positive breast cancer cell lines, especially those with PIK3CA or PTEN mutations, and still worked in models that had become resistant to hormone therapy and to CDK4/6 inhibitors. The tests used cell lines and patient tumours grown in mice (PDX models), so they are preclinical. The paper laid groundwork for the related drug RMC-5552, which has gone into clinical trials.

PubMed shows no other paper that can be tied to this name with the same co-authors, and no official profile was found, so the current position could not be confirmed. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MEN2023: First author: showed that the mTORC1-selective bi-steric inhibitor RMC-6272 overcomes hormone- and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance in breast cancer cell lines and PDX models.

Yang YC.role: Scientist at Revolution Medicines who worked on the company's bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitors, from the breast cancer lab studies of RMC-6272 to the first trial of RMC-5552 in patients
Yang YC.sub: Revolution Medicines, Redwood City, California (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2023 to 2026)
story: Yu Chi Yang is a co-author of two Atlas papers on a new kind of mTOR drug. Rapamycin and its relatives only partly block mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and leave one of its key targets, 4E-BP1, largely untouched. Drugs that block the mTOR enzyme site block mTORC1 fully but also hit mTORC2, which causes side effects such as high blood sugar. Revolution Medicines built bi-steric molecules, which join a rapamycin-like part to an enzyme-site part so that they bind two places at once and prefer mTORC1. MEN2023 showed that one of them, RMC-6272, fully shut down mTORC1, including 4E-BP1, and overcame resistance to hormone therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer cells and in tumours from patients grown in mice. SCH2025 was the first trial of the related drug RMC-5552 in 57 patients with advanced solid tumours. High blood sugar was uncommon (4 percent) and the disease was controlled in 64 percent of patients, but with no comparison group the trial cannot prove that sparing mTORC2 is the reason.
PubMed lists Yang at Revolution Medicines in Redwood City, California, on 17 papers from 2023 to 2026, in the company's work on targeted cancer drugs.
Because Yang is a very common surname, only papers with the Revolution Medicines affiliation were counted. No official profile was found, so training and job title are not given.

highlights.MEN2023: Revolution Medicines co-author on the preclinical study showing that the bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-6272 overcomes drug resistance in breast cancer models.
highlights.SCH2025: Revolution Medicines co-author on the first-in-human phase 1 trial of the bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552 in advanced solid tumours.

Cao Z.role: Veterinary toxicologist at Northeast Agricultural University in Harbin whose group studies how pollutants and food toxins damage the kidney, liver and gut in mice
Cao Z.sub: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin
story: Zheng Cao was senior author of a 2026 Environmental Science & Technology study (MIAO2026) on EDPrB, a liquid-crystal monomer, one of the chemicals used in flat screens that can leak into the environment. In mice, EDPrB built up in the kidney and caused chronic kidney disease. The team traced the harm to overactive mTOR, the cell's growth switch. When mTOR stays on, autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, is held back, and the kidney developed inflammation and fibrosis, a stiff scar tissue. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, prevented the damage, which marked mTOR activation as the first step in the chain. Human kidney cells grown in a dish gave matching results.

The study is written as an adverse outcome pathway, a step-by-step map from the first molecular hit to disease that toxicologists use to judge chemical risks. It is evidence from mice and cultured cells, not from exposed people.

Cao's group at the Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine in Harbin works on how contaminants injure organs. Recent papers from the group show that the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol, a common contaminant of grain, breaks down the gut barrier (2024) and harms the liver through excessive mitophagy, the removal of mitochondria (2025), that the plastic chemical bisphenol F causes kidney inflammation and fibrosis through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (2026), and that a berberine gel can ease mastitis in a mouse model (2026).

highlights.MIAO2026: Senior author: led the mouse and cell study showing that the pollutant EDPrB causes kidney disease through mTOR overactivation, which rapamycin prevented.

Cao Z.lab_name: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University (Harbin, China)

Miao C.role: Researcher in Zheng Cao's group at Northeast Agricultural University who studies how environmental and food toxins damage organs in mice, and first author of the 2026 study tying a screen chemical to kidney disease through mTOR
Miao C.sub: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin (papers 2024–2026)
story: Chenjiao Miao was first author of a 2026 Environmental Science & Technology study (MIAO2026) on EDPrB, a liquid-crystal monomer used in display screens that can escape into the environment. Mice exposed to EDPrB built it up in the kidney and developed chronic kidney disease. The chain of harm started with overactive mTOR, the cell's growth switch. With mTOR stuck on, autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was suppressed, and inflammation and fibrosis, a stiff scar tissue, followed. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, prevented the damage, and human kidney cells in a dish responded in the same way.

The paper lays this out as an adverse outcome pathway, a step-by-step map that regulators can use to judge chemical risk. It shows a mechanism in mice and cells; it does not measure harm in exposed people.

Miao works in Zheng Cao's group in Harbin. Earlier first-author work showed in mice and pig gut cells that the grain mycotoxin deoxynivalenol damages the intestinal barrier through the RhoA/ROCK pathway (2024), and a 2026 first-author paper found that the plastic chemical bisphenol F drives kidney inflammation and fibrosis through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and changes in kidney macrophages.

story: In 2018 Dirk Mossmann, Sujin Park and Michael Hall wrote a review in Nature Reviews Cancer arguing that mTOR signalling and cell metabolism decide each other in cancer. mTOR reads the nutrients a cell has and turns on the making of proteins, fats and nucleotides. In turn, the metabolic state of a tumour cell changes how mTOR signals. A review gathers earlier experiments; it does not report new ones.

Before Basel, Mossmann worked at the University of Freiburg in Germany, at the Institute of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, where Mossmann co-authored work on mitochondrial protein import and a 2018 study linking mutations in the mitochondrial presequence protease to a childhood neurodegenerative disease.

In Basel, Mossmann moved to liver cancer. As first author of a 2023 paper in Cell, Mossmann showed that liver tumours in mice and patients pile up the amino acid arginine, because tumour cells take more of it in and use less. High arginine binds the protein RBM39 and pushes the cells toward a more primitive, dividing state. The team suggested the drug indisulam, which degrades RBM39, as a way to target this. Mossmann also co-authored a 2022 Molecular Cell study on how the transcription factors TEAD2 and E2A shut down acetyl-CoA production to favour tumour growth. A position after 2023 could not be confirmed.

story: Taras Stasyk is a co-author of two Atlas studies about mTORC1 control at the lysosome. An early 2004 review with Lukas Huber described how to purify parts of the cell, such as organelles, before mass spectrometry so that rare signaling proteins can be seen. story: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with a mutated TP53 gene often resists immunotherapy because the tumours are immune-cold: few killer T cells get inside. Priyatosh Nath's 2026 study, with Cherie-Ann Nathan as senior author, tested whether blocking mTOR could change that. A preprint version appeared on bioRxiv in June 2026 and the paper was then published in Neoplasia.

In mouse tumours of this type, including lines resistant to anti-PD-1 therapy, everolimus, an approved mTOR inhibitor, slowed tumour growth and remodelled the tumour surroundings. More CD8 T cells and dendritic cells came in, regulatory T cells that dampen immunity went down, and the HIF-1alpha/VEGFA signal that recruits immune-suppressing myeloid cells and builds blood vessels was reduced. Everolimus also raised the chemokine signals TNF-alpha and CXCL10 and lowered PD-1 and PD-L1, which helped T cells kill again. These are mouse results; the authors propose testing everolimus with immunotherapy in patients likely to fail immunotherapy alone.

PubMed lists Nath at the Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, LSU Health Shreveport, on papers since 2024, including a 2024 review on the growth-factor receptor FGFR2 in cutaneous squamous cell cancer with the same group and a 2025 review on the pharmacology of natural chalcones. The exact title could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.NAT2026: First author: showed in syngeneic TP53-mutant head and neck cancer models that everolimus brings in CD8 T cells, reduces suppressive cells and PD-1/PD-L1, and slows tumour growth.

Nazio F.role: Cell biologist at the University of Rome Tor Vergata who, in Francesco Cecconi's lab, showed how mTOR keeps autophagy switched off by acting on AMBRA1 and the starter kinase ULK1
Nazio F.sub: Department of Biology, University of Rome Tor Vergata (papers to 2026) · Dulbecco Telethon Institute, Cecconi lab (2013)
story: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: when food is short, cells wrap up worn-out parts and break them down for raw materials. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, keeps autophagy off when nutrients are plentiful. Francesca Nazio is first author of a 2013 paper from Francesco Cecconi's group at the Dulbecco Telethon Institute in Rome that explained one way it does this (NAZ2013). The kinase ULK1 starts autophagy. To work well it needs the helper protein AMBRA1 and the enzyme TRAF6, which together add ubiquitin chains to ULK1, stabilise it and help it cluster. mTOR phosphorylates AMBRA1 and so blocks this step; when mTOR is switched off, AMBRA1 is freed and autophagy can begin. The experiments were done in cultured cells.

Nazio has stayed at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, with more than 60 papers on PubMed. Recent work includes a 2024 review with Silvia Campello's group on how cancer cells take up mitochondria from healthy neighbours to gain energy and resist treatment, and a 2026 study on how the heme-making enzyme ferrochelatase shapes the metabolism and staying power of CAR T cells used against the childhood cancer neuroblastoma. The current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.NAZ2013: First author: showed that mTOR blocks autophagy by phosphorylating AMBRA1, preventing TRAF6-driven ubiquitylation, stabilisation and self-association of ULK1.

Nazio F.lab_name: Department of Biology, University of Rome Tor Vergata (Rome, Italy)

Nazemi M.role: Cell biologist in Elena Rainero's lab at the University of Sheffield who studies how the collagen-rich matrix around tumours feeds cancer cells when nutrients run short
Nazemi M.sub: School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield, Elena Rainero lab (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2020 to 2026)
story: Mona Nazemi is the first author of NAZ2026. Breast and pancreatic tumours are packed in collagen I, the main protein of scar-like tissue, and the blood supply in them is poor, so cancer cells are often short of amino acids. The study found that cancer cells sitting on collagen I use their collagen receptor, alpha2beta1 integrin, to switch on mTORC1 and its target S6, and to bring the amino acid transporter LAT1-4F2hc to the cell surface. More transporter at the surface means more essential amino acids get in, and the cells survive. In patient data, high LAT1-4F2hc levels in basal-like breast and pancreatic tumours went with a worse outlook. This links the tumour's surroundings directly to mTORC1, the cell's nutrient sensor.

Nazemi has worked with Elena Rainero at Sheffield since at least 2020, when they wrote a review on how the tumour matrix and cell metabolism talk to each other. In a 2024 PLoS Biology paper, also as first author, Nazemi showed that invasive breast cancer cells starved of amino acids can swallow pieces of the surrounding matrix, break them down in lysosomes and use the released tyrosine and phenylalanine to keep growing.
No official profile was found, so training and current role are given only from the publication record.

highlights.NAZ2026: First author: showed that collagen I activates mTORC1/S6 and brings the LAT1-4F2hc amino acid transporter to the cell surface, helping cancer cells survive nutrient shortage.

Brohée L.role: Cell biologist who studied how lipid metabolism and the lysosome feed into mTORC1, first at the University of Liège and then at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing in Cologne
Brohée L.sub: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Cologne, Cell Growth Control in Health and Age-related Disease group (papers 2021–2023; at the time of the studies) · Laboratory of Connective Tissues Biology, GIGA-Cancer, University of Liège, Belgium (papers 2015–2021)
story: Laura Brohée appears on two Atlas papers about brakes on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2021 Cell study PRE2021 found that G3BP1 and G3BP2, proteins best known from stress granules, also sit on the outer surface of lysosomes and hold the TSC complex there. TSC is the brake that keeps mTORC1 in check, and without the G3BPs it could not reach its target, so mTORC1 over-reacted to amino acids and insulin. The 2023 Nature Cell Biology study NIC2023 found that malonyl-CoA, a building block made during fatty acid synthesis, fits into the same pocket of mTOR that normally binds ATP and blocks it. When fatty acid production slows and malonyl-CoA builds up, mTORC1 activity falls, which links the cell's fat-making capacity to its overall growth. Brohée was a co-author on the first and the second author on the second. Both were mainly cell studies; the 2021 paper added zebrafish experiments on nerve development.

Before Cologne, Brohée worked at the University of Liège in Belgium in the Laboratory of Connective Tissues Biology (Deroanne group), on cancer cell metabolism. A 2021 review on lipin-1 as a cancer target followed.

At the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Brohée's papers list the Cell Growth Control in Health and Age-related Disease group, led by Constantinos Demetriades, which also produced a 2021 Molecular Cell paper on how TSC1 binds lysosomal lipids. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: Gianluca Figlia appears on two Atlas studies about brakes on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2021 Cell paper (PRE2021) found that G3BP1 and G3BP2, proteins best known from stress granules, also sit on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment where mTORC1 is switched on. There they hold the TSC complex, the main off-switch for mTORC1, in place. Without them mTORC1 reacts too strongly to amino acids and insulin. The 2023 Nature Cell Biology paper (NIC2023) showed that malonyl-CoA, a building block made on the way to new fatty acids, fits into the same pocket of mTOR that normally holds ATP and so blocks it. When a cell cannot make fat fast enough, malonyl-CoA rises and slows mTORC1 down. Both results come mainly from cells; the first adds zebrafish experiments, and the second shows the malonyl-CoA effect is conserved across species.

Figlia's path ran through two labs that both linked mTOR to lipids. At ETH Zurich, in Ueli Suter's group, Figlia was second author of a 2014 Cell Reports paper showing in mice that mTORC1 in Schwann cells, the cells that wrap nerves in insulating myelin, drives myelin growth by switching on fat-making genes through SREBP. At the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, in Aurelio Teleman's group, Figlia was first author of a 2020 review on how metabolites control signalling by attaching chemically to proteins, and first author of a 2025 EMBO Journal paper showing that cells sense glutamine for mTORC1 entirely through the kinase GCN2, triggered by the loss of asparagine.
The 2025 paper and a 2026 commentary on TDP-43 disease list Figlia at the Institute of Neuropathology, RWTH Aachen University Hospital.

Nicastro R.role: Cell biologist at the University of Fribourg who studies TORC1 signalling in yeast and mammals, and first author of the discovery that malonyl-CoA is a natural mTORC1 inhibitor
