story: Raffaele Nicastro is the first author of NIC2023, a Nature Cell Biology paper by groups at the University of Fribourg and Constantinos Demetriades's lab. mTOR is a kinase, an enzyme that uses ATP to tag other proteins. The study found that malonyl-CoA, a small molecule made on the way to building fatty acids, fits directly into the mTOR catalytic pocket and competes with ATP. It works like a natural version of the ATP-competitive mTOR drugs. When the fat-making enzyme fatty acid synthase is turned down, malonyl-CoA builds up and dampens mTORC1. This ties the cell's capacity to make fat to its overall growth output. The effect was seen in yeast and mammalian cells, which is why the paper calls it conserved.

Nicastro's PubMed record shows many papers from the University of Fribourg between 2016 and 2026 many of them with Claudio De Virgilio, whose group studies how TORC1 is controlled in yeast. Papers from 2014 and 2015 list an affiliation in Milan, Italy. No official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.NIC2023: First author: showed that malonyl-CoA binds the mTOR catalytic pocket and acts as a conserved, ATP-competitive inhibitor of mTORC1.

Nojima H.role: First author of the 2003 Kobe study showing that raptor grabs mTOR's targets through a short TOS motif, the docking step that lets mTORC1 reach its substrates
Nojima H.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (at the time of the study, 2003)
story: An enzyme like mTOR has to find the right proteins to act on. In 2002 two groups discovered raptor, a partner protein that sits next to mTOR in the complex now called mTORC1, the growth-control complex. One of those groups was Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's team at Kobe University. Hiroki Nojima was first author of their 2003 follow-up in the Journal of Biological Chemistry (NOJ2003).

The study showed that raptor binds two of mTOR's best-known targets, p70 S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, both of which control how fast cells make proteins. Raptor holds them through a short stretch of five amino acids called the TOS motif (TOR signalling motif). When the motif was changed, raptor could no longer bind and mTOR could no longer act on the target. This made raptor the part of mTORC1 that presents substrates to the kinase, a model that has held up in later structural work. The experiments were done in cultured cells and with purified proteins.
PubMed lists Nojima at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University. No other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, so later career steps are not known.

highlights.NOJ2003: First author: showed that raptor binds S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 through their TOS motifs, which lets mTORC1 present these substrates to the kinase.

Granholm AC.role: Neuroscientist of aging who has studied Down syndrome and the Alzheimer's disease that often comes with it since the 1990s, now a professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
Granholm AC.sub: Professor, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus · founding Executive Director, Knoebel Institute for Healthy Aging, University of Denver (from 2015) · Director, Center on Aging, Medical University of South Carolina (14 years) · guest professor in neurosciences, Karolinska Institutet
story: People with Down syndrome carry three copies of chromosome 21, which includes the gene for amyloid precursor protein, and Alzheimer's disease brain changes are common as they age. The 2026 study led by Abigail Nordbeck, with Ann-Charlotte Granholm as senior author, looked at post-mortem hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, from people with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's neuropathology. Using spatial transcriptomics, which reads gene activity while keeping track of where in the tissue it happens, and localized proteomics, the team found that mTOR pathway signalling was altered in particular hippocampal subfields, while insulin signalling was altered mainly in the dentate granule neurons.

The point is that the changes were not uniform across the tissue. Different cell layers showed different disturbances in the two growth and nutrient pathways. The authors call these preliminary observations from a small set of human brains; they describe associations, not causes.

Granholm holds both a dental degree (DDS) and a PhD and has held NIH R01 funding for Down syndrome research since 1994. At the Medical University of South Carolina she directed the Center on Aging for 14 years and the brain bank. In 2015 she moved to the University of Denver as founding executive director of the Knoebel Institute for Healthy Aging, and she holds a guest professorship in neurosciences at the Karolinska Institutet. The group studies healthy aging and age-related neurodegeneration, especially Down syndrome-related Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, using biomarkers, neuropathology and animal models. Granholm is now a professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and part of the Down Syndrome Biobank Consortium run from its Department of Neurosurgery; publications also appear under the names Ann-Charlotte Granholm-Bentley and Lotta Granholm.

highlights.NOR2026: Senior author: led the spatial study of human post-mortem hippocampus showing subfield-specific mTOR and cell-type-specific insulin pathway changes in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's neuropathology.

Nordbeck AJ.sub: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Almost everyone with Down syndrome has an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21, and Alzheimer's disease changes in the brain are common as they age. Abigail Nordbeck's 2026 study, with Ann-Charlotte Granholm as senior author, examined post-mortem hippocampus, the brain region central to forming memories, from people with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's neuropathology.

The team combined spatial transcriptomics, which measures gene activity while keeping its location in the tissue, with localized proteomics, which measures proteins in small chosen regions. mTOR pathway signalling was significantly altered in particular hippocampal subfields, and insulin pathway signalling was altered mainly in dentate granule neurons. In other words, the disturbance is local and cell-type specific rather than spread evenly through the tissue. The authors present these as preliminary observations in human tissue; they show associations and cannot say whether the changes cause the disease or follow from it.

Okazaki H.role: Pharmacologist at Daiichi University of Pharmacy in Fukuoka who studies how the body clock sets the daily rhythm of mTOR in tumours and how to time cancer drugs to match it
Okazaki H.sub: Associate Professor, Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Daiichi University of Pharmacy (2026) · Lecturer (2020–2024) and Assistant Professor (2015–2019) at the same faculty · Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Kyushu University, with Shigehiro Ohdo (to 2013)
story: Hiroyuki Okazaki is first author of a 2013 study from Shigehiro Ohdo's chronopharmacology group at Kyushu University (OKA2013). Chronopharmacology asks whether the time of day a drug is given changes what it does. In mice carrying kidney tumours, the amount of mTOR protein and its active, phosphorylated form rose and fell over 24 hours. The circadian clock set this rhythm through Fbxw7, an enzyme that tags mTOR for destruction. When the mTOR blocker everolimus was given at the time of day when mTOR was high, the mice survived longer than with the same dose at other times. The result is in mice; it has not been tested as a dosing schedule in people.

Okazaki's earlier papers with the Ohdo group (from 2010) also deal with daily rhythms in tumours and the brain, for example a clock-driven rhythm in the transferrin receptor that brings iron into colon cancer cells, and clock disruption in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. From about 2015 Okazaki's papers list the Department of Molecular Biology at Daiichi University of Pharmacy in Fukuoka, still working with Kyushu colleagues on clock-timed drug delivery.

Japan's national research database lists Okazaki as Associate Professor in the Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences at Daiichi University in 2026, after posts there as assistant professor and lecturer. Okazaki's grants continue the same theme: using mTOR and the clock to design cancer chronotherapy, timing pain treatment to daily rhythms, and testing Kampo herbal medicines on mTOR in cancer cells.

highlights.OKA2013: First author: showed in tumour-bearing mice that the clock drives a 24-hour mTOR rhythm through Fbxw7 and that dosing everolimus at the mTOR peak improved survival.

Oki T.role: Hematology researcher who trained at the Institute of Medical Science in Tokyo and in David Scadden's lab at Massachusetts General Hospital, where he imaged mTORC1 activity in leukemia cells inside living mice
Oki T.sub: Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Stem Cell Institute (David Scadden lab, papers 2021–2023) · Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo (Toshio Kitamura lab, papers to 2014)
story: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. In the Atlas study OKI2021, Oki and colleagues built fluorescent reporters that light up when mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is active, and watched AML cells inside the bone marrow of living mice. mTORC1 activity in the leukemia cells fell as the disease advanced. But at the moment chemotherapy was working best, mTORC1 switched back on in the surviving cells, and this was a change inside the cells rather than the survival of a pre-existing group. Blocking mTORC1 at exactly that time killed more AML cells.

The point for the Atlas is timing. mTORC1 activity is not a fixed property of a tumour; it shifts over days, and a drug given at the wrong time may do little. The work was done in mice and has not been tested as a treatment schedule in patients.

PubMed shows Oki working on leukemia biology at the Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo, in Toshio Kitamura's division up to 2014, then at the Center for Regenerative Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Harvard Stem Cell Institute with David Scadden, where he also contributed to a 2023 study of cartilage repair cells.

highlights.OKI2021: First author: imaged mTORC1 activity in AML cells in the bone marrow of living mice and showed that inhibiting mTORC1 at the peak of chemotherapy response improved killing.

O'Reilly KE.role: Physician-scientist who, in Neal Rosen's lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering, showed that blocking mTORC1 with rapamycin-like drugs switches on the survival kinase Akt through a feedback loop, a main reason these drugs worked less well against cancer than hoped
O'Reilly KE.sub: Department of Dermatology, New York University School of Medicine (2009, at the time of the most recent PubMed paper) · Program in Molecular Pharmacology and Chemistry, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, Neal Rosen lab (2006)
story: Kathryn O'Reilly is the first author of ORE2006, one of the most cited papers on why rapamycin-like drugs disappointed as cancer treatments. Normally, when mTORC1 and its target S6K1 are active, they send a brake signal back up the pathway that dampens insulin and growth-factor receptors. O'Reilly and colleagues in Neal Rosen's lab showed that blocking mTORC1 takes that brake off. Signals from receptor tyrosine kinases then rise, and Akt, a kinase that helps cancer cells survive, becomes more active. They saw this in cancer cell lines and also in tumour samples from patients treated with everolimus (RAD001), so it is a real effect in people, not only in a dish. The finding pushed the field toward drugs that block both mTOR and the PI3K/Akt pathway, or mTOR together with growth-factor receptors.

PubMed lists O'Reilly on 11 papers. In 2009, at the Department of Dermatology of New York University School of Medicine and again with Neal Rosen among the co-authors, she was first author of a study of 72 patients with metastatic melanoma, which found that a high level of phosphorylated 4E-BP1, a sign that mTORC1 is driving protein synthesis, went with shorter survival.
A current position could not be confirmed, and the most recent confirmed affiliation (NYU, 2009) is given at the time of that study.

highlights.ORE2006: First author: showed in cancer cells and in patient tumours treated with everolimus that mTORC1 inhibition removes a feedback brake and activates upstream receptor signalling and Akt.

Panchaud N.role: Biochemist who, during a PhD with Claudio De Virgilio in Fribourg, showed that the yeast SEACIT complex switches off TORC1 when amino acids run out, and who later moved into clinical drug development at Novartis
Panchaud N.sub: PhD in Biochemistry, University of Fribourg (De Virgilio lab, at the time of the study) · Associate Clinical Scientist, Novartis (listed 2018; joined 2015 through its postgraduate programme)
story: Cells must stop growing when food runs short. In 2013, Nicolas Panchaud, working in Claudio De Virgilio's yeast lab at the University of Fribourg, was first author of a paper that found one of the switches (PAN2013). TORC1, the yeast version of the growth-control complex mTORC1, is turned on by small proteins called Rag GTPases (Gtr1 and Gtr2 in yeast) when amino acids are plentiful. The team showed that a protein group they named SEACIT acts as a GAP, an 'off button' that makes Gtr1 switch itself off, and that cells without it cannot shut down TORC1 when amino acids are removed. The human counterpart, GATOR1, was described in the same year, so the yeast work helped establish that this brake is shared from yeast to humans. The experiments were done in yeast cells.

Panchaud earned a PhD in Biochemistry at the University of Fribourg. According to a 2018 University of Zurich career event page, Panchaud then joined Novartis in 2015 through its two-year postgraduate programme and was working as an associate clinical scientist, a role in planning and running clinical trials. No more recent position could be confirmed.

highlights.PAN2013: First author: showed in yeast that the SEACIT complex is a GAP for the Rag GTPase Gtr1 and is needed to switch off TORC1 when amino acids are scarce.

Park JM.role: Autophagy researcher in Do-Hyung Kim's University of Minnesota lab who mapped how the kinase ULK1 starts autophagy, and lead author of work showing that AMPK can hold ULK1 back under energy stress
Park JM.sub: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (papers with Do-Hyung Kim, 2013–2023)
story: Ji-Man Park is the first author of PAR2023, a Nature Communications paper from Do-Hyung Kim's lab at the University of Minnesota. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane and breaks them down. The kinase ULK1 starts the process. A textbook model said that AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, switches ULK1 on when energy runs low. In cultured cells starved of glucose or with poisoned mitochondria, the team found the opposite: AMPK held ULK1 and autophagy back. AMPK also shielded the ULK1 machinery from being cut up by caspases, enzymes active in cell death, so autophagy could restart later. This challenges a common reading of how energy stress and autophagy are linked, though it comes from cell culture.

Park's PubMed record shows a long run of ULK1 work in the same lab. As first author, Park showed in 2016 that ULK1 binds and phosphorylates ATG14, a step that passes the mTORC1 signal on to the autophagy machinery, and in 2018 that ULK1 phosphorylates BECN1 (Beclin 1) on serine 30 to drive autophagy. Park also contributed to the lab's 2014 Molecular Cell paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG to slow autophagosome maturation, and co-wrote a 2023 commentary in Autophagy titled "A paradigm shift: AMPK negatively regulates ULK1 activity".
All of these papers list the University of Minnesota. No official profile page was found, so the current position could not be confirmed; the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.PAR2023: First author: found in cultured cells that AMPK restrains ULK1 and autophagy under energy stress and protects the ULK1 machinery from caspase cleavage.

Park JM.lab_name: Do-Hyung Kim Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)

Paul D.role: Postdoctoral fellow in Steven Cappell's lab at the National Cancer Institute who studies how ubiquitin ligases time the start of the cell cycle, and who found that mTOR briefly switches off the APC/C to give cells a burst of glycolysis as they start to divide
Paul D.sub: Postdoctoral fellow, Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (papers 2021–2025) · PhD on ubiquitin ligases
story: Debasish Paul is first author of PAU2025, a Nature paper about the moment a resting cell decides to divide. When a growth signal arrives, mTOR quickly adds a phosphate to CDH1, the helper protein of a large enzyme called APC/C that tags other proteins for destruction. This partly releases CDH1 and briefly switches APC/C off. One of APC/C's usual targets, the glycolysis enzyme PFKFB3, then builds up, and the cell burns more glucose for a while, until a slower-acting phosphatase turns APC/C back on. The study, in human cells, showed that this short pulse of glycolysis is needed for cells to enter the cell cycle.

The finding gives mTOR a new job: besides boosting protein synthesis, it times a metabolic switch by reaching into the cell-cycle machinery. Because many cancers have overactive mTOR, the circuit may also help explain how tumor cells keep their fuel supply high, although the paper itself did not test tumors.

Paul is a postdoctoral fellow in Steven Cappell's lab at the Center for Cancer Research of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda, and the publication record places Paul there from at least 2021. That year the group showed that cells hit by DNA damage early in the cycle often keep going rather than stopping at the classic checkpoint. The lab uses time-lapse imaging of single living cells to follow cell-cycle decisions.

Paul's PhD was on ubiquitin ligases, enzymes that tag other proteins with a small protein called ubiquitin, often marking them for destruction. In the Cappell lab Paul studies how the activity of these enzymes rises and falls as a resting cell re-enters the cell cycle, focusing on the APC/C, and is building fluorescent biosensors that report ubiquitin ligase activity in living cells.

highlights.PAU2025: First author: showed that mTOR phosphorylates CDH1 to briefly inactivate APC/C, letting PFKFB3 build up and boost glycolysis as cells enter the cell cycle.

Paul D.lab_name: Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)

Peng M.role: Immunologist at Tsinghua University who, as a postdoc at Memorial Sloan Kettering, identified Sestrins and SZT2 as brakes on mTORC1 and now studies how T cells grow, specialise and remember
Peng M.sub: Tenured Associate Professor, School of Medicine, Tsinghua University (since 2024) · Associate Professor (2023–2024) and Assistant Professor (2017–2023), Tsinghua University · Research Fellow and Research Associate, Immunology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (2010–2017) · PhD in Immunology, Peking Union Medical College (2010)
story: Min Peng is first author of an Atlas study (PEN2017) about how cells tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that amino acids are scarce. Two protein complexes on the lysosome do this job: GATOR1 switches mTORC1 off, and GATOR2 holds GATOR1 back. The paper showed that a large protein called SZT2 pulls GATOR1 and GATOR2 together into one complex on the lysosome surface. Cells without SZT2 kept mTORC1 switched on even when starved of amino acids, and mice lacking SZT2 died soon after birth. The work, in cells and mice, added SZT2 to the list of parts that let mTORC1 sense nutrients.

Peng studied clinical medicine at Sichuan University and earned a PhD in immunology at Peking Union Medical College in 2010. From 2010 to 2017 Peng worked in the Immunology Program at Memorial Sloan Kettering in New York, in the group of Ming Li, the senior author of the Atlas paper. There Peng also showed that Sestrin proteins act on the Rag GTPases to hold mTORC1 down (Cell, 2014).

In 2017 Peng started a lab at the School of Medicine of Tsinghua University in Beijing and became a tenured associate professor in 2024. The lab studies how T cells, the white blood cells that kill infected and cancerous cells, are activated, divide, specialise and form memory, including the role of metabolism in these steps. It continues the mTOR thread: a 2022 paper from the lab showed that SZT2 keeps blood stem cells in balance by tuning mTORC1 to nutrients. The lab also develops engineered T cell therapies, including a T cell state it calls TIF that can renew itself for a long time while keeping its function.

highlights.PEN2017: First author: showed that SZT2 links GATOR1 and GATOR2 on the lysosome so that mTORC1 shuts off when amino acids run low.

Peng M.lab_name: Peng Lab, School of Medicine, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China)

Perez K.role: Aging researcher and co-founder of the Swiss company EPITERNA, working with Alejandro Ocampo's lab at the University of Lausanne on screening platforms that look for drugs extending lifespan across several species
Perez K.sub: Co-founder, EPITERNA SA, Épalinges · Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of Lausanne, Ocampo lab (papers 2023–2026)
story: Many drugs extend lifespan in one lab animal and then fail in the next. Kevin Perez is first author of a 2026 paper describing a platform built to tackle that problem (PEREZ2026). It tests compounds in yeast, nematode worms, fruit flies, killifish and mice, uses automated imaging and a deep-learning program to spot when each animal dies, and has screened more than 400 compounds under thousands of conditions. By comparing species, it picks out compounds that work in several of them and shows that hits tend to act on known conserved longevity pathways, mTOR among them. The paper is about methods and infrastructure; individual hits still need checking in mammals and eventually people.

Perez is a co-founder of EPITERNA, a start-up set up with Alejandro Ocampo, who leads an aging lab at the University of Lausanne and is the company's CEO. The company aims to develop affordable products that slow aging and delay age-related disease. PubMed lists Perez with both EPITERNA SA and the Ocampo group in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of Lausanne. Earlier work includes a 2023 first-author study showing that mouse models of premature aging with defects in DNA repair have an older 'epigenetic age', measured from DNA methylation, than their real age, unlike other premature aging models, and a 2025 study in which a two-chemical reprogramming cocktail reduced signs of aging in human cells and extended lifespan in worms.

highlights.PEREZ2026: First author of the cross-species screening platform spanning yeast, worms, flies, killifish and mice used to find lifespan-extending compounds that generalise.

Petit CS.role: Cell biologist who showed, in Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale, that folliculin moves onto lysosomes when amino acids run out and is needed to switch on the Rag GTPases
Petit CS.sub: Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Farese and Walther lab (2020, most recent paper) · Department of Cell Biology, Yale University School of Medicine, Shawn Ferguson lab (2012–2013) · Centre de Recherche des Cordeliers, Paris, Sophie Thenet group (2008–2013)
story: Constance Petit is first author of the Atlas study PET2013 from Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, when amino acids are available. Small switch proteins called Rag GTPases do the recruiting. The open question was which protein flips the Rags into their active state.

Petit and colleagues found that folliculin (FLCN), the protein lost in the inherited Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, gathers on lysosomes when amino acids are withdrawn and binds RagA directly. Cells without folliculin could not recruit mTORC1 to lysosomes when amino acids were added back. This placed folliculin at the amino acid switch of mTORC1. The study used cultured human cells. Petit was also a co-author on the 2012 Ferguson lab paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates the transcription factor TFEB at lysosomes (ROC2012).

Before Yale, Petit worked in Sophie Thenet's group at the Centre de Recherche des Cordeliers in Paris on the cellular prion protein and the junctions that seal the gut lining, including a 2012 study on its role in the intestinal barrier and in inflammatory bowel disease. In 2020 PubMed lists Petit as first author in Robert Farese and Tobias Walther's lab at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, showing that blocking sphingolipid synthesis improved survival in a mouse model of motor neuron degeneration. No later position could be confirmed.

highlights.PET2013: First author: showed in human cells that folliculin moves to lysosomes on amino acid withdrawal, binds RagA and is needed for amino acid-driven mTORC1 recruitment.

Petit CS.lab_name: Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)

Roczniak-Ferguson A.role: Cell biologist in Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale who showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates the transcription factor TFEB to control lysosome and autophagy genes, and who studies lysosome biology in neurodegenerative disease
Roczniak-Ferguson A.sub: Department of Cell Biology and Program in Cellular Neuroscience, Neurodegeneration and Repair, Yale University School of Medicine (2012–2026) · Department of Cancer Biology, Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, Albert Reynolds lab (2003–2004)
story: Agnes Roczniak-Ferguson is first author of the Atlas study ROC2012 from Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale. TFEB is a transcription factor, a protein that turns on a set of genes, in this case the genes that build lysosomes and run autophagy, the cell's self-recycling process. The study showed that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, phosphorylates TFEB on the lysosome surface. This keeps TFEB from switching on its target genes. When mTORC1 is switched off, for example by starvation, TFEB becomes active and lysosome and autophagy genes are turned on.

The result tied the same nutrient signal that drives growth to the building of the cell's recycling system: when food is plentiful mTORC1 holds TFEB back, and when it is scarce the cell can build more lysosomes. It was done in cultured human cells.

Earlier, at Vanderbilt University, Roczniak-Ferguson studied p120-catenin, a protein that controls cell-cell adhesion, with Albert Reynolds (2003, 2004). At Yale Roczniak-Ferguson has stayed with lysosome biology in the Ferguson lab: C9orf72, the gene most often mutated in ALS and frontotemporal dementia, binds SMCR8 and affects mTORC1 responses to amino acids (2016); loss of TDP-43 disturbs many organelles (2019); and the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 is switched on at damaged lysosomes through the STING, CASM and GABARAP pathway (2025) and through the chloride transporter ClC-7 (2026).

highlights.ROC2012: First author: showed in human cells that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to control the transcription of lysosome and autophagy genes.

Roczniak-Ferguson A.lab_name: Ferguson Lab, Department of Cell Biology, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)

Pledger ES.role: Researcher in Jamie Cate's lab at UC Berkeley who used ribosome profiling to show that exhausted human T cells shut down a key class of growth-related mRNAs even while mTOR is active
Pledger ES.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley (Cate lab, papers 2025–2026)
story: Erica Pledger was first author of a 2026 RNA Biology paper in this Atlas (PLEDGER2026), first posted as a preprint in 2025. CD8+ T cells are the immune cells that kill infected and cancer cells. When they are stimulated for too long, for example inside a tumour, they become exhausted and stop working well. The team made human CD8+ T cells exhausted in the dish and used ribosome profiling, a method that shows which messenger RNAs are actually being read by ribosomes, to see what proteins the cells were making.

One group of messages stood out: 5' TOP mRNAs, which code for ribosome parts and other protein-making machinery. Their translation is normally switched on by mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In exhausted T cells these messages were strongly held back even though mTOR activity was high, which points to a second layer of control that overrides or bypasses mTOR. The work was done in cultured human cells, not in patients.

Pledger works in Jamie Cate's lab at UC Berkeley, which studies how ribosomes and the initiation factor eIF3 decide which mRNAs are made into protein. PubMed lists two papers with Pledger's name, the preprint and the published version.

highlights.PLEDGER2026: First author: showed by ribosome profiling that exhausted human CD8+ T cells repress 5' TOP mRNAs despite high mTOR activity.

Pledger ES.lab_name: Cate Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)

Porstmann T.role: Cell biologist who, as a researcher in Almut Schulze's laboratory at the Cancer Research UK London Research Institute, showed that the growth kinase Akt drives fat synthesis through SREBP and that this route runs through mTORC1
Porstmann T.sub: Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory, Cancer Research UK London Research Institute, London (papers 2005–2009, at the time of the study)
story: Thomas Porstmann was first author of a 2008 Cell Metabolism paper (POR2008) that connected two big ideas about cell growth. A growing cell has to make more membrane as well as more protein, and membranes are built from fats. SREBP is a family of transcription factors, proteins that switch on genes, and they control the genes for making fatty acids and cholesterol. The study showed in human cells that when the kinase Akt is switched on, the active form of SREBP1 builds up in the nucleus, and that this needs mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, stopped it.

Blocking SREBP did more than lower fat production. It also stopped Akt from making cells bigger, and in fruit flies loss of SREBP reduced cell and organ size. So mTORC1 also orders the lipids for new membranes, on top of speeding up protein production. The work was done in cultured cells and in flies.

The paper grew out of Porstmann's earlier first-author study in Oncogene (2005) in the same laboratory, which used gene-expression arrays to find that Akt switches on cholesterol and fatty acid enzymes through SREBP. In 2009 Porstmann and colleagues summarised the SREBP and mTORC1 link in a Biochemical Society Transactions review. All three papers list the Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory led by Almut Schulze at the Cancer Research UK London Research Institute, now part of the Francis Crick Institute. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.POR2008: First author: showed that Akt-driven activation of SREBP and fat synthesis needs mTORC1, and that SREBP is required for Akt to make cells grow.

Porstmann T.lab_name: Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory (Almut Schulze), Cancer Research UK London Research Institute (London, England, United Kingdom)

Poulsen MM.role: Endocrinologist at Aarhus University Hospital who led one of the first careful human trials of high-dose resveratrol, which found no metabolic benefit in obese men
Poulsen MM.sub: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (papers 2012–2025)
story: Morten Møller Poulsen is first author of the Atlas study POU2013, with Jens Otto Lunde Jørgensen as senior author. Resveratrol, a compound found in red grape skin, had made headlines because it seemed to mimic calorie restriction and protect rodents on rich diets. Poulsen and colleagues gave obese but otherwise healthy men a high dose of resveratrol or a placebo for four weeks and measured insulin sensitivity, fuel use, blood pressure and body composition with precise methods.

Resveratrol changed none of them. The result contradicted the rodent data that had driven the enthusiasm and is a useful reminder that a strong animal result does not guarantee a human one. The trial was short and small, so it cannot rule out effects with longer treatment, but it set a clear benchmark.

Poulsen's earlier work in the same Aarhus group, with Pedersen as senior author, tested resveratrol in rats on a high-fat diet, where it prevented fatty liver (2012), and the group later reported that resveratrol also did not help people with the metabolic syndrome (2017). More recent papers from the Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine follow Danish families with RET gene variants that cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, an inherited cancer syndrome of the thyroid and adrenal glands, in nationwide studies (2019 to 2025).

highlights.POU2013: First author: ran the randomised trial in which four weeks of high-dose resveratrol had no effect on insulin sensitivity, blood pressure or body composition in obese men.

Poulsen MM.lab_name: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (Aarhus, Denmark)

Pyo JO.role: Autophagy researcher in Yong-Keun Jung's group in Korea, and first author of the 2013 study in which mice with an extra dose of the autophagy gene Atg5 lived longer
Pyo JO.sub: Global Research Laboratory, School of Biological Sciences and Bio-MAX Institute, Seoul National University (papers 2008–2013, at the time of the study) · Department of Life Science, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (papers to 2005)
story: Jong-Ok Pyo was first author of a 2013 Nature Communications paper (PYO2013) that tested a simple idea. Autophagy is the cell's self-cleaning system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane bag and sends them to be broken down. Autophagy fades with age, and mTOR, the cell's growth switch, holds it back when nutrients are plentiful. The team made mice that carry extra copies of Atg5, one of the core genes needed to build the autophagy bags. These mice had more autophagy, lived about 17 percent longer at the median, stayed leaner and responded better to insulin, and their cells coped better with oxidative damage.
It showed that turning autophagy up, without blocking mTOR, can lengthen life in a mammal. It is a mouse study, and it does not show that the same would happen in people.

Pyo spent the earlier part of this path in the group of Yong-Keun Jung, first at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology and then at Seoul National University. A 2005 first-author paper in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, written with the autophagy researchers Noboru Mizushima and Yoshinori Ohsumi among the co-authors, showed that Atg5 also takes part in a form of cell death by binding the death-signalling protein FADD. A 2008 first-author paper showed that extra ARC protein protects mouse heart muscle cells from damage when oxygen is cut off, and a 2012 review in Experimental & Molecular Medicine summarised the molecules that drive autophagy. No PubMed record after 2013 was found, and a current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.PYO2013: First author: showed that mice carrying extra Atg5 have more autophagy, live about 17 percent longer and are leaner and more insulin sensitive.

Pyo JO.lab_name: Yong-Keun Jung laboratory, School of Biological Sciences and Bio-MAX Institute, Seoul National University (Seoul, South Korea)

Ramanathan C.role: Circadian biologist at the University of Memphis who showed that mTOR signalling sets the speed and strength of the body's daily clocks
Ramanathan C.sub: Research Associate Professor, College of Health Sciences, University of Memphis · postdoc in circadian functional genomics, University of Memphis · postdoc on the neural basis of day-active behaviour, Michigan State University · PhD, Madurai Kamaraj University (2002)
story: Chidambaram (Chida) Ramanathan is the first author of RAM2018, a PLoS Genetics paper from Andrew Liu's group at the University of Memphis. Almost every cell runs a circadian clock, a set of genes that switch each other on and off over about 24 hours. A master clock in the brain, the SCN, keeps the clocks in organs such as the liver in step. The study started from the observation that mTOR activity itself rises and falls over the day, and asked whether mTOR also feeds back on the clock.

It does. Blocking mTOR made the clock run slower, with a longer period, and weaker, with a flatter rhythm. Turning mTOR up did the reverse. The team saw this in cultured cells, in slices of SCN and liver taken from mice, and in living mice with only one working copy of the mTOR gene, whose daily activity cycle ran longer. This links the cell's main nutrient and growth sensor to the timing of daily rhythms, though the evidence comes from cells and mice.

Ramanathan earned a PhD at Madurai Kamaraj University in India in 2002, then worked as a postdoc at Michigan State University on the brain basis of being active by day, and at the University of Memphis on circadian functional genomics. Ramanathan is now a research associate professor in the College of Health Sciences at the University of Memphis, studying how circadian clocks and their output signals interact with cell metabolism, oxidative stress and ageing.

highlights.RAM2018: First author: showed in cells, mouse tissue slices and mTOR heterozygous mice that mTOR activity sets the period and amplitude of central and peripheral circadian clocks.

Ramanathan C.lab_name: College of Health Sciences, University of Memphis (Memphis, Tennessee, USA)

Feng X.role: Researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases in Chengdu whose group studies how cells in the mouth respond to stress, from chemotherapy tolerance in oral cancer to inflammation in gum disease
Feng X.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases and Research Unit of Oral Carcinogenesis and Management, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (papers 2025–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Xiaodong Feng was senior author of a 2026 Atlas study on why some cancer cells survive cisplatin, a widely used chemotherapy drug (RAO2026). The team ran a genome-wide CRISPR screen, switching off genes one by one across the genome to see which ones change how cells cope with the drug. The surprise was that blocking mTOR, the growth-control kinase, made the cells more tolerant of cisplatin, not less, because it switched on protective autophagy, the cell's recycling system. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5, which brings leucine and other large amino acids into the cell, sat at the centre of this circuit. Adding extra leucine made tumour cells carrying SLC7A5 sensitive to cisplatin again. The work was done in cancer cells and tumour models, not in patients.
The finding matters for drug combinations: mTOR inhibitors are sometimes proposed alongside chemotherapy, and this study suggests that in some tumours they could do the opposite of what is hoped.

PubMed lists Feng at the State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University. A 2025 paper from the same laboratory in International Immunopharmacology, with Pengcheng Rao among the co-authors, showed that a stress response in the gum-lining cells drives inflammation and bone loss in periodontitis. No personal institutional page could be checked, so further details of training and title are not shown.

highlights.RAO2026: Senior author: led the CRISPR screen study showing that mTOR inhibition can protect cancer cells from cisplatin through autophagy, with SLC7A5 and leucine as a way to reverse it.

Feng X.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)

Rao P.role: Researcher at the West China Hospital of Stomatology in Chengdu who led a genome-wide CRISPR screen showing that switching off mTOR can help cancer cells tolerate cisplatin
Rao P.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (papers with Xiaodong Feng, 2025–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Pengcheng Rao was first author of the 2026 Atlas study on cisplatin tolerance (RAO2026). Cisplatin is a platinum chemotherapy drug used against many cancers, including cancers of the head and neck. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, which knocks out genes one at a time across the whole genome, the team asked which genes change how well cancer cells survive the drug. Blocking mTOR, the growth-control kinase, helped the cells survive, because it turned on autophagy, a recycling process that protected them. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5 linked nutrient supply to this response, and giving extra leucine, one of the amino acids it carries, made SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells sensitive to cisplatin again. This was shown in cancer cells and tumour models, not in patients.

Rao also appears, with Xiaodong Feng as a co-author, on a 2025 paper from the same State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases on how stressed gum-lining cells drive inflammation in periodontitis. No personal page was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RAO2026: First author: ran the genome-wide CRISPR screen showing that mTOR inhibition promotes cisplatin tolerance through autophagy and that leucine can reverse it in SLC7A5-expressing cells.

Rao P.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)

Rauch B.role: Researcher in Péter Bai's group at the University of Debrecen who studies how ADP-ribosylating enzymes control fat cell development through AMPK and mTOR
Rauch B.sub: Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (papers 2019–2026)
story: Fat cells form from precursor cells in a process called adipocyte differentiation, which needs mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to be active. In RAUCH2026, Boglarka Rauch and colleagues in Péter Bai's group worked on tankyrases, enzymes that attach chains of ADP-ribose to other proteins and so change how those proteins behave. In a cell line, deleting tankyrase-1 or tankyrase-2 slowed fat cell formation. The cells showed active AMPK, the energy sensor, low mTORC1 activity and blocked autophagy. The defect caused by losing tankyrase-2 could be fixed by NV-5138, a drug that switches mTORC1 on, or by blocking LKB1, the kinase that activates AMPK. Tankyrase-2 was found to ADP-ribosylate LKB1, which suggests that it normally keeps the LKB1-AMPK brake on mTORC1 in check. The findings come from cultured cells only.

Rauch has published with the Bai group in the Department of Medical Chemistry at the University of Debrecen since 2019, including a 2023 screen of bacterial metabolites for effects on breast cancer cell growth. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RAUCH2026: First author: showed in a cell line that tankyrase-2 supports fat cell differentiation through the LKB1-AMPK-mTORC1 axis and ADP-ribosylates LKB1.

Rauch B.lab_name: Bai Lab, Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (Debrecen, Hungary)

Rebsamen M.role: Cell biologist who found that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 is part of the amino acid sensor for mTORC1, and who now leads a group at the University of Lausanne studying transporters in immune signalling and autoimmunity
Rebsamen M.sub: Group leader, Department of Immunobiology, University of Lausanne (from about 2022) · CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine, Vienna, Giulio Superti-Furga lab (about 2013–2022) · University of Lausanne, Juerg Tschopp lab (2008–2012)
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome when amino acids are plentiful. In 2015, as first author of a Nature paper from Giulio Superti-Furga's group at CeMM in Vienna, Manuele Rebsamen showed that SLC38A9, an amino acid transporter in the lysosome membrane, binds the Ragulator-Rag machinery that brings mTORC1 there. Cells with extra SLC38A9 kept mTORC1 active even when amino acids were removed, and cells without it switched mTORC1 on poorly when amino acids returned. These are cell studies.

Rebsamen began in innate immunity. In Juerg Tschopp's lab at the University of Lausanne, Rebsamen co-authored work on how cells detect RNA viruses, including the role of TRADD in the RIG-I antiviral pathway (2008) and inflammasome activation by RIG-I (2009). At CeMM, Rebsamen focused on solute carriers, the large family of membrane transporters, including a 2020 classification of human transporters by what they carry and a 2022 genetic screen for transporters that help cells survive nutrient shortage. Rebsamen was also a co-author of the 2018 Science paper identifying LZTR1 as a regulator of RAS.

Rebsamen now leads a group at the Department of Immunobiology of the University of Lausanne in Epalinges. The lab studies how the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 and its partner TASL control immune signals from Toll-like receptors, and in 2025 and 2026 showed that this complex is needed for antiviral responses and for lupus-like autoimmune disease in mice.

highlights.REB2015: First author: identified SLC38A9 as a lysosomal amino acid transporter that is part of the Ragulator-Rag sensing machinery for mTORC1.

Rebsamen M.lab_name: Rebsamen Lab, Department of Immunobiology, University of Lausanne (Épalinges, Switzerland)

Ren Y.role: Gastric cancer researcher in Yanfeng Hu's surgical group at Nanfang Hospital who studies how tumour bacteria and metabolism shape resistance to immunotherapy
Ren Y.sub: Department of General Surgery and Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (papers 2023–2026)
story: Yingxin Ren is first author of the Atlas study REN2026, with Yanfeng Hu as senior author. Immune checkpoint drugs that block PD-1 release a brake on T cells so they can attack tumours, but many gastric cancers do not respond. The team linked part of this resistance to bacteria living inside the tumour. Streptococcus anginosus was associated with kynurenic acid, a metabolite that raised levels of the integrin ITGA2 in cancer cells.

ITGA2 then held back an mTOR-dependent cascade, which kept cathepsin V (CTSV) expression high and weakened the killing activity of CD8 T cells. In this setting lower mTOR activity sits on the side of immune escape, a reminder that the effect of mTOR depends on cell type and context.

Ren's other papers come from the same group and the Guangdong key laboratory for gastrointestinal tumours: tumour bacteria and their vesicles that improve PD-1 therapy (2026), gut bacteria that tune CD8 T cell immunity through butyrate (2024), an enzyme that protects gastric cancer stem cells from ferroptosis through a cholesterol and mTOR pathway (2024), and imaging probes for lymph nodes and peritoneal spread (2025, 2026).

highlights.REN2026: First author: showed that tumour-associated kynurenic acid drives PD-1 blockade resistance in gastric cancer through an ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis that suppresses CD8 T cells.

Ren Y.lab_name: Yanfeng Hu group, Department of General Surgery, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China)

Robida-Stubbs S.role: Researcher in Keith Blackwell's worm lab at the Joslin Diabetes Center who showed that TOR inhibition and rapamycin extend C. elegans lifespan through the protective factors SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO
Robida-Stubbs S.sub: Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard Stem Cell Institute and Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School (T. Keith Blackwell group, papers 2012–2022)
story: Stacey Robida-Stubbs is first author of an Atlas study (ROB2012) on how blocking TOR lengthens life in the roundworm C. elegans. Lowering TORC1 genetically extended lifespan, and that needed two transcription factors that switch on defence genes: SKN-1, the worm version of Nrf, which protects against oxidative and chemical stress, and DAF-16, the worm FoxO. Rapamycin also extended lifespan, but needed only SKN-1, not DAF-16. The authors traced this difference to rapamycin also acting on TORC2. They also saw that rapamycin switched on a similar Nrf-type protective response in mice.

The paper showed that turning down TOR does more than slow growth: it actively switches on the cell's protective programmes. It also gave an early warning that rapamycin does not act like a pure TORC1 blocker, a theme the Atlas follows into mice and people.

The publication record places Robida-Stubbs in T. Keith Blackwell's group at the Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School from 2012 to at least 2022, including a 2022 Nature Communications paper showing that the stress factor ATF-4 and hydrogen sulfide production help explain why lowering protein synthesis or mTORC1 extends worm lifespan. No profile page was found, so the current role is not confirmed.

highlights.ROB2012: First author: showed in C. elegans that TORC1 inhibition extends lifespan through SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO, while rapamycin's effect needs only SKN-1.

Robida-Stubbs S.lab_name: Blackwell Lab, Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)

Shimobayashi M.lab_name: Clinical and Experimental Endocrinology, Department of Chronic Diseases and Metabolism, KU Leuven (Leuven, Belgium)
Shimobayashi M.role: Metabolism researcher who trained with Michael Hall in Basel on mTOR in fat tissue and now leads a group at KU Leuven studying how fat and liver control sugar and lipid storage
Shimobayashi M.sub: Group leader, Clinical and Experimental Endocrinology, KU Leuven (last-author papers from 2023) · Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (to about 2023)
story: In 2014 Mitsugu Shimobayashi and Michael Hall wrote the review "Making new contacts" in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology. It describes mTOR as a hub in a network: the two mTOR complexes trade signals with other pathways, such as insulin and AMPK signalling, and between them steer how cells take up and use nutrients. A review collects earlier findings and does not add new experiments.

Shimobayashi also appears on two research papers in this Atlas. In a 2013 Science study, a large-scale measurement of phosphorylated proteins showed that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on the cell's own production of pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA. In 2020 a cryo-electron microscopy structure of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution pointed to the tail end of the subunit Rictor as the reason this complex is not blocked by rapamycin. These were cell and protein studies.

In Basel, Shimobayashi worked on mTOR in fat tissue and the whole body. A 2023 paper with Shimobayashi as senior author showed that when mTORC2 is lost in fat, mTORC2 in the liver can step in to keep energy storage and blood sugar in balance in mice. Shimobayashi now runs a group at KU Leuven in Belgium. Its 2025 papers show how a chemical tag on the protein MLX stabilises the sugar-sensing ChREBP-MLX complex on DNA to control carbohydrate and fat metabolism, and test a diet change after incretin-drug treatment in obese mice.

highlights.SHI2014: First author of the review describing the mTOR network and its crosstalk with other metabolic signalling pathways.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author of the 3.2 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 that explains its rapamycin insensitivity.
highlights.ROB2013: Co-author of the phosphoproteomics study showing that mTORC1 turns on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Brignole EJ.lab_name: MIT Cryo-EM Facility, MIT.nano, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Brignole EJ.role: Research scientist who directs the cryo-electron microscopy facility at MIT.nano and whose cryo-EM work helped solve the structures of GATOR1, GATOR2 and Raptor docked on the Rag GTPases for the Sabatini lab
Brignole EJ.sub: Director, MIT cryo-EM facility at MIT.nano (appointed 2017) · research scientist in Catherine Drennan's lab, MIT (from 2010)
story: Edward Brignole is a co-author of three structural papers in the Atlas from David Sabatini's lab, all made with cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In cryo-EM, purified proteins are frozen in a thin layer of ice and photographed thousands of times with an electron beam, and the images are combined into a 3D model. The method needs careful sample preparation and microscope work, which is where an EM specialist comes in.

The three papers solve key parts of how mTORC1 senses amino acids. SHE2018 gives the structure of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rag GTPases off, alone and bound to the Rags, and shows how it does so. ROG2019 shows how Raptor, part of mTORC1, docks onto the Rag-Ragulator complex on the lysosome: one part of Raptor reads the state of RagA and a separate claw reads RagC, and only the right combination lets mTORC1 land. VAL2022 gives the structure of human GATOR2, a large cage-like complex built on an octagonal frame, and maps where the sensors Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 attach. How GATOR2 holds back GATOR1 is still not fully settled.

Brignole joined Catherine Drennan's lab at MIT in 2010 as a research scientist and worked mainly on ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme that makes the building blocks of DNA; the PubMed record shows fifteen joint papers with the Drennan group up to 2023. In late 2017 the Drennan lab announced that Brignole had been appointed to direct MIT's new cryo-EM facility, housed in the MIT.nano building, while keeping up the work with the lab. Running a shared facility means helping groups across MIT, such as the Sabatini lab, turn purified proteins into 3D structures, which is how the Atlas papers came about.

highlights.VAL2022: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure of human GATOR2, a large cage that carries the binding sites for Sestrin2 and CASTOR1.
highlights.ROG2019: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure showing how Raptor docks on Rag-Ragulator to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.SHE2018: Co-author on the cryo-EM structures of GATOR1 alone and bound to the Rag GTPases.

Kraus WE.lab_name: Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and Division of Cardiology, Duke University School of Medicine (Durham, North Carolina, USA)
Kraus WE.role: Preventive cardiologist and exercise physiologist at Duke University who leads long-running trials on how exercise and calorie restriction change human health, and senior author of the CALERIE two-year safety report
Kraus WE.sub: Richard and Pat Johnson University Distinguished Professor, Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Duke University School of Medicine (since 2017) · Professor of Medicine (since 2006) · Duke Molecular Physiology Institute (since 2013) · MD, Duke University (1982)
story: Calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, slows aging in many animals and lowers mTOR activity. CALERIE (Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy) was the first long trial to test it in healthy, non-obese people. William Kraus is last author of the 2016 report on its safety (ROM2016). Over two years, participants aimed to eat 25% fewer calories. The diet was safe overall, with no rise in serious problems, but bone density fell more than in the control group, so bone health needs watching in anyone who tries long-term restriction.

Kraus earned an MD at Duke University in 1982 and trained as an internist and preventive cardiologist, a heart doctor who focuses on stopping disease before it starts. Kraus has been Professor of Medicine at Duke since 2006 and Richard and Pat Johnson University Distinguished Professor since 2017, and is a member of the Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and a professor in the School of Nursing. The group combines studies in people with lab work. It asks how exercise changes the body in healthy people, in people at risk such as those with pre-diabetes, and in people with heart disease or heart failure. It also looks for genes that raise the risk of early heart disease and metabolic syndrome, and studies how signals inside skeletal muscle adapt to exercise, heart failure, aging and spaceflight.

Kraus's PubMed record runs to hundreds of papers from Duke on exercise, heart and metabolic health. A 2026 follow-up of STRRIDE, a supervised exercise trial, found that step counts from wearable devices tracked fitness and heart-health measures better than people's own reports of how much they exercised.

highlights.ROM2016: Last author of the CALERIE report showing that two years of 25% calorie restriction was safe in healthy non-obese adults, apart from greater bone density loss.

Romashkan SV.lab_name: Division of Geriatrics and Clinical Gerontology, National Institute on Aging, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Romashkan SV.role: Physician scientist at the National Institute on Aging who oversees clinical trials in older adults and led the safety analysis of CALERIE, the first long-term trial of calorie restriction in healthy people
Romashkan SV.sub: Division of Geriatrics and Clinical Gerontology, National Institute on Aging (papers 2006–2021; most recent confirmed affiliation 2021)
story: Cutting calories without malnutrition lengthens life in many lab animals, partly by turning down mTOR signalling. CALERIE was the first multicentre trial to ask what two years of calorie restriction does to healthy people who are not obese. Sergei Romashkan was first author of its safety report, ROM2016 in Oncotarget. Participants were assigned at random, two to one, to cut their intake by 25 percent or to eat as usual. There were no deaths and only one serious adverse event in the restriction group, and three people were withdrawn from restriction for safety reasons. Overall, side effects were not more common than in the control group. Bone mineral density at the spine and hip, however, fell more in the restriction group at 12 and 24 months, and the authors advised close monitoring for bone loss and anaemia.

For anyone thinking about calorie restriction, or about drugs meant to mimic it, the trial shows that the approach can be done safely under supervision but is not free of cost to the skeleton. It measured safety in people and did not test mTOR activity directly.

Romashkan works in the Division of Geriatrics and Clinical Gerontology of the National Institute on Aging, where the role centres on large clinical trials in older adults. Romashkan is a co-author of the design paper of the Testosterone Trials, seven coordinated trials of testosterone treatment in older men, and of the pilot of the LIFE physical activity trial. In 2021 Romashkan was first author of a report from an NIA workshop on how to test existing drugs and supplements for senolytic or senomorphic effects, meaning that they remove or quiet senescent cells, in clinical trials.

highlights.ROM2016: First author: reported that two years of 25 percent calorie restriction in non-obese adults was safe overall but lowered bone mineral density more than in controls.

Ruvinsky I.lab_name: Meyuhas Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School (Jerusalem, Israel)
Ruvinsky I.role: Biochemist from Oded Meyuhas's Jerusalem lab who made the mouse in which ribosomal protein S6 cannot be phosphorylated, showing that this mark controls cell size and blood sugar rather than the translation of TOP mRNAs
Ruvinsky I.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School, Jerusalem (papers with Oded Meyuhas, 2005–2009)
story: Igor Ruvinsky is the first author of RUV2005, a Genes & Development paper from Oded Meyuhas's lab at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School. Ribosomal protein S6 sits on the ribosome, the cell's protein-making machine, and is the best-known target of S6 kinase, which mTORC1 switches on. For years people thought that adding phosphate groups to S6 was how cells turned up the translation of 5'TOP mRNAs, the messages that code for ribosome parts. The team made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of S6 were changed to alanine, so S6 could never be phosphorylated. Translation of 5'TOP mRNAs did not change. Instead, cells from these mice made protein and divided faster, yet stayed smaller than normal cells, and rapamycin did not shrink them further. The mice also handled glucose poorly, a sign that their insulin-making beta cells were affected.

This was a clean genetic test of a widely held model, and it moved the role of S6 phosphorylation from translation control to cell size and metabolism. Ruvinsky and Meyuhas summed this up in a 2006 review in Trends in Biochemical Sciences, and a 2009 PLoS ONE paper from the same lab showed that the mutant mice have weak muscles, because their muscle fibres grow less and hold less ATP and phosphocreatine.

These three papers all list the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School. No later record could be tied to this person with confidence, so the current position is not known and the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RUV2005: First author: built and analysed the S6 phosphorylation-dead knock-in mouse, showing that S6 phosphorylation sets cell size and glucose balance but is not needed for 5'TOP mRNA translation.

Saci A.lab_name: Division of Signal Transduction, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Saci A.role: Cell biologist who, in Christopher Carpenter's lab at Beth Israel Deaconess, found that the small GTPase Rac1 binds mTOR and helps set the activity and location of both mTOR complexes
Saci A.sub: Division of Signal Transduction, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, Carpenter lab (2003–2011, at the time of the study)
story: mTOR works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 controls cell growth and protein making, and mTORC2 controls cell shape and survival signals. Abdelhafid Saci is first author of a 2011 paper from Christopher Carpenter's lab at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston (SAC2011). The team found that Rac1, a small switch protein best known for reorganising the cell's internal skeleton, binds mTOR directly and is needed for both complexes to work properly. Rac1 helped bring the complexes to the right places inside the cell, at membranes, and cells without Rac1 activity grew smaller. The work was done in cultured cells. It linked the machinery of cell shape and movement to the machinery of cell growth.

Saci's earlier PubMed record with the Carpenter lab includes a 2003 paper in Immunity showing that the kinase BTK brings lipid-making enzymes to the cell membrane in B cells, which links Saci's work to the PI3K signalling system that sits upstream of mTOR. No current institutional page could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SAC2011: First author: showed in cultured cells that Rac1 binds mTOR, regulates both mTORC1 and mTORC2, guides their location and controls cell size.

Sang Z.lab_name: Jie Wang group, Department of Chemistry, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
Sang Z.role: Chemical biologist at SUSTech in Shenzhen who used a light-activated methionine probe to identify PKM2 as a methionine sensor for mTORC1
Sang Z.sub: Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis and State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Southern University of Science and Technology (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Zixin Sang is first author of the Atlas study SANG2026, from Jie Wang's group in the Department of Chemistry at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only runs when amino acids are available, and cells have dedicated sensor proteins that report each amino acid. For methionine the known sensor, SAMTOR, does not read methionine itself but a product made from it, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). Whether any protein reads free methionine directly was an open question.

Sang and colleagues built a "Trojan" methionine: a copy of the amino acid that cells take up normally but that carries a chemical group which, when hit with light, links the probe to whatever protein is holding it. Fishing out these proteins with chemoproteomics, a method that identifies protein targets of small molecules on a large scale, pointed to PKM2. PKM2 is best known as a glycolysis enzyme, but here it bound methionine through a separate pocket, independently of its enzyme activity, and passed the signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex. The work was done in cultured cells and complements SAMTOR rather than replacing it.

PubMed lists Sang at the Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis and State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics at SUSTech. No other papers or an official page could be tied to this person, so the profile rests on this study.

highlights.SANG2026: First author: used a photo-crosslinking methionine probe and chemoproteomics to show that PKM2 binds methionine and relays it to mTORC1 through GATOR2.

Saucedo LJ.lab_name: Department of Biology, Pacific Lutheran University (Tacoma, Washington, USA)
Saucedo LJ.role: Fruit-fly cell biologist and teacher who, as a postdoc in Bruce Edgar's lab, showed that the small GTPase Rheb drives cell growth in the insulin/TOR pathway
Saucedo LJ.sub: Visiting Assistant Professor of Biology, Pacific Lutheran University · Emeritus Professor of Biology, University of Puget Sound (faculty 2003–2024) · Postdoc and research affiliate, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (1999–2006) · PhD, University of Wisconsin-Madison (1999)
story: Leslie Saucedo is first author of a 2003 paper from Bruce Edgar's lab at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle (SAU2003). Working in the fruit fly Drosophila, the team found that Rheb, a small switch protein of the GTPase family, makes cells grow bigger when it is overactive and smaller when it is missing. Genetic tests placed Rheb in the insulin/TOR network, the system that tells cells whether there is enough food and growth signal to build more protein. The same year other groups showed that the tumour suppressors TSC1 and TSC2 act by switching Rheb off, so Rheb became the direct link between growth signals and TOR. This was work in flies; the human version of the pathway was confirmed later by others.

Saucedo trained in microbiology at the University of Illinois and earned a PhD in Cellular and Molecular Biology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1999, studying the MDM2 cancer gene and the cell's response to UV damage. Postdoctoral work at the Fred Hutchinson Center from 1999 to 2003, and a research affiliate post there until 2006, focused on finding new genes that control cell growth in flies.

In 2003 Saucedo joined the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, rising from visiting assistant professor to full professor (2015) and becoming emeritus in 2024. Research there, much of it with undergraduates, used flies to study how the phosphatase PRL-1, the Src and Ras cancer genes, redox balance and autophagy affect growth. Saucedo now teaches as a visiting assistant professor in biology at Pacific Lutheran University.

highlights.SAU2003: First author: showed in Drosophila that Rheb promotes cell growth as part of the insulin/TOR signalling network.

Knockenhauer KE.role: Structural biologist trained in Thomas Schwartz's MIT lab who helped solve the amino acid sensor structures of Sestrin2 and CASTOR1, and who later moved to drug discovery at Accent Therapeutics
Knockenhauer KE.sub: Accent Therapeutics, Lexington, Massachusetts (papers 2023–2025) · Thomas Schwartz lab, Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (papers 2015–2020)
story: Kevin Knockenhauer is a co-author of two structural papers in the Atlas from David Sabatini's lab, both made in collaboration with Thomas Schwartz's crystallography lab at MIT. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on only when amino acids are present, and dedicated sensor proteins tell it which amino acids are there. SAX2015 solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine and showed the pocket, closed by a lid-like loop, that makes it a leucine sensor. SAX2016 did the same for CASTOR1 and arginine, and showed how arginine binding makes CASTOR1 let go of GATOR2, which releases the brake on mTORC1. Both are structures of purified proteins, backed by tests in cells.

Knockenhauer's PubMed record lists twelve papers with Schwartz between 2015 and 2020; the Schwartz lab works mainly on the structure of the machinery that moves molecules across the nuclear envelope, the double membrane around the nucleus. From 2023 to 2025 the papers list Accent Therapeutics in Lexington, Massachusetts, a drug discovery company. One 2023 paper, for example, describes assays and a crystal structure for the RNA helicase DHX9 as a cancer drug target. The current position is taken from these papers; no official profile was found.

highlights.SAX2016: Co-author on the structure of CASTOR1 bound to arginine, which showed how arginine releases CASTOR1 from GATOR2.
highlights.SAX2015: Co-author on the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine, which revealed its leucine-binding pocket.

Schwartz TU.lab_name: Schwartz Lab, Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Schwartz TU.role: MIT structural biologist who studies how molecules pass across the nuclear envelope, and whose crystallography lab helped solve the leucine and arginine sensor structures upstream of mTORC1
Schwartz TU.sub: Boris Magasanik Professor in Biology, Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology · PhD, Free University of Berlin (2000)
story: Thomas Schwartz is a co-author of two Atlas papers, made with David Sabatini's lab, on how mTORC1 senses amino acids. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on only when amino acids are present, and sensor proteins report on single amino acids. SAX2015 gives the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine and shows a pocket closed by a lid-like loop. SAX2016 gives the structure of CASTOR1 holding arginine and shows how arginine binding makes CASTOR1 release GATOR2, lifting a brake on mTORC1. These are structures of purified proteins, backed by tests in cells. They turned the idea of an amino acid sensor into a picture at the level of atoms.

Schwartz's own research is on communication across biological membranes. The lab uses structural, biochemical and genetic tools to study how signals and molecules move between the nucleus and the cytoplasm through the nuclear envelope, and how the nuclear pore and its transport machinery are built. Schwartz earned a PhD at the Free University of Berlin in 2000 and is now the Boris Magasanik Professor in Biology at MIT.

highlights.SAX2016: Co-author: the Schwartz crystallography lab helped solve the structure of CASTOR1 bound to arginine.
highlights.SAX2015: Co-author: the Schwartz crystallography lab helped solve the structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine.

Saxena A.lab_name: Institute of Medical Genetics, Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom)
Saxena A.role: Clinical research fellow at Cardiff University who coordinated TRON, a placebo-controlled trial testing whether everolimus improves memory and thinking in adults with tuberous sclerosis complex
Saxena A.sub: Clinical Research Fellow, Institute of Medical Genetics, Cardiff University · PhD, Cardiff University (2021), with Julian Sampson
story: Everolimus, an mTOR blocker, is approved for the tumours and seizures of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Many people with TSC also have problems with memory, attention and planning, and mouse studies suggested mTOR blockers might help. Anurag Saxena is first author of the main report of TRON, a trial run from Cardiff that tested this in adults with TSC (SAX2026). Thirty-eight patients were randomised, two on everolimus for every one on placebo, for 24 weeks. Most people in both groups improved on the thinking tests (87% on everolimus, 75% on placebo), which points to practice and placebo effects rather than a clear drug benefit. Side effects were more common on everolimus. The trial was small, so a modest effect cannot be ruled out, but it gives no support for prescribing everolimus for cognition alone.

Saxena coordinated TRON and carried out the clinical assessments as part of a PhD at Cardiff University, completed in 2021 with a thesis on the effect of everolimus on neurocognitive aspects of TSC. The thesis thanks Julian Sampson, the senior author of the trial report, and Derek Jones. Saxena works as a Clinical Research Fellow at Cardiff's Institute of Medical Genetics, with papers on TSC epilepsy, everolimus side effects and the clinical features of mTOR pathway gene mutations.

highlights.SAX2026: First author: reported the TRON randomised trial, in which everolimus did not clearly beat placebo for memory and thinking in adults with TSC.

Scaiola A.lab_name: Ban Lab, Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Scaiola A.role: Structural biologist in Nenad Ban's group at ETH Zurich who solved the 3.2-angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 and works on how ribosomes are built and how new proteins are processed
Scaiola A.sub: Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2018–2026, Nenad Ban group)
story: Alain Scaiola is first author of the Atlas study SCA2020, a detailed three-dimensional picture of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution, sharp enough to place most individual amino acids. The structure was made by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), which freezes purified protein complexes in thin ice and combines hundreds of thousands of electron microscope images into one 3D map. mTORC2 is one of the two mTOR complexes and, unlike mTORC1, it is not blocked directly by rapamycin. The map shows why: the tail end of the protein Rictor covers the site on mTOR where the rapamycin-FKBP12 pair would bind.

Scaiola is also a co-author of STU2018, the earlier and lower-resolution architecture of the mTORC2 core (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8). Both papers came from a joint effort of the groups of Timm Maier at the University of Basel and Nenad Ban at ETH Zurich, and they give drug designers an accurate picture of the complex.

Scaiola's publication record from 2018 to 2026 is in Nenad Ban's group at the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics of ETH Zurich. Most of the work is on the ribosome, the cell's protein-making machine: a 2018 first-author structure of a yeast ribosome subunit caught in the last steps of assembly, and later studies with the Deuerling lab in Konstanz on how the NAC complex guides enzymes that trim and tag new proteins as they leave the ribosome (Nature 2024; Nature Communications 2026). No personal web page was found, so the current job title is not confirmed.

highlights.SCA2020: First author: determined the 3.2-angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 and showed how Rictor's C-terminus blocks rapamycin binding.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the first architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Stuttfeld E.lab_name: Maier Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Stuttfeld E.role: Structural biologist who led the 2018 eLife study that gave the first detailed picture of the human mTORC2 core complex, working in Timm Maier's lab in Basel
Stuttfeld E.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Timm Maier lab (2016–2021, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Biozentrum, University of Basel and Paul Scherrer Institut, Kurt Ballmer-Hofer group (VEGF receptors, 2009–2017)
story: mTORC2 is the second mTOR complex. It controls the kinase Akt, cell survival and the cell skeleton, and unlike mTORC1 it is not blocked by rapamycin. In 2018 Edward Stuttfeld was first author of an eLife paper, with senior authors Nenad Ban and Timm Maier, that used cryo-electron microscopy to show how the four core parts of human mTORC2 (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8) fit together. The structure helped explain why rapamycin does not act on mTORC2. A 2020 follow-up at 3.2 angstrom resolution, on which Stuttfeld is a co-author, pinned this to the tail end of Rictor. These are protein structure studies.

Stuttfeld began in vascular biology. With Kurt Ballmer-Hofer at the Paul Scherrer Institut in Villigen, Stuttfeld wrote a 2009 review on VEGF receptors, the receptors for a growth factor that drives blood-vessel growth, and later co-authored structural studies of VEGF receptors 1, 2 and 3.

In Timm Maier's group at the Biozentrum, Stuttfeld worked on large enzymes and signalling complexes. Besides the mTORC2 papers, Stuttfeld co-authored a 2018 Nature structure of human acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the first enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, and a 2021 eLife study of how DEPTOR binds and regulates both mTOR complexes. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.STU2018: First author: solved the cryo-EM architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author of the 3.2 angstrom mTORC2 structure that traces rapamycin insensitivity to Rictor's C-terminus.

Schalm SS.role: Cell biologist who, in John Blenis's lab, showed that the TOS motif lets raptor grab 4E-BP1 so mTORC1 can phosphorylate it, and who later moved into cancer drug discovery in the biotech industry
Schalm SS.sub: Kymera Therapeutics, Watertown (2025 paper) · Blueprint Medicines, Cambridge, Massachusetts (2022 paper) · Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Harvard University, Tom Maniatis lab (2010) · Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, John Blenis lab (2000–2004)
story: Stefanie Schalm is first author of the Atlas study SCH2003 from John Blenis's lab at Harvard Medical School. It explains how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, recognises one of its main targets. 4E-BP1 is a brake on protein synthesis: while unphosphorylated it holds on to eIF4E, the factor that binds the cap at the start of a messenger RNA. Once mTORC1 adds several phosphate groups, 4E-BP1 lets go and translation can begin.

The paper showed that a short stretch at the end of 4E-BP1, the TOR signalling (TOS) motif, is what binds raptor, the partner protein that hands substrates to mTOR. Without a working TOS motif, raptor could not bind 4E-BP1 and the multiple phosphorylation steps failed, so 4E-BP1 kept blocking translation. It established the TOS motif as a docking signal on 4E-BP1 for mTORC1. The experiments were done in cultured cells.

With Blenis, Schalm also co-wrote a 2004 review on how the PI3-kinase and TOR pathways join to control cell growth.
