By 2010 PubMed lists Schalm in Tom Maniatis's group in Harvard's Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, studying how the receptor kinase Ret phosphorylates protocadherins, adhesion proteins of nerve cells. Later papers list Blueprint Medicines (2022), on a kinase inhibitor approach for fibrolamellar liver cancer, and Kymera Therapeutics (2025), on a drug that degrades the p53 inhibitor MDM2.

highlights.SCH2003: First author: showed in cultured cells that the TOS motif of 4E-BP1 mediates raptor binding and is needed for its multisite phosphorylation by mTORC1.

Schram AM.lab_name: Early Drug Development Service and Gynecologic Medical Oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Schram AM.role: Medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering who runs first-in-human cancer drug trials, including the first trial of RMC-5552, an mTORC1-selective inhibitor
Schram AM.sub: Associate Attending Physician, Gynecologic Medical Oncology and Early Drug Development, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · fellowship in medical oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering · residency in internal medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital · MD, University of Pennsylvania
story: Rapamycin and the related rapalogs only partly block mTORC1, and the newer drugs that fully block mTOR also hit mTORC2, which causes high blood sugar and other side effects. RMC-5552 was designed to do better on both counts: it is a bi-steric drug that binds two sites on mTOR at once and is selective for mTORC1. Alison Schram was first author of the 2025 phase 1 trial in Clinical Cancer Research (SCH2025), the first time the drug was given to people. Fifty-seven patients with advanced solid tumours received rising weekly doses. Treatment-related high blood sugar occurred in only 4 percent of them and never limited the dose, and 64 percent had their disease controlled for a time.

These numbers fit the idea that sparing mTORC2 reduces metabolic side effects. The trial had no comparison group and did not test RMC-5552 against rapamycin or an older mTOR blocker, so it is early evidence and cannot show that sparing mTORC2 is the reason.

Schram studied medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, trained in internal medicine at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston and in medical oncology at Memorial Sloan Kettering. At MSK the work centres on early-phase clinical trials that match new drugs to the molecular changes driving a patient's tumour, in the Early Drug Development Service and in gynecologic medical oncology, where Schram is an associate attending physician.

highlights.SCH2025: First author: reported the first-in-human dose-escalation trial of the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552 in 57 patients with advanced solid tumours.

Sciarretta S.lab_name: Department of Medical-Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies, Sapienza University of Rome, and IRCCS Neuromed (Latina, Italy)
Sciarretta S.role: Cardiologist and heart researcher at Sapienza University of Rome who trained with Junichi Sadoshima on how mTOR and autophagy protect or harm the stressed heart
Sciarretta S.sub: Department of Medical-Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies, Sapienza University of Rome, Latina campus, and IRCCS Neuromed, Pozzilli (2026) · Cardiovascular Research Institute, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, Junichi Sadoshima lab (2014)
story: In 2014 Sebastiano Sciarretta, with Massimo Volpe and Junichi Sadoshima, wrote a review in Circulation Research on what mTOR does in the healthy and the diseased heart. Heart muscle cells need mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to build protein, grow and keep working. But under some kinds of heart stress, too much mTORC1 can block autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and partial inhibition of mTORC1 protected the heart in animal studies. A review gathers earlier findings rather than reporting new experiments, and most of the evidence it covers comes from mice and rats.

PubMed lists Sciarretta at that time at the Cardiovascular Research Institute of Rutgers New Jersey Medical School in Newark, in Sadoshima's group, and at IRCCS Neuromed, a research hospital in Pozzilli, Italy. This shows a career split between the United States and Italy, with work centred on heart failure, autophagy and mTOR signalling.

Sciarretta now works at the Department of Medical-Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies of Sapienza University of Rome, on its Latina campus, together with IRCCS Neuromed. Recent papers include population studies of cardiovascular risk, such as a 2026 study of the oxidative enzyme NOX2 in blood and future heart events in the Moli-sani cohort, as well as clinical case reports.

highlights.SCI2014: First author of the review on mTOR signalling in cardiac physiology and disease.

Shah OJ.lab_name: Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (La Jolla, California, USA)
Shah OJ.role: Cell biologist in Tony Hunter's lab at the Salk Institute who showed that runaway Rheb-mTOR-S6K signalling destroys the insulin receptor's helper proteins IRS1 and IRS2, one half of the discovery of the S6K-IRS feedback loop
Shah OJ.sub: Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (Tony Hunter lab, at the time of the study)
story: When insulin binds its receptor, the signal passes through helper proteins called IRS1 and IRS2 before it reaches Akt and, further down, mTORC1 and its target S6K. O. Jameel Shah's 2004 paper in Current Biology (SHA2004), from Tony Hunter's lab at the Salk Institute, showed what happens when the end of that chain is stuck on. In cultured mammalian cells lacking the TSC brake, constant activity of Rheb, mTOR and S6K led to the loss of IRS1 and IRS2. The cells became resistant to insulin and their survival signalling through Akt weakened.

The paper appeared two months after a companion study by Harrington and colleagues, and together they set out the S6K-to-IRS negative feedback loop. In this loop, an overactive mTORC1 pathway turns down the very insulin signal that feeds it. The work was done in cultured cells.

PubMed lists Shah at the Salk Institute at the time of the study. Because PubMed also indexes an unrelated surgeon with the same initials, a full publication record could not be built safely, and no current position could be confirmed.

highlights.SHA2004: First author: showed in cultured cells that constitutive Rheb/mTOR/S6K signalling depletes IRS1 and IRS2, causing insulin resistance and weaker survival signalling.

Huang RK.lab_name: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus (Ashburn, Virginia, USA)
Huang RK.role: Cryo-electron microscopy specialist who, at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus, helped solve the 2018 and 2019 structures of the protein machines that pass amino acid signals to mTORC1
Huang RK.sub: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus, Ashburn, Virginia (at the time of the studies, 2018–2019)
story: Rick K. Huang is a co-author on two Atlas studies from David Sabatini's laboratory, led by Kuang Shen, that used cryo-electron microscopy to see how amino acid signals reach mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Cryo-EM freezes purified proteins in thin ice and builds a 3D model from many thousands of electron microscope images. The Rag GTPases are a pair of switch proteins on the lysosome surface that pull mTORC1 there when amino acids are present.

The 2018 Nature paper (SHE2018) showed the shape of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rags off when amino acids are scarce, alone and bound to the Rags. It revealed both the part that speeds up the Rags' GTP burning and a second, unexpected grip that holds them in place. The 2019 Cell paper (SHE2019) showed folliculin with its partner FNIP2 sitting on the Rags and on Ragulator, the platform that anchors them to the lysosome. Both studies used purified human proteins and biochemical tests, not cells or animals.
Both papers list Huang at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia. A current position could not be confirmed with certainty.

highlights.SHE2018: Co-author from Janelia: contributed to the cryo-EM structures of GATOR1 alone and bound to the Rag GTPases.
highlights.SHE2019: Co-author from Janelia: contributed to the cryo-EM structure of the FLCN-FNIP2-Rag-Ragulator complex.

Shin HR.lab_name: Children's Medical Center Research Institute at UT Southwestern, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Shin HR.role: Cell biologist who discovered, in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley, that the lysosomal protein LYCHOS senses cholesterol for mTORC1, and who now works at the Children's Medical Center Research Institute at UT Southwestern
Shin HR.sub: Children's Medical Center Research Institute and Department of Pediatrics, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (2025) · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and Paul F. Glenn Center for Aging Research, University of California, Berkeley (Zoncu lab, papers 2018–2022)
story: Hijai Shin was first author of a 2022 Science paper in this Atlas (SHI2022). Earlier work from the same lab had shown that cholesterol inside the lysosome switches on mTORC1, but the sensor was missing. SHI2022 identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein previously known only as GPR155, as a cholesterol sensor for mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Cholesterol binds one end of LYCHOS, and mutating that site weakens mTORC1 activation. When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that normally keeps mTORC1 off, and so lets mTORC1 be recruited to the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. The work was done in human cell lines and with purified proteins. The finding gave cholesterol its own direct line to the growth switch, alongside the sensors for amino acids.

In Zoncu's lab Shin also wrote two first-author reviews, on how galectin proteins detect and signal lysosome damage (Molecular Cell, 2018) and on the lysosome as the place where cell growth and cell breakdown meet (Developmental Cell, 2020). Shin co-authored a 2019 Nature Chemical Biology study from Daniel Nomura's lab showing that covalently targeting the lysosome's proton pump switches on autophagy by inhibiting mTORC1, and a 2021 Nature Cell Biology study on how pancreatic cancer cells protect their lysosomes from membrane stress.

By 2025 PubMed lists Shin at the Children's Medical Center Research Institute and the Department of Pediatrics at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. From there Shin co-wrote, with Zoncu, two commentaries on new structures of LYCHOS that show where cholesterol binds. Shin's exact title in Dallas could not be confirmed.

highlights.SHI2022: First author: identified LYCHOS (GPR155) as the lysosomal cholesterol sensor that lets mTORC1 respond to cholesterol by capturing GATOR1.

Shim JH.lab_name: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Seoul, South Korea)
Shim JH.role: Medicinal chemist in Hyeon Soo Kim's group at the Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine, who designs small molecules, and first author of the study of the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH that switches on mTORC1 through Sestrin2
Shim JH.sub: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Hyeon Soo Kim group, papers 2021–2026)
story: Muscle builds protein when mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on, and the amino acid leucine is one of its main triggers. Leucine works by binding a sensor protein called Sestrin2, which then lets go of the brake on mTORC1. In the Atlas study SHIM2026, Shim and colleagues made DLMEH, a modified form of D-leucine (the mirror-image form of normal leucine) designed as a prodrug, a compound the body converts into the active form. DLMEH bound Sestrin2 about as tightly as ordinary leucine and switched on mTORC1 only when Sestrin2 was present.

In human muscle cells grown in a dish, DLMEH restored protein production. In rats whose muscles were wasted by the steroid dexamethasone, it preserved muscle mass, grip strength and endurance. The rat model mimics steroid-induced muscle loss, not age-related sarcopenia, and no human trial has been done.

On PubMed, Shim's papers come from the Department of Anatomy at Korea University College of Medicine with Hyeon Soo Kim and are mostly chemistry: a 2021 paper on a catalyst that builds molecules with a chosen handedness, and a 2026 paper on a new oral pain-relief compound that blocks the Nav1.7 sodium channel in nerve cells. Rank could not be confirmed.

highlights.SHIM2026: First author: designed the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH and showed it activates mTORC1 through Sestrin2, restoring protein synthesis in human muscle cells and preserving muscle in steroid-treated rats.

Shimada H.lab_name: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Shimada H.role: Obstetrician-scientist from Sapporo Medical University working in the Colorado placenta group of Thomas Jansson, Theresa Powell and Fredrick Rosario on how mTOR controls nutrient transport to the fetus
Shimada H.sub: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (2024–2026) · Visiting researcher, Faculty of Medicine, Sapporo Medical University (2020, 2026) · Researcher, Faculty of Medicine, Sapporo Medical University (2019)
story: The placenta decides how much food reaches a growing baby, and mTORC1, the cell's nutrient and growth sensor, helps set how fast it pumps amino acids across. In the 2026 study led by Hiroshi Shimada, with Fredrick Rosario as senior author, the team compared 46 placentas from healthy term pregnancies. Placentas from boys showed stronger mTORC1 signalling, more System A amino acid transport and higher mitochondrial respiration than placentas from girls, and boys had a higher birth weight relative to placental weight.

This was a snapshot at one time point with no treatment, so it shows an association between fetal sex and placental function, not a cause. It does suggest that male and female pregnancies may need to be analysed separately in placental research.

Shimada is listed by PubMed with both the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Sapporo Medical University in Japan. Earlier work in the Colorado group includes a 2024 review on how placental amino acid transporters are regulated, with mTOR as a key regulator, and a 2025 mouse study in which switching off mTOR only in placental trophoblast cells cut the transport of folate to the fetus and reduced fetal growth.

The Japanese national research database KAKEN lists Shimada at the Faculty of Medicine of Sapporo Medical University, as a researcher in 2019 and as a visiting researcher in 2020 and 2026, in the field of obstetrics and gynecology. There Shimada led an early-career grant from 2019 to 2020 to study how endometriosis, the growth of womb-lining tissue outside the womb, develops, using a new disease model.

highlights.SHIMADA2026: First author: compared 46 term placentas and found higher mTORC1 signalling, amino acid transport and mitochondrial respiration in placentas from male pregnancies.

Sills AM.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Sills AM.role: Researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who worked with common marmosets in Adam Salmon's group and led the 2018 study of long-term rapamycin and blood health in these small primates
Sills AM.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2018–2020; at the time of the study)
story: Aubrey Sills was first author of the 2018 Atlas study (SIL2018), with Adam Salmon as senior author, that gave middle-aged common marmosets rapamycin every day for nine months. Marmosets are small, relatively short-lived monkeys, which makes them useful for testing anti-aging drugs in a primate. Rapamycin blocks mTOR and extends life in mice, and the study asked whether long-term use is safe for the blood system of a primate. In the marmosets, routine blood tests changed only a little. Females had lower rapamycin levels in their blood than males, yet both sexes showed few changes. The authors concluded that blood side effects are unlikely with long-term rapamycin in healthy middle-aged animals of this kind. This is a primate study, not a human one.

Sills also co-authored a 2020 paper in GeroScience from the same institute, with Veronica Galvan and Adam Salmon, that described a method for growing nerve cells and astrocytes from newborn marmoset brains, as a primate model for studying brain aging in a dish. No personal page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on these papers.

highlights.SIL2018: First author: reported that nine months of daily rapamycin caused only minor changes in blood counts in middle-aged marmosets.

Sillito F.lab_name: Chakraverty Lab, UCL Cancer Institute, University College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Sillito F.role: Haematologist at the Royal Marsden Hospital and University College London with a special interest in CAR-T cell therapy and lymphoma, whose PhD showed that forcing mTORC1 on in CD4+ T cells makes them last longer but tire out
Sillito F.sub: Haematologist with a special interest in cellular therapy and high-grade lymphoma, Royal Marsden Hospital and University College London Hospitals (2025–2026) · PhD, UCL Cancer Institute, MRC Clinical Research Fellow (completed 2023) · Specialist haematology training, University College London Hospitals · Medical degree, University College London (2009)
story: Cancer treatments with engineered T cells, such as CAR-T and TCR-T cells, work only if the infused cells survive and keep fighting. In a 2026 Journal of Immunology paper, with Ronjon Chakraverty as senior author, Francesca Sillito made mouse CD4+ helper T cells produce extra RHEB, a protein that switches on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. After transfer into mice the cells first grew more and lasted longer, but over time they became exhausted: they carried brake-like receptors on their surface and divided poorly when they met their target again. CD8+ killer T cells had been reported to react differently to the same change. The study is in mice and warns that boosting mTORC1 in therapeutic T cells has a cost.

Sillito is a haematologist, a doctor who treats blood diseases and blood cancers. Sillito graduated in medicine from University College London in 2009 and completed specialist haematology training at University College London Hospitals; an early case report from 2011 lists Sillito at Basildon University Hospital. With a Medical Research Council clinical research fellowship, Sillito then did a PhD on T-cell therapies at the UCL Cancer Institute, completed in 2023, working with Ronjon Chakraverty and Hans Stauss; with Angelika Holler and Stauss, Sillito wrote a 2020 review on engineering CD4+ T cells to strengthen cancer immunity. The 2026 paper above comes from that work.

Sillito now works at the Royal Marsden Hospital with a special interest in cellular therapy, including CAR-T, and high-grade lymphoma, and is a principal investigator on several cellular therapy and lymphoma trials. As first author in Haematologica (2025), Sillito studied how blood stem-cell clones change after CAR-T therapy and the risk of later myeloid cancers, and has co-authored UK studies of second-line CAR-T treatment for large B-cell lymphoma from University College London Hospitals and the Royal Marsden Hospital.

highlights.SIL2026: First author: enforced RHEB-driven mTORC1 activity in therapeutic CD4+ T cells improved early persistence but led to exhaustion.

Sinclair LV.lab_name: Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology, School of Life Sciences, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Sinclair LV.role: T cell immunologist at the University of Dundee who works out how amino acid supply, through transporters such as SLC7A5, feeds mTORC1 and decides what activated T cells become
Sinclair LV.sub: Senior Researcher, Cell Signalling and Immunology, University of Dundee · long-time member of Doreen Cantrell's group · PhD, University of Dundee · BSc in Immunology, University of Edinburgh
story: When a T cell meets its target, it must grow fast, divide many times and switch on its killing machinery. All of that needs amino acids. Linda Sinclair is first author of a 2013 paper from Doreen Cantrell's group in Dundee that showed how the T cell gets them (SIN2013). Signals from the antigen receptor, the T cell's sensor for infection, switch on the transporter SLC7A5, a channel that carries large amino acids such as leucine into the cell. Mouse T cells lacking SLC7A5 could not keep mTORC1, the growth-control complex, active or keep making the growth protein c-Myc, and they failed to turn into effector cells. The study, done in mouse T cells, made amino acid transport a control point for immune responses rather than a passive supply line.

Sinclair grew up partly in Sweden, studied immunology at the University of Edinburgh and did a PhD at the University of Dundee. Since then Sinclair has worked with Doreen Cantrell on how nutrients steer T lymphocytes. An earlier paper (Nature Immunology, 2008) showed that mTOR controls where T cells travel in the body, and later work found that SLC7A5-driven methionine uptake acts as a metabolic checkpoint for effector T cells (eLife, 2019).

The University of Dundee lists Sinclair as a Senior Researcher in the Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology. Current topics include mTOR signalling, amino acid uptake and autophagy in CD8 killer T cells, with related work on MAIT cells, B cell metabolism and iron handling in dendritic cells.

highlights.SIN2013: First author: showed in mouse T cells that antigen receptors switch on the SLC7A5 amino acid transporter, which sustains mTORC1 and c-Myc and is needed for effector differentiation.

Singh S.lab_name: Lysosomal Health in Ageing, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Singh S.role: Autophagy researcher in Timothy Sargeant's group in Adelaide who measures autophagy directly in human blood cells and led a diet trial testing whether eating less protein switches it on in people
Singh S.sub: Lysosomal Health in Ageing group, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute, and School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Sciences, Adelaide University · PhD, University of Adelaide (2019–2024, supervised by Timothy Sargeant)
story: In mice and in cultured cells, cutting protein lowers mTORC1 activity, and lower mTORC1 releases autophagy, the cell's recycling system. Many diet books assume the same is true for people. Sanjna Singh's 2026 trial in Clinical Nutrition (SIN2026) tested it. In a randomized crossover design, 63 healthy adults each ate a normal-protein diet (20 percent of energy from protein) and a reduced-protein diet (10 percent) for four weeks, in random order. The team then measured autophagic flux in blood immune cells. Flux means how fast material actually moves through the recycling system, which is a stronger test than a single snapshot of autophagy markers.

Flux did not change between the two diets. The study is one of the few human tests of the protein-to-mTORC1-to-autophagy idea with a flux readout, and it suggests that a moderate cut in protein, without eating fewer calories overall, is not enough to raise autophagy in human blood cells. It says nothing about other tissues or about stronger fasting.

Singh did a PhD in Timothy Sargeant's group from 2019 to 2024 on cross-talk between autophagy and efferocytosis, the process by which microglia in the brain clear away dead cells. The group has also worked on lysosomal clearance of the Alzheimer protein tau. In 2025 Singh was first author of a JCI Insight study showing that a single high-protein meal did not change autophagy in human blood cells after one hour, and in 2026 co-wrote a review with Sargeant on what fasting and diet can and cannot do to autophagy.

highlights.SIN2026: First author: led the randomized crossover trial showing that four weeks of reduced protein intake did not change autophagic flux in human blood cells.

Simpson SJ.lab_name: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia)
Simpson SJ.role: Biologist who began with how locusts choose their food and is known for the Geometric Framework for nutrition, which shows that the balance of protein, carbohydrate and fat shapes health and lifespan; inaugural academic director of the Charles Perkins Centre
Simpson SJ.sub: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney · Executive director, Obesity Australia (since 2018) · Inaugural academic director, Charles Perkins Centre (2014–2025) · ARC Federation Fellow, University of Sydney (from 2005) · about 22 years at the University of Oxford · PhD, King's College London (1982) · BSc, University of Queensland (1978)
story: Is it how much we eat, or what we eat, that sets how long we live? In the Atlas study SOL2014, Simpson's group, with first author Samantha Solon-Biet, fed mice 25 diets that differed in protein, carbohydrate, fat and energy content and let them eat freely for life. Total calories did not decide lifespan or metabolic health. The ratio of protein to carbohydrate did: mice on low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets lived longest, and they also had lower mTOR activation in the liver. The study links diet composition to mTOR, the nutrient sensor that rapamycin blocks. It was done in mice.

Simpson studied at the University of Queensland (BSc, 1978) and earned a PhD at King's College London in 1982 on how locust nymphs control their food intake. He then spent about 22 years at the University of Oxford, in Experimental Psychology, Zoology and the University Museum of Natural History. His group, with colleagues including David Raubenheimer, uses the Geometric Framework (nutritional geometry), a way of mapping how animals balance several nutrients at once.

He returned to Australia in 2005 as an ARC Federation Fellow at the University of Sydney and served as the inaugural academic director of the Charles Perkins Centre from 2014 to 2025. Since 2018 he has also been executive director of Obesity Australia. He is a Fellow of the Royal Society (2013) and of the Australian Academy of Science (2007), and a Companion of the Order of Australia (2016).

highlights.SOL2014: Senior author: led the 25-diet mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calorie intake, shaped lifespan and metabolic health, with lower liver mTOR activation on low-protein diets.

Sinclair DA.lab_name: Sinclair Lab, Paul F. Glenn Center for Biology of Aging Research, Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Sinclair DA.role: Geneticist of aging at Harvard Medical School, known for work on sirtuins, NAD+ and the idea that aging stems from a loss of epigenetic information, who appears in this Atlas as a co-author on two mouse lifespan studies
Sinclair DA.credit: Portrait: Sinclair Lab, Harvard Medical School
Sinclair DA.sub: Professor of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, and founding director, Paul F. Glenn Laboratories for the Biological Mechanisms of Aging · conjoint professor, School of Medical Sciences, University of New South Wales · faculty, Harvard Medical School (since 1999) · postdoc, Leonard Guarente lab, MIT · PhD in molecular genetics, University of New South Wales (1995)
story: David Sinclair is a middle author on two Atlas studies about diet, drugs and lifespan in mice. SOL2014, led by Samantha Solon-Biet and Stephen Simpson in Sydney, fed mice diets that differed in their mix of protein, carbohydrate and fat and let them eat freely. Lifespan and heart and metabolic health depended on the ratio of protein to carbohydrate, not on the total calories eaten, and mice on low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets had lower mTOR activation in the liver. STR2012, from the NIA Interventions Testing Program, tested five popular candidates, including resveratrol, green tea extract and curcumin, in genetically mixed mice. None changed lifespan significantly. The paper is a clear example of publishing negative results, which helps others avoid chasing compounds that do not work.

Sinclair earned his PhD in molecular genetics at the University of New South Wales in 1995, studying gene regulation in yeast. He then spent about four years in Leonard Guarente's lab at MIT, where yeast was used as a model of aging, and joined Harvard Medical School in 1999. His lab has worked on sirtuins, a family of enzymes that need the molecule NAD+, on mitochondria, and on partial reprogramming with Yamanaka factors to restore youthful gene activity in mouse tissues. He proposes an 'information theory of aging', in which aging comes from a gradual loss of epigenetic information, the chemical marks that tell each cell which genes to use.

He is Professor of Genetics at Harvard Medical School, founding director of the Paul F. Glenn Laboratories for the Biological Mechanisms of Aging, and a conjoint professor at the University of New South Wales. Some of his claims, including early work on resveratrol as a sirtuin activator and public statements about reversing aging, have been disputed by other researchers.

highlights.SOL2014: Co-author on the mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calorie intake, shaped lifespan and metabolic health, with lower liver mTOR activation on low-protein diets.
highlights.STR2012: Co-author on the Interventions Testing Program report in which none of five popular compounds, including resveratrol, extended mouse lifespan significantly.

Solon-Biet SM.lab_name: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia)
Solon-Biet SM.role: Nutrition and ageing researcher at the Charles Perkins Centre who uses the Geometric Framework to study how protein, carbohydrate and fat intake affect lifespan, metabolism and reproduction in mice
Solon-Biet SM.sub: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney (papers to 2026) · earlier also Centre for Education and Research on Aging, Concord Hospital, and ANZAC Research Institute, Sydney
story: Is it how much we eat, or what we eat, that sets how long we live? In the Atlas study SOL2014, Solon-Biet led an experiment in which mice ate freely from one of 25 diets that differed in protein, carbohydrate, fat and energy content for their whole lives. Calories did not decide lifespan or metabolic health. The ratio of protein to carbohydrate did: low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets gave the longest lives and were associated with lower activation of mTOR, the nutrient sensor, in the liver. The work was done in mice, with Stephen Simpson as senior author.

PubMed lists more than 50 papers by Solon-Biet, nearly all from the Charles Perkins Centre. Earlier records also name the Centre for Education and Research on Aging at Concord Hospital and the ANZAC Research Institute, where Le Couteur's ageing group is based. The papers extend the same diet-mapping approach to the gut microbiome, reproduction and metabolism, for example a 2016 study showing that protein intake shapes which gut bacteria thrive, and a 2026 study showing that different protein, carbohydrate and fat balances suit mouse mothers during pregnancy and during milk feeding.
The current position is stated from the 2026 PubMed affiliation, the Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences at the University of Sydney.

highlights.SOL2014: First author: ran the 25-diet lifelong mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calorie intake, shaped lifespan and metabolic health.

Sparta B.lab_name: Deeds Lab, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Sparta B.role: Quantitative cell biologist who trained in John Albeck's lab at UC Davis, where live single-cell imaging showed that the mTORC1-TFEB signalling axis tracks nutrients and growth factors continuously, and then moved to UCLA as a postdoctoral fellow
Sparta B.sub: Postdoctoral fellow, Eric Deeds lab, University of California, Los Angeles (IRACDA program, 2021 cohort) · PhD, University of California, Davis (John Albeck lab, papers 2015–2023) · BS in Biochemistry, Northeastern University
story: Breanne Sparta was first author of a 2023 eLife paper in this Atlas (SPA2023). Most experiments on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, grind up millions of cells and measure an average at a few time points. This study filmed single living human breast epithelial cells (MCF10A) carrying fluorescent reporters, and followed TFEB, a regulator of lysosomes and autophagy that mTORC1 holds outside the nucleus, together with AMPK and AKT activity. mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusted smoothly to amino acids and insulin whether they were given alone, one after the other or together. At normal body levels of amino acids the three signals rose and fell in step, and these graded changes tracked how fast the cells were making protein. The results come from one cultured cell line.

Sparta studied biochemistry at Northeastern University (BS) and earned a PhD at the University of California, Davis, in John Albeck's lab, with a thesis on how growth and metabolism are coordinated in single living cells. That work also used live-cell reporters. As first author of a 2015 Journal of Biological Chemistry paper, Sparta showed that pulses of ERK activity triggered by the growth factor EGF depend on mechanisms at the receptor. Sparta co-authored a 2017 methods chapter on imaging ERK signalling with fluorescent biosensors, a 2017 modelling study of oscillations in MAPK signalling, and a 2021 Cell Metabolism paper on how single cells pass through temporary phases of resistance to drugs that block mitochondrial energy production.

Sparta then joined Eric Deeds' lab at the University of California, Los Angeles, as a postdoctoral fellow in the IRACDA program (2021 cohort). The research there asks how gene expression varies between cells in multicellular organisms.

highlights.SPA2023: First author: used live single-cell imaging to show that mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusts continuously to amino acids and insulin and tracks protein synthesis.

Spilman P.lab_name: Drug Discovery Lab, Department of Neurology, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Spilman P.role: Neuroscientist who showed, with Veronica Galvan, that long-term rapamycin prevents memory loss in an Alzheimer's mouse model, and who later worked with Dale Bredesen on Alzheimer's drug discovery
Spilman P.sub: Drug Discovery Lab, Department of Neurology, UCLA (2025) · Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (2010)
story: By 2010 rapamycin was known to extend lifespan in mice, but did it help with a specific disease of old age? In the Atlas study SPI2010, Patricia Spilman was first author and Veronica Galvan senior author. Mice engineered to model Alzheimer's disease were fed rapamycin for a long time. The treated mice did not develop the memory problems seen in untreated animals, and they had less amyloid-beta, the protein that forms plaques in the Alzheimer's brain. Neurons of treated mice showed more autophagy, the cell's clean-up process, which suggests one way the drug helped. The study was done in mice and does not show the same effect in people.

PubMed lists 14 papers that Spilman co-authored with Galvan or with Dale Bredesen, from 2007 to 2025. In 2025 Spilman was a co-author of a Scientific Reports paper from the Drug Discovery Lab in UCLA's Department of Neurology describing DDL-218, an orally active small molecule that raised levels of the protein SirT1 in nerve cells carrying ApoE4, the main genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, and in a mouse model.
No official profile page was found, so the current position is not confirmed.

highlights.SPI2010: First author: showed that long-term rapamycin prevented memory deficits and lowered amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's mouse model, with more autophagy in neurons.

Grewal SS.lab_name: Grewal Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
Grewal SS.role: Calgary biochemist who uses fruit flies to work out how nutrients and growth signals such as TOR set the size of cells, organs and the whole animal
Grewal SS.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, and Senior Associate Dean (Research), Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (at Calgary since 2007) · postdoc, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (Seattle) · PhD in Cell and Developmental Biology, Oregon Health & Science University (2001) · BSc in Pharmacology, King's College London (1992)
story: Savraj Grewal is the senior author of the Atlas study SRI2026, done in fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae. A larva has one job: to eat and grow fast before it turns into an adult. Its fat body, a tissue that works like a mix of our liver and fat, senses how much food there is and sends signals that tell the rest of the body how fast to grow. The study found that TOR, the nutrient-sensing growth kinase, keeps the level of TFAM protein low in the fat body. TFAM is the protein that switches on the genes inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. TOR does this after the TFAM message has been made, not by blocking the gene itself. This TOR to TFAM link in one tissue helps decide how fast the whole larva grows. It is fly work, so it shows a mechanism in an animal, not in people.

The paper continues a line of work from the same lab. In 2022 the group showed that food changes the shape and activity of mitochondria in the fat body, and that turning down mitochondrial energy production only in this tissue made larvae grow faster, through secreted signals that boost insulin action. A 2023 paper found that macrophage-like blood cells use their mitochondria in a similar way to influence body growth.

Grewal studied pharmacology at King's College London, earned a PhD in cell and developmental biology at Oregon Health & Science University in 2001, and did postdoctoral research at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center. Grewal joined the University of Calgary in 2007. The Grewal lab uses Drosophila to study the genetic and molecular controls of cell and tissue growth, with a view to cancer and child development. Grewal is a professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and Senior Associate Dean (Research) at the Cumming School of Medicine, and a member of the Arnie Charbonneau Cancer Institute and the Alberta Children's Hospital Research Institute.

highlights.SRI2026: Senior author: the lab showed in fly larvae that TOR keeps the mitochondrial regulator TFAM low in the fat body, and that this link helps set whole-body growth.

Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.lab_name: Grewal Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.role: Fruit fly biologist in Savraj Grewal's Calgary lab who studies how growth signals and mitochondria in one tissue control how fast the whole larva grows
Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Clark H. Smith Brain Tumour Centre and Arnie Charbonneau Cancer Institute, University of Calgary (papers with Savraj Grewal, 2018–2026)
story: Shrivani Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas is the first author of the Atlas study SRI2026, from Savraj Grewal's lab at the University of Calgary. The work was done in fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae. Their fat body senses food and tells the rest of the body how fast to grow. The study found that TOR, the nutrient-sensing growth kinase, keeps the protein TFAM low in the fat body. TFAM switches on the genes inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. TOR acts on TFAM after its message is made, and this link in one tissue helps set the growth rate of the whole animal. It is a fly study and shows a mechanism, not a result in people.

The PubMed record shows a steady path in the same lab. In 2018 Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas was first author of two papers showing that the Ras/ERK growth pathway drives fly growth by boosting the cell's protein-making machinery: tRNA synthesis through the repressor Maf1, and ribosomal RNA synthesis through the factor TIF-IA. In 2022, in Cell Reports, the same team showed that lowering mitochondrial energy production only in the fat body made larvae grow faster, by reducing secreted signals that hold back insulin. A 2023 paper extended the idea to macrophage-like blood cells.
All of these papers list the University of Calgary. No separate official profile was found, so the current position is given as the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SRI2026: First author: showed in fly larvae that TOR keeps the mitochondrial regulator TFAM low in the fat body, which helps set the growth of the whole animal.

Su Y.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
Su Y.role: Cardiologist in Tianjin and Cangzhou who studied how a long non-coding RNA drives necroptotic heart-cell death after a blocked artery is reopened
Su Y.sub: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University · Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou People's Hospital, Hebei (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Yanhong Su is first author of the Atlas study SU2026, with cardiologist Jun Zhang as senior author. When a blocked heart artery is reopened, the returning blood itself causes extra damage, called ischemia-reperfusion injury. Part of that damage comes from necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death in which the cell bursts. The team looked at DLX6-AS1, a long non-coding RNA, which is an RNA molecule that regulates genes without making a protein.

In mice with ischemia-reperfusion injury, DLX6-AS1 levels rose together with the necroptosis markers RIP1, RIP3 and MLKL. In rat heart cells starved of oxygen and then re-oxygenated, extra DLX6-AS1 raised the active forms of PI3K, AKT and mTOR and made necroptosis worse, while blocking DLX6-AS1 reduced cell death. Here the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway sits on the harmful side, the opposite of many heart studies in which AKT signalling protects heart cells. The work is in mice and a rat cell line.

PubMed lists Su at the cardiology departments of Tianjin Medical University and Cangzhou People's Hospital in Hebei province. No other papers or official page could be tied to this person with confidence, so the profile rests on this study.

highlights.SU2026: First author: showed in mice and rat heart cells that the lncRNA DLX6-AS1 promotes necroptosis after ischemia-reperfusion through PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling.

Zhang Jun.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou Central Hospital, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
Zhang Jun.role: Cardiologist at Cangzhou Central Hospital, a teaching hospital of Tianjin Medical University, and senior author of a study on RNA-driven heart-cell death after reperfusion
Zhang Jun.sub: Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou Central Hospital · Tianjin Medical University (affiliations on the 2026 study)
story: Jun Zhang is the senior and corresponding author of the Atlas study SU2026, with Yanhong Su as first author. The study looked at heart damage that happens when blood flow returns after a heart artery has been blocked, known as ischemia-reperfusion injury. Some of the heart cells die by necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death in which the cell bursts open.

The team focused on DLX6-AS1, a long non-coding RNA (an RNA that regulates other genes but does not code for a protein). Its level rose in injured mouse hearts. In rat heart cells put through oxygen loss and return, more DLX6-AS1 switched on PI3K, AKT and mTOR and increased necroptosis, and blocking it reduced the damage. The results come from mice and a cell line, so they point to a possible drug target rather than a treatment.

PubMed lists Zhang at the Department of Cardiology of Cangzhou Central Hospital in Hebei province, which is affiliated with Tianjin Medical University. Jun Zhang is a very common name, and no official page could be matched with confidence, so this profile rests on the affiliation given on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SU2026: Senior author: led the study showing that DLX6-AS1 drives necroptosis through PI3K/AKT/mTOR in heart ischemia-reperfusion injury in mice and rat heart cells.

Sun Z.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Sun Z.role: Hematology researcher in Hangzhou who studies treatment of bone-marrow failure, including the use of sirolimus (rapamycin) in pure red cell aplasia
Sun Z.sub: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Zhejiang Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine) and The First School of Clinical Medicine, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (papers 2026)
story: In pure red cell aplasia, the bone marrow stops making red blood cells while white cells and platelets are spared. The acquired form is often driven by the immune system, so it is treated with immune-suppressing drugs such as ciclosporin. In SUN2026, Zexing Sun and colleagues in Dijiong Wu's group looked back at patients treated at one hospital whose disease had not responded to ciclosporin and who then received sirolimus, the drug also called rapamycin, which blocks mTOR in immune cells. 54.5 percent responded, and 64.3 percent of those whose aplasia was secondary to another disease. Responses did not depend on mutations in STAT3 or STAT5B, genes often altered in the abnormal lymphocytes linked to this disease. The study was retrospective, at one centre, with no randomised control group, so it cannot prove that sirolimus works better than ciclosporin.

Sun works in the Department of Hematology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University in Hangzhou. In 2026 the same group also published a single-centre comparison of stem cell transplant donor types in aplastic anaemia, on which Sun was a co-author. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SUN2026: First author of the retrospective single-centre study in which second-line sirolimus produced responses in ciclosporin-refractory acquired pure red cell aplasia regardless of STAT3/STAT5B status.

Su MY.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
Su MY.role: Structural biologist who solved cryo-EM structures of lysosomal complexes in James Hurley's lab at UC Berkeley and now leads cryo-EM studies of mTORC1 regulators as corresponding author at the Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen
Su MY.sub: Department of Biochemistry, SUSTech Homeostatic Medicine Institute and Institute for Biological Electron Microscopy, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen (papers from 2021) · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences, University of California, Berkeley (Hurley lab, papers 2017–2021)
story: Ming-Yuan Su was first author of SUX2017, a 2017 Molecular Cell paper from James Hurley's lab at UC Berkeley. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is recruited to the lysosome by the Rag GTPases, which sit on a scaffold called Ragulator. The paper combined several structural methods into a 'hybrid' model of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex, giving one of the first detailed pictures of this docking station. It is a protein-level study, which later work built on to explain how nutrients flip the Rag switch.

Su stayed with structures of lysosome-linked machines. As first author of a 2020 Nature paper, Su solved the cryo-EM structure of the C9orf72-SMCR8-WDR41 complex, which is reduced in some forms of ALS and frontotemporal dementia, and showed that it acts as a GTPase-activating protein for ARF proteins. A 2021 Nature Communications paper explained how this activity works and offered a model for related switches, FLCN and NPRL2, that control the Rag GTPases.

Since 2021 PubMed lists Su in the Department of Biochemistry at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen, as corresponding author. The group's cryo-EM work there includes structures of GATOR2 bound to the amino acid sensors CASTOR1 and Sestrin2 (2025), of the KICSTOR and GATOR1-KICSTOR complexes that anchor an mTORC1 brake on the lysosome (2025, with Chun-Yan Lim), and of ubiquitin ligase complexes such as DDB1-AMBRA1 (2023) and COP1-DET1 (2026).

highlights.SUX2017: First author: built the hybrid structural model of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex that docks mTORC1 on the lysosome.

Suzuki C.lab_name: Wagner Lab, Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Suzuki C.role: Structural biologist from Gerhard Wagner's Harvard lab who showed how the tumour suppressor PDCD4 grabs the helicase eIF4A to block the start of protein synthesis
Suzuki C.sub: Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (papers with Gerhard Wagner, 2008–2009)
story: Chikako Suzuki is the first author of SUZ2008, a PNAS paper from Gerhard Wagner's lab at Harvard Medical School. To start making a protein, the cell must unwind the front end of a messenger RNA. The helicase eIF4A does the unwinding, helped by the scaffold protein eIF4G. PDCD4 is a tumour suppressor that blocks this step, and mTORC1 signalling, through S6 kinase, marks PDCD4 for destruction so that translation can go ahead.

Using x-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy and binding measurements on purified proteins, the team showed that both MA3 domains of PDCD4 bind the front part of eIF4A. In doing so PDCD4 competes with eIF4G and with RNA for the same helicase. This explains in physical terms how PDCD4 slows the start of translation. The work is on purified proteins, so it shows a mechanism, not an effect in cells or animals.

Suzuki is also a co-author of a 2009 Cell paper from the same lab, with Nahum Sonenberg's group, that mapped how eIF4A, eIF4G and eIF4H fit together into a working helicase complex. Because this is a common name, only papers shared with Wagner were counted. No later record could be tied to this person, so the current position is not known and the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SUZ2008: First author: solved how both MA3 domains of PDCD4 bind eIF4A and compete with eIF4G and RNA, explaining how PDCD4 blocks translation initiation.

Swarup A.lab_name: Bolger Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Georgia (Athens, Georgia, USA)
Swarup A.role: PhD candidate in Timothy Bolger's lab at the University of Georgia who studies how cancer mutations in the RNA helicase DDX3X change the cell's protein-making response to stress
Swarup A.sub: PhD candidate, BCMB program, Bolger Lab, University of Georgia · master's studies at Maastricht University and Savitribai Phule Pune University · undergraduate degree, Savitribai Phule Pune University
story: Akanksha Swarup is the first author of SWA2026, done in Timothy Bolger's lab at the University of Georgia. DDX3X is an RNA helicase, a protein that unwinds folded messenger RNA so ribosomes can read it. It is often mutated in medulloblastoma, a brain cancer of children. The team copied these cancer mutations into DED1, the yeast version of the gene. The mutant yeast kept growing in rapamycin, the drug that blocks the growth complex TORC1. After TORC1 was blocked, the mutant cells made more protein from messages with simple, unfolded starts, many of them growth messages. This hints at how mutant DDX3X might let tumour cells escape a brake set by TORC1, but it is yeast work and does not show the effect in tumours.

In 2024 Swarup and Bolger also wrote a review in Biomolecules on the role of DDX3X in medulloblastoma. The lab page lists Swarup as a PhD candidate in the Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (BCMB) program. Swarup did undergraduate studies at Savitribai Phule Pune University in India and master's studies at Maastricht University in the Netherlands and Savitribai Phule Pune University.

highlights.SWA2026: First author: modelled medulloblastoma DDX3X mutations in yeast DED1 and found rapamycin-resistant growth with more translation of simple-start growth messages after TORC1 inhibition.

Szwed A.lab_name: Jacinto Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University (Piscataway, New Jersey, USA)
Szwed A.role: Lead author, from Estela Jacinto's Rutgers lab, of a long Physiological Reviews article on how the two mTOR complexes are controlled and what they do in metabolism
Szwed A.sub: Jacinto Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University (at the time of the 2021 review)
story: Angelia Szwed is the first author of SZW2021, a review in Physiological Reviews written with Eugene Kim and Estela Jacinto at Rutgers. mTOR, the cell's central growth kinase, works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 reads nutrients and switches on the making of proteins, fats and nucleotides. mTORC2 responds mostly to growth factors and helps control sugar uptake, survival and the cell's skeleton. The review explains how each complex is switched on and off and what each one does to metabolism, with examples from cancer, immune cells, diabetes and obesity, brain disease and ageing.

For a student, a review of this kind is a map of the field. It is useful for seeing how the many single findings fit together, but it reports other people's experiments and does not add new data of its own.

The Jacinto lab website lists the review on a page for Szwed. PubMed shows no other papers under this name with an mTOR or Rutgers link, and no official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the review.

highlights.SZW2021: First author of a Physiological Reviews article on how mTORC1 and mTORC2 are regulated and how they control metabolism.

Tang B.lab_name: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Tang B.role: Urology researcher at West China Hospital and first author of a study explaining how kidney cancers escape mTOR inhibitor drugs, and how blocking NEK7 restores their effect
Tang B.sub: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Everolimus and temsirolimus, two drugs that block mTOR, are used for advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common kidney cancer. Many tumours stop responding to them. In the Atlas study TAN2026 in Nature Communications, Bo Tang was first author of work that traces one escape route. The protein SPOP attaches a K63-linked chain of ubiquitin, a small tag protein, to ZMYND8. The tag keeps ZMYND8 out of phase-separated droplets, small membrane-less compartments inside the nucleus. Freed ZMYND8 pairs with ZHX2 to switch on the gene for NEK7, and NEK7 activates p70S6K, a growth kinase normally downstream of mTOR, by a route that mTOR drugs cannot block. A PROTAC, a molecule built to make the cell destroy a chosen protein, aimed at NEK7 restored sensitivity to everolimus. The evidence comes from cells and animal models, not from patients.

PubMed lists Tang at the Department of Urology and Institute of Urology of West China Hospital, Sichuan University in Chengdu. Because the name is very common, no other paper was tied to this person with enough confidence to include, and no official profile page was found.

highlights.TAN2026: First author: showed that SPOP-driven ubiquitination of ZMYND8 switches on NEK7 and lets kidney cancer cells activate p70S6K without mTOR, and that a NEK7 degrader restores everolimus sensitivity.

Tao J.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Tao J.role: Fish nutrition researcher at Shanghai Ocean University who studies why carnivorous farmed fish such as largemouth bass handle dietary carbohydrate poorly and how this links to mTOR signalling in the liver
Tao J.sub: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, Shanghai Ocean University (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2023 to 2026)
story: Jiajie Tao is the first author of TAO2026, a study in largemouth bass, a meat-eating fish that is farmed widely in China. Fish feed is cheaper when it contains more starch, but carnivorous fish cope badly with it: their livers fill up with glycogen, the stored form of sugar, much like animals with glucose intolerance. The study asked why. It found that in the bass liver the insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway, which normally turns extra sugar into fat, works poorly. When this route is impaired, more of the sugar ends up stored as glycogen. The work is in fish, so it tells us about how mTOR helps decide where sugar goes in the liver, not directly about people.

PubMed lists Tao at Shanghai Ocean University's Research Centre on Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition on about a dozen papers since 2023, most of them on carbohydrate use in largemouth bass, usually with Songlin Li as senior author. An earlier first-author paper (2023) showed that adding cultures of the gut bacterium Clostridium butyricum to a high-starch diet reduced glycogen build-up in the bass liver and raised insulin-signalling and glycolysis genes.
No official profile was found, so training and position are given only from the publication record.

highlights.TAO2026: First author: showed in largemouth bass that weak insulin-driven mTOR/SREBP1 fat synthesis in the liver goes with glycogen overload on high-carbohydrate feed.

Li S.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Li S.role: Fish nutrition scientist at Shanghai Ocean University who leads research on how largemouth bass and other farmed fish use carbohydrate and other nutrients in their feed
Li S.credit: Portrait: Shanghai Ocean University, College of Fisheries and Life Science
Li S.sub: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition and National Demonstration Center on Experiment Teaching of Fisheries Science, Shanghai Ocean University
story: Songlin Li is the senior (last) author of TAO2026, which studied why largemouth bass, a carnivorous farmed fish, store too much glycogen in the liver when fed starch-rich feed. The team found that the liver's insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway, which would normally turn surplus sugar into fat, is impaired in this fish, so sugar is stored as glycogen instead. The result is from fish, and it adds a comparative view of how mTOR helps share out sugar between storage forms in the liver.

PubMed lists Li at Shanghai Ocean University's Research Centre on Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, and at the university's National Demonstration Center on Experiment Teaching of Fisheries Science, as senior author of more than 30 papers on largemouth bass nutrition. The work tests feed ingredients and additives, such as the gut bacterium Clostridium butyricum (2023), to help fish cope with high-carbohydrate diets, and measures liver metabolism, antioxidant defences and gut bacteria.

Because Li is a very common Chinese surname, only papers with the Shanghai Ocean University fish-nutrition affiliation were counted. No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given.

highlights.TAO2026: Senior author: led the largemouth bass study linking impaired mTOR/SREBP1 lipogenesis to glycogen overload in the liver.

Tiwari A.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Tiwari A.role: Cancer biologist in Anindya Bagchi's lab who found that a tiny protein made from the circular RNA circPVT1 keeps MYC levels high through mTORC1
Tiwari A.sub: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, Anindya Bagchi lab (2026) · Masonic Cancer Center, University of Minnesota, and Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, Gurgaon, India (2014)
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Ashutosh Tiwari is first author of this study. The work continues a long collaboration with Anindya Bagchi: Tiwari is also a co-author of the 2014 Nature paper, from Bagchi's group at the University of Minnesota, which showed that cancers with extra MYC copies depend on PVT1. At that time PubMed listed Tiwari at the Masonic Cancer Center in Minneapolis and at the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute in Gurgaon, India.

In 2026, Tiwari was also a co-author of a second Genes and Development paper from the Bagchi lab, on Honeybadger, another micropeptide made from an alternative transcript, which holds back RAS-MAPK signalling. A formal title for Tiwari's current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.TIW2026: First author: discovered Firefox, a circPVT1-encoded micropeptide that sustains MYC through AKT-mTORC1 signalling.

Bagchi A.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Bagchi A.role: Cancer geneticist and associate professor at Sanford Burnham Prebys who uses chromosome engineering to find cancer genes, known for showing that MYC-amplified cancers depend on the neighbouring gene PVT1
Bagchi A.sub: Associate Professor, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, La Jolla · University of Minnesota, Department of Genetics, Cell Biology and Development and Masonic Cancer Center (2014–2017) · Postdoctoral training, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Alea Mills lab · PhD, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Anindya Bagchi is the senior author, the scientist who led the work. The paper builds on a question Bagchi's lab has followed for more than a decade: why does PVT1 travel with MYC? In 2014, from the University of Minnesota, Bagchi's group showed in Nature that cancers with extra copies of MYC also gain PVT1 and need it, because PVT1 keeps MYC protein stable. A 2016 paper showed MYC and PVT1 working together in breast cancer.

Bagchi earned a PhD at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi and then trained as a postdoctoral fellow at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York with Alea Mills. As first author of a 2007 Cell paper, Bagchi used chromosome engineering in mice, adding or deleting a large stretch of DNA matching human chromosome region 1p36, to identify the chromatin regulator CHD5 as a tumour suppressor that works through the p53 pathway.

Bagchi is now an associate professor in the Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program at Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla, part of its NCI-designated cancer center. The lab continues to engineer large genome rearrangements to find cancer genes and has discovered small proteins hidden in RNAs thought to be non-coding, including Firefox and, in a companion 2026 paper, Honeybadger, which restrains RAS-MAPK signalling. Bagchi also collaborates on brain tumour and pancreatic cancer studies at the institute.

highlights.TIW2026: Senior author of the study that discovered Firefox, a circPVT1-encoded micropeptide that sustains MYC through AKT-mTORC1 signalling.

Tsun ZY.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Tsun ZY.role: Biologist who, as first author in David Sabatini's lab, showed that the tumour suppressor folliculin is a GAP for the RagC and RagD GTPases that carry the amino acid signal to mTORC1
Tsun ZY.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and MIT Department of Biology, Sabatini lab (papers 2011–2015, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is only switched on when amino acids are available. The signal is carried by the Rag GTPases, pairs of small switch proteins that sit on the lysosome. Each Rag can hold GTP or GDP, and the combination decides whether mTORC1 is pulled to the lysosome, where its activator waits. The open question in 2013 was what controls RagC and RagD, one half of each Rag pair.

Zhi-Yang Tsun, first author of the 2013 Molecular Cell paper (TSU2013), found the answer in folliculin, a tumour suppressor protein. Together with its partner FNIP, folliculin acts as a GAP for RagC and RagD, a helper that makes them turn GTP into GDP. Rags in this state bind mTORC1 and bring it to the lysosome when amino acids are present. The work was done in human cells and with purified proteins. Tsun is also a co-author of WAN2015, which showed that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 tells mTORC1 that arginine is available.

PubMed lists Tsun at the Whitehead Institute and the MIT Department of Biology on these papers and as first author of a 2015 review with Richard Possemato on how cancer cells handle amino acids, covering glutamine and serine use and amino acid sensing by mTOR. Tsun is also a co-author of the 2011 Nature study from the same lab that found breast cancers dependent on the serine-synthesis enzyme PHGDH. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.TSU2013: First author: showed in cells and with purified proteins that folliculin-FNIP is a GAP for RagC and RagD, needed for amino acids to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.WAN2015: Co-author on the cell study showing that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 signals arginine sufficiency to mTORC1.

Ullern H.lab_name: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, University of Oslo (Oslo, Norway)
Ullern H.role: Researcher in Helene Knævelsrud's autophagy group at the University of Oslo and first author of a 2026 study of folliculin loss in Birt-Hogg-Dubé kidney cancer
Ullern H.sub: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, and Centre for Cancer Cell Reprogramming, University of Oslo (papers 2025–2026)
story: Halvor Ullern was first author of a 2026 Autophagy Reports paper in this Atlas (ULL2026). Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is an inherited condition in which people carry a faulty copy of the FLCN gene and can develop kidney tumours. Folliculin, the FLCN protein, is part of the switch that controls mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomes and autophagy. In kidney cancer cells from patients, losing FLCN kept TFEB permanently in the nucleus and made mTORC1 overactive. Bulk autophagy, the cell's self-recycling, still ran normally. Even so, the autophagy receptor p62 (SQSTM1) piled up in enlarged clumps, and the same build-up was seen in kidney tumours from a Norwegian group of patients.

The lesson for researchers is practical: a build-up of p62 is often read as a sign that autophagy is blocked, but here it was not. The study used patient-derived cells and tumour samples, so it describes this one cancer type.

Ullern works in Helene Knævelsrud's group in the Department of Molecular Medicine at the University of Oslo. In 2025 Ullern was also first author of a review in the Journal of Molecular Biology on the links between autophagy and sleep. PubMed lists two papers with the name; no further career details were found.

highlights.ULL2026: First author: showed in Birt-Hogg-Dubé kidney cancer cells and patient tumours that p62 accumulates even though bulk autophagy still works.

Um SH.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine (Suwon, South Korea)
Um SH.role: Molecular biologist at Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine whose work centres on the S6 kinases, and first author of the 2004 Nature study showing that mice without S6K1 resist obesity
Um SH.sub: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Suwon (papers 2012–2024) · Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel (2004)
story: Sung Hee Um was first author of a 2004 Nature paper (UMX2004) from the group of George Thomas at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel. S6K1 is a kinase that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on when nutrients and insulin are plentiful. The team bred mice that lack S6K1 entirely. On a normal diet and on a high-fat diet these mice stayed lean as they aged and kept their insulin sensitivity, while normal mice grew fat. The knockout mice burned more fat and their fat cells stayed small.

The study matters because it ties one branch of mTORC1 output directly to weight gain and to insulin resistance, the first step towards type 2 diabetes. It was done in mice, so it shows what removing S6K1 does in a mammal, not what blocking it would do in people.

Um went on to lead work on the S6 kinases at the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, in Suwon, South Korea. As senior author in 2012, Um showed in mice that the sister kinase S6K2 restrains the liver's production of ketone bodies, the fuel made during fasting, by holding back the receptor PPAR-alpha. Later papers from the same department, in 2020 and 2024, found that S6K1 in the cells surrounding a tumour, especially macrophages, helps tumours build blood vessels and spread to the lung in mice.

highlights.UMX2004: First author: showed that mice lacking S6K1 resist age- and diet-induced obesity and stay more insulin sensitive.

Urfer SR.lab_name: Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Urfer SR.role: Veterinarian and epidemiologist of aging at the University of Washington who led the first placebo-controlled rapamycin trial in pet dogs, an early step of the Dog Aging Project
Urfer SR.sub: Acting Assistant Professor, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington (since 2022) · Senior Fellow, Department of Pathology, University of Washington (2016–2019) · postdoc, Department of Pathology, University of Washington (2008–2012) · postdoc, National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH (2007–2008) · Dr. med. vet., University of Bern (2007)
story: Rapamycin extends lifespan in mice, but mice live in cages and die young. Pet dogs share our homes, our air and often our food, and they age faster than we do, so they are a useful middle step between lab animals and people. In 2017 Silvan Urfer was first author of the trial that tested this idea for the first time (URF2017). Twenty-four healthy middle-aged companion dogs received either low-dose rapamycin or a placebo for 10 weeks, and neither owners nor vets knew which. The treated dogs showed no clinical side effects, and heart ultrasound (echocardiography) hinted at better heart function. With so few dogs and such a short course, the study shows that a larger trial is safe to attempt, not that rapamycin slows aging in dogs.

Urfer trained as a veterinarian at the University of Bern in Switzerland and earned the Dr. med. vet. doctorate there in 2007 with work in population genetics. After a short postdoc at the National Human Genome Research Institute in Bethesda, Urfer moved to the Department of Pathology at the University of Washington in Seattle, first as a postdoc and later as a senior fellow, working with Matt Kaeberlein's group on the dog studies that grew into the Dog Aging Project.

Since 2022 Urfer has been an Acting Assistant Professor in the Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology at the University of Washington. The faculty page lists lifespan and survival analysis, comparative medicine, epidemiology, rapamycin and canine cognitive dysfunction, the dog form of dementia, among the research interests.

highlights.URF2017: First author: ran the 10-week placebo-controlled rapamycin trial in 24 middle-aged pet dogs, which found no clinical side effects and possible gains in heart function.

Vellai T.lab_name: Department of Genetics, Eötvös Loránd University (Budapest, Hungary)
Vellai T.role: Hungarian geneticist who showed in 2003 that silencing the TOR gene roughly doubles the lifespan of the worm C. elegans, and who studies autophagy and ageing in worms at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest
Vellai T.sub: Department of Genetics, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, and HUN-REN-ELTE Genetics Research Group · Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (at the time of the 2003 study, with Fritz Müller)
story: Tibor Vellai is the first author of VEL2003, a short Nature paper from Fritz Müller's group at the University of Fribourg in Switzerland. The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans has a single TOR gene. When the team silenced it, the worms lived about twice as long. This was one of the first signs that turning TOR down can lengthen life in an animal. Because worms and mammals are separated by a very long stretch of evolution, the result suggested that the link between TOR and ageing is ancient. It is a worm study and does not by itself show anything about people.

Vellai went on to lead a genetics group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) in Budapest, Hungary. PubMed lists close to a hundred papers with an ELTE or Budapest affiliation under this name, many on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and its role in ageing in C. elegans. A 2025 paper, for example, describes new single-copy reporter genes that track autophagy in the worm and shows that starvation switches autophagy on only after a delay.
Recent papers list the Department of Genetics at ELTE and the HUN-REN-ELTE Genetics Research Group. No official profile page was opened, so the exact title is not given here.

highlights.VEL2003: First author: showed that silencing the single TOR gene of C. elegans roughly doubles worm lifespan.

Munaretto GM.lab_name: Department of Medicine, Universidade do Contestado (Concordia, Brazil)
Munaretto GM.role: Member of the Department of Medicine at Universidade do Contestado in Santa Catarina, Brazil, and senior author of a 2026 meta-analysis of everolimus after heart transplantation
Munaretto GM.sub: Department of Medicine, Universidade do Contestado, Concórdia, Santa Catarina (papers 2026; at the time of the study)
story: After a heart transplant, patients take drugs for life to stop the immune system from attacking the new heart. The standard drugs, calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, can damage the kidneys, and over the years many transplanted hearts develop cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a thickening of the coronary arteries. Everolimus blocks mTOR, which slows the growth of immune cells and of the cells in artery walls. Giancarlo Maruri Munaretto was senior author of a 2026 meta-analysis in JHLT Open (VITTE2026) that pooled 60 studies with 1,786 heart transplant recipients to weigh up everolimus.

A meta-analysis combines the results of many separate studies to get a clearer overall answer. Here, everolimus-based treatment slowed the artery thickening seen on intravascular ultrasound and kept kidney function better when the dose of calcineurin inhibitors was lowered. Deaths were about the same, but side effects and stopping the drug were more common. The study draws on data from people, so it speaks directly to patient care.

PubMed lists Munaretto at the Department of Medicine of Universidade do Contestado in Concordia, Santa Catarina, Brazil, as senior author of one other 2026 meta-analysis, on sealing the needle track with saline to prevent a collapsed lung after CT-guided lung biopsy. No personal page was found to show career stage.

highlights.VITTE2026: Senior author of the meta-analysis showing that everolimus slows cardiac allograft vasculopathy and protects kidney function after heart transplantation, with more side effects.

Vitte SH.lab_name: Hospital de Amor Nossa Senhora (Barretos, Brazil)
Vitte SH.role: Brazilian medical researcher who works on evidence synthesis and cardiometabolic studies, and first author of the 2026 meta-analysis of everolimus in heart transplant recipients
Vitte SH.sub: Hospital de Amor Nossa Senhora, Barretos (VITTE2026, 2026) · Department of Medicine, Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Campinas (2025–2026) · Atherosclerosis and Vascular Biology Laboratory (Aterolab), State University of Campinas (2022–2024)
story: Sofia Helena Vitte was first author of a 2026 meta-analysis in JHLT Open (VITTE2026) on everolimus after heart transplantation. Everolimus is a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTOR and is used to stop the immune system from attacking a new organ. A meta-analysis pools the numbers from many studies to get a clearer answer than any one study gives. This one pooled 60 studies with 1,786 heart transplant recipients.

Everolimus-based treatment slowed cardiac allograft vasculopathy, the narrowing of the transplanted heart's arteries that limits how long the new heart lasts, to about 57 percent of the risk seen without it. When doctors also reduced calcineurin inhibitors, older drugs that damage the kidneys, kidney function was clearly better. Deaths from any cause did not change, but side effects and stopping treatment were more common. This is evidence from transplant patients, pooled across studies of different designs.

PubMed shows Vitte's earlier work at the Atherosclerosis and Vascular Biology Laboratory of the State University of Campinas, on the Brazilian Diabetes Study of people with type 2 diabetes (2022 to 2024), and later at the Department of Medicine of the Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Campinas, including other meta-analyses on exercise after Fontan heart surgery (2025) and on preventing lung collapse after CT-guided lung biopsy (2026). The 2026 everolimus paper lists the Hospital de Amor Nossa Senhora in Barretos.
