highlights.VITTE2026: First author: led the meta-analysis of 60 studies showing that everolimus slows transplant artery disease and protects kidney function in heart recipients, without changing mortality.

Wagle N.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Wagle N.role: Medical oncologist and cancer genomics researcher at Dana-Farber who studies why some patients respond exceptionally well to targeted drugs, including a patient whose tumour carried two activating MTOR mutations
Wagle N.sub: Department of Medical Oncology and Center for Molecular Oncologic Pathology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (at the time of the study, 2014)
story: Most patients in early drug trials see little benefit, but now and then one patient responds far better than anyone else. Studying these 'exceptional responders' can reveal what makes a tumour sensitive. In WAG2014, Nikhil Wagle and colleagues sequenced the tumour of a patient who had an extraordinary response on a phase I trial of everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, combined with pazopanib. The tumour carried two activating mutations in the MTOR gene itself at the same time, which made it dependent on mTOR and so vulnerable to everolimus. Because it is a single patient, the finding generates a hypothesis; it does not show that MTOR mutations predict response in general.

At the time of the study Wagle worked in the Department of Medical Oncology and the Center for Molecular Oncologic Pathology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and at Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School. An official current profile could not be opened for this batch, so later positions are not described here.

highlights.WAG2014: First author: found two concurrent activating MTOR mutations in the tumour of a patient with an exceptional response to everolimus plus pazopanib.

Walter T.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Hospices Civils de Lyon (Lyon, France)
Walter T.role: Medical oncologist in Lyon who specialises in neuroendocrine tumours and led the COMPETE phase 3 trial comparing 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus
Walter T.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Lyon (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Neuroendocrine tumours of the gut and pancreas grow from hormone-making cells. Many carry receptors for the hormone somatostatin on their surface, which can be used to deliver radiation straight to the tumour: a somatostatin-like molecule is linked to a radioactive atom such as lutetium-177, an approach called peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, is a standard drug for these tumours. In WALTER2026, Thomas Walter was first author of COMPETE, a phase 3 randomised trial in 309 patients that compared 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus. Median progression-free survival was 23.9 months with the radioligand and 14.1 months with everolimus, and serious treatment-related side effects were less common (18 percent against 40 percent). The trial was open-label, so patients and doctors knew which treatment was given. For the mTOR field, the result means an mTOR inhibitor was the comparator that a newer therapy beat in this disease.
Walter works in the Department of Medical Oncology at Hôpital Édouard Herriot in Lyon. PubMed lists more than 140 papers under this name on neuroendocrine tumours with Lyon affiliations.

highlights.WALTER2026: First author: reported the COMPETE trial, in which 177Lu-edotreotide gave longer progression-free survival than everolimus with fewer severe side effects.

Wang Q.lab_name: Yang Lab, Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky (Lexington, Kentucky, USA)
Wang Q.role: Cancer biologist in Hsin-Sheng Yang's lab at the University of Kentucky who studies how the tumour suppressor Pdcd4 holds back mTORC2 signalling, protein synthesis and cancer cell invasion
Wang Q.sub: Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology and Markey Cancer Center, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky (Hsin-Sheng Yang lab, papers 2017–2026)
story: Cancer cells burn sugar fast, even when oxygen is plentiful, a habit called aerobic glycolysis. In the Atlas study WANG2026B in Neoplasia, Qing Wang was first author in Hsin-Sheng Yang's lab. The team showed in non-small cell lung cancer cells and in tumours grown in mice that the tumour suppressor Pdcd4 binds Rictor, the core partner of mTOR in the mTORC2 complex, through three positively charged amino acids (R105, K108 and R110). This binding breaks up mTORC2 and lowers its activity. Less mTORC2 means less PFKFB3, an enzyme that speeds up glycolysis, so the cancer cells use less sugar and grow more slowly. The work was done in cells and mouse xenografts.

Wang has worked with Yang in the Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology at the University of Kentucky for several years; PubMed lists 18 papers with both names and this address. Much of the work is on Pdcd4 in colorectal cancer. A 2025 first-author paper showed that Pdcd4 blocks translation of Slug, a protein that helps cancer cells invade, through the 5' untranslated region of its messenger RNA. A 2020 first-author paper found that blocking the IGF-1 receptor in colon cancer cells switches on MEK, a survival signal, which may explain why IGF-1 receptor drugs worked poorly in patients. No official profile page was found.

highlights.WANG2026B: First author: showed in lung cancer cells and xenografts that Pdcd4 binds Rictor, breaks up mTORC2, lowers PFKFB3 and slows glycolysis and tumour growth.

Piatkevich KD.lab_name: Piatkevich Lab, School of Life Sciences, Westlake University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Piatkevich KD.role: Protein engineer who designs fluorescent proteins and biosensors for imaging cells and brains, trained with Vladislav Verkhusha and Edward Boyden, now running a lab at Westlake University
Piatkevich KD.sub: Principal investigator, School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, Hangzhou (papers to 2026) · Media Lab, MIT (Edward Boyden lab, papers around 2018) · Department of Anatomy and Structural Biology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Vladislav Verkhusha lab, papers 2009–2014)
story: Most ways of measuring mTOR activity give a snapshot: you break open the cells at one moment and look. In the Atlas study WANG2026C, Piatkevich's lab built a fluorescent protein ticker tape, a set of self-assembling protein fibres that grow inside a cell and lay down fluorescent colour bands over time, like rings in a tree trunk. Each colour can be tied to the activity of a different signalling pathway, including mTOR, NF-kB, STAT3, NFAT and cAMP. Reading the bands later gives a history of each pathway in each single cell, in culture and in living animals.

Using the mTOR version, the team saw mTOR activity rise and fall in step with the cell division cycle. That supports the idea that mTOR signalling is dynamic, not a fixed on or off state, which is one of the Atlas's current themes. The recording was done in cells and animals, not in people.

On PubMed, Piatkevich's first papers (from 2009) come from Vladislav Verkhusha's lab at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York, on fluorescent timers that change colour as proteins age and on red fluorescent proteins with unusual colour properties. By 2018 the papers come from Edward Boyden's group at the MIT Media Lab, including Archon1, a fluorescent voltage reporter for imaging electrical activity in neurons, found with a robotic cell-picking screen. Recent papers come from Piatkevich's own group at the School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, in Hangzhou, on far-red fluorescent proteins and super-resolution imaging, and the Atlas paper also lists Zhejiang University.

highlights.WANG2026C: Senior author: led the development of the fluorescent protein ticker tape that records the history of mTOR and other pathways in single cells and showed mTOR activity oscillating with the cell cycle.

Zhang Xiaoxiao.lab_name: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University (Guangzhou, China)
Zhang Xiaoxiao.role: Eye specialist at Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital who works on childhood myopia, from school screening and myopia-control lenses to the biology of the sclera in animal models
Zhang Xiaoxiao.sub: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, affiliated with Jinan University (PubMed affiliation 2023–2026) · Optometry and Strabismus Department (2023)
story: Myopia (short-sightedness) usually happens because the eyeball grows too long. The sclera, the tough white outer wall of the eye, has to remodel for that to happen. Xiaoxiao Zhang was senior author of the 2026 FASEB Journal study in this Atlas (WEN2026), which used human scleral cells and guinea pigs whose eyes were covered to induce myopia. Too much autophagy in the sclera, the cell's recycling system, appeared to link low-oxygen stress to the remodelling. Rapamycin injected under the conjunctiva made the myopia worse, the autophagy blocker 3-MA eased it, and atropine eye drops slowed it. The team measured AMPK/mTOR/P70S6K signalling, but the paper does not show that this route causes the effect, and the results come from cells and animals, not children.

A companion 2026 paper from the same Guangzhou group, again with Zhang as last author, traced the low-oxygen signal one step further: in hypoxic scleral cells and in guinea pigs, the HIF-1alpha protein pushed cells towards glycolysis and lactate production, and blocking glycolysis reduced myopic eye growth.

Much of Zhang's other published work is clinical. PubMed lists papers from Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital on a vision screening of more than 170,000 primary school pupils in three Guangzhou districts (2025), on predicting eye growth in children wearing orthokeratology night lenses over six years (2025), on comparing two kinds of myopia-control spectacle lenses (2023), and on eyelid hygiene during orthokeratology (2026). The hospital is affiliated with Jinan University.

highlights.WEN2026: Senior author: led the guinea pig and scleral cell study linking excess scleral autophagy to myopia, in which rapamycin worsened and 3-MA eased experimental myopia.

Wu JJ.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Center for Molecular Medicine, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Wu JJ.role: Researcher in Toren Finkel's laboratory at the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and first author of the 2013 study showing that mice making only a quarter of the normal amount of mTOR live about 20 percent longer
Wu JJ.sub: Center for Molecular Medicine, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH (Toren Finkel lab, papers 2009–2013, at the time of the study)
story: Rapamycin lengthens the life of mice, but a drug can have side effects that muddy the picture. In the Atlas study WUX2013, Wu and colleagues in Toren Finkel's lab at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute took a genetic route instead. They bred mice that make only about 25 percent of the normal amount of mTOR protein. These mice lived about 20 percent longer on average: median lifespan was 28.0 versus 22.9 months in males and 31.5 versus 26.5 months in females.

The slowing of ageing was uneven, which is why the paper calls it segmental and tissue-specific. The mTOR-reduced mice kept better memory and balance in old age, but they lost more bone and were more prone to infection. For the Atlas this is a clean mouse experiment showing that turning mTOR down, not off, can extend life, and that the benefit does not reach every organ.

PubMed lists Wu on several papers with Finkel between 2009 and 2013, including work on Wnt signalling and liver glucose metabolism, and on two studies with Elizabeth Henske's group at Brigham and Women's Hospital on autophagy in tuberous sclerosis complex, a disease in which mTORC1 is overactive. Wu's current position could not be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.WUX2013: First author: led the study of mice engineered to make about a quarter of the normal amount of mTOR, which lived about 20 percent longer with a tissue-by-tissue pattern of slower ageing.

Xiao T.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Xiao T.role: Researcher at the Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study and first author of a 2026 review on how nutrient-sensing pathways steer adult stem cells through life
Xiao T.sub: School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (at the time of the study)
story: Tianxiong Xiao is first author of XIA2026, a review in Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology. It does not report new experiments. It pulls together evidence that four nutrient-sensing systems, mTOR, AMPK, the sirtuins and insulin/IGF-1 signaling, work as one network to decide what adult stem cells do: stay at rest (quiescence), wake up and divide, or turn into specialised cells. Adult stem cells keep tissues such as blood, muscle, gut and brain supplied with new cells, so this decision matters throughout life.

The review argues that with age the network drifts out of balance, for example with mTOR too active, which can wear stem cells out and add to tissue decline. Because it is a review, its framework is a proposal built on mostly animal and cell studies, and the Atlas treats it as a map of ideas rather than as evidence in its own right.

PubMed lists Xiao at the Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Hu C as senior author. No other papers could be tied to this person with confidence, and no profile page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.XIA2026: First author: wrote the review proposing that mTOR, AMPK, sirtuins and insulin/IGF-1 signaling form one network steering adult stem cell fate and ageing.

Xie J.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources, College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Tai'an, Shandong, China)
Xie J.role: Animal nutrition researcher in Ning Jiao's group at Shandong Agricultural University who studies how feed contaminants damage the pig gut, and first author of the piglet study on glutamine and bisphenol A
Xie J.sub: College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Ning Jiao group, papers 2026)
story: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial chemical found in some plastics that can reach animal feed. In the Atlas study XIE2026, Xie, Ning Jiao and colleagues fed piglets BPA and found damage to the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine. Adding the amino acid glutamine to the feed reduced the damage, helped the gut lining stay sealed and restored how the cells' mitochondria produce energy. These changes came with shifts in AMPK and mTOR signalling, the two linked sensors of cell energy and nutrients.
The study shows an association between glutamine, gut repair and AMPK-mTOR signalling in pigs. It does not prove that the mTOR change causes the protection, and it was not done in people.

PubMed lists Xie only in 2026, both times in Jiao's group at the Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources at Shandong Agricultural University in Tai'an. The second paper looked at how the mould toxin zearalenone and its hidden glucoside form harm pig intestinal cells. The career stage (student or staff) could not be confirmed.

highlights.XIE2026: First author: showed in piglets that glutamine reduced bisphenol A damage to the small intestine, with restored mitochondrial energy production and changes in AMPK-mTOR signalling.

Jiao N.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources, College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Tai'an, Shandong, China)
Jiao N.role: Animal nutrition scientist at Shandong Agricultural University who studies how feed contaminants such as mould toxins and bisphenol A harm pigs, and how nutrients like glutamine protect the gut
Jiao N.sub: College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (papers 2021–2026)
story: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial chemical found in some plastics that can reach animal feed. In the Atlas study XIE2026, Jiao's group, with first author Jiayuan Xie, fed piglets BPA and found damage to the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine. Adding the amino acid glutamine reduced the damage, kept the gut lining sealed and restored mitochondrial energy production, alongside changes in AMPK and mTOR signalling, the linked sensors of cell energy and nutrients. It is a pig study, and the mTOR change is an association rather than a proven cause.

PubMed lists Jiao as a corresponding author at Shandong Agricultural University on studies of pigs and pig cells since at least 2021. One line of work follows zearalenone, a mould toxin with oestrogen-like effects, from its impact on the ovaries of young female pigs (2021) to its toxicity in pig intestinal cells (2026). Another line asks whether glutamine protects piglets from BPA: a 2023 paper found that glutamine reduced BPA-driven gut inflammation and shifted the gut bacteria, and the Atlas study extends this to mitochondria and AMPK-mTOR.
Jiao works with Weiren Yang at the Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources in the College of Animal Science and Technology. Academic rank could not be confirmed.

highlights.XIE2026: Senior author: led the piglet study showing that glutamine eased bisphenol A damage to the small intestine, with changes in AMPK-mTOR signalling.

Xu J.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Xu J.role: Researcher in the orthopedics department of Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 review on mTORC2 and its partner RICTOR in immune cells and inflammatory disease
Xu J.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Most writing on mTOR is about mTORC1, the complex that drives growth. Jingting Xu's 2026 review in Inflammation Research, with Fengjing Guo as senior author, collects what is known about the second complex, mTORC2, and its defining partner RICTOR in the immune system. mTORC2 acts through the kinases AKT, SGK1 and PKC.

The review describes how mTORC2 shapes the choice between Th1 and Th2 helper T cells, keeps regulatory T cells stable, helps memory T cells form, and affects B-cell receptor signalling, plasma cell survival, and the behaviour of macrophages, dendritic cells and natural killer cells. In tissues its effect depends on context: it worsens inflammation in osteoarthritis and pancreatitis but restrains pro-inflammatory macrophages in colorectal cancer. Drugs that block both mTOR complexes, such as AZD2014, show early but complicated promise. The paper is a review of published work, not new data.

PubMed lists Jingting Xu at the Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

highlights.XU2026B: First author: wrote the review of mTORC2/RICTOR signalling across T cells, B cells and innate immune cells and its context-dependent role in inflammatory disease.

Guo F.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Guo F.role: Orthopedic researcher at Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and senior author of a 2026 review on how mTORC2 and RICTOR shape immune cells and inflammation
Guo F.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Fengjing Guo is the senior author of a 2026 review, led by Jingting Xu, on mTORC2, the less studied of the two mTOR complexes, and its essential partner RICTOR. mTORC2 passes its signals through the kinases AKT, SGK1 and PKC, and the review follows these signals through T cells, B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells and natural killer cells.

One theme of the review is relevant to an orthopedics department: mTORC2 signalling makes inflammation worse in osteoarthritis, the joint disease in which cartilage wears away, and in pancreatitis, yet it restrains pro-inflammatory macrophages in colorectal cancer. The authors conclude that dual mTORC1/2 inhibitors such as AZD2014 show early but complicated promise. The paper summarises published studies and adds no new experiments.

PubMed lists Guo at the Department of Orthopedics of Tongji Hospital, part of Tongji Medical College of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, where Guo has co-authored papers with Hongbo You, senior author of another osteoarthritis study in this Atlas. Career details could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.XU2026B: Senior author: supervised the review of mTORC2/RICTOR signalling in immune cells and its context-dependent role in inflammatory disease.

Yang HJ.lab_name: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Yang HJ.role: Researcher in Nikola Pavletich's structural biology laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering and co-author of the two Nature papers that showed the atomic structure of mTOR and of mTORC1
Yang HJ.sub: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (Pavletich laboratory, papers 2013 and 2017; at the time of the studies)
story: Hyo J Yang is a co-author of two structure papers from Nikola Pavletich's laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center that changed how mTOR is pictured. Structural biology works out the exact 3D shape of a protein, atom by atom, which shows how it does its job and how drugs fit into it.

The 2013 paper (YAN2013) solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, the part of the protein that adds phosphate groups to its targets. It showed that the active site sits in a deep, narrow cleft, guarded by a section called the FRB domain that acts like a gatekeeper for incoming target proteins. That explained why rapamycin, which binds the FRB domain together with its partner protein FKBP12, blocks mTOR by limiting access to the cleft, and why cancer-causing mutations cluster where they do. The 2017 paper (YAN2017) used cryo-electron microscopy, which images frozen protein complexes with an electron beam, to show the whole mTORC1 complex. It showed how the small protein RHEB, which signals growth, bends mTORC1 into its active shape, and how the inhibitor PRAS40 blocks it. Both papers describe purified proteins, not cells or animals.

These two papers are the only PubMed records for Yang with Pavletich, and no other publication or institutional page could be firmly tied to this name, which is common. The affiliation shown is the one on the papers. Hyo J Yang is a different person from Haijuan Yang, first author of both papers.

highlights.YAN2013: Co-author of the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, which showed the deep active-site cleft guarded by the FRB domain.
highlights.YAN2017: Co-author of the cryo-EM structures showing how RHEB switches mTORC1 on and how PRAS40 blocks it.

Li R.lab_name: Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Li R.role: Toxicologist at Central China Normal University in Wuhan who leads mouse studies of how early-life exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics and plastic additives harms the developing brain
Li R.sub: Key Laboratory of Pesticide and Chemical Biology of the Ministry of Education and Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University
story: Rui Li is the senior (last) author of YANG2026. Young children take in tiny plastic particles from bottles, toys and food containers, often together with DEHP, a chemical that makes plastic soft. In this study, young mice exposed to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP developed brain and behaviour changes that resemble features of autism spectrum disorder, including reduced social behaviour. In their brains mTOR was overactive and autophagy, the cell's recycling system that mTOR normally restrains, was impaired. Treating the mice with rapamycin restored autophagy and improved the social and behavioural problems. The work is in mice, so it shows a possible mechanism, not proof that plastic exposure causes autism in children.

PubMed lists Li as senior author of a series of papers from the School of Life Sciences at Central China Normal University on plastic pollution and the young brain. In 2023 the group reported that combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP caused memory problems, damage in the hippocampus and inflammation in young mice, through a long-lasting stress response in the protein-folding system. In 2025, in ACS Nano, the group showed that polystyrene nanoplastics disturb protein balance in the brain partly through changes in gut bacteria, with the sugar trehalose acting as a link between gut and brain.
Because Li is a very common surname, only papers from this Central China Normal University group were counted. No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given.

highlights.YANG2026: Senior author: led the mouse study linking early-life microplastic and DEHP exposure to mTOR overactivity, impaired autophagy and autism-like behaviour, which rapamycin reversed.

Yang G.lab_name: Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Yang G.role: Researcher in Rui Li's group at Central China Normal University who has led mouse studies on how microplastics, nanoplastics and the plasticiser DEHP affect the young brain
Yang G.sub: School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University, Rui Li group (first-author papers 2023, 2025 and 2026)
story: Ge Yang is the first author of YANG2026, which exposed young mice to polypropylene microplastics and the plastic softener DEHP. The mice developed changes resembling features of autism spectrum disorder. In their brains, mTOR was overactive and autophagy, the recycling process that keeps nerve cells healthy, was impaired. When the mice were given rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, autophagy recovered and the social and behavioural problems improved. Because the work is in mice, it points to a possible mechanism rather than a proven cause in children.

Yang has been first author of three papers from the same group. In 2023 the team showed that combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP caused memory deficits and damage in the hippocampus of young mice. In 2025, in ACS Nano, Yang and colleagues showed that polystyrene nanoplastics upset the balance of proteins in the brain partly through changes in gut bacteria, and that the sugar trehalose could ease this damage.
No official profile was found, so training and current position are given only from the publication record.

highlights.YANG2026: First author: showed in mice that early-life microplastic and DEHP exposure overactivates mTOR, impairs autophagy and causes autism-like behaviour that rapamycin reverses.

Yao JC.lab_name: Department of Gastrointestinal Medical Oncology, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas, USA)
Yao JC.role: Medical oncologist at MD Anderson Cancer Center who led the RADIANT-3 and RADIANT-4 trials that made the mTOR inhibitor everolimus a standard treatment for advanced neuroendocrine tumours
Yao JC.sub: Department of Gastrointestinal Medical Oncology, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston (papers 2011–2026)
story: Neuroendocrine tumours grow from hormone-making cells, for example in the pancreas, gut or lung. They often grow slowly, but once they spread they are hard to treat, and in many of them the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway is switched on. James Yao was first author of RADIANT-3 (YAO2011), a phase 3 trial in the New England Journal of Medicine that randomly assigned 410 patients with advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours to everolimus, an mTOR-blocking drug, or placebo. The time before the cancer grew again more than doubled, from a median of 4.6 months on placebo to 11.0 months on everolimus, and most side effects were mild. The result led to everolimus being approved for this cancer.

Yao then led RADIANT-4, published in the Lancet in 2016, which tested everolimus in 302 patients with non-functional neuroendocrine tumours of the lung or gastrointestinal tract. Median progression-free survival was 11.0 months with everolimus and 3.9 months with placebo. Together the two trials showed that blocking mTOR helps across neuroendocrine tumours from several organs, which is strong evidence from people that mTOR signalling drives these cancers.

PubMed lists Yao at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center throughout this work and, in 2026, in its Department of Gastrointestinal Medical Oncology, with more than 120 papers on neuroendocrine tumours.

highlights.YAO2011: First author of the RADIANT-3 trial showing that everolimus more than doubles progression-free survival in advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

Yin J.lab_name: School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China)
Yin J.role: Structural biologist at Tsinghua University who used cryo-electron microscopy to show how the human amino acid transporter PAT1 (SLC36A1) recognises and moves its cargo
Yin J.sub: State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology and Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Structural Biology, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (affiliation on PubMed papers)
story: Jian Yin is the first author of YIN2026, a structural study of PAT1 (also called SLC36A1), a human transporter that carries small amino acids across membranes together with protons. Earlier work by other groups had shown that PAT1 sits on lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, and helps move amino acids out of them, which affects how mTORC1, the cell's nutrient sensor, is switched on. Yin and colleagues used cryo-electron microscopy, a method that freezes proteins and images them with electrons, to see PAT1 empty and with different amino acids bound. The structures show that the transporter grips many different amino acids in a similar way. The study is about the shape and mechanism of the protein; the mTORC1 link comes from the earlier work.

PubMed lists Yin at Tsinghua University's School of Life Sciences on about a dozen structural papers on membrane transporters, most of them with M. Yang as senior author, from the State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology and the Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Structural Biology.
Because Yin is a common surname, only papers from this Tsinghua structural biology group were counted. No official profile was found, so training and position are not given.

highlights.YIN2026: First author: solved cryo-EM structures of the human proton-coupled amino acid transporter PAT1 (SLC36A1) with and without bound amino acids.

Yu J.lab_name: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (Tianjin, China)
Yu J.role: Anesthesiology researcher at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital and first author of a mouse study showing that breathing hydrogen gas protects memory after sepsis by calming mTOR in brain support cells
Yu J.sub: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital · Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can damage the brain, and survivors often have long-lasting problems with memory and thinking. In the Atlas study YU2026, Yu and colleagues used a mouse model of sepsis and looked at the medial prefrontal cortex, a brain region for planning and memory. mTOR was overactive there, and this stopped oligodendrocyte precursor cells from maturing into the cells that wrap nerve fibres in myelin, the insulation that speeds up signals. The mice lost myelin and did worse in a water maze memory test.

Breathing a high concentration of hydrogen gas lowered mTOR activity, restored oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin, and improved memory. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, had a similar protective effect, and a drug that switches mTOR on (NV-5138) was used to check the mechanism. For the Atlas, this is an example where too much mTOR activity is harmful in the brain. All of the work was done in mice.

Jiafeng Yu is listed in the Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and the Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology, in the group of Yang Yu and Yonghao Yu, which has studied hydrogen therapy in sepsis for several years. No other publication could be tied to this name with confidence.

highlights.YU2026: First author: showed in septic mice that mTOR overactivity blocks myelin repair in the prefrontal cortex and that hydrogen gas or rapamycin restores myelin and memory.

Yu Yang.lab_name: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (Tianjin, China)
Yu Yang.role: Anesthesiologist and researcher at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital who studies hydrogen gas as a treatment for sepsis and its brain damage, and co-senior author of the 2026 study linking hydrogen, mTOR and myelin repair
Yu Yang.sub: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital · Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (papers from at least 2020 to 2026)
story: Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can damage the brain, leaving survivors with memory problems. In the Atlas study YU2026, led by first author Jiafeng Yu with Yang Yu and Yonghao Yu as corresponding authors, septic mice had overactive mTOR in the medial prefrontal cortex. This kept oligodendrocyte precursor cells from maturing into the cells that make myelin, the insulation around nerve fibres, and the mice lost myelin and memory. Breathing high-concentration hydrogen gas lowered mTOR activity, restored myelin and improved memory; rapamycin had a similar effect. The work was done in mice.

Hydrogen gas is studied as a mild antioxidant and anti-inflammatory treatment. On PubMed, Yang Yu appears with Yonghao Yu in the Department of Anesthesiology at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital on earlier hydrogen studies in septic mice, including a 2020 paper showing that hydrogen protected the gut in severe sepsis through the Nrf2 pathway. Rank and training could not be confirmed.

highlights.YU2026: Co-senior (last) author: co-led the mouse study showing that hydrogen gas restores myelin and memory after sepsis by restraining mTOR in the prefrontal cortex.

Yu L.lab_name: Li Yu Lab, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China)
Yu L.role: Cell biologist at Tsinghua University who, as a postdoc at the NIH, found how cells end autophagy and rebuild their lysosomes, and whose own group later discovered the migrasome, a new organelle left behind by migrating cells
Yu L.sub: Professor, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (since 2008) · postdoc, Michael Lenardo lab, Laboratory of Immunology, NIAID, National Institutes of Health · PhD, Peking University
story: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system. During starvation the cell wraps parts of itself in membranes, delivers them to lysosomes (small acid-filled sacs full of digestive enzymes) and breaks them down for raw material. mTOR, the cell's growth controller, is switched off at the start of this process. Li Yu's 2010 Nature paper (YUX2010), done in rat kidney cells in Michael Lenardo's lab at the NIH, asked what happens next. During long starvation, the breakdown products switched mTOR back on. That renewed mTOR activity stopped autophagy and started a repair step the team called autophagic lysosome reformation: new lysosomes budded off from the used autolysosomes, so the cell got its digestive sacs back. The paper reported the same process in several other animal species.

The finding matters because it shows mTOR acting at both ends of autophagy. It is not only the switch that blocks autophagy when food is plentiful. It is also part of the signal that ends autophagy and restores the lysosome pool, which is why a drug that blocks mTOR for a long time can interfere with this recovery step.

Li Yu earned a PhD at Peking University and trained as a postdoc with Lenardo before joining the School of Life Sciences at Tsinghua University in 2008. His group kept working on later steps of autophagy, and in the early 2010s it discovered migrasomes, small vesicle-like structures that form on thin fibres at the back of a moving cell and are left behind when the fibres break. The lab now studies how migrasomes form and what they carry, including their role in delivering signalling molecules during zebrafish organ development.

highlights.YUX2010: First author: showed in rat kidney cells that mTOR is reactivated during prolonged starvation and that this ends autophagy and drives lysosome reformation.

Zeng H.lab_name: Zeng Lab, Division of Rheumatology, Department of Medicine, and Department of Immunology, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Zeng H.role: Immunologist at Mayo Clinic who studies how mTOR signalling and cell metabolism shape T cells in autoimmunity, and who showed as a postdoc that regulatory T cells need mTORC1 to work
Zeng H.sub: Division of Rheumatology, Department of Medicine, and Department of Immunology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester · postdoc, Hongbo Chi lab, Department of Immunology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis (at the time of the study)
story: Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, are the immune system's peacekeepers: they stop other immune cells from attacking the body's own tissues. It had been thought that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, mainly works against Tregs, because rapamycin can help them expand. In ZEN2013, Hu Zeng, working in Hongbo Chi's lab at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, showed in mice that the opposite is also true. When Raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, was removed only from Tregs, the cells lost their suppressive function and the mice developed severe inflammatory disease. mTORC1 was needed to switch on cholesterol and lipid production in Tregs, which they use to keep up their suppressive programme. The study showed that a single signalling hub can both restrain and support the same cell type, depending on context.

Zeng now runs a research group in the Division of Rheumatology and the Department of Immunology at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. The lab studies T cell metabolism and signalling in autoimmune disease, including, in a 2026 study, the immune profile of inflammatory arthritis caused by cancer immunotherapy drugs, which looked driven mainly by T cells rather than autoantibodies.

highlights.ZEN2013: First author: showed in mice that regulatory T cells lacking mTORC1 lose their suppressive function, linking mTORC1 to Treg lipid metabolism.

Li G.lab_name: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (Yantai, China)
Li G.role: Researcher at the College of Life Sciences, Yantai University, and senior author of a mouse study of the plant compound pungenin and hair regrowth
Li G.sub: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Androgenetic alopecia is the common pattern hair loss driven by male hormones. A hormone called DHT shrinks hair follicles, and the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT from testosterone. In the Atlas study ZHAI2026, Li's group, with first author Wencai Zhai, treated mice with DHT to cause hair loss and then applied pungenin, a compound found in plants, to the skin. Hair grew back faster, the follicles made less type II 5-alpha-reductase, and genes in the PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR pathway, which controls cell growth and survival, changed their activity in hair follicle cells.
The mTOR link in this study comes from gene activity measurements in mice, not from blocking or activating mTOR directly, so it shows association rather than cause. It has not been tested in people.
Gang Li is a very common name, and no other publication or official page could be tied to this person with confidence. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.ZHAI2026: Senior author: led the mouse study showing that pungenin on the skin sped hair regrowth in hormone-driven hair loss, with changes in PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR gene activity.

Zhai W.lab_name: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (Yantai, China)
Zhai W.role: Researcher at Yantai University and first author of a mouse study showing that the plant compound pungenin speeds hair regrowth in hormone-driven hair loss
Zhai W.sub: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (at the time of the study, 2026)

In the Atlas study ZHAI2026, Zhai and colleagues in Gang Li's group treated mice with DHT to cause hair loss, then applied pungenin, a plant compound, to the skin. This is the only PubMed record for Wencai Zhai at Yantai University; other papers under the initials Zhai W at Yantai belong to a different person. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.ZHAI2026: First author: ran the mouse experiments showing that pungenin on the skin sped hair regrowth, with lower 5-alpha-reductase and changes in PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR gene activity.

Zhang Jingyue.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Lanzhou University (Lanzhou, China)
Zhang Jingyue.role: Pharmacy researcher at Lanzhou University working with Wen Li on the chemistry and actions of traditional Chinese medicines, from extracting plant compounds to testing a herbal formula in breast cancer models
Zhang Jingyue.sub: School of Pharmacy, Lanzhou University (papers with Wen Li, 2024–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Jingyue Zhang was first author of a 2026 Atlas study on the Xingxiao Pill, a traditional Chinese herbal formula, in breast cancer models (ZHANG2026C). The pill slowed the growth of 4T1 mouse breast cancer cells in culture and of 4T1 tumours in mice. It lowered signalling along the ErbB3/PI3K/AKT/mTOR chain, a relay that carries growth signals from the cell surface down to mTOR, the cell's growth-control kinase, and it changed how the tumours used amino acids. Computer docking pointed to two of the pill's ingredients, cinnamic acid and palmitic acid, as compounds that can bind mTOR. All of this was done in mouse cells and mice, so it does not show an effect in patients.

Zhang's other papers from the School of Pharmacy at Lanzhou University, also with Wen Li as senior author, are on the chemistry side of plant medicines. A 2024 study in Food Chemistry, for example, built magnetic molecularly imprinted polymers, a kind of chemical trap shaped to fit one molecule, to pull the compound glabridin out of licorice waste left over from industrial processing.
No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the Lanzhou University affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.ZHANG2026C: First author: showed in 4T1 cells and mice that the Xingxiao Pill slows breast tumour growth with lower ErbB3/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling and changed amino acid metabolism.

Zhou N.lab_name: Department of Oncology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (Harbin, China)
Zhou N.role: Oncology researcher at the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University and first author of a 2026 study linking a DNA-demethylating enzyme to PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation in lung adenocarcinoma
Zhou N.sub: Department of Oncology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Genes can be silenced by methyl groups attached to their DNA, and enzymes called TET remove those marks to turn genes back on. Nan Zhou's 2026 study, with Y. Wang as senior author, found that in lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, TET1 strips the methyl marks from the control region of the MRPS17 gene. MRPS17 normally helps build the protein-making machinery inside mitochondria, and its overproduction in tumour cells switched on PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, a growth pathway, and made the cells divide, move and invade more.

Reducing MRPS17 pushed cancer cells into apoptosis, programmed cell death, and slowed tumour growth in cell culture and in animal experiments. The study ties an epigenetic switch to the mTOR growth pathway in one cancer type; it has not been tested in patients.
PubMed lists Nan Zhou at the Department of Oncology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

highlights.ZHOU2026: First author: showed that TET1-driven demethylation raises MRPS17 in lung adenocarcinoma, activating PI3K-AKT-mTOR and promoting tumour growth.

You H.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
You H.role: Orthopedic researcher at Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and senior author of a 2026 mouse study showing that the plant compound corilagin slows osteoarthritis by restoring cartilage-cell autophagy
You H.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: In osteoarthritis the cartilage that cushions joints slowly breaks down. Chondrocytes, the cells that maintain cartilage, depend on autophagy, their internal recycling system, and autophagy falls when PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling is too high. The 2026 study led by Ruijia Zhou, with Hongbo You as senior author, tested corilagin, a polyphenol found in several medicinal plants.

Corilagin lowered PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB signalling, the second being a main switch for inflammation. Chondrocytes recovered their autophagic flux and made more extracellular matrix, the material that gives cartilage its strength. In mice with surgically induced osteoarthritis (the DMM model, in which a knee ligament is cut to destabilise the joint), corilagin reduced cartilage erosion and lowered OARSI damage scores. These are cell and mouse results; corilagin has not been tested in people with osteoarthritis.

PubMed lists Hongbo You at the Department of Orthopedics of Tongji Hospital in Wuhan, where You has co-authored papers with Fengjing Guo, senior author of the Atlas review on mTORC2 in inflammation. Career details could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.ZHOU2026B: Senior author: led the study showing that corilagin restores chondrocyte autophagy by damping PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB, reducing cartilage damage in mouse osteoarthritis.

Zhou R.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Zhou R.role: Researcher in the orthopedics department of Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 study on corilagin, a plant polyphenol that protected mouse cartilage by restoring autophagy
Zhou R.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Ruijia Zhou's 2026 study, with Hongbo You as senior author, looked for a way to protect cartilage in osteoarthritis. Cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, need autophagy to clear damaged parts, and too much PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling holds autophagy back. Inflammation driven by NF-kappaB adds to the damage.

Corilagin, a polyphenol from several medicinal plants, damped both PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB in chondrocytes. Autophagy recovered and the cells produced more extracellular matrix, the tough material of cartilage. In mice whose knee joints were destabilised surgically (the DMM model), corilagin reduced cartilage erosion and joint damage scores. The results come from cells and mice only.

PubMed lists Ruijia Zhou at the Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

highlights.ZHOU2026B: First author: showed that corilagin restores chondrocyte autophagy and matrix synthesis via PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB inhibition and reduces cartilage erosion in mice.

Zinzalla V.role: Cell biologist who, in Michael Hall's Basel lab, found that mTORC2 is switched on by binding to ribosomes, and later moved to cancer pharmacology at Boehringer Ingelheim in Vienna
Zinzalla V.sub: Pharmacology and Translational Research, Boehringer Ingelheim RCV, Vienna (2017–2020, most recent confirmed affiliation) · postdoc, Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2008–2012) · University of Milano-Bicocca, Lilia Alberghina group (2005–2007)
story: mTORC2 controls the kinase Akt, but in 2011 it was not clear what switches mTORC2 on. Vittoria Zinzalla, as first author of a Cell paper with Michael Hall, used a genetic screen in yeast and then mammalian cells to find the answer: mTORC2 needs ribosomes, the protein-making machines of the cell. It needs the ribosomes themselves, not ongoing protein synthesis. Active mTORC2 sits on the ribosome, and insulin signalling through PI3K increases this binding. The authors proposed that this link lets mTORC2 respond to how ready a cell is to grow. Data from melanoma and colon cancer cells suggested this may matter in cancer. The work was done in yeast and cultured cells.

Zinzalla trained in yeast cell-cycle research at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy, in Lilia Alberghina's group. As first author in 2007, Zinzalla showed that rapamycin stops yeast cells before they copy their DNA partly by acting on the cell-cycle brake Sic1.

After Basel, Zinzalla moved to industry. PubMed lists Zinzalla at Boehringer Ingelheim RCV in Vienna, in pharmacology and translational research, on a 2017 Cell study that built a living biobank of breast cancer organoids and a 2020 study on switching off the BCL6 gene in lymphoma cells. Zinzalla's current role could not be confirmed.

highlights.ZIN2011: First author: showed that mTORC2 is activated by binding to ribosomes downstream of PI3K.

Bannister CA.lab_name: Human Data Sciences (Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom)
Bannister CA.role: Health data analyst from Craig Currie's group in Cardiff who works with UK primary care records, and first author of the 2014 comparison of survival in people with type 2 diabetes on metformin and people without diabetes
Bannister CA.sub: Human Data Sciences, Cardiff (PubMed affiliation, 2023) · Cochrane Institute of Primary Care and Public Health, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (papers 2013–2018)
story: Metformin is the most common first drug for type 2 diabetes, and it is being studied as a possible anti-ageing drug, partly because it acts on cell energy sensing that feeds into mTOR. In the Atlas study BAN2014, Bannister, Craig Currie and colleagues used UK primary care records to compare people with type 2 diabetes who started on metformin, people who started on a sulphonylurea, and matched people without diabetes. Those started on metformin had slightly longer median survival than the matched non-diabetic group, while those on sulphonylureas had shorter survival.

The study is observational. People prescribed metformin may differ from others in ways the records do not capture, and people who keep taking their medicine tend to be healthier in other ways too, so the result is consistent with a benefit but does not prove one.

On PubMed, Bannister's papers from 2013 to 2018 come from Cardiff University with Currie, using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, a large UK database of anonymised GP records. They include a 2013 study showing that a widely used heart risk calculator for diabetes overestimated risk. A 2023 paper lists Bannister at Human Data Sciences in Cardiff, a company working on an online platform that turns routine health records into disease statistics.

highlights.BAN2014: First author: analysed UK primary care records and found that people with type 2 diabetes started on metformin had slightly longer survival than matched people without diabetes.

Currie CJ.lab_name: Division of Population Medicine, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom)
Currie CJ.role: Pharmacoepidemiologist at Cardiff University who uses large UK primary care databases to study diabetes treatments and their long-term outcomes, and senior author of the 2014 metformin survival study
Currie CJ.sub: Division of Population Medicine, School of Medicine, Cardiff University · Human Data Sciences, Cardiff (PubMed affiliations, 2023) · Cochrane Institute of Primary Care and Public Health, Cardiff University (2013–2014)
story: In the Atlas study BAN2014, Currie's group, with first author Christian Bannister, used UK primary care records to compare people with type 2 diabetes who started on metformin or on a sulphonylurea with matched people without diabetes. People started on metformin had slightly longer median survival than the matched non-diabetic group, while those on sulphonylureas had shorter survival. Metformin acts on the cell's energy sensing, which feeds into mTOR, and is being studied as a possible anti-ageing drug.

The result is observational. Differences between the patients that the records do not capture, and the tendency of people who take their medicine to be healthier in other ways, could explain part of it. It is consistent with a benefit but does not prove one.

On PubMed, Currie is the senior author on a long line of studies from Cardiff University using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, a large database of anonymised GP records, on diabetes drugs, cardiovascular risk and survival. A 2023 paper lists him at both the Division of Population Medicine in Cardiff University's School of Medicine and Human Data Sciences in Cardiff, on a platform that produces disease statistics from routine health records almost in real time.

highlights.BAN2014: Senior author: led the UK records study comparing survival in people with type 2 diabetes on metformin or sulphonylurea with matched people without diabetes.

Ottina KA.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Ottina KA.role: Researcher in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute and HHMI at MIT who contributed to studies of the GATOR1 amino acid off-switch, mTORC1 feedback on growth-factor signalling, and cancer drug resistance
Ottina KA.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Howard Hughes Medical Institute, MIT Department of Biology, Sabatini lab (papers 2011–2014, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: Kathleen Ottina is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab. HSU2011 asked which proteins in a cell carry phosphate tags that depend on mTOR, the growth kinase. The team found that Grb10 is one of the proteins mTORC1 phosphorylates, and that Grb10 then damps signalling from insulin and growth factors through PI3K. This is a feedback loop: active mTORC1 turns down the signals that switch it on. The work was done in cultured cells.

BAR2013 found the off switch for the amino acid signal to mTORC1. A complex the lab named GATOR1 acts as a GAP for the Rag GTPases, a helper that makes these switch proteins turn themselves off when amino acids run low, while a second complex, GATOR2, opposes it. Some cancers carry mutations in GATOR1 genes; in those cell lines mTORC1 stayed on during amino acid starvation and the cells were very sensitive to rapamycin.

PubMed lists Ottina on two more papers from the same lab: a 2011 Genome Research RNAi screen for regulators of TORC1-S6K signalling in fruit-fly cells, and a 2014 Science Signaling study with Kris Wood's lab at Duke University that screened pathway-activating genes for those that let cancer cells survive targeted drugs, pointing to Notch1 in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer. There Ottina is listed at the Whitehead Institute and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the MIT Department of Biology. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.BAR2013: Co-author on the cell study that identified GATOR1 as a GAP that switches off the Rag GTPases, and mTORC1, when amino acids are scarce.
highlights.HSU2011: Co-author on the mTOR-dependent phosphoproteome study that identified Grb10 as an mTORC1 substrate mediating feedback inhibition of growth-factor signalling.

Campone M.lab_name: Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest (Saint-Herblain, France)
Campone M.role: Breast cancer oncologist and general director of the Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest, a co-investigator on the BOLERO-2 trial that brought everolimus into breast cancer care
Campone M.credit: Portrait: Persévérance, fonds de dotation de l'ICO
Campone M.sub: General Director, Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest · Professor of Medical Oncology, University of Angers · Head of Breast Cancer and Translational Research, ICO · Deputy President, Unicancer (since 2019) · MD with oncology certificate, University of Nantes (1998)
story: Mario Campone is a co-author on BOLERO-2, the phase 3 trial that showed mTOR matters in a common cancer. In 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer that had grown despite earlier hormone therapy, adding the mTOR blocker everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review, BAS2012). The idea behind it: cancers that escape hormone therapy often switch on mTOR, so blocking mTOR can restore control. The final report (PIC2014) found a median overall survival of 31.0 months with everolimus and 26.6 months without, a difference that was not statistically significant. Together the two papers show both the real benefit and its limit.

Campone qualified in medicine with a certificate in oncology at the University of Nantes in 1998, with training that included the Beatson Institute in Glasgow, and earned a doctorate in life and health sciences in 2010. story: Most breast cancers grow in response to the hormone estrogen, and hormone therapy is the main treatment. Over time many tumours stop responding, and part of that resistance runs through mTOR. BOLERO-2 (BAS2012) was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women whose hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor. Adding the mTOR inhibitor everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, 10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review. story: Julie St-Pierre is a co-author on two Atlas studies from McGill University about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and energy metabolism. The 2013 Cell Metabolism paper (MOR2013), led by Nahum Sonenberg's group, showed in cells that mTORC1 sets how many mitochondria a cell builds and how hard they work. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations. mTORC1 does this by releasing the brake that 4E-BP proteins put on the production of proteins the mitochondria need. This links the growth signal directly to the energy supply that growth needs.

The 2026 Journal of Endocrinology paper (BCH2026), from Vincent Giguère's group, is a mouse study. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, can cause fatty liver, and adding the antimalarial drug chloroquine made that fatty liver milder. The rescue depended on ERR-alpha, a nuclear receptor that switches on many energy metabolism genes; in mice without it, chloroquine did not help.

St-Pierre studied at Laval University in Quebec (BSc and MSc), earned a doctorate at the University of Cambridge in England, and did postdoctoral research in Europe and the United States, including at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. From 2008 to 2017 St-Pierre was on the faculty of McGill University, rising from assistant to full professor, and co-founded and co-led a metabolomics core facility there for eight years. Metabolomics measures hundreds of small molecules of metabolism at once and gives a snapshot of a cell's metabolic state. In 2018 St-Pierre was also a co-author on the McGill study of how ERR-alpha shapes fatty liver on a high-fat diet. The main research theme is how breast cancer cells change their metabolism, and how those changes can help tumours resist treatment.

In 2017 the University of Ottawa recruited St-Pierre to set up a similar metabolomics facility in its Faculty of Medicine, with a professorship in the Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology. St-Pierre became the university's Associate Vice-President, Research Support and Infrastructure in 2023, and took over as Vice-President, Research and Innovation in October 2024, first on an interim basis. The 2026 paper lists St-Pierre at both the Goodman Cancer Institute in Montreal and the University of Ottawa.

story: Fiona Menzies is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Rubinsztein's lab. As a postdoc at the University of Basel O'Kane helped develop enhancer trapping in Drosophila, a method for finding where and when genes are switched on in the fly. O'Kane is now Professor of Genetics in the Department of Genetics at Cambridge and a Fellow of Churchill College.

The O'Kane lab uses Drosophila to study the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a network of membrane tubes that runs along nerve axons. The group has linked several proteins that are mutated in hereditary spastic paraplegia, an inherited disease in which the longest nerve fibres slowly degenerate, to the formation of this axonal ER, and it images the network by light and electron microscopy.

highlights.KOR2011: Co-author on the paper showing that lysosome position inside the cell tunes mTORC1 activity and autophagy.

highlights.RAV2004: Co-author, providing fly genetics, on the paper showing that mTOR inhibition induces autophagy and reduces Huntington's disease toxicity in fly and mouse models.

Young LR.role: Lung physician-scientist who helped run the first sirolimus trials in lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) and now leads pulmonary medicine at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
Young LR.sub: Chief, Division of Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia · Professor of Pediatrics, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · Vanderbilt University (from 2011) · University of Cincinnati and Cincinnati Children's Hospital (fellowship and six years on faculty)
story: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare lung disease, almost only in women, in which abnormal muscle-like cells with an overactive mTOR pathway slowly fill the lungs with cysts. It can also occur in tuberous sclerosis complex, together with kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas. Lisa Young was a co-author of the two Cincinnati-led trials that first tested sirolimus (rapamycin) against these problems. In the 2008 trial (BIS2008), a year of sirolimus shrank kidney angiomyolipomas in patients with TSC or LAM, though they grew back after the drug stopped. The larger MILES trial (MCC2011) compared sirolimus with placebo in 89 women with LAM: lung function held steady on sirolimus while it kept falling on placebo, and the benefit faded once the drug was stopped. MILES led to sirolimus becoming the standard treatment for LAM.

Young studied at the University of Virginia, earned an MD at Duke University and trained there in both paediatrics and internal medicine. A double fellowship in paediatric pulmonology and adult pulmonary and critical care followed at Cincinnati Children's Hospital and the University of Cincinnati, where Young then spent six years on the faculty, the period of the two trials. In 2011 Young moved to Vanderbilt University and later to Philadelphia.

Young is now Chief of the Division of Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Professor of Pediatrics at the University of Pennsylvania. Research topics include LAM and other rare lung diseases such as Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome and neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia of infancy, as well as lung development, injury and repair.

highlights.BIS2008: Co-author of the Cincinnati trial showing that sirolimus shrinks kidney angiomyolipomas in TSC and LAM.
highlights.MCC2011: Co-author of the MILES trial, in which sirolimus stabilised lung function in women with LAM while it was taken.

Belousova E.role: Child neurologist and epilepsy specialist in Moscow who heads a department of psychoneurology and epileptology and has been a principal investigator in international drug trials for tuberous sclerosis complex
Belousova E.sub: Head, Department of Psychoneurology and Epileptology, Moscow Research Institute of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery (since 2003; at the institute since 1985) · Professor (2007) · Doctor of Medical Sciences (2004) · residency in child neurology, Leningrad · MD, Leningrad Pediatric Medical Institute (1980)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which a faulty TSC1 or TSC2 gene leaves mTOR permanently switched on. Children and adults with TSC grow benign tumours in many organs, including the brain and the kidneys, and most have epilepsy. Elena Belousova is a co-author of both large phase 3 trials of everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, in this disease. In EXIST-1 (FRA2013), 117 patients with brain tumours called subependymal giant cell astrocytomas took everolimus or placebo; the tumours shrank by at least half in 35 percent of patients on the drug and in none on placebo. In EXIST-2 (BIS2013), 118 patients with kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas took part; 42 percent on everolimus had a response, against none on placebo.

These were randomised, placebo-controlled trials in people, and they are among the clearest evidence that blocking mTOR works when a genetic fault is the cause of mTOR overactivity. That does not mean the same benefit applies to people without such a mutation.

Belousova trained in medicine at the Leningrad Pediatric Medical Institute, graduating in 1980, and completed a residency in child neurology in Leningrad. She has worked since 1985 at the Moscow Research Institute of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery and has headed its Department of Psychoneurology and Epileptology since 2003. Her doctoral thesis (2004) was on seizures and epilepsy in children with cerebral palsy, and she became a professor in 2007. Her work covers the diagnosis and treatment of childhood epilepsy, and she has been a principal investigator in international trials in tuberous sclerosis and in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. She was named Honored Physician of the Russian Federation in 2011.

highlights.BIS2013: Co-author of EXIST-2, the phase 3 trial in which everolimus shrank TSC-related kidney angiomyolipomas in 42 percent of patients versus none on placebo.
highlights.FRA2013: Co-author of EXIST-1, the phase 3 trial in which everolimus shrank TSC-related brain tumours in 35 percent of patients versus none on placebo.

Whittemore VH.role: Neuroscientist and NIH program director for epilepsy and ME/CFS research who spent over two decades working for patient organisations, including the Tuberous Sclerosis Alliance

story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which mTOR is stuck on, so benign tumours grow in the brain, kidneys and other organs. Vicky Whittemore is a co-author of EXIST-1 (FRA2013), the phase 3 randomised trial of everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, in 117 people with TSC-related brain tumours called subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. The tumours shrank by at least half in 35 percent of patients on everolimus and in none on placebo. The trial helped make everolimus a standard treatment for these tumours, and it is some of the cleanest evidence in people that blocking mTOR helps when a genetic fault drives it.

Whittemore trained as a neuroscientist: a PhD in anatomy at the University of Minnesota Medical School, postdoctoral work at the University of California, Irvine, and a Fogarty Fellowship at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, followed by a faculty position at the Miami Project to Cure Paralysis at the University of Miami. After her nephew was diagnosed with TSC she moved to patient-led research organisations and spent 23 years in that world, including at the Tuberous Sclerosis Alliance, the Genetic Alliance and CURE Epilepsy.

In August 2011 Whittemore joined the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke as a program director. She oversees grants on the basic mechanisms and genetic causes of epilepsy, including sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and has also overseen the NIH research portfolio on ME/CFS since 2013.

Stitt TN.role: Regeneron scientist who worked in David Glass and George Yancopoulos's muscle program on the 2001 papers showing that the Akt/mTOR pathway drives muscle growth and protects against muscle wasting
Stitt TN.sub: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Tarrytown, New York (affiliation on PubMed papers from the early 1990s to 2007)
story: Trevor Stitt is a co-author of two 2001 Atlas papers from Regeneron that made mTOR central to muscle biology. BOD2001 showed in living mice and rats that switching on Akt makes muscle fibres grow larger, that blocking mTOR with rapamycin stops this growth, and that active Akt can protect muscle from wasting (atrophy). ROM2001 showed in cultured muscle cells (myotubes) that the growth signal IGF-1 enlarges muscle cells through Akt and two branches below it, mTOR and GSK3. Together these papers explain why mTOR is the main switch linking growth signals and exercise to muscle size.

PubMed lists Stitt at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals in Tarrytown, New York, on 23 papers. The earlier ones come from Regeneron's work on growth factors and their receptors in the nervous system. In 1995, as first author in Cell, Stitt reported that the blood-clotting regulator protein S and the related protein Gas6 are the ligands for the Tyro3 and Axl receptor tyrosine kinases. Later papers stay with the muscle program led by David Glass, including a 2004 paper on how IGF-1 and Akt block the switching on of the atrophy enzymes MuRF1 and MAFbx, and a 2007 paper showing that MuRF1 breaks down myosin heavy chain, the main motor protein of muscle.
No official profile was found, so training and current position are not given.

highlights.BOD2001: Co-author on the in vivo study showing that Akt/mTOR signalling drives skeletal muscle hypertrophy and can prevent muscle atrophy.
highlights.ROM2001: Co-author on the cultured-myotube study showing that IGF-1 grows muscle cells through Akt and both its mTOR and GSK3 branches.

Pollizzi KN.role: Immunologist trained in Jonathan Powell's lab at Johns Hopkins who used gene deletions in mice to show how the two mTOR complexes push killer T cells toward effector or memory fates
Pollizzi KN.credit: Portrait: LinkedIn (same photo as JCI author interview)
Pollizzi KN.sub: Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Powell lab, 2011–2016; latest PubMed affiliation)
story: CD8 T cells are the immune system's killer cells. After an infection, most become short-lived effectors that attack, and a few become long-lived memory cells that guard against the next infection. Kristen Pollizzi's 2015 study in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, with Jonathan Powell as senior author, used mice whose T cells lacked Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor to separate the roles of the two mTOR complexes. With Tsc2 gone, mTORC1 stayed switched on: the cells burned glucose hard, made more of the killing molecules IFN-gamma, TNF and granzyme B, and controlled tumours better, but they ended up terminally differentiated, fewer in number after a month, and formed no memory. With Rheb gone, mTORC1 was off while mTORC2 still worked: these cells failed as effectors and kept memory-like features, yet they did not respond when the mice met the same antigen again, which the authors traced to defects in their metabolism.

The message is that mTOR activity tunes the balance between attack and memory, and that a T cell needs the right amount of each complex at the right time. That matters for vaccine design and for cancer treatments that rely on T cells. Pollizzi was also a co-author on the 2011 Nature Immunology paper from the same lab showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages.

PubMed lists 11 papers for Pollizzi between 2011 and 2016, all with the Powell group at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins. They include a 2015 PLoS One study showing that cell size after activation can be used to track mTOR activity and predict whether a T cell becomes an effector or a long-lived cell, and reviews on mTOR and T cell metabolism in Nature Reviews Immunology (2014) and Trends in Immunology (2015). No later publications or current position could be found.

highlights.POL2015: First author: used Tsc2, Rheb and Rictor deletion in T cells to show that constant mTORC1 drives glycolytic, terminally differentiated effectors with no memory, while loss of mTORC1 gives memory-like cells that still fail on rechallenge.
highlights.DEL2011: Co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively program distinct CD4 helper T-cell lineages.

Pollizzi KN.lab_name: Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Department of Oncology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)

Waickman AT.role: Immunologist who trained in Jonathan Powell's mTOR and T cell lab at Johns Hopkins and now studies human immune responses to dengue virus at SUNY Upstate Medical University
Waickman AT.credit: Portrait: The Waickman Lab, SUNY Upstate Medical University
Waickman AT.sub: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, SUNY Upstate Medical University (2025 Upstate news, 2026 PubMed affiliation) · Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Powell lab, around 2011–2016)
story: Adam Waickman appears in this Atlas on two papers from Jonathan Powell's laboratory at Johns Hopkins that split T cell decisions between the two mTOR complexes. The 2011 Nature Immunology paper showed that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages. The 2015 Journal of Clinical Investigation paper did the same for killer (CD8) T cells: constant mTORC1 activity, after deleting Tsc2, produced aggressive but short-lived effector cells with no memory, while removing mTORC1 activity by deleting Rheb gave memory-like cells that still responded poorly to a second encounter with the antigen.

In the same period Waickman co-authored a 2015 PLoS One study from the lab showing that, within one batch of freshly activated CD4 T cells, the larger cells with high mTOR activity become glycolytic effector cells, while the smaller cells with low mTOR activity tend to become long-lived cells and regulatory T cells, a pattern also seen in human T cells.

PubMed lists close to 70 papers under Waickman's name. The recent ones come from the Department of Microbiology and Immunology at SUNY Upstate Medical University in Syracuse and deal with human immunity to dengue virus, including a 2026 Lancet Microbe report on a first-in-human dengue serotype 4 challenge study run with the University of Maryland and the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research. In 2025 Upstate announced a 3.1 million dollar NIH grant for Waickman to study how a second dengue infection becomes life-threatening and to build tools for better dengue diagnosis, vaccines and patient care.

highlights.POL2015: Co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 activity drives effector CD8 T cells at the expense of memory.
highlights.DEL2011: Co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively program distinct CD4 helper T-cell lineages.

Waickman AT.lab_name: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, SUNY Upstate Medical University (Syracuse, New York, USA)

Ikenoue T.role: Gastroenterologist and cancer researcher at the University of Tokyo who trained in Kun-Liang Guan's mTOR lab and now builds mouse models of liver, bile duct and pancreatic cancer driven by the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway
Ikenoue T.sub: Associate Professor, Institute of Medical Science, University of Tokyo (grant records 2010–2022) · Assistant Professor, University of Tokyo Hospital (2012) · research fellow, Kun-Liang Guan lab, Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (papers 2006–2009)
story: mTOR works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 controls growth, and mTORC2 adds a phosphate group to the survival protein Akt. In 2006 it was still unclear which parts were essential for mTORC2. The Atlas study YAN2006, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at the University of Michigan, showed that a protein called Sin1 is one of them. Without Sin1, mTOR and its partner Rictor did not stay together, and the complex could not phosphorylate Akt. Tsuneo Ikenoue was one of the co-authors.

In the Guan lab Ikenoue worked on the same signalling network from several angles. A 2008 paper with Ken Inoki and Guan, with Ikenoue as first author, showed that the tumour suppressor PTEN carries an acetyl tag that changes which partner proteins it binds. Ikenoue also contributed to Michigan studies on mTOR in hypothalamic neurons that control appetite, on the TSC-mTOR pathway in resting T cells, and on Rictor and mTORC2 in blood stem cells and leukaemia.

Back in Japan, Ikenoue is an associate professor at the Institute of Medical Science of the University of Tokyo, according to national grant records that run to 2022. The grants cover gastroenterology and cancer genetics: genetically engineered mice in which Kras activation and loss of Pten cause bile duct cancer, autophagy in Kras-driven pancreatic cancer, and mutations that act through the PI3K-Akt-mTORC1 pathway.

highlights.YAN2006: Co-author of the Guan-lab study showing that Sin1 is required for mTORC2 to assemble and to phosphorylate Akt.
