Finan PM.role: Biochemist and drug-discovery leader who started the PI 3-kinase drug discovery program at Novartis and ran its Developmental and Molecular Pathways group in Cambridge, Massachusetts, before moving into life-science venture investing
Finan PM.sub: Managing Partner, Epidarex Capital (partner since 2014) · Chairman, Enterprise Therapeutics · Global Head of Respiratory Disease Area and UK Site Head, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research · Executive Director, Developmental and Molecular Pathways, Novartis (Cambridge, Massachusetts) · earlier at Cancer Research UK, Yamanouchi Research Institute and Karus Therapeutics · BSc and PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Leeds
story: Peter Finan is a co-author of two Atlas papers from a partnership between Brendan Manning's lab at Harvard and Novartis scientists in Cambridge, Massachusetts. DUV2010 asked what mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on besides protein synthesis. In mouse cells where mTORC1 is stuck in the on position (because the brake protein TSC2 is missing), the team measured thousands of genes and metabolites at once. mTORC1 turned on sugar breakdown (glycolysis), the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and the building of new fats, through the transcription factors HIF1alpha and SREBP. DIB2012 found TBC1D7, a third core protein in the TSC1-TSC2 complex that acts as the brake on mTORC1. Both studies were done in cultured cells.

Finan studied biochemistry and molecular biology at the University of Leeds, where he also did his PhD. He worked at Cancer Research UK, the Yamanouchi Research Institute (now part of Astellas) and Karus Therapeutics, where he was Head of Biology. At Novartis he started the company's PI 3-kinase drug discovery program, which works on the signalling enzymes that sit just upstream of mTOR, and received the Novartis Leading Scientist Award in 2007. As Executive Director of the Developmental and Molecular Pathways platform in Cambridge, Massachusetts, he led target discovery and early drug discovery across cancer, neuroscience, regenerative medicine and inflammation. PubMed lists him at Novartis on papers from the same years on autophagy, rapamycin resistance and chemical tools for the autophagy enzyme VPS34. He later headed the Respiratory Disease Area and the Novartis research site in the UK.

Finan joined the life-science investor Epidarex Capital in 2014 and was named a Managing Partner in July 2026. He chairs Enterprise Therapeutics and sits on the boards of several young biotech companies and of the UK BioIndustry Association.

highlights.DIB2012: Co-author from the Novartis side of the Harvard-Novartis team that identified TBC1D7 as the third core subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, the brake on mTORC1.
highlights.DUV2010: Co-author from Novartis on the study showing that active mTORC1 is enough to switch on glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and fat synthesis in cultured cells.

Murphy LO.role: Cell biologist who led autophagy and mTOR drug discovery at Novartis in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and is now Chief Scientific Officer of Casma Therapeutics, a company that develops drugs acting on the autophagy-lysosome system
Murphy LO.sub: Chief Scientific Officer, Casma Therapeutics · Senior Vice President, Biology, Casma Therapeutics (from 2018) · Entrepreneur-in-residence, Third Rock Ventures · drug discovery group leader, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts)
story: Leon Murphy is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Brendan Manning's Harvard lab and its Novartis collaborators. DUV2010 showed in cultured mouse cells that switching mTORC1, the growth-control complex, permanently on is enough to drive sugar breakdown, the pentose phosphate pathway and the making of new fats, through the transcription factors HIF1alpha and SREBP. DIB2012 added TBC1D7 as a third core part of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, the protein brake that keeps mTORC1 in check.

Murphy trained in biochemistry and cell biology. At the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, he led a drug discovery group working on autophagy, the cell's system for breaking down and recycling its own parts, and on metabolic disease. PubMed shows his main line of work there: why rapamycin switches on autophagy in some cell lines but not others, and how combining it with a second kind of mTOR inhibitor overcomes this (2011); orally available inhibitors of the autophagy enzyme VPS34 (2015); and a CRISPR screen that found TMEM41B as a new autophagy gene (2018).

In 2018 Murphy moved to Third Rock Ventures as an entrepreneur-in-residence and helped found Casma Therapeutics, first as Senior Vice President of Biology and now as Chief Scientific Officer. With Noboru Mizushima he wrote a 2020 review on how to measure autophagy properly, and Casma's recent papers with academic groups study the lysosomal ion channel TRPML1 as a drug target.

highlights.DUV2010: Co-author from Novartis on the map of the metabolic gene program that mTORC1 switches on in cultured cells.

Beckers J.role: Geneticist at Helmholtz Munich and the Technical University of Munich whose group at the Institute of Experimental Genetics runs gene-expression profiling for the German Mouse Clinic
Beckers J.sub: Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic, Helmholtz Munich · Chair of Experimental Genetics, Technical University of Munich, Freising · German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD)
story: Johannes Beckers is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Beckers works at the Institute of Experimental Genetics of Helmholtz Munich in Neuherberg, near Munich, and PubMed records also list the Chair of Experimental Genetics at the Technical University of Munich and the German Center for Diabetes Research. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. In both Atlas papers Beckers appears among the German Mouse Clinic authors. Beckers's own papers centre on measuring which genes are switched on in tissues, for example with Marion Horsch and Martin Irmler, and range from mouse genetics to the effects of air pollution on the lung, as in a 2026 study of wood-smoke aerosols.

highlights.EIS2016: Co-author from the German Mouse Clinic, which contributed phenotyping to the mouse spermidine study.
highlights.NEF2013: Co-author from the German Mouse Clinic on the broad phenotyping that showed rapamycin changes only a few ageing traits in mice.

Huynh T.lab_name: Zoghbi Lab, Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, Texas, USA)
Huynh T.role: Research associate at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston and co-author on a long run of papers from Andrea Ballabio's group on TFEB, the master switch for lysosome and autophagy genes, including the work that tied TFEB to mTOR, starvation and fat metabolism
Huynh T.sub: Research Associate, Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine (Zoghbi Lab) · co-author with the Ballabio, Settembre and Sardiello groups (2011–2026)
story: Cells keep themselves clean with lysosomes, small acid-filled bags that break down worn-out parts, and with autophagy, the process that delivers those parts to the lysosome. In 2011 Carmine Settembre, Andrea Ballabio and colleagues, with Tuong Huynh among the co-authors, showed that one transcription factor, TFEB, switches on a whole programme of autophagy and lysosome genes when cells are starved (SET2011). In that first paper TFEB was controlled by the kinase ERK2. The 2012 follow-up (SET2012) found the link to mTORC1, the growth-control complex that sits on the lysosome surface: when nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB and keeps it out of the nucleus, so the lysosome itself reports its state to the genes that build it.

The 2013 paper (SET2013) moved into living mice. Fasting switched on the TFEB gene in liver, muscle and kidney, and TFEB then boosted its own production in a feed-forward loop. In the liver it drove fat breakdown largely through PGC-1alpha and PPARalpha, and extra liver TFEB protected mice from diet-induced obesity. The most recent paper (FER2026) used kidney-specific mouse models to separate mTORC1 activity from TFEB/TFE3 activity and found that overactive mTORC1, not TFEB/TFE3 alone, is the main driver of kidney cysts and tumours in models of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex.

PubMed lists Tuong Huynh on about a dozen TFEB, lysosome and autophagy papers with the Ballabio, Settembre or Sardiello groups between 2011 and 2026. The early papers give no affiliation for this author; a 2020 paper and the 2026 kidney paper place Huynh at the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, and the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute of Texas Children's Hospital in Houston, where Ballabio's US laboratory is based. The Baylor College of Medicine staff directory lists Tuong B. Huynh as a Research Associate in the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, attached to the Zoghbi Lab.

highlights.SET2011: Co-author on the discovery that TFEB coordinates autophagy and lysosome genes during starvation.
highlights.SET2012: Co-author on the paper showing that mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of TFEB lets the lysosome signal its own state to the nucleus.
highlights.SET2013: Co-author on the mouse study showing that fasting turns on TFEB, which then drives its own gene and liver fat breakdown.
highlights.FER2026: Co-author on the kidney mouse models that identified mTORC1 overactivity as the main driver of cysts and tumours, with TFEB/TFE3 adding to it.

Shackelford DB.lab_name: Shackelford Lab, Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Shackelford DB.role: Cancer biologist at UCLA who studies lung tumours that have lost the LKB1 tumour suppressor, the upstream activator of AMPK, and who trained in Reuben Shaw's lab at the Salk Institute
Shackelford DB.sub: Associate Professor, Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and member, Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center · Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (Reuben Shaw lab, papers 2008–2013)
story: David Shackelford is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Reuben Shaw's lab at the Salk Institute that explain how AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, controls growth and recycling. GWI2008 found a second way AMPK shuts mTORC1 down. Besides activating the TSC2 brake, AMPK directly adds a phosphate group to Raptor, a core part of mTORC1, and this halts growth when energy runs low. EGA2010 showed that AMPK also adds phosphate groups to ULK1, the kinase that starts autophagy, which links low energy to the clearing of damaged mitochondria. Together the two papers describe a metabolic checkpoint: when fuel is short, the cell stops building and starts recycling.

The enzyme upstream of AMPK is LKB1, a tumour suppressor that is lost in many lung cancers. Shackelford's own work has followed that thread. A 2013 Cancer Cell paper from the Shaw lab, with Shackelford as first author, showed in mice that lung tumours lacking LKB1 respond to phenformin, a stronger relative of the diabetes drug metformin, because they cannot cope with the energy stress it causes.

At UCLA, Shackelford is an associate professor in pulmonary and critical care medicine. The lab uses genetically engineered mouse models of non-small cell lung cancer to study signalling and metabolism in tumours with KRAS and LKB1 mutations, tests compounds that selectively kill such tumours, and works on why LKB1-deficient tumours resist immune therapy. The American Lung Association has funded the lab through a Lung Cancer Discovery Award.

highlights.GWI2008: Co-author of the study showing that AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor to switch off mTORC1 when energy is low.
highlights.EGA2010: Co-author of the study showing that AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 to link energy sensing to autophagy and mitophagy.

Oppliger W.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Oppliger W.role: Long-serving Biozentrum researcher who worked for more than two decades in Basel labs, first on how proteins enter mitochondria and then on TOR signalling with Michael Hall
Oppliger W.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (about 2002–2014) · Biozentrum, University of Basel, Gottfried Schatz lab (1991–1997, mitochondrial protein import) · current position not confirmed
story: In 2012 Raul Duran and colleagues in Michael Hall's lab showed that glutaminolysis, the breakdown of the amino acid glutamine, switches on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Glutamine is turned into alpha-ketoglutarate, and this metabolite activates the Rag proteins that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, where it is switched on. The result linked a common nutrient to mTORC1 through a specific chemical step. It was shown in cultured cells. Wolfgang Oppliger is one of the co-authors.

Oppliger's name runs through Biozentrum papers for more than twenty years. In the 1990s, Oppliger co-authored studies from Gottfried Schatz's lab on how proteins made in the cytoplasm are imported into yeast mitochondria, including work on the mitochondrial processing protease (1991) and on how the import machines of the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes work together (1995).

From the early 2000s, Oppliger appears on TOR papers from Michael Hall's group: the 2002 Molecular Cell paper that described the two yeast TOR complexes, a 2005 study of how TOR complex 2 is organised, the 2011 Cell paper showing that mTORC2 is activated by ribosomes, and a 2014 mouse study showing that mTORC1 in the liver controls body temperature, movement and fat metabolism through the hormone FGF21. Oppliger's exact role and current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.DUR2012: Co-author: glutaminolysis activates Rag-mTORC1 signalling through alpha-ketoglutarate.

Astle CM.lab_name: Harrison Laboratory, The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA)
Astle CM.role: Long-time research associate of David Harrison at The Jackson Laboratory, with work on mouse blood stem cells and aging since the 1970s, and a co-author of the Interventions Testing Program papers that showed rapamycin extends mouse lifespan
Astle CM.sub: The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine (papers with David E. Harrison, 1976–2019)
story: C. Michael Astle is a co-author of five Atlas papers from the Interventions Testing Program (ITP) of the US National Institute on Aging. The ITP tests drugs and supplements for effects on lifespan in genetically mixed mice, running the same experiment at three sites (The Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan and UT Health San Antonio) so that a result has to hold up in all three. The 2009 Nature paper (HAR2009) showed that rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, extended lifespan even when started late in life at about 600 days of age. Later papers showed that the gain depends on dose and is larger in females (MIL2011, MIL2014), that acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol extend life mainly in males (HAR2014), and that resveratrol, green tea extract, curcumin and several other popular compounds did not change lifespan (STR2012). Publishing negative results was part of the programme's design. All of this is mouse work.

Astle has worked with David Harrison at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine, for decades. Their first joint PubMed paper, on immune-cell responses in mice, dates from 1976, and PubMed lists more than 50 papers by the two together. Their most recent joint paper in PubMed, from 2019, reported that adding glycine to the diet modestly extended lifespan in ITP mice. On that paper the name appears in full as C Michael Astle, at The Jackson Laboratory.

story: Kevin Flurkey is a co-author of four Atlas papers from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at once. The 2009 Nature paper (HAR2009) showed that rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, extended mouse lifespan even when it was started late in life. Follow-up papers showed that resveratrol and simvastatin did not extend life in the same experiment (MIL2011), that rapamycin's effect grows with dose and is larger in females (MIL2014), and that acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extend lifespan mainly in males (HAR2014). These are mouse results; whether they carry over to people is still open.

Flurkey's PubMed record goes back to 1982, with a paper with Caleb Finch on how levels of the reproductive hormones LH, progesterone and prolactin change with age in female C57BL/6J mice. At The Jackson Laboratory, Flurkey has worked on mouse aging with David Harrison's group, including the ITP studies and, more recently, genetic studies of lifespan in Diversity Outbred mice, a genetically mixed mouse population. A 2025 paper in Genetics, with Gary Churchill's group and Calico Life Sciences, combined three such studies with 2,444 mice and found eight regions of the genome that affect lifespan.

Nadon NL.lab_name: Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Nadon NL.role: Scientist and programme official at the US National Institute on Aging who oversaw research resources for aging biology and helped run the Interventions Testing Program that found rapamycin extends mouse lifespan
Nadon NL.credit: Portrait: NIH Office of Research on Women's Health (video still)
Nadon NL.sub: Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging (at the time of the studies) · Chief, Biological Resources Branch (listed 2013) · earlier research at NINDS, NIH, on myelin genetics (1990)
story: Nancy Nadon appears in this Atlas as a co-author on five reports from the Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which the National Institute on Aging (NIA) funds to test possible anti-aging drugs in mice. The ITP runs each test at three sites at once, in genetically mixed mice, so that a result is less likely to be a quirk of one lab or one mouse strain. The most famous result is HAR2009: rapamycin, which blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, extended lifespan in both sexes even when feeding started late in life. Later reports showed the gain depends on dose and is larger in females (MIL2014), and that resveratrol, simvastatin, green tea extract, curcumin and several other popular compounds did not extend lifespan (MIL2011, STR2012). Acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA did, mostly in males (HAR2014).

Nadon's role was on the funding and organising side. An archived NIA page from 2013 lists Nadon as Chief of the Biological Resources Branch in the Division of Aging Biology, responsible for resource contracts and aged animal resources. Nadon wrote a 2006 review on how to design rodent lifespan studies, describing the problems the ITP had to solve, and was first author of a 2016 overview of the programme with the three site leaders.

Earlier, Nadon did laboratory research. A 1990 paper from NINDS at the NIH, as first author, traced a point mutation in a myelin protein gene that blocks the development of oligodendrocytes, the cells that insulate nerve fibres. The latest PubMed papers date from 2016 to 2018, and no current position could be confirmed.

highlights.HAR2009: Co-author from the NIA, which funds and coordinates the ITP: rapamycin fed from 600 days of age extended mouse lifespan in both sexes.
highlights.MIL2011: Co-author from the NIA: in the same ITP design, rapamycin extended lifespan while resveratrol and simvastatin did not.
highlights.STR2012: Co-author from the NIA on the ITP report in which five popular longevity compounds had no significant effect on lifespan.
