Sharp ZD.lab_name: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Biotechnology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Sharp ZD.role: Molecular biologist at UT Health San Antonio who works on rapamycin and aging in mice, from the Interventions Testing Program lifespan studies to cancer prevention in tumour-prone mice
Sharp ZD.sub: Department of Molecular Medicine and Institute of Biotechnology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · Mays Cancer Center (PubMed affiliations to 2023)
story: Zelton Dave Sharp is a co-author of three Interventions Testing Program (ITP) papers in this Atlas. The ITP, funded by the US National Institute on Aging, tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at once, so a result has to hold up in different labs. In HAR2009, rapamycin added to food from 600 days of age, already late in a mouse's life, extended both median and maximum lifespan in males and females. MIL2011 showed in the same design that rapamycin raised median lifespan by 10 to 18 percent while resveratrol and simvastatin had no effect. MIL2014 found that the gain depends on dose, is larger in females, and works differently from dietary restriction. These were the first convincing drug results for lifespan in mammals, but they are mouse results.

Sharp's own papers follow the same drug. As senior author, Sharp showed in 2013 that rapamycin lengthens the life of mice carrying one faulty copy of the Rb1 tumour suppressor gene by holding back their neuroendocrine tumours, and in 2016 described how mice adapt to long-term rapamycin. Sharp also co-authored a 2019 study linking mTORC1 to muscle fibre damage with age, and in 2023 was first author of a review in Experimental Gerontology calling rapamycin the only drug consistently shown to increase mammalian lifespan.

PubMed lists Sharp in the Department of Molecular Medicine and the Institute of Biotechnology at UT Health San Antonio, with links to the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and the Mays Cancer Center.

highlights.HAR2009: Co-author of the ITP study showing that rapamycin started late in life extends lifespan in both sexes.
highlights.MIL2011: Co-author: rapamycin extended lifespan in the same experiment in which resveratrol and simvastatin did not.
highlights.MIL2014: Co-author: the lifespan gain from rapamycin depends on dose, is larger in females and differs from dietary restriction.

Birsoy K.lab_name: Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, The Rockefeller University (New York, New York, USA)
Birsoy K.role: Cancer metabolism researcher who trained with Jeffrey Friedman and David Sabatini and now heads the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics at The Rockefeller University, using genetic screens to find how cancer cells rewire their metabolism
Birsoy K.sub: Associate Professor and head of the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, The Rockefeller University (title as of 2023) · Postdoc, David Sabatini laboratory, Whitehead Institute and MIT (papers 2012–2015) · PhD, The Rockefeller University, Jeffrey Friedman laboratory
story: Kivanç Birsoy is a co-author of two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute. The 2012 Nature paper (YIL2012) showed in mice that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells, the cells that sit next to intestinal stem cells and support them. With less mTORC1, Paneth cells send signals that make the neighbouring stem cells more numerous and more active. The 2014 Cancer Discovery paper (GRA2014) went through MTOR mutations found in human cancers, identified 33 that switch the pathway on, and showed that cancer cells carrying them were more sensitive to rapamycin in cell culture and in mouse tumour grafts. That suggests the mutations could help pick patients who might respond to mTOR inhibitors.

Birsoy did a PhD at The Rockefeller University in the laboratory of Jeffrey Friedman, the discoverer of the fat hormone leptin, and then joined David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute as a postdoctoral fellow. Birsoy's own first-author work there was on cell metabolism. A 2015 Cell paper used a CRISPR screen to find genes that cells need when their mitochondria are blocked by the drug phenformin. It showed that one essential job of the mitochondrial electron transport chain in dividing cells is to let them make the amino acid aspartate, and that cells without a working chain can grow if they get extra aspartate.

Birsoy returned to Rockefeller to lead the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, and a 2023 profile lists the title as associate professor. The lab studies how cancer cells reprogram metabolic pathways, especially oxidative metabolism, using unbiased genetic screens together with large-scale measurements of metabolites and proteins. A 2026 paper in Cell Chemical Biology, for example, used CRISPR screens to identify TXNDC15 as a missing part of the system that removes faulty proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, with effects on lipid balance.

highlights.GRA2014: Co-author of the study showing that many cancer-associated MTOR mutations switch the pathway on and predict rapamycin sensitivity.
highlights.YIL2012: Co-author of the mouse study showing that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 in Paneth cells and so boosts the neighbouring intestinal stem cells.

Cornu M.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Cornu M.role: Physiologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed in mice that mTORC1 in the liver controls body temperature, movement and fat metabolism through the hormone FGF21
Cornu M.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2012–2018, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Center for Integrative Genomics, University of Lausanne (2014) · current position not confirmed
story: Marion Cornu is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Michael Hall's lab. In the first (2012), mice lacking rictor, the core subunit of mTORC2, only in the liver could not sense that they had eaten. Their livers kept making glucose and made less fat, and the animals had high blood sugar and insulin. Restoring the kinase Akt fixed both problems, which placed Akt as the main route from liver mTORC2 to these outputs. In the second (2013), a large-scale measurement of phosphorylated proteins in cells showed that mTORC1 turns on the production of pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA.

Cornu's own first-author work looked at the opposite case, too much mTORC1 in the liver. In a 2014 PNAS study the team removed TSC1, a brake on mTORC1, from mouse liver. The mice moved less, had lower body temperature and less liver fat. Constant mTORC1 activity drained glutamine from the liver and blood and drove production of the hormone FGF21, which acted on the whole body. With Hall, Cornu also wrote a 2013 review on mTOR in aging, metabolism and cancer.

PubMed also lists Cornu in 2014 at the Center for Integrative Genomics of the University of Lausanne, on a study of insulin-producing beta cells, and in Basel on a 2018 Nature paper identifying the enzyme LHPP as a tumour suppressor in liver cancer. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HAG2012: Co-author: liver-specific loss of mTORC2 left mice unable to switch the liver to fed-state metabolism.
highlights.ROB2013: Co-author: phosphoproteomics showed that mTORC1 activates de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Cybulski N.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Cybulski N.role: Cell biologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed that mTORC2 in fat tissue helps control how big the whole body grows
Cybulski N.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2008–2014, most recent confirmed affiliation) · PhD, University of Basel (2010, with Michael N. Hall) · later address in Montreal, Canada (2014) · current position not confirmed
story: Nadine Cybulski is a co-author of two Atlas mouse studies from Michael Hall's lab. In 2008, mice lacking raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, only in fat tissue stayed lean, resisted diet-induced obesity and burned more energy in their fat. In 2012, mice lacking rictor, the core of mTORC2, only in the liver could not switch the liver to its fed-state programme, so it kept making glucose and made less fat. Both are mouse results.

Cybulski did a PhD in Hall's lab at the Biozentrum. The thesis, "New insights into the 'in vivo' and 'in vitro' functions of mammalian TOR complex 2", was accepted by the University of Basel in 2010, supervised by Hall with Markus Ruegg as co-referee. Cybulski's main paper, as first author in PNAS in 2009, removed rictor from fat tissue. The mice grew larger overall, with bigger organs such as heart, kidney and bone. The mice had high insulin and raised levels of the growth factor IGF1 and its partner protein IGFBP3. The study showed that mTORC2 in fat tissue acts as a brake on growth of the whole body. With Hall, Cybulski also wrote a 2009 review, "TOR complex 2: a signaling pathway of its own", and described mouse cells in which raptor or rictor can be switched off on demand, a tool used by many labs.

Cybulski also co-authored studies with Oded Meyuhas's group in Jerusalem on how mTOR controls translation of a class of messenger RNAs called TOP mRNAs. A 2014 paper gives a later address in Montreal, Canada. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HAG2012: Co-author: liver-specific loss of mTORC2 caused high blood sugar and insulin in mice.
highlights.POL2008: Co-author: fat-specific loss of raptor gave lean mice with more energy use in their fat.

Hidayat S.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Hidayat S.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and worked out how mTOR senses amino acids, and first author of a study showing that a leucine derivative can block amino acid-mTOR signalling
Hidayat S.credit: Portrait: Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Brawijaya
Hidayat S.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: In 2002 two teams, one in Boston and one in Kobe, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Sujuti Hidayat is a co-author of the Kobe paper in Cell (HARA2002). It showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase, two proteins that control protein synthesis, and that silencing raptor in the worm C. elegans mimics loss of TOR. Hidayat is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003) showing that raptor holds these targets through a short TOS motif.

Hidayat's own first-author paper from the same group, published in 2003, tested a chemical cousin of the amino acid leucine. It blocked the amino acid signal to mTOR in human Jurkat cells, a line of immune cells, and stopped them in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. That study lists Hidayat at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University.

PubMed records place Hidayat in the Yonezawa group from 2000 to 2006, on papers about the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work (2000), about how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway (2006), and about the two motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor (2006). A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author: part of the Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and showed it is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase.
highlights.NOJ2003: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that raptor binds mTOR substrates through their TOS motif.

Tokunaga C.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Tokunaga C.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor, and first author of a 2004 review on how mTOR combines amino acid and energy signals
Tokunaga C.sub: Assistant professor (joshu), Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (KAKEN record 2002–2004), Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: Chiharu Tokunaga is a co-author of the 2002 Cell paper from Kobe University (HARA2002) that, together with a Boston study in the same issue, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The Kobe team showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase and that silencing raptor in worms mimics loss of TOR. Tokunaga is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003), which found that raptor holds these two targets through a short TOS motif and so presents them to the kinase.

In 2004 Tokunaga was first author, with Ken-ichi Yoshino and Kazuyoshi Yonezawa, of a review in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications explaining how mTOR brings together two kinds of information, whether amino acids are available and whether the cell has enough energy. PubMed lists Tokunaga at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University on that review.

Other PubMed records from the same group, from 2000 to 2006, include work on the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work, on a leucine derivative that blocks amino acid signalling to mTOR, on how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway, and on the motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor.

Japan's national research grant database (KAKEN) lists Tokunaga as an assistant professor at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University from 2002 to 2004, with grants on the crosstalk between mTOR, which senses nutrients, and AMPK, which senses the cell's energy level. The record lists no later affiliation, so a current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author: part of the Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and showed it is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase.
highlights.NOJ2003: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that raptor binds mTOR substrates through their TOS motif.

Baur JA.lab_name: Baur Lab, Department of Physiology and Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Baur JA.role: Biologist of aging at the University of Pennsylvania whose lab showed that rapamycin's harm to glucose control comes from mTORC2 loss and studies how NAD levels shape health
Baur JA.sub: Professor of Physiology, Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · postdoc, Paul F. Glenn Laboratories, Harvard Medical School (David Sinclair lab, 2006 paper) · PhD research, Department of Cell Biology, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Woodring Wright and Jerry Shay, 2001 paper)
story: Joseph Baur is senior author of an Atlas study (LAM2012) that solved a puzzle about rapamycin. The drug lengthens life in mice, yet long-term use makes them glucose intolerant and insulin resistant, which looks like early diabetes. The team showed that chronic rapamycin, at doses close to those that extend lifespan, gradually disrupts a second mTOR complex, mTORC2, and that loss of mTORC2 in the liver explains the insulin problem: the liver keeps making glucose when it should stop. Mice with genetically lowered mTORC1 activity lived longer with normal glucose handling. So the longevity benefit and the metabolic side effect can be separated, which opened the search for drugs that hit only mTORC1.

Baur did PhD research in the Department of Cell Biology at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas with Woodring Wright and Jerry Shay, showing in 2001 that genes near telomeres, the ends of chromosomes, are silenced in human cells depending on telomere length. As a postdoc at Harvard Medical School in David Sinclair's lab, Baur was first author of the 2006 Nature paper showing that resveratrol improved health and survival of mice on a high-calorie diet.

Today Baur is professor of physiology at the Perelman School of Medicine and the Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism at the University of Pennsylvania. The lab studies basic mechanisms of aging with two main lines. One is NAD, a molecule every cell needs for energy metabolism; the lab identified SLC25A51 as the transporter that carries NAD into mitochondria. The other is rapamycin, where the lab works to separate its longevity effects from side effects, including showing that its effect on blood fats involves loss of mTORC1 signaling in fat cells.

highlights.LAM2012: Senior author: led the work showing that chronic rapamycin causes insulin resistance through mTORC2 loss, separable from its lifespan benefit.

Jørgensen JO.lab_name: Department of Clinical Medicine (Hormone and Bone Diseases), Aarhus University, and Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (Aarhus, Denmark)
Jørgensen JO.role: Clinical professor of endocrinology at Aarhus University who studies growth hormone, the pituitary and adrenal glands and metabolism in people, and senior author of a trial showing that high-dose resveratrol did not improve metabolism in obese men
Jørgensen JO.sub: Clinical Professor, Department of Clinical Medicine (Hormone and Bone Diseases), Aarhus University · Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital
story: Jens Otto Lunde Jørgensen is the senior author of the Atlas study POU2013, with Morten Møller Poulsen as first author. Resveratrol, a compound from grape skins, had looked promising in rodents, where it seemed to copy some effects of calorie restriction. The Aarhus team tested it properly in people: obese men took a high dose or a placebo for four weeks, and the researchers measured insulin sensitivity, how the body burned fuel, blood pressure and body composition.

None of these changed with resveratrol. The trial was short and small, but it was carefully controlled, and it showed that the rodent results did not carry over to this group of people. A later trial from the same Aarhus groups, with Jørgensen as a co-author, found no benefit of resveratrol in the metabolic syndrome either (2017).

Jørgensen's main research line is growth hormone, the pituitary hormone that drives growth in children and shapes fat, muscle and sugar metabolism in adults. The group studies how the hormone acts in muscle and fat, including in people with acromegaly, the condition caused by too much growth hormone. Recent papers show that excess growth hormone causes reversible scarring (fibrosis) in muscle and fat of patients with acromegaly (2026) and compare methods for measuring body composition in acromegaly (2025). A 2014 study from the resveratrol trial examined growth hormone signalling in muscle and fat of obese people.

Jørgensen is a clinical professor (klinisk lærestolsprofessor) in the Department of Clinical Medicine at Aarhus University, in the unit for hormone and bone diseases. The university profile describes research on hormones and metabolism, especially diseases of the pituitary and adrenal glands, with both clinical studies in patients and laboratory work.

highlights.POU2013: Senior author: led the randomised trial in which four weeks of high-dose resveratrol did not change insulin sensitivity, blood pressure or body composition in obese men.

Parmigiani A.lab_name: Budanov Lab, Department of Human and Molecular Genetics, Virginia Commonwealth University (Richmond, Virginia, USA)
Parmigiani A.role: Molecular biologist who worked in Andrei Budanov's lab at Virginia Commonwealth University on Sestrins, stress-induced proteins that hold back mTORC1
Parmigiani A.sub: Department of Human and Molecular Genetics, Goodwin Research Laboratories, Massey Cancer Center, Virginia Commonwealth University (papers with Andrei Budanov, 2014–2019, at the time of the study)
story: Sestrins are proteins that cells make when they are under stress, for example after DNA damage, and they help switch off mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In PAR2014, Anita Parmigiani and colleagues in Andrei Budanov's lab showed in cultured cells how this works. Sestrins bind to GATOR2, a protein complex that normally helps turn mTORC1 on at the lysosome when amino acids are present. By holding GATOR2 back, Sestrins keep the Rag proteins in their inactive state, so mTORC1 cannot be recruited and switched on. The study helped place Sestrins inside the amino acid sensing pathway that controls mTORC1.

Parmigiani published with the Budanov group at Virginia Commonwealth University from 2014 to 2019, on Sestrins and their links to p53, mTORC1 and mTORC2. In a 2019 study of mouse lung cancer and human lung cancer cells, the group found that losing Sestrin2 sped up early tumour growth through AKT, while Sestrins could also slow later stages when nutrients are scarce. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.PAR2014: First author: showed in cultured cells that Sestrins inhibit mTORC1 by acting on the GATOR2 complex.

Lindquist RA.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Lindquist RA.role: Researcher in David Sabatini's group at the Whitehead Institute who ran large image-based RNAi screens for regulators of TORC1 signaling and helped build the CellProfiler image-analysis software
Lindquist RA.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, Sabatini lab (papers 2006–2011, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: Robert Lindquist is a co-author on two cell-biology papers from David Sabatini's lab that changed how the field thinks about mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2007 paper (SAN2007) found PRAS40, a brake that sits inside mTORC1. When insulin is missing, PRAS40 holds the complex back. Insulin switches on the kinase Akt, Akt tags PRAS40 with a phosphate, and the brake lets go. This helped explain how a hormone sets how strongly mTORC1 works.

The 2008 paper (SAN2008) answered a different question: how does mTORC1 know that amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are available? The answer was the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bind raptor, part of mTORC1. When amino acids are present, the Rags bring mTORC1 to the place in the cell where its activator Rheb sits. Both findings come from experiments in cultured cells.

Lindquist's own line of work in the lab was screening technology. He is first author of a 2011 Genome Research paper that knocked down genes one by one in fruit-fly cells grown on printed microarrays and read the effect on TORC1-S6K signaling by microscope, which found new regulators of the pathway. He was also a co-author of the 2006 Genome Biology paper describing CellProfiler, open-source software that measures cell features in microscope images, and of the 2008 follow-up CellProfiler Analyst. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.SAN2008: Co-author on the cell study showing that the Rag GTPases bind raptor and tell mTORC1 that amino acids are present.
highlights.SAN2007: Co-author on the cell study that identified PRAS40 as an insulin-controlled brake inside mTORC1.

Medina DL.lab_name: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) and Department of Translational Medical Science, University of Naples Federico II (Pozzuoli, Campania, Italy)
Medina DL.role: Cell biologist at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine in Naples who showed how TFEB, the master switch for lysosome genes, is controlled by calcium released from lysosomes, and who works on lysosomal storage diseases
Medina DL.credit: Portrait: TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine)
Medina DL.sub: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli · Department of Translational Medical Science, University of Naples Federico II (papers 2011–2026)
story: Diego Medina is a co-author of the 2012 EMBO Journal paper from Andrea Ballabio's group at TIGEM (SET2012) that showed how the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, talks to the nucleus. When nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1, the growth-control complex, sits on the lysosome surface and adds a phosphate group to the transcription factor TFEB, which keeps TFEB outside the nucleus. When mTORC1 is blocked, when the cell is starved, or when lysosomes are under stress, TFEB moves into the nucleus and switches on genes for new lysosomes and for autophagy. The study was done in cultured cells and gave a simple explanation of how cells match their recycling capacity to their needs.

Medina's own first-author papers fill in other parts of the TFEB story. A 2011 Developmental Cell paper showed that TFEB also drives lysosomal exocytosis, in which lysosomes fuse with the cell surface and empty their contents outside, and that this cleared stored material in models of lysosomal storage diseases. A 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper showed that calcium released from the lysosome through the channel MCOLN1 switches on the phosphatase calcineurin, which removes the phosphate that mTORC1 put on TFEB, so TFEB can enter the nucleus. In mice this route was needed for TFEB activation during starvation and exercise.

PubMed lists Medina at TIGEM in Pozzuoli, near Naples, on more than 50 papers, and in 2026 also at the Department of Translational Medical Science of the University of Naples Federico II, on work on autophagy and inflammation in intestinal organoids from people with coeliac disease.

highlights.SET2012: Co-author of the study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB on the lysosome and that blocking mTORC1 sends TFEB into the nucleus to switch on lysosome genes.

Carling D.lab_name: Cellular Stress Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences, Imperial College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Carling D.role: Biochemist who heads the Cellular Stress group at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences in London and has spent decades working out how the energy sensor AMPK is switched on and what it controls
Carling D.credit: Portrait: MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences
Carling D.sub: Head, Cellular Stress Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (formerly MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, later MRC London Institute of Medical Sciences), Hammersmith Hospital Campus, Imperial College London (group founded 1992)
story: AMPK is the cell's fuel gauge. When energy runs low, the ratio of AMP and ADP to ATP rises, AMPK switches on, and it turns off energy-hungry processes such as mTORC1-driven growth. In 2011 a Nature paper led by Bing Xiao and Steve Gamblin, with David Carling as a co-author, showed how this works in atomic detail. AMP binding protects AMPK from losing the phosphate group that keeps it active. ADP binding at one site gives the same protection without directly switching the enzyme on, so ADP, which is more abundant than AMP, can also signal low energy. The team also solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex. This is a protein and cell study.

Carling heads the Cellular Stress group at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences on the Hammersmith Hospital campus of Imperial College London. The group was founded in 1992, when the institute was the MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, and it studies how AMPK regulates metabolism and how this links to cancer, obesity and fatty liver disease. With the same structural biology team, Carling followed the 2011 paper with a 2013 study showing how a synthetic drug-like molecule binds and activates AMPK.

The group's recent collaborations ask what AMPK and related signals mean for whole animals. They include a 2024 Nature study in which blocking the signalling protein IL-11 extended healthy lifespan in mice, a 2025 study on AMPK in the cells that make myelin in the brain, and a 2026 study in which directly activating AMPK with a drug extended lifespan in yeast, worms and flies.

highlights.XIA2011: Co-author of the study that solved the structure of active mammalian AMPK and showed how ADP binding protects it from inactivation.

Gamblin SJ.lab_name: Scientific Platforms, The Francis Crick Institute (London, England, United Kingdom)
Gamblin SJ.role: Structural biologist and Fellow of the Royal Society who solved the crystal structure of active mammalian AMPK, the cell's energy sensor and the main counterweight to mTORC1, and who now directs the scientific platforms of the Francis Crick Institute
Gamblin SJ.sub: Director of Scientific Platforms, The Francis Crick Institute · Director of Science Operations, Crick (from 2015) · Director of Research (2011) and Joint Head of the Division of Molecular Structure (2005), MRC National Institute for Medical Research, Mill Hill · group leader, NIMR Division of Protein Structure (from 1994) · postdoc, Stephen Harrison lab, Harvard University · PhD in enzymology and crystallography with Herman Watson, University of Bristol
story: AMPK is the cell's fuel gauge. When energy runs low, the cell has more AMP and ADP (the spent forms of the energy carrier ATP), AMPK switches on, and one of the first things it does is put the brakes on mTORC1 so that the cell stops spending energy on growth. The 2011 Nature paper XIA2011, with Steven Gamblin as senior author, from his group at the MRC National Institute for Medical Research in London, showed how AMPK reads these signals. AMP binding to AMPK's regulatory gamma part protected the enzyme from losing the phosphate group that keeps it switched on. ADP binding to one site gave the same protection, though it did not directly activate the enzyme the way AMP does. The team also solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex, giving a 3D picture of how the energy-sensing part talks to the enzyme part.

The finding changed the textbook picture: ADP, which is far more plentiful than AMP in a stressed cell, can also keep AMPK on. That makes the energy brake on mTORC1 more sensitive than had been thought. The work was done with purified proteins and cells.

Gamblin studied biochemistry at the University of Bristol and did a PhD there with Herman Watson on enzymes and protein crystallography, followed by postdoctoral work in Stephen Harrison's lab at Harvard. In 1994 he set up his own lab in the new Division of Protein Structure at the National Institute for Medical Research, using structural biology to study proteins involved in disease. He became Joint Head of the Division of Molecular Structure in 2005 and the institute's Director of Research in 2011, the year he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. When NIMR became part of the Francis Crick Institute he became its Director of Science Operations in 2015, and he is now Director of Scientific Platforms, overseeing the shared technology facilities. He is also a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences and a member of EMBO.

highlights.XIA2011: Senior author: showed that AMP and ADP protect AMPK from dephosphorylation and solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex.

Qiu Z.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Hubei University of Chinese Medicine (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Qiu Z.role: Pharmacologist and Professor at Hubei University of Chinese Medicine who studies how natural medicines act on liver and kidney disease, including fatty liver disease and drug-induced organ damage
Qiu Z.sub: Professor and doctoral supervisor, School of Pharmacy, Hubei University of Chinese Medicine (since 2023) · Associate Professor (2021–2023) · Visiting scholar, University of Minnesota Medical School (2019–2020) · Lecturer (2015–2018) · PhD in Basic Medicine, Wuhan University (2014)
story: Zhenpeng Qiu was senior author of a 2026 Atlas study on tacrolimus, a drug given after organ transplants to stop the immune system from rejecting the new organ (GAO2026). Over years of use, tacrolimus slowly damages the kidneys. In mice and kidney cells, the team found that astragaloside IV, a compound from the medicinal plant Astragalus, protected the kidney by turning down mTOR. With mTOR quieter, the transcription factor TFEB moved into the nucleus and switched on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, which tacrolimus had suppressed. The authors point to the mTOR-TFEB-GADD45alpha axis as a possible drug target. This is preclinical work, with no data from patients.

Qiu trained in pharmacy at South-Central Minzu University and earned a PhD in Basic Medicine at Wuhan University in 2014. Qiu joined the School of Pharmacy at Hubei University of Chinese Medicine as a lecturer in 2015, spent 2019 to 2020 as a visiting scholar at the University of Minnesota Medical School, and became a professor and doctoral supervisor in 2023.

According to the university profile, Qiu's group works on the molecular pharmacology and toxicology of natural medicines and traditional Chinese medicine, with a main focus on chronic liver disease: fatty liver disease, the inflammatory form called steatohepatitis, and liver cancer that grows out of it, as well as fatty acid metabolism in metabolic disease.

highlights.GAO2026: Senior author: led the mouse and cell study showing that astragaloside IV protects the kidney from tacrolimus by lowering mTOR and restoring TFEB-driven autophagy.

Gile B.lab_name: Research and Development Lab, Simmaron Research (Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA)
Gile B.role: Researcher in Simmaron Research's laboratory in Milwaukee who works on low-dose rapamycin as a possible treatment for ME/CFS and led the 2026 analysis of its effects on purine metabolism
Gile B.sub: Research and Development Lab, Simmaron Research, at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee (papers 2025–2026)
story: ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome) is a long-term illness with severe fatigue that gets worse after effort. Simmaron Research, a non-profit research group, has been testing whether low doses of rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, can ease it. Brooke Gile was first author of the 2026 Atlas study from this programme (GIL2026). In patients who improved on rapamycin, blood levels of several purines, small molecules used to build DNA and carry energy, shifted in a pattern that fits lower activity of the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase in white blood cells. In lab experiments, the same purine changes harmed mitochondria and made microglia, the brain's immune cells, more inflammatory.

The study had no placebo group, so it cannot show that rapamycin caused the improvement in fatigue. The links to mitochondria and microglia come from lab tests and were not measured in the patients themselves.

Gile was also a co-author of the first paper from the same trial, published in 2025, which reported that 6 mg of rapamycin a week was tolerated without serious side effects and that most patients who stayed in the study reported less fatigue, with blood markers suggesting better autophagy, the cell's recycling system. PubMed lists Gile at the Simmaron Research and Development Lab at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee in that paper. No personal page was found, so training and job title are not shown.

highlights.GIL2026: First author: linked rapamycin response in an uncontrolled ME/CFS pilot to shifts in blood purines and tested the purine effects on mitochondria and microglia in the lab.

Roy A.role: Neuroscientist who studies brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease and now leads research on ME/CFS as Chief Scientific Officer of the nonprofit Simmaron Research
Roy A.sub: Chief Scientific Officer and Section Chief, Neurobiology, Simmaron Research · Adjunct Professor and member, Milwaukee Institute for Drug Discovery, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee (since 2024) · Assistant Professor, Department of Neurobiology, Rush University Medical Center · PhD in neuroscience, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago
story: ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome) is a long-lasting illness with severe fatigue that gets worse after effort, and it has no approved treatment. Avik Roy was senior author of a 2026 pilot study in the Journal of Translational Medicine (GIL2026) in which people with ME/CFS took low-dose rapamycin, the classic mTOR blocker. Fatigue went down. In blood plasma from the patients who responded, purine chemicals (building blocks of DNA and of energy carriers) shifted in a way that fits lower activity of the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase in their white blood cells. Lab experiments then suggested that altered purines can weaken mitochondria and push microglia, the brain's immune cells, into an inflammatory state.

The study was observational, without a placebo group, so it cannot show that rapamycin caused the improvement. The mitochondrial and microglial effects come from lab assays and were not measured in the patients.

Roy earned a PhD in neuroscience at Rush University Medical Center in Chicago and has been an assistant professor in its Department of Neurobiology. Much of the earlier work concerned glial activation and inflammation in Parkinson's disease, including the finding that loss of the gene for the protein BPOZ2 contributes to Lewy body pathology and the death of dopamine neurons, which won a Rapid Response Innovation Award from the Michael J. Fox Foundation. Roy is now Chief Scientific Officer and head of neurobiology at Simmaron Research, a nonprofit that studies ME/CFS, and since 2024 an adjunct professor and member of the Milwaukee Institute for Drug Discovery at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee.

highlights.GIL2026: Senior author: led the uncontrolled pilot linking low-dose rapamycin to lower fatigue and shifted purine metabolism in people with ME/CFS.

Zong Y.lab_name: Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Zong Y.role: Pathologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who works on the diagnosis of kidney and genitourinary tumours, senior author of a 2026 study proposing GPR143 as a marker for kidney tumours driven by the FLCN/TSC/mTOR-TFE pathway
Zong Y.sub: Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (by 2024 to present) · Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of California Los Angeles (earlier)
story: Some kidney tumours are driven by faults in one signalling chain: the genes FLCN, TSC1/TSC2 and MTOR, which control mTORC1, and the TFE family of transcription factors that sit downstream. These tumours can look like other kidney cancers under the microscope, and getting the diagnosis right matters for treatment and for spotting inherited syndromes such as Birt-Hogg-Dube and tuberous sclerosis complex. The 2026 study in Virchows Archiv, led by Q. Li with Yang Zong as senior author, tested GPR143, a protein that can be stained in tissue sections.

GPR143 staining was both sensitive and specific for renal tumours with FLCN/TSC/MTOR-TFE alterations, which makes it a practical addition to the tests pathologists already use. The study is based on human tumour samples and is a diagnostic tool, not a treatment.

Zong was at the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine of the University of California Los Angeles, where a 2024 Modern Pathology paper as first author described the genetic diversity of embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumours arising from testicular germ cell tumours; that paper notes the move to the University of Wisconsin-Madison. In Madison Zong also co-authored a 2026 study on the CXCL13-CXCR5 signal that draws CD8 T cells into clear cell renal cell carcinoma. A lab or profile page could not be checked.

highlights.LI2026: Senior author: led the study showing that GPR143 immunostaining is a sensitive and specific marker for renal tumours with FLCN/TSC/MTOR-TFE pathway alterations.

Ouyang G.lab_name: Division of Hepatobiliary Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (Nanning, China)
Ouyang G.role: Liver surgery researcher at Guangxi Medical University and senior author of a 2026 study in which the plant compound notoginsenoside R1 eased paracetamol liver injury by boosting autophagy
Ouyang G.sub: Division of Hepatobiliary Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (2026) · Department of General Surgery, Liuzhou People's Hospital affiliated to Guangxi Medical University (2024)
story: An overdose of acetaminophen (paracetamol) is one of the commonest causes of sudden liver failure. Guoqing Ouyang is last author of a 2026 study testing notoginsenoside R1, a compound from the medicinal plant Panax notoginseng, in this kind of injury (LIS2026). The compound reduced liver cell death and oxidative damage, and it worked by boosting autophagy, the cell's recycling system, through changes in MAPK and mTOR signalling. mTOR normally holds autophagy back, so easing it lets damaged cells clean up. The work was done in laboratory models; there is no evidence yet that the compound helps people with overdose.

Ouyang's PubMed record is in liver disease at Guangxi Medical University in Nanning. Recent papers include a 2024 study, as first author from Liuzhou People's Hospital affiliated to the university, that grouped liver cancers by genes of a cell-death programme called PANoptosis and built a survival score, and work with Songqing He's hepatobiliary surgery group on alcohol-related liver disease. A Frontiers profile lists Ouyang at the Division of Hepatobiliary Surgery of the First Affiliated Hospital as a doctoral-level researcher, but no institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the 2026 paper.

highlights.LIS2026: Last author: led the study showing that notoginsenoside R1 eases acetaminophen liver injury by promoting protective autophagy via MAPK/mTOR.

Lv N.lab_name: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (Nanjing, China)
Lv N.role: Researcher at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine who led a mouse study showing that the age-related loss of Lamtor5, a part of the lysosomal platform that helps switch on mTORC1, drives immune ageing through inflammation
Lv N.sub: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Nianyin Lv is the first author of LV2026. mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of lysosomes, with the help of a protein complex called the Ragulator (LAMTOR1 to LAMTOR5) that anchors the docking machinery there. The study found that one of these proteins, Lamtor5, falls with age in macrophages, the immune cells that eat debris and germs. When Lamtor5 is lost, macrophages age early and release signals through the cGAS-STING pathway, a DNA-sensing alarm system, that spread inflammation to other tissues and push the whole body toward ageing. Putting Lamtor5 back into old mice reversed the immune ageing and eased other ageing signs. The work is in mice and gives a link between lysosomes, mTOR signalling and inflammation in old age.

PubMed shows other papers under the same initials at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, but they could not be tied to this researcher with confidence, so they are not used here. No official profile was found, so training and current position are not given.

highlights.LV2026: First author: showed in mice that age-related loss of the lysosomal mTOR-docking protein Lamtor5 drives macrophage ageing and body-wide ageing through cGAS-STING inflammation.

Shi L.lab_name: Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Shi L.role: Immunologist at Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou whose group showed in mice that losing the lysosomal mTOR-activating protein Lamtor5 with age pushes macrophages into senescence and spreads inflammation
Shi L.sub: Key Laboratory of Artificial Organs and Computational Medicine, Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (papers 2024–2026)
story: Liyun Shi is senior author of an Atlas study (LV2026) on why the immune system ages. Lamtor5 is one of the five small proteins of the Ragulator complex, the platform on the lysosome surface where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. The team found that Lamtor5 levels fall with age in mouse macrophages, the immune cells that clean up debris and fight infection. Without enough Lamtor5 the macrophages became senescent, a state in which cells stop dividing but release inflammatory signals. The study traced this to the cGAS-STING pathway, an alarm system that senses DNA in the wrong place in the cell, and showed that the inflammation spread to other tissues. Restoring Lamtor5 in old mice reduced these signs of immune ageing.

The finding links a component of the mTOR machinery to inflammaging, the low-level chronic inflammation of old age. It is a mouse study, so whether Lamtor5 behaves the same way in human immune cells remains open.

PubMed lists Shi at the Institute of Translational Medicine of Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou on the Atlas paper and on a 2024 study, with clinical partners, of how gut bacteria and a population of macrophages drive bowel inflammation in children with glycogen storage disease type Ib. No official profile page was found, so the exact current title is not confirmed.

highlights.LV2026: Senior author: led the mouse study showing that age-related loss of Lamtor5 drives macrophage senescence and cGAS-STING inflammation, reversed by restoring Lamtor5.

Martins-Branco D.lab_name: Scientific and Medical Division, European Society for Medical Oncology (Lugano, Switzerland)
Martins-Branco D.role: Portuguese medical oncologist focused on breast cancer who moved from clinical research at the Institut Jules Bordet to the scientific division of the European Society for Medical Oncology
Martins-Branco D.sub: Scientific and Medical Division, European Society for Medical Oncology, Lugano (2026 paper) · Academic Trials Promoting Team, Institut Jules Bordet, Université libre de Bruxelles (papers 2022–2026) · Breast Multidisciplinary Clinic, Instituto Português de Oncologia de Lisboa Francisco Gentil (earlier papers)
story: Diogo Martins-Branco is first author of EVERGREEN (MAR2026), a study of women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite hormone therapy combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor, today's standard first treatment. The question was whether adding everolimus, an mTOR blocker, to the next hormone therapy still helps. Across several centres, patients given everolimus went a little longer before the cancer grew again (median 5.0 versus 4.3 months) but did not clearly live longer.

Everolimus was approved for this kind of breast cancer before CDK4/6 inhibitors existed, so doctors need to know whether it still works after them. EVERGREEN gives a cautious answer: a small benefit, best kept for selected patients. The study looked back at patient records and was not randomised, so differences in who received the drug may have shaped the result.

Martins-Branco trained and worked as a medical oncologist in Lisbon, publishing from the breast clinic of the Instituto Português de Oncologia de Lisboa on topics such as using genomic tests to spare women chemotherapy. From about 2022 the papers list the Academic Trials Promoting Team at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels, which designs and runs large academic breast cancer trials, and work there included reviews on antibody-drug conjugates. A 2026 paper on the ESMO scale for ranking cancer gene targets lists the Scientific and Medical Division of the European Society for Medical Oncology in Lugano, Switzerland, which appears to be the current post.

highlights.MAR2026: First author: led the multicentre EVERGREEN analysis showing a modest progression-free survival gain from everolimus after CDK4/6 inhibitor failure.

de Azambuja E.lab_name: Academic Trials Promoting Team, Institut Jules Bordet, Université libre de Bruxelles (Brussels, Belgium)
de Azambuja E.role: Brazilian-born medical oncologist at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels who designs and runs large academic breast cancer trials
de Azambuja E.sub: Head of the Medical Support Team, Academic Trials Promoting Team, Institut Jules Bordet, Brussels · PhD, Université libre de Bruxelles (2015) · PhD, Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil (2007)
story: Evandro de Azambuja is senior author of EVERGREEN (MAR2026), a study of women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Adding everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR, to the next hormone therapy gave a modest delay in cancer growth (median 5.0 versus 4.3 months) without a clear gain in survival. The study used records from several centres and was not randomised, so the result guides careful selection of patients rather than settling the question.

Everolimus reached breast cancer care through the BOLERO-2 trial in 2012, before CDK4/6 inhibitors became standard. EVERGREEN checks whether that old evidence still holds in today's treatment order, which is the kind of practical question academic trial groups exist to answer.

De Azambuja holds a PhD from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul in Porto Alegre, Brazil (2007), and a second PhD from the Université libre de Bruxelles (2015). At the Institut Jules Bordet de Azambuja heads the medical support team of the Academic Trials Promoting Team, a unit that runs international breast cancer trials. The main research interest is the design and conduct of large clinical trials in breast cancer, including studies of HER2-targeted drugs. De Azambuja also serves on the advisory board of the Anticancer Fund.

highlights.MAR2026: Senior author: supervised the multicentre EVERGREEN analysis of everolimus after CDK4/6 inhibitor failure in advanced breast cancer.

Bo S.lab_name: Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, Hubei University of Medicine (Xiangyang, China)
Bo S.role: Cardiothoracic surgery researcher in Xiangyang who tests natural compounds against lung cancer cells, including gambogic acid acting on the AKT and mTOR pathway
Bo S.sub: Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, affiliated with Hubei University of Medicine (papers 2021–2026)
story: Su Bo is first author of the Atlas study BO2026, which tested gambogic acid, a yellow compound from the resin of the gamboge tree, on lung cancer cells. The study had two parts. In the computer part, network pharmacology and molecular docking (a simulation of how well a molecule fits into a protein) suggested that gambogic acid binds most tightly to AKT and to S6K1, a kinase that mTORC1 switches on to drive growth. In the lab part, the compound killed A549 lung cancer cells and pushed them into apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death.

The study did not measure whether gambogic acid directly blocks the mTOR enzyme, and it had no animal or human data. Docking predicts possible binding but does not prove it, so the link to mTOR remains a hypothesis to test.

PubMed lists Bo at the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery of Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, a hospital of Hubei University of Medicine. An earlier paper from the same department (2021) followed the same approach with purpurin, another plant-derived compound, which killed A549 lung cancer cells through oxidative stress and lower PI3K/AKT signalling. No official profile page was found.

highlights.BO2026: First author: combined docking with cell experiments to show that gambogic acid kills A549 lung cancer cells and is predicted to bind AKT and S6K1.

Dąbkowska A.lab_name: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences (Warsaw, Poland)
Dąbkowska A.role: Leukemia researcher in Warsaw who works on new drug combinations for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including mTORC1 inhibitors that make leukemia cells easier targets for anti-CD20 antibodies
Dąbkowska A.sub: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences · Department of Immunology, Medical University of Warsaw (papers with Malgorzata Firczuk, 2024–2026)
story: B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) is the most common childhood cancer. Antibody drugs such as rituximab attack cells that carry the surface protein CD20, but many BCP-ALL cells show little CD20, so the antibodies have few places to grab. In DAB2026, Agnieszka Dąbkowska and colleagues in Malgorzata Firczuk's group found that drugs blocking mTORC1, the growth-control complex, raise CD20 on these leukemia cells. The route runs through AKT and the transcription factor FOXO1, and the treated cells also move a step further along B-cell maturation. As a result, anti-CD20 antibodies killed leukemia cells better, including in high-risk disease with deletions in the IKZF1 gene. The study gives a laboratory rationale for combining mTORC1 inhibitors with CD20-targeted antibodies; it is not a clinical trial.

Dąbkowska works with the Firczuk group at the Mossakowski Medical Research Institute of the Polish Academy of Sciences and the Department of Immunology of the Medical University of Warsaw. In 2024 Dąbkowska was a co-author of a study showing that blocking the antioxidant enzyme peroxiredoxin-1 together with a DNA repair pathway makes Philadelphia-positive B-ALL much more sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.DAB2026: First author: showed that mTORC1 inhibitors raise CD20 on B-cell precursor ALL cells via AKT-FOXO1 and improve the effect of anti-CD20 antibodies.

Firczuk M.lab_name: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences (Warsaw, Poland)
Firczuk M.role: Immunologist in Warsaw who leads research on the weak points of B-cell leukemias and lymphomas, from the thioredoxin antioxidant system to combinations of mTORC1 inhibitors with antibody drugs
Firczuk M.sub: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences · Department of Immunology, Medical University of Warsaw
story: In DAB2026, Malgorzata Firczuk's group in Warsaw asked whether blocking mTORC1, the growth-control complex, could help antibody drugs that target CD20, a protein on the surface of B cells. In B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, CD20 is often low. The team found that mTORC1 inhibitors raise CD20 through AKT and the transcription factor FOXO1 and push the leukemia cells towards a more mature B-cell state, which made anti-CD20 antibodies work better, including in high-risk disease with IKZF1 deletions. This is preclinical work that supports testing the combination; it does not show benefit in patients.

Firczuk works at the Department of Immunology of the Medical University of Warsaw and the Laboratory of Immunology of the Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences, and has about two dozen PubMed papers on leukemia and lymphoma. A recurring theme is how leukemia cells handle oxidative stress. In 2024, as senior author, Firczuk reported that the antioxidant enzyme peroxiredoxin-1 is high in Philadelphia-positive B-ALL, and that blocking the thioredoxin system together with a DNA repair route called non-homologous end joining makes these cells much more sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

highlights.DAB2026: Senior author: led the study showing that mTORC1 inhibition raises CD20 and improves anti-CD20 antibody efficacy in B-cell precursor ALL.

Deniz O.lab_name: Nutrient Sensing group (Hietakangas lab), Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and Institute of Biotechnology, University of Helsinki (Helsinki, Finland)
Deniz O.role: Doctoral researcher in Ville Hietakangas's nutrient-sensing group in Helsinki, and first author of the fruit-fly study that found Spalt-related to be a stress-activated brake on mTORC1-driven growth
Deniz O.sub: Doctoral Researcher, Nutrient Sensing group, University of Helsinki
story: Onur Deniz was first author of a 2026 EMBO Journal study in fruit flies (DEN2026). When an animal runs short of nutrients it has to stop building new tissue and storing fat. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is the main switch for that building work. The study found that a transcription factor called Spalt-related (Salr), a protein that turns genes on and off, holds mTORC1-driven growth and fat storage back in the fat body, the fly organ that does the jobs of our liver and fat tissue.

Salr is switched on by the integrated stress response, a cell-wide alarm system that reacts to stress such as missing amino acids. It works side by side with FoxO, the better-known starvation regulator, rather than taking orders from it. So the fly has at least two separate brakes on growth that respond to different signals. The work was done in flies, and whether a similar Salr brake works in mammals was not tested here.

Deniz is listed as a doctoral researcher in the Nutrient Sensing group led by Ville Hietakangas at the University of Helsinki. The group page quotes Deniz's aim as finding new physiological regulators of nutrient sensing.

highlights.DEN2026: First author: identified Spalt-related as a brake on mTORC1-driven growth and fat storage in the fly fat body, switched on by the integrated stress response.

Hietakangas V.lab_name: Nutrient Sensing group, Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and Institute of Biotechnology (HiLIFE), University of Helsinki (Helsinki, Finland)
Hietakangas V.role: Professor of gene regulation at the University of Helsinki who uses fruit flies to study how animals sense nutrients and how diet controls growth, metabolism and stem cells
Hietakangas V.sub: Professor of Gene Regulation and group leader, MetaScale Centre of Excellence, University of Helsinki · postdoc with Stephen Cohen, EMBL Heidelberg and Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory, Singapore (papers 2007–2009) · doctoral work with Lea Sistonen, Turku Centre for Biotechnology, Turku (papers 2003–2005)
story: Ville Hietakangas was senior author of the 2026 fruit-fly study in this Atlas (DEN2026). It found that a transcription factor called Spalt-related (Salr) restrains mTORC1, the growth-control complex, when nutrients are scarce. Salr limits growth and fat storage in the fat body, the fly's equivalent of liver and fat tissue. It is switched on by the integrated stress response, a cell-wide alarm system, and works alongside FoxO rather than below it. The result adds a second, separate brake to the picture of how a starving animal stops growing. It was shown in flies only.

Hietakangas began in a very different area. Papers from 2003 to 2005 with Lea Sistonen at the Turku Centre for Biotechnology in Finland describe how heat shock factors, proteins that protect cells under stress, are controlled by chemical tags called SUMO. As a postdoc with Stephen Cohen, first at EMBL in Heidelberg and then at the Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory in Singapore, Hietakangas moved to growth signalling in flies. A 2007 Genes & Development paper showed that TOR complex 2, the second mTOR complex, acts as a booster that widens the range of AKT signalling, and that it matters most when the pathway is overactive, as in tumour-like overgrowth. In 2009 Hietakangas and Cohen wrote an Annual Review of Genetics overview of how nutrition controls tissue growth.

The Hietakangas group in Helsinki studies nutrient sensing: how cells read the animal's nutritional state and turn it into changes in gene activity, including sensing of sugar and the nutrient control of intestinal stem cells. The university presents this basic research as relevant to diabetes and fatty liver. Hietakangas is Professor of Gene Regulation at the Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and the Institute of Biotechnology, and a group leader in the MetaScale Centre of Excellence.

highlights.DEN2026: Senior author: led the fly study showing that Spalt-related, switched on by the integrated stress response, restrains mTORC1-driven growth alongside FoxO.

Pirscoveanu DF.lab_name: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (Craiova, Romania)
Pirscoveanu DF.role: Neurology researcher in Craiova who works with Aurel Popa-Wagner on aging and stroke, and first author of a 2026 review on why mTOR-type lifespan gains shrink from worms to mammals
Pirscoveanu DF.sub: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (2026) · Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing, University Hospital Essen (2025 affiliation)
story: Blocking TOR, the yeast and worm version of mTOR, can lengthen the life of a roundworm several-fold, yet rapamycin extends mouse lifespan by a much smaller fraction. The 2026 review led by Denisa Pirscoveanu, with Aurel Popa-Wagner as senior author, asks why. It compares data from the worm C. elegans, the fruit fly and rodents and argues that in simple animals aging is steered by a few high-leverage pathways, while in mammals it is spread across many tissues with backup systems, feedback, hormones, gut microbes and the complications of getting a drug to the right place in the body.

The authors call this a shift from pathway leverage to system-level buffering. It is a synthesis of earlier results, not a new experiment, and it gives a framework for why a pathway like mTOR can matter a great deal in mammals while any single drug still has a limited effect on lifespan.

PubMed places Pirscoveanu in the Department of Neurology at the University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova in 2026 and, in 2025, at the Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing of University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen, where Popa-Wagner also works. Their joint papers since 2025 include work on immune genes and post-stroke damage in the aging rat brain.

highlights.PIR2026: First author: wrote the cross-species review arguing that TOR-pathway lifespan gains fall in mammals because aging there is buffered across many tissues and systems.

Popa-Wagner A.lab_name: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (Craiova, Romania)
Popa-Wagner A.role: Neuroscientist of brain aging and stroke recovery working between Craiova and Essen, senior author of a 2026 review on the limits of extending lifespan through the mTOR pathway
Popa-Wagner A.sub: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova · Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing, University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen
story: In worms and flies, turning down TOR signalling can stretch lifespan dramatically. In mice, rapamycin also works, but the gain is far smaller. The 2026 review led by Denisa Pirscoveanu, with Aurel Popa-Wagner as senior author, offers an explanation: in simple organisms aging runs through a few dominant pathways, whereas in mammals it emerges from many organs talking to each other, with redundant genes, hormonal feedback, gut microbes and drug-handling differences that soften the effect of any single intervention.

For readers of this Atlas the useful message is about expectations. mTOR remains a central aging pathway in mammals, but the review argues that its leverage is diluted by system-level buffering. The paper is a synthesis of published data across species, not a new experiment.

PubMed lists Popa-Wagner at both the Department of Neurology of the University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova and the Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing at University Hospital Essen. Recent papers with this group study stroke in the aging rat brain, for example how immune genes active during early brain development contribute to post-stroke damage in old male rats.

highlights.PIR2026: Senior author: led the cross-species review proposing that mTOR-pathway lifespan gains shrink in mammals because of multi-tissue buffering and redundancy.

Song H.lab_name: Oh Lab, Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (Gwangju, South Korea)
Song H.role: Researcher in Chang-Myung Oh's lab at GIST who tested urolithin A, a gut-microbe product, in mice with a stiff-heart form of heart failure
Song H.sub: Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (papers with Chang-Myung Oh)
story: Hangyul Song is the first author of SONH2026, a study in Experimental and Molecular Medicine from Chang-Myung Oh's lab at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) in South Korea. It deals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): the heart still pumps out a normal share of its blood with each beat, but the muscle is stiff and thick and fills poorly. HFpEF is common in older people with obesity and diabetes and has few good treatments.

Urolithin A is made by gut bacteria from compounds in foods such as pomegranates and walnuts. In mice with HFpEF it eased heart stiffness, thickening and scarring. In heart cells it switched on AMPK, the energy sensor, and lowered mTOR activity. That restored mitophagy, the clearing of damaged mitochondria. Urolithin A also changed the gut microbiome and lowered ceramides, fatty molecules that harm heart cells. The results come from mice and cell models, not from patients.
PubMed lists several papers shared by Song and Oh. No separate profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SONH2026: First author: showed in HFpEF mice that urolithin A restores mitophagy through AMPK activation and mTOR inhibition and lowers ceramides through the gut microbiome.

Oh CM.lab_name: Oh Lab, Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (Gwangju, South Korea)
Oh CM.role: Metabolism researcher at GIST in South Korea whose lab studies heart and metabolic disease in mice, including how urolithin A protects the stiff heart in HFpEF
Oh CM.sub: Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (at the time of the 2026 study)
story: Chang-Myung Oh is the senior author of SONH2026, with Hangyul Song as first author. The study looks at heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), in which the heart pumps a normal share of blood per beat but its muscle is stiff and fills poorly. Urolithin A, a compound that gut bacteria make from foods such as pomegranates, improved heart function and structure in HFpEF mice. It activated AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, turned down mTOR, and so restored mitophagy, the removal of damaged mitochondria. It also lowered blood ceramides, fatty molecules linked to heart damage, through changes in the gut microbiome. These findings come from mice and cell models.

PubMed lists more than seventy papers under this name with a GIST affiliation. No official profile page could be opened, so the title and training are not given here, and the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SONH2026: Senior author: led the mouse study showing that urolithin A protects the HFpEF heart through the AMPK-mTOR-mitophagy axis and the gut-ceramide axis.

Mugale MN.lab_name: Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute (Lucknow, India)
Mugale MN.role: Toxicologist at CSIR-CDRI in Lucknow whose group studies how organs such as the liver and lung are injured and scarred, and how hormones and drugs change that process
Mugale MN.sub: Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow · also affiliated with the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR)
story: Fibrosis is scarring: after repeated injury, an organ fills with stiff connective tissue and stops working well. Madhav Mugale is last author, the group leader, of a 2026 rat study on liver fibrosis caused by the toxin carbon tetrachloride (VER2026). Male rats given testosterone kept their mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in better shape, and their autophagy, the cell's recycling system, kept flowing: the protein p62 did not pile up and markers of working autophagy such as LC3B and Beclin-1 stayed higher. mTOR activity was maintained. Castrated rats did worse, with more damaged mitochondria and more cell death. The study suggests that male hormones help the liver cope with toxic injury in rats; it did not test people.

PubMed lists more than 90 papers with Mugale, all from the Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine at CSIR-CDRI, a national drug research institute in Lucknow, from 2019 onward. They cover safety testing of drug ingredients, models of lung and liver fibrosis, and collaborations with CDRI pharmacology groups on diabetes and insulin resistance in mice. Mugale is also affiliated with the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), which runs CSIR's doctoral programmes. No official profile page was found, so job title and training are not given.

highlights.VER2026: Last author: led the rat study showing that testosterone preserves mitochondrial health and autophagic flux, with sustained mTOR activity, in toxin-induced liver fibrosis.

Zhu L.lab_name: Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University (Hefei, China)
Zhu L.role: Environmental health researcher at Anhui Medical University and first author of a 2026 mouse study on how the solvent trichloroethylene damages the liver when the LKB1/AMPK energy sensor is missing
Zhu L.sub: Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Trichloroethylene is an industrial solvent used to degrease metal, and workers exposed to it can develop liver injury. Lifu Zhu's 2026 study, with J. Zhang as senior author, asked why some livers are hit harder. The focus was LKB1 and AMPK, a pair of enzymes that sense low energy in the cell and normally hold mTOR in check.

In mice lacking LKB1/AMPK, trichloroethylene caused worse liver injury. mTOR-regulated mitophagy, the clean-up of damaged mitochondria, failed, and mitochondrial DNA leaked out of the mitochondria, where it can trigger inflammation. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, and drugs that activate AMPK protected the liver. The work is in mice only, with no human data, and suggests the LKB1/AMPK/mTOR axis as a possible target.

PubMed lists Lifu Zhu at the Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University in Hefei. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.ZHU2026: First author: showed in mice that LKB1/AMPK loss worsens trichloroethylene liver injury by impairing mTOR-regulated mitophagy, and that rapamycin or AMPK activation protects.

Jibrin W.lab_name: Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology, School of Medicine, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Jibrin W.role: Researcher at the University of Dundee School of Medicine who led a 2026 cell-culture test of whether rapamycin can shield sperm-precursor cells from the cancer drug cisplatin
Jibrin W.sub: School of Medicine, University of Dundee (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy drug used against many childhood and adult cancers. It kills dividing cells, and that includes the cells in the testis that will later make sperm, so boys treated for cancer can become infertile as adults. In mouse ovaries, earlier work had suggested that rapamycin, a drug that switches off mTOR (the cell's growth-control kinase), can put egg-cell precursors into a quieter state and protect them from chemotherapy. Wafiya Jibrin was first author of the 2026 Atlas study that asked whether the same trick works for the male side (JIB2026).

The team exposed GC6-spg cells, a mouse cell line that behaves like spermatogonia (the stem-like cells that give rise to sperm), to cisplatin with and without rapamycin. Rapamycin did not reduce the damage. The result is a useful negative one: a protective strategy reported in female fertility models cannot simply be carried over to the testis. It was shown only in a cell line in a dish, not in animals or in patients.

The study came from Federica Lopes's group in the School of Medicine at the University of Dundee, which works on fertility preservation for young cancer patients. PubMed lists no other papers under this name, and no institutional page could be found, so the Dundee affiliation shown is the one on the 2026 paper.

highlights.JIB2026: First author: tested rapamycin as a shield for a mouse spermatogonial cell line exposed to cisplatin and found that it gave no protection.

Lopes F.lab_name: Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology, School of Medicine, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Lopes F.role: Reproductive biologist and Lecturer at the University of Dundee who studies how chemotherapy damages the immature testis and ovary, with the aim of protecting the future fertility of children treated for cancer
Lopes F.sub: Lecturer, Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology, School of Medicine, University of Dundee · earlier research at the University of Edinburgh (Biomedical Sciences and MRC Centre for Reproductive Health, papers 2013–2022)
story: Federica Lopes was senior author of the 2026 Atlas study (JIB2026) that tested whether rapamycin, a drug that switches off mTOR, could protect sperm-precursor cells from cisplatin. In female fertility models, earlier reports had suggested that rapamycin keeps egg-cell precursors in a resting state and so spares them from chemotherapy. In this study, done on a mouse spermatogonial cell line (GC6-spg) in a dish, rapamycin gave no protection. The finding warns against assuming that a fertility-sparing drug which helps the ovary will also help the testis.

The question fits a long line of Lopes's own work. At the University of Edinburgh, working with Norah Spears and Rod Mitchell, Lopes cultured whole prepubertal mouse testes and ovaries and exposed them to cancer drugs at doses seen in patients. These studies showed that the irinotecan metabolite SN38 killed germ cells in the young testis but spared the ovary (2016), that carboplatin is no less damaging to young gonads than the older drug cisplatin (2020), and that a single exposure to cisplatin or doxorubicin harms spermatogonial stem cells and lowers sperm production weeks later (2020). Work on human fetal and prepubertal testis tissue then showed that the supporting Sertoli cells survive platinum drugs, which keeps open the option of restoring fertility by stem-cell transplant (2022).

Lopes is now a Lecturer in Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology at the University of Dundee School of Medicine, where the university lists a PhD project on fertility preservation for boys with cancer. Recent Dundee papers also cover embryo culture conditions in the IVF laboratory (2025) and access to fertility care in low- and middle-income countries (2024).

highlights.JIB2026: Senior author: led the Dundee study showing that rapamycin did not protect a mouse spermatogonial cell line from cisplatin damage.
